Due to the symmetry of the problem, the admissible values $a_{1}$ and $1 / a_{1}$ leads to the same central configuration. Then, there exists exactly two $(2, n)$-crowns when $m=1$ and $n$ is even.

The equation $H(a)=1$ can be written as

$$
S_{n} \frac{a^{3}-1}{a^{2}}=\left(a^{2}-1\right) \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{\cos \theta_{k}}{d_{k}^{3 / 2}}
$$

where $\theta_{k}=(2 k-1) \pi / n$ and $d_{k}=1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \theta_{k}, k=1, \ldots, n$. Clearly $a=1$ is a solution (that was already known), so considering $a \neq 1$ we have to solve the equation

$$
g_{1}(a):=S_{n} \frac{a^{2}+a+1}{a^{2}(a+1)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{\cos \theta_{k}}{d_{k}^{3 / 2}}=: g_{2}(a)
$$

From Lemma 5 (see Appendix) we have the following properties:

1. $g_{i}(1 / a)=a^{3} g_{i}(a), i=1,2$;
2. $\exists A>0$ such that for all $a>A, g_{2}(a)<g_{1}(a)$;
3. when $n$ is even, $g_{2}(1)>g_{1}(1)$;
4. when $n$ is even, $g_{1}$ and $g_{2}$ are decreasing functions in $(1, \infty)$.

From the first property we have that if $a_{1}$ is a solution of $g_{1}(a)=g_{2}(a)$, so it is $1 / a_{1}$. Thus we only look for solutions in the interval $(1, \infty)$. Using the second and third properties and applying Bolzano's theorem, there exists at least one solution. Finally, from the last property, the solution must be unique.

In other to obtain an exact number of twisted $(2, n)$-crowns we we should be able to prove that the function $H$ is strictly increasing. We have not succeeded in that. All the numerical experiments done support the conclusion that the number is exactly three. See Figure 3, where the set of curves $m=H(a)$ is plotted for three different values of $n$.

# 4 Convex twisted $(2, n)$-crowns 

We will discuss in this section whether the central configurations obtained are convex or concave. It is not difficult to see that, given $2 n$ bodies in two $n$-gons of radius 1 and $a$, respectively, the configuration is convex if and only if

$$
a \in \mathcal{C}_{n}=\left(\cos \left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right), \frac{1}{\cos \left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right)}\right)
$$

For any $n \geq 3$ we have seen that the set of admissible values consists in three disjoint intervals. From now on we will focus our interest on the interval that contains the value $a=1$, that we call the central admissible interval, $\mathcal{A}_{2 C}(n)$. Our purpose is to prove the following statement.

Proposition 3. Consider twisted $(2, n)$-crowns of radius 1 and $a$, with masses 1 and $m$ respectively. Let $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ given in Proposition 1 (for $n=3$ ) and Proposition 2 and Conjecture 1 (for $n \geq 4)$.

1. for $n=3, \mathcal{A}_{2}(3) \cap \mathcal{C}_{3}=\mathcal{A}_{2 C}(3)$, that is, a twisted $(2,3)$-crown is convex if and only if a belongs to the central admissible interval, $\mathcal{A}_{2 C}(3)$.
2. for $n=4, \mathcal{A}_{2}(4) \cap \mathcal{C}_{4}=\mathcal{C}_{4}$, that is, if the twisted $(2,4)$-crown is convex then a belongs to the central admissible interval, $\mathcal{A}_{2 C}(4)$, but not all the values of a within $\mathcal{A}_{2 C}(4)$ correspond to convex configurations.
3. For $n \geq 5$, if the twisted $(2, n)$-crown is convex, then a belongs to the central admissible interval.

Proof. For $n=3$, by Proposition 1 we have that

$$
z_{1}<\frac{7}{16}<\cos \left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=\frac{1}{2}<\frac{8}{13}<\frac{1}{z_{2}}
$$

Therefore, using Theorem 1,

$$
\mathcal{C}_{3} \cap \mathcal{A}_{2}(3)=\left(\frac{1}{z_{2}}, z_{2}\right)=\mathcal{A}_{2 C}(3)
$$

For $n=4$, and by Proposition 2, $F(a)<0$ for $a \in\left(z_{1}, z_{2}\right)$, and $F(a)>0$ otherwise. Using the expression of $F(a)$ for $n=4$ (see the proof of Proposition 2 in the Appendix) we have that

$$
F\left(\cos \left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{8}{5 \sqrt{5}}<0
$$

Therefore, $z_{1}<\cos (\pi / 4)$ and

$$
\mathcal{C}_{4} \cap \mathcal{A}_{2}(4)=\mathcal{C}_{4} \subset\left(z_{1}, \frac{1}{z_{1}}\right)=\mathcal{A}_{2 C}(4)
$$

Finally for $n \geq 5$, by Theorem 3 the central admissible interval is $\left(z_{1}, 1 / z_{1}\right)$ and by Lemma 4 we have that $\frac{1}{z_{2}}<1-\frac{1}{n}<z_{1}$. Using the fact that $1-\frac{1}{n}<\cos (\pi / n)$ we obtain that

$$
\mathcal{C}_{n} \cap\left(\left(0, \frac{1}{z_{2}}\right) \cup\left(z_{2} \infty\right)\right)=\emptyset
$$

Therefore,

$$
\mathcal{C}_{n} \cap \mathcal{A}_{n}=\left\{\begin{array}{c}
\mathcal{C}_{n} \subset\left(z_{1}, \frac{1}{z_{1}}\right) \\
\text { or } \\
\left(z_{1}, \frac{1}{z_{1}}\right)
\end{array}\right.
$$

For $n \geq 5$ we have not been able to proof that all the convex central configurations correspond exactly with the central admissible interval, although the numerical explorations point in that direction. In Table 2 we show the values of central admissible intervals for some values of $n$.

Figure 4: For $5 \geq n \geq 5000$, the difference $\Delta_{n}=z_{1}-\cos (\pi / n)$ (in logarithmic scale).

Figure 4 we show, for $n \in(5,5000)$ the difference $\Delta_{n}=z_{1}-\cos (\pi / n)$ in logarithmic scale. We can see that the difference is always positive, which implies that $\mathcal{C}_{n} \cap \mathcal{A}_{2}(n)=\left(z_{1}, \frac{1}{z_{1}}\right)=\mathcal{A}_{2 C}(n)$.

Combining the results of Proposition 3 and Theorems 2 and 4, we have the following summary on convex central configurations.

1. For $n=3$, let $m^{*}$ be the bifurcation value given by Theorem 2. Then, for any positive value $m$ there exists at least one convex twisted $(2,3)$-crown and
(a) for any $m \in\left(1, m^{*}\right)$, there exist exactly three different convex twisted $(2,3)$-crowns,
(b) for any $m \in\left(m^{*}, \infty\right)$ there exists only one convex twisted $(2,3)$-crown,
(c) for $m=1, m^{*}$ the number of different convex twisted $(2,3)$-crowns is exactly two.

When $m=1$, the two convex twisted $(2,3)$-crowns where already numerically computed by Moeckel in an unpublished report.
2. For $n=4$, there exists a value for the mass ratio $m=\bar{m}$ such that

(a) for any $m \in[1, \bar{m}]$, there exists exactly one convex twisted $(2,4)$-crown,
(b) for any $m \in(\bar{m}, \infty)$ there exists no convex twisted $(2,4)$-crown.

The approximate value of $\bar{m}$ is $H(1 / \cos (\pi / 4))=16.05679941$.
3. For $n \geq 5$, if $H(1 / \cos (\pi / n))>0$, then for $m \leq H(1 / \cos (\pi / n))$, there exists at least one convex twisted $(2, n)$-crown. On the contrary, if $H(1 / \cos (\pi / n))<0$, then for all values of $m$ there exists at least one convex twisted $(2, n)$-crown.

# 5 Appendix 

We include here a detailed proof of some of the results presented in the paper. We have listed first all the lemmas, and then the propositions. In some cases, one can convince himself of the certainty of the results simply by plotting the graphic of a function. Nevertheless, we give an analytical proof of each one of them.

Lemma 2. Let $H$ be the function given in (11). For $n=3$ the following statements hold.

1. the function $H$ has only two critical points for $a>1, a^{*} \in\left(1, z_{2}\right)$ and $a^{* *} \in\left(1 / z_{1},+\infty\right)$, where $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ are given in Proposition 1,
2. the equation $H(a)=a$ has only one positive solution at $a=1$.

Proof. Recall that $H(a)=a^{2} \frac{F(a)}{G(a)}$, and for $n=3, F$ is given by (14) and

$$
G(a)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}-a^{3}\left(\frac{2-a}{\left(1+a^{2}-a\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{1}{(1+a)^{2}}\right)
$$

We start proving the first statement. The numerator of $H^{\prime}(a)$ can be written as

$$
-3 \sqrt{3} a \sqrt{1+a^{2}-a}\left(2 \sqrt{1+a^{2}-a} q(a)-(1+a) p(a)\right)
$$

where $p$ and $q$ are the following polynomials of degree 10 :

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(a)= & 4 a^{10}-a^{9}-23 a^{8}-(2 \sqrt{3}+23) a^{7}-(17 \sqrt{3}+1) a^{6} \\
& +(42 \sqrt{3}+8) a^{5}-(17 \sqrt{3}+1) a^{4}-(2 \sqrt{3}+23) a^{3}-23 a^{2}-a+4 \\
q(a)= & 2 a^{10}-(2+\sqrt{3}) a^{9}-(2 \sqrt{3}-2) a^{8}-(2 \sqrt{3}-2) a^{7}-(12 \sqrt{3}+2) a^{6} \\
& -(13 \sqrt{3}-4) a^{5}-(12 \sqrt{3}+2) a^{4}-(2 \sqrt{3}-2) a^{3}-(2 \sqrt{3}-2) a^{2} \\
& -(2+\sqrt{3}) a+2
\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $H^{\prime}(a)=0$ is equivalent to solve

$$
g_{1}(a)=\frac{2 \sqrt{1+a^{2}-a}}{1+a}=\frac{p(a)}{q(a)}=g_{2}(a)
$$

Recall that we look for the solutions of $g_{1}(a)=g_{2}(a)$ in the interval $[1, \infty)$. On one hand, the function $g_{1} \in \mathcal{C}^{1}$, is positive, $g_{1}(1)=1$, increases in $[1, \infty)$, and $\lim _{a \rightarrow \infty} g_{1}(a)=2$. On the other hand, $g_{2}(1)=\frac{76+3728 \sqrt{3}}{6563}<1$ and $\lim _{a \rightarrow \infty} g_{2}(a)=2$. Furthermore, we will prove that the function $g_{2}$, for $a \geq 1$, has only one pole $u \in(46 / 16,47 / 16)$, a zero $v \in(47 / 16,3)$, only one critical point $w \in(5,6)$ which is a local maximum, and the function increases in $(1, u) \cup(u, w)$ and decreases $(w,+\infty)$. From all of the above properties of the functions $g_{1}$ and $g_{2}$, there exist only two values $a^{*} \in(1, u)$ and $a^{* *} \in(v, w)$ at which $H^{\prime}(a)=0$. See Figure 5. Finally, using a Bolzano's argument and the bounds of $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ given in Proposition $1 a^{*}<25 / 16<z_{2}$ and $a^{* *}>3>1 / z_{1}$.


Figure 5: Functions $g_{1}(a)$ and $g_{2}(a)$ used in the proof of Lemma 2

We have to prove the behavior of the function $g_{2}$ stated above. Notice that the polynomials satisfy that $a^{10} p(1 / a)=p(a)$ and $a^{10} q(1 / a)=q(a)$. That means that if $a$ is a zero of one of the polynomials, so it is $1 / a$. Applying this property and Descarte's rule, $q(a)$ has only one zero at $a=u \geq 1$, and, by Bolzano's theorem, $u \in(46 / 16,47 / 16)$. To determine the number of zeros of $p(a)$, we consider the polynomial $p(1+a)$. Applying again Descarte's rule, $p(1+a)$ has only one positive zero, and therefore, $p(a)$ has only one zero at $a=v \geq 1$, which is located in $(47 / 16,3)$. Looking at the sign of the polynomials $p(a)$ and $q(a), g_{2}(a)>0$ for $a \in[1, u) \cup(v,+\infty)$ and $g_{2}(a)<0$ for $a \in(u, v)$.

It remains to see that $g_{2}$ has only one critical point in $(1, \infty), a=w>u$. We need to solve

$$
p^{\prime}(a) q(a)-p(a) q^{\prime}(a)=-(3+2 \sqrt{3})(a+1)(a-1) r(a)=0
$$

where $r(a)$ is a polynomial of degree 16 that can be written as

$$
r(a)=r_{1}(a)-r_{2}(a)
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_{1}(a)= & 2\left(a^{16}+1\right)+(220-106 \sqrt{3}) a^{3}\left(a^{10}+1\right)+(1507-744 \sqrt{3}) a^{4}\left(a^{8}+1\right) \\
r_{2}(a)= & (88 \sqrt{3}-140) a\left(a^{14}+1\right)+(109 \sqrt{3}-182) a^{2}\left(a^{12}+1\right)+(1276-574 \sqrt{3}) a^{5}\left(a^{6}+1\right) \\
& +(264 \sqrt{3}-356) a^{6}\left(a^{4}+1\right)+(3868-1814 \sqrt{3}) a^{7}\left(a^{2}+1\right)+(560 \sqrt{3}-351) a^{8}
\end{aligned}
$$

By Descarte's rule, $r(a+2)$ has only one positive solution, so that $r(a)$ has only one zero greater than 2 , which is located $a=w \in(5,6)$. The polynomials $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ are positive and increasing for $a>0$, and

$$
r_{1}(1)<r_{2}(1), \quad r_{1}(2)<r_{2}(2)
$$

Therefore, $r(a)<0$, for $a \in(1,2)$, so that it has no zeros in that interval, and $w$ is the only critical point of $g_{2}$ for $a>1$. This concludes the proof of the first item.

The second statement claims that the only positive solution of $H(a)=a$ is $a=1$. The equation can be written as $a F(a)=G(a)$, and after a simplification, it can be written as

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\left(a^{2}-1\right)=\frac{a(a-1)\left(a^{2}-a+1\right)}{\left(a^{2}-a+1\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{a\left(1-a^{2}\right)}{(1+a)^{2}}
$$

Clearly the equation has $a=1$ as a solution. Simplifying by the term $a-1$ at both sides we obtain

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}(a+1)=\frac{a}{\left(a^{2}-a+1\right)^{1 / 2}}-\frac{a}{(1+a)}
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}(a+1)+\frac{a}{(1+a)}=\frac{a}{\left(a^{2}-a+1\right)^{1 / 2}}
$$

The study of the derivative of the functions of both sides of the equations leads quickly to the conclusion that the equation has no positive solutions. Therefore, $a=1$ is the only positive solution of $H(a)=0$. This concludes the proof.

Lemma 3. Let $F$ be the function defined in (11) for $n \geq 4$. Then

1. $F(1)=S_{n}-C_{21}(1)<0$;
2. $\lim _{a \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{F(a)}{a}=S_{n}+\frac{n}{2}$;
3. $\lim _{a \rightarrow+\infty} F(a)=+\infty$.

Proof. The first two results correspond to Lemma 1.2.4 of the first Chapter of . Notice that the notation used by the author is different from the one used here. The last result is obtained from Lemma 1 and the fact that $G(0)=S_{n}>0$.

Lemma 4. Let be $n \geq 5$ and suppose that $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ are the only positive solutions of $F(a)=0$. Then

$$
0<1-\frac{1}{n}<z_{1}<1<\frac{1}{z_{1}}<\frac{n}{n-1}<z_{2}
$$

Proof. This result correspond to Lemma 1.2.5 of the first Chapter of .
Lemma 5. Let be $n \geq 4$ and

$$
g_{1}(a)=S_{n} \frac{a^{2}+a+1}{a^{2}(a+1)}, \quad g_{2}(a)=\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{\cos \theta_{k}}{d_{k}^{3 / 2}}
$$

where $d_{k}=1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \theta_{k}$, and $\theta_{k}=(2 k-1) \pi / n$ for $k=1, \ldots, n$. They satisfy the following properties:

1. $g_{i}(1 / a)=a^{3} g_{i}(a), i=1,2$;
2. $\exists A>1$ such that for all $a>A, g_{2}(a)<g_{1}(a)$;

3. if $n$ is even, then $g_{2}(1)>g_{1}(1)$;
4. if $n$ is even, then $g_{1}$ and $g_{2}$ are decreasing functions in $(1, \infty)$.

Proof. The first item is a straightforward computation. The second one comes from the limit

$$
\lim _{a \rightarrow \infty} \frac{g_{2}(a)}{g_{1}(a)}=\lim _{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \frac{g_{2}(1 / \varepsilon)}{g_{1}(1 / \varepsilon)}=\lim _{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \frac{\varepsilon^{2}(1+\varepsilon) g_{2}(\varepsilon)}{S_{n}\left(\varepsilon^{2}+\varepsilon+1\right)}=0
$$

Now let us consider $n=2 m$ with $m \geq 2$. Then

$$
g_{2}(a)=2 \sum_{k=1}^{[m / 2]} \frac{\cos \theta_{k}}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \theta_{k}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{\cos \theta_{k}}{\left(1+a^{2}+2 a \cos \theta_{k}\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

where [$\cdot$] denotes the floor function, and

$$
g_{2}^{\prime}(a)=-6 \sum_{k=1}^{[m / 2]} \cos \theta_{k}\left(\frac{a-\cos \theta_{k}}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \theta_{k}\right)^{5 / 2}}-\frac{a+\cos \theta_{k}}{\left(1+a^{2}+2 a \cos \theta_{k}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right)
$$

Notice that $\cos \theta_{k}>0$ for $k=1, \ldots,[m / 2]$. Thus, to prove the forth statement we only need to see that

$$
\frac{a-\cos \theta_{k}}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \theta_{k}\right)^{5 / 2}}-\frac{a+\cos \theta_{k}}{\left(1+a^{2}+2 a \cos \theta_{k}\right)^{5 / 2}}>0
$$

which is equivalent to see that

$$
\left(a-\cos \theta_{k}\right)^{2}\left(1+a^{2}+2 a \cos \theta_{k}\right)^{5}-\left(a+\cos \theta_{k}\right)^{2}\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \theta_{k}\right)^{5}>0
$$

The property follows from the fact that the polynomial

$$
q=(a-b)^{2}\left(1+a^{2}+2 a b\right)^{5}-(a+b)^{2}\left(1+a^{2}-2 a b\right)^{5}>0
$$

for all $a>1$ and $0<b \leq 1$.
Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_{1}(1) & =\frac{3}{8} \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \frac{1}{\sin (k \pi / n)}=\frac{3}{8}\left(1+2 \sum_{k=1}^{m-1} \frac{1}{\sin (k \pi / n)}\right) \\
& <\frac{3}{8}\left(1+\frac{n-2}{\sin (\pi / n)}\right) \\
g_{2}(1) & =\frac{2}{8} \sum_{k=1}^{m} \frac{\cos \theta_{k}}{\sin ^{3}\left(\theta_{k} / 2\right)}=\frac{2}{8}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{[m / 2]} \frac{\cos \theta_{k}}{\sin ^{3}\left(\theta_{k} / 2\right)}+\sum_{k=[m / 2]+1}^{m} \frac{\cos \theta_{k}}{\sin ^{3}\left(\theta_{k} / 2\right)}\right) \\
& >\frac{2}{8}\left(\frac{\cos (\pi / n)}{\sin ^{3}(\pi /(2 n))}+\sum_{k=[m / 2]+1}^{m} \frac{\cos \theta_{k}}{(\sqrt{2} / 2)^{3}}\right)>\frac{2}{8}\left(\frac{\cos (\pi / n)}{\sin ^{3}(\pi / 2 n)}-n \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\
& \geq \frac{2}{8}\left(\frac{1-\pi /(2 n)}{(\pi /(2 n))^{3}}-n \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)=\frac{2}{8}\left(\left(\frac{2 n}{\pi}\right)^{3}-\left(\frac{2 n}{\pi}\right)^{2}-n \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where we have used that $n \geq 4$, and $\cos x \geq 1-x / 2$ and $\sin (x / 2) \leq x / 2$ for $x \leq \pi / 4$. Then,

$$
8\left(g_{2}(1)-g_{1}(1)\right)>\frac{16}{\pi^{3}} n^{3}-\frac{8}{\pi^{2}} n^{2}-n \sqrt{2}-3-3 \frac{n-2}{\sin (\pi / n)}
$$

Taking $x=\pi / n$, it is enough to see that

$$
16-8 x-\pi \sqrt{2} x^{2}-3 x^{3} \leq 3 x^{2} \frac{\pi-2 x}{\sin x}
$$

for $x \in(0, \pi / 4]$. The polynomial is decreasing, while the function on the right is increasing, and the inequality holds for $x=\pi / 4$. This concludes the proof.

Proposition 1. Let $F$ be the function defined in (11). Then, for $n=3$, the following statements hold.

1. The equation $F(a)=0$ has exactly two positive solutions, denoted by $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$;
2. $3 / 8<z_{1}<7 / 16$ and $25 / 16<z_{2}<13 / 8$;
3. $F(a)<0$ for $a \in\left(z_{1}, z_{2}\right)$ and $F(a)>0$ for $a \in\left(0, z_{1}\right) \cup\left(z_{2}, \infty\right)$.

Proof. For $n=3$ the functions $C_{12}$ and $C_{21}$ are

$$
C_{12}(a)=\frac{2-a}{\left(1+a^{2}-a\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{1}{(1+a)^{2}}, \quad C_{21}(a)=\frac{2 a-1}{\left(1+a^{2}-a\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{1}{(1+a)^{2}}
$$

and the function $F$ is

$$
F(a)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} a-\frac{2 a-1}{\left(1+a^{2}-a\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1}{(1+a)^{2}}
$$

$F(a)=0$ is equivalent to $g_{1}(a)=g_{2}(a)$ where

$$
g_{1}(a)=\left(1+a^{2}-a\right)^{3 / 2}, \quad \text { and } \quad g_{2}(a)=\frac{3(2 a-1)(1+a)^{2}}{\sqrt{3} a^{3}+2 \sqrt{3} a^{2}+\sqrt{3} a-3}
$$

The function $g_{1} \in \mathcal{C}^{1}$, is positive, decreases in $(0,1 / 2)$, increases in $(1 / 2, \infty), g_{1}(1 / 2)=3 \sqrt{3} / 8$ and $\lim _{a \rightarrow \infty} g_{1}(a)=+\infty$.

The function $g_{2}$ has only one positive zero at $a=1 / 2$, and using Descarte's rule and a Bolzano's argument, there exists only one pole at $a=c \in(5 / 8,3 / 4)$. Furthermore, $g_{2}(a)<0$ for $a \in$ $(1 / 2, c)$ and positive otherwise, and $\lim _{a \rightarrow+\infty} g_{2}(a)=6 / \sqrt{3}$. Its derivative is

$$
g_{2}^{\prime}(a)=3 \sqrt{3} \frac{(1+a)\left(a^{3}+3 a^{2}+(3-6 \sqrt{3}) a+1\right)}{\left(\sqrt{3} a+2 \sqrt{3} a^{2}+\sqrt{3} a^{3}-3\right)^{2}}
$$

and, using again Descarte's rule and Bolzano's theorem, it has only two positive zeros, one located in $(0,1 / 2)$, which is a local maximum, and one in $(23 / 16,3 / 2)$, which is a local minimum. We denote by $a_{m}$ the local minimum.

First we show that there exits only one solution of $g_{1}(a)=g_{2}(a)$ in $(0,1 / 2)$, denoted by $z_{1}$. This is a direct consequence of the fact that $g_{1}(0)=g_{2}(0)=1, g_{1}$ decreases in the interval $(0,1 / 2)$, $g_{2}^{\prime}(0)>0$ and $g_{2}$ has unique critical point which is a local maximum in the same interval.

Next we show that there exits only one solution of $g_{1}(a)=g_{2}(a)$ in $(c, \infty)$, denoted by $z_{2}$. Recall that the function $g_{2}$ decreases for $\left(c, a_{m}\right)$, increases for $a>a_{m}$, and has a horizontal asymptote

when $a \rightarrow \infty$, whereas the function $g_{1}$ tends to infinity. Thus, at least there must exists one solution. Moreover, $g_{1}^{\prime}(a)$ is an increasing function, so that $g_{1}^{\prime}(a)>g_{1}^{\prime}(1)=3 / 2$ for $a>1$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_{2}^{\prime}(a) & \leq 3 \sqrt{3} \frac{(1+a)\left(5 a^{3}+(3-6 \sqrt{3}) a\right)}{\left(\sqrt{3} a+2 \sqrt{3} a^{2}+\sqrt{3} a^{3}\right)^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{a} \frac{(1+a)\left(5 a^{3}-5 a\right)}{\left((1+a)^{4}\right)^{2}} \\
& =\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{a} \frac{a-1}{(a+1)^{2}} \leq \frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{8}
\end{aligned}
$$

for $a>1$. Therefore, there cannot exist more than one solution to the equation $g_{1}(a)=g_{2}(a)$. See Figure 6.


Figure 6: Functions $g_{1}(a)$ and $g_{2}(a)$ used in the proof of Proposition 1

It is clear from the above that $z_{1}<1 / 2$ and $c<z_{2}$. In fact, using Bolzano's theorem, it can be shown that

$$
z_{1} \in(3 / 8,7 / 16) \quad \text { and } \quad z_{2} \in(25 / 16,13 / 8)
$$

Finally, from the fact that $F(1 / 4)>0, F(1)<0$ and $F(2)>0$ we have that $F(a)$ is negative for $z \in\left(z_{1}, z_{2}\right)$, and positive otherwise. This concludes the proof.

Proposition 2. Let $F$ be the function defined in (11). Then, for $n \geq 4$, the following statements hold.

1. The equation $F(a)=0$ has at least two positive solutions, denoted by $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$.
2. Suppose that $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ are the only positive solutions of $F(a)=0$. Then
(a) $z_{1}<1<z_{2}$ and $z_{1} z_{2}>1$.
(b) $F(a)<0$ for $a \in\left(z_{1}, z_{2}\right)$, and $F(a)>0$ for $a \in\left(0, z_{1}\right) \cup\left(z_{2}, \infty\right)$.

Proof. The first statement follows from Lemma 3 and Bolzano's Theorem applied in the intervals $[\epsilon, 1]$ and $[1,1 / \epsilon]$ for $\epsilon$ small enough. Furthermore, it is clear that $z_{1}<1<z_{2}$, and supposing that they are the only positive solutions of $F(a)=0$, we get easily that $F(a)<0$ for $a \in\left(z_{1}, z_{2}\right)$, and $F(a)>0$ for $a \in\left(0, z_{1}\right) \cup\left(z_{2}, \infty\right)$. We remark that this fact was already known by Roberts, and proved in .

From Lemma 4 the property $z_{1} z_{2}>1$ follows immediately for $n \geq 5$. For $n=4$, the result of that lemma is not true (it can be checked numerically). We claim that, when $n=4, F(2 / 3)>0$ and $F(3 / 2)<0$. Using the fact that $F(1)<0$ and $\lim _{a \rightarrow+\infty} F(a)=+\infty$, we get that $2 / 3<z_{1}<1$ and $z_{2}>3 / 2$, so in particular $z_{1} z_{2}>1$.

The proof of the claim relies on the fact that for $n=4$ we can write $F(a)=f_{1}(a)-f_{2}(a)-f_{3}(a)$ where

$$
f_{1}(a)=\left(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) a, \quad f_{2}(a)=\frac{2 a-\sqrt{2}}{\left(1+a^{2}-a \sqrt{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}, \quad f_{3}(a)=\frac{2 a+\sqrt{2}}{\left(1+a^{2}+a \sqrt{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

The following equalities and bounds are straightforward computations from which we obtain that $F(2 / 3)>0$ and $F(3 / 2)<0$.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
f_{1}(2 / 3)=\frac{1}{6}(1+2 \sqrt{2})>\frac{3}{5}, & f_{1}(3 / 2)=\frac{3}{8}(1+2 \sqrt{2})<\frac{3}{2} \\
f_{2}(2 / 3)=-9 \frac{3 \sqrt{2}-4}{(13-6 \sqrt{2})^{3 / 2}}<\frac{-1}{5}, & f_{2}(3 / 2)=8 \frac{3-\sqrt{2}}{(13-6 \sqrt{2})^{3 / 2}}>\frac{13}{10} \\
f_{3}(2 / 3)=9 \frac{3 \sqrt{2}+4}{(13+6 \sqrt{2})^{3 / 2}}<\frac{4}{5}, & f_{3}(3 / 2)=8 \frac{3+\sqrt{2}}{(13+6 \sqrt{2})^{3 / 2}}>\frac{3}{10}
\end{array}
$$

These computations conclude the proof of the proposition.

# CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS OF THE SYMMETRIC RESTRICTED 4-BODY PROBLEM 


#### Abstract

We consider the symmetric planar $(3+1)$-body problem with finite masses $m_{1}=m_{2}=1$, $m_{3}=\mu$ and one small mass $m_{4}=\epsilon$. We count the number of central configurations of the restricted case $\epsilon=0$, where the finite masses remain in an equilateral triangle configuration, by means of the bifurcation diagram with $\mu$ as the parameter. The diagram shows a folding bifurcation at a value consistent with that found numerically by Meyer  and it is shown that for small $\epsilon>0$ the bifurcation diagram persists, thus leading to an exact count of central configurations and a folding bifurcation for small $m_{4}>0$.


Key words: restricted 4-body problem, central configuration, analytic continuation
AMS Subject classification: 70F

## 1. Introduction

Consider $N$ bodies with positive masses $m_{i}, i=1, \ldots, N$, moving under their mutual gravitational attraction. Let $\mathbf{q}_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ be their positions relative to the center of mass. The motion is governed by Newton's law

$$
m_{i} \ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{i}=\frac{\partial U}{\partial \mathbf{q}_{i}}, \quad i=1, \ldots, N
$$

Here the Newtonian potential, taking the gravitational constant as unit, is

$$
U=\sum_{1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{q_{i j}}
$$

where $U: \mathbb{R}^{3 n} \backslash \Delta \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, \Delta=\cup_{i<j} \Delta_{i j}$ is the set of collisions, $\Delta_{i j}=$ $\left\{\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \mathbf{q}_{2}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{N}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{3 N}: \mathbf{q}_{i}=\mathbf{q}_{j}\right\}$, and $q_{i j}=\left\|\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right\|$ for $1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant N$ denote the Euclidean distance between the $i$ th and $j$ th particle.

A configuration of the $N$ particles is a central configuration at time $t$ if there exists some scalar $\lambda$ such that $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{q}}_{i}=-\lambda \mathbf{q}_{i}$ for $i=1, \ldots, N$. By replacing the acceleration vector $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{q}}_{i}$ by the force vector these equations become

$$
\frac{\partial U}{\partial \mathbf{q}_{i}}+\lambda m_{i} \mathbf{q}_{i}=0, \quad i=1, \ldots, N
$$

There are many reasons for studying central configurations in the $N$-body problem, they allow us to obtain the unique solutions of the $N$-body problem that can be described explicitly . They also play a main role in the topological changes of the integral manifolds , and they are limiting configurations for total collapsing particles  or parabolic total escape .

The problem of determining the central configurations of $N$ bodies is classical. For $N=3$, it is completely solved: there are three collinear and two equilateral triangle configurations. Moulton  solved this problem for arbitrary $N$ collinear particles. For general non-collinear and $N \geqslant 4$, central configurations are not yet all known, although the problem has been completely solved by Albouy for the planar case and equal masses . Wintner  shows that the only non-planar central configuration of four arbitrary masses is that of a regular tetrahedron.

One possible approach towards counting and understanding the bifurcations of central configurations when some masses are taken as parameters, is to proceed from a restricted problem when one or several masses are set equal to zero, while the primaries are located at a known central configuration of fewer bodies. This approach has been followed by Xia , Meyer  and Meyer and Schmidt , Albouy and Llibre , among others. In fact the study of central configuration for restricted problems goes back to Euler and Lagrange in the study of the socalled 'restricted 3-body problem'. For $N=4$ particles the initial contributions are due to Lindwow in 1923 who studied the case of three equal aligned masses , and Pedersen  who studied the case of three arbitrary masses in an equilateral triangle configuration and a fourth massless particle moving in the same plane of the primaries.

In this paper we consider a 4-body problem where the primaries $m_{1}, m_{2}$ and $m_{3}$ are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. We also assume that two primaries have equal masses say $m_{1}=m_{2}=1$, the third particle has mass $m_{3}=\mu$; a fourth infinitesimal mass $m_{4}$ (i.e. we will consider it to be zero as well as small and positive) and axis of symmetry of the triangle passing through $m_{4}$. We shall call this the symmetric restricted 4-body problem. This problem is a particular case of that studied by Arenstorf  where the primaries have arbitrary masses with a fourth infinitesimal mass moving in the same plane. He first concludes that for $m_{4}=0$ there are exactly 8,9 or 10 planar central configurations depending on whether the normalized masses lie inside, on or outside a closed curve, which is the degeneracy locus of a potential function in the simplex of masses $m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}=1$. He then concludes that every central configuration of the restricted problem can be continued uniquely to either 8 or 10 planar central configuration for sufficiently

small $m_{4}>0$. He conjectured that when there are just 9 , then exactly one of them is not continuable to $m_{4}>0$.

Previously, Simó in 1978  presented a complete numerical study of the central configurations of the planar 4-body problem including the restricted cases which in the simplex of masses $m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}+m_{4}=1$ correspond to one of their faces. He found a closed curve of degeneracy for the restricted case.

On the other hand, Meyer  considered the symmetric planar restricted 4-body problem, and proved that the bifurcation he obtain actually occurs in the full 4-body problem with one small mass. He showed that a folding bifurcation occurs at some value of the ratio of masses of the primaries, and that central configurations for the restricted case can be continued to the full symmetric 4-body problem under some conditions (see Section 4 of this paper).

The structure of the paper is as follows: In Section 2 we set the equations of the symmetric problem with the mass of the apsidal particle as parameter $\mu$. We determine the exact number of central configurations and their bifurcations for the restricted case $m_{4}=0$ with $\mu$ as the parameter. In Section 3, we perform the analytic continuation of the central configurations found in the previous section to small $m_{4}>0$ including the particular value $\mu^{*}$ where a folding bifurcation occurs for $m_{4}=0$. This value coincides with that obtained previously by Meyer  and lies on the locus of degeneracy found by Arenstorf, thus disproving his conjecture.

# 2. The Symmetric Restricted 4-Body Problem 

Consider four particles located as follows: Two equal masses of unit magnitude are located at points $P_{1}(x, \eta), P_{2}(-x, \eta)$. The third and fourth particles of masses $\mu$ and $\epsilon$ are located along the line perpendicular to the segment $P_{1}, P_{2}$ with coordinates $P_{\mu}(0, \eta+z)$ and $P_{\epsilon}(0, \eta+z-w)$, respectively. Fixing the center of mass at the origin leads to

$$
\eta=-\frac{\mu z+\epsilon(z-w)}{2+\mu+\epsilon}
$$

so $x>0, z, w \in \mathbb{R}$ can be considered as independent coordinates. Positive (negative) values of $z$ represents configurations with the particle of mass $\mu$, which subsequently will be called the apsidal particle, upside (down) the segment $P_{1} P_{2}$; positive (negative) values of $w$ represent configurations with the particle of mass $\epsilon$ down (up) the apsidal particle (see Figure 1).

The negative of the potential $U$ and the mass matrix $M$ in these coordinates are

$$
U=\frac{1}{2 x}+\frac{2 \epsilon}{\sqrt{x^{2}+(-w+z)^{2}}}+\frac{2 \mu}{\sqrt{x^{2}+z^{2}}}+\frac{\epsilon \kappa \mu}{w}
$$


where $\kappa=\operatorname{sign}(w)$, and

$$
M=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
2 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \frac{2(\mu+\epsilon)}{2+\mu+\epsilon} & -\frac{2 \epsilon}{2+\mu+\epsilon} \\
0 & -\frac{2 \epsilon}{2+\mu+\epsilon} & \frac{\epsilon(2+\mu)}{2+\mu+\epsilon}
\end{array}\right)
$$

This can be deduced by writing down the kinetic energy

$$
T=\dot{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \mu(\dot{\eta}+\dot{z})^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \epsilon(\dot{\eta}+\dot{z}-\dot{w})^{2}
$$

and eliminating $\eta$ using (2).
The inverse of the mass matrix is

$$
M^{-1}=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\frac{1}{2} & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \frac{1}{\epsilon}+\frac{1}{\mu} & \frac{1}{\mu} \\
0 & \frac{1}{\mu} & \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{\mu}
\end{array}\right)
$$

The equations for central configurations $Q=(x, z, w)$

$$
M^{-1} \nabla U(Q)+\lambda Q=0
$$

yields the system

$$
\begin{aligned}
& -\frac{1}{4 x^{2}}-\frac{\epsilon x}{\left(x^{2}+(w-z)^{3}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{\mu x}{\left(x^{2}+z^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}+\lambda x=0 \\
& -\frac{\kappa \epsilon}{w^{2}}-\frac{\epsilon(z-w)}{\left(x^{2}+(w-z)^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}+-\frac{(2+\mu) z}{\left(x^{2}+z^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}+\lambda z=0 \\
& -\frac{\kappa(\epsilon+\mu)}{w^{2}}+\frac{2(z-w)}{\left(x^{2}+(w-z)^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{2 z}{\left(x^{2}+z^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}+\lambda w=0
\end{aligned}
$$

The restricted case corresponds to $\epsilon=0$. If $z \neq 0$ then one can eliminate the Lagrange multiplier among the equations above leading to two homogeneous equations in $x, z, w$ which can be written in terms of the ratios $\alpha=w / x$ and $\beta=z / x$. The first equation involves only $\beta$,

$$
2+\mu=\frac{4 \mu+\left(1+\beta^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}{4}
$$

from which the unique real and positive solution $\beta=\sqrt{3}$ is read off (a symmetric solution occurs at $\beta=-\sqrt{3}$, but will be omitted in what follows). Thus primaries form an equilateral triangle configuration with the apsidal particle above the base. Having fixed positions for the primaries, our goal is to describe the position of the massless particle along the vertical axis.

Substitution of $\beta=\sqrt{3}$ in the second equation leads to an equation in $\alpha$ and $\mu$

$$
\mu\left(\frac{\alpha^{3}-8 \kappa}{8 \alpha^{3}}\right)=\frac{1}{\alpha}\left(\frac{8(\alpha-\sqrt{3})+\sqrt{3}\left(1+(\alpha-\beta)^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}{4\left(1+(\alpha-\beta)^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}\right)-\frac{1}{4}
$$

which can be solved for $\mu$,

$$
\mu(\alpha)=\frac{2 \alpha^{2}(\alpha-\sqrt{3})\left(8-\left(1+(\alpha-\sqrt{3})^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}\right)}{\left(\alpha^{3}-8 \kappa\right)\left(1+(\alpha-\sqrt{3})^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

where $\kappa=1$ for $\alpha \geqslant 0$ and $\kappa=-1$ for $\alpha<0$.
We follow the notation shown in Figure 2. Notice that the graph of $\mu(\alpha)$ presents a local maximum at

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \alpha=\alpha_{0}=1.4514804909908971 \ldots \\
& \mu\left(\alpha_{0}\right)=\mu_{0}=1.46889555399367761 \ldots
\end{aligned}
$$

a local minimum at the origin, and a horizontal asymptote where $\lim _{\alpha \rightarrow \pm \infty} \mu(\alpha)=$ -2 , and two vertical asymptotes at $\alpha= \pm 2$.


We will now describe briefly the configuration the infinitesimal mass adopts as we decrease the parameter $\mu$ from $\infty$ up to include negative values, along the series (curves) marked $A, B^{\prime}, B^{\prime \prime}, C$ and $D$.

Since $\beta=\sqrt{3}$ the primaries remain in an equilateral configuration. In the series $A$, the particle of mass $\epsilon=0$ lays above the apsidal particle; as $\mu \downarrow 0$ the infinitesimal mass approaches a collision with the apsidal particle. The configuration $\alpha=0$ with $\mu=0$ corresponds to the Lagrangian equilateral point $L_{5}$ in the restricted 3-body problem with equal masses. In series $B^{\prime}$ and $B^{\prime \prime}$ the infinitesimal mass lays in the interior of the equilateral triangle formed by the primaries. For the particular value of $\mu=\mu_{0}$, where $\mu^{\prime}(\alpha)$ vanishes, a folding bifurcation occurs at a point with $\alpha=\alpha_{0}>2 / \sqrt{3}$ so the infinitesimal mass lays just below the barycenter. The two branches named $B^{\prime}$ and $B^{\prime \prime}$ bifurcate from this special value; as $\mu$ decreases from $\mu_{0}$ to zero along series $B^{\prime}$ the $\epsilon$-particle ends up with collision with the $\mu$ particle; the series $B^{\prime \prime}$ ends up for non-negative values of $\mu$ at $\alpha=\sqrt{3}$ where the infinitesimal mass is aligned with the primaries of mass 1 . By continuing through negative values of $\mu$ the series $B^{\prime \prime}$ approaches line $\alpha=2$ as $\mu \downarrow-\infty$, thus the infinitesimal particle approaches the lower vertex of a trapezoidal configuration, more precisely, its position lays in the intersection of the circle with center at the apsidal particle and radius 2 (the length of the equilateral triangle) and the bisectrix of the segment joining the primaries of mass 1 .

For $\mu \downarrow 0$ along series $C$ the infinitesimal mass lays below the base of the equilateral triangle and ends up with a value of $\alpha=2 \sqrt{3}$ with the infinitesimal mass at the vertex of a rhombus. Since $\lim _{\alpha \rightarrow \infty} \mu(\alpha)=-2$, we have a bifurcation 'at infinity'.

Series $D$ exists only for $\mu$ negative. It is originated from the bifurcation 'at infinity' of series $C$. As $\mu \downarrow-\infty$ from the asymptotic value $\mu(-\infty)=-2$, the configuration $\alpha$ of particle $\epsilon$ decreases monotonically from $\alpha=\infty$ where the particle of mass $\epsilon$ comes from above particle $\mu$, up to $\alpha=-2$ where the particles form a kite-shaped conguration with particle $\epsilon$ above particle $\mu$.

Note that the case of negative masses has no physical meaning and it has been considered here only for mathematical purposes.

In summary, the number of central configurations where the primaries form an equilateral triangle are the following

| Value of $\mu$ | Number of central configurations |
| :-- | :-- |
| $\mu>\mu_{0}$ | 2 |
| $\mu=\mu_{0}$ | 3 |
| $0<\mu<\mu_{0}$ | 4 |
| $\mu=0$ | 3, one with double collision |
| $-2<\mu<0$ | 2 |
| $\mu=-2$ | 1 |
| $\mu<-2$ | 2 |

# 3. Analytic Continuation for Small Values of $\epsilon$ 

In this section we will prove that bifurcation diagrams obtained in the previous section for $\epsilon=0$ persist for small $\epsilon$, for all ratios $\alpha=w / x$, except $\alpha=0$ which corresponds to collision of the infinitesimal particle with the apsidal particle.

Consider the full set of equations obtained by elimination of the Lagrange multiplier $\lambda$ in (5)-(7), that is, without setting $\epsilon=0$. These can be written in the form

$$
F(\alpha, \beta, \mu, \epsilon)=0, \quad G(\alpha, \beta, \mu, \epsilon)=0
$$

From Section 2 the series $A, B \equiv B^{\prime} \cup B^{\prime \prime}$ and $C$ are the graphs of functions $\mu_{i}(\alpha), i=A, B, C$ defined for $\alpha \in I_{1}=(-\infty, 0), I_{2}=(0,2), I_{3}=(2, \infty)$, respectively, such that

$$
F\left(\alpha, \sqrt{3}, \mu_{i}(\alpha), 0\right)=0, \quad G\left(\alpha, \sqrt{3}, \mu_{i}(\alpha), 0\right)=0
$$

Our goal is to show that these equations admit solutions $\mu^{(i)}\left(\alpha, \epsilon\right), \beta^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon)$, $i=A, B, B^{\prime}, C$ defined for small $\epsilon$ such that $\mu^{(i)}(\alpha, 0)=\mu_{i}(\alpha), \beta^{(i)}(\alpha, 0)=\sqrt{3}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}
& F\left(\alpha, \beta^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon), \mu^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon), \epsilon\right)=0 \\
& G\left(\alpha, \beta^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon), \mu^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon), \epsilon\right)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

To show this we compute the Jacobian determinant

$$
\Delta=\left|\begin{array}{ll}
\frac{\partial F}{\partial \beta} & \frac{\partial F}{\partial \mu} \\
\frac{\partial G}{\partial \beta} & \frac{\partial G}{\partial \mu}
\end{array}\right|
$$

evaluated at $\alpha \in I_{i}, \beta=\sqrt{3}, \mu=\mu_{i}(\alpha)$ and $\epsilon=0$. A short computation shows that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta= & 72(\alpha-2 \kappa) \alpha^{2}\left(4+2 \alpha+\alpha^{2}\right) \\
& \cdot\left(256-512 \sqrt{3} \alpha+1408 \alpha^{2}-768 \sqrt{3} \alpha^{3}+816 \alpha^{4}-\right. \\
& \left.-192 \sqrt{3} \alpha^{5}+88 \alpha^{6}-8 \sqrt{3} \alpha^{7}+\alpha^{8}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

vanishes for $\alpha=0,2 \kappa$. When $\alpha=0$ a binary collision occurs, but we are not interested on its continuation. For $\alpha=2 \kappa$ there is no central configuration for $\epsilon=0$. The last polynomial factor can be factored as

$$
(\alpha-\sqrt{3}+\mathrm{i})^{4}(\alpha-\sqrt{3}-\mathrm{i})^{4}
$$

where $\mathrm{i}=\sqrt{-1}$. Therefore it has only complex roots.
Remark. By considering any compact interval $K$ in the $\alpha$-axis not containing $\alpha=0$ nor $\alpha= \pm 2$, one can even prove the stronger result.

THEOREM 3.1. Consider a compact interval $K$ not containing $\alpha=0, \pm 2$. Then there exists $\epsilon_{0}>0$ and $\mu^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon)$ defined for all $\alpha \in K$ and $|\epsilon|<\epsilon_{0}$ such that Equation (10) are satisfied.

# 3.1. CRITICAL POINTS OF $\beta(\alpha, \epsilon), \mu(\alpha, \epsilon)$ 

In order to prove that the bifurcation diagram in Figure 2 persists for small $\epsilon$, it is necessary to show that there are no critical points of the analytic extensions $\mu^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon)$ for $\epsilon=0$. We complete the picture by analyzing also the critical point of the complementary surface $\beta^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon)$. We conjecture that $\beta^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon)$ has a saddle singularity for $\alpha=2 / \sqrt{3} \equiv \alpha_{\text {bar }}$, which corresponds to the infinitesimal mass laying at the barycenter of the triangle of the primaries.

THEOREM 3.2. Let $i=A, B, C, D$ denote any of the analytic extensions $\mu^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon), \beta^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon)$ given by (10), and $I_{i}$ the corresponding domains on the $\alpha$-axis, then
(a) $\left(\alpha_{\text {bar }}, 0\right)$ is the unique critical point of the analytic extension $\beta^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon), i=C$, for small $\epsilon$.
(b) For each $i=A, B, C$ and $\alpha \in I_{i},(\alpha, 0)$ is a regular point of the analytic extension $\mu^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon)$. In particular the folding bifurcation in the $\alpha-\mu$ plane persists for fixed but small $\epsilon$.
Proof. Taking derivatives with respect to $\epsilon$ in Equation (10) it follows

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial F}{\partial \beta} \frac{\partial \beta}{\partial \epsilon}+\frac{\partial F}{\partial \mu} \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial \epsilon}=-\frac{\partial F}{\partial \epsilon} \\
& \frac{\partial G}{\partial \beta} \frac{\partial \beta}{\partial \epsilon}+\frac{\partial G}{\partial \mu} \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial \epsilon}=-\frac{\partial G}{\partial \epsilon}
\end{aligned}
$$

It is readily verified that as a function of $(\alpha, \beta, \mu, \epsilon)$

$$
\frac{\partial F}{\partial \mu}=0
$$

in particular,

$$
\frac{\partial F}{\partial \beta}\left(\alpha, \sqrt{3}, \mu_{i}(\alpha), 0\right) \frac{\partial \beta}{\partial \epsilon}(\alpha, 0)=-\frac{\partial F}{\partial \epsilon}\left(\alpha, \sqrt{3}, \mu_{i}(\alpha), 0\right)
$$

An explicit computation shows that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial F}{\partial \epsilon}\left(\alpha, \sqrt{3}, \mu_{i}(\alpha), 0\right)= \\
& \quad-32\left(-16+16 \sqrt{3} \alpha-20 \alpha^{2}+4 \sqrt{3} \alpha^{3}+\kappa \sqrt{1+(\sqrt{3}-\alpha)^{2}} \alpha^{3}-\alpha^{4}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

and it vanishes only for $\alpha_{\text {bar }}=2 \sqrt{3} / 3$ (thus $\kappa=1$ ), the remaining roots being complex. Since the factor

$$
\frac{\partial F}{\partial \beta}(\alpha, \sqrt{3}, \mu_{i}(\alpha), 0)=-18 \alpha^{2}\left(16-16 \sqrt{3} \alpha+20 \alpha^{2}-4 \sqrt{3} \alpha^{3}+\alpha^{4}\right)
$$

does not vanish for $\alpha=\alpha_{\text {bar }}$, if follows that $(\partial \beta / \partial \epsilon)\left(\alpha_{\text {bar }}, 0\right)=0$.
A further analysis of the type of singularity would reveal the type of singularity although it requires the computation of higher order derivatives. Strong numerical evidence shows that the critical point is of saddle type.

Next, we study the possible singularities of $\mu^{(i)}(\alpha, \epsilon)$. Since $(\partial \mu / \partial \alpha)(\alpha, 0) \neq$ 0 , except for $\alpha=\alpha_{0}$ it is enough to compute the value of $(\partial \mu / \partial \epsilon)\left(\alpha_{\text {bar }}, 0\right)$. A straightforward computation of $\partial \mu / \partial \epsilon$ from expressions (11) yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial \beta}{\partial \epsilon}\left(\alpha_{0}, 0\right)=-1.4593385456713914 \\
& \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial \epsilon}\left(\alpha_{0}, 0\right)=0.8560203602197306
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore there are no critical points for the analytic extension $\mu(\alpha, \epsilon)$.

# 4. Remarks 

We have shown that the bifurcation diagram in Figure 2 persists for small positive $\epsilon$. In particular the surface $\mu(\alpha, \epsilon)$ presents a folding for a value of $\mu_{0}$ given in (8). Meyer  (see also $$ ) has given sufficient conditions on the self-potential of the restricted $(n+1)$-body problem, say $V(x, y, \mu)$, where $\mathbf{r}_{n+1}=u=(x, y)$ is the position of the infinitesimal mass, and depending on a parameter $\mu$, for a planar central configurations of $n$-bodies which is non-degenerate at some value of $\mu=\bar{\mu}$ could be continued analytically into the full planar $(n+1)$-body problem, namely if $V$ has a fold catastrophe at $(\bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{\mu})$

$$
V_{x}=V_{y}=V_{x y}=V_{y y}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad V_{x x} \neq 0, V_{y u} \neq 0, V_{y y y} \neq 0
$$

and

$$
V_{y \mu} \cdot V_{y y y}<0
$$

then for small $\epsilon>0$ the number of central configurations is two for $\mu<\mu^{*}(\epsilon)$, none for $\mu>\mu^{*}(\epsilon)$ and a degenerate central configuration for $\mu=\mu^{*}(\epsilon)$, where $\mu(\epsilon)$ is a smooth function such that $\mu(0)=\bar{\mu}$. Then he considers the example of the restricted 4-body problem with the primaries at an equilateral triangle central configuration with two equal masses $1-\mu$ and the third mass $2 \mu$. Finally, he verifies numerically the hypothesis for a value of $\mu=\bar{\mu} \approx 0.423448$.

In the notation of this paper Meyer's parameter $\tilde{\mu}$ corresponds to the mass of the apsidal particle (Figure 1) with $\epsilon=0$ that is to our value of $\mu$ given by

$$
\frac{\mu}{2+\mu}=\frac{2 \tilde{\mu}}{(1-\tilde{\mu})+(1-\tilde{\mu})}=\tilde{\mu}
$$

which leads to our value of

$$
\mu=\frac{2 \tilde{\mu}}{(1-\tilde{\mu})}
$$

substituting Meyer's value of $\tilde{\mu}$ gives

$$
\mu=1.46889 \ldots
$$

this value coincides with the value of $\mu_{0}$ given in (8) within machine precision.

# Central configurations on the plane with $N$ heavy and $k$ light bodies 

#### Abstract

We study the problem of planar central configurations with $N$ heavy bodies and $k$ bodies with arbitrary small masses. We derive the equation which describe the limit of light masses going to zero, which can be seen as the equation for central configurations in the anisotropic plane. Using computer rigorous computations we compute all central configurations for $N=2$ and $k=3,4$ and for the derived limit problem. We show that the results are consistent.

## 1 Introduction

The main problem of the classical celestial mechanics is the $n$-body problem, i.e. the description of the motion of $n$ point masses under their mutual Newtonian gravitational forces. This problem is entirely solved for $n=2$, while for $n \geq 2$ only partial results exist.
A central configuration, denoted here as CC, is an initial configuration, such that if the particles were all released with zero velocity, they would collapse toward the center of mass at the same time. In the planar case, CCs are initial positions for periodic solutions of the $n$-body problem where bodies move on a Keplerian elliptical orbits preserving the shape of the configuration. The circular orbits give rise to solutions for which the configuration rotates at constant angular speed. This is called a relative equilibrium solution (see Figure 1). The other orbits give rise to solutions where radius and the angular speed are not constant.

If we give the particles an appropriate angular velocity such that gravitational forces $F_{i}$ balance (equilibrate) centrifugal forces $R_{i}$, they will move along circular orbits.

# 1.1 The state of the art 

It is conjectured in  that there are finitely many isometry classes of CCs. The conjecture appears as the sixth problem of Smale's eighteen problems for the 21st century . We refer to this problem in short as CC finiteness. From among abundant literature on the subject, let us mention two important works  and  which aim at studying the problem in the most general setting and provide results for $n=4$ and $n=5$ with (almost) arbitrary masses. In  the authors give a computer assisted proof of CC finiteness for $n=4$ for any system of positive masses; in  the problem for $n=4$ is proven without computer assistance and the finiteness for $n=5$ is proven for arbitrary positive masses with the possible exception of those CCs where quintuples of positive masses belongs to a given codimension 2 subvariety of the mass space. It is interesting to note that when masses are equal, there are finitely many isometry classes of CCs and this case belongs to the aforementioned subvariety (see ). A common feature of these works is that they give a quite poor estimate for the maximum number of CCs. In this context it is worth to mention the work of Simo, based on extensive numerical studies. In  he gives the number of CCs for all possible masses for $n=4$.
The papers  which are concerned with CC finiteness for all masses study the polynomial equations derived from the equations for CC using the algebraic geometry tools. The approach we pursue is different as we study the equations for CCs using rigorous numerics. While our results published so far (see ) refer to the equal masses case, our program allows to process boxes in the mass space, hence in principle we can cover the whole mass space and find the number of CCs with all masses. However, there are several obstacles in the case of different masses: some of the masses approaching zero and possible bifurcations. In the current paper, we try to overcome the former problem.

### 1.2 Our contribution

We look for CCs in the situation when the massess of certain bodies approach zero as the positions of these bodies move closer together (approaching the same point). We derive equations for this limit problem, which can be seen as the equations for central configurations in the anisotropic plane. Our results can be seen as a generalization of the results by Xia , where the case of two light bodies was considered. We perform computer assisted proofs of full listings of CCs in the anisotropic plane for $k=3,4$. The anisotropy parameters correspond to CCs for two heavy bodies with equal masses and $k$ light bodies with very small equal masses in the neighborhood of Lagrange point $L_{4}$ of the restricted two body problem. We also perform rigorous computations of all CCs for $(2+k)$-body problem in the corresponding region of configuration space. The results of both computations are in very good agreement.
The content of the paper is as follows. In Section 2 we recall equations for central configurations. In Section 3 we derive the reduced set of equations for CCs where we remove the rotational symmetry and the system of equations becomes amenable to a direct application of the implicit function theorem. In Section 4 the limit of vanishing masses is studied, the limit problem is derived and basic theorem about

the continuation of solutions of the limit problem is proved. In Section 5 we study general properties of the limit problem and we establish some a priori bounds. In Section 6 we find analytically several solutions of the limit problem. In Section 7 we present computer assisted proofs for the limit problem with $k=3,4$ and corresponding CCs for $(2+k)$-bodies with $k=3,4$.
Proofs which are either very simple, or analogous to those in  are contained in Appendix A.

# 1.3 Notation 

Throughout the paper we use the following notation:

- body - point characterized by its position $q \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ and the mass $m$;
- CC - central configuration
- $\mathrm{CC}_{n}$ - central configuration of $n$ point masses (bodies); $q \in \mathrm{CC}_{n}-q=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$ is a central configuration of $n$ bodies;
- $r_{i j}=\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|$, where $q_{i}, q_{j}$ are positions of bodies.

Usually we use letters $p$ and $q$ for light and heavy bodies, respectively. Uppercase $P$ and $Q$ denote their respective configurations, with subscripts and superscripts indicating the number of bodies and vector of masses. Both these parameters are consider constant when solving the equations for central configurations (see equation (1)).

- $Q_{N}^{m}$ and $P_{k}^{\mu}$, where
$-\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}\right)$ - configuration of heavy bodies with masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$, respectively; we use $m=\left(m_{i}\right)_{i=1, \ldots, N}$
$-\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{k}\right)$ - configuration of light bodies with masses $\mu_{1}, \ldots, \mu_{k}$, respectively; use $\mu=$ $\left(\mu_{i}\right)_{i=1, \ldots, k}$
$-x \in \operatorname{RE}\left(Q_{N}\right)-x$ is a relative normalized $C C$ in the restricted $(N+1)$-body problem for the configuration $Q_{N}$ (see Definition 3);
$-\mathrm{CC}\left(W, Q_{N}^{m}, x, \mu\right)$ - central configuration of potential $W$ induced by $\left(Q_{N}, x\right)$ for $\mu$ (see Definition 4).

If we indicate masses explicitly we sometimes omit superscripts and just we write $Q_{N}$ or $P_{k}$.
When we focus only on light bodies we use:

- $\operatorname{rbp}(k, a, b)-\mathrm{CC}$ of restricted $k$ light body problem (see Definition5), solutions of the anisotropic central configuration problem (71).


## 2 Central configurations

Assume there are a group $Q_{N}^{m} \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)^{N}$ of $N$ celestial bodies interacting with each other gravitationally (i.e. due to inverse square Law of Gravitation; gravitational constant is normalized $G=1$ ). The central configuration problem is to find positions of bodies satisfying the following system of equations

$$
\lambda m_{i}\left(q_{i}-c\right)=\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\ j \neq i}}^{N} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}\left(q_{i}-q_{j}\right)=: f_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n
$$

where $c$ is a center of mass of the configuration and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$is a scaling factor. It is well-known (see for example ) that in equations (1) we can set $c=0$ obtaining

$$
-\lambda m_{i} q_{i}=\sum_{j \neq i} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|^{3}}\left(q_{j}-q_{i}\right)=\frac{\partial U_{N}}{\partial q_{i}}, \quad i=1,2, \ldots, N
$$

where

$$
U_{N}=\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq N} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|}
$$

Definition 1.  A normalized central configuration $Q_{N} \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)^{N}$ is a central configuration with $\lambda=1$ and $c=0$.

From now on we focus on normalized central configurations.
We can reformulate equations (2) with $\lambda=1$ as the problem of finding critical points for certain potential function. Let us define potential

$$
V\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i} q_{i}^{2}}{2}+U_{N}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i} q_{i}^{2}}{2}+\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq N} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|}
$$

Note that for $\lambda=1$ the equations (2) become

$$
\frac{\partial V}{\partial q_{i}}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}\right)=0, \quad i=1, \ldots, N
$$

# 3 The reduced system of equations for CC 

The goal of this section is to derive a set of equations (the reduced system of equations), which gives all (equivalence classes of) CCs and which no longer has $\mathcal{S O}(d)$-symmetry, where $d$ is the dimension of the space. In our case $d=2$ that means that we eliminate rotations around the origin. This section is an extension of the results of Section 5 in  and Section 3 in .
For the future use we introduce the function $F: \Pi_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \Pi_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{R}^{d}$ given by

$$
F_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)=q_{i}-\sum_{j, j \neq i} \frac{m_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}\left(q_{i}-q_{j}\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n
$$

Then the system for normalized central configurations

$$
q_{i}=\sum_{j, j \neq i} \frac{m_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}\left(q_{i}-q_{j}\right)=: \frac{1}{m_{i}} f_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n
$$

becomes

$$
F\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)=0
$$

It is well known (see  and the literature given there) that for any $\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right) \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right)^{n}$ holds

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} f_{i} & =0 \\
\sum_{i=1}^{n} f_{i} \wedge q_{i} & =0
\end{aligned}
$$

where $v \wedge w$ is the exterior product of vectors, the result being an element of exterior algebra. If $d=2$ or 3 it can be interpreted as the vector product of $v$ and $w$ in dimension 3 . The identities (8) and (9) are

easy consequences of the third Newton's law (the action equals reaction) and the requirement that the mutual forces between bodies are in direction of the other body.
Consider system (6). After multiplication of $i$-th equation by $m_{i}$ and addition of all equations using (8) we obtain (or rather recover) the center of mass equation

$$
\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{i}\right) c=\sum_{i} m_{i} q_{i}=0
$$

We can take the equations for $n$-th body and replace it with (10) to obtain an equivalent system

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{i} & =\sum_{j, j \neq i} \frac{m_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}\left(q_{i}-q_{j}\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n-1 \\
q_{n} & =-\frac{1}{m_{n}} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} m_{i} q_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

# 3.1 Non-degenerate solutions of full and reduced systems 

Following Moeckel  we state the following definition for any $d$, but we are interested in $d=2$, here.

Definition 2. We say that a normalized central configuration $q=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$ is non-degenerate if the rank of $D F(q)$ is equal to $d n-\operatorname{dim} \mathcal{S O}(d)$. Otherwise the configuration is called degenerate.

The idea of the above notion of degeneracy is to allow only for the degeneracy related to the rotational symmetry of the problem, because by setting $\lambda=1$ in (1) and keeping the masses fixed we removed the scaling symmetry.

### 3.1.1 The center of mass reduction

We write the system (11) obtained from (7) after removing the $n$-th body using the center of mass equation (condition (10)) as

$$
F_{\text {red }}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)=0
$$

where $F_{\text {red }}: \Pi_{i=1}^{n-1} \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \Pi_{i=1}^{n-1} \mathbb{R}^{d}$. To be precise we have

$$
F_{\text {red }, i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)=F_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n-1
$$

where

$$
q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)=-\frac{1}{m_{n}} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} m_{i} q_{i}
$$

Lemma 1. If $q=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\right)$ is a normalized CC. Then

$$
\operatorname{rank}\left(D F_{\operatorname{red}}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right)=\operatorname{rank}\left(D F\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\right)\right)-d
$$

An easy proof is left to reader.
For any configuration $q$ we set

$$
R_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)=m_{i} q_{i}-f_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n
$$

With the above notation the system (7) becomes

$$
R\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)=\left(R_{1}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right), \ldots, R_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)\right)=0
$$

For any $\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right) \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)^{n-1}$ we define

$$
\tilde{R}_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)=R_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n
$$

Obviously $\operatorname{rank}(D \tilde{R})(q)=\operatorname{rank}\left(D F_{\text {red }}\right)(q)$. Observe that for any $\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right) \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right)^{n-1}$ holds

$$
\tilde{R}_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)=-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \tilde{R}_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)
$$

Indeed, by (6) we have

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} m_{i} q_{i}
$$

and by $(13)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right) & =-\frac{1}{m_{n}} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} m_{i} q_{i} \\
& =-\frac{1}{m_{n}} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right) & =m_{n} q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right) \\
& =-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Now from (17) and (19) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{R}_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right) & =R_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right) \\
& =m_{n} q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)-f_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right) \\
& =-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} m_{i} q_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right) \\
& =-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \tilde{R}_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Observe that from (9) it follows that for any configuration $\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$ holds

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} q_{i} \wedge R_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)=0
$$

In particular for $q_{n}=q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)$ we obtain from (20) and (18)

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 & =\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} q_{i} \wedge \tilde{R}_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)+q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right) \wedge \tilde{R}_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right) \\
& =\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\left(q_{i}-q_{n}\right) \wedge \tilde{R}_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

# 3.2 The reduced system $\mathcal{R S}$ 

The system of equations (6) is degenerate due to the presence of the $S O(d)$-symmetry. In this section we remove this symmetry and introduce the reduced system of equations. Let us set $d=2$. We use the notation $\tilde{R}_{i}=\left(\tilde{R}_{i, x}, \tilde{R}_{i, y}\right)$. Let us fix $k_{1} \in\{1, \ldots, n-1\}$, and consider the following set of equations

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{i} & =\frac{1}{m_{i}} f_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right), \quad i \in\{1, \ldots, n-1\}, i \neq k_{1} \\
x_{k_{1}} & =\frac{1}{m_{k_{1}}} f_{k_{1}, x}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $f_{i}=\left(f_{i, x}, f_{i, y}\right)$. In the sequel, we use the abbreviation $\mathcal{R S}$ to denote the reduced system (22). $\mathcal{R S}$ coincides with (11) with the equation for $y_{k_{1}}$ dropped. Observe that $\mathcal{R S}$ has $2(n-1)-1$ equations for $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$. To obtain the same number of variables we set $q_{k_{1}, y}=0 . \mathcal{R S}$ no longer has $O(2)$ as a symmetry group, but still it is symmetric with respect to the reflections against the coordinate planes. Using the notation introduced in Section 3.1.1 $\mathcal{R S}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{R}_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right) & =0, \quad i \in\{1, \ldots, n-1\}, i \neq k_{1} \\
\tilde{R}_{k_{1}, x}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right) & =0
\end{aligned}
$$

with the requirement that $y_{k_{1}}=0$. The next theorem addresses the question: whether from $\mathcal{R S}$ we obtain the solution of (6)?

Theorem 2. If $q=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$ is a solution of $\mathcal{R S}$ and

$$
x_{k_{1}} \neq x_{n}
$$

then it is a normalized central configuration, i.e. it satisfies (6).
Proof. Without any loss of the generality we can assume that $k_{1}=n-1$. We need to show that $\tilde{R}_{n-1, y}(q)=0$. From (21) and (23) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 & =\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\left(q_{i}-q_{n}\right) \wedge \tilde{R}_{i}(q)=\left(q_{n-1}-q_{n}\right) \wedge \tilde{R}_{n-1}(q) \\
& =\left(x_{n-1}-x_{n}\right) \tilde{R}_{n-1, y}(q)
\end{aligned}
$$

and our assertion follows immediately.
Observe that in the proof we did not use the assumption that $y_{k_{1}}=0$.

### 3.3 The non-degenerate CC and the reduced system

Theorem 3. Assume that $q=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$ is a non-degenerate normalized CC. Then in a suitable coordinate system and after some permutation of bodies $q$ is a non-degenerate solution of $\mathcal{R S}$.

Proof. From the non-degeneracy assumption it follows that

$$
\operatorname{rank}(D F(q))=2 n-1
$$

From this and Lemma 1 we obtain

$$
\operatorname{rank}\left(D \tilde{R}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right)=\operatorname{rank}\left(D F_{\operatorname{red}}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)\right)=2(n-1)-1
$$

Assume that we have $q_{n-1}=\left(x_{n-1}, 0\right), x_{n-1} \neq x_{n}$ (see condition (24) in Theorem 2), $x_{n-1} \neq 0$ and consider $\mathcal{R S}$ on the subspace $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-2} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ and $x_{n-1} \in \mathbb{R}$. Now $\mathcal{R S}$ has the same number of equations and variables equal to $2(n-1)-1$. We want to show that the Jacobian matrix of this reduced system

has the rank $2(n-1)-1$, which implies that $q$ is a non-degenerate solution of $\mathcal{R S}$. We have that $D \tilde{R}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& {\left[\begin{array}{c}
D \tilde{R}_{1, x} \\
D \tilde{R}_{1, y} \\
D \tilde{R}_{2, x} \\
D \tilde{R}_{2, y} \\
\ldots \\
D \tilde{R}_{n-1, x} \\
D \tilde{R}_{n-1, y}
\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cccccc}
\frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{1, x}}{\partial x_{1}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{1, x}}{\partial y_{1}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{1, x}}{\partial x_{2}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{1, x}}{\partial y_{2}}, & \ldots, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{1, x}}{\partial x_{n-1}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{1, x}}{\partial y_{n-1}} \\
\frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{1, y}}{\partial x_{1}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{1, y}}{\partial y_{1}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{1, y}}{\partial x_{2}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{1, y}}{\partial y_{2}}, & \ldots, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{1, y}}{\partial x_{n-1}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{1, y}}{\partial y_{n-1}} \\
\frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{2, x}}{\partial x_{1}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{2, x}}{\partial y_{1}}, & \ldots, & \ldots, & \ldots, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{2, x}}{\partial x_{n-1}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{2, x}}{\partial y_{n-1}} \\
\frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{2, y}}{\partial x_{1}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{2, y}}{\partial y_{1}}, & \ldots, & \ldots, & \ldots, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{2, y}}{\partial x_{n-1}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}_{2, y}}{\partial y_{n-1}}
\end{array}\right]} \\
& =\left[\begin{array}{cccccc}
\frac{\partial \tilde{R}}{\partial x_{1}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}}{\partial y_{1}}, & \ldots, & \ldots & \ldots & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}}{\partial x_{n-1}}, & \frac{\partial \tilde{R}}{\partial y_{n-1}}
\end{array}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Observe that the jacobian matrix of $\mathcal{R S}$ is equal $D \tilde{R}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)$ with removed the last column (which is consequence of the restriction to $y_{n-1}=0$ ) and the last row (which is consequence of dropping the equation $\tilde{R}_{n-1, y}=0$ ). We need to show that such removal does not change the rank of the matrix. From (21) we have

$$
0=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\left(q_{i}-q_{n}\right) \wedge \tilde{R}_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)
$$

By taking partial derivatives of the above equation with respect to $x_{j}$ and $y_{j}$ and evaluating at $q$ (we have $\tilde{R}_{i}(q)=0$ ) we obtain

$$
0=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\left(q_{i}-q_{n}\right) \wedge D \tilde{R}_{i}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n-1}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\left(\left(x_{i}-x_{n}\right) D \tilde{R}_{i, y}-\left(y_{i}-y_{n}\right) D \tilde{R}_{i, x}\right)
$$

The above equation is the linear combination of the rows in the matrix $D \tilde{R}$. If $x_{n-1}-x_{n} \neq 0$, then the last row can be expressed as the linear combination of other rows, hence it can be removed from the matrix without changing its rank.
Now we show that last row $\frac{\partial \tilde{R}}{\partial y_{n-1}}$ is a linear combination of other rows. Let $O(t)$ be the rotation by angle $t$. It acts on configuration $q$ as follows $q_{i}(t)=O(t) q_{i}$ and $q(t)=\left(q_{1}(t), \ldots, q_{n-1}(t), q_{n}(t)\right)$ is a normalized central configuration if $q$ is. Observe that $\frac{d}{d t} q_{i}(t)_{t=0}=\left(-y_{i}, x_{i}\right)$. From the rotational symmetry we have

$$
\tilde{R}(O(t) q)=0
$$

By taking the derivative with respect to the angle for $t=0$ we obtain

$$
0=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\left(-\frac{\partial \tilde{R}}{\partial x_{i}} y_{i}+\frac{\partial \tilde{R}}{\partial y_{i}} x_{i}\right)
$$

If $x_{n-1} \neq 0$, then we can express $\frac{\partial \tilde{R}}{\partial y_{n-1}}$ (the last column in the matrix $D \tilde{R}$ ) in terms of other columns. Therefore we can remove the last row and the last column from the matrix $D \tilde{R}(q)$ without decreasing its rank. Therefore the rank of $\mathcal{R S}$ is $2(n-1)-1$, which shows the non-degeneracy of $q$ as the solution of $\mathcal{R S}$.

Now the question remains: whether we can always achieve that $x_{n-1} \neq x_{n}$ and $x_{n-1} \neq 0$. First we take any $q_{i_{0}} \neq 0$ (there can be only one body at the origin) and we chose coordinate frame so that $q_{i_{0}}=\left(x_{i_{0}}, 0\right)$. Then we look for $j \neq i_{0}$ such that $x_{j} \neq x_{i_{0}}$. Observe that due to (10) such $j$ always exists. Now we change the numeration of bodies so that $i_{0} \rightarrow n-1$ and $j \rightarrow n$.

Remark 4. From the proof of the above theorem it follows that a normalized CC, such that $x_{n-1}=x_{n}$ and $y_{n-1}=0$ is always a degenerate solution of $\mathcal{R S}$.

Theorem 5. Assume that $q=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$ is a non-degenerate solution of $\mathcal{R S}$, such that $x_{n-1} \neq x_{n}$. Then $q$ is a non-degenerate normalized central configuration.

An easy proof is left to reader.

# 4 CCs for $(N+k)$-bodies 

### 4.1 Some a-priori bounds for normalized CCs

Let us recall two theorems from : first states an upper bound on the size of a normalized CC; second states the lower bound for distances between bodies in normalized CC. We use them repeatedly in the sequel.

Theorem 6. [MZ19, Thm. 11] Given positive masses $m_{i}, i=1, \ldots, n$. Let $M=\sum_{i} m_{i}$. Assume $q=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$ is a normalized $C C_{n}$. Then

$$
\max _{i}\left|q_{i}\right| \leqslant M^{1 / 3} \begin{cases}n-1, & n \geqslant 2 \\ \left(2^{1 / 3}+2^{-2 / 3}\right)(n-2)^{2 / 3}, & n \geqslant 4\end{cases}
$$

In this theorem was stated for $M=1$, but a simple scaling argument gives factor $M^{1 / 3}$.
Theorem 7. [MZ19, Thm. 6] Given positive masses $m_{i}, i=1, \ldots, n$. Let $M=\sum_{i} m_{i}$. Assume that a normalized $C C_{n}$ satisfies $\left|q_{i}\right| \leqslant R$ for $i=1, \ldots, n$. Then

$$
r_{i j}>\frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{M R^{2}}, \quad 1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n
$$

### 4.2 Study of the limit of small masses going to zero

To study central configurations with several masses going to zero we need the notion of the restricted central configuration problem.

Definition 3. Let $Q_{N}^{m}=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{N}\right) \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)^{N}$ with masses $m=\left(m_{i}\right)_{i=1, \ldots, N}$. A potential $V_{\text {res }}$ for the restricted $(N+1)$-body problem induced by configuration $Q_{N}^{m}$ for $p \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ is defined by

$$
V_{\mathrm{res}}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, p\right)=\frac{p^{2}}{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i}}{\left|p-q_{i}\right|}
$$

Let $x^{*}$ be a solution of

$$
\frac{\partial V_{\mathrm{res}}}{\partial p}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, x^{*}\right)=0
$$

Then $x^{*}$ is called a relative normalized CC in the restricted $(N+1)$-body problem for the configuration $Q_{N}^{m}$ - in short $x^{*} \in \operatorname{RE}\left(Q_{N}^{m}\right)$.
The solution $x^{*}$ is called non-degenerate, if $\frac{\partial^{2} V_{\text {res }}}{\partial p^{2}}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, x^{*}\right)$ is an isomorphism ${ }^{1}$.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{1}$ Everywhere we write $\frac{\partial V_{\text {res }}}{\partial q_{i}}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, y\right)$ or $\frac{\partial V_{\text {res }}}{\partial p}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, x\right)$, we have in mind that the potential $V_{\text {res }}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, p\right)$ is a function of $N+1$ variables $\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}, p\right)$ and it means the derivative with respect to variables $q_{i}$ or $p$, respectively, at the point $\left(Q_{N}^{m}, x\right)$.

We are interested in the $(N+k)$-body problem, where there is $N$ heavy and $k$ light bodies. The meaning of the next theorem (Theorem 8) is as follows: in the central configuration the light bodies gather in several clusters around $x^{*} \in \operatorname{RE}\left(Q_{N}\right)$, i.e. solutions of (32) (see Fig. 2). The crosses indicate the possible positions of $x^{*} \in \operatorname{RE}\left(Q_{N}^{m}\right)$.

We use a parameter $\varepsilon$ to describe the behaviour of masses and positions with $\varepsilon$ tending to zero. For the masses, we assume that $\mu_{j} \rightarrow 0$ for $j=1, \ldots, k$ and the example we have in mind is $\mu_{j}=\varepsilon \tilde{\mu}_{j}$ with $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$ and $\tilde{\mu}_{j}$ being some positive constants. For $m_{i}(\varepsilon)$ we assume that they converge to some non-zero $\bar{m}_{i}$.
For the positions, we consider a normalized central configuration $\left(Q_{N}(\varepsilon), P_{k}(\varepsilon)\right)$ for the $(N+k)$-bodies with masses $m_{i}(\varepsilon)$ and $\mu_{j}(\varepsilon)$. From Theorem 6 it follows that we can find a subsequence of $\left\{\varepsilon_{s}\right\}_{s \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that the $\left(Q_{N}\left(\varepsilon_{s}\right), P_{k}\left(\varepsilon_{s}\right)\right)$ are converging to some limit. We want to investigate the nature of this limit.
Theorem 8. Let $\left(m_{1}(\varepsilon), \ldots, m_{N}(\varepsilon), \mu_{1}(\varepsilon), \ldots, \mu_{k}(\varepsilon)\right)$ are positive masses depending on parameter $\varepsilon$ (which might be discrete or continuous) and a sequence of normalized CC for these masses $\left(q_{1}(\varepsilon), \ldots, q_{N}(\varepsilon), p_{1}(\varepsilon), \ldots, p_{k}(\varepsilon)\right)$, such that for $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$ holds

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{i}(\varepsilon) & \rightarrow \bar{m}_{i}>0, \quad i=1, \ldots, N \\
\mu_{i}(\varepsilon) & \rightarrow 0, \quad i=1, \ldots, k \\
q_{i}(\varepsilon) & \rightarrow \bar{q}_{i}, \quad p_{j}(\varepsilon) \rightarrow \bar{p}_{j}, \quad i=1, \ldots, N \quad j=1, \ldots, k
\end{aligned}
$$

Then
(A) $\bar{Q}_{N}=\left(\bar{q}_{1}, \ldots, \bar{q}_{N}\right)$ is a normalized CC for masses $\left(\bar{m}_{1}, \ldots, \bar{m}_{N}\right)$,
(B) $\bar{p}_{j} \in \operatorname{RE}\left(\bar{Q}_{N}\right)$ for $j=1, \ldots, k$.

Proof. First define a pleiad $\mathcal{P}$ (of light bodies) - a set of indices of light bodies such that all bodies in the pleiad have the same limit point when $\varepsilon$ tends to 0 .
Note that a pleiad may contain one or several light bodies. For the pleiad $\mathcal{P}$ by $\bar{p}(\mathcal{P})$ we denote the corresponding limit point. Let us divide all light bodies into $n_{\mathrm{cl}}$ pleiades $\mathcal{P}_{i}$, with $i=1, \ldots, n_{\mathrm{cl}}$.
Since limit points of different pleiades are different and there is a finite number $n_{\mathrm{cl}}$ of these points, thus we can take $\delta_{\mathcal{P}}>0$ such that holds

$$
\left|\bar{p}\left(\mathcal{P}_{s}\right)-\bar{p}\left(\mathcal{P}_{t}\right)\right|>\delta_{\mathcal{P}}
$$

for all $s, t=1, \ldots, n_{\mathrm{cl}}, s \neq t$. Let us set

$$
\begin{aligned}
M(\varepsilon) & =\sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i}(\varepsilon)+\sum_{j=1}^{k} \mu_{j}(\varepsilon) \\
\bar{M} & =\lim _{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} M(\varepsilon)=\sum_{i=1}^{N} \lim _{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} m_{i}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{m}_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

Justification of the below facts constitutes the main part of the proof:
Lemma 9. Under the assumptions of Theorem 8, the limit configuration of heavy bodies does not contain any collision (i.e. $\exists r_{\mathrm{H}}>0:\left|\bar{q}_{i}-\bar{q}_{j}\right| \geq r_{\mathrm{H}}, \quad\left|q_{i}(\varepsilon)-q_{j}(\varepsilon)\right| \geq r_{\mathrm{H}}$ for $i, j=1, \ldots, N, i \neq j, \varepsilon \leq \varepsilon_{0}$ ).

Lemma 10. Under the assumptions of Theorem 8, the light bodies cannot converge to any of the heavy bodies, (i.e. $\exists r>0 \forall i, j:\left|\overline{q_{i}}-\overline{p_{j}}\right| \geq r>0$ ).

Proof. (of Lemma 9) First we show the existence of a lower bound for $r_{i j}(\varepsilon)=\left|q_{i}(\varepsilon)-q_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|, i, j=$ $1, \ldots, N$, i.e. a lower bound for mutual distances between the heavy bodies.
From Theorem 7 we have that the distance $r_{i j}(\varepsilon)$ between any pair of heavy bodies in CC has lower bound

$$
r_{i j}(\varepsilon)>\frac{m_{i}(\varepsilon) m_{j}(\varepsilon)}{M(\varepsilon) R(\varepsilon)^{2}}
$$

where $R(\varepsilon)=\max \left\{\max _{i=1, \ldots, N}\left|q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right|, \max _{j=1, \ldots, k}\left|p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|\right\}$. From Theorem 6 we know an upper bound on $R(\varepsilon)$

$$
R(\varepsilon) \leqslant M(\varepsilon)^{1 / 3}\left\{\begin{array}{cc}
N+k-1, & N+k \geqslant 2 \\
\left(2^{1 / 3}+2^{-2 / 3}\right)(N+k-2)^{2 / 3}, & N+k \geqslant 4
\end{array}\right.
$$

hence

$$
r_{i j}(\varepsilon)>\frac{m_{i}(\varepsilon) m_{j}(\varepsilon)}{M(\varepsilon)^{5 / 3}(N+k-1)^{2}}
$$

Passing to the limit $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$ in (40) we obtain

$$
\left|\bar{q}_{i}-\bar{q}_{j}\right| \geq \overline{m_{i}} \overline{m_{j}}\left(\bar{M}^{5 / 3}(N+k-1)^{2}\right)^{-1}, \quad i, j=1, \ldots, N, i \neq j
$$

This establishes the existence of $r_{\mathrm{H}}>0$ (subscript H is for heavy bodies ) and $\varepsilon_{0}>0$, such that

$$
\left|\bar{q}_{i}-\bar{q}_{j}\right| \geq r_{\mathrm{H}}, \quad\left|q_{i}(\varepsilon)-q_{j}(\varepsilon)\right| \geq r_{\mathrm{H}}, \quad i, j=1, \ldots, N, i \neq j, \varepsilon \leq \varepsilon_{0}
$$

This completes the proof of Lemma 9.
Proof. (of Lemma 10) We are going to show that the light bodies cannot converge to any of the heavy bodies. That means that there exists $r>0$, such that for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$

$$
\left|q_{i}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right| \geq r, \quad i=1, \ldots, N, \quad j=1, \ldots, n_{\mathrm{cl}}
$$

We know that $\lim _{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} q_{i}(\varepsilon)=\bar{q}_{i}$ and $\lim _{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} p_{j}(\varepsilon)=\bar{p}\left(\mathcal{P}_{j}\right)$, thus in fact we show that there exists $r>0$, such that

$$
\left|\bar{q}_{i}-\bar{p}\left(\mathcal{P}_{j}\right)\right| \geq r, \quad i=1, \ldots, N, \quad j=1, \ldots, n_{\mathrm{cl}}
$$

Since all light bodies in a pleiad converge to the same limit point, from (36) it follows that there exists $\varepsilon_{1}>0$ such that for all $s, t=1, \ldots, n_{\mathrm{cl}}, s \neq t$ holds

$$
\left|p_{j}(\varepsilon)-p_{l}(\varepsilon)\right| \geq \delta_{\mathcal{P}}, \quad j \in \mathcal{P}_{s}, l \in \mathcal{P}_{t}, \quad \varepsilon<\varepsilon_{1}
$$

i.e. we have a uniform positive lower bound for the distance between the light bodies in different pleiades. By contradiction, assume that for some $i_{0}$ and some pleiad $\mathcal{P}_{s}$ we have

$$
\left|\bar{q}_{i_{0}}-\bar{p}\left(\mathcal{P}_{s}\right)\right|=0
$$

Let us take

$$
r<\min \left\{r_{\mathrm{H}} \sqrt{m_{\min }\left(r_{\mathrm{H}}^{2} \bar{M}^{2 / 3}(N+k-1)+4 \bar{M}\right)^{-1}}, \frac{1}{2} r_{\mathrm{H}}\right\}
$$

where $m_{\min }=\min \left\{m_{i}: i=1, \ldots, N\right\}$.
For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ holds

$$
\left|q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right| \leq r, \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{P}_{s}
$$

Let us fix $\varepsilon<\min \left\{\varepsilon_{0}, \varepsilon_{1}\right\}$ satisfying (47). Let $j_{0} \in \mathcal{P}_{s}$ be such that

$$
\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right| \geq\left|p_{j}(\varepsilon)-q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right|, \quad j \in \mathcal{P}_{s}
$$

i.e. $p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)$ is the point in the pleiad $\mathcal{P}_{s}$ which is furthest away from $q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)$.

Consider now the direction connecting $p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)$ with $q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)$. Without loss of the generality, we can assume that the direction is the $x$-coordinate direction, i.e. $y\left(p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)=y\left(q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)$, where by $x(p), y(p)$ denote $x$ and $y$ components of $p \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$, respectively. In such situation the $x$-component of forces acting on $p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)$ coming from the heavy body $i_{0}$ and all other light bodies in the pleiad $\mathcal{P}_{s}$ have the same sign (see Fig. 3).


Figure 3: The $x$-component of forces acting on $p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)$ coming from the heavy body $i_{0}$ and all other light bodies $p$ in the pleiad $\mathcal{C}_{s}$ have the same sign; pleiades of light bodies are symbolically visualized by grey circles.
