Let us rewrite (2) with $\lambda=1$ for $x$-component of the equation corresponding $p_{j_{0}}$-th body. We group terms to highlight which terms are dominating and we take an absolute value of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left|\frac{m_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\left(x\left(p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)-x\left(q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)\right)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}+\sum_{j \in \mathcal{P}_{s}, j \neq j_{0}} \frac{\mu_{j}(\varepsilon)\left(x\left(p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)-x\left(p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right)\right)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}\right| \\
& =\left|\sum_{i \neq i_{0}, i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i}(\varepsilon)\left(x\left(p_{j_{0}}\right)-x\left(q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right)\right)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}+\sum_{j \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}} \frac{\mu_{j}(\varepsilon)\left(x\left(p_{j_{0}}\right)-x\left(p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right)\right)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}-x\left(p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)\right|
\end{aligned}
$$

We show that, if $r$ is small enough, lhs of (49) dominates rhs of (49). First, observe that the inequalities (50)-(52) are true (we precede each equation with a short proof).
Since our choice of $j_{0}$ is such that the expressions $x\left(p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)-x\left(q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)$ and $x\left(p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)-x\left(p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right)$ for $j \in \mathcal{P}_{s}$ have the same sign (see Fig. 3) we obtain

$$
\operatorname{lhs}(49) \geq\left|\frac{m_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\left(x\left(p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)-x\left(q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)\right)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}\right|=\frac{m_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right|^{2}} \geq \frac{m_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)}{r^{2}}
$$

hence

$$
\left|\frac{m_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\left(x\left(p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)-x\left(q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)\right)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}+\sum_{j \in \mathcal{P}_{s}, j \neq j_{0}} \frac{\mu_{j}(\varepsilon)\left(x\left(p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)-x\left(p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right)\right)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}\right| \geq \frac{m_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)}{r^{2}}
$$

By Lemma 9, conditions (47), (46)) and the triangle inequality there is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|\sum_{i \neq i_{0}, i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i}(\varepsilon)\left(x\left(p_{j_{0}}\right)-x\left(q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right)\right)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}\right| & \leq \sum_{i \neq i_{0}, i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i}(\varepsilon)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right|^{2}} \\
& \leq \sum_{i \neq i_{0}, i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i}(\varepsilon)}{\left(\left|q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)-q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right|-\left|q_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)-p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right|\right)^{2}} \\
& \leq \sum_{i \neq i_{0}, i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i}(\varepsilon)}{\left(r_{\mathrm{H}}-r\right)^{2}} \leq\left(\sum_{i \neq i_{0}, i=1}^{N} m_{i}(\varepsilon)\right) \frac{1}{\left(r_{\mathrm{H}} / 2\right)^{2}} \\
& \leq \frac{4 M(\varepsilon)}{r_{\mathrm{H}}^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

hence

$$
\left|\sum_{i \neq i_{0}, i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i}(\varepsilon)\left(x\left(p_{j_{0}}\right)-x\left(q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right)\right)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}\right| \leq \frac{4 M(\varepsilon)}{r_{\mathrm{H}}^{2}}
$$

By (44) we obtain

$$
\left|\sum_{j \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}} \frac{\mu_{j}(\varepsilon)\left(x\left(p_{j_{0}}\right)-x\left(p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right)\right)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}\right| \leq \sum_{j \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}} \frac{\mu_{j}(\varepsilon)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|^{2}} \leq \sum_{j \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}} \frac{\mu_{j}(\varepsilon)}{\delta_{P}^{2}} \leq\left(\sum_{j \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}} \mu_{j}(\varepsilon)\right) \frac{1}{\delta_{P}^{2}}
$$

hence

$$
\left|\sum_{j \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}} \frac{\mu_{j}(\varepsilon)\left(x\left(p_{j_{0}}\right)-x\left(p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right)\right)}{\left|p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}\right| \leq\left(\sum_{j \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}} \mu_{j}(\varepsilon)\right) \frac{1}{\delta_{P}^{2}}
$$

Finally, from Theorem 6 we have

$$
\left|x\left(p_{j_{0}}(\varepsilon)\right)\right| \leq M^{1 / 3}(\varepsilon) R(\varepsilon)
$$

Notice that by (50)-(53) we have

$$
\frac{m_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)}{r^{2}} \leq \operatorname{lhs}(49)=\operatorname{rhs}(49) \leq M^{1 / 3}(\varepsilon) R(\varepsilon)+\frac{4 M(\varepsilon)}{r_{\mathrm{H}}^{2}}+\left(\sum_{j \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}} \mu_{j}(\varepsilon)\right) \frac{1}{\delta_{P}^{2}}

hence

$$
r^{2} \geq m_{i_{0}}(\varepsilon)\left(M^{1 / 3}(\varepsilon) R(\varepsilon)+\frac{4 M(\varepsilon)}{r_{\mathrm{H}}^{2}}+\left(\sum_{j \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}} \mu_{j}(\varepsilon)\right) \frac{1}{\delta_{P}^{2}}\right)^{-1}
$$

Passing to the limit $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
r^{2} & \geq m_{\min }\left(\bar{M}^{2 / 3}(N+k-1)+\frac{4 \bar{M}}{r_{\mathrm{H}}^{2}}\right)^{-1} \\
& =m_{\min } r_{\mathrm{H}}^{2}\left(r_{\mathrm{H}}^{2} \bar{M}^{2 / 3}(N+k-1)+4 \bar{M}\right)^{-1}
\end{aligned}

Hence

$$
r \geq r_{\mathrm{H}} \sqrt{m_{\min }\left(r_{\mathrm{H}}^{2} \bar{M}^{2 / 3}(N+k-1)+4 \bar{M}\right)^{-1}}
$$

However, this contradicts (46), completing the proof of Lemma 10.
(A) Now we prove that $\left(\bar{q}_{1}, \ldots, \bar{q}_{N}\right)$ is a normalized CC for the $N$-body problem.

Let us rewrite (2) for $i=1, \ldots, N$ in the following way:

$$
q_{i}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{N} \frac{m_{j}(\varepsilon)\left(q_{i}(\varepsilon)-q_{j}(\varepsilon)\right)}{\left|q_{i}(\varepsilon)-q_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}+\sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{\mu_{j}(\varepsilon)\left(q_{i}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right)}{\left|q_{i}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}
$$

Lemmas 9 and 10 imply that when $\varepsilon$ tends to 0 , denominators in the above equations are bounded from below by some positive numbers. Hence we obtain

$$
\bar{q}_{i}=\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{N} \frac{\bar{m}_{j}\left(\bar{q}_{i}-\bar{q}_{j}\right)}{\left|\bar{q}_{i}-\bar{q}_{j}\right|^{3}}
$$

showing that $\bar{Q}_{N}$ is $\mathrm{CC}_{N}$ for masses $\bar{m}_{1}, \ldots, \bar{m}_{N}$. This completes the proof of part (A).
(B) It remains to prove that $\bar{p}_{j} \in \operatorname{RE}\left(\bar{Q}_{N}\right)$ for $j=1, \ldots, k$. Write equations (2) for the light bodies as follows

$$
\mu_{j} p_{j}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\mu_{j} m_{i}(\varepsilon)\left(p_{j}(\varepsilon)-q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right)}{\left|p_{j}(\varepsilon)-q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}+\sum_{i=1, i \neq j}^{k} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}(\varepsilon)\left(p_{j}(\varepsilon)-p_{i}(\varepsilon)\right)}{\left|q_{j}(\varepsilon)-p_{i}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}
$$

Let us take a pleiad $\mathcal{P}_{s}$. Bodies of that pleiad converge to $p^{*}=\bar{p}\left(\mathcal{P}_{s}\right)$, when $\varepsilon$ tends to 0 . Notice that for $\Theta(\varepsilon)=\sum_{j \in \mathcal{P}_{s}} \mu_{j}(\varepsilon)$

$$
c(\varepsilon)=\frac{1}{\Theta(\varepsilon)} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{P}_{s}} \mu_{j}(\varepsilon) p_{j}(\varepsilon)
$$

is a center of mass of $\mathcal{P}_{s}$ and $c(\varepsilon) \rightarrow p^{*}$. We add equations (55) for $j \in \mathcal{P}_{s}$ and divide by $\Theta(\varepsilon)$ to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
c(\varepsilon) & =\frac{1}{\Theta(\varepsilon)} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{P}_{s}} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\mu_{j}(\varepsilon) m_{i}(\varepsilon)\left(p_{j}(\varepsilon)-q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right)}{\left|p_{j}(\varepsilon)-q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}+\frac{1}{\Theta(\varepsilon)} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{P}_{s}} \sum_{\substack{i=1 \\
i \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}}}^{\substack{k \\
k}} \frac{\mu_{j}(\varepsilon) \mu_{i}(\varepsilon)\left(p_{j}(\varepsilon)-p_{i}(\varepsilon)\right)}{\left|p_{i}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}} \\

i \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}}}^{\substack{k \\
k}} \mu_{i}(\varepsilon) \sum_{j \in \mathcal{P}_{s}} \frac{\mu_{j}(\varepsilon)}{\Theta(\varepsilon)} \frac{\left(p_{j}(\varepsilon)-p_{i}(\varepsilon)\right)}{\left|p_{i}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

From Lemma 10 it follows that $p^{*} \neq \bar{q}_{i}$ and

$$
\frac{p_{j}(\varepsilon)-q_{i}(\varepsilon)}{\left|p_{j}(\varepsilon)-q_{i}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}} \rightarrow \frac{p^{*}-\bar{q}_{i}}{\left|p^{*}-\bar{q}_{i}\right|^{3}}
$$

and since by (36) $p^{*} \neq \bar{p}_{j}$ for $j \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}$ we have

$$
\frac{p_{i}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)}{\left|p_{i}(\varepsilon)-p_{j}(\varepsilon)\right|^{3}} \rightarrow \frac{p^{*}-\bar{p}_{j}}{\left|p^{*}-\bar{p}_{j}\right|^{3}}, \quad i \in \mathcal{P}_{s}, j \notin \mathcal{P}_{s}
$$

Taking this into account when passing to the limit $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$ in (56) we obtain

$$
p^{*}=\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\bar{m}_{i}\left(p^{*}-\bar{q}_{i}\right)}{\left|p^{*}-\bar{q}_{i}\right|^{3}}
$$

Therefore $p^{*}$ is a relative normalized central configuration for the restricted $(N+1)$-problem with the configuration $\bar{Q}_{N}$.
This completes the proof of part (B) and the proof of the whole theorem.

# 4.3 The shape of the pleiads of light bodies 

To better understand the behavior of pleiad of light bodies in the limit of vanishing masses, we investigate in more details the potential $V$ given in (3). First, we separate the interactions between bodies into three groups: heavy-heavy, heavy-light and light-light. Thus we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
V\left(Q_{N}, P_{k}\right)= & \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i} q_{i}^{2}}{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\left(\sum_{j=i+1}^{N} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|}\right) \\
& +\sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{\mu_{j} p_{j}^{2}}{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{m_{i} \mu_{j}}{\left|q_{i}-p_{j}\right|}\right) \\
& +\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\left(\sum_{j=i+1}^{k} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{\left|p_{i}-p_{j}\right|}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where heavy bodies are $Q_{N}=\left(q_{i}\right)_{i=1, \ldots, N}$ with masses $m=\left(m_{i}\right)_{i=1, \ldots, N}$ (hereinafter referred to as $Q_{N}^{m}$ ) and light bodies are $P_{k}=\left(p_{j}\right)_{j=1, \ldots, k}$ with masses $\mu=\left(\mu_{j}\right)_{j=1, \ldots, k}$ (hereinafter referred to as $P_{k}^{\mu}$ ).
Then (see Def. 3)

$$
V\left(Q_{N}^{m}, P_{k}^{\mu}\right)=V\left(Q_{N}^{m}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{k} \mu_{j} V_{\mathrm{res}}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, p_{j}\right)+\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq k} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{\left|p_{i}-p_{j}\right|}
$$

Let us denote

$$
W\left(Q_{N}^{m}, P_{k}^{\mu}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^{k} \mu_{j} V_{\mathrm{res}}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, p_{j}\right)+\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq k} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{\left|p_{i}-p_{j}\right|}
$$

thus

$$
V\left(Q_{N}^{m}, P_{k}^{\mu}\right)=V\left(Q_{N}^{m}\right)+W\left(Q_{N}^{m}, P_{k}^{\mu}\right)
$$

Now, equations (4) for CC become

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial V}{\partial q_{i}}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial q_{i}}\left(Q_{N}^{m}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{k} \mu_{j} \frac{\partial V_{\mathrm{res}}}{\partial q_{i}}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, p_{j}\right)=0, \quad \underline{i=1, \ldots, N} \\
& \frac{\partial V}{\partial p_{j}}=\frac{\partial W}{\partial p_{j}}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, P_{k}^{\mu}\right)=\mu_{j}\left(\frac{\partial V_{\mathrm{res}}}{\partial p}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, p_{j}\right)+\sum_{\substack{1 \leq i \leq k, i \neq j}} \frac{\mu_{i}\left(p_{j}-p_{i}\right)}{\left|p_{j}-p_{i}\right|^{3}}\right)=0, \quad \underline{j=1, \ldots, k}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let us focus on (59). We fix a $Q_{N}^{m}$. From Theorem 8 we expect that the light bodies will form pleiades (clusters) close to points belonging to $\operatorname{RE}\left(Q_{N}^{m}\right)$. Let us fix $x^{*} \in \operatorname{RE}\left(Q_{N}^{m}\right)$ and consider a cluster $P_{k}^{\mu}=$ $\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{k}\right)$ of $k$ light bodies around $x^{*}$, i.e. $p_{j} \approx x^{*}$ for $j=1, \ldots, k$. Since positions of heavy bodies are fixed, in the following part, we omit the argument $Q_{N}^{m}$ in $V_{\text {res }}$. We expand $V_{\text {res }}\left(p_{i}\right)$ into Taylor series at the point $x^{*}$ up to the second order term ${ }^{2}$ and by (32) we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
W\left(Q_{N}^{m}, P_{k}^{\mu}\right)= & \sum_{j=1}^{k} \mu_{j}\left(V_{\mathrm{res}}\left(x^{*}\right)+\frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p^{2}} V_{\mathrm{res}}\left(x^{*}\right)\left(p_{j}-x^{*}\right)^{2}+g\left(Q_{N}^{m}, x^{*}, p_{j}\right)\right) \\
& +\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq k} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{\left|p_{i}-p_{j}\right|}
\end{aligned}
$$

Definition 4. Let $Q_{N}^{m}=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}\right)$ with masses $m=\left(m_{i}\right)_{i=1, \ldots, N}$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$. Let $\mu=\left(\mu_{j}\right)_{j=1, \ldots, k}$ be some constant positive real numbers. The critical points of

$$
\widetilde{W}\left(x, Q_{N}^{m}, P_{k}^{\mu}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{\mu_{j}}{2} \frac{\partial^{2} V_{\mathrm{res}}}{\partial p^{2}}\left(Q_{N}, x\right)\left(p_{j}, p_{j}\right)+\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq k} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{\left|p_{i}-p_{j}\right|}
$$

with fixed $x, Q_{N}^{m}$, i.e. solutions $P_{k}=\left(p_{j}\right)_{j=1, \ldots, k}$ of

$$
\frac{\partial \widetilde{W}}{\partial p_{j}}\left(x, Q_{N}^{m}, P_{k}^{\mu}\right)=0, \quad \text { for } j=1, \ldots, k
$$

are called CC of potential $\widetilde{W}$ induced by $\left(Q_{N}^{m}, x\right)$ for $\mu$. We write $P_{k} \in C C\left(\widetilde{W}, Q_{N}^{m}, x\right)$ for $\mu$.

The following theorem is the main result in this section and the main motivation behind the notion of CC of potential $\widetilde{W}$ induced by $\left(Q_{N}^{m}, x\right)$. It can be seen as the generalization of the unstated explicitly result from , where case $k=2$ was considered in Section 2.

Theorem 11. Assume that

- $\hat{Q}_{N}^{m}=\left(\hat{q}_{1}, \ldots, \hat{q}_{N}\right)$ is a non-degenerate normalized CC with masses $m=\left(m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}\right)$,
- $x^{*} \in \operatorname{RE}\left(\hat{Q}_{N}^{m}\right)$ and $x^{*}$ is non-degenerate,
- $\hat{P}_{k}^{\widetilde{\mu}}=\left(\hat{p}_{1}, \ldots, \hat{p}_{k}\right)$ is a non-degenerate central configuration of potential $\widetilde{W}$ induced by $\left(\hat{Q}_{N}^{m}, x^{*}\right)$ for some positive real numbers $\widetilde{\mu}=\left(\widetilde{\mu}_{1}, \ldots, \widetilde{\mu}_{k}\right)$ and $\sum_{i} \widetilde{\mu}_{i}=1$.

Then, for sufficiently small $\Theta>0$, there exists a normalized non-degenerate central configuration:

$$
Q_{N+k}=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}, p_{1}, \ldots, p_{k}\right)
$$

with masses $m_{i}$, for $i=1, \ldots, N$ and $\mu_{j}=\Theta \widetilde{\mu}_{j}$, for $j=1, \ldots, k$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{i} & =\hat{q}_{i}+\mathcal{O}(\Theta) \\
p_{j} & =x^{*}+\Theta^{1 / 3} \hat{p}_{j}+\mathcal{O}\left(\Theta^{2 / 3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

We are given positions of $\hat{Q}_{N}^{m} \in \mathrm{CC}_{N}, x^{*} \in \operatorname{RE}\left(\hat{Q}_{N}^{m}\right)$ and $\hat{P}_{k}^{\widetilde{\mu}} \in \mathrm{CC}\left(\widetilde{W}, \hat{Q}_{N}^{m}, x^{*}\right)$ for $\widetilde{\mu}$ marked in black. Light red circles symbolize balls around $\hat{Q}_{N}^{m}$ and $x^{*}$. Dark red points indicate $\mathrm{CC}_{N+k}$.

Proof. In the proof we will use the implicit function theorem applied to reduced system in the sense defined in Section 3.2. In view of Theorem 3 we can assume that configuration $\hat{Q}_{N}^{m}$ is a solution of $\mathcal{R S}$ with $\hat{q}_{N}$ being computed by the center of mass condition, $\hat{q}_{N-1, y}=0, \hat{q}_{N-1, x} \neq \hat{q}_{N, x}$.
In the proof we use the notation introduced in (61), therefore from (58) and (64), it follows that a solution of the below system (66), with $\delta=\Theta^{1 / 3}$ as a parameter (to have analytic dependence on the parameter) and $q_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$, for $i=1, \ldots, N-2, q_{N-1, x} \in \mathbb{R}, x \in \mathbb{R}, \widetilde{p}_{j} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}, j=1, \ldots, k$ as variables to be solved for, gives rise to a solution of $\mathcal{R} \mathcal{S}$ for $(N+k)$-bodies with masses $m_{i}$ for $i=1, \ldots, N$ and $\mu_{j}=\Theta \widetilde{\mu}_{j}$ for $j=1, \ldots, k$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial V}{\partial q_{i}}\left(Q_{N}^{m}\right)+\Theta \sum_{j=1}^{k} \widetilde{\mu}_{j} \frac{\partial V_{\mathrm{res}}}{\partial q_{i}}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, p_{j}\left(\Theta, x, \widetilde{p}_{j}\right)\right) & =0, \quad \underline{i=1, \ldots, N-2} \\
\frac{\partial V}{\partial q_{N-1, x}}\left(Q_{N}^{m}\right)+\Theta \sum_{j=1}^{k} \widetilde{\mu}_{j} \frac{\partial V_{\mathrm{res}}}{\partial q_{N-1, x}}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, p_{j}\left(\Theta, x, \widetilde{p}_{j}\right)\right) & =0 \\
\frac{\partial V_{\mathrm{res}}}{\partial p}\left(Q_{N}^{m}, x\right) & =0 \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \widetilde{p}_{j}}\left(\widetilde{W}\left(x, Q_{N}^{m}, \widetilde{P}_{k}\right)+\Theta^{\frac{1}{3}} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \widetilde{\mu}_{i} g\left(Q_{N}^{m}, x, \widetilde{p}_{i}\right)\right) & =0, \quad \underline{j=1, \ldots, k}
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
q_{N}\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N-1}, p_{1}, \ldots, p_{j}\right)=-\frac{1}{m_{N}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} m_{i} q_{i}+\Theta \sum_{j=1} \hat{p}_{j} p_{j}\left(\Theta, x, \tilde{p}_{j}\right)\right)
$$

By the implicit function theorem ${ }^{3}$, we know that for sufficiently small $\delta>0$, the system (66) has unique, nondegenerate solution. These solutions are

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{i}(\delta) & =\hat{q}_{i}+\mathcal{O}\left(\delta^{3}\right) \\
x(\delta) & =x^{*}+\mathcal{O}\left(\delta^{3}\right) \\
\widetilde{p}_{j}(\delta) & =\hat{p}_{j}+\mathcal{O}(\delta)
\end{aligned}
$$

Written in terms of $\Theta$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{i}(\Theta) & =\hat{q}_{i}+\mathcal{O}(\Theta) \\
x(\Theta) & =x^{*}+\mathcal{O}(\Theta) \\
\widetilde{p}_{j}(\Theta) & =\hat{p}_{j}+\mathcal{O}\left(\Theta^{1 / 3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

From the above, (62) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{j}(\Theta) & =x(\Theta)+\Theta^{1 / 3} \widetilde{p}_{j}(\Theta) \\
& =\left(x^{*}+\mathcal{O}(\Theta)\right)+\Theta^{1 / 3}\left(\hat{p}_{j}+\mathcal{O}\left(\Theta^{1 / 3}\right)\right) \\
& =x^{*}+\Theta^{1 / 3} \tilde{p}_{j}+\mathcal{O}\left(\Theta^{2 / 3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Observe that

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{N-1}(\Theta)-x_{N}(\Theta) & =\hat{x}_{N-1}+\mathcal{O}(\Theta)-\left(\frac{1}{m_{N}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} m_{i} x_{i}+\Theta \sum_{j=1} \hat{p}_{j} p_{j, x}(\Theta)\right)\right) \\
& =\hat{x}_{N-1}-\hat{x}_{N}+\mathcal{O}(\Theta)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore for sufficiently small $\Theta$ from Theorem 2 it follows that our solution of $\mathcal{R S}$ is a normalized central configuration.
The configuration is non-degenerate by Theorem 5 , because it is a non-degenerate solution of $\mathcal{R S}$ and $x_{n-1} \neq x_{n}$.

# 5 The limit equation for light bodies, some a priori bounds 

In this section we start investigation of the critical points of the potential $\widetilde{W}\left(x^{*}, Q_{N}^{m}, P_{k}^{\mu}\right)$ with fixed $x^{*}$ and $Q_{N}^{m}$. Since we focus on the light bodies, we drop $\left(x^{*}, Q_{N}^{m}\right)$ and all tildes in notation. By a suitable rotation we diagonalize a quadratic form $\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p^{2}} V_{\text {res }}\left(Q_{N}, x^{*}\right)$, which becomes

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial q^{2}} V_{\mathrm{res}}\left(Q_{N}, x^{*}\right)((x, y),(x, y))=\frac{a x^{2}}{2}+\frac{b y^{2}}{2}
$$

\begin{array}{ll}
\mu_{i} a x_{i}=\sum_{j, j \neq i} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)}{r_{i j}^{3}}, & \forall i \in\{1, \ldots, k\} \\
\mu_{i} b y_{i}=\sum_{j, j \neq i} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}\left(y_{i}-y_{j}\right)}{r_{i j}^{3}}, & \forall i \in\{1, \ldots, k\}
\end{array}
$$

Observe also that for $a=b>0$ we obtain the problem normalized central configurations (with $a$ being an inverse of the gravitational constant). If $a \neq b$, then the rotational symmetry is broken, so system (71) can be seen as the central configuration problem in anisotropic space.

System of equations (71) has the same scaling properties as the system of equations (2), hence we can scale masses and variables $\left(x_{i}, y_{i}\right)$ so that $\sum_{i} \mu_{i}=1$ (this is our choice in CAP discussed later in the paper). We can also scale $a, b$ and variables $\left(x_{i}, y_{i}\right)$ to obtain $|a|=1$ (or $|b|=1$ ), hence only the ratio $\frac{a}{b}$ matters.

After adding equations (71) for $x_{i}$ 's and $y_{i}$ 's separately we obtain

$$
c=\sum_{i} \mu_{i} p_{i}=0
$$

We see that the center of mass for solutions for (71) is at the origin, just as in the case of $\mathrm{CC}_{N}$.

# 5.1 Moment of inertia-like quantities 

This is an adaptation of the well known identities for central configurations (see [MZ19, Sec. 2 and 3]) to the present context.

Lemma 12. Assume that

$$
M=\sum_{i} \mu_{i}=1
$$

For solutions of (71) hold

$$
\begin{aligned}
a\left(\sum_{i} \mu_{i} x_{i}^{2}\right) & =a\left(\sum_{i<j} \mu_{i} \mu_{j}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)^{2}\right)=\sum_{i<j} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)^{2} \\
b\left(\sum_{i} \mu_{i} y_{i}^{2}\right) & =b\left(\sum_{i<j} \mu_{i} \mu_{j}\left(y_{i}-y_{j}\right)^{2}\right)=\sum_{i<j} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}\left(y_{i}-y_{j}\right)^{2} \\
a\left(\sum_{i} \mu_{i} x_{i}^{2}\right) & +b\left(\sum_{i} \mu_{i} y_{i}^{2}\right)=\sum_{i<j} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{r_{i j}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Proof. See Appendix A.1.

Since the rightmost expressions in $(74 \mathrm{a}, 74 \mathrm{~b})$ are positive we immediately obtain the following conclusion.
Conclusion 13. The number of solutions of (71) is:

- If $a, b \leq 0$, then there are no solutions.
- If $a \leq 0$ and $b>0$, then all solutions are on the $y$ axis $\left(\forall i: x_{i}=0\right)$. By the Moulton's Theorem (see ), there are $k$ ! solutions, one for each ordering of the bodies on the $y$ axis.
- If $a>0$ and $b \leq 0$, then all solutions are on the $x$ axis $\left(\forall i: y_{i}=0\right)$. By the Moulton's Theorem (see ) there are $k$ ! solutions, one for each ordering of the bodies on the $x$ axis.

Thus the only non-trivial case is $a, b>0$. In this case, from the Moulton Theorem, we also have collinear solutions on $x$ and $y$ axes.

# 5.2 Lower bound for the distance between bodies 

Just like in from the Lemma 12 we derive the lower bound for $r_{i j}$ provided that we have an upper bound for $I=\sum_{i} \mu_{i} r_{i}^{2}$.
Lemma 14. Assume (73) and $a, b>0$. If $P_{k}^{\mu}$ is a solution of (71), then for any bodies $p_{i}, p_{j}$ in $P_{k}^{\mu}$

$$
r_{i j} \geq \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{\max \{a, b\} R^{2}}
$$

where $R=\max _{i}\left|p_{i}\right|$.
Proof. See Appendix A. 2

### 5.3 Upper bound for the size

This is an adaptation of the upper bound on the size of the normalized central configurations from [MZ19, Sec. 3.2] recalled in the present paper as Theorem 6.
From Conclusion 13 it follows we cannot have both $a \leq 0$ and $b \leq 0$, hence we assume $a>0$ or $b>0$.
Theorem 15. Assume that $a>0$ or $b>0$. Assume $P_{k}^{\mu}$ is a solution of (71) and $M=\sum_{i} \mu_{i}$. If $a>0$, then

$$
\max _{i}\left|x_{i}\right| \leqslant \begin{cases}(n-1)\left(\frac{M}{a}\right)^{1 / 3}, & n \geqslant 2 \\ \left(2^{1 / 3}+2^{-2 / 3}\right)(n-2)^{2 / 3}\left(\frac{M}{a}\right)^{1 / 3}, & n \geqslant 4\end{cases}
$$

and if $b>0$, then

$$
\max _{i}\left|y_{i}\right| \leqslant \begin{cases}(n-1)\left(\frac{M}{b}\right)^{1 / 3}, & n \geqslant 2 \\ \left(2^{1 / 3}+2^{-2 / 3}\right)(n-2)^{2 / 3}\left(\frac{M}{b}\right)^{1 / 3}, & n \geqslant 4\end{cases}
$$

Proof. See Appendix A. 3

## 6 Analytical solutions for CCs in anisotropic plane

### 6.1 Collinear solutions

As it was noticed at the end of Subsection 5.1, by the Moulton Theorem , there are $k$ ! collinear solutions on both $x$ and $y$ axes. The next theorem states that if $a \neq b$ there are no other collinear solutions.

Theorem 16. Assume that $\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{k}\right)$ is collinear $C C$ for the restricted problem (71) with $a \neq b$. Then either $x_{i}=0$ for all $i=1, \ldots, n$, or $y_{i}=0$ for all $i=1, \ldots, n$.

Proof. See Appendix A.4.
6.2 $k=2$

For $k=2$ all the solutions are collinear and contained in coordinate axes.

# 6.3 $k=3$ with equal masses 

For $k=3$ by the Moulton Theorem we have $2 \cdot 3$ ! collinear solutions contained in coordinate axes.
It appears that there exists only one type of non-collinear solutions described in the next subsection. The computer assisted proof reported in Section 7.4 confirms this for a particular values $a=3 / 4$ and $b=9 / 4$.

### 6.3.1 The isosceles triangle

Theorem 17. Assume that $a, b>0$ and $\mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=\mu_{3}=\mu$ and

$$
\frac{b}{a}>\frac{5}{12}
$$

Then there exists a solution of (71) which forms an isosceles triangle symmetric with respect to the $x$ axis. Moreover, if we denote by $s$ the side and by $r$ the base of the triangle, then

- $s=\left(\frac{3 \mu}{a}\right)^{1 / 3}$
- $r=\left(\frac{2 \mu}{b-\frac{a}{3}}\right)^{1 / 3}$.

Proof. See Appendix A.5.
The geometry of the triangle is given by

$$
\frac{s}{r}=\left(\frac{3}{2} \frac{b-\frac{a}{3}}{a}\right)^{1 / 3}=\left(\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{b}{a}-\frac{1}{3}\right)\right)^{1 / 3}
$$

From Theorem 17 we obtain two isosceles triangles: one is obtained from the other by the reflection with respect to the $y$ axis. If $\frac{12}{5}>\frac{b}{a}>\frac{5}{12}$ then from Theorem 17 follows that we have two isosceles triangles with the reflectional symmetry with respect to the $x$ axis and two other isosceles triangles with the reflectional symmetry with respect to the $y$ axis (see Figure 5). For $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{5}{12}$ the isosceles triangle becomes singular and becomes the collinear solution on the the $y$ axis.



Figure 5: Orientations of isosceles triangles: two black for $b / a>5 / 12$ and two red for $a / b>5 / 12$.

# $6.4 \quad k=4$ with equal masses 

For $k=4$ by the Moulton Theorem we have $2 \cdot 4$ ! collinear solutions contained in coordinate axes. From Theorem 16 we see that there are no other collinear solutions.
We can analytically prove the existence of two types of non-collinear solutions for equal mass case: a rhombus and a rectangle, both symmetrical with respect to $x$ and $y$ axes. There exist other types of solutions, see Section 7.4.2 for the computer assisted proof of full list for equal mass case and $a=3 / 4$ and $b=9 / 4$.

### 6.4.1 Rhombus

Theorem 18. Assume $a, b>0$. Assume that $\sum_{i=1}^{4} \mu_{i}=1$ and $\mu_{i}=\mu$ for $i=1,2,3,4$. Then there exists a solution of (71) which forms a rhombus (consisting from points $( \pm x, 0),(0, \pm y)$, for some positive $x, y$ ) symmetrical with respect to $x$ and $y$ axes. Moreover, if we denote by $k=\frac{9}{x}$ the ratio of diagonals and by $r$ the length of the sides, then

- $k$ is a unique solution to

$$
\frac{8 k^{3}+\left(k \sqrt{1+k^{2}}\right)^{3}}{8 k^{3}+\left(\sqrt{1+k^{2}}\right)^{3}}=\frac{a}{b}
$$

- $r>\left(\frac{9 \mu}{4 \min \{a, b\}}\right)^{1 / 3}$
- in the above range, $r$ is a unique solution to

$$
\left(\frac{2 \mu}{a r^{3}-2 \mu}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}+\left(\frac{2 \mu}{b r^{3}-2 \mu}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}=4
$$

Proof. See Appendix A.6.

### 6.4.2 Rectangle

Theorem 19. Assume $a, b>0$. Assume that $\sum_{i=1}^{4} \mu_{i}=1$ and $\mu_{i}=\mu$ for $i=1,2,3,4$. Then there exists solution of (71) which forms a rectangle (consisting of points of the form $( \pm x, \pm y)$ for some positive $x, y$ ) symmetrical with respect to $x$ and $y$ axes. Moreover, if we denote by $d=2 r$ the diagonal and by $\varphi$ the angle between diagonal and the $x$ axis, then

- $\varphi$ is a unique solution to

$$
\tan ^{3}(\varphi) \frac{\cos ^{3}(\varphi)+1}{\sin ^{3}(\varphi)+1}=\frac{a}{b}
$$

- $r>\left(\frac{\mu}{2 \min \{a, b\}}\right)^{1 / 3}$
- in the above range, $r$ is a unique solution to

$$
\left(\frac{\mu}{4 a r^{3}-\mu}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}+\left(\frac{\mu}{4 b r^{3}-\mu}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}=1
$$

Proof. See Appendix A.7.

# 7 Computer assisted results for CCs with heavy and light bodies and corresponding problems in anisotropic plane 

In this section we discuss and compare results obtained from two programs, first is the program for central configurations (PGU) described in  and the second program (PHU), which solves the problem defined in Section 5 .

### 7.1 PGU - about the program

The program for rigorous computations of all CC for N -body problem for fixed set of masses $m_{i}$ is described in . The program, if successful, returns all central configurations. It solves rigorously the reduced system $\mathcal{R S}$ (discussed in Section 3.2) and the necessary condition for the program to succeed is that all solutions of $\mathcal{R S}$ are non-degenerate.
On input, the program accepts a box in the configuration space of the reduced system $\mathcal{R S}$ and then uses binary subdivision to produce boxes (covering the initial box) which satisfy one of the following conditions:
(C1) there is no solution in a box
(C2) there is exactly one solution (non-degenerate) in a box
(C3) cannot decide rigorously if (C1) or (C2) is satisfied and the size of the box is below some threshold
The program always stops. If there are no undecided boxes, i.e. satisfying (C3), then we know that all normalized central configuration are in boxes satisfying (C2).

### 7.2 PHU - about the program

PHU looks for all solutions of system of equations (71) for given $a, b$ and masses $\mu_{i}>0$ such that $\sum \mu_{i}=1$. This allows us to obtain $\operatorname{rbp}(k, a, b)$ with the coefficients $a, b$ (see Section 5).
The basic idea of the program is the same as in the case of PGU: for a given initial box we use the binary subdivision algorithm to produce a set of boxes satisfying conditions (C1)-(C3) and covering the initial box. The initial box was chosen to contain all possible solutions according to the upper bound on the size of solution from Theorem 15. If it turns out that there are no boxes satisfying (C3), then we obtained all solutions of system of equations (71) and all solutions are non-degenerate.
In the program we use the following tests:

- using the Krawczyk operator (discussed in ) we can: decide that a box satisfies (C1) or (C2) or we can reduce the size of the box
- for boxes containing pairs of close bodies we check the condition from Lemma 14, where we obtained lower bound for the distance between bodies. This test allows us to remove boxes with very close bodies during the binary subdivision process.


# 7.3 Two heavy and $k$-light bodies 

We perform our computations for $(2+k)$-problem with $k=3,4$. We are interested in the neighborhood of relative equilibria in the restricted 3-body problem. It is well known (see for example ) that in the restricted 3-body problem we have five relative equilibria: three collinear with the primaries (called $L_{1}, L_{2}, L_{3}$ ) and two triangular ones denoted by $L_{4}$ and $L_{5}$, which form an equilateral triangle with the primaries. $L_{4}$ and $L_{5}$ are mutually symmetric with respect to the line passing through the primaries. $L_{4}$ and $L_{5}$ are mutually symmetric with respect to the line passing through the primaries. See Figure 6.

Two heavy bodies (primaries) are depicted as black dots. Light bodies (red) at the Lagrange points $\left(L_{1}, \ldots, L_{5}\right)$ are in equilibrium.

It turns out that for collinear relative equilibria $L_{i}, i=1,2,3$ we have $a>0$ and $b<0$, which in view of Conclusion 13 makes the $\operatorname{rbp}(k, a, b)$ problem not interesting. We focus on $L_{4}$ (for $L_{5}$ the situation is symmetric). In Lemma 22 we computed values of $a$ and $b$ for the equal masses case. These are

$$
a=\frac{3}{4}, \quad b=\frac{9}{4}
$$

We will use them in the computations PHU computations reported below. For PHU computations we assume that we have

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k} \mu_{i}=1, \quad \mu_{i}=\frac{1}{k}
$$

In this paper we run PGU with two heavy masses close to $1 / 2$ and $k$-light bodies with small masses, for $k=3,4$. The heavy masses are located close to $( \pm 0.5,0)$ and the light bodies were located in box around $L_{4}$ (see Appendix A.8).
We refer to the notation introduced in Section 3.2 and we obtain $\mathcal{R S}$ in the following way. First, we set $n=N+k$. Then we order bodies: $\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{k}\right)$ are light bodies, $q_{k+1}=q_{n-1}$ and $q_{k+2}=q_{n}$ are heavy bodies. We set $k_{1}=n-1$, this means that one heavy body is placed on the $x$ axis and the second one is computed from the center of mass condition (11b).

### 7.3.1 A comparison of PGU and PHU

By Theorem 11 we know that the non-degenerate relative equilibria of a restricted $(N+1)$-body problem combined with non-degenerate solutions for $k$ bodies in the $W$-potential can be extended to solutions of $Q_{N+k}$ central configuration problem. In the future work we hope do rigorously this continuation, so

that we will have a rigorous result for central configuration for an explicit range of small masses from zero up to some macroscopic quantity, from which cc could be continued using other tools, like Krawczyk operator.
However, for a present moment, we will just compare the results from both programs. For this end we identify solutions from PHU with those from PGU as follows.
Following the coordinate change from Theorem 11 (see (61b, 61c)) for solutions of PGU we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tilde{p_{i}}=\frac{p_{i}-c}{\Theta^{1 / 3}} \\
& \tilde{\mu_{i}}=\frac{\mu_{i}}{\Theta}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\tilde{p_{i}}$ are normalized coordinates $p_{i}$ of small bodies obtained by PGU, $\mu_{i}$ - masses of small bodies before normalization, $\Theta=\sum \mu_{i}$ and $c$ is a center of masses $\mu_{i}$.
Observe that in (61c) we have $x^{*}$ while in (85a) we have $c$ - the center of masses of light bodies. However from Theorem 11 it follows that

$$
c=x^{*}+\mathcal{O}\left(\Theta^{2 / 3}\right)
$$

The obtained values $\tilde{p}_{i}$ are then compared to those from PHU. The agreement is quite satisfactory for the values of masses considered, thus supporting our hope for the possibility of rigorous continuation.
In our discussion below we give approximate values, in fact we use midpoints of exact bounds obtained by our programs. The width of those bounds are very small, therefore it makes sense to using midpoints in comparison. For exact bounds refer to report files attached in the Appendix ??.
Below, we also present demonstrative pictures of solutions. Pictures are created in Mathematica  with midpoints of the intervals bounding the soultion. Labels of bodies in $a b$-potential are colored blue, in $(2+k)$-body problem - red. The role of ordering and colors of bodies is only to illustrate the compatibility of solutions.

# A Technical proofs omitted in the main paper 

## A. 1 Proof of Lemma 12

We show the identity (74a) - the proof of (74b) is analogous.

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{i}^{2} & =x_{i}\left(x_{i}-\sum_{j} \mu_{j} x_{j}\right) & & \text { (since (72) implies } \sum_{i} \mu_{i} x_{i}=0 \text { ) } \\
& =x_{i}\left(x_{i} \sum_{j} \mu_{j}-\sum_{j} \mu_{j} x_{j}\right) & & \text { (use (73)) } \\
& =x_{i}\left(\sum_{j} \mu_{j}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)\right) & &
\end{aligned}
$$

Now we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i} \mu_{i} x_{i}^{2} & =\sum_{i} \sum_{j} \mu_{i} \mu_{j}\left(x_{i}^{2}-x_{i} x_{j}\right) \\
& =\sum_{i<j} \mu_{i} \mu_{j}\left(x_{i}^{2}-2 x_{i} x_{j}+x_{j}^{2}\right) \\
& =\sum_{i<j} \mu_{i} \mu_{j}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i} \mu_{i} n x_{i}^{2} & =\sum_{i} \sum_{j, j \neq i} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right) x_{i}}{r_{i j}^{3}} \\
& =\sum_{i<j} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

From (74a, 74b) the equation (74c) is obvious:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a\left(\sum_{i} \mu_{i} x_{i}^{2}\right)+b\left(\sum_{i} \mu_{i} y_{i}^{2}\right) & =\sum_{i<j} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)^{2}+\sum_{i<j} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}\left(y_{i}-y_{j}\right)^{2} \\
& =\sum_{i<j} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{r_{i j}}
\end{aligned}
$$

# A. 2 Proof of Lemma 14 

From Lemma 12 we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \left\{a, b\right\} \sum_{i} \mu_{i}\left(x_{i}^{2}+y_{i}^{2}\right) & \geq a\left(\sum_{i} \mu_{i} x_{i}^{2}\right)+b\left(\sum_{i} \mu_{i} y_{i}^{2}\right) \\
& =\sum_{i<j} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{r_{i j}}>\frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{r_{i j}}
\end{aligned}
$$

From the above using (73) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_{i j} & >\frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{\max \left\{a, b\right\} \sum_{i} \mu_{i}\left(x_{i}^{2}+y_{i}^{2}\right)} \\
& >\frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{\max \{a, b\} R^{2} \sum_{i} \mu_{i}} \\
& =\frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{\max \{a, b\} R^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

## A. 3 Proof of Theorem 15

For the proof of Theorem 15 we will need the following result.
Lemma 20. Let

$$
M=\sum_{i} \mu_{i}
$$

Assume that $a>0$ or $b>0$. Assume $P_{k}^{\mu}$ is a solution of (71). Let $R=\left|x_{i_{0}}\right|=\max _{i}\left|x_{i}\right|$. If $a>0$, then for all $\varepsilon \in(0, R /(n-1))$ holds

$$
R-(n-2) \varepsilon<\frac{M}{a \varepsilon^{2}}
$$

Analogously, let $R=\left|y_{i_{0}}\right|=\max _{i}\left|y_{i}\right|$. If $b>0$, then for all $\varepsilon \in(0, R /(n-1))$ holds

$$
R-(n-2) \varepsilon<\frac{M}{b \varepsilon^{2}}
$$

Proof. Let us fix any $\varepsilon \in(0, R /(n-1))$. We can assume that

$$
p_{i_{0}}=\left(R, y_{i_{0}}\right)
$$

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a minimal subset (cluster) of indices of bodies satisfying the following conditions

- $i_{0} \in \mathcal{C}$

- if $j \in \mathcal{C}$ and $\left|p_{k}-p_{j}\right| \leqslant \varepsilon$, then $k \in \mathcal{C}$

The cluster $\mathcal{C}$ can be constructed as follows: We start with $i_{0} \in \mathcal{C}$. Then we add all bodies which are not farther than $\varepsilon$ from the bodies already in $\mathcal{C}$. We repeat this until the set $\mathcal{C}$ stabilizes, which happens after at most $n-1$ steps. From assumption about $\varepsilon$ and $R$ it follows that

$$
R>(n-1) \varepsilon
$$

Observe that (91) implies that $\mathcal{C} \neq\{1, \ldots, n\}$. Indeed (91) and (90) imply that $x_{i}>0$ for all $i \in \mathcal{C}$. This and the center of mass condition (72) implies that $\mathcal{C}$ cannot contain all bodies. This implies that the process of building $\mathcal{C}$ must stop after at most $n-2$ steps. Therefore we obtained a cluster $\mathcal{C}$ with the following properties

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{i} & \in \overline{B\left(p_{i_{0}},(n-2) \varepsilon\right)}, \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{C} \\
\left|p_{i}-p_{j}\right| & >\varepsilon, \quad i \in \mathcal{C}, j \notin \mathcal{C}
\end{aligned}
$$

$R>(n-1) \varepsilon$ and $r=(n-2) \varepsilon$; the darkened area is the region where all the bodies from cluster are located.

Note that

$$
\sum_{\substack{i, j \in \mathcal{C} \\ i \neq j}} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)=0
$$

thus by adding equations for $x$ 's in (71) for $i \in \mathcal{C}$ we obtain

$$
a \sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}} \mu_{i} x_{i}=\sum_{\substack{i, j \in \mathcal{C} \\ i \neq j}} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)}{r_{i j}^{3}}+\sum_{\substack{i \in \mathcal{C} \\ j \notin \mathcal{C}}} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)}{r_{i j}^{3}}
$$

Let

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{\mathcal{C}} & =\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}} \mu_{i} \\
c_{\mathcal{C}} & =\frac{1}{\mu_{\mathcal{C}}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}} \mu_{i} x_{i} \\
F_{\mathcal{C}} & =\frac{1}{\mu_{\mathcal{C}}} \sum_{\substack{i \in \mathcal{C} \\
j \notin \mathcal{C}}} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)}{r_{i j}^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Observe that (94) could be now rewritten as

$$
a \cdot c_{\mathcal{C}}=F_{\mathcal{C}}
$$

It is easy to see (cf. (92)) that for $i \in \mathcal{C}$ : $x_{i} \geqslant R-(n-2) \varepsilon>0$, hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|c_{\mathcal{C}}\right| & =\frac{1}{\mu_{\mathcal{C}}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}} \mu_{i} x_{i} \\
& \geqslant R-(n-2) \varepsilon
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|F_{\mathcal{C}}\right| & \leqslant \frac{1}{\mu_{\mathcal{C}}} \sum_{\substack{i \in \mathcal{C} \\
j \notin \mathcal{C}}} \frac{\mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{r_{i j}^{2}} \leqslant \frac{1}{\varepsilon^{2}} \frac{1}{\mu_{\mathcal{C}}} \sum_{\substack{i \in \mathcal{C} \\
j \notin \mathcal{C}}} \mu_{i} \mu_{j} \\
& =\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{2}} \frac{1}{\mu_{\mathcal{C}}}\left(\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}} \mu_{i}\right) \cdot\left(\sum_{j \notin \mathcal{C}} \mu_{j}\right)=\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{2}} \sum_{j \notin \mathcal{C}} \mu_{j}<\frac{M}{\varepsilon^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence from the above and (95) we obtain

$$
a(R-(n-2) \varepsilon) \leqslant\left|a \cdot c_{\mathcal{C}}\right|=\left|F_{\mathcal{C}}\right|<\frac{M}{\varepsilon^{2}}
$$

This completes the proof of (88). The proof of (89) is analogous.

Proof of Theorem 15 We focus on the estimate on $R=\max _{i}\left|x_{i}\right|$. From Lemma 20 we have the following implication for any $\varepsilon$ :

$$
\text { if }(n-1) \varepsilon<R \text {, then } R<(n-2) \varepsilon+\frac{M}{a \varepsilon^{2}}
$$

Therefore

$$
R \leq g(\varepsilon):=\max \left((n-1) \varepsilon,(n-2) \varepsilon+\frac{M}{a \varepsilon^{2}}\right)
$$

We look for minimum of $g(\varepsilon)$. It is easy to see that

$$
\begin{aligned}
g(\varepsilon) & =(n-1) \varepsilon, \quad \text { for } \varepsilon \geq\left(\frac{M}{a}\right)^{1 / 3} \\
g(\varepsilon) & =g_{2}(\varepsilon):=(n-2) \varepsilon+\frac{M}{a \varepsilon^{2}}, \quad \text { for } \varepsilon \leq\left(\frac{M}{a}\right)^{1 / 3}
\end{aligned}
$$

The function $g_{2}(\varepsilon)$ has a global minimum at $\varepsilon_{0}=\left(\frac{2 M}{(n-2) a}\right)^{1 / 3}$ and

$$
g\left(\varepsilon_{0}\right)=\left(\frac{M}{a}\right)^{1 / 3}\left(2^{1 / 3}+2^{-2 / 3}\right)(n-2)^{2 / 3}
$$

Now $\varepsilon_{0} \leq\left(\frac{M}{a}\right)^{1 / 3}$ iff $n \geq 4$, therefore

$$
\begin{gathered}
\min g(\varepsilon)=(n-1)\left(\frac{M}{a}\right)^{1 / 3}, \quad \text { for } n \geq 2 \\
\min g(\varepsilon)=\left(\frac{M}{a}\right)^{1 / 3}\left(2^{1 / 3}+2^{-2 / 3}\right)(n-2)^{2 / 3}, \quad \text { for } n \geq 4
\end{gathered}
$$

# A. 4 Proof of Theorem 16 

We divide by $\mu_{i}$ the equations (71) and take differences for $x_{i}$ 's and $y_{i}$ 's separately. Then we obtain system (71) written in matrix form as

$$
A\left[\begin{array}{c}
x_{1}-x_{2} \\
x_{2}-x_{3} \\
\cdots \\
x_{k-1}-x_{k}
\end{array}\right]=a\left[\begin{array}{c}
x_{1}-x_{2} \\
x_{2}-x_{3} \\
\cdots \\
x_{k-1}-x_{k}
\end{array}\right] \quad \text { and } \quad A\left[\begin{array}{c}
y_{1}-y_{2} \\
y_{2}-y_{3} \\
\cdots \\
y_{k-1}-y_{k}
\end{array}\right]=b\left[\begin{array}{c}
y_{1}-y_{2} \\
y_{2}-y_{3} \\
\cdots \\
y_{k-1}-y_{k}
\end{array}\right]
$$

where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{(k-1) \times(k-1)}$ is matrix with

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{i j}= & -\delta_{i j}-\chi_{[1, i-1]}(j)\left(\sum_{t=1}^{j} \frac{\mu_{t}}{r_{i t}^{3}}\right)+\chi_{[i, n-1]}(j)\left(\sum_{t=j+1}^{k} \frac{\mu_{t}}{r_{i t}^{3}}\right) \\
& +\chi_{}(j)\left(\sum_{t=1}^{j} \frac{\mu_{t}}{r_{i+1 t}^{3}}\right)-\chi_{[i+1, n-1]}(j)\left(\sum_{t=j+1}^{k} \frac{\mu_{t}}{r_{i+1 t}^{3}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\delta_{i j}$ is Kronecker delta and $\chi_{}$ is the characteristic function of the interval $$, i.e.

$$
\chi_{}(j)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
1, & l \leq j \leq p \\
0, & \text { otherwise }
\end{array}\right.
$$

For example, matrix $A$ for $k=3$ is:

$$
A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\frac{\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}}{r_{12}^{2}}+\frac{\mu_{3}}{r_{13}^{2}}, & \mu_{3}\left(\frac{1}{r_{12}^{2}}-\frac{1}{r_{23}^{2}}\right) \\
\mu_{1}\left(\frac{1}{r_{13}^{2}}-\frac{1}{r_{12}^{2}}\right), & \frac{\mu_{2}+\mu_{3}}{r_{23}^{2}}+\frac{\mu_{1}}{r_{13}^{2}}
\end{array}\right]
$$

Observe from (97) we see that for any solution of (71) the $x$-differences and $y$-differences are eigenvectors of $A$ of different eigenvalues $a, b$, respectively or are zero. This with collinearity assumption implies that the solution must be on the coordinate axis. The precise argument goes as follows.
From collinearity it follows that there exist $\lambda_{i} \neq 0, i=2, \ldots, k-1$ such that

$$
\left[x_{i}-x_{i+1}, y_{i}-y_{i+1}\right]=\lambda_{i}\left[x_{1}-x_{2}, y_{1}-y_{2}\right]
$$

For the proof it is enough to show that $x_{1}-x_{2}=0$ or $y_{1}-y_{2}=0$.
We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
{\left[x_{1}-x_{2}, x_{2}-x_{3}, \ldots, x_{k-1}-x_{k}\right] } & =\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)\left[1, \lambda_{2}, \ldots, \lambda_{k-1}\right] \\
{\left[y_{1}-y_{2}, y_{2}-y_{3}, \ldots, y_{k-1}-y_{k}\right] } & =\left(y_{1}-y_{2}\right)\left[1, \lambda_{2}, \ldots, \lambda_{k-1}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Let

$$
\Lambda=\left[1, \lambda_{2}, \ldots, \lambda_{k-1}\right]^{t}
$$

thus we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
A\left(\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right) \Lambda\right)=a\left(\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right) \Lambda\right) \\
A\left(\left(y_{1}-y_{2}\right) \Lambda\right)=b\left(\left(y_{1}-y_{2}\right) \Lambda\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

Since $a \neq b$, then either $x_{1}-x_{2}=0$ or $y_{1}-y_{2}$. Hence we obtain our conclusion.

# A. 5 Proof of Theorem 17 

Since we are looking for an isosceles triangle symmetrical with respect to the $x$ axis and since the center of mass is at the origin, we can assume that

$$
p_{1}=(x, 0), \quad p_{2}=\left(-\frac{x}{2}, y\right), \quad p_{3}=\left(-\frac{x}{2},-y\right)
$$

where $x \neq 0$ and $y \neq 0$, since the solution cannot be collinear. Without loss of generality, assume $x, y>0$.
A sample isosceles triangle with $x, y>0$.
Then we have

$$
r=r_{23}=2 y, \quad s=r_{12}=r_{13}=\sqrt{\frac{9 x^{2}}{4}+y^{2}}
$$

From the above, it is easy to see that the system (71) can be reduced to

$$
\begin{aligned}
a x & =\frac{3 \mu x}{r_{12}^{3}} \\
b y & =\frac{\mu y}{r_{12}^{3}}+\frac{2 \mu y}{r_{23}^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $x \neq 0$ and $y \neq 0$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
a & =\frac{3 \mu}{r_{12}^{3}} \\
b & =\frac{\mu}{r_{12}^{3}}+\frac{2 \mu}{r_{23}^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_{12}^{3} & =\frac{3 \mu}{a} \\
r_{23}^{3} & =\frac{2 \mu}{b-\frac{a}{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

For the equation (100b) to make sense, the denominator must be positive $\left(r=r_{23}>0\right)$, thus

$$
b>\frac{a}{3}
$$

Note that (101) is compatibile with the assumtion (78). From (98) we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{3} & =\frac{\mu}{4\left(b-\frac{a}{3}\right)} \\
x^{2} & =\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{2}\left(r_{12}^{2}-y^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

To have a real solution, we demand $r_{12}^{2}-y^{2}>0$, which implies (78).

# A. 6 Proof of Theorem 18 

Assume that the rhombus is as on the figure below:

$$
p_{1}=(x, 0) \quad p_{2}=(0, y) \quad p_{3}=(-x, 0) \quad p_{4}=(0,-y)
$$

where $x>0$ and $y>0$. Ratio of diagonals is $k=y / x>0$.

It is easy to see that the system (71) can be reduced to the following two equations

$$
\begin{aligned}
a & =\mu \frac{2}{r^{3}}+\mu \frac{1}{4 x^{3}} \\
b & =\mu \frac{2}{r^{3}}+\mu \frac{1}{4 y^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $y=k x$, it holds that $r=x \sqrt{1+k^{2}}$ and we can wrtite

$$
\begin{aligned}
a & =\frac{\mu}{x^{3}}\left(\frac{2}{\left(\sqrt{\left(1+k^{2}\right)}\right)^{3}}+\frac{1}{4}\right) \\
b & =\frac{\mu}{x^{3}}\left(\frac{2}{\left(\sqrt{\left(1+k^{2}\right)}\right)^{3}}+\frac{1}{4 k^{3}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the corresponding sides of (104a) and (104b) we obtain (79). The lhs of (79),

$$
f(k)=\frac{8 k^{3}+k^{3}\left(\sqrt{1+k^{2}}\right)^{3}}{\left(\sqrt{1+k^{2}}\right)^{3}+8 k^{3}}
$$

is strictly increasing, $\lim _{k \rightarrow \infty} f(k)=\infty$ and $f(0)=0$, so equation (79) has exactly one solution (see Fig. 17a).
By (103a) we have

$$
a=\mu \frac{2}{r^{3}}+\mu \frac{1}{4 x^{3}}>\mu \frac{2}{r^{3}}+\mu \frac{1}{4 r^{3}}=\frac{9 \mu}{4 r^{3}}
$$

and analogously from (103b) we obtain

$$
b>\frac{9 \mu}{4 r^{3}}
$$

Combining (105) and (106) we get the lower bound for $r$, namely

$$
r^{3}>\max \left(\frac{9 \mu}{4 a}, \frac{9 \mu}{4 b}\right)=\frac{9 \mu}{4 \min (a, b)}
$$

And again using (103), we compute $x^{2}$ and $y^{2}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} & =r^{2}\left(\frac{\mu}{4\left(a r^{3}-2 \mu\right)}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} \\
y^{2} & =r^{2}\left(\frac{\mu}{4\left(b r^{3}-2 \mu\right)}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Observe that from (107) it follows that denominators in the above equations are positive. Hence

$$
r^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}\left(\frac{\mu}{4\left(a r^{3}-2 \mu\right)}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}+r^{2}\left(\frac{\mu}{4\left(b r^{3}-2 \mu\right)}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}
$$

and we obtain (80). Using lhs of (80) we define a function

$$
g_{1}(r)=\left(\frac{2 \mu}{a r^{3}-2 \mu}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}+\left(\frac{2 \mu}{b r^{3}-2 \mu}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}
$$

The equation (80) has exactly one solution, with $r>\left(\frac{2 \mu}{\min \{a, b\}}\right)^{1 / 3}$ (see Fig. 17b)

where $x, y>0, x=r \cos (\varphi)$ and $y=r \sin (\varphi)$.

and afterwards to

is strictly increasing for $\varphi \in[0, \pi / 2), \lim _{\varphi \rightarrow \pi / 2} f(\varphi)=\infty$ and $f(0)=0$, so equation (81) has unique solution in $[0, \pi / 2)$ (see Fig. 18a).

hence

and we obtain (82). Using lhs of (80) define a function

# A. 8 Computation of $a, b$ at $L_{4}$ in the restricted three body problem 

We assume that point of mass $m_{i}$ is located at $p_{i}, i=1,2$ where

$$
p_{1}=(-1 / 2,0), \quad p_{2}=(1 / 2,0)
$$

The masses are normalized to $m_{1}+m_{2}=1$. The zero-mass (third) body has an unknown location $z=(x, y)$. The equation for relative equilibria is $\nabla V(z ; m)=0$, where

$$
V(z ; m)=\frac{1}{2}\|z-c\|^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{3} m_{i}\left\|z-p_{i}\right\|^{-1}
$$

where $c=\sum_{i=1}^{2} m_{i} p_{i}$ is the center of mass.
It is well known (see for example ) that we have five relative equilibria: three collinear with the primaries (called $L_{1}, L_{2}, L_{3}$ ) and two triangular $L_{4}$ and $L_{5}$, which form an equilateral triangle with the primaries. $L_{4}$ and $L_{5}$ are mutually symmetric with respect to the line passing through the primaries. For any choice of positive masses $m_{1}, m_{2}$, such that $m_{1}+m_{2}=1$, we have $L_{4}=(0, \sqrt{3} / 2)$ and $L_{5}=$ $(0,-\sqrt{3} / 2)$.
Expressions in the lemma below are computed using Mathematica program .

## Lemma 21.

$$
D^{2} V\left(L_{4}\right)=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\frac{3}{4} & \frac{3}{4} \sqrt{3}\left(2 m_{1}-1\right) \\
\frac{3}{4} \sqrt{3}\left(2 m_{1}-1\right) & \frac{9}{4}
\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\frac{3}{4} & \frac{3}{4} \sqrt{3}\left(m_{1}-m_{2}\right) \\
\frac{3}{4} \sqrt{3}\left(m_{1}-m_{2}\right) & \frac{9}{4}
\end{array}\right]
$$

The matrix $D^{2} V\left(L_{4}\right)$ is positive definite. Its eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \lambda_{2}=\frac{3}{2}\left(1-\sqrt{3 m_{1}^{2}-3 m_{1}+1}\right)=\frac{3}{2}\left(1-\sqrt{1-3 m_{1} m_{2}}\right) \\
& \lambda_{1}=\frac{3}{2}\left(\sqrt{3 m_{1}^{2}-3 m_{1}+1}+1\right)=\frac{3}{2}\left(1+\sqrt{1-3 m_{1} m_{2}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

and satisfy the following conditions

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{3} & >\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2} \geq \frac{3}{2} \\
\lambda_{1} & <\frac{3}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \\
\lambda_{2} & =\frac{9 m_{1} m_{2}}{4}+O\left(\left(m_{1} m_{2}\right)^{2}\right)

Proof. Expressions for $\lambda_{1,2}$ can be checked by direct computation. It remains to establish the remaining inequalities. Since

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_{2} & =\frac{3}{2}\left(1-\sqrt{1-3 m_{1} m_{2}}\right) \\
& =\frac{3}{2}\left(1-\left(1-\frac{3 m_{1} m_{2}}{2}+O\left(\left(m_{1} m_{2}\right)^{2}\right)\right)\right) \\
& =\frac{9 m_{1} m_{2}}{4}+O\left(\left(m_{1} m_{2}\right)^{2}\right)
