On the vertical boundary $x=\sqrt{3}, P$ is also strictly increasing with a minimum of approximately 12,818 at $y=2-\sqrt{3}$. Finally, for the lower boundary, in order to handle the $\sqrt{x^{2}+1}$ term, we introduce the auxiliary variable $u$ and consider the ideal in $\mathbb{Q}$ generated by the polynomials $P(x, y=-x+u)$

and $u^{2}-x^{2}-1$. Computing a Gröbner basis for this ideal to eliminate $u$, we obtain a polynomial in $x$ that has no roots for $1 / \sqrt{3}<x<\sqrt{3}$. Since $P(1,-1+\sqrt{2})>0$, we conclude that $P>0$ on the entire lower boundary. (The minimum value is the same as the value attained on the diagonal.) This shows that $P$ is strictly positive on $\mathcal{C}$.

Although the specific location of the critical point $z$ is unknown, we do know that it must correspond to some point $(\hat{x}, \hat{y})$ in the reduced configuration space $\mathcal{C}$. Since $F(\hat{x}, \hat{y})>P(\hat{x}, \hat{y})>0$, it follows that the index of $z$ is +1 .

Remark 5.3. Using MATLAB , we evaluated $F$ on a $300 \times 300$ grid on $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ to check numerically that $F>0$. The minimum value of $F$ is approximately 342.71 , attained at the point $(1 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3})$, which is the same location for the minimum of $P$. It appears that $F$ is an increasing function of $y$ on $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$.

# 5.4 Proof of Main Theorem 

Theorem 5.4. Given four positive masses $m_{1}, m_{3}, m_{2}=m_{4}$ and any ordering with bodies 2 and 4 positioned opposite each other, there exists a unique convex kite central configuration.

Proof: Without loss of generality, we can assume that the bodies are ordered consecutively in the counterclockwise direction. A convex kite central configuration with this ordering corresponds to a critical point $z \in \mathcal{N}_{\text {cvex }}$ that is a rest point (zero) of the gradient vector field $X$ defined in Lemma 3.1. Let $Z \subset \mathcal{N}_{\text {cvex }}$ be the set of all zeros of $X$ contained in the space of normalized convex configurations. By Corollary 4.3, this set is nonempty.

By Theorem 4.1, there exists a smooth manifold $\mathcal{M} \subset \mathcal{N}_{\text {cvex }}$ with boundary for which $X$ points outward on the boundary. We have $Z \subset M$ by construction. Since $\mathcal{M}$ is diffeomorphic to a closed disk, it has Euler characteristic 1. Each $z \in Z$ is an isolated zero of the vector field $X$ with index equal to +1 . The zeros are isolated because there are a finite number of them . Let $N$ be the number of elements in $Z$, that is, the total number of equivalence classes of convex kite central configurations with our prescribed ordering. Then, by the Poincaré-Hopf Index Theorem, we have

$$
1=\chi(\mathcal{M})=\sum_{z \in Z}^{N} i(z)=\sum_{z \in Z}^{N} 1
$$

from which it follows quickly that $N=1$.

Corollary 5.5. A convex kite central configuration $z \in \mathcal{N}$ is a nondegenerate local minimum of $V=$ $U \mid \mathcal{N}$.

Proof: Without loss of generality, we can assume that $z \in M$. Nondegeneracy follows from Lemma 5.2. If $z$ were not a local minimum, then there would exist an additional critical point $z^{*} \in M$ corresponding to the minimum value of $V$ on $\mathcal{M}$. But then $z^{*}$ would be a convex kite central configuration with the same ordering as $z$, contradicting uniqueness.

Remark 5.6. If we expand the configuration space to include all convex configurations (not just kites), then the convex kite c.c.'s are local minima of the full four-body potential function $U(q)$ restricted to the mass ellipsoid $I(q)=1$. This follows from the same argument used in the proof of the corollary along with the fact that any convex central configuration with masses $m_{1}, m_{3}, m_{2}=m_{4}$ must necessarily be a kite $$.

Remark 5.7. One advantage of using the Poincaré-Hopf Index Theorem is that computing the Poincaré index is easier than computing the Morse index or proving that $z$ is a minimum of the restricted potential function. This should prove fruitful for problems set in higher dimensional spaces.

# 6 Concave Kites 

In this section we discuss the concave kite central configurations. Much of our work is numerical in nature and concurs with the results of Leandro . The setup is similar to the convex setting except that now $y=b-c$ is negative. Positivity of the masses leads to two different types of concave configurations. We find a degenerate family of concave kites and a mass map that is two-to-one.

Without loss of generality, we assume that the third body $\left(m_{3}\right)$ lies in the interior of the triangle formed by the other three bodies and that bodies 1,2 , and 4 are arranged in counterclockwise order (see right plot in Figure 1). Recall that $x=a+c, y=b-c, r_{13}=x+y$, and $r_{24}=2 d$. Central configurations of this type lie in the interior of

$$
\mathcal{N}_{\text {cave }}=\left\{z \in \mathcal{N}: y \leq 0, x+y \geq 0, \text { and } d \geq 0\right\}
$$

Unlike the convex case, the gradient flow points inwards on the boundary $y=0$ of $\mathcal{N}_{\text {cave }}$, so the Poincaré-Hopf Index Theorem does not apply. In this case, the minimum value of $\left.U\right|_{\mathcal{N}_{\text {cave }}}$ may be located on the boundary $y=0$. In contrast to the convex setting, there are values of the masses for which there does not exist a concave kite central configuration (although $m_{2}=m_{4}$, the central configuration need not be symmetric). This fact was previously noted in .

### 6.1 The reduced configuration space $\mathcal{C} \mathcal{V}_{1} \cup \mathcal{C} \mathcal{V}_{2}$

The reduction and change of variables from $z=(a, b, c, d)$ to $(\hat{x}, \hat{y})$, as well as the formulas for the mass ratios given in (33) and (34), are still valid in the concave setting. However, since $\hat{y}<0$, we obtain different relations between the mutual distances. Positivity of the masses and equation (14) imply that

$$
r_{23}, r_{13}<\lambda^{-1 / 3}<r_{12}, r_{24}
$$

This means that each edge of the exterior triangle is larger than any of the interior edges. In addition, equation (34) implies that $r_{12}>r_{24}$ if and only if $r_{23}>r_{13}$. In other words, each of the congruent legs of the exterior triangle is larger than the base of the triangle if and only if each of the congruent interior edges is larger than the third interior edge.

Thus we have two types of concave kite configurations. We will refer to the concave configurations satisfying $r_{12}>r_{24}$ (and consequently $r_{23}>r_{13}$ ) as Type 1. Using (29) and the defining inequalities, Type 1 configurations lie in the space

$$
\mathcal{C} \mathcal{V}_{1}=\left\{(\hat{x}, \hat{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: \sqrt{3}<\hat{x}<2+\sqrt{3},-\sqrt{3}<\hat{y}<-\frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{x}-\frac{1}{\hat{x}}\right)\right\}
$$

Concave configurations with $r_{12}<r_{24}$ (and consequently $r_{23}<r_{13}$ ) will be denoted as Type 2. These configurations lie in the space

$$
\mathcal{C} \mathcal{V}_{2}=\left\{(\hat{x}, \hat{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: 1<\hat{x}<\sqrt{3},-\frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{x}-\frac{1}{\hat{x}}\right)<\hat{y}<0\right\}
$$

(see Figure 4). The closures of these two sets intersect in a special point at $(\sqrt{3},-1 / \sqrt{3})$, which corresponds to the well-studied $1+3$-gon central configuration. This configuration satisfies $r_{12}=r_{24}=2$,

The reduced configuration space for the different types of concave kite central configurations. The red curve consists of degenerate central configurations.
$r_{23}=r_{13}=2 / \sqrt{3}$, and $m_{1}=m / 2=m_{2}=m_{4}$. It consists of three equal mass at the vertices of an equilateral triangle and a body of arbitrary mass located at the center. This is the only kite configuration with an arbitrary mass; each configuration in $\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{C} \mathcal{V}_{1}$, or $\mathcal{C} \mathcal{V}_{2}$ has a unique value of the normalized masses that makes it central. We note the similarity of our bow-tie shaped configuration space in Figure 4 with the sets $\Pi_{1}$ and $\Pi_{3}$ in Fig. 4 of .

As with the convex case, the boundary curves (dashed curves in Figure 4) correspond to central configurations where one or more masses vanish. These configurations are central configurations of either the restricted four-body problem or the $1+3$-body problem. For example, the boundary $\hat{y}=0$ contains solutions to the restricted four-body problem, but with the three primaries forming a collinear central configuration. Unlike the convex kites, it is possible for three bodies of a concave kite central configuration to be nearly collinear.

Using MATLAB, we computed the index for each type of concave kite by evaluating $F(\hat{x}, \hat{y})$ from the proof of Lemma 5.2 on a $300 \times 300$ grid in both $\mathcal{C V}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{C V}_{2}$. The results are shown in Figure 4 and summarized in Table 1. Interestingly, there is a curve of degenerate central configurations (red curve) containing examples of each type. These are configurations where $F=0$ and the modified Hessian is singular.

Note that the degeneracy curve passes through the $1+3$-gon. It is possible to compute the exact mass values for this particular degeneracy. Plugging in $\hat{x}=\sqrt{3}, \hat{y}=-1 / \sqrt{3}, m_{1}=m / 2$, and $m_{3}=1-3 m / 2$ into inequality (36) yields a quadratic inequality in $m$ that is readily solved. We find that the $1+3$-gon

|  | Mutual Distances | Index | Degeneracies |
| :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: |
| Type 1 | $r_{12}>r_{24}>r_{23}>r_{13}$ | $\begin{gathered} +1 \text { or }-1 \\ \text { (majority }+1) \end{gathered}$ | Yes |
| Type 2 | $r_{24}>r_{12}>r_{13}>r_{23}$ | $\begin{gathered} +1 \text { or }-1 \\ \text { (majority }-1) \end{gathered}$ | Yes |
| $1+3$-gon | $r_{12}=r_{24}$ and $r_{23}=r_{13}$ | $\begin{aligned} & m>m^{*} \Longrightarrow+1 \\ & m<m^{*} \Longrightarrow-1 \end{aligned}$ | $m^{*}=\frac{207-16 \sqrt{3}}{338}$ |

Table 1: Summary of information for the different types of concave kite central configurations. We did not compute the index of the degenerate central configurations.
is degenerate for $m=m^{*}$, where

$$
m^{*}=\frac{207-16 \sqrt{3}}{338} \approx 0.530435
$$

From this we compute the ratio between the interior mass $m_{3}$ and one of the outer equal masses at the degeneracy to be $(81+64 \sqrt{3}) / 249$, which matches the value previously computed by Schmidt  and Leandro . The $1+3$-gon is a local min for $m>m^{*}$ and a saddle for $m<m^{*}$.

# 6.2 The mass map 

Next we consider the mass map $\widehat{M}$ from the configuration space $\mathcal{C V}_{1} \cup \mathcal{C V}_{2}$ to the mass triangle $m_{1}+m_{3}+m=1, m, m_{1}, m_{3} \geq 0$. Two coordinates of this map are given by

$$
m_{1}(\hat{x}, \hat{y})=\frac{\hat{y}\left(s_{23}-s_{24}\right)\left(s_{23}-s_{13}\right)}{S\left[\hat{x}\left(s_{13}-s_{12}\right)+\hat{y}\left(s_{13}-s_{23}\right)\right]} \quad \text { and } \quad m_{3}(\hat{x}, \hat{y})=\frac{\hat{x}\left(s_{12}-s_{24}\right)\left(s_{12}-s_{13}\right)}{S\left[\hat{x}\left(s_{13}-s_{12}\right)+\hat{y}\left(s_{13}-s_{23}\right)\right]}
$$

where $s_{i j}=r_{i j}^{-3}$ and $S=s_{13}+s_{24}-s_{12}-s_{23}$. While each of these expressions are defined and positive on $\mathcal{C V}_{1} \cup \mathcal{C V}_{2}$, they are undefined, taking the form $0 / 0$, at the $1+3$-gon $\left(x^{*}, y^{*}\right)=(\sqrt{3},-1 / \sqrt{3})$ because of its free mass parameter. Nevertheless, limiting values of the masses exist at the $1+3$-gon. Consider a line segment in $\mathcal{C V}_{1} \cup \mathcal{C V}_{2}$ of slope $k$, with $k<-2 / 3$, passing through $\left(x^{*}, y^{*}\right)$. Using a first-order Taylor expansion, it is straight-forward to compute that

$$
\lim _{(x, y) \rightarrow\left(x^{*}, y^{*}\right)} m_{1}(x, y)=\frac{6+9 k}{18-\sqrt{3}+27 k} \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{(x, y) \rightarrow\left(x^{*}, y^{*}\right)} m_{3}(x, y)=\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{18-\sqrt{3}+27 k}
$$

The limiting values satisfy $m_{3}=1-3 m_{1}$, which is equivalent to $m_{1}=m / 2$, as expected for the $1+3$-gon.
The image of the mass map $\widehat{M}$ projected into the $m_{1} m_{3}$-plane is shown in Figure 5. The figure was created by computing the image of 20 equally spaced vertical lines in both $\mathcal{C V}_{1}$ (red and orange curves) and $\mathcal{C V}_{2}$ (blue and green curves). The image of the red degeneracy curve from Figure 4 is shown in magenta and the masses for the $1+3$-gon are shown on the black line $m_{3}=1-3 m_{1}$. There are several interesting features revealed by this image.

- $\widehat{M}$ does not cover the full mass space (see also Figure 6). There are mass values for which there does not exist a concave kite central configuration (e.g., $m_{1}=0.25, m_{3}=0.4$ ). This holds even

The image of the different concave configurations under the mass map $\widehat{M}$ projected into the $m_{1} m_{3}$-plane.
if we interchange $m_{1}$ and $m_{3}$, and $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$ (moving body 1 to the interior of the triangle). The value of $m_{1}$ is bounded above by 0.42345 and for each $m_{1}$, there is a maximum allowable value for the interior mass $m_{3}$ determined by the image of the degeneracy curve.

- As indicated by the intersections in the figure, $\widehat{M}$ is a two-to-one map. For those mass values where a concave kite exists, most have one configuration of each type (e.g., a point of intersection between a blue curve and an orange curve). However, for mass values located above the black line and below the magenta curve, the two pre-images are of the same type. This can be seen, for example, in the lower right part of the figure, where different green curves intersect each other. Moving across the black line in Figure 5, one of the pre-images of $\widehat{M}$ will pass through the 1+3-gon and then flip its type of configuration.
- Any curve that meets the magenta curve must be tangent to it. This follows because the mass map is not invertible on the degeneracy curve. The derivative of $\widehat{M}$ evaluated at any degenerate point is a rank one matrix.


# 7 Linear Stability 

In this section we numerically investigate the spectral and linear stability of the relative equilibria that arise from the kite central configurations. We find that nearly all of the kite relative equilibria are linearly unstable. The only stable solutions occur for the convex case, very close to the lower

The image of the mass map for the concave kites only covers a portion of the normalized mass triangle $m_{1}+m_{3}+m=1$ (boundaries of this triangle shown in cyan).
boundary of $\mathcal{C}$. Surprisingly, all of the concave solutions are unstable, even those with a "dominant" mass (where one body is substantially larger than the others). In agreement with Moeckel's conjectures (see problems 15 and 16 in ), the linearly stable solutions found correspond to nondegenerate local minima of $\left.U\right|_{\mathcal{N}}$ and contain a dominant mass. Specifically, we compute that the infimum of the mass ratio $m_{1} /\left(m_{2}+m_{3}+m_{4}\right)$ over the set of linearly stable solutions is $(25+3 \sqrt{69}) / 2 \approx 24.9599$. Detailed plots showing the different eigenvalue structures for the two types of concave solutions are provided, revealing some interesting bifurcation curves.

# 7.1 An invariant subspace for the nontrivial eigenvalues 

We first provide an overview and definition of linear stability of relative equilibria in the planar $n$-body problem (see ). Here we work in the full phase space, utilizing the Hamiltonian structure of the problem. Given the correct initial momentum, a central configuration $q \in \mathbb{R}^{2 n}$ will rigidly rotate about its center of mass with angular velocity $\omega=\sqrt{\lambda}$, where $\lambda=U(q) / I(q)$ is the same value given in the defining c.c. equation (3). After changing to rotating coordinates, the linear stability of this circular periodic solution is determined by regarding the relative equilibrium as a fixed point in the rotating frame. As with our initial setup, we will assume that the center of mass of $q$ is at the origin and that $I(q)=1$. Linearizing about the relative equilibrium gives the $4 n \times 4 n$ stability matrix

$$
\Lambda=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\omega K & M^{-1} \\
D^{2} U(q) & \omega K
\end{array}\right]
$$

where $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n}, m_{n}\right\}$ and $K$ is the $2 n \times 2 n$ block-diagonal matrix with $J=\left[\begin{array}{cc}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{array}\right]$ on the diagonal.

The stability matrix has two "trivial" eigenspaces that arise from the symmetries of the problem. The linear subspace

$$
W_{1}=\operatorname{span}\{(q, 0),(K q, 0),(0, M q),(0, K M q)\}
$$

is invariant under $\Lambda$ with eigenvalues $0,0, \pm \omega i$. These eigenvalues are a result of the rotational symmetry ( $q$ is not isolated) and the homogeneity of $U$. The linear subspace

$$
W_{2}=\operatorname{span}\left\{\left(\xi_{n}, 0\right),\left(K \xi_{n}, 0\right),\left(0, M \xi_{n}\right),\left(0, K M \xi_{n}\right)\right\}
$$

where $\xi_{n}=(1,0,1,0, \ldots, 1,0)$, is also invariant under $\Lambda$ with eigenvalues $\pm \omega i, \pm \omega i$. These eigenvalues come from the conservation of the center of mass and linear momentum.

Thus, any relative equilibrium will contain the eight trivial eigenvalues $0,0, \pm \omega i, \pm \omega i, \pm \omega i$. It is standard to call $q$ a nondegenerate relative equilibrium if the remaining $4 n-8$ eigenvalues are nonzero. It is spectrally stable if the nontrivial eigenvalues lie on the imaginary axis. Linear stability is defined using the skew inner product $\Omega$. For vectors $v, w \in \mathbb{C}^{4 n}$, let

$$
\Omega(v, w)=v^{T} \mathbb{J} w, \text { where } \mathbb{J}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
0 & I_{2 n} \\
-I_{2 n} & 0
\end{array}\right] \text { and } I_{2 n} \text { is the } 2 n \times 2 n \text { identity matrix. }
$$

Let $W$ denote the skew-orthogonal complement of $W_{1} \cup W_{2}$, that is,

$$
W=\left\{v \in \mathbb{C}^{4 n}: \Omega(v, w)=0 \forall w \in W_{1} \cup W_{2}\right\}
$$

Using the fact that $\Omega(v, \Lambda w)=-\Omega(\Lambda v, w)$, it is easy to see that $W$ is also an invariant subspace under $\Lambda$. The nontrivial eigenvectors all lie in $W$. Therefore, we call a relative equilibrium linearly stable if it is spectrally stable and if $\Lambda$ is diagonalizable when restricted to $W$.

We note that there exists a vector $\chi \in \mathbb{R}^{2 n}$ in the null space of the modified Hessian $M^{-1} D^{2} U(q)+\lambda I_{2 n}$ if and only if the vector $(\chi,-\omega K M \chi)$ is in the kernel of $\Lambda$. Hence $q$ is nondegenerate when regarded as a central configuration (in the same sense as Definition 3.3) if and only if it is a nondegenerate relative equilibrium.

Next we focus on the linear stability of the kite relative equilibria. In order to determine stability, we need to find the eight nontrivial eigenvalues of $\Lambda$. Suppose that $q=(a, 0,-c, d,-b, 0,-c,-d)$ is a kite central configuration with center of mass at the origin and moment of inertia $I(q)=1$. We will use the mass inner product

$$
\langle v, w\rangle=v^{T} M w, \quad \text { for } v, w \in \mathbb{R}^{8}
$$

where $M=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{2}, m_{3}, m_{3}, m_{4}, m_{4}\right\}$. Recall that $m_{2}=m_{4}=m / 2$ and that the masses have been normalized by $m_{1}+m_{3}+m=1$. The vectors $q, K q, \xi_{4}$, and $K \xi_{4}$ are mutually orthogonal and of unit length with respect to this inner product.

More accurate numerical computations can be achieved by restricting $\Lambda$ to $W$, the skew orthogonal complement of $W_{1} \cup W_{2}$, which is an eight-dimensional vector space. In order to find a basis for $W$, we first extend $q, K q, \xi_{4}$, and $K \xi_{4}$ to an $M$-orthonormal basis for $\mathbb{R}^{8}$. We take a geometric approach and use the oriented areas $\Delta_{i}$ of the triangles obtained by deleting the $i$ th body . For our setup, we have

$$
\Delta_{1}=-d(b-c), \Delta_{3}=-d(a+c), \quad \text { and } \quad \Delta_{2}=\Delta_{4}=\frac{1}{2} d(a+b)
$$

Define the vector $u_{1}=\left(\Delta_{1} / m_{1}, 0, \Delta_{2} / m_{2}, 0, \Delta_{3} / m_{3}, 0, \Delta_{4} / m_{4}, 0\right)$. It is straight-forward to check that the vectors $u_{1}$ and $-K u_{1}$ are each $M$-orthogonal to $q, K q, \xi_{4}$, and $K \xi_{4}$.

Next we use Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization to obtain an orthogonal vector $u_{2}$. Recall that

$$
\operatorname{proj}_{w}(v)=\frac{<v, w>}{<w, w>} w
$$

is the projection of the vector $v$ onto $w$. Suppose that $v \in \mathbb{R}^{8}$ is an arbitrary vector. Define

$$
u_{2}=v-\left(\operatorname{proj}_{q}(v)+\operatorname{proj}_{K q}(v)+\operatorname{proj}_{\xi_{4}}(v)+\operatorname{proj}_{K \xi_{4}}(v)+\operatorname{proj}_{u_{1}}(v)+\operatorname{proj}_{-K u_{1}}(v)\right)
$$

The vector $u_{2}$ is $M$-orthogonal to the six vectors $q, K q, \xi_{4}, K \xi_{4}, u_{1}$, and $-K u_{1}$. It is nonzero if $v$ does not lie in the span of these six vectors.

Taking $v=(1,0,0,0,0,0,0,0)$ in (39) yields the vector

$$
\begin{aligned}
u_{2}= & \left(1-m_{1} a^{2}-m_{1}-\frac{\Delta_{1}^{2}}{m_{1}<u_{1}, u_{1}>}, 0, m_{1} a c-m_{1}-\frac{\Delta_{1} \Delta_{2}}{m_{2}<u_{1}, u_{1}>},-m_{1} a d\right. \\
& \left.m_{1} a b-m_{1}-\frac{\Delta_{1} \Delta_{3}}{m_{3}<u_{1}, u_{1}>}, 0, m_{1} a c-m_{1}-\frac{\Delta_{1} \Delta_{4}}{m_{4}<u_{1}, u_{1}>}, m_{1} a d\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $a d>0$, we know that $u_{2}$ is nonzero. Finally, let $\widehat{u_{1}}=u_{1} /\left\|u_{1}\right\|$ and $\widehat{u_{2}}=u_{2} /\left\|u_{2}\right\|$ (norm taken with respect to our inner product). The vectors $\widehat{u_{1},}-K \widehat{u_{1}}, \widehat{u_{2}}$, and $-K \widehat{u_{2}}$ form an $M$-orthonormal basis for the orthogonal complement of $\operatorname{span}\left\{q, K q, \xi_{4}, K \xi_{4}\right\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{8}$. This in turn implies that the vectors

$$
\left(\widehat{u_{1}}, 0\right),\left(-K \widehat{u_{1}}, 0\right),\left(\widehat{u_{2}}, 0\right),\left(-K \widehat{u_{2}}, 0\right),\left(0, M \widehat{u_{1}}\right),\left(0,-M K \widehat{u_{1}}\right),\left(0, M \widehat{u_{2}}\right),\left(0,-M K \widehat{u_{2}}\right)
$$

form a basis for $W$. Using this basis, we see that the nontrivial eigenvalues are equal to the eigenvalues of the $8 \times 8$ matrix

$$
\Lambda_{W}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\omega K & I_{4} \\
\widehat{A} & \omega K
\end{array}\right]
$$

where $\widehat{A}$ is the restriction of $M^{-1} D^{2} U(q)$ to $\operatorname{span}\left\{\widehat{u_{1},}-K \widehat{u_{1}}, \widehat{u_{2},}-K \widehat{u_{2}}\right\}$. The entries of $\widehat{A}$ can be computed numerically using our inner product. For example, the first entry on the main diagonal is simply $<\widehat{u_{1}}, M^{-1} D^{2} U(q) \widehat{u_{1}}>$. Due to the symmetry of the kites and our choice of vectors, half the entries in $\widehat{A}$ vanish (specifically, $\widehat{a}_{i j}=0$ if $i+j \equiv 1 \bmod 2$ ).

The matrix $\Lambda_{W}$ is Hamiltonian and therefore has an even characteristic polynomial. The eigenvalues consist of real pairs $\pm a_{j}$, pure imaginary pairs $\pm b_{j} i$, or complex quadruplets $\pm a_{j} \pm b_{j} i$. The relative equilibrium is linearly stable if it has four distinct imaginary pairs of eigenvalues.

# 7.2 Convex case 

For the convex kites, most of the relative equilibria are unstable, except for a small neighborhood about the lower boundary in $\mathcal{C}$.

Proposition 7.1. There is an open neighborhood in $\mathcal{C}$ about the lower boundary curve $r_{12}=r_{13}$ for which the corresponding kite relative equilibria are linearly stable.

Proof: This is a direct application of the work of Corbera et al. (see Corollary 1 in ). The authors show that the convex critical points of the $1+3$-body problem (which includes the lower boundary of $\mathcal{C}$ ) are nondegenerate minima of a special potential function $V(\theta)$. By the main theorem in , this implies that for each point $\left(\hat{x}, \hat{y}=-\hat{x}+\sqrt{\hat{x}^{2}+1}\right)$ on the lower boundary of $\mathcal{C}$, there is a smooth family

of linearly stable relative equilibria converging to $(\hat{x}, \hat{y})$. These relative equilibria must be kites because $m_{2}=m_{4}$.

Starting on the lower boundary of $\mathcal{C}$ and increasing $\hat{y}$, stability can be lost in one of two ways. Either a pair of pure imaginary eigenvalues collides at the origin and then splits into a real pair, or two pairs of pure imaginary eigenvalues merge on the imaginary axis and then break off into a complex quadruplet (a Krein collision). In either case, we have repeated roots at the bifurcation and the discriminant of the characteristic polynomial of $\Lambda_{W}$ must vanish. Since the entries of $\Lambda_{W}$ vary continuously in $(\hat{x}, \hat{y})$, so to does this discriminant. Thus there is an open inequality which guarantees a linear stable family persists locally.

The stability diagram for the convex case is plotted in the reduced configuration space $\mathcal{C}$ in Figure 7. The plots were created in MATLAB using the eig command to compute the eigenvalues of $\Lambda_{W}$. Given a point $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}) \in \mathcal{C}$, we scale and shift the configuration using equations (20)-(23) to obtain the vector $q \in \mathbb{R}^{8}$ with center of mass at the origin and $I(q)=1$. The relative equilibrium is considered linearly stable if the real parts of the nontrivial eigenvalues are less than $1 \times 10^{-10}$ and the eigenvalues are distinct. Eigenvalues were normalized by dividing by $\omega$. Stability is lost through a Krein collision, which occurs on the red boundary curve shown in the left plot. As shown in the right plot, the size of the stable region is quite small, less than 0.004 in the vertical direction.

Stability diagrams for the convex case, showing a small neighborhood of linearly stable relative equilibria near the lower boundary of $\mathcal{C}$. The right plot is a $250 \times 250$ grid of sample points within 0.005 (vertically) of the lower boundary. The vertical axis $(\epsilon)$ indicates the distance between $\hat{y}$ and the lower boundary. Red points correspond to linearly stable solutions, while blue points are unstable.

# 7.3 Concave case 

None of the concave kite relative equilibria are spectrally stable. The configurations with a dominant mass are located close to the boundary $r_{23}=r_{13}$, which contains critical points of the $1+3$-body problem (blue dashed curve in Figure 4). The third body (largest mass) in the interior of the triangle is roughly equidistant to the other three smaller bodies. We checked numerically that the configurations on the boundary are either local maxima or saddles of the special potential function $V(\theta)$ defined in . It follows by the main theorem in  that the nearby kite relative equilibria (both types) are linearly unstable. Between the two types is the $1+3$-gon relative equilibrium (equilateral triangle with an arbitrary mass at the center), but this is known to be unstable for any value of the central mass .

Detailed stability diagrams for both the Type 1 and 2 concave configurations were created using MATLAB (see Figures 8 and 9). Each color represents a different structure for the eight nontrivial eigenvalues, as indicated by the triple (fully complex, real, pure imaginary). For example, eigenvalues for points in the magenta regions $(8,0,0)$ consist of two complex quadruplets, while the eigenvalues in the large blue regions $(4,2,2)$ consist of a complex quadruplet, a real pair, and a pure imaginary pair. Two of the nine possible combinations of eigenvalues do not exist for either type: four real pairs $(0,8,0)$ and the stable case of four pure imaginary pairs $(0,0,8)$.

Stability diagram for the Type 1 concave kite relative equilibria. Each colored region represents a different eigenvalue structure, as indicated by the triple (fully complex, real, pure imaginary).

There are several interesting bifurcation curves apparent in Figures 8 and 9, where the eigenvalue structure changes. Some of these curves match the degenerate curves shown in Figure 4. For example, moving from an orange region $(4,0,4)$ into a blue region $(4,2,2)$, one pair of pure imaginary eigenvalues merge at the origin (a degeneracy) and then switch over to a pair of real eigenvalues. Krein collisions occur when passing from a cyan region $(0,2,6)$ into a blue region $(4,2,2)$, or traveling from an orange region $(4,0,4)$ into a magenta region $(8,0,0)$. A third example occurs when two pairs of real eigenvalues merge on the real axis and then break off into a complex quadruplet, a scenario that transpires when moving from a neon green region $(4,4,0)$ into a magenta region $(8,0,0)$. For those bifurcations where the


Stability diagram for the Type 2 concave kite relative equilibria.
eigenvalues pass through the origin (a degeneracy), but which are not on the curve shown in Figure 4, these must feature eigenvectors that break the symmetry of the kite (perturbations that exit $\mathcal{C} \mathcal{V}_{1}$ or $\mathcal{C} \mathcal{V}_{2}$ ). The corresponding kite central configurations are degenerate in the full four-body problem.

# 7.4 Relative size of the dominant mass 

Our final computation explores the masses of the linearly stable solutions, focusing on the size of the largest mass with respect to the sum of the others. For the stable convex kites, the largest mass is $m_{1}$. Consider the mass ratio

$$
\psi=\frac{m_{1}}{m_{2}+m_{3}+m_{4}}=\frac{m_{1}}{1-m_{1}}
$$

evaluated on the set of all linearly stable solutions. This ratio is infinite on the lower boundary of $\mathcal{C}$ since $m=m_{3}=0$ there, and numerical experiments show that it is decreasing as a function of $\hat{y}$. It follows that the minimum value of $\psi$ will occur on the red boundary curve from the left plot in Figure 7.

A graph of $\psi$ evaluated along the stability boundary is shown in Figure 10. It is an increasing function of $\hat{x}$, with a minimum value around 25 . Careful numerical calculations near the boundary point $(\hat{x}, \hat{y})=(1 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3})$ indicate that the infimum of $\psi$ is

$$
\frac{25+3 \sqrt{69}}{2} \approx 24.959936
$$

The exact value is obtained from Routh's critical mass ratio $\rho_{r}=(1-\sqrt{69} / 9) / 2$ for the restricted three-body problem, where the two primaries have masses $\rho$ and $1-\rho$. Placing an infinitesimal mass at each of the Lagrange triangle points $L_{4}$ and $L_{5}$ yields a four-body central configuration that is equivalent

The mass ratio $\psi=m_{1} /\left(m_{2}+m_{3}+m_{4}\right)$ evaluated along the stability boundary curve from the left plot in Figure 7. For each $\hat{x}$, in order for the convex kite relative equilibrium to be linearly stable, the mass ratio must be greater than the value given by this curve.
to the kite c.c. for $(\hat{x}, \hat{y})=(1 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3})$. This is a limiting configuration for a linearly stable family of relative equilibria in the four-body problem, provided $\rho<\rho_{r}$. Substituting $m_{1}=1-\rho_{r}$ into the mass ratio $\psi$ gives the value shown in (40). These numerical results provide further evidence for Moeckel's dominant mass conjecture.


# ON THE CENTERED CO-CIRCULAR CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS FOR THE N-BODY PROBLEM 

#### Abstract

For the power-law potential $n$-body problem, we study a special kind of central configurations where all the masses lie on a circle and the center of mass coincides with the center of the circle. It is also called the centered cocircular central configuration. We get some symmetry results for such central configurations. We show that for positive numbers $\alpha>0$ and integers $n \geq 3$ satisfying $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc ^{n} \frac{j \pi}{n} \leq 1+\frac{\alpha}{4}$, the regular $n$-gon with equal masses is the unique centered co-circular central configuration for the $n$-body problem with power-law potential $U_{\alpha}$. It quickly follows that for the Newtonian $n$ body problem (in the case $\alpha=1$ ) and $n \leq 6$, the regular $n$-gon is the unique centered co-circular central configuration.


## 1. Introduction and the Main Result

The $n$-body problem concerns the motion of $n$ point masses $m_{k}>0$ and their positions $x_{k} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}, k=1, \ldots, n$. For $n \geq 2$ and $\alpha \geq 0$, this motion can be governed by a power-law potential:

$$
m_{k} \ddot{x}_{k}=\frac{\partial U_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{x})}{\partial x_{k}}, \quad k=1,2, \ldots, n
$$

where $\boldsymbol{x}=\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)^{T}$, and in a slight abuse of notation,

$$
U_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{x})= \begin{cases}\sum_{1 \leq j<k \leq n} \frac{m_{j} m_{k}}{\left|x_{j}-x_{k}\right|^{\alpha}}, & \alpha \neq 0 \\ \sum_{1 \leq j<k \leq N} m_{j} m_{k} \log \left|x_{j}-x_{k}\right|, & \alpha=0\end{cases}
$$

When $\alpha=1$, it is the classical Newtonian $n$-body problem, and for the limiting case $\alpha=0$, it corresponds to an N-Vortex Problem. In order to avoid collisions, we consider the configuration space

$$
\mathbf{X} \backslash \triangle=\left\{\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)^{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 n}: x_{j} \neq x_{k} \quad \text { when } \quad j \neq k\right\}
$$

and give the following definition of central configurations.
Definition 1. A configuration $\boldsymbol{x}=\left(x_{1}, x_{2} \ldots, x_{n}\right)^{T} \in \mathbf{X} \backslash \triangle$ is called a central configuration (CC for short) for masses $\boldsymbol{m}=\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n}\right)^{T}$ if there exists some constant $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ such that

$$
\sum_{\substack{j \neq k \\ j=1}}^{n} \frac{x_{j}-x_{k}}{\left|x_{j}-x_{k}\right|^{\alpha+2}} m_{j} m_{k}=-\frac{\lambda}{\alpha} m_{k}\left(x_{k}-c_{0}\right), \quad k=1,2, \ldots, n
$$

or simply

$$
\frac{\partial U_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{x})}{\partial x_{k}}=-\lambda m_{k}\left(x_{k}-c_{0}\right), \quad k=1,2, \ldots, n
$$

where the center of mass is defined as $c_{0}=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{n} m_{k} x_{k}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} m_{k}}$.
Central configurations play "central" role in the $n$-body problem  such as in the analysis of collision orbits or expanding gravitational systems. It also gives rise to a family of simple and explicit periodic solutions . For instance, a planar central configuration can naturally give rise to a relative equilibrium motion where every mutual distance $r_{j k}=\left|x_{j}-x_{k}\right|$ stays constant.

The equations for central configurations (1.1) are invariant under rotations, translations and dilations. Thus we always consider equivalent classes of central configurations modulo these symmetries. The study of Newtonian central configurations dates back to Euler  and Lagrange  who studied the 3-body case. There are only five classes of central configurations for the Newtonian 3-body problem, three Euler collinear CCs and two Lagrange equilateral triangle CCs. Although centuries have passed since then, a complete understanding of CCs remains elusive. When $n>3$, it is almost impossible to solve the equations of central configurations (1.1) for any given masses. A longstanding problem, known as the finiteness problem, is for any given positive masses whether there are only finitely many equivalent classes of CCs. It is proposed by Wintner  and listed by Smale  as the sixth problem on his list of problems for this century. Albouy et al.  also list it as the 9th open problem in celestial mechanics. For the collinear case, Moulton  showed that there are exactly $n!/ 2$ equivalent classes of CCs for the $n$-body problem. Most recently, using BKK theory in algebraic geometry, Hampton and Moeckel  proved the finiteness of the number of equivalent classes of CCs for n $=4$. For 5 bodies in the plane, Albouy and Kaloshin  showed the the number is finite, except perhaps if the masses belong to an explicit codimension 2 subvariety of the space of positive masses. For the spatial 5 -body central configuration, Hampton and Jenson  showed the finiteness, apart from some explicitly given special cases of mass values.

In this paper, we study a special kind of central configuration where all the masses lie on a circle and the center of mass coincides with the center of the circle. In what follows we call it centered co-circular central configurations as in . There are also many work on the co-circular central configurations which is not centered (see  and references therein). There is an open question asked by Chenciner  when he studied the choreography solutions in the $n$-body problem.
Is the regular n-gon with equal masses the sole central configuration such that all the bodies lie on a circle and the center of mass coincides with the center of the circle?

The regular $n$-gon central configuration with equal masses is the trivial one. It gives rise to the trivial choreography solution where each body moves (with equal time spacings) on the same circle. If there were some other centered co-circular central configurations we can immediately have a choreography solution with unequal time spacings between the bodies and maybe unequal masses. Chenciner's question is also listed as Problem 12 in a collection of important open problems in celestial mechanics. The first one who answered the question was Hampton. He proved that the only four-body centered co-circular CC is the square with equal masses . Llibre and Valls  studied the case $n=5$. All the above results are just in the Newtonian case $\alpha=1$. A big progress is the work of Cors et al. who study the general co-circular configurations with power-law potential $U_{\alpha}(\alpha \geq 0)$. They

proved that, for any choice of positive masses, if such a central configuration exists, it is unique. It quickly follows that when the masses are all equal, the only solution is the regular $n$-gon. In that paper, they also give a positive answer to Chenciner's question for the power law potential $U_{0}$ (in the case $\alpha=0$ ). They proved that, in the n-vortex problem the only possible centered co-circular central configuration is the regular $n$-gon with equal vorticities. Our main result is
Theorem 1.1. For all the integers $n \geq 3$ and real numbers $\alpha>0$ satisfying

$$
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc ^{\alpha} \frac{j \pi}{n} \leq 1+\frac{\alpha}{4}
$$

the regular n-gon CC with equal masses is the unique central configuration for power-law potential $U_{\alpha}$, such that all the bodies lie on a circle, and the center of mass coincides with the center of the circle.

We notice that the function $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc ^{\alpha} \frac{j \pi}{n}$ is increasing with respect to $n$ and $\alpha$, separately. For any given integer $n>0$, we can get a positive answer to Chenciner's question for the $n$-body problem with power-law potential $U_{\alpha}$ in the case $\alpha=\alpha(n)$ is sufficiently small. For the classical Newtonian case $\alpha=1$, a direct computation shows that

$$
\frac{1}{6} \sum_{j=1}^{6-1} \csc \frac{j \pi}{6}=\frac{5}{6}+\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{9}<1+\frac{1}{4}
$$

Corollary 1.1. In the Newtonian $n(\leq 6)$ body problem, the regular n-gon CC with equal masses is the unique central configuration, such that all the bodies lie on a circle, and the center of mass coincides with the center of the circle.

This paper is organized as follows: In Section 2 we derive the equations for the centered co-circular CC. Following the approach of Cors et al., we can see the centered co-circular CC as the unique minimum of a new function for any given positive masses (see Lemma 2.2). In Section 3, we provide some symmetry results and lemmas of centered co-circular CCs by the uniqueness of minimum. We also give a positive answer to Chenciner's question for any power-law potential in the 3 and 4-body problem. In Section 4 we prove Theorem 1.1 based on the lemmas in Section 3.

# 2. EQUATIONS FOR CENTERED CO-CIRCULAR CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS 

We suppose that $n$ positive masses $\boldsymbol{m}=\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n}\right)^{T} \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$ lie on a unit circle centered at origin in the complex plane. Their positions are $\boldsymbol{q}=$ $\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)^{T} \in \mathbb{C}^{n}$ where $q_{j}=e^{\sqrt{-1} \theta_{j}}=\cos \theta_{j}+\sqrt{-1} \sin \theta_{j}$. Without loss of generality, let $\theta_{j} \in(0,2 \pi]$ and in order to avoid collisions, we suppose

$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}=\left(\theta_{1}, \theta_{2}, \ldots, \theta_{n}\right)^{T} \in \mathcal{K}=\left\{\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: 0<\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<\cdots<\theta_{n} \leq 2 \pi\right\}
$$

Thus when the mass vector $\boldsymbol{m}$ is given, their order is also determined. Under these notations, the potential $U_{\alpha}$ can be written as

$$
U_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta})=\sum_{j<k} \frac{m_{j} m_{k}}{r_{j k}^{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}=2^{-\alpha} \sum_{j<k} \frac{m_{j} m_{k}}{\left|\sin ^{a} \frac{\theta_{1}-\theta_{j}}{2}\right|}
$$

where

$$
r_{j k}=\left|q_{j}-q_{k}\right|=\left|2 \sin \frac{\theta_{j}-\theta_{k}}{2}\right|=\sqrt{2-2 \cos \left(\theta_{j}-\theta_{k}\right)}
$$

is the mutual distance between $q_{j}$ and $q_{k}$. Then by (1.1), they form a centered co-circular CC if and only if

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\sum_{j \neq k}^{n} \frac{m_{j}\left(1-q_{j} / q_{k}\right)}{r_{j k}^{\alpha+2}}=\frac{\lambda}{\alpha}, \quad k=1,2, \ldots, n \\
\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j} q_{j}=0
\end{array}\right.
$$

Actually the last equations can also be deduced from the first $n$ equations by multiplying each of them by $m_{k} q_{k}$ and taking summation. Writing their real and imaginary part separately, we have

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\alpha m_{k} \sum_{j \neq k}^{n} \frac{m_{j}}{r^{\alpha+2}} \sin \left(\theta_{j}-\theta_{k}\right)=0 \\
\sum_{j \neq k}^{n} \frac{m_{j}}{r_{j k}^{\alpha}}=\tilde{\lambda} \\
\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j} \cos \theta_{j}=\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j} \sin \theta_{j}=0
\end{array}\right.
$$

where $\tilde{\lambda}=\frac{2 \lambda}{\alpha}=\frac{2 U_{n}}{M}$. Seeing $U_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta})=\sum_{j<k} \frac{m_{j} m_{k}}{r_{j k}^{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}$ as a function of varibles $\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}$, and noticing that

$$
U_{-2}(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta})=\sum_{j<k} m_{j} m_{k} r_{i j}^{2}=\sum_{j<k} m_{j} m_{k}\left(2-2 \cos \left(\theta_{j}-\theta_{k}\right)\right)
$$

these equations are equivalent to

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_{k}} U_{\alpha}=0, \quad \frac{\partial}{\partial m_{k}} U_{\alpha}=\tilde{\lambda}, \quad k=1,2, \ldots, n \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_{k}} U_{-2}=0, \quad \frac{\partial}{\partial m_{k}} U_{-2}=2 M, \quad k=1,2, \ldots, n
\end{gathered}
$$

or more compactly

$$
\begin{gathered}
\left.\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} U_{\alpha}\right|_{(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta})}=\mathbf{0}, \quad \nabla_{\boldsymbol{m}} U_{\alpha} \|_{(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta})}=\tilde{\lambda} \mathbf{1} \\
\left.\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} U_{-2}\right|_{(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta})}=\mathbf{0}, \quad \nabla_{\boldsymbol{m}} U_{-2} \|_{(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta})}=2 M \mathbf{1}
\end{gathered}
$$

where the vectors $\mathbf{0}=(0,0, \ldots, 0)^{T}$ and $\mathbf{1}=(1,1, \ldots, 1)^{T}$. Thus $\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}$ form a centered co-circular central configuration if and only if the equations (2.1) and (2.2) hold (if and only if the equations (2.1) hold). So if $\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}$ satisfy (2.1) and (2.2), we simply denote

$$
(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathcal{C C}
$$

Cors et al. notice that $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} U_{\alpha}=\mathbf{0}$ means $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is a critical points of $U_{\alpha}$ when the positive mass vector $\boldsymbol{m}$ is given. By computing the corresponding Hessian matrix of $U_{\alpha}$, they showed that this critical point is a minimum and is unique up to translation which can be removed by specifying $\theta_{n}=2 \pi$. Let

$$
\mathcal{K}_{0}=\left\{\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathcal{K} \mid \theta_{n}=2 \pi\right\}, \quad \mathcal{C C}_{0}=\left\{(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathcal{C C} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathcal{K}_{0}\right\}
$$

their result can be expressed as follows:

Lemma 2.1. For any given positive mass vector $\boldsymbol{m} \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$, there exists a unique $\varphi_{\boldsymbol{m}} \in \mathcal{K}_{0}$ such that $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} U_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \varphi_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)=\mathbf{0}$. Moreover, this critical point is a minimum.

They also figure out that for any given positive mass vector $\boldsymbol{m}$, a centered cocircular central configuration (if exists), namely $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, should be the unique minimum of the function $U_{\alpha}$. That is to say

$$
(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0} \Rightarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}=\varphi_{\boldsymbol{m}}
$$

Let

$$
f_{K}(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta})=U_{\alpha}+\frac{U_{-2}}{K}
$$

where $K \geq \frac{2^{3+n}}{\alpha}$ is some constant, we can extend the above lemma a little bit:
Lemma 2.2. For any given positive mass vector $\boldsymbol{m} \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$ and real number $K \geq$ $\frac{2^{3+n}}{\alpha}$, there exists a unique $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}} \in \mathcal{K}_{0}$ such that $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)=\mathbf{0}$. Moreover, this critical point is a minimum and $(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$ implies $\boldsymbol{\theta}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}$.

Proof. For any given number $\beta \neq 0$, we compute that

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial \theta_{i} \partial \theta_{j}} U_{\beta}=\frac{-\beta m_{i} m_{j}\left(1+\beta \cos ^{2} \frac{\theta_{j}-\theta_{i}}{2}\right)}{\left[2 \sin \frac{\theta_{j}-\theta_{i}}{2}\right] \beta+2}, \quad \text { if } i \neq j \\
\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial \theta_{i}^{2}} U_{\beta}=-\sum_{j \neq i}^{n} \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial \theta_{i} \partial \theta_{j}} U_{\beta}
\end{array}\right.
$$

So we have

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial \theta_{i}^{2}} f_{K}=-\sum_{j \neq i}^{n} \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial \theta_{i} \partial \theta_{j}} f_{K}
$$

and for $i \neq j$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial \theta_{i} \partial \theta_{j}} f_{K} & =m_{i} m_{j}\left[\frac{-\alpha\left(1+\alpha \cos ^{2} \frac{\theta_{j}-\theta_{i}}{2}\right)}{\left|2 \sin \frac{\theta_{j}-\theta_{i}}{2}\right| \alpha+2}+\frac{2-4 \cos ^{2} \frac{\theta_{j}-\theta_{i}}{2}}{K}\right] \\
& \leq m_{i} m_{j}\left[\frac{-\alpha\left(1+\alpha \cos ^{2} \frac{\theta_{j}-\theta_{i}}{2}\right)}{2^{\alpha+2}}+\frac{2-4 \cos ^{2} \frac{\theta_{j}-\theta_{i}}{2}}{K}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

When $K \geq \frac{2^{3+n}}{\alpha}$, we have

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial \theta_{i} \partial \theta_{j}} f_{K} \leq m_{i} m_{j}\left[\frac{-\alpha\left(1+\alpha \cos ^{2} \frac{\theta_{j}-\theta_{i}}{2}\right)}{2^{\alpha+2}}+\frac{\alpha}{2^{2+\alpha}}-\frac{4 \cos ^{2} \frac{\theta_{j}-\theta_{i}}{2}}{K}\right] \leq 0
$$

Thus the Hessian matrix $D^{2} f_{K}=\left(\frac{\partial^{2} f_{K}}{\partial \theta_{i} \partial \theta_{j}}\right)_{n \times n}$ is diagonally dominant. So the quadratic form $u^{T}\left(D^{2} f_{K}\right) u \geq 0$, where the equality holds if and only if $u$ is a scalar multiple of $\mathbf{1}$ (see Remark 1 below). This vector corresponds to the translational invariance of $f_{K}$, which can be removed by specifying $\theta_{n}=2 \pi$. Since $\lim _{\boldsymbol{\theta} \rightarrow \partial \mathcal{K}_{0}} f_{K}(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta})=+\infty$, there exists a unique critical point (which is a minimum) $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}} \in \mathcal{K}_{0}$ of $f_{K}$.

So if $(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$ is a centered co-circular $\mathrm{CC},(2.1)$ and (2.2) are satisfied and thus $\boldsymbol{\theta}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}$ is the unique minimum of the function $f_{K}, K \geq \frac{2^{3+n}}{\alpha}$. We point out that because (2.2) can be deduced from (2.1), $\varphi_{\boldsymbol{m}}$ in Lemma 2.1 is equal to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}$ in this lemma.

Remark 1. We say $A=\left(a_{i j}\right)_{n \times n}$ is a diagonally dominant matrix, if $\left|a_{i i}\right| \geq$ $\sum_{j \neq i}\left|a_{i j}\right|$ for $i=1,2, \ldots, n$. A symmetric diagonally dominant real matrix with nonnegative diagonal entries is positive semidefinite. Moreover, if the off-diagonal entries of the symmetric real matrix $A$ are non-positive and $a_{i i}=-\sum_{j \neq i} a_{i j}>0$ for $i=1,2, \ldots, n$ (i.e., $A \mathbf{1}=0$ ), then $A$ is positive semidefinite and the vector $\mathbf{1}$ is its unique zero eigenvector. To see the uniqueness, we suppose there is another vector $\boldsymbol{v}=\left(v_{1}, \ldots, v_{n}\right)^{T}$ not parallels to $\mathbf{1}$ such that $A \boldsymbol{v}=\mathbf{0}$. Then we can choose $j_{0}$ such that $v_{j_{0}} \geq v_{j}, \forall j=1,2, \ldots, n$ and $v_{j_{0}}>v_{j_{1}}$ for some $j_{1}$. It is not difficult to check that the $j_{0}$-th element of $A \boldsymbol{v}$ is strictly greater than zero, contradicts with $A \boldsymbol{v}=\mathbf{0}$.

# 3. SYMMETRY OF CENTERED CO-CIRCULAR CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS 

In this section, we study the symmetry of centered co-circular CCs. It is intuitional that a reflection or a cyclic permutation of the co-circular CC is also a co-circular CC. More precisely, if we denote

$$
P=\left(\begin{array}{cccccc}
0 & 1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & \ldots & 0 & 0 \\
. & . & . & \ldots & . & . \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \ldots & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 0 & \ldots & 0 & 0
\end{array}\right) S=\left(\begin{array}{cccccc}
0 & 0 & \ldots & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \ldots & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
. & . & \ldots & . & . \\
1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \ldots & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right)
$$

and let $G=<P, S>$ be the dihedral group generated by the matrix $P$ and $S$. Then for all $g \in G$, we have

$$
(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathcal{C C} \Leftrightarrow(g \boldsymbol{m}, g \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathcal{C C}
$$

This is because (2.1) and (2.2) are invariant if we take the same permutation on indices of $\boldsymbol{m}$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ simultaneously. Moreover, to restrict the angles $\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathcal{K}_{0}$, we can let

$$
\mathcal{P}=\left(\begin{array}{cccccc}
-1 & 1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 & 0 \\
-1 & 0 & 1 & \ldots & 0 & 0 \\
. & . & . & \ldots & . & . \\
-1 & 0 & 0 & \ldots & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \ldots & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right) \mathcal{S}=\left(\begin{array}{cccccc}
0 & 0 & \ldots & 0 & -1 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & \ldots & -1 & 0 & 1 \\
. & . & \ldots & . & . & . \\
-1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & \ldots & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right)
$$

then $\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathcal{K}_{0}$ if and only if $\mathcal{P}^{h} \mathcal{S}^{l} \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathcal{K}_{0}, \forall h, l \in \mathbb{Z}$. For any $g=P^{h} S^{l} \in G$, letting $\tilde{g}=\mathcal{P}^{h} \mathcal{S}^{l}$, we can define the group representation

$$
g \cdot(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta})=(g \boldsymbol{m}, \tilde{g} \boldsymbol{\theta})
$$

We also recall that for given positive mass vector $\boldsymbol{m}$, the unique minimum of $\left.f_{K}\right|_{\mathcal{K}_{0}}$ always exists (see Lemma 2.2), and we denote it as $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}} \in \mathcal{K}_{0}$. It will be a centered co-circular CC if it also satisfies the second part of equations (2.1) and (2.2).
Lemma 3.1. Suppose $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$ form a centered co-circular central configuration, then
(1) $g \cdot\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}, \forall g \in G$;
(2) $f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)=f_{K}\left(g \boldsymbol{m}, \tilde{g} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \leq f_{K}\left(g \boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)$ and $\tilde{g} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{g m}}$;
(3) $\boldsymbol{m}=g \boldsymbol{m}$ implies $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}=\tilde{g} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}$.

Proof. For $\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathcal{K}_{0}$ which means $0<\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<\cdots<\theta_{n}=2 \pi$, we have

$$
\mathcal{P} \boldsymbol{\theta}=\left(\theta_{2}-\theta_{1}, \theta_{3}-\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{n}-\theta_{1}, \theta_{1}-\theta_{1}+2 \pi\right) \in \mathcal{K}_{0}
$$

$$
\mathcal{S} \boldsymbol{\theta}=\left(2 \pi-\theta_{n-1}, 2 \pi-\theta_{n-2}, \ldots, 2 \pi-\theta_{1}, 2 \pi\right) \in \mathcal{K}_{0}
$$

They are the rotation or reflection on indices of the configuration $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ plus a translation. Since (2.1) and (2.2) are invariant by this group action, we have

$$
(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0} \Leftrightarrow(P \boldsymbol{m}, \mathcal{P} \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0} \Leftrightarrow(S \boldsymbol{m}, \mathcal{S} \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0} \Leftrightarrow g \cdot(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}
$$

Then

$$
f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)=f_{K}\left(g \boldsymbol{m}, \hat{g} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)
$$

follows and the uniqueness of the minimum implies that $\hat{g} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{g} \boldsymbol{m}}$. Applying Lemma 2.2, we have the following inequality

$$
f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)=f_{K}\left(g \boldsymbol{m}, \hat{g} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \leq f_{K}\left(g \boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)
$$

where the equality holds if and only if $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}=\hat{g} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}$. So if $\boldsymbol{m}=g \boldsymbol{m}$, we will always have the equality, then $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}=\hat{g} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}$. This finishes the proof.

This lemma tells us that, for a centered co-circular CC, the symmetry of the distribution of the masses can imply the the symmetry of the configuration. For example, if $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$ and $\boldsymbol{m}=P \boldsymbol{m}$ (i.e., all the masses are equal), we will have $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}=\mathcal{P} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}$, which is just the equal-mass regular $n$-gon CC.

Corollary 3.2. For all integers $n \geq 3$ and real numbers $\alpha>0$, if all the masses are equal, then the unique centered co-circular central configuration for power-law potential $U_{\alpha}$ is the equal-mass regular n-gon central configuration.

Let the matrix

$$
H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}}=\left(r_{j k}^{-\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)+\frac{1}{K} r_{j k}^{2}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)\right)_{n \times n}
$$

which is determined by the mass vector $\boldsymbol{m}$ (seeing $r_{i j}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ as indirect variables) and consider the function

$$
h_{\boldsymbol{m}}(\boldsymbol{y})=f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)=\sum_{j<k}\left(\frac{y_{j} y_{k}}{r_{j k}^{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}+\frac{y_{j} y_{k} r_{j k}^{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{K}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{y}^{T} H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}} \boldsymbol{y}, \quad \boldsymbol{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}
$$

Then $h_{\boldsymbol{m}}(\boldsymbol{y})$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree 2 .
If $\boldsymbol{m}$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}$ also satisfy the second part of (2.1) and (2.2), i.e., $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$ is a centered co-circular CC, we have

$$
D h_{\boldsymbol{m}}(\boldsymbol{m})=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{m}} f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)=\left(\tilde{\lambda}+\frac{2 M}{K}\right) \mathbf{1}
$$

Writing $h_{\boldsymbol{m}}(\boldsymbol{y})$ in its Taylor series at the point $\boldsymbol{m}$, we get

$$
h_{\boldsymbol{m}}(\boldsymbol{y})=f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(\tilde{\lambda}+\frac{2 M}{K}\right)\left(y_{j}-m_{j}\right)+\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{m})^{T} H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{m})
$$

where $H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}}$ happens to be the Hessian of $h_{\boldsymbol{m}}(\boldsymbol{y})$ at the point $\boldsymbol{m}$.
So $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$ and $\sum_{j=1}^{n} y_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{i}$ would imply
(3.1) $f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)-f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)=\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{m})^{T} H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{m})=f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)$.

Moreover, for $\boldsymbol{y}=g \boldsymbol{m}$, we have the following lemma.

Lemma 3.3. For the positive mass vector $\boldsymbol{m}$, if

$$
\boldsymbol{m}^{T}(g-I)^{T} H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}}(g-I) \boldsymbol{m}<0, \quad \text { for some } g \in G
$$

or

$$
f_{K}\left(g \boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)<f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right), \text { for some } g \in G
$$

then there is no centered co-circular central configuration for $\boldsymbol{m}$.
Proof. We give the proof by contradiction. Suppose $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C} \mathcal{C}_{0}$, then the two conditions are equivalent by (3.1) in the above discussion. However Lemma 3.1 imply that

$$
f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)=f_{K}\left(g \boldsymbol{m}, \hat{g} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \leq f_{K}\left(g \boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)
$$

which is a contradiction.

This lemma is our first criterion to exclude any positive mass vector $\boldsymbol{m}$ which can not form a centered co-circular CC, although it seems quite hard to compute $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}$ or the matrix $H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}}$.

Lemma 3.4. Suppose $n$ positive masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n}$ form a centered co-circular central configuration, then exchange the positions of any two unequal masses $m_{i}, m_{j}$, the value of $f_{K}$ will strictly decrease.
Proof. Suppose $\boldsymbol{m}=\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n}\right)^{T}$ and $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C} \mathcal{C}_{0}$. Let

$$
\boldsymbol{m}^{\prime}=\left(m_{1}, \ldots, m_{j-1}, m_{k}, m_{j+1}, \ldots, m_{k-1}, m_{j}, m_{k+1}, \ldots, m_{n}\right)
$$

by (3.1) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_{\boldsymbol{m}}\left(\boldsymbol{m}^{\prime}\right) & =f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(\boldsymbol{m}^{\prime}-\boldsymbol{m}\right) H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}}\left(\boldsymbol{m}^{\prime}-\boldsymbol{m}\right)^{T} \\
& =f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)+\left(m_{k}-m_{j}\right)\left(r_{j k}^{-\alpha}+\frac{1}{K} r_{j k}^{2}\right)\left(m_{j}-m_{k}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

which implies

$$
f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}^{\prime}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)<f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right), \quad \text { if } \quad m_{j} \neq m_{k}
$$

This lemma shows us some positive possibility of Chenciner's question because the centered co-circular CC is some kind of minimum by Lemma 2.2.

Corollary 3.5. The equal-mass equilateral triangle $C C$ is the unique centered cocircular central configuration for the general power-law potential 3-body problem.

Proof. By Corollary 3.2, it is enough to show that all the masses are equal and we give the proof by contradiction. Suppose there is a 3 -body centered co-circular central configuration $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C} \mathcal{C}_{0}$ with unequal masses. Without loss of generality, we suppose $m_{1} \neq m_{2}$, then

$$
\boldsymbol{m}=\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}\right)^{T} \neq\left(m_{2}, m_{1}, m_{3}\right)^{T}=S \boldsymbol{m}
$$

Lemma 3.4 implies $f_{K}\left(S \boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)<f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)$, but by Lemma 3.3 there is no centered co-circular CC for such $\boldsymbol{m}$, contradicts.

Corollary 3.6. The equal-mass square $C C$ is the unique centered co-circular central configuration for the general power-law potential 4-body problem.

Proof. Suppose $\boldsymbol{m}=\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}, m_{4}\right)$ and $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$, then $S \boldsymbol{m}=\left(m_{3}, m_{2}, m_{1}, m_{4}\right)$ and $P^{2} S \boldsymbol{m}=\left(m_{1}, m_{4}, m_{3}, m_{2}\right)$ can also form co-circular central configurations. Applying Lemma 3.3 and 3.4, a similar discussion to the proof of Corollary 3.5 implies that $m_{1}=m_{3}, m_{2}=m_{4}$, thus $\boldsymbol{m}=S \boldsymbol{m}=P^{2} S \boldsymbol{m}$. By Lemma 3.1, we have

$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}=\mathcal{S} \boldsymbol{\theta}=\mathcal{P}^{2} \mathcal{S} \boldsymbol{\theta}
$$

which implies $\boldsymbol{\theta}=\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi, \frac{3 \pi}{2}, 2 \pi\right)$, a square. It is an easy exercise to show that the four masses should be equal to form a CC when the configuration is a square. There is also another more general result, Theorem 1 in , $n \geq 4$ masses located at the vertices of a regular polygon form a central configuration with homogeneous potential $U_{\alpha}(\alpha \geq 0)$ if and only if all the masses are equal.

It is more complicated when $n \geq 5$ because the order of masses will change by just exchanging two unequal masses, unless the mass vector has some highly symmetry. Corbera and Valls  studies a special case where all the masses are equal except one for the general power-law potential $n$-body problem. Using Lemma 3.3 and 3.4 , we can have a much simpler proof.

Corollary 3.7. In the general power-law potential $n$-body problem, there are no centered co-circular central configurations having all the masses equal except one.

Proof. Without loss of generality, suppose the mass vector is

$$
\boldsymbol{m}=\left(1, \ldots, 1, m_{n}\right)
$$

We give the proof by contradiction and suppose $m_{n} \neq 1$ and $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$. Because $(I-P) \boldsymbol{m}=\left(0, \ldots, 0,1-m_{n}, m_{n}-1\right)$, then Lemma 3.4 implies

$$
f_{K}\left(P \boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)<f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)
$$

which contradicts with Lemma 3.3.

Moreover, we have
Corollary 3.8. In the general power-law potential $n$-body problem, when $n$ is odd there are no centered co-circular central configurations having all the masses equal except two.

Proof. Without loss of generality, suppose the mass vector is

$$
\boldsymbol{m}=\left(1, \ldots, 1, m_{k}, 1, \ldots, 1, m_{n}\right)
$$

According to the previous corollary, it is enough to prove $m_{k}=1$ if $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$. Now suppose $m_{k} \neq 1$ and $n$ is an odd number, we have

$$
(I-S) \boldsymbol{m}=\left(0, \ldots, 0, m_{k}-1,0, \ldots, 0,1-m_{k}, 0, \ldots, 0,0\right)
$$

Then by Lemma 3.4,

$$
f_{K}\left(S \boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)<f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)
$$

contradicts with Lemma 3.3.

# 4. Proof of Theorem 1.1 

In this section we prove our main theorem. We give the proof by contradiction and throughout this proof we set $K=\frac{2^{3+\alpha}}{\alpha}$ for simplicity. Suppose $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$, and let

$$
\mathcal{H}_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}}=\left(\frac{2 U_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)}{M^{2}}+\frac{2}{K}\right) J_{n}-H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}}
$$

where $J_{n}$ is the $n \times n$ matrix of ones which means every element of $J_{n}$ is equal to one.

Lemma 4.1. If $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$ and $2^{\alpha+1} \frac{U_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)}{M^{2}} \leq 1+\frac{\alpha}{4}$, the symmetric matrix $\mathcal{H}_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}}$ is positive semi-definite and the only zero eigenvector is $\boldsymbol{m}$.

Proof. Let the diagonal matrix $\mathcal{M}=\operatorname{diag}\left\{m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n}\right\}$, then to prove this lemma is equivalent to prove that the symmetric matrix $\mathcal{M}^{T} \mathcal{H}_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}} \mathcal{M}$ is positive semi-definite and the only zero eigenvector is $\mathbf{1}$. Since $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$, then the second part of (2.1) and (2.2) imply that

$$
H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}} \boldsymbol{m}=\left(\frac{2 U_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)}{M}+\frac{2 M}{K}\right) \mathbf{1}
$$

Thus $\mathcal{H}_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}} \boldsymbol{m}=\mathbf{0}$ which implies

$$
\mathcal{M}^{T} \mathcal{H}_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}} \mathcal{M} \mathbf{1}=\mathbf{0}
$$

The condition $2^{\alpha+1} \frac{U_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)}{M^{2}} \leq 1+\frac{\alpha}{4}$ implies

$$
\frac{2 U_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)}{M^{2}} \leq \frac{1}{2^{\alpha}}+\frac{\alpha}{2^{2+\alpha}}=\frac{1}{2^{\alpha}}+\frac{2}{K}
$$

and a direct computation shows that for $r_{i j} \in(0,2]$ and $K=\frac{2^{3+\alpha}}{\alpha}$,

$$
\frac{1}{r_{i j}^{\alpha}}+\frac{r_{i j}^{2}}{K} \geq \frac{1}{2^{\alpha}}+\frac{4}{K}
$$

Thus the off-diagonal entries of the matrix $\mathcal{M}^{T} \mathcal{H}_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}} \mathcal{M}$

$$
m_{i} m_{j}\left[\left(\frac{2 U_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)}{M^{2}}+\frac{2}{K}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{r_{i j}^{\alpha}}+\frac{r_{i j}^{2}}{K}\right)\right] \leq 0
$$

Together with (4.1), we see that the matrix $\mathcal{M}^{T} \mathcal{H}_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}} \mathcal{M}$ is diagonally dominant and thus positive semi-definite. Moreover the vector $\mathbf{1}$ is its unique zero eigenvector(see Remark 1).

This lemma implies that, for unequal positive masses $\boldsymbol{m}$ and $2^{\alpha+1} \frac{U_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)}{M^{2}} \leq$ $1+\frac{\alpha}{4}$,

$$
\boldsymbol{m}^{T}(P-I)^{T} H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}}(P-I) \boldsymbol{m}<0
$$

Applying Lemma 3.3, we have the following corollary.
Corollary 4.2. A necessary condition for unequal positive masses $\boldsymbol{m}$ to form a centered co-circular central configuration, namely $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$, is that

$$
2^{\alpha+1} \frac{U_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)}{M^{2}}>1+\frac{\alpha}{4}
$$

Considering $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}$ is hard to compute and noticing that $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}$ is a minimum, we have the following corollary which can be seen as our second criterion to judge whether a masses vector $\boldsymbol{m}$ can not form a centered co-circular CC.

Corollary 4.3. For any given positive unequal masses $\boldsymbol{m}$, if there is some $\varphi \in \mathcal{K}_{0}$ such that

$$
2^{\alpha+1} \frac{U_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\varphi})}{M^{2}} \leq 1+\frac{\alpha}{4}
$$

then it can not be a centered co-circular central configuration, namely $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \notin$ $\mathcal{C} \mathcal{C}_{0}$.

We have already known that, the regular $n$-gon CC with equal masses is the trivial centered co-circular central configuration. When we consider the regular $n$-gon CC , it is interesting to notice that $\mathcal{H}_{\alpha, \mathbf{1}}, J_{n}, H_{\alpha, \mathbf{1}}$ are all circulant matrices $$.

An $n \times n$ matrix $C=\left(c_{k j}\right)$ is called circulant if $c_{k j}=c_{k-1, j-1}$ where $c_{0, j}$ and $c_{k, 0}$ are identified with $c_{n, j}$ and $c_{k, n}$, respectively. Thus every circulant matrix $C$ can be represented as $C=\sum_{j=1}^{n} c_{1 j} P^{j-1}$, then they all have the same eigenvectors $\boldsymbol{v}_{k}=\left(\xi_{k-1}, \xi_{k-1}^{2}, \cdots, \xi_{k-1}^{n}\right)^{T}$, where $\xi_{k}=e^{\frac{2 k a}{n} \sqrt{-1}}$ denote the $n$ complex $n$th roots of unity.

So considering the regular $n$-gon CC with equal masses $\left(\mathbf{1}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathbf{1}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$, if

$$
2^{\alpha+1} \frac{U_{\alpha}\left(\mathbf{1}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathbf{1}}\right)}{n^{2}}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc ^{\alpha} \frac{j \pi}{n} \leq 1+\frac{\alpha}{4}
$$

then by Lemma 4.1, $\mathcal{H}_{\alpha, \mathbf{1}}$ will be positive semi-definite with only one zero eigenvalue. This implies that the eigenvalues of $H_{\alpha, \mathbf{1}}$ are negative except the first one corresponding to the eigenvector $\boldsymbol{v}_{1}=\mathbf{1}$. So for all unequal masses $\boldsymbol{m}$, we have

$$
\frac{\boldsymbol{m}^{T} H_{\alpha, \mathbf{1}} \boldsymbol{m}}{M^{2}}<\frac{\mathbf{1}^{T} H_{\alpha, \mathbf{1}} \mathbf{1}}{n^{2}}
$$

We notice that $f_{K}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{m}^{T} H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}} \boldsymbol{m}$, so by Lemma 2.2

$$
\frac{\boldsymbol{m}^{T} H_{\alpha, \boldsymbol{m}} \boldsymbol{m}}{M^{2}} \leq \frac{\boldsymbol{m}^{T} H_{\alpha, \mathbf{1}} \boldsymbol{m}}{M^{2}} \leq \frac{\mathbf{1}^{T} H_{\alpha, \mathbf{1}} \mathbf{1}}{n^{2}}
$$

Suppose there exist some unequal masses $\boldsymbol{m}$ to form a centered co-circular CC, namely $\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right) \in \mathcal{C C}_{0}$, the above inequality implies

$$
\frac{2 U_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)+2 M^{2}}{M^{2}}<\frac{2 U_{\alpha}\left(\mathbf{1}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathbf{1}}\right)+2 n^{2}}{n^{2}}
$$

then

$$
2^{\alpha+1} \frac{U_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\boldsymbol{m}}\right)}{M^{2}}<1+\frac{\alpha}{4}
$$

So Theorem 1.1 follows by Corollary 4.3.

# Central configurations of nested rotated regular tetrahedra 

## A B S T R A C T

In this paper we prove that there are only two different classes of central configurations with convenient masses located at the vertices of two nested regular tetrahedra: either when one of the tetrahedra is a homothecy of the other one, or when one of the tetrahedra is a homothecy followed by a rotation of Euler angles $\alpha=\gamma=0$ and $\beta=\pi$ of the other one.

We also analyze the central configurations with convenient masses located at the vertices of three nested regular tetrahedra when one them is a homothecy of the other one, and the third one is a homothecy followed by a rotation of Euler angles $\alpha=\gamma=0$ and $\beta=\pi$ of the other two.

In all of these cases we have assumed that the masses on each tetrahedron are equal but masses on different tetrahedra could be different.
