## Keywords:

n-body problem
Spatial central configurations
Nested regular tetrahedra

## 1. Introduction

The equations of motion of the $N$-body problem in the three-dimensional Euclidean space are

$$
m_{i} \ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{i}=-\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{N} G m_{i} m_{j} \frac{\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}}{\left|\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right|^{3}}, \quad i=1, \ldots, N
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ is the position vector of the point mass $m_{i}$ in an inertial coordinate system and $G$ is the gravitational constant which can be taken equal to 1 by choosing the unit of time conveniently. We fix the center of mass $\sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i} \mathbf{q}_{i} / \sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i}$ of the system at the origin of $\mathbb{R}^{3 N}$. The configuration space of the $N$-body problem in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is

$$
\mathscr{E}=\left\{\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{N}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{3 N}: \sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i} \mathbf{q}_{i}=0, \mathbf{q}_{i} \neq \mathbf{q}_{j}, \text { for } i \neq j\right\}
$$

Given positive masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$ a configuration $\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{N}\right) \in \mathscr{E}$ is central if there exists a positive constant $\lambda$ such that

$$
\ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{i}=-\lambda \mathbf{q}_{i}, \quad i=1, \ldots, N
$$

that is, if the acceleration $\ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{i}$ of each point mass $m_{i}$ is proportional to its position $\mathbf{q}_{i}$ relative to the center of mass of the system and is directed towards the center of mass. In a central configuration system (1) can be written as

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{N} m_{i} \frac{\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}}{\left|\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right|^{3 / 2}}=\lambda \mathbf{q}_{i}, \quad i=1, \ldots, N
$$


Therefore a central configuration $\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{N}\right) \in \mathcal{E}$ of the $N$-body problem with positive masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$ is a solution of (2) with $\lambda>0$.

Two central configurations in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ are in the same class if there exist a rotation and a homothecy of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ which transform one into the other.

A general rotation in the three-dimensional Euclidean space having the origin of coordinates fixed is an element of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ that can be parametrized by using the Euler angles $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ via the rotation matrix $\mathcal{R}$ given by

$$
\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\cos \gamma & \sin \gamma & 0 \\
-\sin \gamma & \cos \gamma & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \cos \beta & \sin \beta \\
0 & -\sin \beta & \cos \beta
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\cos \alpha & \sin \alpha & 0 \\
-\sin \alpha & \cos \alpha & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right)
$$

where $\alpha \in[0,2 \pi), \beta \in[0, \pi]$ and $\gamma \in[0,2 \pi)$; see  for more details.
Consider two regular tetrahedra with vertices $\mathbf{q}_{i}$ and $\mathbf{q}_{i+4}$ for $i=1, \ldots, 4$ respectively. We say that these two tetrahedra are nested if they have the same center and the positions of the vertices of the two tetrahedra satisfy the relation $\mathbf{q}_{i+4}=$ $\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{q}_{i}$ for all $i=1, \ldots, 4$, for some scale factor $\rho$ and for some rotation matrix $\mathcal{R}$. Notice that if $\rho=1$, then $R \neq I d$ where Id denotes the identity matrix.

In a similar way if we consider three regular tetrahedra with vertices $\mathbf{q}_{i}, \mathbf{q}_{i+4}$ and $\mathbf{q}_{i+8}$ for $i=1, \ldots, 4$ respectively, then these three tetrahedra are called nested if they have the same center and the positions of the vertices of the three tetrahedra satisfy the relations $\mathbf{q}_{i+4}=\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{q}_{i}$ and $\mathbf{q}_{i+8}=R \mathcal{R}^{\prime} \mathbf{q}_{i}$ for all $i=1, \ldots, 4$, for some scale factors $\rho$ and $R$ and for some rotation matrices $\mathcal{R}$ and $\mathcal{R}^{\prime}$.

The configuration formed by four equal masses located at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron is central for the four-body problem; see for instance . In  and in  it is proved that the configuration formed by four equal masses $m_{1}$ located at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron and four additional masses $m_{2}$ located at the vertices of a second nested regular tetrahedron is central for the eight-body problem when $\mathcal{R}=I d$ and the ratio of the masses $m_{2} / m_{1}$ and the scale factor $\rho$ satisfy a convenient relation. In  it is proved that this kind of central configuration is also central when $\mathcal{R}$ is the rotation matrix of Euler angles $\alpha=0, \beta=\pi$ and $\gamma=0$. In Section 2 we summarize these results and we prove that these are the two unique classes of central configurations formed by two nested regular tetrahedra of the eight-body problem; see Theorem 2.

In Section 3 we provide a new class of central configurations of the 12-body problem consisting of three nested regular tetrahedra with one of them rotated with respect to the other two by a rotation matrix with Euler angles $\alpha=0, \beta=\pi$ and $\gamma=0$. Of course on each tetrahedron the four masses located on its vertices are equal; see Result 3. The central configurations of the 12-body problem consisting of three nested regular tetrahedra when $\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{R}^{\prime}=I d$ have been described in .

# 2. Two nested tetrahedra 

In this section we study the spatial central configurations of the eight-body problem with the masses located at the vertices of two nested regular tetrahedra. In particular we give all classes of central configurations formed by two nested regular tetrahedra of the eight-body problem

We assume that the masses on each tetrahedron are equal but the masses on different tetrahedra can be different. Taking conveniently the unit of masses we can assume that the masses of the tetrahedron with scale factor 1 are equal to 1 , that is $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=m_{4}=1$, and those of the tetrahedron with scale factor $\rho$ are equal to $m$, that is $m_{5}=m_{6}=m_{7}=m_{8}=m$. We also choose the unit of length in such a way that the edges of the tetrahedron with scale factor 1 have length 2.

Recall that the set of spatial central configurations is invariant under homothecies and rotations of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. So without loss of generality we can assume that $\rho \geqslant 1$ and that the positions of the vertices of the tetrahedron with scale factor 1 are $\mathbf{a}_{1}=(0,0, \sqrt{3 / 2})^{T}, \mathbf{a}_{2}=(0,2 / \sqrt{3},-1 / \sqrt{6})^{T}, \mathbf{a}_{3}=(1,-1 / \sqrt{3},-1 / \sqrt{6})^{T}$ and $\mathbf{a}_{4}=(-1,-1 / \sqrt{3},-1 / \sqrt{6})^{T}$.

In what follows a configuration of two nested regular tetrahedra means the configuration consisting of four equal masses $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=m_{4}=1$ at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron having the positions $\mathbf{a}_{i}$ for $i=1, \ldots, 4$ and four additional masses $m_{5}=m_{6}=m_{7}=m_{8}=m$ at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron having positions $\mathbf{q}_{i+4}=\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}$ for $i=1, \ldots, 4$, for some scale factor $\rho \geqslant 1$ and for some rotation matrix $\mathcal{R}$.

We say that two configurations of two nested regular tetrahedra with rotation matrices $\mathcal{R}$ and $\mathcal{R}^{\prime}$ respectively are in the same class if $\mathcal{R}$ and $\mathcal{R}^{\prime}$ are such that the set $\left\{\mathbf{q}_{5}, \mathbf{q}_{6}, \mathbf{q}_{7}, \mathbf{q}_{8}\right\}$ is the same for $\mathcal{R}$ and $\mathcal{R}^{\prime}$; that is, if $\left\{\mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{1}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{2}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{3}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{4}\right\}=$ $\left\{\mathcal{R}^{\prime} \mathbf{a}_{1}, \mathcal{R}^{\prime} \mathbf{a}_{2}, \mathcal{R}^{\prime} \mathbf{a}_{3}, \mathcal{R}^{\prime} \mathbf{a}_{4}\right\}$.

As usual $\langle\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}\rangle=\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathbf{v}$ denotes the scalar product of the vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$.
Lemma 1. Let

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f(i)=\sum_{j=1}^{4} \frac{3 / 2-\rho\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle}{\left(3 \rho^{2} / 2-2 \rho\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle+3 / 2\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& g(i)=\sum_{j=1}^{4} \frac{3 \rho / 2-\left\langle\mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle}{\left(3 \rho^{2} / 2-2 \rho\left\langle\mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle+3 / 2\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

for $i=1, \ldots, 4$.

A configuration of two nested regular tetrahedra is central for the eight-body problem if and only if one of the following statements holds.
(a) $f(1)=f(2)=f(3)=f(4), g(1)=g(2)=g(3)=g(4), 2 f(1) / 3-1 /\left(2 \rho^{3}\right) \neq 0$,

$$
\lambda=1 / 2+2 m f(i) / 3>0 \text { and } m=\frac{2 g(1) /(3 \rho)-1 / 2}{2 f(1) / 3-1 /\left(2 \rho^{3}\right)}>0
$$

(b) $f(1)=f(2)=f(3)=f(4), g(1)=g(2)=g(3)=g(4), 2 f(1) / 3-1 /\left(2 \rho^{3}\right)=2 g(1) /(3 \rho)-1 / 2=0$ and $\lambda=1 / 2+2 m f(i) / 3>0$ and $m>0$.
Proof. It is easy to check that for the configuration of two nested tetrahedra, system (2) can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{4} \frac{\mathbf{a}_{i}-\mathbf{a}_{j}}{\left|\mathbf{a}_{i}-\mathbf{a}_{j}\right|^{3}}+m \sum_{j=1}^{4} \frac{\mathbf{a}_{i}-\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}}{\left|\mathbf{a}_{i}-\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}\right|^{3}}=\lambda \mathbf{a}_{i} \\
& \sum_{j=1}^{4} \frac{\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}-\mathbf{a}_{j}}{\left|\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}-\mathbf{a}_{j}\right|^{3}}+m \sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{4} \frac{\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}-\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}}{\left|\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}-\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}\right|^{3}}=\lambda \rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

for $i=1, \ldots, 4$. We take the scalar product of the $i$-th equation of (3) with the vector $\mathbf{a}_{i}$ and the scalar product of the $i$-th equation of (4) with the vector $\mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{4} \frac{\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathbf{a}_{i}\right\rangle-\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle}{\left|\mathbf{a}_{i}-\mathbf{a}_{j}\right|^{3}}+m \sum_{j=1}^{4} \frac{\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathbf{a}_{i}\right\rangle-\rho\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle}{\left|\mathbf{a}_{i}-\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}\right|^{3}}=\lambda\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathbf{a}_{i}\right\rangle \\
& \sum_{j=1}^{4} \frac{\rho\left\langle\mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}\right\rangle-\left\langle\mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle}{\left|\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}-\mathbf{a}_{j}\right|^{3}}+m \sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{4} \frac{\rho\left\langle\mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}\right\rangle-\rho\left\langle\mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle}{\left|\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}-\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}\right|^{3}}=\lambda \rho\left\langle\mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}\right\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

for $i=1, \ldots, 4$. It is easy to check that $\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathbf{a}_{i}\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}\right\rangle=3 / 2,\left\langle\mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle,\left|\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}-\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}\right|^{3}=\rho^{3}\left|\mathbf{a}_{i}-\mathbf{a}_{j}\right|^{3}$ and

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{4} \frac{\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathbf{a}_{i}\right\rangle-\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle}{\left|\mathbf{a}_{i}-\mathbf{a}_{j}\right|^{3}}=\frac{3}{4}
$$

for all $i=1, \ldots, 4$. On the other hand

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left|\mathbf{a}_{i}-\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}\right|=\left(3 \rho^{2} / 2-2 \rho\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle+3 / 2\right)^{1 / 2} \\
& \left|\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}-\mathbf{a}_{j}\right|=\left(3 \rho^{2} / 2-2 \rho\left\langle\mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{i}, \mathbf{a}_{j}\right\rangle+3 / 2\right)^{1 / 2}
\end{aligned}
$$

So Eqs. (5) and (6) become

$$
\frac{3}{4}+m f(i)=\frac{3}{2} \lambda, \quad g(i)+m \frac{3}{4 \rho^{2}}=\frac{3 \rho}{2} \lambda
$$

for $i=1, \ldots, 4$. In short, the configuration consisting of two nested tetrahedra is central if and only if $(\lambda, m)$ is a solution of (7) satisfying that $\lambda>0$ and $m>0$.

From the first equation of (7) we have that $\lambda=1 / 2+2 m f(i) / 3$ for $i=1, \ldots, 4$; this implies that $f(1)=f(2)=f(3)=$ $f(4)$. From the second equation of (7) we have $\lambda=2 g(i) /(3 \rho)+m /\left(2 \rho^{3}\right)$ for $i=1, \ldots, 4$, so $g(1)=g(2)=g(3)=g(4)$. Equating the two expressions for $\lambda$ for $i=1$ we have that if $2 f(1) / 3-1 /\left(2 \rho^{3}\right) \neq 0$, then

$$
m=\frac{2 g(1) /(3 \rho)-1 / 2}{2 f(1) / 3-1 /\left(2 \rho^{3}\right)}
$$

This proves statement (a).
Moreover if $2 f(1) / 3-1 /\left(2 \rho^{3}\right)=2 g(1) /(3 \rho)-1 / 2=0$, then the solution of (7) is $\lambda=1 / 2+2 m f(i) / 3>0$ and $m>0$, which concludes the proof of statement (b).

Theorem 2. The following statements hold.
(a) There are two unique classes of central configurations of two nested regular tetrahedra:
(a.1) The class of configurations of Type I with $\left\{\mathbf{q}_{5}, \mathbf{q}_{6}, \mathbf{q}_{7}, \mathbf{q}_{8}\right\}=\left\{\rho \mathbf{a}_{1}, \rho \mathbf{a}_{2}, \rho \mathbf{a}_{3}, \rho \mathbf{a}_{4}\right\}$.
(a.2) The class of configurations of Type II with $\left\{\mathbf{q}_{5}, \mathbf{q}_{6}, \mathbf{q}_{7}, \mathbf{q}_{8}\right\}=\left\{\rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{1}, \rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{2}, \rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{3}, \rho \mathcal{R} \mathbf{a}_{4}\right\}$ and

$$
\mathcal{R}=P=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & -1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -1
\end{array}\right)
$$

These two classes of configurations are shown in Fig. 1.

Proof of Theorem 2. We know that the spatial central configurations are invariant under rotations of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. Consider the rotation

$$
A=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
1 / 2 & \sqrt{3} / 2 & 0 \\
1 /(2 \sqrt{3}) & -1 / 6 & 2 \sqrt{2} / 3 \\
\sqrt{2 / 3} & -\sqrt{2} / 3 & -1 / 3
\end{array}\right)
$$

It is easy to check that $A \mathbf{a}_{1}=\mathbf{a}_{2}, A \mathbf{a}_{2}=\mathbf{a}_{3}, A \mathbf{a}_{3}=\mathbf{a}_{1}$ and $A \mathbf{a}_{4}=\mathbf{a}_{4}$. Since the rotation $A$ leaves invariant the tetrahedron with scale factor 1 , it also must leave invariant the one with scale factor $\rho$. This means that the sets $\left\{\mathbf{q}_{5}, \mathbf{q}_{6}, \mathbf{q}_{7}, \mathbf{q}_{8}\right\}$ and $\left\{A \mathbf{q}_{5}, A \mathbf{q}_{6}, A \mathbf{q}_{7}, A \mathbf{q}_{8}\right\}$ must be the same. Then either $A \mathbf{q}_{5}=\mathbf{q}_{5}$, or $A \mathbf{q}_{5}=\mathbf{q}_{6}$, or $A \mathbf{q}_{5}=\mathbf{q}_{7}$, or $A \mathbf{q}_{5}=\mathbf{q}_{8}$. On the other hand, by Lemma 1 the rotation matrix $\mathcal{R}$ provides a central configuration of two nested tetrahedra if $f(1)=f(2)=f(3)=f(4)$ and $g(1)=g(2)=g(3)=g(4)$.

We start analyzing the solutions of the system $\mathbf{f}_{5}=A \mathbf{q}_{5}-\mathbf{q}_{5}=0$ where

$$
\mathbf{f}_{5}=\left(\begin{array}{c}
\frac{\sin \beta(\sqrt{3} \sin \gamma-3 \cos \gamma)}{\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{2 \sqrt{2}}}
\end{array}\right)
$$

From the first equation of $\mathbf{f}_{5}=0$ we have that $\beta=0$, or $\beta=\pi$, or $\gamma=\pi / 3$, or $\gamma=4 \pi / 3$. It is easy to check that $\beta=0$ and $\beta=\pi$ do not provide solutions of the full system $\mathbf{f}_{5}=0$. If $\gamma=\pi / 3$, then there is a unique solution of $\mathbf{f}_{5}=\mathbf{0}$ with $\beta \in[0, \pi]$, the solution $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)=(\alpha, 2 \arctan (1 / \sqrt{2}), \pi / 3)=\sigma_{1}(\alpha)$. When $\gamma=4 \pi / 3$ the system $\mathbf{f}_{5}=\mathbf{0}$ has a unique solution with $\beta \in[0, \pi]$ which is given by $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)=(\alpha, 2 \arctan \sqrt{2}, 4 / 3)=\sigma_{2}(\alpha)$. These two solutions of $\mathbf{f}_{5}=\mathbf{0}$ leave invariant the tetrahedron with scale factor $\rho$.

It only remains to find the values of $\alpha$ for which $\sigma_{1}(\alpha)$ and $\sigma_{2}(\alpha)$ satisfy that $f(1)=f(2)=f(3)=f(4)$ and $g(1)=g(2)=g(3)=g(4)$. The functions $f(i)$ and $g(i)$ evaluated at $\sigma_{1}(\alpha)$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f(1)=f(2)=f(3)=-\frac{\sqrt{2}(\rho-3)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+F(\alpha)+F(\alpha+2 \pi / 3)+F(\alpha+4 \pi / 3) \\
& f(4)=\frac{\sqrt{2 / 3}}{(\rho+1)^{2}}-\frac{3 \sqrt{2}(\rho-3)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& g(1)=\frac{3 \sqrt{2}(3 \rho-1)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2 / 3}}{(\rho+1)^{2}} \\
& g(2)=g(3)=g(4)=\frac{\sqrt{2}(3 \rho-1)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+G(\alpha)+G(\alpha+2 \pi / 3)+G(\alpha+4 \pi / 3)
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& F(\alpha)=\frac{\sqrt{6}(8 \rho \cos \alpha+\rho+9)}{\left(9 \rho^{2}+16 \rho \cos \alpha+2 \rho+9\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& G(\alpha)=\frac{\sqrt{6}(9 \rho+8 \cos \alpha+1)}{\left(9 \rho^{2}+16 \rho \cos \alpha+2 \rho+9\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

We must find the values of $\alpha$ for which $\sigma_{1}(\alpha)$ is a solution of the system $e_{1}(\alpha)=f(1)-f(4)=0$ and $e_{2}(\alpha)=g(1)-g(2)=$ 0 . We consider the additional equation

$$
e(\alpha)=\frac{e_{1}(\alpha)+e_{2}(\alpha)}{\rho-1}=H_{0}-H(\alpha)-H(\alpha+2 \pi / 3)-H(\alpha+4 / \pi / 3)=0
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& H_{0}=\frac{8 \sqrt{2}}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& H(\alpha)=\frac{8 \sqrt{6}(1-\cos \alpha)}{\left(9 \rho^{2}+16 \rho \cos \alpha+2 \rho+9\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $H_{0}>0$ for all $\rho \geqslant 1$ and $H(\alpha) \geqslant 0$ for all $\rho \geqslant 1$ and $\alpha \in[0,2 \pi)$. Next we prove that $e(\alpha) \leqslant 0$ for all $\rho \geqslant 1$ and $\alpha \in[0,2 \pi)$. First we find the minimum values of the function $h(\alpha)=H(\alpha)+H(\alpha+2 \pi / 3)+H(\alpha+4 / \pi / 3)$.

It is easy to check that $h(\alpha)$ is a periodic function of period $2 \pi / 3$. Moreover $h(2 \pi / 3-\alpha)=h(\alpha)$ so it is sufficient to study the behaviour of $h(\alpha)$ for $\alpha \in[0, \pi / 3]$. The possible minima of $h(\alpha)$ are given by the solutions of $h^{\prime}(\alpha)=0$ where

$$
h^{\prime}(\alpha)=H^{\prime}(\alpha)+H^{\prime}(\alpha+2 \pi / 3)+H^{\prime}(\alpha+4 \pi / 3)
$$

and

$$
H^{\prime}(\alpha)=\frac{8 \sqrt{6}\left(9 \rho^{2}-8 \rho \cos \alpha+26 \rho+9\right) \sin \alpha}{\left(9 \rho^{2}+16 \rho \cos \alpha+2 \rho+9\right)^{5 / 2}}
$$

In order to solve the equation $h^{\prime}(\alpha)=0$, we eliminate the radicals and the denominators of the equation by using the procedure described in the Appendix and we set $c=\cos \alpha$. The result is the polynomial equation

$$
21233664(c-1)(c+1)(2 c-1)^{2}(2 c+1)^{2} \rho^{2} E(c, \rho)=0
$$

in the variable $c$ with coefficients depending on $\rho$ where $E(c, \rho)$ is a polynomial of degree 21 in $c$. Notice that we are only interested in solutions of $h^{\prime}(\alpha)=0$ with $\alpha \in[0, \pi / 3]$, so we only consider solutions of (8) with $c \in[1 / 2,1]$.

We solve symbolically with the help of the algebraic manipulator Mathematica the equation $E(c, \rho)=0$. We see that only three of the 21 solutions $c(\rho)$ are real for all $\rho \geqslant 1$; one satisfies $c(\rho) \geqslant 1.8638527724 \ldots$ for all $\rho \geqslant 1$, another one satisfies $c(\rho) \geqslant 1.9150397104 \ldots$, and finally the third one $c(\rho)=\tilde{c}(\rho)$ satisfies $\tilde{c}(\rho) \in[0.5088804885 \ldots, 1]$ for $\rho \in\left[1, \rho^{*}\right]$ and $\tilde{c}(\rho)>1$ for $\rho>\rho^{*}$. Here $\rho^{*}=6.1180170733 \ldots$ is the unique real solution of $E(1, \rho)=0$ with $\rho \geqslant 1$. Two of the solutions of $E(c, \rho)=0$ are real for $\rho \in\left[1, \rho^{*}\right]$ and in $\mathbb{C} \backslash \mathbb{R}$ for $\rho>\rho^{*}$; moreover for these two real solutions $c(\rho) \notin[1 / 2,1]$. The rest of the solutions of $E(c, \rho)=0$ are in $\mathbb{C} \backslash \mathbb{R}$ for all $\rho \geqslant 1$. In short, there is a unique solution $c(\rho)=\tilde{c}(\rho)$ with $\rho \in\left[1, \rho^{*}\right]$ satisfying that $c(\rho) \in[1 / 2,1]$. This solution provides a solution of the initial equation $h^{\prime}(\alpha)=0$ only when $\rho=\rho^{*}$ and $c=1$. Consequently the solutions of (8) with $c(\rho) \in[1 / 2,1]$ that provide solutions of $h^{\prime}(\alpha)=0$ are $c=1 / 2$ and $c=1$ for all $\rho \geqslant 1$. Therefore $h^{\prime}(\alpha)=0$ has two unique solutions in the interval $[0, \pi / 3]$ that are independent of $\rho$, $\alpha=0$ which corresponds to a minimum and $\alpha=\pi / 3$ which corresponds to a maximum. Thus the minimum values of $h(\alpha)$ in the interval $[0,2 \pi)$ are $\alpha=0, \alpha=2 \pi / 3$ and $\alpha=4 \pi / 3$. Furthermore $h(0)=h(2 \pi / 3)=h(4 \pi / 3)=H_{0}$. Consequently $e(\alpha) \leqslant 0$ for all $\rho \geqslant 1$ and $e(\alpha)=0$ if and only if $\alpha=0, \alpha=2 \pi / 3$ or $\alpha=4 \pi / 3$. It is easy to check that all these solutions satisfy the system $e_{1}(\alpha)=0$ and $e_{2}(\alpha)=0$. On the other hand, in a similar way it can be proved that the solutions of the system $e_{1}(\alpha)=0$ and $e_{2}(\alpha)=0$ for $\rho=1$ are also $\alpha=0, \alpha=2 \pi / 3$ or $\alpha=4 \pi / 3$.

In short, there are three rotations for $\sigma_{1}(\alpha)$ that satisfy conditions of Lemma 1 ; they have Euler rotation angles $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (0,2 \arctan (1 / \sqrt{2}), \pi / 3) \\
& (2 \pi / 3,2 \arctan (1 / \sqrt{2}), \pi / 3) \\
& (4 \pi / 3,2 \arctan (1 / \sqrt{2}), \pi / 3)
\end{aligned}
$$

All these rotations give configurations of Type II.
Proceeding in a similar way with the solution $\sigma_{2}(\alpha)$ we obtain three additional rotations that satisfy the conditions of Lemma 1; they have Euler rotation angles $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (\pi / 3,2 \arctan \sqrt{2}, 4 \pi / 3) \\
& (\pi, 2 \arctan \sqrt{2}, 4 \pi / 3) \\
& (5 \pi / 3,2 \arctan \sqrt{2}, 4 \pi / 3)
\end{aligned}
$$

All these rotations give configurations of Type I.
We have just proved that all the rotations satisfying $\mathbf{f}_{5}=\mathbf{0}$ and the conditions of Lemma 1 provide configurations of either Type I or Type II.

By using similar arguments, we find all the rotations that satisfy the system $A \mathbf{q}_{5}-\mathbf{q}_{5}=\mathbf{0}$, for $i=6,7,8$, and the conditions of Lemma 1; moreover we see that all these rotations provide configurations of either Type I or Type II. The Euler rotation angles $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ of those rotations classified by the type of configuration that they provide are given in Tables 1-3.

In short, all rotations that satisfy conditions of Lemma 1 provide configurations of either Type I or Type II. This completes the proof of statement (a).

Statement (b) is proved in  by using the choice of the units of mass and length that we use here and it is proved in  with a different choice of the units. Here by using Lemma 1 we give a new and shorter proof of this result. Indeed, statement

(b) is an immediate consequence of Lemma 1 together with statement (a). In statement (a) we have proved that if $\mathbf{q}_{5}=\rho \mathbf{a}_{1}$, $\mathbf{q}_{6}=\rho \mathbf{a}_{2}, \mathbf{q}_{7}=\rho \mathbf{a}_{3}$, and $\mathbf{q}_{8}=\rho \mathbf{a}_{4}$ then the hypotheses of Lemma 1 hold. Statement (c) is proved in  by using choices of the units of mass and length different to the ones used here. Statement (c) is also an immediate consequence of Lemma 1 together with statement (a). As above in statement (a) we have proved that if $\mathbf{q}_{5}=\rho P \mathbf{a}_{1}, \mathbf{q}_{6}=\rho P \mathbf{a}_{2}, \mathbf{q}_{7}=\rho P \mathbf{a}_{3}$, and $\mathbf{q}_{8}=\rho P \mathbf{a}_{4}$ then the hypotheses of Lemma 1 hold. So applying this Lemma 1 we obtain the expressions of $\lambda$ and $m$ which provide a central configuration if $\lambda>0$ and $m>0$. We see that $2 f(1) / 3-1 /\left(2 \rho^{3}\right)=0$ at $\rho=\alpha_{2}$ and $2 g(1) /(3 \rho)-1 / 2=0$ at $\rho=\alpha_{1}$; in particular, $\lambda>0$ and $m>0$ when $\rho \in\left[1, \alpha_{1}\right) \cup\left(\alpha_{2}, \infty\right)$. Moreover $m=m(\rho)$ is decreasing in the interval $\left[1, \alpha_{2}\right)$ with $m(1)=1$ and $\lim _{\rho \rightarrow \alpha_{2}^{-}} m(\rho)=-\infty$, it is decreasing in the interval $\left(\alpha_{2}, \alpha_{3}\right)$, increasing in the interval $\left(\alpha_{3}, \infty\right)$, the point $\rho=\alpha_{3}$ is a minimum with $m(\rho)=m_{0}$ and $\lim _{\rho \rightarrow \alpha_{2}^{+}} m(\rho)=\infty$ and $\lim _{\rho \rightarrow+\infty} m(\rho)=\infty$. These properties of $m(\rho)$ together with the fact that the faces of the nested tetrahedra intersect when $1 \leqslant \rho \leqslant 3$ prove statements (c.1), (c.2), (c.3), and (c.4).

# 3. Three nested tetrahedra 

In this section we study the spatial central configurations of the 12-body problem when the masses are located at the vertices of three nested regular tetrahedra with scale factors $1, \rho$ and $R$ and some of them rotated with respect to the others by a rotation of Euler angles $\alpha=0, \beta=\pi$ and $\gamma=0$ (i.e. by a rotation with rotation matrix $P$ ). Taking conveniently the unit of masses we can assume that all the masses of the tetrahedron with scale factor 1 are equal to 1 . We also choose the unit of length in such a way that the edges of the tetrahedron with scale factor 1 have length 2 . Without loss of generality we can assume that the configuration has only one rotated tetrahedron which could be either the inner, the middle or the outer one. This is due to the fact that central configurations are invariant under rotations and a configuration with two rotated tetrahedra can be transformed into a configuration with only one rotated tetrahedron by performing a rotation of Euler angles $\alpha=0, \beta=\pi$ and $\gamma=0$. Central configurations are also invariant under homothecies, so we can assume that the rotated tetrahedron is the one with scale factor $\rho$, and that $1 \leqslant \rho<R$ when the rotated tetrahedron is the middle one, $1<R \leqslant \rho$ when the rotated tetrahedron is the outer one, and finally $0<\rho<1<R$ when the rotated tetrahedron is the inner one (see Fig. 2). We define

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathcal{O}_{m}=\left\{(\rho, R) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: 1 \leqslant \rho<R\right\} \\
& \mathcal{O}_{v}=\left\{(\rho, R) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: 1<R \leqslant \rho\right\} \\
& \mathcal{O}_{i}=\left\{(\rho, R) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: 0<\rho<1<R\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Result 3. Consider four equal masses $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=m_{4}=1$ at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron with edge length 2 having positions $\mathbf{a}_{1}, \mathbf{a}_{2}, \mathbf{a}_{3}$ and $\mathbf{a}_{4}$. Consider four additional equal masses $m_{5}=m_{6}=m_{7}=m_{8}=m$ at the vertices of a second nested

regular tetrahedron having positions $\mathbf{q}_{i+4}=\rho P \mathbf{a}_{i}$ for all $i=1, \ldots, 4$ with $\rho>0$. Finally we consider four additional equal masses $m_{9}=m_{10}=m_{11}=m_{12}=M$ at the vertices of a third nested regular tetrahedron having positions $\mathbf{q}_{i+8}=R \mathbf{a}_{i}$ for all $i=1, \ldots, 4$ with $R>1$ (see Fig. 2). Then the following statements hold.
(a) Such configuration is central for the spatial 12-body problem when $m=m(\rho, R)$ and $M=M(\rho, R)$ are given by the expression (11) and $(R, \rho) \in \mathscr{D}=\left\{(R, \rho) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: \operatorname{det}(A) \neq 0, m(R, \rho)>0, M(R, \rho)>0, \rho>0, R>1\right\}$ (see (11) for the definition of $A$ and see Fig. 3 for the plot of $\mathscr{D}$ ).
(b) The set $\mathscr{D}$ is formed by the disjoint union of the sets $\mathscr{D}_{i}$ for $i=1, \ldots, 6$ defined in Fig. 3. Then the regions $\mathscr{D}_{i}$ provide central configurations of the 12-body problem with the masses located at the vertices of three nested regular tetrahedra satisfying the following.
(b.1) The rotated tetrahedron is the inner one and it intersects only the middle one when $(\rho, R) \in \mathscr{D}_{2} \cap \mathcal{O}_{i}$, it intersects the middle one and the outer one when $(\rho, R) \in \mathscr{D}_{4} \cap \mathcal{O}_{i}$, and the three tetrahedra do not intersect when $(\rho, R) \in \mathscr{D}_{1}$.
(b.2) The rotated tetrahedron is the middle one and it intersects only the inner one when $(\rho, R) \in \mathscr{D}_{2} \cap \mathcal{O}_{m}$ and when $(\rho, R) \in \mathscr{D}_{3} \cap\{\rho \leqslant 3\}$, it intersects the inner one and the outer one when $(\rho, R) \in \mathscr{D}_{5} \cap \mathcal{O}_{m} \cap\{\rho \leqslant 3\}$ and when $(\rho, R) \in \mathscr{D}_{4} \cap \mathcal{O}_{m}$, it intersects only the outer one when $(\rho, R) \in \mathscr{D}_{5} \cap \mathcal{O}_{m} \cap\{\rho>3\}$, and the three tetrahedra do not intersect when $(\rho, R) \in \mathscr{D}_{3} \cap\{\rho>3\}$.
(b.3) The rotated tetrahedron is the outer one and it intersects only the middle one when $(\rho, R) \in \mathscr{D}_{5} \cap \mathcal{O}_{n} \cap\{\rho>3\}$, it intersects the inner one and the middle one when $(\rho, R) \in \mathscr{D}_{5} \cap \mathcal{O}_{n} \cap\{\rho \leqslant 3\}$, and the three tetrahedra do not intersect when $(\rho, R) \in \mathscr{D}_{6}$.
(c) Let

$$
m(M, \rho, R)=\frac{\rho^{2}(\rho+2 f(\rho, 1))}{2 \rho^{3} f(1, \rho)+1}-M \frac{2 \rho^{2}\left(\rho g_{1}(R)-f(\rho, R)\right)}{2 \rho^{3} f(1, \rho)+1}
$$

and $M_{0}(\rho, R)=\left(\rho^{2}(\rho+2 f(\rho, 1))\right) / 2 \rho^{2}\left(\rho g_{1}(R)-f(\rho, R)\right)$ (see (9) for the definitions of $f$ and $\left.g_{1}\right)$, and let $\mathbf{p}=\left(p_{1}, p_{2}\right)=$ $(1.5094116757 \ldots, 1.9479968088 \ldots)$ and $\mathbf{q}=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}\right)=(1.9926247501 \ldots, 31.4606148079 \ldots)$ be the solutions of the system $\operatorname{det}(A)=\operatorname{det}\left(A_{2}\right)=\operatorname{det}\left(A_{3}\right)=0$ (see (11) for the definitions of $A_{2}$ and $\left.A_{3}\right)$. Then the following statements hold.
(c.1) For each $M>M_{0}(\mathbf{p})=0.1252891302 \ldots$ and $m=m(M, \mathbf{p})=-0.4001317738 \cdots+3.1936671053 \ldots M$ we have a central configuration of the spatial 12-body problem when $(\rho, R)=\mathbf{p}$. In this configuration the rotated tetrahedron is the middle one and it intersects the inner one and the outer one.
(c.2) For each $M>M_{0}(\mathbf{q})=25204.620455 \ldots$ and $m=m(M, \mathbf{q})=-3.5811747685 \cdots+0.0001420840585 \ldots M$ we have a central configuration of the spatial 12-body problem when $(\rho, R)=\mathbf{q}$. In this configuration the rotated tetrahedron is the middle one and it intersects only the inner one.

The values of the masses $m(\rho, R)$ and $M(\rho, R)$ that provide central configurations on sets $\mathscr{D}_{i}$ are analyzed in Section 3.1.
We call the previous result Result 3 instead of Theorem 3 because part of its proof is performed numerically with the help of Mathematica.

Proof of Result 3. The positions and the values of the masses have been taken so that the center of mass of the configuration is located at the origin of coordinates.

We substitute the positions and the values of the masses into (2). After some computations we obtain that system (2) over the three nested tetrahedra configuration with $R>1$ is equivalent to the system $A x=b$, or more precisely

$$
\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & f(1, \rho) & g_{1}(R) \\
\rho & -1 /\left(2 \rho^{2}\right) & f(\rho, R) \\
R & f(R, \rho) & -1 /\left(2 R^{2}\right)
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{l}
\lambda \\
m \\
M
\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}{c}
1 / 2 \\
-f(\rho, 1) \\
g_{2}(R)
\end{array}\right)
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f(x, y)=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(y-3 x)}{\left(3 x^{2}-2 y x+3 y^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{(2 / 3)^{3 / 2}}{(x+y)^{2}} \\
& g_{1}(x)=-\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(x+3)}{\left(3 x^{2}+2 x+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{(2 / 3)^{3 / 2}}{(x-1)^{2}} \\
& g_{2}(x)=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(3 x+1)}{\left(3 x^{2}+2 x+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{(2 / 3)^{3 / 2}}{(x-1)^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $3 x^{2}-2 y x+3 y^{2}>0$ in $D=\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: x>0, y>0\right\}$, the function $f(x, y)$ is defined for all $(x, y) \in D$. The functions $g_{1}(x)$ and $g_{2}(x)$ are defined for all $x>1$; moreover

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 1^{+}} g_{1}(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 1^{+}} g_{2}(x)=+\infty
$$

On the other hand $f(x, y)<0$ for all $(x, y) \in D$. Indeed the set $D$ can be written as $D=\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: y=a x, x>0, a>0\right\}$. It is easy to check that $f(x, a x)=f_{1}(a) / x^{2}$ where

$$
f_{1}(a)=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(a-3)}{\left(3 a^{2}-2 a+3\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{(2 / 3)^{3 / 2}}{(a+1)^{2}}
$$

As in the Appendix we find the zeros of $f_{1}(a)$ by reducing the problem to find the zeros of a polynomial of one variable and we see that $f_{1}(a)=0$ has no real solutions for $a>0$. In particular $f_{1}(a)<0$ for $a>0$.

If $\operatorname{det}(A) \neq 0$, then the solution of system (9) is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \lambda=\lambda(\rho, R)=\frac{\operatorname{det}\left(A_{1}\right)}{\operatorname{det}(A)}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{det}(A)}\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
1 / 2 & f(1, \rho) & g_{1}(R) \\
-f(\rho, 1) & -1 /\left(2 \rho^{2}\right) & f(\rho, R) \\
g_{2}(R) & f(R, \rho) & -1 /\left(2 R^{2}\right)
\end{array}\right|, \\
& m=m(\rho, R)=\frac{\operatorname{det}\left(A_{2}\right)}{\operatorname{det}(A)}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{det}(A)}\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 1 / 2 & g_{1}(R) \\
\rho & -f(\rho, 1) & f(\rho, R) \\
R & g_{2}(R) & -1 /\left(2 R^{2}\right)
\end{array}\right|, \\
& M=M(\rho, R)=\frac{\operatorname{det}\left(A_{3}\right)}{\operatorname{det}(A)}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{det}(A)}\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & f(1, \rho) & 1 / 2 \\
\rho & -1 /\left(2 \rho^{2}\right) & -f(\rho, 1) \\
R & f(R, \rho) & g_{2}(R)
\end{array}\right| .
\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $\lambda(\rho, R), m(\rho, R)$ and $M(\rho, R)$ gives a central configuration of the 12-body problem if and only if $R$ and $\rho$ are such that $\lambda(\rho, R)>0, m(\rho, R)>0$ and $M(\rho, R)>0$.

It is easy to check that

$$
\operatorname{det}(A)=\frac{\rho}{2 R^{2}} f(1, \rho)+\frac{1}{4 R^{2} \rho^{2}}+R f(\rho, R) f(1, \rho)-f(R, \rho) f(\rho, R)+\frac{R}{2 \rho^{2}} g_{1}(R)+\rho f(R, \rho) g_{1}(R)
$$

We analyze the sign of $\operatorname{det}(A)$ on the boundaries of the regions $\mathcal{O}_{m}, \mathcal{O}_{a}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{1}$.
Clearly

$$
\lim _{\rho \rightarrow 0^{+}} \operatorname{det}(A)=\operatorname{sign}\left(\frac{1}{4 R^{2}}+\frac{R}{2} g_{1}(R)\right) \cdot \infty
$$

The level curves $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$. The dashed lines correspond to the boundaries of the regions $\sigma_{m}, \sigma_{v}$ and $\sigma_{i}$.

$$
\text { and from }(10)
$$

$$
\lim _{R \rightarrow 1^{+}} \operatorname{det}(A)=\operatorname{sign}\left(\frac{1}{2 \rho^{2}}+\rho f(1, \rho)\right) \cdot \infty
$$

We solve the equation $f_{2}(R)=1 /\left(4 R^{2}\right)+R g_{1}(R) / 2=0$ as in the Appendix and we see that it has no real solutions for $R>1$; moreover $f_{2}(R)>0$ for all $R>1$. Solving the equation $f_{3}(\rho)=1 /\left(2 \rho^{2}\right)+\rho f(1, \rho)=0$ as in the Appendix we find two unique real roots $\rho=b_{1}=0.7152231486 \ldots$ and $\rho=b_{2}=6.5360789462 \ldots$ Moreover $f_{3}(\rho)>0$ for $\rho \in$ $(0, b 1) \cup\left(b_{2}, \infty\right)$ and $f_{3}(\rho)<0$ for $\rho \in\left(b_{1}, b_{2}\right)$. In short, $\lim _{\rho \rightarrow 0^{+}} \operatorname{det}(A)=+\infty$ for all $R>1, \lim _{R \rightarrow 1^{+}} \operatorname{det}(A)=+\infty$ when $\rho \in(0, b 1) \cup\left(b_{2}, \infty\right)$ and $\lim _{R \rightarrow 1^{+}} \operatorname{det}(A)=-\infty$ when $\rho \in\left(b_{1}, b_{2}\right)$. The regions of these two limits are indicated in Fig. 4.

After some computations we see that when $\rho=1$ and $R>1$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{det}(A)= & f_{4}(R)=-\frac{-9+9 \sqrt{2}+\sqrt{6}}{36 R^{2}}+\frac{3 \sqrt{6} R\left(R^{2}+2 R+1\right)-8}{27(R-1)^{2}(R+1)^{2}}+\frac{2\left(3 \sqrt{3} R(R+1)^{2}+R(R+1)^{2}-4\right)}{27(R+1)^{4}} \\
& +\frac{8\left(3 R^{2}-10 R+3\right)}{\left(3 R^{2}-2 R+3\right)^{3}}-\frac{2(9+\sqrt{3})(R-3) R}{9\left(3 R^{2}-2 R+3\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{8\left(5 R^{2}-2 R+1\right)}{3 \sqrt{3}(R-1)^{2}(R+1)\left(3 R^{2}-2 R+3\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& -\frac{(R+3)\left(9 \sqrt{2} R^{3}+18 \sqrt{2} R^{2}+9 \sqrt{2} R-8 \sqrt{3}\right)}{9(R+1)^{2}\left(3 R^{2}+2 R+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{8\left(3 R^{2}+8 R-3\right)}{\left(3 R^{2}-2 R+3\right)^{3 / 2}\left(3 R^{2}+2 R+3\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the equation $f_{4}(R)=0$ as in the Appendix and we find two real solutions with $R>1$; they are $R=c_{1}=$ $1.3711124500 \ldots$ and $R=c_{2}=28.2412927769 \ldots$. Moreover $f_{4}(R)>0$ for $R \in\left(c_{1}, c_{2}\right)$ and $f_{4}(R)<0$ for $R \in\left(1, c_{1}\right)$ $\cup\left(c_{2}, \infty\right)$.

For $R=\rho$ and $\rho>1$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{det}(A)= & f_{5}(\rho)=\frac{\left(-18+9 \sqrt{2}-2 \sqrt{3}\right)(\rho-3)}{9 \rho\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{-2-6 \sqrt{3}+3 \sqrt{6}}{27(\rho-1)^{2} \rho} \\
& +\frac{\left(18-9 \sqrt{2}+2 \sqrt{3}\right)(\rho+3)}{9 \rho\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{2+6 \sqrt{3}-3 \sqrt{6}}{27 \rho(\rho+1)^{2}}-\frac{29+12 \sqrt{3}}{108 \rho^{4}}
\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the equation $f_{5}(\rho)=0$ as in the Appendix and we see that it has no real solutions with $\rho>1$. Moreover $f_{5}(R)<0$ for all $\rho>1$.

Notice that $\operatorname{det}(A)$ is continuous for all $\rho>0, R>1$. This means that if $\operatorname{det}(A)$ has different signs on two different curves $\gamma_{1}$ and $\gamma_{2}$, then there exist an odd number of curves of zeros of $\operatorname{det}(A)$ (taking into account their multiplicities) between $\gamma_{1}$ and $\gamma_{2}$, whereas if $\operatorname{det}(A)$ has the same sign on the curves $\gamma_{1}$ and $\gamma_{2}$, then there exist an even number (that could be 0 ) of curves of zeros of $\operatorname{det}(A)$ (taking into account their multiplicities) between $\gamma_{1}$ and $\gamma_{2}$. Moreover these curves are continuous.

By analyzing the sign of $\operatorname{det}(A)$ on the boundary of $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ we have seen that $\operatorname{det}(A)>0$ on $\left\{(\rho, R) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: \rho=0, R>1\right\}$ $\cup\left\{(\rho, R) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: \rho \in\left(0, b_{1}\right), R=1\right\} \cup\left\{(\rho, R) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: \rho=1, R \in\left(c_{1}, c_{2}\right)\right\}$, that $\operatorname{det}(A)<0$ on $\left\{(\rho, R) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: \rho=1\right.$, $\left.R \in\left(1, c_{1}\right)\right\} \cup\left\{(\rho, R) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: \rho=1, R \in\left(c_{2},+\infty\right)\right\}$ and that $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$ at the points $\left(1, c_{1}\right)$ and $\left(1, c_{2}\right)$. Therefore on $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ there exists a curve $\Gamma_{1}$ starting at the point $\left(b_{1}, 1\right)$ and passing through the point $\left(1, c_{1}\right)$ and another one $\Gamma_{2}$ coming from $R=+\infty$ and passing through the point $\left(1, c_{2}\right)$ on which $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$ (see Fig. 4).

On the boundary of $\mathcal{C}_{m}$ we have that $\operatorname{det}(A)<0$ everywhere with the exception of the set $\left\{(\rho, R) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: \rho=1, R \in\right.$ $\left.\left(c_{1}, c_{2}\right)\right\}$ and $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$ at the points $\left(1, c_{1}\right)$ and $\left(1, c_{2}\right)$. Therefore we can guarantee the existence of a curve in $\mathcal{C}_{m}$ with $R \in\left(c_{1}, c_{2}\right)$ on which $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$. This curve starts at the point $\left(1, c_{1}\right)$, so it is the continuation on the region $\mathcal{C}_{m}$ of the curve $\Gamma_{1}$. By plotting the level curves $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$ with the help of Mathematica (see Fig. 4), we see that the curve $\Gamma_{2}$ can be continued to the region $\mathcal{C}_{m}$ and that the curves $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ do not coincide.

Finally on the boundary of $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ we have that $\operatorname{det}(A)<0$ everywhere with the exception of the set $\left\{(\rho, R) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: \rho \in\right.$ $\left.\left(b_{2},+\infty\right), R=1\right\}$ and $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$ at the point $\left(b_{2}, 1\right)$. Therefore there exists a curve $\Gamma_{3}$ on $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ starting at the point $\left(b_{2}, 1\right)$ and going to $\rho=+\infty$ (see again Fig. 4).

By plotting the level curves $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$ for larger values of $\rho$ and $R$ we see that these are the unique three curves with $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$.

Now we analyze the sign of $\operatorname{det}\left(A_{2}\right)$ on the boundaries of $\mathcal{C}_{m}, \mathcal{C}_{n}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{i}$. From (11) we have that

$$
\operatorname{det}\left(A_{2}\right)=g_{1}(R) g_{2}(R) \rho+\frac{\rho}{4 R^{2}}+\frac{f(\rho, 1)}{2 R^{2}}+\frac{1}{2} R f(\rho, R)+R f(\rho, 1) g_{1}(R)-f(\rho, R) g_{2}(R)
$$

Since the procedure is exactly the same as that for the sign of $\operatorname{det}(A)$ we omit the computations and we just summarize the results in Table 4.

The plot of the level curves $\operatorname{det}\left(A_{2}\right)=0$ is given in Fig. 5. As in the previous case the plot of these level curves for larger values of $\rho$ and $R$ does not provide new curves with $\operatorname{det}\left(A_{3}\right)=0$.


Fig. 5. The level curves $\operatorname{det}\left(A_{2}\right)=0$. The dashed lines correspond to the boundaries of the regions $\mathcal{O}_{m}, \mathcal{O}_{a}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{i}$.


Fig. 6. The level curves $\operatorname{det}\left(A_{3}\right)=0$. The dashed lines correspond to the boundaries of the regions $\mathcal{O}_{m}, \mathcal{O}_{a}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{i}$.

Since $f(R, \rho)<0$ and $g_{2}(R)>0$ in the region $\rho>0, R>1$, from the third equation of (9) we have that if $m>0$ and $M>0$, then $\lambda>0$. So it is not necessary to find the set of level curves $\operatorname{det}\left(A_{1}\right)=0$.

Analyzing the sign of $m$ and $M$ on the regions $\mathcal{O}_{m}, \mathcal{O}_{a}$, and $\mathcal{O}_{i}$ we prove that the region $\mathfrak{D}=\left\{(R, \rho) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: \operatorname{det}(A) \neq\right.$ $0, m(R, \rho)>0, M(R, \rho)>0, \rho>0, R>1\}$ where the solution of (9) given by (11) gives a central configuration of the spatial 12-body problem is the one plotted in Fig. 2. This proves statement (a).

It is easy to check that the faces of the rotated tetrahedron, which has scale factor $\rho$, intersect those of the tetrahedron with scale factor 1 when $\rho \in[1 / 3,3]$, and they intersect those of the tetrahedron with scale factor $R$ when $R \in[\rho / 3,3 \rho]$. Moreover the rotated tetrahedron can be either the inner, the middle or the outer one. Statement (b) can be proved by analyzing these geometric properties of the three nested tetrahedra in the regions $\mathfrak{D}_{i}$ for $i=1, \ldots, 6$ (see Fig. 7 for more details).

Finally we analyze the solution of (9) at the points $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$. The numerical values of $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ can be found by solving the system $\operatorname{det}(A)=\operatorname{det}\left(A_{2}\right)=\operatorname{det}\left(A_{3}\right)=0$.


Fig. 7. Geometric properties of the nested tetrahedra in $\mathscr{D}$. Using this notation we obtain ten different regions $\{a\}:\left\{\left\{a, 1, R\right\}, \rho^{\circ} 1, \rho^{\circ} 8\right\},\{b\}:\left\{\left\{a, 1, R\right\}, \rho \cap 1, \rho^{\circ} 8\right\},\{c\}:\left\{\left\{a, 1, R\right\}, \rho \cap 1, \rho \cap R\right\},\{d\}:\left\{\left\{1, \rho, R\right\}, \rho \cap 1, \rho^{\circ} 8\right\},\{e\}:\left\{\left\{1, \rho, R\right\}, \rho \cap 1, \rho \cap R\right\},\right.$ $\left.\left\{f\right\}:\left\{\left\{1, \rho, R\right\}, \rho^{\circ} 1, \rho^{\circ} R\right\},\{g\}:\left\{\left\{1, \rho, R\right\}, \rho^{\circ} 1, \rho \cap R\right\},\{h\}:\left\{\left\{1, R, \rho\right\}, \rho \cap 1, \rho \cap R\right\},\{i\}:\left\{\left\{1, R, \rho\right\}, \rho^{\circ} 1, \rho \cap R\right\},\{j\}:\left\{\left\{1, R, \rho\right\}, \rho^{\circ} 1, \rho^{\circ} R\right\}\right]$. These ten regions are limited by the dashed and continuous lines in the figures.

Let

$$
\bar{A}(\rho)=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
1 & f(1, \rho) \\
\rho & -1 /\left(2 \rho^{2}\right)
\end{array}\right)
$$

We note that $\operatorname{det}(\bar{A}(\rho))=-f_{3}(\rho)$, so $\operatorname{det}(\bar{A}(\rho)) \neq 0$ for all $\rho \neq b_{1}$ and $\rho \neq b_{2}$. In particular, $\operatorname{det}\left(\bar{A}\left(p_{1}\right)\right) \neq 0$ and $\operatorname{det}\left(\bar{A}\left(q_{1}\right)\right) \neq 0$.

Since $\operatorname{det}(A)=\operatorname{det}\left(A_{3}\right)=0$ and $\operatorname{det}(\bar{A}(\rho)) \neq 0$, system (9) is equivalent to the system

$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc}
1 & f(1, \rho) \\
\rho & -1 /\left(2 \rho^{2}\right)
\end{array}\right)\binom{\lambda}{m}=\binom{1 / 2-M g_{1}(R)}{-f(\rho, 1)-M f(\rho, R)}
$$

and it has infinitely many solutions which are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda & =\lambda(M)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{det}(\bar{A})}\left|\begin{array}{cc}
1 / 2-M g_{1}(R) & f(1, \rho) \\
-f(\rho, 1)-M f(\rho, R) & -1 /\left(2 \rho^{2}\right)
\end{array}\right| \\
& =-\frac{4 \rho^{2} f(1, \rho) f(\rho, 1)-1}{2\left(2 \rho^{3} f(1, \rho)+1\right)}-M \frac{2 \rho^{2} f(1, \rho) f(\rho, R)+g_{1}(R)}{2 \rho^{3} f(1, \rho)+1} \\
m & =m(M)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{det}(\bar{A})}\left|\begin{array}{cc}
1 & 1 / 2-M g_{1}(R) \\
\rho & -f(\rho, 1)-M f(\rho, R)
\end{array}\right| \\
& =\frac{\rho^{2}(\rho+2 f(\rho, 1))}{2 \rho^{3} f(1, \rho)+1}-M \frac{2 \rho^{2}\left(\rho g_{1}(R)-f(\rho, R)\right)}{2 \rho^{3} f(1, \rho)+1}
\end{aligned}
$$

This solution provides a central configuration of the 12-body problem when $\lambda(M)>0, m(M)>0$ and $M>0$. Moreover $m(M)=0$ when $M=\left(\rho^{2}(\rho+2 f(\rho, 1))\right) /\left(2 \rho^{2}\left(\rho g_{1}(R)-f(\rho, R)\right)\right)$.

Evaluating (12) at the point $\mathbf{p}$ we get $\lambda=0.3706146625 \cdots+0.6060692429 \ldots M$, and $m=-0.4001317738 \cdots+$ $3.1936671053 \ldots M$. Moreover this solution provides a central configuration of the 12-body problem when $M>$

$0.1252891302 \ldots$. Finally evaluating (12) at the point $\mathbf{q}$ we get the solution $\lambda=-0.0001803428746 \cdots+$ $0.00001606707675 \ldots M$, and $m=-3.5811747685 \cdots+0.0001420840585 \ldots M$, which provides a central configuration of the 12-body problem when $M>25204.620455 \ldots$. This completes the proof of statement (c).

# 3.1. The functions $m(\rho, R)$ and $M(\rho, R)$ 

In this section we analyze some of the properties of the functions $m(\rho, R)$ and $M(\rho, R)$ on the regions $\mathscr{D}_{i}$ for $i=1, \ldots, 6$. After some tedious computations we can prove that

$$
\lim _{R \rightarrow \infty} M(\rho, R)= \begin{cases}+\infty & \text { if } \rho \in K_{1} \\ -\infty & \text { if } \rho \in K_{2}\end{cases}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& K_{1}=(0,0.501930 \ldots) \cup(0.715223 \ldots, 1.992306 \ldots) \cup(6.536078, \infty) \\
& K_{2}=(0.501930 \ldots, 0.715223 \ldots) \cup(1.992306 \ldots, 6.536078 \ldots) \\
& \lim _{\rho \rightarrow \infty} M(\rho, R)=m_{l}(R), \quad \lim _{\rho \rightarrow 0} M(\rho, R)=m_{l}(R) \\
& \lim _{R \rightarrow \infty} m(\rho, R)=m_{l l}(\rho), \quad \lim _{\rho \rightarrow \infty} m(\rho, R)=+\infty, \quad \lim _{\rho \rightarrow 0} m(\rho, R)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

where $m_{l}(\rho)$ and $m_{l l}(\rho)$ are the solutions given in Theorem 2.
With the help of Mathematica, we plot the functions $m(\rho, R)$ and $M(\rho, R)$ defined in (11) on the regions $\mathscr{D}_{i}$ for $i=$ $1, \ldots, 6$. We also find numerically the minimum and the maximum values of $m$ and $M$ in each region. The results that we have obtained are the following.

(a) The plot of $m(\rho, R)$ on the region $\mathcal{D}_{1}$. Here $m \in(0,0.000347182 \ldots)$.

(b) The plot of $M(\rho, R)$ on the region $\mathcal{D}_{1}$. Here $M \in(0, \infty)$.

On the region $\mathscr{D}_{1}$ the function $m(\rho, R)$ is equal to zero on the boundaries $\rho=0$ and $m(\rho, R)=0$. Moreover on the boundary $M(\rho, R)=0$ and when $R \rightarrow+\infty$ the behaviour of $m(\rho, R)$ is equal to that of the function $m_{l l}(\rho)$ with $\rho \in(0,0.152996 \ldots)$. From the plot of $m(\rho, R)$ we see that its maximum value is reached either on $M(\rho, R)=0$, or when $R \rightarrow \infty$. Thus on $\mathscr{D}_{1}$ we have that $m \in\left(0, \bar{m}_{0}\right)$ with $\bar{m}_{0}=0.000347182 \ldots$. Clearly the function $M(\rho, R)$ is equal to zero on the boundary $M(\rho, R)=0$ and the behaviour of $M(\rho, R)$ on the boundary $\rho=0$ is equal to $m_{l}(R)$ which tends to infinity as $R \rightarrow \infty$. Therefore $M \in(0,+\infty)$ on $\mathscr{D}_{1}$.

(c) The plot of $m(\rho, R)$ on the region $\mathcal{D}_{2}$. Here $m \in(0, \infty)$.

(d) The plot of $M(\rho, R)$ on the region $\mathcal{D}_{3}$. Here $M \in(25204.62 \ldots, \infty)$.

Clearly the function $m(\rho, R)$ on $\mathscr{D}_{2}$ is equal to zero on the boundary $m(\rho, R)=0$ and it tends to infinity when we approach the boundary $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$. Therefore on $\mathscr{D}_{2}$ we have that $m \in(0,+\infty)$. The function $M(\rho, R)$ also tends to infinity when we approach the boundary $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$. Moreover, from the plot of $M(\rho, R)$, we see that its minimum value is reached on the boundary $m(\rho, R)=0$; in particular, it is reached at the point $\mathbf{q}$ and the minimum value is $M=M_{0}(\mathbf{q})=25204.620455 \ldots$ (see Result 3 for the definitions of $\mathbf{q}$ and $M_{0}(\mathbf{q})$ ).


(e) The plot of $m(\rho, R)$ on the region $\mathcal{D}_{3}$. Here $m \in(0, \infty)$.

(f) The plot of $M(\rho, R)$ on the region $\mathcal{D}_{3}$. Here $M \in(11625.1167 \ldots, \infty)$.

On $\mathscr{D}_{3}$ clearly the function $m(\rho, R)$ is equal to zero on the boundary $m(\rho, R)=0$ and tends to infinity on the boundary $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$, so $m \in(0,+\infty)$ on $\mathscr{D}_{3}$. The function $M(\rho, R)$ also tends to infinity on $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$. Moreover, from the plot of $M(\rho, R)$, we see that its minimum value is reached on the boundary $m(\rho, R)=0$; in particular, it is reached at the point $(\rho, R)=(2.7556 \ldots, 24.7316 \ldots)$ and the minimum value is $M=11625.1167 \ldots$.

(g) The plot of $m(\rho, R)$ on the region $\mathcal{D}_{4}$. Here $m \in(0, \infty)$.

(h) The plot of $M(\rho, R)$ on the region $\mathcal{D}_{4}$. Here $M \in(0, \infty)$.

The set $\mathscr{D}_{4}$ is delimited by the curves $\operatorname{det}(A)=0, M(\rho, R)=0$, and finally, near $\mathbf{p}$, the curve $m(\rho, R)=0$ (see Result 3 for the definition of $\mathbf{p}$ ). Clearly $m(\rho, R)$ (resp., $M(\rho, R)$ ) is equal to zero on the curve $m(\rho, R)=0$ (resp., $M(\rho, R)=0$ ) and tends to infinity when we approach $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$. Therefore $m \in(0, \infty)$ and $M \in(0, \infty)$ on $\mathscr{D}_{4}$.

(i) The plot of $m(\rho, R)$ on the region $\mathcal{D}_{5}$. Here $m \in(0, \infty)$.

(j) The plot of $M(\rho, R)$ on the region $\mathcal{D}_{5}$. Here $M \in(0, \infty)$.

The set $\mathscr{D}_{5}$ is also delimited by the curves $\operatorname{det}(A)=0, M(\rho, R)=0$, and $m(\rho, R)=0$. So $m \in(0, \infty)$ and $M \in(0, \infty)$ on $\mathscr{D}_{5}$.

(k) The plot of $m(\rho, R)$ on the region $\mathcal{D}_{6}$. Here $m \in(14997.0524 \ldots, \infty)$.

(l) The plot of $M(\rho, R)$ on the region $\mathcal{D}_{6}$. Here $M \in(0, \infty)$.

From the plot of $m(\rho, R)$, we see that the minimum value of $m(\rho, R)$ is reached on the boundary $M(\rho, R)=0$; in particular, it is reached at the point $(\rho, R)=(21.62574 \ldots, 2.56200 \ldots)$ and the minimum value is $m=14997.0524 \ldots$. Moreover $m(\rho, R) \rightarrow+\infty$ when $\rho \rightarrow+\infty$. Therefore $m \in(14997.0524 \ldots, \infty)$ on $\mathscr{D}_{6}$. On the other hand clearly $M(\rho, R)$ is equal to zero on $M(\rho, R)=0$ and $M(\rho, R) \rightarrow m_{l}(R)$ as $\rho \rightarrow+\infty$. So $M \in(0, \infty)$.

## Appendix

In this Appendix we analyze the solutions of the equations of the form $F(x)=0$ when $F$ is a rational function containing radicals. These kinds of equations are solved by following the steps below.
(1) We eliminate the denominators of the fractions which appear in $F(x)$ by multiplying the equation $F(x)=0$ by the least common multiple of all the denominators.
(2) We eliminate the radicals of the resulting equation by isolating in a convenient way one or more radicals on one side of the equation and squaring both sides of the equation. If the resulting equation still contains radicals, then we repeat the process again. At the end we obtain a polynomial equation.
(3) We find numerically all the solutions of the polynomial equation obtained in step 2.
(4) Finally we cheek which of these solutions are really solutions of the initial equation $F(x)=0$.

Now we detail how to group the radicals in step 2 for each of the kinds of equations that appear in this work after applying step 1.
(a) Equations with one radical: $\alpha_{1} \sqrt{a}+\alpha_{2}=0$. We eliminate the radicals by applying step 2 in the following way:

$$
\left(\alpha_{1} \sqrt{a}\right)^{2}=\left(-\alpha_{2}\right)^{2}
$$

(b) Equations of the form $\alpha_{1} \sqrt{a}+\alpha_{2} \sqrt{b}+\alpha_{3} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b}+\alpha_{4}=0$. Apply step 2 in the following way:

$$
\left(\alpha_{1} \sqrt{a}+\alpha_{2} \sqrt{b}\right)^{2}=\left(-\alpha_{3} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b}-\alpha_{4}\right)^{2}
$$

We obtain an equation with one radical of the form $\beta_{1} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b}+\beta_{2}=0$.
(c) Equations of the form $\alpha_{1} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b}+\alpha_{2} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{c}+\alpha_{3} \sqrt{b} \sqrt{c}=0$. Apply step 2 in the following way:

$$
\left(\alpha_{1} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b}\right)^{2}=\left(-\alpha_{2} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{c}-\alpha_{3} \sqrt{b} \sqrt{c}\right)^{2}
$$

We obtain an equation with one radical of the form $\beta_{1} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b}+\beta_{2}=0$.
---

# On the central configurations in the spatial 5-body problem with four equal masses 


#### Abstract

We analyze the families of central configurations of the spatial 5-body problem with four masses equal to 1 when the fifth mass $m$ varies from 0 to $+\infty$. In particular we continue numerically, taking $m$ as a parameter, the central configurations (which all are symmetric) of the restricted spatial $(4+1)$-body problem with four equal masses and $m=0$ to the spatial 5-body problem with equal masses (i.e. $m=1$ ), and viceversa we continue the symmetric central configurations of the spatial 5-body problem with five equal masses to the restricted $(4+1)$-body problem with four equal masses. Additionally we continue numerically the symmetric central configurations of the spatial 5-body problem with four equal masses starting with $m=1$ and ending in $m=+\infty$, improving the results of AlvarezRamírez et al. (Discrete Contin Dyn Syst Ser S 1: 505-518, 2008). We find four bifurcation values of $m$ where the number of central configuration changes. We note that the central configurations of all continued families varying $m$ from 0 to $+\infty$ are symmetric.

# 1 Introduction 

A configuration of $n$ bodies is central if the force due to acceleration on each body is proportional to the position vector of the body with respect to the center of mass. Central configurations are very important in the study of the $n$-body problem; for instance, they allow to compute all the homographic solutions, every motion starting and ending in a total collision is asymptotic to a central configuration, and every parabolic motion of the $n$ bodies is asymptotic to a central configuration (Saari and Hulkower 1981; Chenciner 1998). For the 3-body problem the set of central configurations is completely known, but the problem of finding the central configurations when $n>3$ is far to be completely solved. We only know the entire set of central configurations in some particular cases where some of the masses are equal or the configurations satisfy some geometrical properties.

The objective of this paper is to study the central configurations of the spatial 5-body problem with four equal masses when the non equal mass varies from 0 to infinity. More precisely, we will continue numerically all the symmetric central configurations of the spatial 5 -body problem with the five masses equal to 1 to the restricted spatial $(4+1)$-body problem with four masses equal to 1 and a fifth infinitesimal mass, and vice versa; that is, we vary the non equal mass from 1 to 0 , and viceversa. This study completes the one presented in Alvarez-Ramírez et al. (2008) where the authors continue numerically the symmetric central configurations from the spatial 5-body problem with the five masses equal to 1 to the restricted spatial $(1+4)$-body problem with four infinitesimal masses equal to $m=0$ and a fifth mass equal to 1 . Note that the study in Alvarez-Ramírez et al. (2008) is equivalent to study the symmetric central configurations of the 5-body problem with four masses equal to 1 varying the fifth mass $1 / m$ from 1 to infinity. This explains why the work of this paper completes the study of Alvarez-Ramírez et al. (2008). Thus the work done in Alvarez-Ramírez et al. (2008) and the one in the present paper provide a skeleton of the families of symmetric central configurations of the spatial 5-body problem with four equal masses and their bifurcations. The results that we have obtained are represented in Fig. 1. Each one of the families of classes of central configurations which appear in Fig. 1 are described later on.

This paper is structured as follows, in Sect. 2 we provide the equations for the central configurations of the spatial 5-body problem. In Sect. 3 we give a brief summary of the known results on symmetric central configurations for the spatial 5-body problem with five equal masses, we provide all the symmetric classes of central configurations of this problem and the positions of a representative of each class. In Sect. 4 we give all the classes of central configurations of the spatial restricted $(4+1)$-body problem with four equal masses and one infinitesimal, and we also give a representative of each class. In Sect. 5 we continue numerically the known families of central configurations from the spatial restricted $(4+1)$ body problem with 4 equal masses to the spatial 5-body problem with equal masses, and vice versa, taking one of the masses $m$ as a parameter. The results that we obtain are summarized in Sect. 6. In Sect. 7 we revisit and improve the work in Alvarez-Ramírez et al. (2008).

## 2 Equations of central configurations in the 5-body problem

The spatial 5-body problem is given by

$$
m_{i} \ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{i}=-\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\ j \neq i}}^{5} G m_{i} m_{j} \frac{\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}, \quad i=1, \ldots, 5
$$


Fig. 1 Connections between the families of classes of central configurations of the 5-body problem with four equal masses when the non-equal mass goes from 0 to $+\infty$. The four equal masses are represented by a small black ball whereas the non-equal mass is represented by a circle

where $\mathbf{q}_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ is the position vector of the body with mass $m_{i}$ in an inertial coordinate system, $r_{i j}=\left|\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right|$ is the distance between the masses $m_{i}$ and $m_{j}$, and $G$ is the gravitational constant which can be taken equal to one by scaling the time.

In these coordinates the configuration space of the spatial 5-body problem is

$$
\mathcal{P}=\left\{\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{5}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{3 n}: \mathbf{q}_{i} \neq \mathbf{q}_{j}, \text { for } i \neq j\right\}
$$

It is known that given $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{5}$ the configuration $\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{5}\right) \in \mathcal{P}$ is central if the acceleration vector of each body is a common scalar multiple of its position vector (with respect to the center of mass). That is, if there exists a positive constant $\lambda$ such that

$$
\ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{i}=-\lambda\left(\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{m}\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, 5
$$

where

$$
\mathbf{q}_{m}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{5} m_{i} \mathbf{q}_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{5} m_{i}}
$$

is the position vector of the center of mass of the system. In other words, the given configuration $\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{5}\right) \in \mathcal{P}$ of the 5 -body problem with positive masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{5}$ is central if there exists $\lambda$ such that $\left(\lambda, \mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{5}\right)$ is a solution of the system

$$
\lambda\left(\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{m}\right)=\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\ j \neq i}}^{5} m_{j} \frac{\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}, \quad i=1, \ldots, 5
$$

We say that two central configurations belong to the same class if they are invariant under rotations, scaling and permutations of the particles with equal masses.

We assume that the center of mass $\mathbf{q}_{m}$ of the system is fixed at the origin of coordinates. Then system (1) can be written as

$$
\mathbf{f}_{i}=0, \quad i=1, \ldots, 5
$$

where

$$
\mathbf{f}_{i}=\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\ j \neq i}}^{5} m_{j} \frac{\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}-\lambda \mathbf{q}_{i}
$$

Since the center of mass is at the origin the following linear combination of the $\mathbf{f}_{i}$ 's

$$
m_{1} \mathbf{f}_{1}+m_{2} \mathbf{f}_{2}+m_{3} \mathbf{f}_{3}+m_{4} \mathbf{f}_{4}+m_{5} \mathbf{f}_{5}=0
$$

is satisfied. So, if the mass $m_{i} \neq 0$ then the vectorial function $\mathbf{f}_{i}$ is a linear combination of the other ones, and we can eliminate the equation $\mathbf{f}_{i}=0$ from system (2).

Without loss of generality we can assume that the mass $m_{1}$ is fixed at $\mathbf{q}_{1}=(0,0,1)$. We also can fix $x_{3}=0$, this avoids the rotation of the configuration except when the mass $m_{3}$ is located on the $z$-axis. In this last case, to avoid rotations we should fix a variable different from $x_{3}$. Moreover if $m_{i} \neq 0$ we can isolate $\left(x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i}\right)$ from the equation $\mathbf{q}_{m}=0$. Thus, assuming that $m_{2} \neq 0$, we can fix the variables $x_{2}, y_{2}$ and $z_{2}$ as follows

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{2}=-\frac{m_{4} x_{4}+m_{5} x_{5}}{m_{2}}, \quad y_{2}=-\frac{m_{3} y_{3}+m_{4} y_{4}+m_{5} y_{5}}{m_{2}} \\
& z_{2}=-\frac{m_{1}+m_{3} z_{3}+m_{4} z_{4}+m_{5} z_{5}}{m_{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, from the third component of the vectorial equation $\mathbf{f}_{1}=0$ we get

$$
\lambda=-\sum_{i=2}^{5} \frac{m_{i}\left(z_{i}-1\right)}{\left(x_{i}^{2}+y_{i}^{2}+\left(z_{i}-1\right)^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

Therefore system (2) can be reduced to a set of eleven equations, denoted by $e_{i}$ for $i=$ $1, \ldots 11$, and eight unknowns, namely, the position variables $y_{3}, z_{3}, x_{4}, y_{4}, z_{4}, x_{5}, y_{5}, z_{5}$. Clearly these eleven equations are not all independent.

We note that if $m_{2}=0$, then we can proceed in the same way by taking a mass $m_{i} \neq 0$ instead of $m_{2}$ and we would arrive to a similar set of equations but with different unknowns.

In short the problem of finding the central configurations of the 5-body problem is reduced to find the solutions of a system of eleven equations and eight unknowns.

# 3 Spatial central configurations in the 5-body problem with equal masses 

Faugère and Kotsireas (1999), and Kotsireas and Lazard (2002) by using linear algebra and Gröbner bases studied the central configurations of the spatial 5-body problem with equal masses. In Faugère and Kotsireas (1999) the authors showed that a convex central configuration of this problem has always a plane of symmetry, see also the Habilitation Thesis of Albouy, section 3.4, first theorem, page 92 (Albouy 1997). In Kotsireas and Lazard (2002) the authors classified the symmetric spatial central configurations with axial symmetry in the 5-body problem with equal masses. In particular, they found four classes of central configurations having an axis of symmetry, two convex and two concave (see Fig. 2), and they conjectured that these are all the central configurations of the spatial 5-body problem with equal masses. Alvarez-Ramírez et al. (2008) proved that if there are other central configurations of the 5-body problem with equal masses they must be non-symmetric. Lee and Santoprete (2009) used a computer algebra algorithm, which is devised to find all the isolated solutions of a polynomial system, to find all the isolated central configurations of the 5-body problem with equal masses. They did not find anything more than the central configurations of Kotsireas and Lazard.

Next we describe these four classes of symmetric central configurations given in Kotsireas and Lazard (2002), and we also give the positions $\mathbf{q}_{i}$ and the mutual distances $r_{i j}$ for a representative of each class in the variables that we are working, see Alvarez-Ramírez et al. (2008) for more details. Without loss of generality we assume that $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=m_{4}=$ $m_{5}=1$.

# 4 Central configuration in the restricted spatial $(4+1)$-body problem with four equal masses 

The restricted $(4+1)$-body problem is a particular case of the 5-body problem with 4 equal masses plus an infinitesimal mass, where the four particles with positive masses are disposed in a central configuration. From now on, when we say the spatial $(4+1)$-body problem we mean the restricted spatial $(4+1)$-body problem.

It is known that the planar 4-body problem with equal masses has three different classes of central configurations. These consist of a square, an equilateral triangle with one mass at its barycenter, and an isosceles triangle with another mass on its axis of symmetry, see Albouy (1995). However, there exists a unique class of spatial central configurations of the 4-body problem given by the regular tetrahedron, see for instance Lehmann-Filhés (1891).

In the following subsections we shall discuss the central configurations of the spatial $(4+1)$-body problem for each class of central configurations of the planar and spatial 4-body problem with equal masses.

### 4.1 Central configurations of the $(4+1)$-body problem with four masses at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron

Santos (2004) proved that all central configurations of the $(4+1)$-body problem with the four positive equal masses forming a regular tetrahedron have either two planes of symmetry (planar type symmetry), or one axis of symmetry (axis type symmetry). Using these symmetries he found the central configurations of the problem, in particular, he proved that there are 25 central configurations of which 12 are non-convex. Later, Tsai (2012) found the same result using Gröebner bases. These 25 central configurations provide 6 different classes of central configurations. Leandro (2008) gives a different proof of the fact that the spatial central configurations of the restricted $(4+1)$-body problem with equal masses are symmetric.

Next we describe these 6 classes and we give the positions $\mathbf{q}_{i}$ and the mutual distances $r_{i j}$ for a representative of each class in the variables that we are working, see Santos (2004) for more details.

We will assume that $m_{1}=\cdots=m_{4}=1$ and that the positions of the vertices of the tetrahedron are $\mathbf{q}_{1}=(0,0,1), \mathbf{q}_{2}=\left(-\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{1}{3}\right), \mathbf{q}_{3}=\left(0,-\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{1}{3}\right), \mathbf{q}_{4}=$ $\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{1}{3}\right)$. Then we have the following mutual distances

$$
r_{12}=r_{13}=r_{14}=r_{23}=r_{24}=r_{34}=2 \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}
$$

( $T_{b}$ ) Axis and planar type symmetry simultaneously: (1 cc) The infinitesimal mass is located at the barycenter of the tetrahedron; that is, $\mathbf{q}_{5}=(0,0,0)$ (see Fig. 3).
