# Convex central configurations of the $n$-body problem which are not strictly convex 


#### Abstract

It is well-known that if a planar central configuration for the Newtonian 4body problem is convex, then it must be strictly convex. In some literature, same conclusion were believed to hold for the case of five or even more bodies but rigorous treatments are absent. In this paper we provide concrete examples of central configurations which are convex but not strictly convex. Our examples include planar central configurations with five bodies and spatial central configurations with seven bodies.


## 1. InTRODUCTION

The classical $n$-body problem concerns the motion of $n$ mass points moving in space in accordance with Newton's law of gravitation:

$$
\ddot{q}_{k}=\sum_{i \neq k} \frac{m_{i}\left(q_{i}-q_{k}\right)}{\left|q_{i}-q_{k}\right|^{3}}, \quad k=1,2, \cdots, n
$$

Here $q_{k} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}(1 \leq d \leq 3)$ is the position of mass $m_{k}>0$. Alternatively the system (1) can be written

$$
m_{k} \ddot{q}_{k}=\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{k}} U(q), \quad k=1,2, \cdots, n
$$

where

$$
U(q):=\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq n} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|}
$$

is the potential of the system. The position vector $q=\left(q_{1}, \cdots, q_{n}\right) \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right)^{n}$ is often referred to as the configuration of the system, and vectors $\left\{q_{k}\right\}$ are vertices of the configuration $q$.

Let $M=m_{1}+\cdots+m_{n}$ be the total mass and

$$
\hat{q}=\frac{1}{M}\left(m_{1} q_{1}+\cdots+m_{n} q_{n}\right)
$$

be the mass center of the configuration $q$. The set $\Delta$ of collision configurations is the algebraic variety defined by

$$
\Delta=\left\{q \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right)^{n}: q_{i}=q_{j} \text { for some } i \neq j\right\}
$$

A configuration $q \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right)^{n} \backslash \Delta$ is called a central configuration if there exists some positive constant $\lambda$, called the multiplier, such that

$$
-\lambda\left(q_{k}-\hat{q}\right)=\sum_{i \neq k} \frac{m_{i}\left(q_{i}-q_{k}\right)}{\left|q_{i}-q_{k}\right|^{3}}, \quad k=1,2, \cdots, n
$$

The assumption that $\lambda$ being positive is redundant as it can be easily verified that there is no negative $\lambda$ that can possibly satisfy (3). The definition of central configuration can be extended to cases with some zero masses but we shall only consider positive masses throughout this paper.

The set of central configurations are invariant under three classes of transformations on $\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right)^{n}$ which act equitably on each copy of $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ : translations $\left(q_{k} \mapsto q_{k}+a, a \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\right)$, scalings $\left(q_{k} \mapsto \mu q_{k}, \mu \neq 0\right)$, and orthogonal transformations $\left(q_{k} \mapsto A q_{k}, A \in O(d)\right)$. Scaling a central configuration with multiplier $\lambda$ by multiplying $\mu$ results in a central configuration with multiplier $\lambda /|\mu|^{3}$. Conventionally two central configurations are considered equivalent if one can be obtained from the other via translations, scalings, and $S O(d)$-actions. This clearly defines an equivalence relation on central configurations, and two central configurations are different in that aspect if they differ from each other by a reflection with respect to a hyperplane in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. The term "central configurations" is often referred to equivalence classes of central configurations.

There are several reasons why central configurations are of special importance in the study of the $n$-body problem, see  for details.

Without loss of generality we consider only central configurations $q$ with mass centers $\hat{q}$ at the origin. In this case, using the Leibniz formula for the moment of inertia

$$
\mathcal{I}(q):=\sum_{k=1}^{n} m_{k}\left|q_{k}\right|^{2}=\frac{1}{M} \sum_{i<j} m_{i} m_{j}\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|^{2}
$$

the system (3) can be written in a compact form

$$
-\frac{\lambda}{2} \nabla \mathcal{I}(q)=\nabla U(q)
$$

or equivalently,

$$
\sum_{i \neq k} m_{i}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{1}{\left|q_{i}-q_{k}\right|^{3}}\right)\left(q_{i}-q_{k}\right)=0, \quad k=1,2, \cdots, n
$$

By suitable scaling, we may assume without loss of generality that the multiplier $\lambda$ is equal to the total mass $M$. Then equations for central configurations become

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{i}\left(1-s_{i k}\right)\left(q_{i}-q_{k}\right)=0, \quad k=1,2, \cdots, n
$$

where

$$
s_{i j}=\frac{1}{\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|^{3}} \quad \text { for } i \neq j ; \quad s_{i i}=1 \quad \text { for each } i
$$

This is the system of equations we will be working with.
The convex hull $\operatorname{Conv}(q)$ of the configuration $q \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right)^{n}$ is the convex hull in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for its vertices $\left\{q_{k}\right\}$. We say the configuration $q$ is convex if each $q_{k}$ is on the boundary of $\operatorname{Conv}(q)$ (as a subset of $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ); it is strictly convex if no $q_{k}$ is on the convex hull for other vertices. Concave configurations are configurations which are not strictly convex. Strictly concave configurations are configurations which are not convex. The dimension of a configuration $q$ is defined as the dimension $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Conv}(q)$ of $\operatorname{Conv}(q)$.

Strictly convex and strictly concave configurations are clearly two open sets in $\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right)^{n}$ and their boundaries intersect at configurations that are both convex and concave (convex but not strictly convex, in other words). The intersection also includes some collision configurations. According to the above definition, a collinear configuration $q$ (i.e. $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Conv}(q) \leq 1$ ) in $\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right)^{n} \backslash \Delta$ with $n \geq 3$ is concave if $d=1$ but is both convex and concave if $d \geq 2$. Likewise, a coplanar configuration $q$ (i.e. $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Conv}(q) \leq 2$ ) with $n \geq 4$ is convex if $d \geq 3$, or $d=2$ and no $q_{k}$ is in the interior of the convex hull for other vertices, or $d=2$ and $q$ is collinear. In literature the terms convex and concave configurations are often referred to noncollinear configurations.

Other than the 12 collinear central configurations , the planar four-body problem $(d=2)$ has at least 14 concave central configurations , and at least 6 non-collinear convex central configurations, one for each of the 6 cyclic orderings of the four bodies . It follows easily from the perpendicular bisector theorem  that all of these convex central configurations are strictly convex. By calculating the derivative of the normalized potential on the boundary of the set of convex configurations, Xia shows that no local minimum can possibly fall on this boundary, following from which he provides a simple alternative proof for the existence of a convex central configuration for each of the 6 cyclic orderings. There it was proposed that such a method may also work for the planar five-body problem, or even planar and spatial $n$-body problems in general [8, §2]. In [7, §2 and §8-Theorem 8.1] Williams also claimed that convex five-body central configurations cannot have three masses

along the same line. Our main result shows the existence of central configurations which disprove above stated assertions.

Theorem 1. For some positive masses there are 2-dimensional central configurations for the 5 -body problem which are convex but not strictly convex. For some positive masses there are 3-dimensional central configurations for the 7-body problem which are convex but not strictly convex.

# 2. Planar central configurations with five bodies 

In this section we construct a 2-dimensional central configuration with five bodies which is convex but not strictly convex.

Consider a planar convex configuration $q \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)^{5}$ whose convex hull $\operatorname{Conv}(q)$ is an isosceles trapezoid. Vertices are

$$
q_{1}=\left(-\alpha,-\gamma_{1}\right), \quad q_{2}=\left(\alpha,-\gamma_{1}\right), \quad q_{3}=\left(-\beta, \gamma_{2}\right), \quad q_{4}=\left(\beta, \gamma_{2}\right)
$$

where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma_{1}, \gamma_{2}$ are positive numbers. The fifth vertex $q_{5}$ is located $\left(0,-\gamma_{1}\right)$, making the configuration $q$ convex but not strictly convex.

Let $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{5}=1, m_{3}=m_{4}=\mu$. The height $\gamma=\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}$ of the isosceles trapezoid and $\gamma_{1}, \gamma_{2}$ are related by

$$
\gamma_{1}=\frac{2 \mu \gamma}{3+2 \mu}, \quad \gamma_{2}=\frac{3 \gamma}{3+2 \mu}
$$

so that the mass center $\hat{q}$ of the configuration $q$ is at the origin.
Apparently we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& s_{13}=s_{24}=\left((\alpha-\beta)^{2}+\gamma^{2}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
& s_{14}=s_{23}=\left((\alpha+\beta)^{2}+\gamma^{2}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
& s_{35}=s_{45}=\left(\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
& s_{15}=s_{25}=8 s_{12}=\alpha^{-3} \\
& s_{34}=(2 \beta)^{-3} \\
& s_{i j}=s_{j i} \text { for any } i, j
\end{aligned}
$$

From these symmetries, in (5) equations for $k=1,2$ are identical, equations for $k=3,4$ are also identical. Equations (5) for central configurations become

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(1-s_{12}\right)\left(q_{2}-q_{1}\right)+\mu\left(1-s_{13}\right)\left(q_{3}-q_{1}\right)+\mu\left(1-s_{14}\right)\left(q_{4}-q_{1}\right)+\left(1-s_{15}\right)\left(q_{5}-q_{1}\right) & =0 \\
\left(1-s_{13}\right)\left(q_{1}-q_{3}\right)+\left(1-s_{23}\right)\left(q_{2}-q_{3}\right)+\mu\left(1-s_{34}\right)\left(q_{4}-q_{3}\right)+\left(1-s_{35}\right)\left(q_{5}-q_{3}\right) & =0 \\
\left(1-s_{15}\right)\left(q_{1}-q_{5}\right)+\left(1-s_{25}\right)\left(q_{2}-q_{5}\right)+\mu\left(1-s_{35}\right)\left(q_{3}-q_{5}\right)+\mu\left(1-s_{45}\right)\left(q_{4}-q_{5}\right) & =0
\end{aligned}
$$

This is actually a system of six equations with positive unknowns $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \mu$, and $s_{i j}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\left(1-s_{12}\right) \alpha+\mu\left(1-s_{13}\right)(\alpha-\beta)+\mu\left(1-s_{14}\right)(\alpha+\beta)+\left(1-s_{15}\right) \alpha & =0 \\
\left(1-s_{13}\right)(-\alpha+\beta)+\left(1-s_{23}\right)(\alpha+\beta)+2 \mu\left(1-s_{34}\right) \beta+\left(1-s_{35}\right) \beta & =0 \\
-\left(1-s_{15}\right) \alpha+\left(1-s_{25}\right) \alpha-\mu\left(1-s_{35}\right) \beta+\mu\left(1-s_{45}\right) \beta & =0 \\
\mu\left(1-s_{13}\right) \gamma+\mu\left(1-s_{14}\right) \gamma & =0 \\
\left(1-s_{13}\right) \gamma+\left(1-s_{23}\right) \gamma+\left(1-s_{35}\right) \gamma & =0 \\
\mu\left(1-s_{35}\right) \gamma+\mu\left(1-s_{45}\right) \gamma & =0
\end{aligned}
$$

The third identity is obvious as it follows immediately from (6). The fourth and the sixth identities are equivalent to

$$
s_{13}+s_{14}=2, \quad s_{35}=1
$$

These two identities together with $s_{14}=s_{23}$ imply the fifth identity in (7). The second identity in (7) can therefore be simplified to

$$
\mu\left(1-s_{34}\right) \beta=\left(1-s_{13}\right) \alpha
$$

By (6), (8), (9), the first identity in (7) can be written

$$
\left(3-10 s_{12}\right)\left(s_{34}-1\right)+2\left(s_{13}-1\right)^{2}=0
$$

The system (7) is now reduced to (8), (9), (10).
We will soon see that every variable can be expressed in terms of $s_{13}=\theta$. Observe that

$$
(2-\theta)^{-\frac{2}{3}}=s_{14}^{-\frac{2}{4}}=(\alpha+\beta)^{2}+\gamma^{2}, \quad \theta^{-\frac{2}{3}}=s_{13}^{-\frac{2}{4}}=(\alpha-\beta)^{2}+\gamma^{2}
$$

Thus

$$
\alpha=\left(\frac{\theta^{-\frac{2}{3}}+\left(2-\theta\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}-2}{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}, \quad \beta=\frac{(2-\theta)^{-\frac{2}{3}}-\theta^{-\frac{2}{3}}}{4 \alpha}
$$

both of which are positive since

$$
2-\theta=s_{14}<s_{13}=\theta \in(1,2)
$$

Every $s_{i j}$ can now be expressed in terms of $\theta$ via (6) and (8), and so is $\gamma=\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}$. In terms of $\theta,(10)$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(3 \sqrt{2}\left(\theta^{-\frac{2}{3}}+(2-\theta)^{-\frac{2}{3}}-2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}-5\right)\left(1-\frac{\left((2-\theta)^{-\frac{2}{3}}-\theta^{-\frac{2}{3}}\right)^{3}}{2 \sqrt{2}\left(\theta^{-\frac{2}{3}}+(2-\theta)^{-\frac{2}{3}}-2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\right) \\
+ & \left((2-\theta)^{-\frac{2}{3}}-\theta^{-\frac{2}{3}}\right)^{3}(\theta-1)^{2}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R(\theta)$ be the function in (11). Then it increases on $[1.4,1.6]$ from $R(1.4) \approx-0.647$ to $R(1.6) \approx 0.866$. The unique root $\theta^{*}$ in there is approximately 1.506654 . One can easily check that the corresponding $\gamma, \mu$ are both strictly positive. This proves the existence of a 2-dimensional central configuration for the five-body problem with suitable masses.

Numerical data accurate to the 24th decimal places are given in table 1. Figure 1 shows a homographic solution for this particular central configuration with period $2 \pi$ and eccentricity 0.6 .

From (4), central configurations are exactly the set of critical points of the normalized potential $\tilde{U}=\sqrt{\mathcal{I}} U$. The central configuration we found is of local minimum type as one can easily check that eigenvalues of $D^{2} \tilde{U}$ are all positive, except the two zero eigenvalues due to the invariance under rotations and scalings. Therefore, the idea of perturbing the intermediate mass $q_{5}$ downward so as to decrease the normalized potential (see ) is not applicable to this case.

A convex but not strictly convex central configuration with five bodies.

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\theta=1.506654068878065383203023, & \mu=11.23156072828415553841745 \\
\alpha=0.425756342462430700206462, & \gamma_{1}=0.767184777048876570481630 \\
\beta=0.493679334448944202819131, & \gamma_{2}=0.102459239050841954854995
\end{array}
$$

Table 1. Numerical data for the example of planar five-body central configuration.

Same calculations can be carried out for the more general case with $m_{5}=\nu$ as a new parameter. The system is reduced to (8), (9), and an identity similar to (10):

$$
\left(2+\nu-(2+8 \nu) s_{12}\right)\left(s_{34}-1\right)+2\left(s_{13}-1\right)^{2}=0
$$

Following the procedure demonstrated above we may reduce (12) to an equation in $\theta=s_{13}$ with an additional parameter $\nu$. By solving the equation numerically, as $\nu$ increases the mass $\mu$ increases and the shape of the isosceles trapezoid deforms closer and closer to a rectangle. Figure 2 shows one central configuration with $\nu=10^{-4}$ and the other one with $\nu=10^{4}$. The corresponding $\mu$ are approximately 2.758 and 81952.332 , respectively. The one with $\nu=10^{4}$ is of local minimum type but the one with $\nu=10^{-4}$ is not. A degenerate central configuration is found when $\nu$ reaches a threshold value around 0.518085751 , for which case $\mu$ is approximately 7.215 .

Central configurations with $\nu=10^{-4}$ (left) and $\nu=10^{4}$ (right).

# 3. SPATIAL CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS WITH SEVEN BODIES 

In this section we construct a 3-dimensional central configuration with seven bodies which is convex but not strictly convex. Its convex hull is an octahedron with two planes of symmetry. The idea is to add two mass points along the vertical line through the circumcenter of a horizontal five-body isosceles trapezoidal configuration similar to the one in the previous section.

Consider a 3-dimensional configuration $q \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{3}\right)^{7}$ with vertices

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
q_{1}=(-\alpha,-\zeta, 0), & q_{2}=(\alpha,-\zeta, 0), & q_{3}=(-\beta, \gamma-\zeta, 0) \\
q_{4}=(\beta, \gamma-\zeta, 0), & q_{5}=(0,-\zeta, 0), & q_{6}=(0, \delta-\zeta, \eta) \\
q_{7}=(0, \delta-\zeta,-\eta) &
\end{array}
$$

Here $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \eta$ are all assumed to be positive. The term $\delta$ is given by

$$
\delta=\frac{-\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}}{2 \gamma}
$$

so that $q_{6}$ and $q_{7}$ are equally distant from the vertices $q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3}, q_{4}$ of a trapezoid. The configuration is clearly convex but not strictly convex as $q_{5}$ is the midpoint of the edge $\overline{q_{1} q_{2}}$.

Let $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{5}=1, m_{3}=m_{4}=\mu, m_{6}=m_{7}=\nu$. By setting

$$
\zeta=\frac{2(\mu \gamma+\nu \delta)}{3+2 \mu+2 \nu}
$$

the mass center $\dot{q}$ of the configuration $q$ is exactly the origin. We will show that $q$ is indeed a central configuration for some positive $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \eta, \mu$, and $\nu$.

The main idea is the same as the planar case. First we write down equations of central configurations in terms of $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \eta, \mu, \nu$, and $s_{i j}$ 's, and then look for solutions with all of these variables positive. Each $s_{i j}$ can be easily expressed in terms of $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \eta$ and are subject to some symmetry constraints. By straightforward reductions, variables $\mu$ and $\nu$ can be also easily expressed in terms of these four variables, and we are left with four equations with four variables.

We begin with some observations on $s_{i j}$ 's:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& s_{13}=s_{24}=\left((\alpha-\beta)^{2}+\gamma^{2}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
& s_{14}=s_{23}=\left((\alpha+\beta)^{2}+\gamma^{2}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
& s_{35}=s_{45}=\left(\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
& s_{15}=s_{25}=8 s_{12}=\alpha^{-3} \\
& s_{34}=(2 \beta)^{-3} \\
& s_{17}=s_{27}=s_{37}=s_{47}=s_{16}=s_{26}=s_{36}=s_{46}=\left(\alpha^{2}+\delta^{2}+\eta^{2}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
& s_{56}=s_{57}=\left(\delta^{2}+\eta^{2}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
& s_{67}=(2 \eta)^{-3} \\
& s_{i j}=s_{i j} \quad \text { for any } i, j
\end{aligned}
$$

Using merely symmetries among $s_{i j}$ 's, equations (5) are reduced to cases $k=1,3,5,7$ and they are expressed in terms of $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \eta, \mu, \nu$, and $s_{12}, s_{13}, s_{14}, s_{34}, s_{35}, s_{17}, s_{57}, s_{67}$. The

third component of (5) is clearly zero when $k=1,3,5$, and the first component of (5) is also zero when $k=5,7$. There are seven equations left:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha\left(3-10 s_{12}\right)+\mu \alpha\left(2-s_{13}-s_{14}\right)+2 \nu \alpha\left(1-s_{17}\right)+\mu \beta\left(s_{13}-s_{14}\right) & =0 \\
\mu \gamma\left(2-s_{13}-s_{14}\right)+2 \nu \delta\left(1-s_{17}\right) & =0 \\
\alpha\left(s_{13}-s_{14}\right)+\beta\left(3-s_{13}-s_{14}-s_{35}\right)+2 \mu \beta\left(1-s_{34}\right)+2 \nu \beta\left(1-s_{17}\right) & =0 \\
\gamma\left(3-s_{13}-s_{14}-s_{35}\right)+2 \nu(\gamma-\delta)\left(1-s_{17}\right) & =0 \\
\mu \gamma\left(1-s_{35}\right)+\nu \delta\left(1-s_{57}\right) & =0 \\
2\left(\mu(\gamma-\delta)-\delta)\left(1-s_{17}\right)-\delta\left(1-s_{57}\right)\right. & =0 \\
2(1+\mu)\left(1-s_{17}\right)+\left(1-s_{57}\right)+2 \nu\left(1-s_{67}\right) & =0
\end{aligned}
$$

For brevity we keep the notation $\delta$ in these equations. One can easily check linear dependence of the second, fourth, fifth, and the sixth equations. By the substitutions

$$
\begin{aligned}
s_{35} & =\frac{\nu \delta}{\mu \gamma}\left(1-s_{57}\right)+1 \\
s_{57} & =1-\frac{2(\mu \gamma-\mu \delta-\delta)}{\delta}\left(1-s_{17}\right) \\
s_{17} & =\frac{\mu \gamma}{2 \nu \delta}\left(2-s_{13}-s_{14}\right)+1
\end{aligned}
$$

the system is reduced to three equations, two of which can be used to determine masses $\mu$ and $\nu$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu & =\frac{\alpha\left(s_{14}-s_{13}\right)}{\beta\left(s_{13}+s_{14}-2 s_{34}\right)} \\
\nu & =\frac{\mu \gamma}{\delta} \sqrt{\frac{2-s_{13}-s_{14}}{2\left(1-s_{67}\right)}}
\end{aligned}
$$

In particular we have $s_{13}+s_{14}-2 s_{34}<0$, since $s_{14}<s_{13}$. The remaining equation can be written

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(3-10 s_{12}\right)\left(s_{13}+s_{14}-2 s_{34}\right) \\
= & \left(s_{13}-s_{14}\right)^{2}+\frac{\alpha(\delta-\gamma)}{\beta \delta}\left(s_{13}-s_{14}\right)\left(2-s_{13}-s_{14}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

With the help of (13) and (16), equations (15) and (17) are now four equations in four unknowns $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \eta$. The Newtonian method converges rapidly near $(0.4,0.5,0.87,0.77)$, and resulting masses $\mu$ and $\nu$ are both positive. This shows the existence of a central configuration with seven bodies which is convex but not strictly convex, and finishes the proof of Theorem 1.

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\alpha=0.396619093609962801426587, & \gamma=0.871188462806049795533515 \\
\beta=0.495555327813506194775772, & \eta=0.772004237900502489476959 \\
\delta=0.486253980284487121746795, & \zeta=0.777294735425231051490145 \\
\mu=14.09290585257097996322574, & \nu=0.540451308652400689509046
\end{array}
$$

Table 2. Numerical data for the example of spatial seven-body central configuration

Numerical data accurate to the 24th decimal places are given in table 2. Figure 3 shows the corresponding central configuration. This central configuration is not of local minimum type since the second derivative of the normalized potential $D^{2} \tilde{U}$ has two negative eigenvalues that are approximately -134.616 and -66.881 .

As in the previous section, we may consider the more general case with $m_{5}=\sigma$ as a parameter, then obtain a family of convex spatial central configurations which are not strictly convex. The spectrum of $D^{2} \tilde{U}$ evaluated at the central configuration varies with $\sigma$ and, among those we computed, the number of negative eigenvalues are two or three. A degenerate central configuration can be obtained when $\sigma \approx 0.504336299$.


Figure 3. A convex but not strictly convex central configuration with seven bodies.

Convex central configurations which are not strictly convex should be rare; we have searched miscellaneous seemly possible candidates and the one in this section is the only one we found for the spatial seven-body central configuration.

Now we finish this paper with some remarks on spatial central configurations with less bodies. There is no 3-dimensional convex central configuration with five bodies which is

not strictly convex. If there were, then there would be a plane $\pi$ which contains exactly four masses. One way of excluding this possibility is by using a spatial version of the perpendicular bisector theorem [5, pp.511]. Another simple approach is by using a result in  which implies in this case that the four masses on $\pi$ must be cocircular, thus forming a strictly convex polygon. Consequently, since the fifth body is not on $\pi$, the configuration is strictly convex.

It would be interesting to know if there exists any 3-dimensional convex central configuration with six bodies which is not strictly convex. We don't know the answer. A case we find difficult to exclude is a hexahedron with an isosceles triangular base and with three collinear bodies on its top which fall on the perpendicular bisecting plane of the base.

# Continuation and bifurcations of concave central configurations in the four and five body-problems for homogeneous force laws 

Alan Almeida Santos ${ }^{\mathrm{a}, *}$, Marcelo Marchesin ${ }^{\mathrm{b}}$, Ernesto Pérez-Chavela ${ }^{\mathrm{c}, 1}$, Claudio Vidal ${ }^{\mathrm{d}}$<br>${ }^{a}$ Departamento de Matemática, Campus Prof. Alberto Carvalho, Universidade Federal de Sergipe, Av. Ver. Olímpio Grande, s/n, Itabaiana, SE CEP 49510-200, Brazil<br>${ }^{\mathrm{b}}$ Department of Mathematics, Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, Av. Antônio Carlos, 6627, Belo Horizonte, MG CEP 31270-901, Brazil<br>${ }^{c}$ ITAM, Department of Mathematics, Calle Río Hondo No. 1, Col. Progreso Tizapan, México, D.F. 01080, Mexico<br>${ }^{d}$ Departamento de Matemática, Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad del Bío Bío, Casilla 5-C, Concepción, VIII-Región, Chile

A B S T R A C T

The central configurations given by an equilateral triangle and a regular tetrahedron with equal masses at the vertices and a body at the barycenter have been widely studied in  and  due to the phenomena of bifurcation occurring when the central mass has a determined value $m^{*}$. We propose a variation of this problem setting the central mass as the critical value $m^{*}$ and letting a mass at a vertex to be the parameter of bifurcation. In both cases, 2 D and 3 D , we verify the existence of bifurcation, that is, for a same set of masses we determine two new central configurations. The computation of the bifurcations, as well as their pictures have been performed considering homogeneous force laws with exponent $a<-1$.

## 1. Introduction

In the classical Newtonian $n$-body problem the unique explicit solutions which are known until now are the homographic solutions, characterized by the fact that their configurations are invariant up to rotations and scaling, and in which each body describes a Keplerian orbit. These particular solutions are generated by initial configurations called central configurations (see  for details) and are, certainly the most celebrated of them. More precisely, let be $\mathbb{E}$ a finite dimensional Euclidean vector space; $\mathbf{q}_{1}, \cdots, \mathbf{q}_{n} \in \mathbb{E}$ the position vectors; $m_{1}, \cdots, m_{n}$ the masses given by $n$ positives numbers; $a$ a negative real number; $M=\sum m_{i}$ the
total mass of the system and $\mathbf{q}_{G}=\frac{1}{M} \sum m_{i} \mathbf{q}_{i}$ the center of mass of the system, we can then give the following definition:

Definition 1. A configuration $\mathbf{q}=\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \cdots, \mathbf{q}_{n}\right) \in \mathbb{E}^{n}$ is a central configuration (cc by short) for the masses $m_{1}, \cdots, m_{n}$ if there exists a constant $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ such that

$$
\lambda\left(\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{G}\right)=\sum_{j \neq i} m_{j}\left\|\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right\|^{2 a}\left(\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right), \quad \forall i=1, \cdots, n
$$

When $a=-3 / 2$ we have the Newtonian case and when $a=-1$ the vortex case.
Technically, central configurations are zeros of a system of $n$ equations with $n$ vectorial variables and $n$ positive parameters. In some special cases, e.g., when all masses are equal, some quite simple solutions having well-defined positions can be obtained in a trivial way. In effect, we can verify easily that any regular $n$-gon is a central configuration. If we add any additional mass at the origin, we still get a central configuration. A regular simplex of $n$ points on an affine subspace $n-1$ dimensional is a central configuration no matter the values of the masses at the vertices. Other symmetric configurations like rhombus, kites and pyramids exist for systems with some equal masses $$.

As zeros of systems of equations with many parameters, it is expected that bifurcation phenomena arise. This happens if the Jacobian of the system becomes degenerate for some values of the parameters at a given trivial solution. This type of question has been approached in many works. In , the authors proved the existence of bifurcations at the neighborhood of the following planar central configurations: the equilateral triangle with equal masses at the vertices and a fourth mass $m^{*}$ at the barycenter and the square with equal masses at the vertices and a fifth mass $m^{* *}$ at the center. In  Meyer studied the continuation of central configurations from the restricted $(3+1)$-body problem with two equal masses $1-\mu$ and a third mass $2 \mu$ forming an equilateral triangle to the full 4-body problem. He proved that for small values of the fourth mass, there are central configurations degenerated which undergo bifurcation for specific values of the parameter $\mu$. The same bifurcation analysis was applied in  to show the existence of four branches of central configurations which arise from the regular tetrahedron with a critical mass at the barycenter. In , by using the $S_{4}$-equivariance of equations defining Dziobek's configurations, three new branches of bifurcations were found improving the previous result.

In this paper we investigate bifurcations arising from two concave central configurations in the 4 and 5 -body problem. In the former case, we consider the equilateral triangle with masses $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{4}=1$ at the vertices and a mass $m_{3}=m$ at the barycenter. For any non-negative value of $m$, this is a central configuration. In , Palmore showed that $m^{*}=\frac{81+64 \sqrt{3}}{249}$ is the unique value of m for which, this central configuration is degenerate. Unlike the analysis performed by Schmidt and Meyer , which have considered the mass at the barycenter as the bifurcation parameter, we set $m_{4}=1+\varepsilon$ and $m=m^{*}$, so that at $\varepsilon=0$ we verify that the system of equations undergo a bifurcation producing symmetric and non symmetric central configurations for $\varepsilon$ near zero. The $S_{2}$-equivariance of the equations and the Implicit Function Theorem (IFT for shorting) are applied in a singular case as in , and they will be the main tools in the proof of existence. For $m \neq m^{*}$ the equilateral triangle is non-degenerate and so, it can be continued in a neighborhood of $\varepsilon=0$ as a family of isosceles triangles.

In the five body problem, we consider the regular tetrahedron with masses $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=m_{5}=1$ at the vertices and a mass $m_{4}=m$ at the barycenter. By setting $m_{4}=m^{* *}=\frac{10368+1701 \sqrt{6}}{54952}$ as in , we proceed to the bifurcation analysis in a similar way, as in the former case, but taking into account that the equations present an $S_{3}$-equivariance. The fact that in this case one has a biggest system entails some extra difficulties, however still in this case, the equations present $S_{3}$ instead $S_{2}$-equivariance, so the computations can be reduced significantly and allows us to show the existence of several branches of central configurations emanating from the tetrahedron.

A remarkable note about this work is that in both cases, the existence of bifurcations was carried out considering the exponent $a<-1$. That is, our results are valid for any potential of the homogeneous family.

After the introduction where we give the preliminaries of the problems to be studied here, the paper is organized as follows: In Section 2 we define Dziobek's configurations and characterize the central configurations of $n$ bodies in dimension $n-2$ through them. In Section 3 we prove that the $c c$ with equilateral triangle shape and a mass other than $m^{*}$ at the barycenter can be continued to a symmetric family of $c c$ and we study the bifurcation phenomena when one of the masses located at one vertex of the equilateral triangle crosses the value 1 and $m^{*}$ is located at the barycenter. Section 4 is dedicated to the study of concave $c c$ formed by a regular tetrahedron with a mass at the barycenter. First we prove that the above $c c$ can be continued to a symmetrical family of $c c$ and finally we analyze the bifurcation phenomena following the same strategy as in the triangular case.

# 2. Equations for Dziobek's configurations 

Given $n$ points $\mathbf{q}=\left(q_{1}, \cdots, q_{n}\right)$ in an Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}$, we define the dimension of the configuration $\mathbf{q}$ as the number

$$
\operatorname{dim}\left[q_{1}-q_{i}, \cdots, q_{n}-q_{i}\right]
$$

which is independent of the chosen point $q_{i}$ and where the brackets  mean the vectorial space generated by the list of vectors in there.

If the dimension of $\mathbf{q}$ is exactly $n-2$ then there exists a non-zero $n$-tuple, $X=\left(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ unique up to a factor such that

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} q_{i}=0
$$

Let $\mathbf{q}$ be a configuration associated to $n$ positive masses, then we can define a Dziobek configuration as following

Definition 2. A Dziobek configuration is a configuration of $n$ particles such that there exists a non-zero $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfying (2) and such that for some $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$

$$
\frac{\lambda}{M}-s_{i j}^{a}=\frac{x_{i} x_{j}}{m_{i} m_{j}}
$$

where $s_{i j}=\left\|q_{i}-q_{j}\right\|^{2}$.
In , it is shown that Dziobek's configurations are central configurations of dimension at most $n-2$ and any central configuration of dimension exactly $n-2$ is a Dziobek configuration.

If we define the quantities $t_{i}=\sum_{j \neq i} s_{i j} x_{j}$ then equations (2) are equivalent to

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad t_{i}=t_{j} \quad \text { for all } i, j
$$

so central configurations of dimension $n-2$ associated to $n$ positive masses $m_{j}$ are given by the following system

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} & =0 \\
t_{i} & =t_{j} \\
\frac{\lambda}{M}-s_{i j}^{a} & =\frac{x_{i} x_{j}}{m_{i} m_{j}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Remark 1. The constant $\lambda$ required in Definition 2 is the Lagrange multiplier associated to the central configuration. It is not difficult to see that two homothetic Dziobek configurations satisfy the same equations (4) for different values of $\lambda$. In the calculations of Dziobek configurations, we set an appropriate value for $\lambda$.

Remark 2. If two masses are equal, e.g. $m_{1}=m_{2}$, then for a Dziobek configuration, the equality $x_{1}=x_{2}$ is equivalent to a symmetry with respect to the segment $q_{1} q_{2}$. This is because the function $\varphi(s)=\frac{\lambda}{M}-s^{a}$ is increasing for $a<-1$ and according to (3), for all $j \neq 1,2$ we have

$$
x_{1}=x_{2} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \frac{x_{1} x_{j}}{m_{1} m_{j}}=\frac{x_{2} x_{j}}{m_{2} m_{j}} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \varphi\left(s_{1 j}\right)=\varphi\left(s_{2 j}\right)
$$

from where follows the identities $s_{1 j}=s_{2 j}$.

# 3. The equilateral triangle with a mass at the barycenter 

Consider the system (4) with $n=4$ and masses $m_{1}=m_{2}=1, m_{3}=m$ and $m_{4}=1+\varepsilon$. In order that the equilateral triangle with the squares of the mutual distances $s_{12}^{0}=s_{14}^{0}=s_{24}^{0}=3$ and $s_{13}^{0}=s_{23}^{0}=s_{34}^{0}=1$ be a solution for $\varepsilon=0$ we must have $\lambda=m+3^{1+a}$. This central configuration of the 4 -body problem will be called simply concave equilateral triangle leaving implied the occurrence of a fourth mass at the barycenter. The values for the variables $x$ 's corresponding to the concave equilateral triangle are

$$
x_{1}^{0}=x_{2}^{0}=x_{4}^{0}=k \quad \text { and } \quad x_{3}^{0}=-3 k
$$

where $k=\sqrt{\frac{m}{3+m}\left(1-3^{a}\right)}$.
By using the third equation in (4) we can express the six squares of the mutual distances in terms of oriented areas $x_{i}$. Besides, from the first equation in (4) we insert $x_{3}=-x_{1}-x_{2}-x_{4}$ into equations $t_{i}=t_{j}$ to get a system of three equations, three variables $X=\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{4}\right)$ and one parameter $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}$ given by the functions:

$$
\begin{gathered}
F_{1}(X, \varepsilon)=x_{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-x_{1} x_{2}\right)^{1 / a}+x_{3}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{1} x_{3}}{m}\right)^{1 / a}+x_{4}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{1} x_{4}}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}-t_{4} \\
F_{2}(X, \varepsilon)=x_{1}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-x_{1} x_{2}\right)^{1 / a}+x_{3}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{2} x_{3}}{m}\right)^{1 / a}+x_{4}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{2} x_{4}}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}-t_{4} \\
F_{3}(X, \varepsilon)=\sum_{j=1}^{2} x_{j}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{j} x_{3}}{m}\right)^{1 / a}+x_{4}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{3} x_{4}}{m(1+\varepsilon)}\right)^{1 / a}-t_{4}
\end{gathered}
$$

where $m>0$ and $a<-1$ are fixed and

$$
t_{4}=x_{1}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{1} x_{4}}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}+x_{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{2} x_{4}}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}+x_{3}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{3} x_{4}}{m(1+\varepsilon)}\right)^{1 / a}
$$

Calling $F=\left(F_{1}, F_{2}, F_{3}\right): \mathbb{R}^{3} \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{3}$, we have $F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)=(0,0,0)$ for any $m>0$. Observe also that $F$ is $S_{2}$-equivariant, that is

$$
F(\sigma \cdot X, \varepsilon)=\sigma \cdot F(X, \varepsilon)
$$

for $\sigma:\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{4}\right) \mapsto\left(x_{2}, x_{1}, x_{4}\right)$ and its first derivative must satisfy

$$
D_{X} F(\sigma \cdot X, \varepsilon) \cdot \sigma=\sigma \cdot D_{X} F(X, \varepsilon)
$$

Take into account that $\sigma \cdot X^{0}=X^{0}$, we have that the derivative $D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)$ is a linear transformation that commutes with $\sigma$. Therefore, it is a matrix of the form

$$
D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
b & c & d \\
c & b & d \\
e & e & f
\end{array}\right)
$$

The calculations of the first partial derivative of $F$ with respect to $X$ evaluated at $\left(X^{0}, m, 0\right)$ give us

$$
\begin{gathered}
b=\left.\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}\right|_{\left(X^{0}, 0\right)}=-3-\frac{k^{2}}{a}\left(\frac{9}{m}+3^{1-a}\right)=-d \\
c=\left.\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial x_{2}}\right|_{\left(X^{0}, 0\right)}=0 \\
e=\left.\frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial x_{1}}\right|_{\left(X^{0}, 0\right)}=-1+\frac{k^{2}}{a}\left(\frac{9}{m}+3^{1-a}\right)=d-4 \\
f=\left.\frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial x_{4}}\right|_{\left(X^{0}, 0\right)}=2+2 \frac{k^{2}}{a}\left(\frac{9}{m}+3^{1-a}\right)=2 d-4
\end{gathered}
$$

With the above values, the determinant below is easily obtained

$$
\left|D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)\right|=4 d^{2}(d-3)
$$

The factor $d-3$ is negative for any $a<-1$ and $m>0$, whereas the factor $d$ is zero if, and only if, the mass $m$ is equal to

$$
m^{*}=3 \frac{3^{a}-a-1}{3^{-a}+a-1}
$$

Proposition 1. For $a<-1$, the value of $m^{*}$ is in the interval $(0,1)$.
Proof. First we observe that $m^{*}=3 \frac{3^{a}-a-1}{3^{-a}+a-1}>3 \frac{3^{a}-a-1}{3^{-a}}>0$ for all $a<-1$.
Now, on one hand the derivative of $m^{*}$ with respect to $a$ is

$$
\frac{d m^{*}}{d a}=3 \frac{\left(1-3^{-a}\right)\left(\log (3) a 3^{a}-\log (3) 3^{a}-3^{a}+\log (3) a+\log (3)+1\right)}{\left(3^{-a}+a-1\right)^{2}}
$$

and on the other hand, the derivative of the numerator with respect to $a$ is

$$
\log ^{2}(3)\left(3^{a}(a-1)+(a+1) 3^{-a}\right)
$$

which is negative for $a<-1$. Thus the numerator of $\frac{d m^{*}}{d a}$ is a decreasing function on $(-\infty,-1)$, this implies that it reaches its minimum at $a=-1$. Since $\left.\frac{d m^{*}}{d a}\right|_{a=-1}=4(\log (3)-1)$ we get that $\frac{d m^{*}}{d a}>0$ on $(-\infty,-1)$.

Finally, it is easy to verify that

$$
\lim _{a \rightarrow-\infty} m^{*}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad m^{*}(-1)=1
$$

which proves the stated.
Remark 3. In the Newtonian case with $a=-3 / 2$, the value of $m^{*}$ agrees with that found by Meyer-Schmidt in  and by Palmore in , that is $m^{*}=\frac{81+64 \sqrt{3}}{249}$.

# 3.1. Continuation 

By a straightforward application of the Implicit Function Theorem, we have the
Theorem 1. For every $a<-1$ and $0<m \neq m^{*}$, there exists $\varepsilon_{0} \in \mathbb{R}$ such that the concave equilateral triangle $\left(X^{0}, 0\right)$ can be continued to a symmetric family of concave central configurations $X(\varepsilon)$ defined for $|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_{0}$ and having isosceles shape given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{1}(\varepsilon)=k+\alpha \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right) \\
& x_{2}(\varepsilon)=k+\alpha \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right) \\
& x_{4}(\varepsilon)=k+\beta \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are well-defined functions of $m$ and $a$.
Proof. If $0<m \neq m^{*}$, then $\left|D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)\right| \neq 0$ and the Implicit Function Theorem can be applied to the equation $F(X, \varepsilon)=(0,0,0)$ near the trivial solution $\left(X^{0}, 0\right)$, ensuring the existence of a unique curve $X(\varepsilon) \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ defined on an interval $\left(-\epsilon_{0}, \epsilon_{0}\right)$ and such that

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(X(\varepsilon), \varepsilon) & =(0,0,0) \\
X(0) & =X^{0}
\end{aligned}
$$

The $S_{2}$-equivariance of $F$ implies that $(\sigma \cdot X(\varepsilon), \varepsilon)$ is also solution for $F=0$. By the local uniqueness of the implicit function we must have

$$
\sigma \cdot X(\varepsilon)=X(\varepsilon) \quad \Rightarrow \quad x_{1}(\varepsilon)=x_{2}(\varepsilon)
$$

By Remark 2, the central configurations given by $F=0$, which are continuation of $X^{0}$ in a neighborhood of $\varepsilon=0$, are symmetric with respect to the segment $q_{1} q_{2}$, that is

$$
s_{13}(\varepsilon)=s_{23}(\varepsilon) \quad \text { and } \quad s_{14}(\varepsilon)=s_{24}(\varepsilon)
$$

for any $\varepsilon \in\left(-\varepsilon_{0}, \varepsilon_{0}\right)$.
By multiplying the derivative $\left.\frac{\partial F}{\partial \varepsilon}\right|_{\left(X^{0}, 0\right)}$ by the matrix $-D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)^{-1}$ we obtain the expression of $X(\varepsilon)$ at the first order in $\varepsilon$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{1}(\varepsilon)=k+\alpha \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right) \\
& x_{2}(\varepsilon)=k+\alpha \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right) \\
& x_{4}(\varepsilon)=k+\beta \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The expressions for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \alpha=\frac{k^{3} p(m, a)}{6 \cdot 3^{a}\left(1-3^{a}\right)\left(m+3^{1+a}\right)\left(3^{-a}+a-1\right)\left(m-m^{*}\right)} \\
& \beta=\frac{k^{3} q(m, a)}{6 \cdot 3^{a}\left(1-3^{a}\right)\left(m+3^{1+a}\right)\left(3^{-a}+a-1\right)\left(m-m^{*}\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\begin{gathered}
p(m, a)=2 a 3^{a} m^{2}+\left[3^{1+a}\left(3 a+(a+1) 3^{a}\right)-3\right] m \\
+3^{a+2}\left[3^{2 a}+(a+1) 3^{a}+3^{a}+a-3\right]-\frac{2\left(1-3^{a}\right) 3^{3+2 a}}{m} \\
q(m, a)=2 \cdot 3^{a} m^{2}\left(3^{1-a}+a-3\right)+m\left[3^{a+1}\left(3^{a}(a-11)+3(a+2)\right)+15\right] \\
+3^{a+2}\left[9+a+3^{a}(a-4)-5 \cdot 3^{2 a}\right]+\frac{4\left(1-3^{a}\right) 3^{3+2 a}}{m}
\end{gathered}
$$

Thus we have proved the theorem.
Note that $p(m, a)$ is a sum of negative terms for $a<-1$ so that the sign of $\alpha$ is defined by the difference $m-m^{*}$. On the other hand, it is not possible to give a complete description of the continuation in terms of the parameter $\varepsilon$ because the signal of $\beta$ is undefined due to the third term in the expression of $q(m, a)$.

However, for the particular value $a=-3 / 2$ which corresponds to the Newtonian case, we can make a complete analysis of the central configurations given by (10). In this case we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
x_{1}(\varepsilon)=k+\alpha \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right) \\
x_{2}(\varepsilon)=k+\alpha \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right) \\
x_{3}(\varepsilon)=-3 k+\gamma \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right) \\
x_{4}(\varepsilon)=k+\beta \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

where

$$
\begin{gathered}
\alpha=-\frac{k^{3}\left[18 m^{3}+(55 \sqrt{3}+81) m^{2}+(241-3 \sqrt{3}) m+12(3 \sqrt{3}-1)\right]}{2(59-21 \sqrt{3}) m(\sqrt{3} m+1)\left(m-m^{*}\right)} \\
\beta=\frac{k^{3}\left[54(2 \sqrt{3}-1) m^{3}+(245 \sqrt{3}+27) m^{2}+(395-33 \sqrt{3}) m+24(3 \sqrt{3}-1)\right]}{2(59-21 \sqrt{3}) m(\sqrt{3} m+1)\left(m-m^{*}\right)} \\
\gamma=-(2 \alpha+\beta)=-\frac{3 k^{3}[(36 \sqrt{3}-30) m+49 \sqrt{3}-27]}{2(59-21 \sqrt{3})(\sqrt{3} m+1)}
\end{gathered}
$$

Clearly, we see that the sign of $\gamma$ is negative for all $m>0$ while

$$
\begin{aligned}
& m<m^{*} \Rightarrow \alpha>0 \text { and } \beta<0 \\
& m>m^{*} \Rightarrow \alpha<0 \text { and } \beta>0
\end{aligned}
$$

Considering that

$$
s_{i j}(\varepsilon)=\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{i} x_{j}}{m_{i} m_{j}}\right)^{-2 / 3}
$$

and remembering that $M=m+3+\varepsilon, m_{4}=1+\varepsilon$ and $\lambda=m+3^{-1 / 2}$, we can obtain the derivatives of $s_{i j}$ at $\varepsilon=0$ in terms of the mass $m$. After some tedious calculations we obtain

Table 1
Behavior of $s_{i j}(\varepsilon)$ in a small neighborhood of $\varepsilon=0$.

|  | $0<m<m^{*}$ | $m>m^{*}$ |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| $s_{12}(\varepsilon)$ | increasing | decreasing |
| $s_{13}(\varepsilon)$ | decreasing | increasing |
| $s_{14}(\varepsilon)$ | indefinite | increasing |
| $s_{34}(\varepsilon)$ | increasing | decreasing |

$$
s_{i j}(\varepsilon)=s_{i j}^{0}+v_{i j}(m) \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right)
$$

where

$$
\begin{gathered}
v_{12}(m)=-\frac{2}{9} \frac{(54 \sqrt{3}-18) m^{2}+(36-\sqrt{3}) m+2+3 \sqrt{3}}{\lambda(6 \sqrt{3}-5)\left(m-m^{*}\right)} \\
v_{13}(m)=\frac{2}{27} \frac{(45-8 \sqrt{3}) m+6 \sqrt{3}-5}{\lambda(6 \sqrt{3}-5)\left(m-m^{*}\right)} \\
v_{14}(m)=\frac{2}{9} \frac{(27 \sqrt{3}-9) m^{2}+(45-8 \sqrt{3}) m-2-3 \sqrt{3}}{\lambda(6 \sqrt{3}-5)\left(m-m^{*}\right)} \\
v_{34}(m)=-\frac{2}{27} \frac{(36-\sqrt{3}) m+21 \sqrt{3}-4}{\lambda(6 \sqrt{3}-5)\left(m-m^{*}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

All coefficients $v_{i j}(m)$ have well-defined sign for each $m>m^{*}$, whereas for $m<m^{*}$ only $v_{14}(m)$ has a change of sign on the interval $\left(0, m^{*}\right)$. In fact, to see this just make $m=0$ and $m=m^{*}$ in the numerator of the expression. Nevertheless, we can draw the behavior of central configurations given by the equation $F(X, \varepsilon)=0$ in a small neighborhood of $\left(X^{0}, 0\right)$ for all $m \neq m^{*}$ (see Table 1, Figs. 1 and 2).

# 3.2. Bifurcation 

Now, we consider the problem

$$
F_{i}\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{4}, \varepsilon\right)=0, \quad i=1,2,3
$$

where we set $m_{3}=m^{*}$. At the point $\left(X^{0}, 0\right)$, the matrix (7) is given by

$$
D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 \\
-4 & -4 & -4
\end{array}\right)
$$

We make some transformations, following the Liapunov-Schmidt reduction process. If $L=D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)$ then we have that

$$
\operatorname{ker}\{L\}=\left\{\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{4}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{3} / x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{4}=0\right\}, \quad \operatorname{Im}\{L\}=\{(0,0, x): x \in \mathbb{R}\}
$$

By taking, $u_{1}=(1,0,-1), u_{2}=(0,1,-1)$ and $u_{3}=(0,0,-1)$ we proceed the following change of variables

$$
\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{4}\right)=y_{1} \cdot u_{1}+y_{2} \cdot u_{2}+y_{3} \cdot u_{3}
$$

so that

$$
x_{1}=y_{1}, \quad x_{2}=y_{2}, \quad x_{4}=-y_{1}-y_{2}-y_{3} \quad \text { and } \quad x_{3}=y_{3}
$$

Let $G(Y, \varepsilon)=F(X(Y), \varepsilon)$ be the new functions defining the Dziobek's configurations on the plane after the change of variables. We get that

$$
\begin{gathered}
G_{1}\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3}, \varepsilon\right)=y_{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-y_{1} y_{2}\right)^{1 / a}+y_{3}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{y_{1} y_{3}}{m^{*}}\right)^{1 / a} \\
-\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}+\frac{y_{1}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}-y_{1}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}+\frac{y_{1}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a} \\
-y_{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}+\frac{y_{2}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}-y_{3}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}+\frac{y_{3}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)}{m^{*}(1+\varepsilon)}\right)^{1 / a} \\
G_{2}\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3}, \varepsilon\right)=y_{1}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-y_{1} y_{2}\right)^{1 / a}+y_{3}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{y_{2} y_{3}}{m^{*}}\right)^{1 / a} \\
-\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}+\frac{y_{2}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}-y_{1}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}+\frac{y_{1}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a} \\
-y_{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}+\frac{y_{2}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}-y_{3}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}+\frac{y_{3}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)}{m^{*}(1+\varepsilon)}\right)^{1 / a} \\
G_{3}\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3}, \varepsilon\right)=y_{1}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{y_{1} y_{3}}{m^{*}}\right)^{1 / a}+y_{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{y_{2} y_{3}}{m^{*}}\right)^{1 / a} \\
-\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}+\frac{y_{3}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)}{m^{*}(1+\varepsilon)}\right)^{1 / a}-y_{1}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}+\frac{y_{1}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a} \\
-y_{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}+\frac{y_{2}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}-y_{3}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}+\frac{y_{3}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}\right)}{m^{*}(1+\varepsilon)}\right)^{1 / a}
\end{gathered}
$$

where $\lambda=m^{*}+3^{1+a}, M=3+m^{*}+\varepsilon$ and $k=\sqrt{\frac{m^{*}}{3+m^{*}}\left(1-3^{a}\right)}$.

By construction we have

$$
D_{Y} G\left(Y^{0}, 0\right)=D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right) \cdot D_{Y} X=\left(\begin{array}{lll}
0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 4
\end{array}\right)
$$

Since the change of variables (11) is $S_{2}$-equivariant, the $S_{2}$-equivariance of $F$ remains in $G$ so that the equation $G_{3}(Y, \varepsilon)=0$ is $S_{2}$-invariant.

The strategy to calculate the central configurations near the concave equilateral triangle consists of solving the equation $G_{3}=0$ for $y_{3}$ in terms of $\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\right)$, insert it into $G_{1}$ and $G_{2}$ and solve the remaining bifurcation problem.

In order to study the bifurcation problem

$$
G\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3}, \varepsilon\right)=(0,0,0), \quad G(k, k,-3 k, 0)=(0,0,0)
$$

we only need two properties of $G$ to know, the analyticity around the trivial solution $(k, k,-3 k, 0)$ and the $S_{2}$-equivariance. In view of this, we firstly make a translation $y_{i} \rightarrow y_{i}+k(i=1,2)$ and $y_{3} \rightarrow y_{3}-3 k$ in the expression of $G$. We have adopted the following notation for its Taylor's series around the trivial root $(0,0,0,0)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
G_{1}(Y, \varepsilon)= & b_{4} \varepsilon+2 b_{22} y_{1} y_{2}+b_{22} y_{2}^{2}+b_{33} y_{3}^{2}+b_{13} y_{1} y_{3}+b_{23} y_{2} y_{3} \\
& +b_{14} y_{1} \varepsilon+b_{24} y_{2} \varepsilon+b_{34} y_{3} \varepsilon+b_{44} \varepsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(3) \\
G_{2}(Y, \varepsilon)= & b_{4} \varepsilon+2 b_{22} y_{1} y_{2}+b_{22} y_{1}^{2}+b_{33} y_{3}^{2}+b_{13} y_{2} y_{3}+b_{23} y_{1} y_{3} \\
& +b_{14} y_{2} \varepsilon+b_{24} y_{1} \varepsilon+b_{34} y_{3} \varepsilon+b_{44} \varepsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(3) \\
G_{3}(Y, \varepsilon)= & 4 y_{3}+c_{4} \varepsilon+c_{11} y_{1}^{2}+c_{11} y_{2}^{2}+c_{33} y_{3}^{2}+c_{12} y_{1} y_{2}+c_{13} y_{1} y_{3} \\
& +c_{13} y_{2} y_{3}+c_{14} y_{1} \varepsilon+c_{14} y_{2} \varepsilon+c_{34} y_{3} \varepsilon+c_{44} \varepsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(3)
\end{aligned}
$$

The above expressions are due to the $S_{2}$-equivariance of $G$. The derivatives of $G_{1}, G_{2}$ and $G_{3}$ at $(0,0,0,0)$ are given by

$$
\begin{gathered}
G_{1}=G_{2}=G_{3}=0 \\
\frac{\partial G_{1}}{\partial y_{1}}=\frac{\partial G_{1}}{\partial y_{2}}=\frac{\partial G_{2}}{\partial y_{1}}=\frac{\partial G_{2}}{\partial y_{2}}=0 \\
b_{4}=\frac{\partial G_{1}}{\partial \varepsilon}=\frac{\partial G_{2}}{\partial \varepsilon}=3 \sqrt{\frac{3^{a}\left(3^{a}-a-1\right)}{1-3^{a}}}>0 \\
b_{11}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^{2} G_{1}}{\partial y_{1}^{2}}=0 \\
b_{22}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^{2} G_{1}}{\partial y_{2}^{2}}=-\frac{6 k 3^{1-a}}{2 a}+\frac{k^{3}(1-a)}{2 a^{2}}\left(3^{1-2 a}+\frac{27}{m^{* 2}}\right)>0 \\
b_{12}=\frac{\partial^{2} G_{1}}{\partial y_{2} \partial y_{1}}=-\frac{6 k 3^{1-a}}{a}+\frac{k^{3}(1-a)}{a^{2}}\left(3^{1-2 a}+\frac{27}{m^{* 2}}\right)=2 b_{22} \\
c_{4}=\frac{\partial G_{3}}{\partial \varepsilon}=\frac{6 k}{a}\left[\frac{\lambda\left(3^{-a}-1\right)}{\left(3+m^{*}\right)^{2}}-k^{2}\left(\frac{2}{m^{*}}+3^{-a}\right)\right]
\end{gathered}
$$

$$
\begin{gathered}
c_{11}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^{2} G_{3}}{\partial y_{1}^{2}}=\frac{k}{2 a}\left[\left(\frac{12}{m^{*}}-2 \cdot 3^{1-a}\right)+\frac{k^{2}(1-a)}{a}\left(\frac{45}{m^{* 2}}-3^{1-2 a}\right)\right] \\
c_{12}=\frac{\partial^{2} G_{3}}{\partial y_{2} \partial y_{1}}=\frac{k}{a}\left[\frac{6}{m^{*}}-4 \cdot 3^{1-a}+\frac{36 k^{2}(1-a)}{a m^{* 2}}\right]
\end{gathered}
$$

By solving $G_{3}=0$ for $y_{3}$ through the IFT, we get a unique analytical function $y_{3}=W\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\right)$ defined on an invariant neighborhood $V$ of $(0,0,0)$.

Lemma 1. The function $W\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\right)$ guaranteed by the IFT is $S_{2}$-invariant.
Proof. Let $\sigma:\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right) \mapsto\left(y_{2}, y_{1}\right)$ be the non-trivial permutation of $S_{2}$. From $S_{2}$-invariance of $G_{3}$ we have for all $y=\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right) \in V$ and $\varepsilon$ small

$$
G_{3}(y, W(\sigma \cdot y, \varepsilon), \varepsilon)=G_{3}(\sigma \cdot y, W(\sigma \cdot y, \varepsilon), \varepsilon)=0
$$

That is, $W(\sigma \cdot y, \varepsilon)$ also solves $G_{3}=0$ locally. By uniqueness of the implicit solution, we must have

$$
W(\sigma \cdot y, \varepsilon)=W(y, \varepsilon), \quad \forall y \in V \text { and } \varepsilon \text { small. }
$$

Now we write the power series for $W$ in a small neighborhood of $(0,0,0)$ and insert it into the third equation of (14). By comparison of coefficients we get up to order 2

$$
\begin{aligned}
W\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\right)= & -\frac{c_{4}}{4} \varepsilon-\frac{c_{11}}{4} y_{1}^{2}-\frac{c_{11}}{4} y_{2}^{2}-\frac{c_{12}}{4} y_{1} y_{2}+\left(\frac{c_{4} c_{13}}{16}-\frac{c_{14}}{4}\right) y_{1} \varepsilon \\
& +\left(\frac{c_{4} c_{13}}{16}-\frac{c_{14}}{4}\right) y_{2} \varepsilon+\left[\frac{c_{34} c_{4}}{16}-\frac{c_{4}^{2} c_{33}}{64}-\frac{c_{44}}{4}\right] \varepsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(3)
\end{aligned}
$$

With this, we turn back to the bifurcation problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tilde{G}_{1}\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\right)=G_{1}\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, W\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\right), \varepsilon\right)=0 \\
& \tilde{G}_{2}\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\right)=G_{2}\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, W\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\right), \varepsilon\right)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

The Taylor's series expansion for these functions are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tilde{G}_{1}\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\right)=b_{4} \varepsilon+2 b_{22} y_{1} y_{2}+b_{22} y_{2}^{2}+\left(b_{14}-\frac{b_{13} c_{4}}{4}\right) y_{1} \varepsilon \\
& \quad+\left(b_{24}-\frac{b_{23} c_{4}}{4}\right) y_{2} \varepsilon+\left(b_{44}-\frac{b_{34} c_{4}}{4}+\frac{b_{33} c_{4}^{2}}{16}\right) \varepsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(3) \\
& \tilde{G}_{2}\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\right)=b_{4} \varepsilon+2 b_{22} y_{1} y_{2}+b_{22} y_{1}^{2}+\left(b_{14}-\frac{b_{13} c_{4}}{4}\right) y_{2} \varepsilon \\
& \quad+\left(b_{24}-\frac{b_{23} c_{4}}{4}\right) y_{1} \varepsilon+\left(b_{44}-\frac{b_{34} c_{4}}{4}+\frac{b_{33} c_{4}^{2}}{16}\right) \varepsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(3)
\end{aligned}
$$

Proposition 2. The system $\tilde{G}_{1}=\tilde{G}_{2}=0$ does not admit a differentiable solution $y(\varepsilon)=\left(y_{1}(\varepsilon), y_{2}(\varepsilon)\right)$ defined around $\varepsilon=0$

Proof. If it did, we would have $\tilde{G}(y(\varepsilon), \varepsilon)=0$ whose differentiation at $(0,0,0)$ would furnish

$$
D_{y} \tilde{G}(y(0), 0) \cdot y^{\prime}(0)+\frac{\partial \tilde{G}}{\partial \varepsilon}(y(0), 0)=0
$$

However by (12), we have $D_{y} \tilde{G}(y(0), 0)=0$ and $\tilde{G}_{\varepsilon} \neq 0$ so the above equation is impossible.

Now we solve the equation $\tilde{G}_{1}\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\right)=0$ for $\varepsilon$ by writing it as an analytic function of $\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)$

$$
\varepsilon\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)=-\frac{b_{22}}{b_{4}} y_{2}^{2}-\frac{2 b_{22}}{b_{4}} y_{1} y_{2}+\mathcal{O}(3)
$$

The last equation to be solved is

$$
H\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)=\tilde{G}_{2}\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)\right)=0
$$

but such $H\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)$ is analytic in a small neighborhood of $(0,0)$ and satisfy

$$
H(0,0)=0 \quad \text { and } \quad D_{y} H(0,0)=(0,0)
$$

Lemma 2. If $H(x, y)$ is an analytic function defined on a neighborhood of the origin $(0,0)$, such that $H(x, x)=0$ then

$$
H(x, y)=(x-y) \cdot h(x, y)
$$

where $h(x, y)$ is analytic in a neighborhood of $(0,0)$.
Proof. By defining $\hat{H}(\xi, \eta)=H(\xi+\eta, \xi-\eta)$ for $(\xi, \eta)$ near the origin, we have that $\hat{H}$ is analytic in a small neighborhood of $(0,0)$ and $\hat{H}(\xi, 0)=0$. Therefore, in the Taylor's series of $\hat{H}(\xi, \eta)$ all coefficients of the powers of $\xi^{n}$ must be zero so that the series of $\hat{H}$ has a factor $\eta$. Thus

$$
H(x, y)=(x-y) \cdot h(x, y)
$$

The function (18) satisfies the conditions of Lemma 2. In fact, from the $S_{2}$-equivariance of $\tilde{G}$ we have the identity

$$
\tilde{G}_{2}\left(y_{2}, y_{1}, \varepsilon\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)\right)=\tilde{G}_{1}\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \varepsilon\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)\right)=0
$$

for all $\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)$ near $(0,0)$. Thus

$$
H(t, t)=\tilde{G}_{2}(t, t, \varepsilon(t, t))=0
$$

for all $t$ near 0 .
By Lemma 2, we have that

$$
H\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)=\left(y_{1}-y_{2}\right) \cdot h\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)
$$

By replacing the series of $\varepsilon\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)$ into $\tilde{G}_{2}$ we obtain

$$
H\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)=b_{22}\left(y_{1}^{2}-y_{2}^{2}\right)+\mathcal{O}(3)
$$

Comparing with (19) and remembering that the Taylor series is unique, we have that

$$
h\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)=b_{22}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}\right)+\mathcal{O}(2)
$$

Thus, the equation $h\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)=0$ can be solved for $y_{1}=\tau\left(y_{2}\right)$ defined in a neighborhood of $y_{2}^{0}=0$ such that $\tau(0)=0$. From the factorization (19), we see that the equation $H\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)=0$ has two analytic branches at the neighborhood of $y_{2}^{0}=0$ given by

$$
y_{1}=y_{2} \quad \text { and } \quad y_{1}=-y_{2}+\mathcal{O}(2)
$$

In order to write the bifurcation branches, we undo the translation of variables $y_{i}$ and we introduce a small parameter $t$ by setting $y_{2}=k+t$. Writing the expressions of $y_{1}, y_{3}$ and $\varepsilon$ in terms of $t$ we have only two families of central configurations given by the system $G(Y, \varepsilon)=0$ near the concave equilateral triangle with masses $m_{1}=m_{2}=1, m_{3}=m^{*}$ and $m_{4}=1$, where $Y=\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3}\right)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { I: }\left\{\begin{array}{l}
y_{1}=k+t \\
y_{2}=k+t \\
\varepsilon=-\frac{3 b_{22}}{b_{4}} t^{2}+\mathcal{O}(3) \\
y_{3}=-3 k+\left(\frac{3 c_{4} b_{22}}{4 b_{4}}-\frac{c_{11}}{2}-\frac{c_{12}}{4}\right) t^{2}+\mathcal{O}(3)
\end{array}\right. \\
& \text { II: }\left\{\begin{array}{l}
y_{1}=k-t+\mathcal{O}(2) \\
y_{2}=k+t \\
\varepsilon=\frac{b_{22}}{b_{4}} t^{2}+\mathcal{O}(3) \\
y_{3}=-3 k+\left(-\frac{c_{4} b_{22}}{4 b_{4}}-\frac{c_{11}}{2}+\frac{c_{12}}{4}\right) t^{2}+\mathcal{O}(3)
\end{array}\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

The family I has symmetry with respect to the bisector of the segment $q_{1} q_{2}$ and it exists for $\varepsilon<0$ whereas the family II is non symmetric and it exists for $\varepsilon>0$.

However, the concept of bifurcation involves a change in the number of roots of the corresponding equation when the parameter crosses the critical point $\varepsilon=0$. That is, the bifurcation is verified if, for any $\varepsilon \neq 0$, we have two or more values for $Y=\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3}\right)$ satisfying the equation $G(Y, \varepsilon)=0$. In order to see this, note that the function $\varepsilon(t)$ has a relative maximum and a relative minimum in family I and family II, respectively. So, e.g., in family II, for every $\varepsilon>0$ sufficiently small there exist two values $t_{1}<0<t_{2}$ such that $\varepsilon\left(t_{1}\right)=\varepsilon=\varepsilon\left(t_{2}\right)$. Consequently, associated to that $\varepsilon$ we will have two values for the $Y$ variables. For the family I the argument is analogous.

With all the above we have the following result.

Theorem 2. For every $a<-1$, the concave equilateral triangle with vertices $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{4}=1$ and a mass $m_{3}=m^{*}$ at the barycenter, experiences a bifurcation when the mass $m_{4}$ crosses the value 1. More precisely, there is a $\delta>0$ such that for any $1-\delta<m_{4}<1$ we have two concave central configurations coming from the bifurcation presenting a symmetry type axes and for any $1<m_{4}<1+\delta$ we have two concave central configurations without symmetry.

In the case of continuation, the coefficients depend on the mass $m$ and the exponent $a$, while in the study of bifurcation, the coefficients depend only on the exponent. So, we can sketch the behavior of two bifurcation branches. By using that

$$
s_{i j}=\left(\frac{\lambda}{m^{*}+3+\varepsilon(t)}-\frac{x_{i} x_{j}}{m_{i} m_{j}}\right)^{-2 / 3}
$$

we write the power series expansion of $t$ for the two families.

$$
s_{i j}^{I, I I}(\varepsilon)=s_{i j}^{0}+w_{i j}^{I, I I} t+\mathcal{O}\left(t^{2}\right)
$$

Table 2
Behavior of the two families of bifurcation as a function of parameter $t$.

| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| $\varepsilon(t)$ | negative | positive |
| $s_{12}(t)$ | increasing | indefinite |
| $s_{13}(t)$ | decreasing | increasing |
| $s_{14}(t)$ | decreasing | decreasing |

Fig. 4. Family II: with $m_{1}=m_{2}=1, m_{3}=m^{*}$ and $m_{4}=1+\varepsilon$, for each $\varepsilon>0$ one has two non symmetric concave central configurations.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { I: }\left\{\begin{array}{l}
w_{12}^{I}=-\frac{2 \cdot 3^{1-a} \cdot k}{a}>0 \\
w_{13}^{I}=w_{23}^{I}=\frac{3 \cdot k}{m^{*} \cdot a}<0 \\
w_{14}^{I}=w_{24}^{I}=\frac{k \cdot 3^{1-a}}{a}<0 \\
w_{34}^{I}=-\frac{6 \cdot k}{m^{*} \cdot a}>0
\end{array} \quad \text { II: }\left\{\begin{array}{l}
w_{12}^{I I}=0 \\
w_{13}^{I I}=-\frac{3 \cdot k}{m^{*} \cdot a}>0 \\
w_{23}^{I I}=\frac{3 \cdot k}{m^{*} \cdot a}<0 \\
w_{14}^{I I}=\frac{k \cdot 3^{1-a}}{a}<0 \\
w_{24}^{I I}=-\frac{k \cdot 3^{1-a}}{a}>0 \\
w_{34}^{I I}=0
\end{array}\right.\right.\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

In Table 2 we show the behavior of both families in terms of the sign of $\varepsilon$ and the mutual distances. In Fig. 3 we show the two symmetric concave families of central configurations coming from Family 1. Fig. 4 shows two non symmetric families of concave central configurations.

In , the authors found numerically a non-symmetric concave central configuration in the four body problem. We observe that, since in their example $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=1$ and $m_{4}=0.992$, it does not belong to our Family II of non-symmetric concave central configurations.

# 4. The regular tetrahedron with a mass at the barycenter 

Now, consider the system (4) with $n=5$ and masses $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=1, m_{4}=m$ and $m_{5}=1+\varepsilon$. In order that the regular tetrahedron with the squares of the mutual distances $s_{12}^{0}=s_{13}^{0}=s_{15}^{0}=s_{23}^{0}=s_{25}^{0}=$ $s_{35}^{0}=8 / 3$ and $s_{14}^{0}=s_{24}^{0}=s_{34}^{0}=s_{45}^{0}=1$ be a solution for $\varepsilon=0$ we must have $\lambda=m+4 \cdot \rho^{a}$ in which $\rho=8 / 3$. This central configuration of the 5 -body problem will be called simply concave regular tetrahedron leaving implied the occurrence of a fifth mass at the barycenter. The values for variables $x$ 's corresponding to the concave regular tetrahedron are

$$
x_{1}^{0}=x_{2}^{0}=x_{3}^{0}=x_{5}^{0}=k \quad \text { and } \quad x_{4}^{0}=-4 k
$$

where $k=\sqrt{\frac{m}{4+m}\left(1-\rho^{a}\right)}$.
In this case, we insert $x_{4}=-x_{1}-x_{2}-x_{3}-x_{5}$ into the equations $t_{i}=t_{j}$ in (4) to get a system of four equations, four variables $X=\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{5}\right)$ and one parameter $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}$ given by the functions

$$
\begin{aligned}
& F_{1}(X, \varepsilon)=\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\
j \neq 1}}^{4} x_{j}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{1} x_{j}}{m_{j}}\right)^{1 / a}+x_{5}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{1} x_{5}}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}-t_{5} \\
& F_{2}(X, \varepsilon)=\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\
j \neq 2}}^{4} x_{j}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{j} x_{2}}{m_{j}}\right)^{1 / a}+x_{5}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{2} x_{5}}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}-t_{5} \\
& F_{3}(X, \varepsilon)=\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\
j \neq 3}}^{4} x_{j}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{j} x_{3}}{m_{j}}\right)^{1 / a}+x_{5}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{3} x_{5}}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}-t_{5} \\
& F_{4}(X, \varepsilon)=\sum_{j=1}^{3} x_{j}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{j} x_{4}}{m}\right)^{1 / a}+x_{5}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{4} x_{5}}{m(1+\varepsilon)}\right)^{1 / a}-t_{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $m>0$ and $a<-1$ are fixed and

$$
t_{5}=\sum_{j=1}^{3} x_{j}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{j} x_{5}}{1+\varepsilon}\right)^{1 / a}+x_{4}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{4} x_{5}}{m(1+\varepsilon)}\right)^{1 / a}
$$

Calling $F=\left(F_{1}, F_{2}, F_{3}, F_{4}\right): \mathbb{R}^{4} \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{4}$, we have $F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)=(0,0,0,0)$ for any $m>0$. Observe also that $F$ is $S_{3}$-equivariant, that is

$$
F(\sigma \cdot X, \varepsilon)=\sigma \cdot F(X, \varepsilon)
$$

for any permutation in $\Sigma_{4}=\left\{\sigma \in S_{4}: \sigma(4)=4\right\}$ and so, its first derivative must satisfy

$$
D_{X} F(\sigma \cdot X, \varepsilon) \cdot \sigma=\sigma \cdot D_{X} F(X, \varepsilon)
$$

Taking into account that $\sigma \cdot X^{0}=X^{0}$, we have that the derivative $D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)$ is a linear transformation that commutes with every $\sigma \in \Sigma_{4}$. Therefore, it can be represented as a matrix of the form

$$
D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)=\left(\begin{array}{llll}
b & c & c & d \\
c & b & c & d \\
c & c & b & d \\
e & e & e & f
\end{array}\right)
$$

The computation of the first partial derivatives of $F$ with respect to $X$ evaluated at $\left(X^{0}, m, 0\right)$ gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}
& b=\left.\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}\right|_{\left(X^{0}, 0\right)}=-\rho-\frac{k^{2}}{a}\left(\frac{16}{m}+2 \rho^{1-a}\right)=-d \\
& c=\left.\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial x_{2}}\right|_{\left(X^{0}, 0\right)}=0 \\
& e=\left.\frac{\partial F_{4}}{\partial x_{1}}\right|_{\left(X^{0}, 0\right)}=2-\rho+\frac{k^{2}}{a}\left(\frac{12}{m}+\rho^{1-a}\right) \\
& f=\left.\frac{\partial F_{4}}{\partial x_{5}}\right|_{\left(X^{0}, 0\right)}=2+\frac{k^{2}}{a}\left(\frac{28}{m}+3 \rho^{1-a}\right)=e-b
\end{aligned}
$$

With the above values, the determinant is easily obtained

$$
\left|D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)\right|=b^{3}(4 e-b)
$$

The factor $b-4 e$ is positive for any $a<-1$ and $m>0$, whereas the factor $b$ is zero if, and only if, the mass $m$ is equal to

$$
m^{* *}=2 \frac{3 \rho^{a}-2 a-3}{2 \rho^{-a}+a-2}
$$

Proposition 3. For all $a<-1$, the value of $m^{* *}$ is positive.
Proof. By labeling $n(a)=3 \rho^{a}-2 a-3$ and $d(a)=2 \rho^{-a}+a-2$ we have for any $a<-1$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& n^{\prime}(a)=3 \rho^{a} \ln (\rho)-2<3 \frac{3}{8} \ln (e)-2<0 \\
& d^{\prime}(a)=1-2 \rho^{-a} \ln (\rho)<1-2 \rho \ln (\rho)<0
\end{aligned}
$$

so that both functions are decreasing on $(-\infty,-1)$ implying that they reach their minima at $a=-1$. Since $n(-1)=3 \rho^{-1}-1>0$ and $d(-1)=2 \rho-3>0$, we get that $m^{* *}>0$ on $(-\infty,-1)$.

Remark 4. In the Newtonian case with $a=-3 / 2$, the value of $m^{* *}$ agrees with that found by Meyer and Schmidt in , that is $m^{* *}=\frac{10368+1701 \sqrt{6}}{54952}$. Moreover, it is worth noting that in terms of $m^{* *}$, the expression for $b$ becomes

$$
b=-\frac{\left(2 \rho^{-a}+a-2\right) \cdot\left(m-m^{* *}\right) \cdot \rho}{a \cdot(4+m)}
$$

which shows that $b>0$ if and only if $m>m^{* *}$.

# 4.1. Continuation 

Analogously to Theorem 1, we have the
Theorem 3. For every $a<-1$ and $0<m \neq m^{* *}$, there exists $\varepsilon_{0} \in \mathbb{R}$ such that the concave regular tetrahedron $\left(X^{0}, 0\right)$ can be continued to a symmetric family of concave central configurations $X(\varepsilon)$ defined for $|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_{0}$ and with symmetry axis type given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{1}(\varepsilon) & =k+\alpha \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right) \\
x_{2}(\varepsilon) & =k+\alpha \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right) \\
x_{3}(\varepsilon) & =k+\alpha \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right) \\
x_{4}(\varepsilon) & =-4 k+\gamma \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right) \\
x_{5}(\varepsilon) & =k+\beta \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\gamma=-(3 \alpha+\beta)$ and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are well-defined functions of $m$ and $a$.
Proof. If $0<m \neq m^{* *}$, then $\left|D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)\right| \neq 0$ and the IFT can be applied to the equation $F(X, \varepsilon)=$ $(0,0,0)$ near the trivial solution $\left(X^{0}, 0\right)$, ensuring the existence of a unique curve $X(\varepsilon) \in \mathbb{R}^{4}$ defined on an interval $\left(-\varepsilon_{0}, \varepsilon_{0}\right)$ and such that

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(X(\varepsilon), \varepsilon) & =(0,0,0) \\
X(0) & =X^{0}
\end{aligned}
$$

The $S_{3}$-equivariance of $F$ implies that $(\sigma \cdot X(\varepsilon), \varepsilon)$ is also a solution for $F=0$. By the local uniqueness of the implicit function we must have

$$
\forall \sigma \in \Sigma_{4}, \quad \sigma \cdot X(\varepsilon)=X(\varepsilon) \quad \Rightarrow \quad x_{1}(\varepsilon)=x_{2}(\varepsilon)=x_{3}(\varepsilon)
$$

By Remark 2, the central configurations given by $F=0$, which are continuation of $X^{0}$ in a neighborhood of $\varepsilon=0$, present a symmetry axis type, that is

$$
s_{1 i}(\varepsilon)=s_{2 i}(\varepsilon)=s_{3 i}(\varepsilon), \quad i \in\{4,5\}
$$

for any $\varepsilon \in\left(-\varepsilon_{0}, \varepsilon_{0}\right)$.
By multiplying the derivative $\left.\frac{\partial F}{\partial \varepsilon}\right|_{\left(X^{0}, 0\right)}$ by the matrix $-D_{X} F\left(X^{0}, 0\right)^{-1}$ we obtain the expression for $\alpha=\left.\frac{d x_{1}}{d \varepsilon}\right|_{\left(X^{0}, 0\right)}$ and $\beta=\left.\frac{d x_{5}}{d \varepsilon}\right|_{\left(X^{0}, 0\right)}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \alpha=\frac{32 k\left(1-\rho^{a}\right) p(m, a)}{(b-4 e) b a^{2}(4+m)^{3} \rho^{a}} \\
& \beta=\frac{32 k\left(1-\rho^{a}\right) q(m, a)}{(b-4 e) b a^{2}(4+m)^{3} \rho^{a}}
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(m, a)= & \frac{a}{3} m^{3}+\frac{2}{3}\left[a\left(3+\rho^{a}\right)-\frac{2\left(1-\rho^{2 a}\right)}{\rho^{a}}\right] m^{2} \\
& +\frac{4}{3}\left[2 a\left(1+\rho^{a}\right)-\left(1-\rho^{a}\right)\left(11+3 \rho^{a}\right)\right] m-32\left(1-\rho^{a}\right) \rho^{a} \\
q(m, a)= & \frac{1}{3}\left[a+8 \frac{1-\rho^{a}}{\rho^{a}}\right] m^{3}+\frac{2}{3}\left[\frac{2\left(7+13 \rho^{a}\right)\left(1-\rho^{a}\right)}{\rho^{a}}+a\left(3+\rho^{a}\right)\right] m^{2} \\
& +4\left[\left(15+7 \rho^{a}\right)\left(1-\rho^{a}\right)+\frac{2 a\left(1+\rho^{a}\right)}{3}\right] m+96\left(1-\rho^{a}\right) \rho^{a}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus we have proved the theorem.

As in Theorem 1, it's not possible to give a complete description for the behavior of the solution $X(\varepsilon)$ independently of the exponent $a$, so in order to show how the solution $X(\varepsilon)$ behaves, we analyze the particular value $a=-3 / 2$ which corresponds to the Newtonian case, in this case we can make a complete analysis of the central configurations given by (27). We compute

$$
\begin{gathered}
\alpha=-\frac{k\left(1-\rho^{a}\right) \tilde{p}(m)}{2^{2} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot(b-4 e) b a^{2}(4+m)^{3} \rho^{a}} \\
\beta=\frac{k \cdot\left(1-\rho^{a}\right) \tilde{q}(m)}{2^{2} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot(b-4 e) b a^{2}(4+m)^{3} \rho^{a}} \\
\gamma=-(3 \alpha+\beta)=-\frac{4 k\left(1-\rho^{a}\right) m\left(m-m^{* *}\right)(16 m+32+3 \sqrt{6})(64 \sqrt{6}-63)}{3^{3} \cdot(b-4 e) b a^{2}(4+m)^{3} \rho^{a}}
\end{gathered}
$$

where

$$
\begin{gathered}
\tilde{p}(m)=1728 m^{3}+(10368+8084 \sqrt{6}) m^{2}+(63783-2160 \sqrt{6}) m \\
+10368 \sqrt{6}-5832 \\
\tilde{q}(m)=(16384 \sqrt{6}-10944) m^{3}+(51404 \sqrt{6}+17280) m^{2} \\
+(188433-11664 \sqrt{6}) m+31104 \sqrt{6}-17496
\end{gathered}
$$

Since $b>0$ if, and only if $m>m^{* *}$, we see that the sign of $\gamma$ is negative for all $m>0$ while

$$
\begin{aligned}
& m<m^{* *} \Rightarrow \alpha>0 \text { and } \beta<0 \\
& m>m^{* *} \Rightarrow \alpha<0 \text { and } \beta>0
\end{aligned}
$$

Considering that

$$
s_{i j}(\varepsilon)=\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-\frac{x_{i}(\varepsilon) x_{j}(\varepsilon)}{m_{i} m_{j}}\right)^{1 / a}
$$

and remembering that $M=m+4+\varepsilon, m_{5}=1+\varepsilon$ and $\lambda=m+4 \rho^{-3 / 2}$, we can obtain the derivatives of $s_{i j}$ at $\varepsilon=0$ in terms of the mass $m$. After some tedious calculations we get

$$
s_{i j}(\varepsilon)=s_{i j}^{0}+v_{i j}(m) \varepsilon+\mathcal{O}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\right)
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_{12}(m) & =-\frac{64(16 \sqrt{6}-9) m^{2}+12(3 \sqrt{6}+64) m+243}{3 \cdot(64 \sqrt{6}-63) \cdot(8 m+3 \sqrt{6}) \cdot\left(m-m^{* *}\right)} \\
v_{14}(m) & =-\frac{8(56 \sqrt{6}-45) m+27(16-3 \sqrt{6})}{4 \cdot(21 \sqrt{6}-128) \cdot(8 m+3 \sqrt{6}) \cdot\left(m-m^{* *}\right)} \\
v_{15}(m) & =\frac{64(16 \sqrt{6}-9) m^{2}+12(320-39 \sqrt{6}) m-243}{3 \cdot(64 \sqrt{6}-63) \cdot(8 m+3 \sqrt{6}) \cdot\left(m-m^{* *}\right)} \\
v_{45}(m) & =\frac{8(40 \sqrt{6}-9) m+81(16-\sqrt{6})}{4 \cdot(21 \sqrt{6}-128) \cdot(8 m+3 \sqrt{6}) \cdot\left(m-m^{* *}\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

All coefficients $v_{i j}(m)$ have well-defined sign for each $m>m^{* *}$, whereas for $m<m^{* *}$ only $v_{15}(m)$ has a change of sign on the interval $\left(0, m^{* *}\right)$. In fact, to see this, just make $m=0$ and $m=m^{* *}$ in the numerator
