# 9. Proof of Theorem 4 

We consider $3 n$ masses at the vertices of three nested polyhedra with the same number of vertices as in Propositions 6-10. We consider and additional mass $m_{0}=\mu$ located at the origin. It is easy to cheek that the equations of the spatial central configurations (1) for the $3 n+1$-body problem with the mass $m_{0}$ located at the origin are

$$
\begin{aligned}
n e x_{0} & =\sum_{j=1}^{N}-\frac{m_{j} x_{j}}{\left(x_{j}^{2}+y_{j}^{2}+z_{j}^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=0 \\
n e y_{0} & =\sum_{j=1}^{N}-\frac{m_{j} y_{j}}{\left(x_{j}^{2}+y_{j}^{2}+z_{j}^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=0 \\
n e z_{0} & =\sum_{j=1}^{N}-\frac{m_{j} z_{j}}{\left(x_{j}^{2}+y_{j}^{2}+z_{j}^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=0 \\
n e x_{i} & =e x_{i}+\frac{\mu x_{i}}{\left(x_{j}^{2}+y_{j}^{2}+z_{j}^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=0 \\
n e y_{i} & =e y_{i}+\frac{\mu y_{i}}{\left(x_{j}^{2}+y_{j}^{2}+z_{j}^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=0 \\
n e z_{i} & =e z_{i}+\frac{\mu z_{i}}{\left(x_{j}^{2}+y_{j}^{2}+z_{j}^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

for $i=1, \ldots, N$, where $e x_{i}, e y_{i}$ and $e z_{i}$ are defined as in (2).
Notice that in Propositions 6-10 the positions $\left(x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i}\right)$ and the values of the masses $m_{i}$ have been taken so that the center of mass of the problem is located at the origin. Moreover all the vertices in the same polyhedron are at the same distance $d$ from the origin. Therefore equations $n e x_{0}=0, n e y_{0}=0$ and $n e z_{0}=0$ are always satisfied.

Proceeding in a similar way than in Sections 3-7, we prove that, for the nested polyhedra configurations of the $3 n+1$ body problem, system (15) can be reduced to a system of the form $A X=b$ where $A$ and $X$ are given as in (3),

$$
b=\left(\beta+\gamma \mu, g(\rho, 1)+\frac{\gamma \mu}{\rho^{2}}, g(R, 1)+\frac{\gamma \mu}{R^{2}}\right)
$$

and $\gamma=x_{i} / d^{3}>0$ for some $i$. Proceeding as in Section 2 we prove that Proposition 5 remains valid when we replace condition (iv) by the following condition: $\beta x+\gamma \mu\left(x^{3}-1\right) / x^{2}-g(x, 1)>0$ for all $x>\alpha(\mu)$ and some $\alpha(\mu)>1$, and $\beta x+\gamma \mu\left(x^{3}-1\right) / x^{2}-g(x, 1)<0$ for $1<x<\alpha(\mu)$.

Notice that the function $\beta x+\gamma \mu\left(x^{3}-1\right) / x^{2}$ is increasing and positive for all $x>1$. On the other hand it is easy to check that the functions $g(x, 1)$ are decreasing for all type of polyhedra and that $\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} g(x, 1) /\left(1 /(x-1)^{2}\right)=c$ for some constant $c$ which depends on the chosen polyhedra. Moreover $\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} g(x, 1)=+\infty$. Therefore equation $\beta x+\gamma \mu\left(x^{3}-1\right) / x^{2}-g(x, 1)=0$ has a unique real solution $x=\alpha(\mu)$ with $\alpha(\mu)>1$ for all $\mu \geqslant 0$ such that $\beta x+\gamma \mu\left(x^{3}-1\right) / x^{2}-g(x, 1)>0$ for $x>\alpha(\mu)$, and $\beta x+\gamma \mu\left(x^{3}-1\right) / x^{2}-g(x, 1)<0$ for $1<x<\alpha(\mu)$. Moreover $\alpha(\mu) \rightarrow \alpha$ when $\mu \rightarrow 0$ and $\alpha(\mu) \rightarrow 1$ when $\mu \rightarrow+\infty$. In short we have proved Theorem 4.

## Appendix

In this appendix we analyze the resolution of equations of the form $F(x)=0$ when $F$ is a rational function containing radicals. These type of equations are solved by following the next steps.

1. We eliminate the fractions by multiplying equation $F(x)=0$ by the least common denominator of $F(x)$.
2. We eliminate the radicals of the resulting equation by isolating in a convenient way one or more radicals on one side of the equation and squaring both sides of the equation. If the resulting equation still contains radicals, then we repeat the process again. At the end we obtain a polynomial equation.
3. We find numerically all the solutions of the polynomial equation obtained in steep (2).
4. We check which of these solutions are really solutions of the initial equation $F(x)=0$.

Now we detail how to group the radicals in steep (2) for each type of equations that appear in this work after applying steep (1).
(a) Equations with one radical: $\alpha_{1} \sqrt{a}+\alpha_{2}=0$. We eliminate the radicals by applying steep (2) in the following way

$$
\left(\alpha_{1} \sqrt{a}\right)^{2}=\left(-\alpha_{2}\right)^{2}
$$

(b) Equations of the form: $\alpha_{1} \sqrt{a}+\alpha_{2} \sqrt{b}+\alpha_{3} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b}=0$. Applying steep (2) in the following way

$$
\left(\alpha_{1} \sqrt{a}+\alpha_{2} \sqrt{b}\right)^{2}=\left(-\alpha_{3} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b}\right)^{2}
$$

we obtain an equation with one radical of the form $\beta_{1} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b}+\beta_{2}=0$.
(c) Equations of the form $\alpha_{1} \sqrt{b} \sqrt{c} \sqrt{d}+\alpha_{2} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{c} \sqrt{d}+\alpha_{3} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b} \sqrt{d}+\alpha_{4} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b} \sqrt{c}+\alpha_{5} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b} \sqrt{c} \sqrt{d}=0$. Applying steep (2) by grouping the terms in the following way

$$
\left(\alpha_{1} \sqrt{b} \sqrt{c} \sqrt{d}+\alpha_{2} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{c} \sqrt{d}\right)^{2}=\left(-\alpha_{3} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b} \sqrt{d}-\alpha_{4} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b} \sqrt{c}-\alpha_{5} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b} \sqrt{c} \sqrt{d}\right)^{2}
$$

we obtain an equation of the form $\beta_{1} \sqrt{c}+\beta_{2} \sqrt{d}+\beta_{3} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b}+\beta_{4} \sqrt{c} \sqrt{d}+\beta_{5}=0$. Applying steep (2) to this equation in the following way

$$
\left(\beta_{1} \sqrt{c}+\beta_{2} \sqrt{d}+\beta_{4} \sqrt{c} \sqrt{d}+\beta_{5}\right)^{2}=\left(-\beta_{3} \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b}\right)^{2}
$$

we obtain an equation with three radicals of the form $\gamma_{1} \sqrt{c}+\gamma_{2} \sqrt{d}+\gamma_{3} \sqrt{c} \sqrt{d}+\gamma_{4}=0$. Finally, applying steep (2) again in the following way

$$
\left(\gamma_{1} \sqrt{c}+\gamma_{2} \sqrt{d}\right)^{2}=\left(-\gamma_{3} \sqrt{c} \sqrt{d}-\gamma_{4}\right)^{2}
$$

we obtain an equation with one radical.

# Central Configurations of the Restricted Problem in $E^{4}$ 

An old technique in celestial mechanics is to reduce a problem with $2 n$ degrees of freedom to a problem with two degrees of freedom in order to approximate asymptotically the flow of the dynamical system. Such is the case with the reduction of the three-body problem in the plane $E^{2}$ to the (circular) restricted problem of three bodies where the motion of the primaries is independent of the two degree of freedom problem associated with the third body. One decouples the differential equations of the six degree of freedom system by choosing a known solution of the two-body problem and then by defining the two degree of freedom problem along this chosen solution. In principle we want to consider this procedure in the $(n+1)$-body problem by defining restricted problems of $n+1$ bodies that correspond to central configurations of the $n$-body problem. We choose to work in Euclidean space $E^{4}$ with a non-Newtonian potential to take advantage of a setting with a richer structure. However, these methods can be used in Euclidean space $E^{3}$ with the Newtonian potential and the proofs of comparable theorems follow directly. The reason we choose to study central configurations is their importance in building homographic solutions of the $n$-body problem.

We prove the existence of many central configurations of the restricted problem of $n+1$ bodies in Euclidean space $E^{4}$ by topological methods. We analyze the configurations by critical-point theory. Compare $$.

An important reason for the study of central configurations of the restricted problem is their use in generating by induction central configurations of the $(n+1)$-body problem. The induction is carried out by using the implicit function theorem on nondegenerate central configurations of the restricted problem.

There are two examples of this use of the restricted problem in the literature. One is the induction of the Lagrange and Euler central configurations in the three-body problem from their appearance in the restricted three-body problem. The other is the induction of collinear central configurations of $n+1$ bodies from their appearance in the restricted $(n+1)$-body problem.

We limit ourselves here to studying the existence of central configurations of a restricted $(n+1)$-body problem which is defined with respect to an arbitrarily chosen central configuration of the $n$-body problem. In  we prove comparable results for central configurations of the $(n+1)$-body problem by generalizing the methods of proof found here.

# 1. Restricted $n+1$-Body Problem in $E^{4}$ 

We define a central configuration of the restricted problem of $n+1$ bodies with respect to a central configuration of the $n$-body problem.

The configuration space of the $n$-body problem is given as a subset of $\left(E^{4}\right)^{n}$. For a given choice of the masses $\left(m_{i}\right) \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$, let $M-\Delta$ denote the subset of configurations which is given by

$$
M-\Delta=\left\{\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in\left(E^{4}\right)^{n} \mid \sum m_{i} x_{i}=0 \text { and } x_{i} \neq x_{j}, i \neq j\right\}
$$

Let $S_{m}-\Delta \subset M-\Delta$ be the excised sphere defined by

$$
S_{m}-\Delta=\left\{x \in M-\Delta \left\lvert\, \frac{1}{2} \sum m_{i}\left\|x_{i}\right\|^{2}=1\right.\right\}
$$

The potential function of the $n$-body problem in $E^{4}$ is

$$
V_{m}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)=-\sum_{i<j} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left\|x_{i}-x_{j}\right\|^{2}}
$$

A configuration $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{m}-\Delta$ is a central configuration if and only if $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)$ is a critical point of the potential $V_{m} \mid\left(S_{m}-\Delta\right)$.

Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{m}-\Delta$ be a central configuration. Then it follows that the configuration satisfies

$$
\lambda m_{i} x_{i}=-\operatorname{grad}_{i} V_{m}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)
$$

for some $\lambda \in \mathbb{R} \backslash\{0\}$ and for all $i=1, \ldots, n$. Here $\operatorname{grad}_{i} V_{m}$ denotes the gradient of $V_{m}$ by $x_{i}$. By the homogeneity of $V_{m}$ it follows that $\lambda=V_{m}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)$ holds.

The potential function of the restricted problem of $n+1$ bodies with respect to the central configuration $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{m}-\Delta$ is defined by $V$ : $E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ where

$$
V(x)=-\sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{2}}+\lambda \frac{1}{2}\|x\|^{2}
$$

The constant $\lambda=V_{m}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)<0$ is the Lagrange multiplier. Here (and throughout the paper) we have suppressed the dependence of $V$ on the configuration $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)$.

A central configuration of the restricted problem is defined as the configuration $\left(\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right), x\right) \in S_{m}-\Delta \times\left(E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}\right)$, where $x$ is a critical point of $V$.

We compute the linear map $D V(x)$ as

$$
D V(x)(v)=-2 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}}\left\langle x_{i}-x, v\right\rangle+\lambda\langle x, v\rangle
$$

for all $v \in E^{4}$. At a critical point, $x \in E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$, we have $D V(x)=0$ so that $x$ satisfies

$$
\lambda x=2 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}}\left(x_{i}-x\right)
$$

Consequently,

$$
\left(\lambda+2 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}}\right) x=2 \sum \frac{m_{i} x_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}}
$$

holds.
Remark. This equation has the form which $x_{k}$ satisfies in the central configuration; i.e., for all $k=1, \ldots, n$, we have

$$
\lambda m_{k} x_{k}=2 \sum_{i \neq k} \frac{m_{i} m_{k}}{\left\|x_{i}-x_{k}\right\|^{4}}\left(x_{i}-x_{k}\right)
$$

Proposition 1. Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{m}-\Delta$ be a central configuration. The critical points of $V: E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ lie in a compact subset of the domain.

Proof. We must show that a critical point is bounded away from $\left\{\left\{x_{i}\right\}, \infty\right\}$. By the equation of the critical point

$$
\lambda x=2 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}}\left(x_{i}-x\right)
$$

we observe that $\|x\|$ cannot be arbitrarily large. Also as $x \rightarrow x_{k}$ for any $k$, the term $\left\|x_{k}-x\right\|^{-3}\left(x_{k}-x\right)$ becomes arbitrarily large. Therefore, the equality must fail to hold for $\left\|x-x_{k}\right\|$ sufficiently small. Consequently, we find that $\|x\|<N$ and for each $k,\left\|x-x_{k}\right\|>\varepsilon$ must hold for some $N>0$ and $\varepsilon>0$.

Proposition 2. Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{m}-\Delta$ be a central configuration. If $V: E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a nondegenerate function, then $V$ has only finitely many critical points.

This follows directly from Proposition 1 and the fact that each nondegenerate critical point is isolated.

We show the way in which the critical-point equation can be used to compute the degeneracy of a critical point $x$ of $V$.

The Hessian of $V$ at a critical point $x \in E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ is the symmetric bilinear form $D^{2} V(x)$ which is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}
D^{2} V(x)(v, w)= & -2 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}}\left(\frac{4\left\langle x_{i}-x, v\right\rangle\left\langle x_{i}-x, w\right\rangle}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{2}}-\langle v, w\rangle\right) \\
& +\lambda\langle v, w\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

for all $(v, w) \in E^{4} \times E^{4}$. We denote by $H_{x}(v, v)$ the associated quadratic form. We write $H_{x}(v, v)$ in the form

$$
H_{x}(v, v)=-8 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{6}}\left\langle x_{i}-x, v\right\rangle^{2}+\left(\lambda+2 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}}\right)\|v\|^{2}
$$

Identify $E^{4}$ with $\mathbb{H}$, the division algebra of quaternions with basis $\{1, i, j, k\}$. For any $v \in \mathbb{H}$, let $i v, j v, k v$ denote the vectors produced by multiplying $v$ by $i, j, k$. Then $\{v, i v, j v, k v\}$ is an orthogonal set. Consequently, we have the equality

$$
H_{x}(v, v)+H_{x}(i v, i v)+H_{x}(j v, j v)+H_{x}(k v, k v)=4 \lambda\|v\|^{2}<0
$$

If $x \in E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ is a critical point of $V$, let $\operatorname{ind}(x)$ denote the index of $V$ at $x$, the maximal dimension of a subspace of $E^{4}$ on which $D^{2} V(x)$ is negative definite. The calculation above shows that for any critical point of $V$, we have $\operatorname{ind}(x) \geqslant 1$. We denote by $\operatorname{rank}(x)$, the rank of $V$ at $x$.

Thus we have proved the following.
Theorem 1. Let $x \in E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ be a critical point of $V$. Then $\operatorname{ind}(x) \geqslant 1$ holds.

Corollary 1.1. If $x$ is a critical point of $V$, then $\operatorname{rank}(x) \geqslant 1$.
Our next theorems concern collinear, planar and three-dimensional central configurations in $E^{4}$. Choose a line $E^{1} \subset E^{4}$ and let $S_{1}-\Delta$ denote the intersection of $\left(E^{1}\right)^{n}$ with $S_{m}-\Delta$. Similarly, let $S_{2}-\Delta$ and $S_{3}-\Delta$ denote the intersections of $\left(E^{2}\right)^{n}$ and $\left(E^{3}\right)^{n}$ with $S_{m}-\Delta$. For all these theorems we fix $\left(m_{i}\right) \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$.

Let $V_{k}$ denote the restriction $V \mid\left(E^{k}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}\right)$ for $k=1,2,3$. We always assume for subsequent calculations that the set $\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ spans $E^{k}$ when we refer to the function $V_{k}$. Clearly a critical point of $V_{k}$ is a critical point of $V$. Let $H_{k}(v, v)$ denote the Hessian $D^{2} V_{k}(v, v)$ for $v \in E^{k}$. If $x$ is a critical point of $V_{k}$, we denote the index of $x$ with respect to $V_{k}$ by $\operatorname{ind}_{k}(x)$.

Theorem 2. Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{1}-\Delta$ be a collinear central configuration so that for all $i, x_{i} \in E^{1}$. Then $V$ has $n+1$ nondegenerate saddle points in $E^{1}$ and in any plane $E^{2}$ containing $E^{1}$, there are two maxima, nondegenerate with respect to $V_{2}$.

Theorem 3. Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{2}-\Delta$ be a planar (noncollinear) central configuration with $x_{i} \in E^{2}$ for all $i$. Then every critical point $x \in E^{2}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ is a saddle point of $V$ in $E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$. For any space $E^{3}$ containing $E^{2}$, there are two maxima in $E^{3} \backslash E^{2}$, nondegenerate with respect to $V_{3}$.

Theorem 4. Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{3}-\Delta$ be a three-dimensional central configuration with $x_{i} \in E^{3}$ for all $i$. Then every critical point $x \in E^{3}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ of $V$ is a saddle point. In $E^{4}$ there are two nondegenerate maxima $x \in E^{4} \backslash E^{3}$ of $V$.

The importance of these theorems is seen by the fact that a complete description of the general critical point set is given by the nature of the central configuration as well as the imbedding space. In particular, the methods used here may be extended to the case of finite masses, the $(n+1)$ body problem .

Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{k}-\Delta$ be a central configuration and let $x \in E^{k}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ be a critical point of $V_{k}$. The Hessian $D^{2} V(x)$ splits as

$$
D^{2} V(x)=D^{2} V_{k}(x) \oplus\left(D^{2} V_{k}\right)^{\perp}(x)
$$

where $\left(D^{2} V_{k}\right)^{\perp}(x)$ is the Hessian restricted to $E^{4-k}$ which is orthogonal to $E^{k}$.
In order to compute the degeneracies of $D^{2} V(x)$ we need the following facts.

Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{1}-\Delta$ be a collinear central configuration so that $x_{i} \in E^{1}$ for all $i$. If $x \notin E^{1}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$, then there are two directions $v_{1}, v_{2} \in E^{4}$ such that for all $i,\left\langle x_{i}-x, v_{1}\right\rangle=0=\left\langle x_{i}-x, v_{2}\right\rangle$ and $\left\langle v_{1}, v_{2}\right\rangle=0$.

Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{2}-\Delta$ be a planar central configuration, $x_{i} \in E^{2}$ for all $i$. If $x \notin E^{2}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$, then there is a vector $v \in E^{4}$ such that for all $i$, $\left\langle x_{i}-x, v\right\rangle=0$.

Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{3}-\Delta$ be a three-dimensional central configuration. If $x \notin E^{3}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$, then for any $v \in E^{4}$, there is an $i$ such that $\left\langle x_{i}-x, v\right\rangle \neq 0$.

# 2. Proof of Theorem 2 

Theorem 2 states that the collinear central configurations always lead to nondegenerate critical points of the potential $V_{2}$. In order to show that there are only two maxima of $V_{2}$ we proceed as follows.

Proposition 3. Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{1}-\Delta$ be a collinear central configuration ordered on $E^{1}$ by $x_{1}<\cdots<x_{n}$. There are always $n+1$ critical points of $V_{1}$.

Proof. Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{1}-\Delta$ be a collinear central configuration. The masses $\left(m_{i}\right) \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$ are linearly ordered on $E^{1}$ by $x_{1}<\cdots<x_{n}$. For any $x \in$ $E^{1}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$, we see that $H(v, v)<0$ for $v \in E^{1}$. Thus, every critical point of $V_{1}$ is a maximum. For $m_{i}$ and $m_{i+1}$, two adjacent masses, $V_{1} \rightarrow-\infty$ as $x \rightarrow$ $x_{i}, x_{i+1}$. Thus, there is a critical point of $V_{1}$ between $x_{i}$ and $x_{i+1}$. As every such critical point is a maximum of $V_{1}$, there is only one between every pair of adjacent masses. This accounts for $n-1$ critical points of $V_{1}$ on $E^{1}$. But for $x<x_{1}$ and $x>x_{n}$, the same behavior occurs for $V_{1} \rightarrow-\infty$ as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$. Thus there are precisely $n+1$ critical points of $V_{1}$ on $E^{1}$.

Proposition 4. Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{1}-\Delta$ be a collinear central configuration; let $E^{2}$ be a plane that contains $E^{1}$. Every critical point of $V_{2}$, $x \in E^{2} \backslash E^{1}$, is a nondegenerate maximum. Thus there are only two such critical points.

Proof. Let $x \in E^{2} \backslash E^{1}$ be a critical point of $V_{2}$. Then

$$
\left(\lambda+2 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}}\right) x=2 \sum \frac{m_{i} x_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}}
$$

implies that $\lambda+2 \sum\left(m_{i} / \| x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}\right)=0$ must be satisfied. At this critical point we evaluate $H_{2}(v, v)$ as

$$
H_{2}(v, v)=-8 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{6}}\left\langle x_{i}-x, v\right\rangle^{2} \leqslant 0
$$

for every $v \in E^{2}$. The inequality $H_{2}(v, v)<0$ holds as $\left\{x_{i}-x\right\}$ spans $E^{2}$. Therefore, we have proved that $x \in E^{2} \backslash E^{1}$ is a nondegenerate maximum of $V_{2}$. Reflection across $E^{1}$ is an involution of $E^{2}$ which leaves invariant the set of critical points of $V_{2}$. As $E^{2} \backslash E^{1}$ has two components, there are two maxima of $V_{2}$, one maximum in each component. This completes the proof.

We have shown that there are $n+3$ critical points of $V_{2}$ in $E^{2}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$. There are at least two nondegenerate maxima (in $E^{2} \backslash E^{1}$ ) and there are $n+1$ critical points in $E^{1}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$. By a simple topological argument we show that the $n+1$ critical points of $V_{2}$ in $E^{1}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ are (possibly degenerate) saddle points with index equal to 1 .

The Betti numbers of $E^{2}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ are $\beta_{0}=1$ and $\beta_{1}=n$. The critical points of $V_{2}$ are isolated. Thus, we may write using Morse theory that $\mu_{0}-\mu_{1}=$ $\beta_{0}-\beta_{1}=1-n$, where $\mu_{0}$ is the number of maxima and $\mu_{1}$ is the number of saddle points. The inequality ind $(x) \geqslant 1$ shows that there is no other

contribution. But from above we know that $\mu_{0}+\mu_{1}=1+n$. Thus, we obtain $\mu_{0}=2$ and $\mu_{1}=n+1$.

From these topological facts we may obtain an analytic fact as follows. Let $v \in E^{2}$ be orthogonal to $E^{1}$. As each $x \in E^{1}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ is a saddle point, and as the Hessian splits in a pair of directions $\left(E^{1},\left(E^{1}\right)^{\perp}\right)$ it follows that $H_{2}(v, v) \geqslant 0$ must hold. Consequently, we have

$$
\lambda+2 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}} \geqslant 0
$$

In order to show that each critical point $x \in E^{1}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ of $V_{2}$ is a nondegenerate saddle, we must show that the Hessian is positive definite in the direction $v \in\left(E^{1}\right)^{\perp}$. We need the following sharp results.

Proposition 5. Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{1}-\Delta$ be a collinear central configuration such that $x_{i} \in E^{1}$ for all $i$ and $x_{1}<\cdots<x_{n}$. The critical points of $V_{1}, x \in E^{1}$ such that $x<x_{1}$ and $x>x_{n}$ are in the intervals $\left(x_{1}-\alpha_{1}, x_{1}\right)$ and $\left(x_{n}, a_{n}+x_{n}\right)$, where $\alpha_{1}^{4}=-2 m_{1} / \lambda$ and $\alpha_{n}^{4}=-2 m_{n} / \lambda, \lambda=V_{m}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)$.

Proof. Identify $E^{1}$ with $\mathbb{R}$. We write the equation for $x_{1}$ as

$$
\lambda m_{1} x_{1}=2 \sum_{i \neq 1} \frac{m_{1} m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x_{1}\right\|^{4}}\left(x_{i}-x_{1}\right)
$$

Consequently, we have the inequality

$$
\lambda x_{1}>2 \sum_{i \neq 1} \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{3}}
$$

for $x<x_{1}$. But $D V_{1}(x)$ can be written as

$$
D V_{1}(x)=-2 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{3}}+\lambda x \quad \text { for } \quad x<x_{1}
$$

By setting $\alpha_{1}=\left(-2 m_{1} / \lambda\right)^{1 / 4}$ we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}
D V_{1}\left(x_{1}-\alpha_{1}\right) & =-2 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x_{1}+\alpha_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\lambda\left(x_{1}-\alpha_{1}\right) \\
& =-2 \sum_{i \neq 1} \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x_{1}+\alpha_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\lambda x_{1}>0
\end{aligned}
$$

holds. But $V_{1} \rightarrow-\infty$ as $x \rightarrow x_{1}$. Thus, the critical point $x<x_{1}$ of $V_{1}$ lies in the interval $\left(x_{1}-\alpha_{1}, x_{1}\right)$. A similar calculation yields the result for the critical point $x>x_{n}$.

Theorem 5. Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{1}-\Delta$ be a collinear central configuration such that $x_{i} \in E^{1}$ for all $i$ and $x_{1}<\cdots<x_{n}$. Then the inequality

$$
-\lambda \leqslant 2 \frac{m_{i}+m_{i+1}}{\left\|x_{i}-x_{i+1}\right\|^{4}}
$$

is satisfied for $i=1, \ldots, n-1$.
Proof. The equations of the critical point are

$$
\lambda m_{k} x_{k}=2 \sum_{i \neq k} \frac{m_{i} m_{k}}{\left\|x_{i}-x_{k}\right\|^{4}}\left(x_{i}-x_{k}\right)
$$

for $k=1, \ldots, n$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda\left(x_{k}-x_{k+1}\right)= & 2 \sum_{i \neq k, k+1} m_{i}\left(\frac{x_{i}-x_{k}}{\left\|x_{i}-x_{k}\right\|^{4}}-\frac{x_{i}-x_{k+1}}{\left\|x_{i}-x_{k+1}\right\|^{4}}\right) \\
& -2 \frac{m_{k}+m_{k+1}}{\left\|x_{k}-x_{k+1}\right\|^{4}}\left(x_{k}-x_{k+1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Take the inner product of each side with $\left(x_{k}-x_{k+1}\right)$. Then we have

$$
-\lambda=2 \frac{m_{k}+m_{k+1}}{\left\|x_{k}-x_{k+1}\right\|^{4}}+\text { nonpositive terms. }
$$

Consequently, $-\lambda \leqslant 2\left(m_{k}+m_{k+1}\right) /\left\|x_{k}-x_{k+1}\right\|^{4}$ holds for all $k=1, \ldots, n-1$.
The proof of Theorem 2 follows immediately from Theorem 5. We estimate $H_{2}(v, v), v \in\left(E^{1}\right)^{\perp},\|v\|=1$ as

$$
H_{2}(v, v)=\lambda+2 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}}>2\left(\sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}}-\frac{m_{k}+m_{k+1}}{\left\|x_{k}-x_{k+1}\right\|^{4}}\right)
$$

But for $x_{k}<x<x_{k+1}$ in $E^{1}$, we have

$$
\frac{m_{k}}{\left\|x_{k}-x\right\|^{4}}+\frac{m_{k+1}}{\left\|x_{k+1}-x\right\|^{4}}>\frac{m_{k}+m_{k+1}}{\left\|x_{k}-x_{k+1}\right\|^{4}}
$$

This holds for every critical point $x \in E^{1}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ of $V_{2}, x_{1}<x<x_{n}$.
At the two critical points $x<x_{1}$ and $x>x_{n}$, Proposition 5 shows that $H_{2}(v, v)>0$ for $v \in\left(E^{1}\right)^{\perp},\|v\|=1$. We need only use the inequalities

$$
\frac{m_{1}}{\left\|x_{1}-x\right\|^{4}}>-\frac{\lambda}{2}
$$

for $x \in\left(x_{1}-\alpha_{1}, x_{1}\right)$ and

$$
\frac{m_{n}}{\left\|x_{n}-x\right\|^{4}}>-\frac{\lambda}{2}
$$

for $x \in\left(x_{n}, a_{n}+x_{n}\right)$ that result from Proposition 5.
Consequently, $H_{2}(v, v)>0$ for $v \in\left(E^{1}\right)^{\perp}$. The plane $E^{2}$ containing $E^{1}$ was selected arbitrarily. Therefore, in every direction $v \in E^{4}$ which is orthogonal to $E^{1}, H(v, v)>0$ holds. Thus, $x \in E^{1}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ is a nondegenerate saddle point of $V$.

This completes the proof of Theorem 2.

# 3. Homology Critical Points 

Let us consider the case that $V$ has only isolated critical points in $E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$. Let $c_{1}<\cdots<c_{r}<0$ be the (finitely many) critical values of $V$. Set $c_{0}=-\infty$ and for any $j, 1 \leqslant j \leqslant r$; define $W_{j}=V^{-1}\left(c_{j-1}, c_{j}\right)$. Let $\Lambda_{j}$ be the set of critical points at the critical level $c_{j}$. For any $i, 0 \leqslant i \leqslant 4$, define $\mu_{i}(j)$ by

$$
\mu_{i}(j)=\operatorname{rank} H_{4-j}\left(W_{j} \cup \Lambda_{j}, W_{j}\right)
$$

and

$$
\mu_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{r} \mu_{i}(j)
$$

Then the numbers $\left\{\mu_{i}\right\}$ satisfy the Morse inequalities.
The same definitions may be used for the real analytic function $V$ in case nonisolated critical points exist. There are only finitely many critical levels in this case and the strata of critical points are nondegenerate critical manifolds (by the fact that ind $(x) \geqslant 1$ holds at a critical point).

In the proofs of Theorems 3 and 4 which follow we use the notation of $\sigma_{i}$ and $\mu_{i}$ for the sum of homology ranks. In Theorem 3, $\left\{\sigma_{i}\right\}$ refers to the critical points of $V_{2}: E^{2}-\left\{x_{i}\right\} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and $\left\{\mu_{i}\right\}$ refers to the critical points of $V_{3}: E^{3}-\left\{x_{i}\right\} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, where $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{3}-\Delta$ is a planar central configuration. In the definitions above, $V$ and $E^{4}$ are replaced by $V_{k}, E^{k}$, $k=2,3$. In Theorem 4, $\left\{\sigma_{i}\right\}$ refers to the critical points of $V_{3}: E^{3}-\left\{x_{i}\right\} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and $\left\{\mu_{i}\right\}$ is defined as above, where $\left(x_{i}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{3}-\Delta$ is a threedimensional central configuration.

# 4. Proof of Theorem 3 

We turn now to the proof of Theorem 3. Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{2}-\Delta$ be a planar central configuration with constant $\lambda=V_{m}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)$. Let $x \in$ $E^{2}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ be a critical point of $V_{2}$. If $x$ is a saddle point of $V_{2}$, then $\operatorname{ind}_{2}(x)=1$ follows from ind ${ }_{2}(x) \geqslant 1$. Also, $x$ is isolated (whether the saddle point is degenerate or not). If $x$ were not isolated, then as $V_{2}$ is real analytic in $E^{2}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$, it follows that $x$ must lie in a one-dimensional arc of critical points. Consequently, $x$ would be a maximum. Therefore, the possible critical points of $V_{2}$ are (isolated) saddles, isolated maxima and circles of maxima.

Choose a space $E^{3}$ which contains $E^{2}$. Let $x \in E^{3} \backslash E^{2}$ be a critical point of $V_{3}$. Then it follows from the critical-point equation that $\lambda+$ $2 \sum\left(m_{i} /\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}\right)=0$ holds for $x \in E^{3} \backslash E^{2}$. The set $\left\{x_{i}-x\right\}$ spans $E^{3}$. Therefore, $\left\langle x_{i}-x, v\right\rangle \neq 0$ for every $v \in E^{3}$ and for some $i=1, \ldots, n$. We find that

$$
H_{3}(v, v)=-8 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{6}}\left\langle x_{i}-x, v\right\rangle^{2}<0
$$

for every $v \in E^{3}$. Thus $x \in E^{3} \backslash E^{2}$ is a nondegenerate maximum of $V_{3}$. As $E^{3} \backslash E^{2}$ has two components there are two maxima, one in each component.

We take the cases (i) that the critical points of $V_{2}$ are isolated and (ii) that $V_{2}$ has nonisolated critical points.

Case (i). With the homology interpretation of Morse theory we let $\sigma_{0}$ be the number of maxima of $V_{2}$ and $\sigma_{1}$ be the number of saddle points of $V_{2}$. Each saddle point has index 1.

Let $x \in E^{2}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ be a degenerate critical point of $V_{2}$. Then there is a vector $v \in E^{2}$ such that $H_{2}(v, v)=0$. But $\left\{x_{i}-x\right\}$ spans $E^{2}$ for we have excluded $\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ collinear. Consequently, $\left\langle x_{i}-x, v\right\rangle \neq 0$ holds for some $i$. Thus $H_{2}(v, v)=0$ requires that

$$
\left(2 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x^{4}\right\|}+\lambda\right)\|v\|^{2}=8 \sum \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{6}}\left\langle x_{i}-x, v\right\rangle^{2}>0
$$

It follows that if $v \in E^{4}$ is orthogonal to $E^{2}$, then $H(v, v)>0$ so that $x$ is a degenerate saddle point of $V$ in $E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ with $\operatorname{ind}(x)=1$.

Let $x \in E^{2}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ be a nondegenerate saddle point of $V_{2}$. Then there is a $v \in E^{2}$ such that $H_{2}(v, v)>0$. Consequently, $H(j v, j v)=H(k v, k v)>$ $H_{2}(v, v)>0$ where we have identified $E^{2}$ with $\mathbb{C} \subset \mathbb{N}$ and $j v, k v$ represent multiplication by the units, $v=v_{1}+v_{2} i$.

Thus, every critical point of $V_{3}$ in $E^{3}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ is isolated. Let $\mu_{0}$ be the number of maxima of $V_{3}$. Let $\mu_{1}$ and $\mu_{2}$ be given the homology interpretation as in Section 3 with $k=3$.

The following equations are satisfied by $\sigma_{0}, \sigma_{1}, \mu_{0}, \mu_{1}, \mu_{2}$.
(i) $\sigma_{0}-\sigma_{1}=1-n$,
(ii) $\mu_{0}-\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}=1+n$,
(iii) $\mu_{0}+\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}-\left(\sigma_{0}+\sigma_{1}\right)=2$.

Combining these equations we find that $\mu_{1}=\sigma_{0}$ and $\mu_{0}+\mu_{2}=\sigma_{1}+2$.
Now $\sigma_{1}$ is the number of saddle points of $V_{2}$ so that each saddle point of $V_{2}$ contributes to $\mu_{2}$. Thus, we find $\mu_{2} \geqslant \sigma_{1}$. But by the existence of two maxima of $V_{3}$ in $E^{3} \backslash E^{2}$, we have $\mu_{0} \geqslant 2$. We conclude that $\mu_{0}=2, \mu_{1}=\sigma_{0}$, $\mu_{2}=\sigma_{1}$ whether or not the critical points of $V_{2}$ are degenerate. This shows again that for each critical point of $V_{2}$ we have $H(v, v) \geqslant 0$ for $v \in E^{4}$, orthogonal to $E^{2}$.

Case (ii). In this case we want to show that $V_{3}$ has only two maxima, both nondegenerate, even when there are (possibly) nonisolated maxima of $V_{3}$. Any degenerate critical point of $V_{2}$ in $E^{2}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ is a saddle point of $V_{3}$. Using the homology interpretation of the Morse inequalities we have as in (i) that $\mu_{1}=\sigma_{0}$ and $\mu_{0}+\mu_{2}=\sigma_{1}+2$. Here $\mu_{0} \geqslant 2$ holds as before. Now any critical point which makes a homology contribution to $\sigma_{1}$ also contributes to $\mu_{2}$. Thus we find that $\mu_{2} \geqslant \sigma_{1}$. Consequently $\mu_{0}=2$ and $\mu_{2}=\sigma_{1}$.

This completes the proof of Theorem 3.

# 5. Proof of Theorem 4 

Finally, we prove Theorem 4. Let $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{3}-\Delta$ be a central configuration. As before, we conclude for each critical point $x \in E^{4} \backslash E^{3}$ of $V$ that $\lambda+2 \sum\left(m_{i} /\left\|x_{i}-x\right\|^{4}\right)=0$ holds. Consequently, as in the other cases, we find that every critical point $x \in E^{4} \backslash E^{3}$ of $V$ is a nondegenerate maximum. As there are only two components of $E^{4} \backslash E^{3}$, we have only two such maxima.

Case (i). Isolated critical points. Let $\sigma_{0}, \sigma_{1}, \sigma_{2}$ be as defined in Section 3 for the contributions in homology of the critical points of $V_{3}$ in $E^{3}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$.

Let $\mu_{0}, \mu_{1}, \mu_{2}, \mu_{3}$ be the contributions in homology of the critical points of $V$ in $E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ as defined above.

The Betti numbers of $E^{3}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ are $\beta_{0}=1, \beta_{2}=n$ and those of $E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ are $\beta_{0}=1, \beta_{3}=n$. Consequently, $\left\{\sigma_{i}\right\}$ and $\left\{\mu_{i}\right\}$ satisfy
(i) $\sigma_{0}-\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{2}=1+n$,
(ii) $\mu_{0}-\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}-\mu_{3}=1-n$,
(iii) $\sum \mu_{i}-\sum \sigma_{i}=2$.

These equations lead to $\mu_{0}+\mu_{2}=2+\sigma_{1}$ and $\mu_{1}+\mu_{3}=\sigma_{0}+\sigma_{2}$.

Every $x \in E^{3}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ such that $x$ contributes to $\sigma_{1}$ also contributes to $\mu_{2}$. Thus $\mu_{2} \geqslant \sigma_{1}$ holds. By the fact that $\mu_{0} \geqslant 2$, we conclude that $\mu_{0}=2$ and $\mu_{2}=\sigma_{1}$. Also every $x \in E^{3}-\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ which contributes to $\sigma_{0}$ or $\sigma_{2}$, respectively, contributes to $\mu_{1}$ or $\mu_{3}$. Consequently, $\mu_{1} \geqslant \sigma_{0}$ and $\mu_{3} \geqslant \sigma_{2}$ hold. Thus, we conclude that $\mu_{1}=\sigma_{0}, \mu_{3}=\sigma_{2}$ and the proof is complete.

Case (ii). Nonisolated critical points. As in case (i) any critical point which makes a contribution in homology to $\sigma_{1}$ also contributes to $\mu_{2}$. Thus we find that $\mu_{2} \geqslant \sigma_{1}$ and $\mu_{0} \geqslant 2$. Consequently, $\mu_{0}=2$ and $\mu_{2}=\sigma_{1}$ as in the proof of Theorem 3.

This completes the proof of Theorem 4.

# 5. Critical Points of Regular Central Configurations 

A central configuration $\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in S_{m}-\Delta$ is regular in $E^{4}$ if $\left\{x_{i}\right\}$ spans $E^{4}$.

If $V: E^{4}-\left\{x_{i}\right\} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a nondegenerate function, then the numbers of critical points of index $k$, denoted by $\mu_{4-k}$, must be given by the Morse inequalities. The Betti numbers of the domain are $\beta_{0}=1, \beta_{3}=n$.

We have $\sum \mu_{l} \geqslant 1+n, \mu_{0}-\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}-\mu_{3}=1-n, \mu_{4}=0(\operatorname{ind}(x) \geqslant 1)$, $\mu_{0} \geqslant 1, \mu_{1}-\mu_{0} \geqslant-1, \mu_{2}-\mu_{1}+\mu_{0} \geqslant 1$.

If the critical points of $V$ are isolated, then the same inequalities hold, where the numbers $\mu_{k}$ are given a homology interpretation.

# On stacked central configurations with $n$ bodies when one body is removed 

## A B STR ACT

A stacked central configuration is a central configuration of the $n$-body problem for which a proper subset of the bodies is already in a central configuration. In this paper we study all the possibilities of stacked central configurations for the $n$-body problem when one body is removed. The results have simple and analytic proofs.

## 1. Introduction

In celestial mechanics the classical $n$-body problem consists in the study of the motion of $n$ point bodies with positive masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{n}$, interacting among themselves through no other forces than their mutual gravitational attraction according to Newton's gravitational law . Consider such bodies with position vectors $r_{1}, \ldots, r_{n}$, where $r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}, d=2,3$. The equations of motion are given by

$$
\ddot{r}_{i}=-\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\ j \neq i}}^{n} \frac{m_{j}}{r_{i j}^{2}}\left(r_{i}-r_{j}\right)
$$

for $i=1,2, \ldots, n$. Here the gravitational constant is taken equal to 1 and $r_{i j}=\left|r_{i}-r_{j}\right|$ is the Euclidean distance between the bodies at $r_{i}$ and $r_{j}$.

Note that Eq. (1) is not well defined if $r_{i j}=0$. So we consider configurations $r=\left(r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{n}\right)$ out of the collision set, assuming $r_{i j} \neq 0$ for all $i \neq j$. We also consider the inertial barycentric system, that is, the origin of the inertial system is the center of mass of the system, which is given by $\mathcal{C}_{n}=\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j} r_{j} / \mathcal{M}_{n}$, where $\mathcal{M}_{n}=m_{1}+\cdots+m_{n}$ is the total mass.

The $n$-body problem is not solvable by direct integration via quadratures when $n>2$. So, the study of particular solutions becomes very important. One interesting case of a particular solution is the homographic one: the initial form of the configuration is preserved in the time evolution. In other words, the motions are given by dilations or rotations (centered at the center of mass).

The first homographic solutions for the three-body problem were found by Euler . In Euler's solutions three bodies move on conical sections, but on a straight line at each fixed instant. Lagrange  studied other homographic solutions for

the three-body problem, in which the bodies are orbiting around the center of mass of the system on conical sections at the vertices of an equilateral triangle in each fixed instant.

At a given instant $t=t_{0}$ the $n$ bodies are in a central configuration if there exists $\lambda \neq 0$ such that $\vec{r}_{i}=\lambda r_{i}$, referred to the inertial barycentric system, for all $i=1, \ldots, n$. By a simple computation we have $\lambda=-U / I$, where

$$
U=\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq n} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{r_{i j}}, \quad I=\frac{1}{\mathcal{M}_{n}} \sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq n} m_{i} m_{j} r_{i j}^{2}
$$

are the Newtonian potential and the moment of inertia of the $n$ bodies, respectively.
Two central configurations $\left(r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{n}\right)$ and $\left(\vec{r}_{1}, \vec{r}_{2}, \ldots, \vec{r}_{n}\right)$ of the $n$ bodies are related if we can pass from one to the other through a dilation or a rotation (centered at the center of mass). So we can study classes of central configurations defined by the above equivalence relation.

Taking into account this equivalence there are exactly five classes of central configurations in the three-body problem. The finiteness of the number of central configurations performed by $n$ bodies with positive masses is a question posed by Chazy in , Wintner in , and reformulated to the planar case by Smale in . This problem has an affirmative answer when $n=4$. See . Alternatively, see  for a proof of the finiteness when $n=4$ and a partial answer when $n=5$. This question is open when $n>5$.

It is important to emphasize that the computation of central configurations is reduced to a resolution of a set of algebraic equations, since by (1) we have

$$
\lambda r_{i}=-\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\ j \neq i}}^{n} \frac{m_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}\left(r_{i}-r_{j}\right)
$$

for each instant of time and $i=1, \ldots, n$. The expressions in Eq. (3) are called the equations of central configurations.
A powerful tool for studying central configurations in the planar $n$-body problem is provided by the so called planar Laura-Andoyer equations. Consider $n$ non-collinear bodies with masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{n}$ and positions $r_{1}, \ldots, r_{n}, r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$. Then the planar Laura-Andoyer equations are given by

$$
f_{i j}=\sum_{\substack{k=1 \\ k \neq i, j}}^{n} m_{k}\left(R_{i k}-R_{j k}\right) \Delta_{i j k}=0
$$

for $1 \leq i<j \leq n$, where $R_{i j}=r_{i j}^{-3}$ and $\Delta_{i j k}=\left(r_{i}-r_{j}\right) \wedge\left(r_{i}-r_{k}\right)$ is twice the oriented area defined by the triangle with vertices at $r_{i}, r_{j}$ and $r_{k}$. The $n(n-1) / 2$ Laura-Andoyer equations are equivalent to the equations of central configurations in (3). See  or , for instance.

The spatial Laura-Andoyer equations are defined analogously. Consider $n$ non-planar bodies with masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{n}$, and positions $r_{1}, \ldots, r_{n}$, with $r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$. Then the spatial Laura-Andoyer equations are given by

$$
f_{i j i}=\sum_{\substack{k=1 \\ k \neq i, j, l}}^{n} m_{k}\left(R_{i k}-R_{j k}\right) \Delta_{i j l k}=0
$$

for $i<j, l \neq i, l \neq j, i, j, l=1, \ldots, n$, where $R_{i j}=r_{i j}^{-3}$ and $\Delta_{i j l k}=\left(r_{i}-r_{j}\right) \wedge\left(r_{i}-r_{l}\right) \cdot\left(r_{i}-r_{k}\right)$ is six times the oriented volume defined by the tetrahedron with vertices at $r_{i}, r_{j}, r_{l}$ and $r_{k}$.

The knowledge of central configurations allows us to compute homographic solutions ; there is a relation between central configurations and the bifurcations of the hypersurfaces of constant energy and angular momentum ; if the $n$ bodies are moving towards a simultaneous collision then the bodies tend to the set of central configurations . See also the Refs. .

Hampton  provides a new family of planar central configurations for the five-body problem with an interesting property: two bodies can be removed and the remaining three bodies are already in a central configuration. Such configurations are called stacked central configurations.

Here we adopt the following nomenclature: a central configuration is called $(n, k)$-stacked when the $n$ bodies are in a central configuration and we can remove $0<k<n$ bodies such that the remaining $n-k$ bodies are already in a central configuration. Without loss of generality, the $k$ bodies to be removed are those of position vectors $r_{n-k+1}, r_{n-k+2}, \ldots, r_{n}$.

Some (5, 2)-stacked planar central configurations were studied by Llibre and Mello , and by Llibre, Mello and PerezChavela . Stacked central configurations in the spatial five-body and seven-body problems were studied by Santos  and Hampton and Santoprete , respectively.

Fernandes and Mello  studied (5, 1)-stacked planar central configurations. The authors conclude that the only noncollinear (5, 1)-stacked planar central configuration is formed by four bodies in a co-circular central configuration and one body of arbitrary mass at the center of the circle.

In this paper we extend the results of  studying the general case of $(n, 1)$-stacked central configurations. The two main results are the following.

Theorem 1. Consider the planar non-collinear n-body problem with $n \geq 4$. Then the only $(n, 1)$-stacked central configurations are formed by $n-1$ bodies in a co-circular central configuration and one body (to be removed) of arbitrary mass at the center of the circle.

Theorem 2. Consider the spatial non-planar n-body problem with $n \geq 4$. Then the only $(n, 1)$-stacked central configurations are formed by $n-1$ bodies in a co-spherical central configuration and one body of arbitrary mass at the center of the sphere.

The proofs of Theorems 1 and 2 are given in Sections 2 and 3, respectively.
The $(n, 1)$-stacked central configurations have the following fundamental property: they are the only non-collinear central configurations in which we can vary the value of one mass of the configuration keeping the positions and other masses fixed and still have a central configuration.

# 2. Proof of Theorem 1 

The proof of Theorem 1 is divided into two lemmas.
Lemma 3. In order to have an $(n, 1)$-stacked central configuration it is necessary that the central configuration of the $n$ bodies does not depend on the value of the mass of the body to be removed, that is $m_{n}$.
Proof. The planar Laura-Andoyer equations $f_{i j}=0$ must be satisfied for the $n$ bodies. So, consider the Laura-Andoyer equations with $i \neq n$ and $j \neq n$. These equations can be written as

$$
f_{i j}=\sum_{k \neq i, j, n} m_{k}\left(R_{i k}-R_{j k}\right) \Delta_{i j k}+m_{n}\left(R_{i n}-R_{j n}\right) \Delta_{i j n}=0
$$

for all indices $i$ and $j$ such that $0<i<j<n$. Note that in (6) the parts under summation are exactly the Laura-Andoyer equations for $n-1$ bodies, which must vanish too. So, as we consider $m_{n}>0$, the following equations are necessary conditions in order to have an $(n, 1)$-stacked central configuration:

$$
\left(R_{i n}-R_{j n}\right) \Delta_{i j n}=0
$$

for all indices $i$ and $j$ such that $0<i<j<n$. Remember that in equations $f_{i n}=0$ the masses $m_{n}$ do not appear. Thus the lemma is proved.

The next lemma says that the remaining $n-1$ bodies must be on a circle with center at $r_{n}$.
Lemma 4. In order to have an $(n, 1)$-stacked central configuration it is necessary that the remaining $n-1$ bodies must be in a co-circular central configuration with center at $r_{n}$.
Proof. By hypothesis the configuration must be non-collinear, so in Eq. (7) at least one $\Delta_{i j n}$ is different from zero. Without loss of generality, consider $\Delta_{12 n} \neq 0$. From

$$
\left(R_{1 n}-R_{2 n}\right) \Delta_{12 n}=0
$$

we have

$$
R_{1 n}-R_{2 n}=0
$$

which implies that $r_{1 n}=r_{2 n}=d>0$. Thus, $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ belong to a circle with radius $d$ and center at $r_{n}$. We can classify the other indices into two sets

$$
\mathfrak{C}_{1}=\left\{j: \Delta_{1 j n}=0\right\}
$$

and

$$
\mathfrak{C}_{2}=\left\{j: \Delta_{1 j n} \neq 0\right\}
$$

that is $\mathfrak{C}_{1}$ contains the indices of the bodies whose vector positions are collinear with $r_{1}$ and $r_{n}$, while $\mathfrak{C}_{2}$ contains the indices of the bodies whose vector positions are not collinear with $r_{1}$ and $r_{n}$. For $j \in \mathfrak{C}_{2}$ and from

$$
\left(R_{1 n}-R_{j n}\right) \Delta_{1 j n}=0
$$

we have

$$
R_{1 n}-R_{j n}=0
$$

Thus, $r_{j n}=r_{1 n}=d>0$ for all $j \in \mathfrak{C}_{2}$. Then $r_{1}, r_{2}$ and $r_{j}$ belong to the circle of radius $d$ and center at $r_{n}$ for all $j \in \mathfrak{C}_{2}$. To complete the proof of the lemma we need to show that $\mathfrak{C}_{1}$ has at most one element. Suppose, by contradiction, that there exist two indices $b, c \in \mathfrak{C}_{1}$. So $\Delta_{1 b n}=0$, which implies that $\Delta_{2 b n} \neq 0$. From

$$
\left(R_{2 n}-R_{b n}\right) \Delta_{2 b n}=0
$$


Fig. 1. There is no position for $r_{c}$ out of the collision set.
we have

$$
R_{2 n}-R_{b n}=0
$$

which implies that $r_{b n}=r_{2 n}=d>0$. Thus $r_{b}$ belongs to the circle of radius $d$ and center at $r_{n}$. As the central configurations are out of the collision set, $r_{b}$ must be diametrically opposite to $r_{1}$. Now consider the index $c \in \mathfrak{C}_{1}$. So $\Delta_{1 c n}=0$, which implies that $\Delta_{2 c n} \neq 0$. From

$$
\left(R_{2 n}-R_{c n}\right) \Delta_{2 c n}=0
$$

we have

$$
R_{2 n}-R_{c n}=0
$$

which implies that $r_{c n}=r_{2 n}=d>0$. Here we have a contradiction, since, in this case, $r_{c}$ coincides with either $r_{1}$ or $r_{b}$. See Fig. 1. The lemma is proved.

Lemma 4 has the following corollary.
Corollary 5. In a non-collinear ( $n, 1$ )-stacked planar central configuration the polygon formed by the position vectors of the remaining $n-1$ bodies is convex.

The proof of Theorem 1 follows from Lemmas 3 and 4.

# 3. Proof of Theorem 2 

The proof of Theorem 2 is divided into two lemmas.
Lemma 6. In order to have an ( $n, 1$ )-stacked spatial central configuration it is necessary that the central configuration of the $n$ bodies does not depend on the value of the mass of the body to be removed, that is $m_{n}$.

The proof of Lemma 6 is similar to the proof of Lemma 3. The main difference is the use of spatial Laura-Andoyer equations. In other words, the following equations are necessary to an ( $n, 1$ )-stacked spatial central configuration:

$$
\left(R_{i n}-R_{j n}\right) \Delta_{i j k n}=0
$$

for all $1 \leq i<j \leq n$ and $k \neq i, j, n$.
The equations in (8) have some geometrical implications for the central configuration.
Lemma 7. In order to have an ( $n, 1$ )-stacked spatial central configuration it is necessary that the remaining $n-1$ bodies must be co-spherical.

Proof. By hypothesis the configuration must be non-coplanar, so in Eq. (8) at least one $\Delta_{i j k n}$ is different from zero. Without loss of generality, consider $\Delta_{123 n} \neq 0$. From

$$
\left(R_{1 n}-R_{2 n}\right) \Delta_{123 n}=0
$$

we have

$$
R_{1 n}-R_{2 n}=0
$$

which implies that $r_{1 n}=r_{2 n}=d>0$. Thus, $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ belong to a sphere with radius $d$ and center at $r_{n}$.


Fig. 2. Example of a $(5,1)$-stacked spatial central configuration.

We can classify the other indices into two sets

$$
\mathfrak{D}_{1}=\left\{j: \Delta_{12 j n}=0\right\}
$$

and

$$
\mathfrak{D}_{2}=\left\{j: \Delta_{12 j n} \neq 0\right\}
$$

that is $\mathfrak{D}_{1}$ contains the indices of the bodies whose vector positions are coplanar with $r_{1}, r_{2}$ and $r_{n}$, while $\mathfrak{D}_{2}$ contains the indices of the bodies whose vector positions are not coplanar with $r_{1}, r_{2}$ and $r_{n}$. For $j \in \mathfrak{D}_{2}$, we have

$$
\left(R_{1 n}-R_{j n}\right) \Delta_{12 j n}=0
$$

which implies that

$$
R_{1 n}-R_{j n}=0
$$

Thus, $r_{j n}=r_{1 n}=d>0$ for all $j \in \mathfrak{D}_{2}$. Then $r_{1}, r_{2}$ and $r_{j}$ belong to the sphere of radius $d$ and center at $r_{n}$ for all $j \in \mathfrak{D}_{2}$. To complete the proof of the lemma note that the index 3 does not belong to $\mathfrak{D}_{1}$; thus $r_{3 n}=d$. Take now the equations in (8) for which the first index is 3 and the second belongs to $\mathfrak{D}_{1}$. So

$$
\left(R_{3 n}-R_{j n}\right) \Delta_{3 j 1 n}=0
$$

and thus

$$
R_{3 n}-R_{j n}=0
$$

which implies that $r_{j n}=r_{3 n}=d>0$ for all $j \in \mathfrak{D}_{1}$, that is $r_{j n}=d>0$ for all $j$ such that $1 \leq j<n$. The lemma is proved.
In short, Theorem 2 is proved from Lemmas 6 and 7.
The only possibility of a central configuration with $n$ bodies for which a proper subset of $n-1$ bodies also form a central configuration is given by $n-1$ bodies in a central configuration on a sphere $S$ and one body of arbitrary mass at the center of $S$.

Little is known about co-spherical central configurations. See  for some results on co-spherical kite central configurations. Platonic polyhedrons with bodies of equal masses at the vertices and one body of arbitrary mass at their geometrical barycenters are examples of $(n, 1)$-stacked spatial central configurations. See Fig. 2.

Pyramidal central configurations are also examples of $(n, 1)$-stacked spatial central configurations. See . In particular, these central configurations are the only possible $(n, 1)$-stacked spatial central configurations with a proper planar subset of the bodies which form a planar central configuration. See Fig. 3.

The study of pyramidal central configurations requires a better understanding of co-circular central configurations. See the work of Roberts and Cors  for the explanation of the case $n=4$. The general case still remains open.

# 4. Concluding remarks 

In Theorem 1 (Theorem 2, respectively) we have characterized the $(n, 1)$-stacked central configuration for the planar non-collinear (spatial non-planar, respectively) $n$-body problem, $n \geq 4$. On the basis of the proofs of Theorems 1 and 2 the following problem arises: What can be said about the center of mass of an $(n, 1)$-stacked central configuration?

This problem will be investigated in a future work.


Fig. 3. Example of an $(n, 1)$-stacked spatial central configuration with a planar subset of bodies that also form a central configuration.

# Twisted stacked central configurations for the spatial seven-body problem 

## 1. Introduction and main results

The classical $n$-body problem concerns with the motion of $n$ mass points moving in space according to Newton's second law and the gravitational law:

$$
m_{i} \ddot{x}_{i}=\sum_{k \neq i} \frac{m_{k} m_{i}\left(x_{k}-x_{i}\right)}{\left|x_{k}-x_{i}\right|^{3}}, \quad i=1,2, \ldots, n
$$

Here $x_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ is the position of mass $m_{i}>0$. Alternatively, system (1.1) can be rewritten as

$$
m_{i} \ddot{x}_{i}=\frac{\partial U(x)}{\partial x_{i}}, \quad i=1,2, \ldots, n
$$

where

$$
U(x)=U\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)=\sum_{1 \leq k<j \leq n} \frac{m_{k} m_{i}}{\left|x_{k}-x_{j}\right|}
$$

is the Newtonian potential of system (1.1). The position vector $x=\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{3}\right)^{n}$ is often referred to the configuration of the system; the vectors $x_{i}(i=1,2, \ldots, n)$ are vertices of the configuration $x$.


Let $M=m_{1}+\cdots+m_{n}$ be the total mass and

$$
c=\frac{1}{M}\left(m_{1} x_{1}+\cdots+m_{n} x_{n}\right)
$$

be the center of mass of the configuration $x$. Because the potential is singular when two particles have the same position, it is natural to assume that the configuration avoids the set

$$
\Delta=\left\{x \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{3}\right)^{n}: x_{i}=x_{j} \text { for some } i \neq j\right\}
$$

A configuration $x=\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{3}\right)^{n} \backslash \Delta$ is called a central configuration if there exists some positive constant $\lambda$, called the multiplier, such that

$$
-\lambda\left(x_{i}-c\right)=\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{n} \frac{m_{j}\left(x_{j}-x_{i}\right)}{\left|x_{j}-x_{i}\right|^{3}}, \quad i=1,2, \ldots, n
$$

It is easy to see that a central configuration remains a central configuration after a rotation in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and a scalar multiplication. More precisely, let $A \in S O(3)$ and $a>0$, if $x=\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)$ is a central configuration, so are $A x=\left(A x_{1}, A x_{2}, \ldots, A x_{n}\right)$ and $a x=\left(a x_{1}, a x_{2}, \ldots, a x_{n}\right)$.

Two central configurations are said to be equivalent if one can be transformed to another by a scalar multiplication and a rotation. In this paper, when we say a central configuration, we mean a class of central configurations as defined by the above equivalence relation.

The study of central configuration goes back to Euler and Lagrange. For $n=3$, it is a classical result there are three collinear, called Euler, central configurations and one equilateral triangular, called Lagrange, central configurations. For $n=4$, Moulton  proved that there is exactly one collinear central configuration for each arrangement of the mass points on the line.

There are several reasons why central configurations are of special importance in the study of the $n$-body problem; see [2-4] for details.

A stacked central configuration is a central configuration in which a proper subset of the $n$ bodies is already on a central configuration. This class of central configuration of 5-body problem was introduced by Hampton in . The work of  was complemented by Llibre in .

Zhang and Zhou  showed the existence of double pyramidal central configurations of $N+2$-body problem. Hampton and Santoprete  provided some examples of stacked central configurations for the spatial 7-body problem where the bodies are arranged as concentric three and two dimensional simplex.

Mello and Fernandes  provided new examples of stacked central configuration for spatial 7-body problem where the four bodies are at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron and the other three bodies are located at the vertices of an equilateral triangle in the exterior of regular tetrahedron. In this paper, we show the existence of the twisted stacked central configurations of the 7-body problem. The spatial central configuration considered here satisfies (see Fig. 1): the position vectors $x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}$ and $x_{4}$ are at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron $\Sigma$; the position vectors $x_{5}, x_{6}$ and $x_{7}$ are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle $\Pi$; the triangle $\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right)$ and the triangle $\left(x_{5}, x_{6}, x_{7}\right)$ have twisted angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$.

Without loss of generality, we can assume that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{1}=(1,0,0), \quad x_{2}=\left(-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 0\right), \quad x_{3}=\left(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 0\right), \quad x_{4}=(0,0, \sqrt{2}) \\
& x_{5}=\left(\frac{1}{2} x, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} x, z\right), \quad x_{6}=(-x, 0, z), \quad x_{7}=\left(\frac{1}{2} x,-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} x, z\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $x>0$ is the radius of the circle that contains the equilateral triangle $\Pi$ and $z \in \mathbb{R}$ is the signed distance between the plane that contains $x_{1}, x_{2}$ and $x_{3}$ and the plane that contains $\Pi$.

The main results of this paper are the following.
Theorem 1.1. According to Fig. 1, in order that the seven mass points are in a central configuration, the following statements are necessary:

1. The masses $m_{1}, m_{2}$ and $m_{3}$ must be equal.
2. The masses $m_{5}, m_{6}$ and $m_{7}$ must be equal.

Theorem 1.2. There exist points $P_{0}\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right) \in T^{-1}(0) \cap D_{1}$ such that the seven bodies take the coordinates

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{1}=(1,0,0), \quad x_{2}=\left(-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 0\right), \quad x_{3}=\left(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 0\right), \quad x_{4}=(0,0, \sqrt{2}) \\
& x_{5}=\left(\frac{1}{2} x_{0}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} x_{0}, z_{0}\right), \quad x_{6}=\left(-x_{0}, 0, z_{0}\right), \quad x_{7}=\left(\frac{1}{2} x_{0},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} x_{0}, z_{0}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Then there are positive solutions of $m_{1}, m_{4}, m_{5}$ such that these bodies form a spatial central configuration according to Fig. 1.


Fig. 1. The configuration of the spatial seven-body problem.

# 2. Proof of Theorem 1.1 

For the spatial central configurations, instead of working with Eq. (1.4), we consider the Dziobek-Laura-Andoyer equations (see , p. 295)

$$
g_{i j h}=\sum_{k=1, k \neq i, j, h}^{n} m_{k}\left(d_{i k}-d_{j k}\right) \Delta_{i j h k}=0
$$

for $1 \leq i<j \leq n, h=1,2, \ldots, n, h \neq i, j$. Here $d_{i j}=\frac{1}{\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)^{2}}$ and $\Delta_{i j h k}=\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right) \wedge\left(x_{i}-x_{h}\right) \cdot\left(x_{i}-x_{k}\right)$. Thus $\Delta_{i j h k}$ gives six times the signed volume of the tetrahedron formed by the bodies with positions $x_{i}, x_{j}, x_{h}$ and $x_{k}$.

For the 7-body problem, Eq. (2.1) is a system of 105 equations. According to Fig. 1, our class of configurations with seven bodies must satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}
& d_{12}=d_{13}=d_{14}=d_{23}=d_{24}=d_{34}=3^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
& d_{15}=d_{17}=d_{25}=d_{26}=d_{36}=d_{37}=\left(1+x^{2}-x+z^{2}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
& d_{16}=d_{27}=d_{35}=\left((1+x)^{2}+z^{2}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
& d_{45}=d_{46}=d_{47}=\left(x^{2}+(z-\sqrt{2})^{2}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\
& d_{56}=d_{57}=d_{67}=(\sqrt{3} x)^{-3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Due to the assumption (1.5) and the definition of $\Delta_{i j h k}$, we have several symmetries in the signed volumes. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Delta_{1235}=\Delta_{1236}=\Delta_{1237} \\
& \Delta_{1256}=\Delta_{1257}=\Delta_{1357}=\Delta_{1376} \\
& \Delta_{1267}=\Delta_{1356}=\Delta_{2357} \\
& \Delta_{5671}=\Delta_{5672}=\Delta_{5673}
\end{aligned}
$$

and much more ones.
By using the symmetries and the properties of $\Delta_{i j h k}$, we obtain the following results.
Lemma 2.1. In order to have a spatial central configuration according to Fig. 1, a necessary condition is that the masses $m_{1}, m_{2}$ and $m_{3}$ must be equal.
Proof. It is sufficient to consider the equations $g_{567}=0$ and $g_{576}=0$. Consider the expressions of $g_{567}$ and $g_{576}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& g_{567}=m_{1}\left(d_{15}-d_{16}\right) \Delta_{5671}+m_{2}\left(d_{25}-d_{26}\right) \Delta_{5672}+m_{3}\left(d_{35}-d_{36}\right) \Delta_{5673}+m_{4}\left(d_{45}-d_{46}\right) \Delta_{5674}=0 \\
& g_{576}=m_{1}\left(d_{15}-d_{17}\right) \Delta_{5761}+m_{2}\left(d_{25}-d_{27}\right) \Delta_{5762}+m_{3}\left(d_{35}-d_{37}\right) \Delta_{5763}+m_{4}\left(d_{45}-d_{47}\right) \Delta_{5764}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

By assumption (1.5) and symmetries (2.2), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& g_{567}=\left(m_{1}-m_{3}\right)\left(d_{15}-d_{16}\right) \Delta_{5671}=0 \\
& g_{576}=\left(m_{2}-m_{3}\right)\left(d_{25}-d_{27}\right) \Delta_{5762}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

For our class of central configurations, we have $d_{15}-d_{16} \neq 0, d_{25}-d_{27} \neq 0, \Delta_{5671} \neq 0, \Delta_{5672} \neq 0$. So the above equations hold if and only if $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}$. So the statement 1 of Theorem 1.1 is proved.

Lemma 2.2. If the configuration according to Fig. 1 is a central configuration, a necessary condition is that the masses $m_{5}, m_{6}$ and $m_{7}$ must be equal.
Proof. It is sufficient to consider the equations $g_{123}=0$ and $g_{132}=0$. Consider the expressions of $g_{123}$ and $g_{132}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& g_{123}=m_{4}\left(d_{14}-d_{24}\right) \Delta_{1234}+m_{5}\left(d_{15}-d_{25}\right) \Delta_{1235}+m_{6}\left(d_{16}-d_{26}\right) \Delta_{1236}+m_{7}\left(d_{17}-d_{27}\right) \Delta_{1237}=0 \\
& g_{132}=m_{4}\left(d_{14}-d_{34}\right) \Delta_{1324}+m_{5}\left(d_{15}-d_{35}\right) \Delta_{1325}+m_{6}\left(d_{16}-d_{36}\right) \Delta_{1326}+m_{7}\left(d_{17}-d_{37}\right) \Delta_{1327}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

By assumption (1.5) and symmetries (2.2), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}

& g_{132}=\left(m_{5}-m_{6}\right)\left(d_{15}-d_{35}\right) \Delta_{1325}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

For our class of central configurations, we have $d_{16}-d_{26} \neq 0, d_{15}-d_{35} \neq 0, \Delta_{1236} \neq 0, \Delta_{1325} \neq 0$. So the above equations hold if and only if $m_{5}=m_{6}=m_{7}$. Hence the statement 2 of Theorem 1.1 is proved.

We restrict the set of admissible masses to $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=\alpha$ and $m_{5}=m_{6}=m_{7}=\beta$. Substituting $m_{1}=m_{2}=$ $m_{3}=\alpha$ and $m_{5}=m_{6}=m_{7}=\beta$ into Eq. (2.1), one can easily verify that the following equations are already satisfied:

& g_{237}=g_{247}=g_{274}=g_{345}=g_{354}=g_{453}=g_{461}=g_{472}=0 \\
& g_{561}=g_{562}=g_{563}=g_{564}=g_{567}=g_{571}=g_{572}=g_{573}=0 \\

While the remaining 66 equations can be put into 6 sets of equivalent equations.

Lemma 2.3. Under our assumptions and in the set $T^{-1}(0)$, the remaining 54 equations in the set $2,3, \ldots, 6$ are satisfied if $g_{152}=g_{153}=g_{154}=0$ are satisfied.

Proof. Consider the expressions of $g_{157}$ and $g_{153}-g_{152}$ :

From Lemma 2.3, in order to study central configurations according to Fig. 1 in the set $T^{-1}(0)$, it is sufficient to study the following 3 equations:

$$
g_{152}=0, \quad g_{153}=0, \quad g_{154}=0

Denote by $A=\left(a_{i j}\right)$ the matrix of the coefficients of the homogeneous linear system in the variables $\alpha, m_{4}, \beta$ defined by Eqs. (2.4). Thus

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
a_{11}=\left(d_{13}-d_{35}\right) \Delta_{1523}, & a_{12}=\left(d_{14}-d_{45}\right) \Delta_{1524}, & a_{13}=\left(d_{16}+d_{17}-2 d_{56}\right) \Delta_{1526} \\
a_{21}=\left(d_{12}-d_{25}\right) \Delta_{1532}, & a_{22}=\left(d_{14}-d_{45}\right) \Delta_{1534}, & a_{23}=\left(d_{17}-d_{57}\right) \Delta_{1537} \\

Let $x=\left(\begin{array}{c}\mu \\ \beta\end{array}\right)$. Then in order to get the spatial central configuration like Fig. 1, we need to find positive solution $\alpha, m_{4}, \beta$ of the following system:

$$
A x=0
$$

where $T=0$.
By elementary computation we have $\operatorname{det}(A)=0$, since the third row of $A$ is a linear combination of the first two rows. Thus in the set $T^{-1}(0)$ Eq. (2.5) have nontrivial solutions.

# 3. The existence of spatial central configurations 

Consider the expression of $T$ :

$$
T=\left(d_{16}-d_{46}\right) \Delta_{1456}+\left(d_{17}-d_{47}\right) \Delta_{1457}
$$

Now we study the sign of each term of $T$. The term $\left(d_{16}-d_{46}\right)$ is negative if $z>\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(1-2 x)$, positive if $z<\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(1-2 x)$ and vanishes on the straight line $z=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(1-2 x)$. The term $\Delta_{1456}$ is negative if $z<\sqrt{2}(1+x)$, positive if $z>\sqrt{2}(1+x)$ and vanishes on the straight line $z=\sqrt{2}(1+x)$. The term $\left(d_{17}-d_{47}\right)$ is negative if $z>\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(1+x)$, positive if $z<\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(1+x)$ and vanishes on the straight line $z=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(1+x)$. The term $\Delta_{1457}$ is negative if $z<\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(2-x)$, positive if $z>\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(2-x)$

Fig. 2. The regions $D_{1}$ and $D_{2}$.
and vanishes on the straight line $z=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(2-x)$. Thus the connected components of the set $T^{-1}(0)$ are restricted to the set $D_{1} \cup D_{2}$, where

$$
D_{1}=D_{11} \cup D_{12}, \quad D_{2}=D_{21} \cup D_{22}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
& D_{11}=\left\{(x, z) \mid 0<x \leq 1, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(2-x)<z<\sqrt{2}(1+x)\right\} \\
& D_{12}=\left\{(x, z) \mid x>1, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(1+x)<z<\sqrt{2}(1+x)\right\} \\
& D_{21}=\left\{(x, z) \mid 0<x \leq 1, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(1-2 x)<z<\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(1+x)\right\} \\
& D_{22}=\left\{(x, z) \mid x>1, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(1-2 x)<z<\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(2-x)\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

See Fig. 2.
In order to prove the existence of positive solutions of (2.5) in the set $T^{-1}(0)$, it is sufficient to prove that the entries in each row of $A$ change the signs. So if the entries of some row of $A$ have the same signs, there are no admissible masses such that the bodies are in a central configuration according to Fig. 1.

Let

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathcal{A}_{1}=D_{2} \cap\left\{(x, z) \mid 2 x^{2}+x-z^{2}<1\right\} \\
& \mathcal{A}_{2}=D_{2} \cap\left\{(x, z) \mid x^{2}-x+1+z^{2}>3\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

and $\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{1} \cup \mathcal{A}_{2}$, see Fig. 3. Then we have the following lemma for $(x, z) \in \mathcal{A}$.


Fig. 3. The regions $\mathcal{A}_{1}, \mathcal{A}_{2}$ and $\mathscr{B}$.

Lemma 3.1. In the set $\mathcal{A}$, there are no spatial central configurations according to Fig. 1.
Proof. Consider the entries $a_{31}=\left(d_{12}-d_{25}\right) \Delta_{1542}+\left(d_{13}-d_{35}\right) \Delta_{1543}$ and $a_{33}=\left(d_{16}-d_{56}\right) \Delta_{1546}+\left(d_{17}-d_{57}\right) \Delta_{1547}$. It is simple to see $\Delta_{1542}>0, \Delta_{1543}>0, \Delta_{1546}>0$ and $\Delta_{1547}>0$ for $(x, z) \in \mathcal{A}$. While $d_{12}-d_{25}, d_{13}-d_{35}, d_{16}-d_{56}, d_{17}-d_{57}$ are negative for $(x, z) \in \mathcal{A}_{1}$, and $d_{12}-d_{25}, d_{13}-d_{35}, d_{16}-d_{56}, d_{17}-d_{57}$ are positive for $(x, z) \in \mathcal{A}_{2}$. Thus the entries $a_{31}$ and $a_{33}$ have the same signs. The lemma is proved.

Now we prove the existence of spatial central configuration according to Fig. 1 for some points in the set $D_{1}$.
Proof of Theorem 1.2. Since the matrix $A$ is singular in the set $T^{-1}(0)$, there are nontrivial solutions of (2.5) in the set $T^{-1}(0)$. In order to simplify our analysis, we consider the following subset of $D_{1}$ (see Fig. 3):

$$
\mathscr{B}=\mathscr{B}_{1} \cup \mathscr{B}_{2}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}

& \mathscr{B}_{2}=\left\{(x, z) \in D_{1}: \frac{\sqrt{10}}{2} \leq x<\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{2}<z<\sqrt{3-x^{2}}+\sqrt{2}\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

In the set $\mathscr{B}$, the entries of the matrix $A$ have the following signs:

$$
A=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
- & + \\ + & + \\ + & 0
\end{array}\right)
$$

Consider the set

$$
\mathscr{L}=\mathscr{B} \cap\{(x, z): 1.09419029<x<1.69932798, T=0\}
$$

Without loss of generality, let $\alpha=1$. It is easy to see that the mass

$$
\beta=-\frac{\left(d_{12}-d_{25}\right) \Delta_{1542}+\left(d_{13}-d_{35}\right) \Delta_{1543}}{\left(d_{16}-d_{56}\right) \Delta_{1546}+\left(d_{17}-d_{57}\right) \Delta_{1547}}
$$

is positive. By direct computation, the mass

$$

is increasing in $(1.09419029,1.69932798)$ about $x$ in the set $\mathscr{L}$ and $m_{4}(1.09419029)=0$. So at every point in the set $\mathscr{L}$, we have nontrivial positive solutions of (2.5). The proof of Theorem 1.2 is complete.
