The typical initial interval is $_{k}=\left[x_{1}\right]_{k_{1}} \times\left[y_{1}\right]_{k_{2}} \times\left[x_{3}\right]_{k_{3}} \times\left[y_{3}\right]_{k_{4}}$ where $\left[x_{1}\right]_{k_{1}}=$ $\left[\frac{k_{1}}{N_{1}}, \frac{k_{1}+1}{N_{1}}\right]$ refers to the $k_{1}$-th subinterval for $x_{1}$ and the others are similar.

Step 2. The initial interval $_{k}$ is ruled out if one of the six functions $f_{i j}\left(_{k}\right)$ doesn't contain zero. The rest intervals are candidates for the existence of solutions and they are labeled as $_{k}, k=0,1,2, \cdots, k_{\text {end }}$. If no intervals are left, then there is no solution for the given mass in the given configuration space and we stop. Otherwise, go to next step.

Step 3. The Krawczyk operator is used as a part of iteration process for each interval $_{k}$ from Step 2:

Let $F(x)=\left[f_{12}(x), f_{13}(x), f_{14}(x), f_{23}(x)\right]$.

1. given $_{k} \subseteq \underline{\mathbf{U}} \subset \mathbf{R}^{4}$
2. Compute $=K\left(\operatorname{mid}_{k},_{k}, F\right)$
3. if $ \subset \operatorname{int}_{k}$ and the diameter $d=\bar{y}-\underline{y}$ of $$ is smaller than the error tolerance, then return success and $$ and go to Step 4
elseif $ \subset \operatorname{int}_{k}$ and the diameter $d=\bar{y}-\underline{y}$ of $$ is not smaller than the error tolerance, then go to 2 by replacing $_{k}$ by $$
elseif $_{k} \subset$, then bisect the longest side of the interval $_{k}$ and go to Step 2 for the two smaller intervals
elseif $_{k} \cap=\emptyset$, then return no solution in $_{k}$
elseif $_{k} \cap \neq \emptyset$, then set $_{k+1}:= \cap_{k}$ and go to Step 2
Step 4. If Step 3 returns success and $, f_{24}()$ and $f_{34}()$ are evaluated. If both contain zero, then $$ is a central configuration for the given mass vector $m_{0}$ and it returns a unique solution $$.

In SageMath 9.6, there are two styles for printing intervals: 'brackets' style and 'question' style. In question style, we print the "known correct" part of the number, followed by a question mark. The question mark indicates that the preceding digit is possibly wrong by $\pm 1$. In the report of the computation results, we may use either of them.

If only one solution is obtained at the end of the program, it implies the existence of a unique central configuration in the given order as in Figure 2. Two examples are provided to demonstrate the numerically rigorous proof of the existence and uniqueness of the convex central configurations for a given mass.

Example 3.4. For $m_{0}=$, there is a unique convex central configuration and $x_{1}=$ $-1 . ? e-20, y 1=1.0000000000000000000 ?, x_{3}=-1 . ? e-20$, $y_{3}=-1.00000000000000000000 ?$.

In this case, we take $N_{1}=20$. Each side of the configuration is partitioned into 20 smaller intervals with length about 0.05 to 0.0733 . There are $20^{4}=160,000$ intervals in total to check in Step 2. Most of them are ruled out because at least one of the six functions $f_{i j}$ contains no zero. Among them only 52 intervals are left for Krawczyk operator in Step 3. Then only one of these intervals returns the above unique solution and others return no solution. We also note that no bisection is needed for these intervals. So we conclude that there is a unique central configurations for this mass $m_{0}$ in the given ordering. This way we recover the well known result (): The square is the only convex central configuration in the planar 4-body problem with equal masses.

Example 3.5. For $m_{0}=[0.2,1,0.3,0.4]$, there is a unique convex central configuration and $x_{1} \in[0.15385328707521665441880634609065,0.15385328707521665448042670172252]$,
$y_{1} \in[1.4086619698548151890849667722929,1.4086619698548151891412057380232]$, $x_{3} \in[0.11611158428853550145374041262273,0.11611158428853550155068635233120]$, $y_{3} \in[-1.484878202646704369219144317714,-1.484878202646704369133519439332]$.

In this case, we take $N_{1}=15$. Each side of the configuration is partitioned into 15 smaller intervals with length about 0.0667 to 0.0977 . There are totally $15^{4}=50,625$ intervals to check in Step 2. Only 62 intervals are left for Krawczyk operator in Step 3. But this time, 60 of them return no solutions. Two of them are bisected their intervals and went back to Step 2. Only one of them returns the above unique solution and others return no solution. We still have the conclusion that there is a unique central configurations for this mass $m_{0}$ in the given ordering.

This completes the proof of Theorem 2.4 for the given mass $m_{0}$ at the meshed grid points. To get the proof for all masses, we have to fill in the gaps among the discrete masses by the

Cartesian product of intervals. Here we employ implicit function theorem to produce such domains. Note that for any central configuration $x_{0}=x_{0}\left(m_{0}\right)=\left[x_{10}, y_{10}, x_{30}, y_{30}\right]$ with the corresponding mass $m_{0}, F\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)=0$. By implicit function theorem, if a nondegeneracy condition on $\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)$ is fulfilled, there exist two radius $r>0$ and $\varepsilon>0$, and a unique function $x=x(m)$ in the neighborhood $B\left(x_{0}, r\right)$ of $x_{0}$ and $B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$ of $m_{0}$ such that $x_{0}=x\left(m_{0}\right)$ and $F(x(m), m) \equiv 0$. Since $m_{2}=1$ is fixed once and for all, $m_{0}$ means $m_{0}=\left(m_{10}, m_{30}, m_{40}\right)$ when $m_{0}$ is considered as a variable. Hence

$$
B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)=\left\{\left(m_{1}, m_{3}, m_{4}\right) \mid \sqrt{\left(m_{1}-m_{10}\right)^{2}+\left(m_{3}-m_{30}\right)^{2}+\left(m_{4}-m_{40}\right)^{2}}<\varepsilon\right\}
$$

In the next section, we will refine the implicit function theorem to estimate the radius $r$ and $\varepsilon$ of the neighborhoods of the concerning point. For each such mass neighborhood, we prove the existence and uniqueness of convex central configuration.

# 4 Implicit Function Theorem: existence, uniqueness and size of valid domain 

Before we introduce the implicit function theorem (IFT) and its applications to our case, we first briefly go over the notations and the definitions that are used in this paper following , especially the norm we used should be consistent. For $x=\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{n}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{n},\|x\|=$ $\sqrt{x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\cdots+x_{n}^{2}}$ is the standard Euclidean norm. For a given real number $r>0$ and $x_{0} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,

$$
B\left(x_{0}, r\right)=\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n} \mid\left\|x-x_{0}\right\|<r\right\}
$$

denotes the open ball of radius $r$ centered at $x_{0}$. For given positive integers $n_{1}, n_{2} \in \mathbb{N}$, the norm $\|A\|$ of a linear map $A: \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n_{2}}$ is defined by

$$
\|A\|:=\sup \left\{\|A x\| \mid x \in B(0,1) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}\right\}
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\|A\|=\sup \left\{\|A x\| \mid x \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}} \text { and }\|x\|=1\right\} \text { or }\|A\|=\sup \left\{\frac{\|A x\|}{\|x\|} \mid x \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}\right\}
$$

with $\|A x\|$ the norm of $A x$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}}$. The standard Euclidean norm is easily computed in Matlab by using the command 'norm'.

For our later purpose, let

$$
\begin{aligned}
f: \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}} \times \mathbb{R}^{n_{2}} & \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}} \\
(x, m) & \mapsto f(x, m)
\end{aligned}
$$

be a multivariable vector-valued function. $f$ has the form $f=\left(f_{1}, f_{2}, \cdots, f_{n_{1}}\right)$ with components $f_{1}, f_{2}, \cdots, f_{n_{1}}: \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}} \times \mathbb{R}^{n_{2}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ multivariable real-valued functions of $(x, m)$. For our problem $f(x, m)$ is a function of position $x$ with mass parameter $m . D_{x} f\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)$ and $D_{m} f\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)$ are Jacobian matrices of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $m$ respectively.

The second derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ is an array of $n_{1}$ Hessian matrices one for each component $f_{j}$ :

$$
D_{x}^{2} f=\left[H_{x}\left(f_{1}\right), H_{x}\left(f_{2}\right), \cdots, H_{x}\left(f_{n_{1}}\right)\right]
$$

whose norm $\left\|D_{x}^{2} f\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)\right\|$ is computed as

$$
\left\|D_{x}^{2} f\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)\right\|=\sup \left\{\left\|D_{x}^{2} f\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)(v, w)\right\| v \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}, w \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}} \text { and }\|v\|=\|w\|=1\right\}
$$

The second derivative $D_{x} D_{m} f\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)$ of $f$ with respect to variables $m$ and then variable $x$ is defined similarly.

Now it is ready to state IFT.

# 4.1 Implicit Function Theorem 

We start with a useful lemma.
Lemma 4.1. Given a continuous map $\varphi: \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right) \times U \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}$ with $\operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right) \subset \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}$ a closed ball and $U \subset \mathbb{R}^{n_{2}}$ an open subset and a fixed point $x_{0} \in U$, the function

$$
\begin{aligned}
l: U & \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \\
x & \mapsto l(x):=\max _{y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)}\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)\right\|
\end{aligned}
$$

is continuous on $U$.
Proof. By triangle inequality, for any $x_{1} \in U$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)\right\| & \leq\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{1}\right)\right\|+\left\|\varphi\left(y, x_{1}\right)-\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)\right\| \\
& \leq \max _{y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)}\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{1}\right)\right\|+\max _{y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)}\left\|\varphi\left(y, x_{1}\right)-\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)\right\| \\
& \leq \max _{y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)}\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{1}\right)\right\|+l\left(x_{1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

So

$$
l(x)=\max _{y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)}\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)\right\| \leq \max _{y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)}\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{1}\right)\right\|+l\left(x_{1}\right)
$$

that is

$$
l(x)-l\left(x_{1}\right) \leq \max _{y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)}\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{1}\right)\right\|
$$

Similarly, we have

$$
l\left(x_{1}\right)-l(x) \leq \max _{y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)}\left\|\varphi\left(y, x_{1}\right)-\varphi(y, x)\right\|
$$

So $\forall x_{1} \in U$, we have

$$
\left|l(x)-l\left(x_{1}\right)\right| \leq \max _{y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)}\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{1}\right)\right\|
$$

Take a closed ball $\operatorname{clB}\left(x_{1}, r_{x_{1}}\right) \subset U$, then $\varphi$ is uniformly continuous on $\operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right) \times \operatorname{clB}\left(x_{1}, r_{x_{1}}\right)$. Thus, $\forall \varepsilon>0, \exists \delta>0$, if $\left\|\left(y_{3}, x_{3}\right)-\left(y_{2}, x_{2}\right)\right\|<\delta$, then $\left\|\varphi\left(y_{3}, x_{3}\right)-\varphi\left(y_{2}, x_{2}\right)\right\|<\varepsilon$. So for $x \in U$ such that $\left\|x-x_{1}\right\|<\delta$, we have $\left\|\left(y, x\right)-\left(y, x_{1}\right)\right\|<\delta,\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{1}\right)\right\|<\varepsilon$ for any $y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)$ which means that

$$
\left|l(x)-l\left(x_{1}\right)\right|<\varepsilon
$$

The proof is complete.
Now we use the lemma to prove a version of implicit function theorem used on the estimation of the valid domain.

Theorem 4.2. Let $Y \subset \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}, X \subset \mathbb{R}^{n_{2}}$ be nonempty open sets. Let $Y \times X \ni(y, x) \mapsto f(y, x) \in$ $\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}$ be a $\mathscr{C}^{1}$ map. For $\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right) \in Y \times X$, suppose $D_{y} f\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)$ is invertible. Then for any neighborhood $\mathscr{O}\left(y_{0}\right)$ of $y_{0}$, there is a neighborhood $\mathscr{O}\left(x_{0}\right)$ of $x_{0}$ and a unique continuous map $g: \mathscr{O}\left(x_{0}\right) \rightarrow \mathscr{O}\left(y_{0}\right)$ such that

1. $g\left(x_{0}\right)=y_{0}$,
2. $f(g(x), x)=f\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)$ for all $x \in \mathscr{O}\left(x_{0}\right)$,
3. $g$ is continuous at point $x_{0}$.

Proof. The proof is based on Banach Fixed-Point Theorem.
Let $T:=D_{y} f\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)$ and $\omega_{0}=f\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)$. Define

$$
\begin{aligned}
\varphi: Y \times X & \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}} \\
(y, x) & \mapsto \varphi(y, x):=y-T^{-1}\left(f(y, x)-\omega_{0}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Then $\varphi(y, x)=y$ iff $f(y, x)=\omega_{0}$. We will show that $\varphi(\cdot, x)$ has a fixed point. From the definition of $\varphi$, we have

$$
D_{y} \varphi(y, x)=I-T^{-1} D_{y} f(y, x)
$$

Since $D_{y} \varphi(y, x)$ is continuous and $D_{y} \varphi\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)=0$, there exists $r>0$ such that $\left\|D_{y} \varphi(y, x)\right\| \leq$ $\frac{1}{2}$ for any $y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)$ and $x \in \mathrm{~B}\left(x_{0}, \varepsilon_{1}\right)$. By the Mean Value Inequality,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)-y_{0}\right\| & =\left\|\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)-\varphi\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)\right\| \\
& \leq \sup _{0 \leq t \leq 1}\left\|D_{y} \varphi\left((1-t) y_{0}+t y, x_{0}\right)\right\|\left\|y-y_{0}\right\| \\
& \leq \frac{1}{2}\left\|y-y_{0}\right\| \leq \frac{r}{2}, \forall y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

For each $x$, let $l(x):=\max _{y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)}\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)\right\|$ as in the previous Lemma 4.1. Since $l(x)$ is continuous by the lemma and $l\left(x_{0}\right)=0$, there exists $\varepsilon \in\left(0, \varepsilon_{1}\right)$ such that

$$
l(x)<\frac{r}{2}, \forall x \in \mathrm{~B}\left(x_{0}, \varepsilon\right)
$$

For each $x \in \mathrm{~B}\left(x_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$, we have

$$
\left\|\varphi(y, x)-y_{0}\right\| \leq\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)\right\|+\left\|\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)-y_{0}\right\|<\frac{r}{2}+\frac{r}{2}=r, \forall y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)
$$

Thus, for each $x \in \mathrm{~B}\left(x_{0}, \varepsilon\right), \varphi(\cdot, x)$ maps

$$
\operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right) \ni y \mapsto \varphi(y, x) \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)
$$

For $y_{1}, y_{2} \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)$ and $x \in \mathrm{~B}\left(x_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$,

$$
\left\|\varphi\left(y_{1}, x\right)-\varphi\left(y_{2}, x\right)\right\| \leq \max _{0 \leq t \leq 1}\left\|D_{y} \varphi\left((1-t) y_{1}+t y_{2}, x\right)\right\|\left\|y_{1}-y_{2}\right\| \leq \frac{1}{2}\left\|y_{1}-y_{2}\right\|
$$

Hence by Banach Fixed-Point Theorem, for each $x \in \mathrm{~B}\left(x_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$, there exists a $g(x) \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)$ such that $\varphi(g(x), x)=g(x)$ or equivalently $f(g(x), x)=\omega_{0}$.

Based on the proof of the implicit function theorem, one can get the following estimate about the size of the valid domain.

Theorem 4.3. (, Proposition 3.12) Let $Y \subset \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}$ and $X \subset \mathbb{R}^{n_{2}}$ be two nonempty open sets. Let $f: Y \times X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}$ be a $\mathscr{C}^{2}$ map. For some $\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right) \in Y \times X, D_{y} f\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)$ is invertible. Define

$$
L_{x}:=\left\|D_{x} f\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)\right\|, M_{y}:=\left\|\left(D_{y} f\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)\right)^{-1}\right\|
$$

and for any given $R_{1}>0, R_{2}>0$, define

$$
\begin{aligned}
K_{y y} & :=\sup _{y \in \mathrm{~B}\left(y_{0}, R_{1}\right)}\left\|D_{y}^{2} f\left(y, x_{0}\right)\right\| \\
K_{x x} & :=\sup _{(y, x) \in \mathrm{B}\left(\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right), R_{2}\right)}\left\|D_{x}^{2} f(y, x)\right\| \\
K_{x y} & :=\sup _{(y, x) \in \mathrm{B}\left(\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right), R_{2}\right)}\left\|D_{x} D_{y} f(y, x)\right\|
\end{aligned}
$$

Then for all $r \leq \min \left\{P, R_{2}\right\}$ with $P:=\min \left\{\frac{1}{2 M_{y} K_{y y}}, R_{1}\right\}$, and $\varepsilon \leq \min \left\{\sqrt{R_{2}^{2}-r^{2}}, \frac{1}{4 M_{y} K_{x y}}\right\}$ satisfying

$$
M_{y}\left(L_{x}+K_{x y} r+K_{x x} \varepsilon\right) \varepsilon<\frac{r}{2}
$$

$\forall x \in \mathrm{~B}\left(x_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$ there exists a unique $g(x) \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)$ such that $f(g(x), x)=f\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)$.
Proof. Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{y} \varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right) & =\int_{0}^{1} D_{y}^{2} \varphi\left((1-s) y_{0}+s y, x_{0}\right)\left(y-y_{0}\right) \mathrm{d} s \\
& =-T^{-1} \int_{0}^{1} D_{y}^{2} f\left((1-s) y_{0}+s y, x_{0}\right)\left(y-y_{0}\right) \mathrm{d} s
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\left\|D_{y} \varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)\right\| \leq M_{y} K_{y y}\left\|y-y_{0}\right\|, \forall y \in \mathrm{~B}\left(y_{0}, R_{1}\right)
$$

by noting $T=D_{y} f\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)$ as in the previous proof. From the Mean Value Inequality,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)-y_{0}\right\| & =\left\|\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)-\varphi\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)\right\| \\
& \leq \max _{0 \leq t \leq 1}\left\|D_{y} \varphi\left((1-t) y_{0}+t y, x_{0}\right)\right\|\left\|y-y_{0}\right\| \\
& \leq M_{y} K_{y y}\left\|y-y_{0}\right\|\left\|y-y_{0}\right\| \\
& \leq M_{y} K_{y y} P\left\|y-y_{0}\right\| \\
& \leq \frac{1}{2}\left\|y-y_{0}\right\|, \forall y \in \mathrm{~B}\left(y_{0}, P\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
P:=\min \left\{\frac{1}{2 M_{y} K_{y y}}, R_{1}\right\}
$$

Using again the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{x} \varphi(y, x) & =D_{x} \varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)+\int_{0}^{1} D_{x}^{2} \varphi\left(y,(1-s) x_{0}+s x\right)\left(x-x_{0}\right) \mathrm{d} s \\
& =D_{x} \varphi\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)+\int_{0}^{1} D_{y} D_{x} \varphi\left((1-s) y_{0}+s y, x_{0}\right)\left(y-y_{0}\right) \mathrm{d} s \\
& +\int_{0}^{1} D_{x}^{2} \varphi\left(y,(1-s) x_{0}+s x\right)\left(x-x_{0}\right) \mathrm{d} s
\end{aligned}
$$

By triangle inequality and submultiplicative property of induced norms we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|D_{x} \varphi(y, x)\right\| & \leq\left\|D_{x} \varphi\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)\right\|+\int_{0}^{1}\left\|D_{y} D_{x} \varphi\left((1-s) y_{0}+s y, x_{0}\right)\right\|\left\|(y-y_{0})\right\| \mathrm{d} s \\
& +\int_{0}^{1}\left\|D_{x}^{2} \varphi\left(y,(1-s) x_{0}+s x\right)\right\|\left\|(x-x_{0})\right\| \mathrm{d} s \\
& \leq M_{y}\left(L_{x}+K_{x y}\left\|y-y_{0}\right\|+K_{x x}\left\|x-x_{0}\right\|\right), \forall(y, x) \in \mathrm{B}\left(\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right), R_{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

From the Mean Value Inequality,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)\right\| & \leq \max _{0 \leq t \leq 1}\left\|D_{x} \varphi\left(y,(1-t) x_{0}+t x\right)\right\|\left\|x-x_{0}\right\| \\
& \leq M_{y}\left(L_{x}+K_{x y}\left\|y-y_{0}\right\|+K_{x x}\left\|x-x_{0}\right\|\right)\left(\left\|x-x_{0}\right\|\right),(y, x) \in \mathrm{B}\left(\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right), R_{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

For a given $r \leq \min \left\{P, R_{2}\right\}$, we need the inequality

$$
\left\|\varphi(y, x)-\varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)\right\| \leq \frac{r}{2}
$$

hold for all $y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)$, and all $x \in \mathrm{~B}\left(x_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$. Requring

$$
M_{y}\left(L_{x}+K_{x y} r+K_{x x} \varepsilon\right) \varepsilon \leq \frac{r}{2}
$$

will suffice. One can solve the inequality above to get a respective

$$
\varepsilon \leq \min \left\{\sqrt{R_{2}^{2}-r^{2}}, \frac{1}{4 M_{y} K_{x y}}\right\}
$$

for a given $r \leq \min \left\{P, R_{2}\right\}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{y} \varphi(y, x) & =D_{y} \varphi\left(y, x_{0}\right)+\int_{0}^{1} D_{x} D_{y} \varphi\left(y,(1-s) x_{0}+s x\right)\left(x-x_{0}\right) \mathrm{d} s \\
& =D_{y} \varphi\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)+\int_{0}^{1} D_{y}^{2} \varphi\left((1-s) y_{0}+s y, x_{0}\right)\left(y-y_{0}\right) \mathrm{d} s \\
& +\int_{0}^{1} D_{x} D_{y} \varphi\left(y,(1-s) x_{0}+s x\right)\left(x-x_{0}\right) \mathrm{d} s, \forall y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Noting $D_{y} \varphi\left(y_{0}, x_{0}\right)=0$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|D_{y} \varphi(y, x)\right\| & \leq \int_{0}^{1}\left\|D_{y}^{2} \varphi\left((1-s) y_{0}+s y, x_{0}\right)\right\|\left\|\left(y-y_{0}\right)\right\| \mathrm{d} s \\
& +\int_{0}^{1}\left\|D_{x} D_{y} \varphi\left(y,(1-s) x_{0}+s x\right)\right\|\left\|\left(x-x_{0}\right)\right\| \mathrm{d} s \\
& \leq M_{y} K_{y y}\left\|y-y_{0}\right\|+M_{y} K_{x y}\left\|x-x_{0}\right\| \\
& \leq \frac{3}{4}, \forall y \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right), \forall x \in \mathrm{~B}\left(x_{0}, \varepsilon\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

From the Mean Value Inequality,

$$
\left\|\varphi\left(y_{1}, x\right)-\varphi\left(y_{2}, x\right)\right\| \leq \max _{0 \leq t \leq 1}\left\|D_{y} \varphi\left((1-t) y_{1}+t y_{2}, x\right)\right\|\left\|y_{1}-y_{2}\right\| \leq \frac{3}{4}\left\|y_{1}-y_{2}\right\|
$$

for $y_{1}, y_{2} \in \operatorname{clB}\left(y_{0}, r\right)$ and $x \in \mathrm{~B}\left(x_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$.
Combining Theorem 4.3 and our setting about the central configurations, we have immediately

Theorem 4.4. Let $F=\left[F_{1}, F_{2}, F_{3}, F_{4}\right]=\left[f_{12}, f_{13}, f_{14}, f_{23}\right]$. Then $F$ is a map from $\mathbf{U} \times\left(\mathbb{R}^{+}\right)^{3} \ni$ $(x, m)$ to $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ where the admissible region $\mathbf{U} \subset \mathbb{R}^{4}$ is defined in Theorem 2.3. Since $m_{2}$ is fixed to be 1 as the largest value once and for all, the mass vector $m \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{+3}\right)$ is then $m=$ $\left[m_{1}, m_{3}, m_{4}\right] \in(0,1]^{3}$. Let $x_{0} \in \mathbf{U}$ be a central configuration for $m_{0}$ such that $F\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)=0$ and $D_{x} F\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)$ is nonsingular. Define

$$
L_{m}:=\left\|D_{m} F\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)\right\|, \quad M_{x}:=\left\|\left(D_{x} F\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)\right)^{-1}\right\|
$$

and for given $R_{1}>0, R_{2}>0$, set

$$
\begin{gathered}
K_{x x}:=\sup \left\{\left\|D_{x}^{2} F\left(x, m_{0}\right)\right\|\left|x \in B\left(x_{0}, R_{1}\right)\right\}\right. \\
K_{m m}:=\sup \left\{\left\|D_{x}^{2} F(x, m)\right\|\left|(x, m) \in B\left(\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right), R_{2}\right)\right\}\right.
\end{gathered}
$$

and

$$
K_{x m}:=\sup \left\{\left\|D_{x} D_{m} F(x, m)\right\|\left|(x, m) \in B\left(\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right), R_{2}\right)\right\}\right.
$$

Set $P:=\min \left\{\frac{1}{2 M_{x} K_{x x}}, R_{1}\right\}$. Then for all $r \leq \min \left\{P, R_{2}\right\}$ and $\varepsilon \leq \min \left\{\sqrt{R_{2}^{2}-r^{2}}, \frac{1}{4 M_{x} K_{x m}}\right\}$ satisfying

$$
M_{x}\left(L_{m}+K_{x m} r+K_{m m} \varepsilon\right) \varepsilon \leq r / 2
$$

$F(x, m)=0$ has a unique solution on $B\left(x_{0}, r\right)$ for any given $m \in B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$.
Remark 4.5. In our computation program, in order to have a large existence and uniqueness neighborhood about $\left(x_{0}, m_{0}\right)$, we choose $r=\min \left\{P, R_{2}\right\}$ and $\varepsilon$ be the maximum value satisfying the inequality (22) or we take

$$
\varepsilon=\min \left\{\frac{-M_{x}\left(L_{m}+K_{x m} r\right)+\sqrt{\left(M_{x}\left(L_{m}+K_{x m} r\right)\right)^{2}+2 M_{x} K_{m m} r}}{2 M_{x} K_{m m}}, \sqrt{R_{2}^{2}-r^{2}}, \frac{1}{4 M_{x} K_{x m}}\right\}
$$

These two values strongly depend on $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$.
We give an example to illustrate our computation program to show that there exists a unique convex central configuration for any masses in the corresponding $\varepsilon$-neighborhood.

Example 4.6. Let $x_{0}$ be the unique convex central configuration for mass $m_{0}$ with $m_{0}=$ $[0.2,1,0.3,0.4]$ and $x_{0}=\left[x_{10}, y_{10}, x_{30}, y_{30}\right]$ as given in Example 3.5. To compute $r$ and $\varepsilon$, we take

$$
\begin{gathered}
x_{10}=0.1538532870752166, y_{10}=1.4086619698548151 \\
x_{30}=0.1161115842885355, y_{30}=-1.4848782026467043
\end{gathered}
$$

Let $R_{1}=0.1$ and $R_{2}=0.2$. By direct computation, $M_{x}=3.193848, L_{m}=0.591292, K_{x x}=$ 1.880567, $K_{x m}=1.9330632, K_{m m}=2.160289$. Then $r=0.083247$ and $\varepsilon=0.016540$. Theorem 4.4 affirms that there exists a unique solution $x=x(m)$ in $x \in B\left(x_{0}, r\right)$ for $m \in B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$.

If we choose $R_{1}=0.2$ and $R_{2}=0.2$, then we have $r=0.066053$, and $\varepsilon=0.013632$. This illustrates that the values of $r$ and $\varepsilon$ depend on the choices of $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$. In our computations, we take $R_{1}=0.1$ and $R_{2}=0.2$ to have a larger $\varepsilon$.

To complete the proof of the uniqueness of the convex central configuration for any $m \in B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$, it is necessary to prove that any $x \in \hat{\mathbf{U}} \backslash B\left(x_{0}, r\right)$ is not a solution of the central configuration equations for this $m$. We have to change the balls to intervals in order to use interval arithmetic. Let

$$
I\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)=\left[m_{10}-\varepsilon, m_{10}+\varepsilon\right] \times\left[m_{30}-\varepsilon, m_{30}+\varepsilon\right] \times\left[m_{40}-\varepsilon, m_{40}+\varepsilon\right]
$$

be a mass interval centered at $m_{0}$ with radius $\varepsilon$. Let

$$
I\left(x_{0}, r\right)=\left[x_{10}-r, x_{10}+r\right] \times\left[y_{10}-r, y_{10}+r\right] \times\left[x_{30}-r, x_{30}+r\right] \times\left[y_{30}-r, y_{30}+r\right]
$$

be a position interval centered at $x_{0}$ with radius $r$. Then

$$
I\left(x_{0}, \frac{r}{2}\right) \subseteq B\left(x_{0}, r\right)
$$

and

$$
I\left(m_{0}, \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \subseteq B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right) \subseteq I\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)
$$

It is easy to prove the following lemma and its proof is omitted.
Lemma 4.7. Suppose there exists a unique solution $x=x(m)$ in $x \in B\left(x_{0}, r\right)$ for $m \in B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$. If any $x \in \overline{\mathbf{U}} \backslash I\left(x_{0}, \frac{r}{2}\right)$ is not a solution for any $m \in I\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$, then there exists a unique solution $x=x(m)$ in $\mathbf{U}$ for $m \in B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$. If any $x \in \overline{\mathbf{U}} \backslash I\left(x_{0}, \frac{r}{2}\right)$ is not a solution for any $m \in I\left(m_{0}, \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$, then there exists a unique solution $x=x(m)$ in $\mathbf{U}$ for $m \in I\left(m_{0}, \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$.

To show that any $x \in \overline{\mathbf{U}} \backslash I\left(x_{0}, \frac{r}{2}\right)$ is not a solution for any $m \in I\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$, we first divide the interval $\overline{\mathbf{U}} \backslash I\left(x_{0}, \frac{r}{2}\right)$ into smaller ones $$ and then we check that at least one of $f_{i j}\left(, I\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)\right)$ doesn't contain zeros. We need to make sure that the union of $$ covers the whole region out of the position ball. This shows that the mass ball $B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$ is a uniqueness mass ball. In Example 4.6, $I\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)=\left[0.183460297345220,0.216539702654780\right] \times$ $\left[0.283460297345220,0.316539702654780\right] \times[0.383460297345220,0.416539702654780]$ and $I_{x_{0}}=\left[0,0.112229923080813\right] \times[0.268,1.733] \times \times[-1.733,-0.268]$ is one of the eight intervals in the closure of $\overline{\mathbf{U}} \backslash I\left(x_{0}, \frac{r}{2}\right)$. But the six functions $f_{i j}\left(I_{x_{0}}, I\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)\right)$ all contain zeros. We split the position interval $I_{x_{0}}$ into two subintervals by bisecting the longest sides and then check whether $f_{i j}$ contains zeros on the subintervals. Repeat the process until it proves that at least one of $f_{i j}$ doesn't contain zeros in the subintervals. By this way, it confirms that $B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$ is a uniqueness mass ball in $\mathbf{U}$.

Note that one may worry that there exists an $m$ in $B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$ near boundary whose solution $x$ is also near the boundary of $B\left(x_{0}, r\right)$. Then such $x$ falls in $\overline{\mathbf{U}} \backslash I\left(x_{0}, \frac{r}{2}\right)$. If such case exists, our method can not confirm the uniqueness of $B\left(m_{0}, r\right)$. But we can apply our method to a smaller mass intervals $I\left(m_{0}, \frac{\varepsilon}{N}\right) \subseteq B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$ for an appropriate $N \geq \sqrt{3}$ and prove $B\left(m_{0}, \frac{\varepsilon}{N}\right)$ is a uniqueness mass ball. Fortunately, this case doesn't occur in our program. All mass balls $B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$ in our program are uniqueness mass balls. To accelerate the numerical computations, we can produce the uniqueness mass interval $I\left(m_{0}, \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$ to cover the mass space by checking that at least one of $f_{i j}\left(, I\left(m_{0}, \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\right)$ doesn't contain zeros for all small intervals $$ out of the corresponding position ball.

# 5 Proof of the Theorem 1.1 

To prove the uniqueness of convex central configurations in Theorem 1.1, we create finite many uniqueness mass balls $B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$ so that the union of such balls can cover the whole mass space $[0.6,1]^{3}$. Here we describe the procedures to produce the uniqueness mass balls.

Step 1: Divide the mass space $[0.6,1]^{3}$ into a grid with equal side length $[0.6,1]$ for $M_{1}$ segments, such that $m_{i k}=0.6+\frac{0.4 k}{M_{1}}$ for $i=1,3,4$ and $k=0,1,2, \ldots, M_{1}$. The value of $M_{1}$ is determined based on experimental results. We choose $M_{1}=40$.

Step 2: For each $m_{0}=\left[m_{1 k_{1}}, 1, m_{3 k_{3}}, m_{4 k_{4}}\right]$ at a meshed grid point in Step 1, applying the algorithm (interval arithmetic computation and Krawczyk operator) in Section 3, we can prove there is a unique central configuration $x_{0}$. Now the proof of Theorem 2.4 is complete.

Step 3: For such central configuration $x_{0}$ for $m_{0}$, applying the implicit function theorem in Section 4, we can find a uniqueness mass ball $B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$, where $\varepsilon$ is a small positive number such that the central configuration is unique for all masses in the ball $B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$ as guaranteed by Theorem 4.4 and Lemma 4.7.

Step 4: Check whether the union of all the uniqueness balls covers the mass space $[0.6,1]^{3}$. This follows from the fact that the compact mass space $[0.6,1]^{3}$ can be covered by a finitely many uniqueness mass balls and the fact that we can refine our mesh points so that the uniqueness balls overlap ensuring that any mass point is in at least one uniqueness ball.

Therefore, by Step 2 and Step 3, there exists a unique central configuration for any mass point in the meshed space, and by Step 4, this uniqueness extends to the entire mass space $[0.6,1]^{3}$. Thus, Theorem 1.1 is proven.

Initially, set $M_{1}=5$. We find that the radius $\varepsilon$ of the uniqueness mass ball is between 0.0092119 and 0.016393 with an overall average radius about 0.01258436 . If the minimum of the radius of the uniqueness mass balls is $\varepsilon_{0}$, we can cover the whole mass space by choosing $M_{1}>\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{20 \varepsilon_{0}}$ since a uniqueness ball $B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon_{0}\right)$ contains an interval centered at $m_{0}$ with each side length $\frac{2 \sqrt{3} \varepsilon_{0}}{3}$. If $\varepsilon_{0}=0.009, M_{1}>38$. In our program, we use $M_{1}=40$ and totally 64000 uniqueness mass balls are computed to cover the whole mass space $[0.6,1]^{3}$. According to Lemma 4.7, our program confirms the uniqueness of the mass ball $B\left(m_{0}, \varepsilon\right)$ for each mass $m_{0}$ at the mesh grid in Step 1.

# 6 Conclusions and Remarks 

By combining the interval analysis and implicit function theorem, we give a computer assisted proof about the uniqueness of convex central configuration for any given mass vector $m \in[0.6,1]^{3}$ in a fixed order in the planar 4-body problem. This closed domain can be enlarged and improved further without modifying our method and program. So the conjecture is hopefully true for all masses except for those near the mass vector with one or more component being zeros.

However we find that it becomes more and more time consuming when we approach the boundary of the mass space because $\varepsilon$ becomes smaller and smaller. This suggests the potential singular behavior when we take the limit to the boundary of the mass space.

For example, let's consider the mass space $([0.1,1])^{3}$ and let $M_{1}=10$. We determine that the radius $\varepsilon$ of the uniqueness mass ball lies between 0.0001436 and 0.02125 , with an average radius of approximately 0.00998445 . By using the minimum radius $\varepsilon_{0}=0.0001436$, we can cover the entire mass space with $M_{1}>5428$ and a total number of uniqueness mass balls equal to approximately $1.6 \times 10^{11}$. It will take a rather long time to finish the computation using the current program, and it seems unpractical without further refinement of our current program.

Reflecting further on our methods, we find the following mathematical problems may be interesting. (1) Given a function $f$ on a closed domain $D \subset \mathbb{R}^{k}$, for each point $q \in D$, we can find an open ball $B\left(q, r_{q}\right)$ with radius depending on the point $q$ and some property of the function $f$ (e.g. the valid domain for implicit function theorem in the current paper). In such a way, we get an open covering of the compact set $D$, and in principle we can select a finite number of them to cover $D$. Now the question is whether one can find an optimal one as in sphere packing problem. Here we are deliberately vague to allow refinements and variations. (2) Even more interesting problem would be trying to refine and optimize the size of the valid domain for the implicit function theorem with or without the conditions about the second order derivatives of the mapping. There is very few literature concerning this fundamental topic, and we leave to future research.

Yet from this perspective we also notice the following interesting result establishing the conjecture about the uniqueness of the convex central configurations for masses $m_{1}, m_{3}, m_{4}$ in the following form near zeros in a given order.
Lemma 6.1. (, Theorem 2) Given $\mu_{i}>0(i=1,3,4)$, there exists $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ such that for $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0}$, the four masses $m=\left[\varepsilon \mu_{1}, 1, \varepsilon \mu_{3}, \varepsilon \mu_{4}\right]$ admit a unique convex central configuration for a given order.

Now we cannot merge the statement into our framework because $\varepsilon_{0}$ is theoretical and not given a concrete numerical value. Note also there are other possibilities to investigate for

masses approaching zero. It seems still a challenging problem even numerically to verify the conjecture.

The final remark is that even we can prove the conjecture with computer assistance, it is still desirable to have a conceptual/analytical proof.


# On Co-Circular Central Configurations in the Four and Five Body-Problems for Homogeneous Force Law 

#### Abstract

We study the central configurations (cc for short) for four masses arranged on a common circle (called co-circular cc) in two different situations, namely with no mass inside and later adding a fifth mass at the center of the circle. In the former, we focus the kite shape configurations by proving the existence of a one-parameter family of cc which goes from the kite containing an equilateral triangle up to the square shape. After, by putting a fifth mass at the center, we feature the planar cc of five bodies as a tensor of corange two see, "Albouy and Chenciner (Invent Math 131:151-184, 1998)" and we prove that cc is stacked see, "Hampton (Nonlinearity 18:2299-2304, 2005b)" in a such way that the center of mass of the four bodies should be the center of the circle. We emphasize that our approach includes not only the Newtonian force law, but the homogeneous ones with exponent $a \leq-1$.


# 1 Introduction 

It is known that, in the Newtonian $N$-body problem, the simplest possible motions are those whose configurations are invariant up to rotation and scaling, and where each body describes a Keplerian orbit. Only few special configurations of particles are allowed in these motions, the so called central configurations . More precisely, let $\mathbb{E}$ be a finite dimensional vector space, $\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{n} \in \mathbb{E}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{n}$ be $n$ positives numbers, $a$ be a negative real number, $M=\sum m_{i}$ be the total mass and $\mathbf{q}_{G}=\frac{1}{M} \sum m_{i} \mathbf{q}_{i}$ be the center of mass of these particles.
Definition 1 A configuration $\mathbf{q}=\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{N}\right) \in \mathbb{E}^{N}$ is a central configuration for the masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{n}$ if there exists a constant $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ such that

$$
\lambda\left(\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{G}\right)=\sum_{j \neq i} m_{j}\left\|\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right\|^{2 a}\left(\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right)
$$

for all $i=1 \ldots, n$. When $a=-3 / 2$ we have the Newtonian case and when $a=-1$ the vortex case.

Many questions have arisen about the set of central configurations, denoted $c c$ for short. So far, the main conjecture, still open, is the Chazy-Wintner-Smale conjecture: given $N$-positive masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$ interacting by the Newtonian potential, the set of equivalence classes of central configurations is finite. In the case $N=3$, the central configurations were completely classified by Euler  and Lagrange : for any choice of three positive masses there are only five distinct affine equivalence classes, two equilateral configurations and three collinear configurations. For $N=4$, the conjecture was proved first in the case of equal masses by Albouy in , and in the general case by Hampton and Moeckel in  with a proof based on symbolic and exact integer computations which were carried out by computer. For $N=5$ recent progress can be found in  and .

Another type of question is proving the existence of central configurations with a given geometric shape. In this direction, there are many works, e.g., $$. Our present paper is also included in this list. In fact, we propose to study central configurations of four masses on a circle in two distinct situations, namely, without and with a fifth mass located at the center of the circle, regardless of the negative value of the exponent $a \in(-\infty,-1]$.

We remark that in , the authors have considered the problem to describe all co-circular central configuration of the four body-problem. They carried out a thorough study of this type of cc, including our result, in which only the Newtonian case was considered. However, we emphasize that the present work deals with central configurations for homogeneous force laws. At this point it is important to justify why we take the exponent $a$ varying in the range $(-\infty,-1]$. Indeed, new phenomena can arise when considering other force laws that are not inversely proportional to the square of the distance as for example, a flat homographic solution of the three body-problem with force proportional to the cube of distance $(a=-2)$ that is not planar and which appear in the $\S 374$ bis of . Also, the number of planar cc of four equal masses which depends on the value of the exponent $a$ : for $a=-1 / 2$ and for a certain value $a^{*} \in(-3 / 2,-1)$ one has two planar cc, namely, the square and the equilateral triangle with a mass at the barycenter while for the Newtonian force law where $a=-3 / 2$, we have one more cc, the isosceles triangle with a mass on the axis of symmetry. In , Simó and Albouy conjectured that there is a unique central configuration of four equal mass with a given axis of symmetry and no other symmetry, for any $a$ in some interval containing the exponent $-3 / 2$.

We are going to proceed as follows: in Sect. 4, we put four points on a common circle by imposing that they form a central configuration and we deduce some geometric properties. In

the Sect. 5, we write the equations defining the kite-shape central configurations. After that, by setting the exponent $a=-1$ (vortex problem) in Sect. 5.1, we succeed in solving that system of equations explicitly. We obtain a one-parameter family of central configurations which goes from the kite with three masses at the vertices of an equilateral triangle (which is a central configuration of the restricted $3+1$ body-problem) up to the square with equal masses. In Sect. 5.2, for homogeneous force laws with $a<-1$, we prove the existence of that same parameterized family of cc, but in an implicit and global way. Finally in Sect. 6, we consider configurations of four masses on a common circle with a fifth mass located at its geometric center. By applying the results of Sect. 4, we shown that the central configurations with that shape are stacked so that the four bodies on the circle form a co-circular central configuration whose center of mass coincides with the center of the circle. In particular, if we take $a=-3 / 2$ (the Newtonian case) then, by , we have that the unique central configuration of this five body-problem is the square with four equal masses at the corners and an arbitrary mass at the center. Here, we decided to apply the tensorial approach presented in  aiming to introduce a new way of studying central configurations in the planar five body-problem. Hampton's paper  has motivated us to work with this tool.

# 2 General Aspects 

If we set $s_{i j}=\left\|\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right\|^{2}$ and replace $\mathbf{q}_{G}$ by its expression, the Eq. (1.1) becomes

$$
\sum_{j \neq i} m_{j} S_{i j}\left(\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right)=0
$$

where $S_{i j}=-s_{i j}^{a}+\lambda / M$. The constant $\lambda$ corresponds to the Lagrange multiplier in the variational point of view and one can show that it is positive for any central configuration as defined above in (1).

We will work with the tensorial viewpoint in a attempt to obtain an alternative description for central configurations of the planar five body-problem. This will be important later in Sect. 6. Further details of the tensorial approach are found in . For brevity, we will state only the main properties of central configurations that arise from this approach and that will be used in the proof of our results.

In this context, a relative configuration of $n$ points, up to rigid movements, in general position in a vector space $\mathbb{E}$ of dimension $d$ will be a positive tensor $\beta \in \mathcal{D} \vee \mathcal{D}$ of range $d$ where $\mathcal{D}=\mathbb{R}^{n} /\langle(1, \ldots, 1)\rangle$. If $\mathbf{q}_{i}=\left(q_{i 1}, q_{i 2}, \ldots, q_{i d}\right)$ then we write $\beta$ as

$$
\beta=\mathrm{X}_{1} \otimes \mathrm{X}_{1}+\mathrm{X}_{2} \otimes \mathrm{X}_{2}+\cdots+\mathrm{X}_{d} \otimes \mathrm{X}_{d}
$$

where $\mathrm{X}_{j}=\left(q_{1 j}, \ldots, q_{n j}\right) \in \mathcal{D}$ is the class of vector whose coordinates are the $n$ projections of the configuration on the $j$ axis in the space $\mathbb{E}$, and the set $\left\{\mathrm{X}_{1}, \ldots, \mathrm{X}_{d}\right\}$ is linearly independent in $\mathcal{D}$.

It is not difficult to see that $\beta$ admits the following decomposition

$$
\beta=-\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i<j} s_{i j}\left(\mathbf{e}_{i} \otimes \mathbf{e}_{j}+\mathbf{e}_{j} \otimes \mathbf{e}_{i}\right)
$$

where $\mathbf{e}_{i}$ is the class of the canonical vector $\mathbf{e}_{i}=(0, \ldots, 1, \ldots, 0)$ of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The tensor $\beta$ is interpreted as a positive symmetric bilinear form of range $d$ on the dual space $\mathcal{D}^{*}=\{\mathbf{x} \in$ $\left.\mathbb{R}^{n} / \sum x_{i}=0\right\}$ and as such, it has a matrix representation as follows

$$
\beta=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
0 & s_{12} & \cdots & s_{1 n} \\
s_{12} & 0 & \cdots & s_{2 n} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
s_{1 n} & s_{2 n} & \cdots & 0
\end{array}\right)
$$

This representation takes into account the identification

$$
\operatorname{Bil}\left(\mathcal{D}^{*}\right)=\operatorname{Bil}\left(\mathbb{R}^{n}\right) /\left\{\left(x_{i}+y_{j}\right)_{n \times n}\right\}
$$

The set of positive symmetric bilinear forms of range $d$ on $\mathcal{D}^{*}$ is a differentiable manifold and it will be denoted here by $(\mathcal{D} \vee \mathcal{D})_{+, d}$. Details of this geometric model are explained in either  or .

Now let $\Phi(s)=\frac{\lambda}{M} s-\frac{1}{a+1} s^{a+1}$ be a primitive of the function $\varphi(s)=-s_{i j}^{a}+\frac{\lambda}{M}$ and consider the function $g:(\mathcal{D} \vee \mathcal{D})_{+, d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ defined by the rule

$$
g(\beta)=\sum_{i<j} m_{i} m_{j} \Phi\left(s_{i j}\right)
$$

As stated in , we give the definition of relative central configuration
Definition 2 A relative central configuration of dimension $d$ for the masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{n}$ is a positive tensor $\beta \in(\mathcal{D} \vee \mathcal{D})_{+, d}$ such that

$$
\beta \circ d g(\beta)=0 \in \mathcal{D} \otimes \mathcal{D}^{*}
$$

where the symbol $\circ$ denotes the contraction of tensors.
The connection between the tensorial Eq. (2.3) and the usual definition of $c c$ becomes clear when we see (2.1) as a product of matrices $\mathbf{X} \cdot A=0$ where $\mathbf{X}$ is a $d \times n$ configuration matrix whose columns are the position vectors $\mathbf{q}_{i}$ and $A$ is the $n \times n$ matrix with entries:

$$
A_{i j}=m_{i} S_{i j} \quad(i \neq j) \quad A_{j j}=-\sum_{i \neq j} A_{i j}
$$

Multiplying on the left $\mathbf{X} \cdot A=0$ by $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}$ and using that the columns of $A$ are in $\mathcal{D}^{*}$, we obtain the matrix form of Eq. (2.3). See  for details.

By calling the differential $d g(\beta)=\alpha$ we have that

$$
\alpha=\sum_{i<j} \frac{\partial g}{\partial s_{i j}} d s_{i j}=\sum_{i<j} m_{i} m_{j} \varphi\left(s_{i j}\right) \xi_{i j} \otimes \xi_{i j}
$$

where $\xi_{i j}=\mathbf{e}_{i}-\mathbf{e}_{j} \in \mathcal{D}^{*}$.
At this point, some remarks should be placed
Remark 1 The tensor $\alpha$ is a symmetric bilinear form on the quotient space $\mathcal{D}$ and if we denote its range by $r$ then, the Eq. (2.3) gives us an important estimative

$$
d+r \leq n-1
$$

Sometimes we call the range of $\alpha$ as the co-range of $\beta$.
Remark 2 The set $\left\{\xi_{i j} \otimes \xi_{i j}\right\}_{1 \leq i<j \leq n}$ is a basis of the linear space $\mathcal{D}^{*} \vee \mathcal{D}^{*}$ and so, $\alpha=0$ if, and only if, $\varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)=0$ for all pair $(i, j)$, that is,

$$
s_{i j}=s_{0}=\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}\right)^{1 / a}
$$

The configuration of $n$ points in which the mutual distances $s_{i j}$ are all equal has dimension $n-1$ and generalizes Lagrange (equilateral triangle) for three bodies and Lehmann-Filhès (regular tetrahedron) for four bodies. This central configuration will be denoted by

$$
\beta_{0}=-\frac{s_{0}}{2} \sum_{i<j}\left(\mathbf{e}_{i} \otimes \mathbf{e}_{j}+\mathbf{e}_{j} \otimes \mathbf{e}_{i}\right)
$$

Remark 3 In , Albouy proved that a relative central configuration must satisfy the radial minimization estimate

$$
\left\langle\beta_{0}, \alpha\right\rangle<0
$$

# 3 Dziobek's Configurations 

Let $\beta$ be a relative central configuration of the $n$ body-problem.
Definition 3 We call $\beta$ a Dziobek configuration if it has corange one.
Thus, taking into account that $\alpha=d g(\beta)$ is a symmetric tensor and has range one, the relative configuration $\beta$ is a Dziobek configuration if, and only if, there is a real number $\eta \neq 0$ and a non null vector $\Delta \in \mathcal{D}^{*}$ such that

$$
\alpha=\eta \Delta \otimes \Delta
$$

By following , this identity and the radial minimization estimate in (2.5) imply that $\eta<0$ and we can take it as being $\eta=-1$ to normalize the vector $\Delta$ up to multiples.

After some computations in the tensorial notation (see ), one sees that the definition (3) can be rewritten by saying that a relative central configuration $\beta$ for the masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{n}$ is Dziobek iff there exists a non-null vector $\Delta \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{k \neq i} s_{i k} \Delta_{k}=\sum_{k \neq j} s_{j k} \Delta_{k} \\
& \sum_{k=1}^{n} \Delta_{k}=0 \\
& -s_{i j}^{a}+\frac{\lambda}{M}=\frac{\Delta_{i}}{m_{i}} \frac{\Delta_{j}}{m_{j}}, \quad 1 \leq i<j \leq n
\end{aligned}
$$

The range of a Dziobek configuration satisfies ${ }^{1} \operatorname{rg}(\beta) \leq n-2$. It is proved in , that if $\beta$ is a central configuration of dimension exactly $n-2$, then $\beta$ is a Dziobek configuration. Moreover, the vector $\Delta$ in Eqs. (3.1) and (3.2) is unique, up to a factor, and the normalization of $\eta$ makes it unique up to orientation. The uniqueness implies that the $\Delta$ 's coordinates are proportional to the oriented areas (or volumes) of the simplex of $n-1$ vertices. For example, $\left|\Delta_{1}\right|$ is proportional to the area (or volume) of the simplex given by the vertices $\left(q_{2}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$, and so on.

Remark 4 In terms of the Dziobek approach, it is clear that the set of variables $\left\{\ldots, \Delta_{j}, \ldots\right.$, $\left.s_{i j}, \ldots\right\}$ solves the system (3.1)-(3.3) with multiplier $\lambda$ if and only if, for any $c \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$, the set $\left(\ldots, \sqrt{c} \Delta_{j}, \ldots, c^{1 / a} s_{i j}, \ldots\right)$ also solves the same system with multiplier $c \lambda$. So, fixing the
multiplier $\lambda$ corresponds to choosing a unique central configuration in the class of homothety. In what follows, we will take $\lambda=1$ with the aim to eliminate the invariance by homotheties and we will normalize the total mass by taking $M=1$.

# 4 Central Configurations for Four Bodies on a Circle 

In this section, we will consider a central configuration of four bodies with the masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}$ and $m_{4}$ arranged on a common circle and derive some geometric properties, which will be important later. In this case, we have four non collinear points in the plane that makes the configuration to have dimension exactly two and puts us in position to apply the Dziobek approach [Eqs. (3.1)-(3.3)]. An interesting question raised by Albouy and cited in  asks: to characterize all the four-body central configurations which lie on a common circle. In the next section, we will go exactly on this direction, aiming to get a complete description about a particular symmetric central configuration of four bodies on a common circle for any gravitational potential, not only for the Newtonian one.

We proceed as follows: by supposing that the points $\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{4}$ satisfy the Eqs. (3.1)(3.3), which is a system of ten equations, ten variables and four parameters, we impose the configuration to be co-circular. This is equivalent to making $t_{i}=\sum_{k \neq i} s_{i k} \Delta_{k}=0$ for all $i$ (it is not difficult to prove this fact) and so, we get another equation while one of the masses becomes dependent variable. Initially, we take $m_{4}$ in order to be this new variable so that we must solve a system of 11 equations, 11 variables $\left(s_{12}, s_{13}, \ldots, s_{34}, \Delta_{1}, \ldots, \Delta_{4}, m_{4}\right)$ and three parameters $\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}\right)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& t_{i}=\sum_{k \neq i} s_{i k} \Delta_{k}=0, \quad i=1, \ldots, 4 \\
& \sum_{j=1}^{4} \Delta_{j}=0 \\
& -s_{i j}^{a}+1=\frac{\Delta_{i} \Delta_{j}}{m_{i} m_{j}}, \quad 1 \leq i<j \leq 4
\end{aligned}
$$

which correspond to the equations defining the central configurations of the co-circular four body-problem with multiplier $\lambda=1$.

A very intuitive result about co-circular central configurations of four points states the following

Lemma 1 Let $\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{4}\right)$ be a co-circular central configuration of the four body-problem whose diagonals of the polygon are the segments $\left[\mathbf{q}_{1} \mathbf{q}_{2}\right]$ and $\left[\mathbf{q}_{3} \mathbf{q}_{4}\right]$. Let $R$ be the radius of the circle. Then
(a) the center of the circle is in the interior of the convex hull of the four co-circular points.
(b) at least one of the sides must be greater than $\sqrt{2} R$.

Proof Any co-circular configuration is strictly convex and we can label the four points so that the following distribution of signals holds

$$
\Delta_{3}, \Delta_{4}<0<\Delta_{1}, \Delta_{2}
$$

Also, $\Delta_{1}, \Delta_{2}, \Delta_{3}$ and $\Delta_{4}$ correspond to the oriented areas of the triangles (234), (431), (124) and (321), respectively.

The configuration is assumed to be central, so that, by the Eq. (4.3) and inequalities (4.4) one has

$$
\varphi\left(s_{13}\right), \varphi\left(s_{23}\right), \varphi\left(s_{24}\right), \varphi\left(s_{14}\right)<0<\varphi\left(s_{12}\right), \varphi\left(s_{34}\right)
$$

and since $\varphi(s)=-s^{a}+1$ is a increasing function one has

$$
s_{13}, s_{23}, s_{24}, s_{14}<1<s_{12}, s_{34}
$$

In order to prove item (a), we suppose that the center of the circle is not in the interior of the convex hull of the four points. Then, without loss of generality, we can apply a rotation on the configuration so that

$$
q_{1}=(R, 0) \quad \text { and } \quad q_{i}=\left(x_{i}, y_{i}\right)
$$

where $y_{i} \geq 0$ and $-R \leq x_{i}<R, \forall i=2,3,4$. Let's write the determinants $\Delta_{i}$ as

$$
\Delta_{2}=\left|\begin{array}{lll}
1 & 1 & 1 \\
x_{4} & x_{3} & R \\
y_{4} & y_{3} & 0
\end{array}\right| \quad \Delta_{3}=\left|\begin{array}{lll}
1 & 1 & 1 \\
R & x_{2} & x_{4} \\
0 & y_{2} & y_{4}
\end{array}\right| \quad \Delta_{4}=\left|\begin{array}{lll}
1 & 1 & 1 \\
x_{3} & x_{2} & R \\
y_{3} & y_{2} & 0
\end{array}\right|
$$

Once $\Delta_{2}>0$, we have that

$$
y_{4}\left(R-x_{3}\right)>y_{3}\left(R-x_{4}\right)
$$

and since both sides are non negative, we have

$$
y_{4}^{2}\left(R-x_{3}\right)^{2}>y_{3}^{2}\left(R-x_{4}\right)^{2}
$$

For all $i=1, \ldots, 4$ we have satisfied the equations $y_{i}^{2}=R^{2}-x_{i}^{2}$. After replacing $y_{i}$ and canceling the terms $R-x_{i}$, we get

$$
\left(R+x_{4}\right)\left(R-x_{3}\right)>\left(R+x_{3}\right)\left(R-x_{4}\right)
$$

which leads us to

$$
\frac{R+x_{4}}{R-x_{4}}>\frac{R+x_{3}}{R-x_{3}} \Rightarrow x_{4}>x_{3}
$$

Likewise, the inequalities $\Delta_{3}<0$ and $\Delta_{4}<0$ show that

$$
-R \leq x_{3}<x_{2}<x_{4}<x_{1}=R
$$

from where it follows that

$$
0<s_{14}<s_{12}<s_{13} \leq 4 R^{2}
$$

But, $s_{12}<s_{13}$ contradicts (4.5) and the configuration could not be central. Thus, for a co-circular central configuration, the center of the circle is in the interior of the convex hull.

The proof of item (b) is as follows. The sides of the polygon $\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{4}\right)$ are the bases of isosceles triangles whose equal sides correspond to the radius $R$. By assertion a, the respective angles $\alpha_{i j}$ of each triangle are in the interval $(0, \pi)$ and their sum is worth $2 \pi$. Note that $\alpha_{i j}$ satisfy (see Fig. 1)

$$
\sin \frac{\alpha_{i j}}{2}=\frac{r_{i j}}{2 R}, \quad\left(r_{i j}=\left\|\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right\|\right)
$$

If all of the lengths $r_{i j}<\sqrt{2} R$, then

$$
0<\sin \frac{\alpha_{i j}}{2}<\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \Rightarrow 0<\alpha_{i j}<\frac{\pi}{2}
$$

Fig. 1 Proof of Lemma 1


In this case, the sum of all angles would be less than $2 \pi$ which is a contradiction. The assertion (b) is proved.

Remark 5 A consequence of the above lemma (item b), is that in a co-circular central configuration of four bodies, we should have

$$
\varphi\left(R^{2}\right)<\varphi\left(2 R^{2}\right)<\varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)<0
$$

for some pair of indices.

# 5 Co-Circular Kite Central Configurations 

From now on, we will consider kite-shape central configurations which are not a square. According to the main result in , for any value of $a<0$, this type of symmetry is characterized by the constraints

$$
\Delta_{3}<\Delta_{4}<0<\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{2}
$$

or equivalently, by $m_{1}=m_{2}$ and $m_{3}<m_{4}$.
Let four co-circular points $\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \mathbf{q}_{2}, \mathbf{q}_{3}, \mathbf{q}_{4}\right)$ form a kite configuration where the segments $\left[\mathbf{q}_{1} \mathbf{q}_{2}\right]$ and $\left[\mathbf{q}_{3} \mathbf{q}_{4}\right]$ are the diagonals. Let $s_{13}=s_{23}=x, s_{14}=s_{24}=y, s_{34}=d$ and $s_{12}=l$ be the square of the mutual distances (see Fig. 2).

The Eqs. (4.1) and (4.2) become

$$
\begin{aligned}
& t_{1}=l \Delta_{2}+x \Delta_{3}+y \Delta_{4}=0 \\
& t_{2}=l \Delta_{1}+x \Delta_{3}+y \Delta_{4}=0 \\
& t_{3}=2 x \Delta_{1}+d \Delta_{4}=0 \\
& t_{4}=2 y \Delta_{1}+d \Delta_{3}=0 \\
& 2 \Delta_{1}+\Delta_{3}+\Delta_{4}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

By adding $t_{3}$ and $t_{4}$, we have that $d=x+y$. From $t_{3}=0$ and $t_{4}=0$, we isolate $\Delta_{3}$ and $\Delta_{4}$ to insert them into $t_{1}=0$. So, we obtain

$$
d l=4 x y
$$

Moreover, $\Delta_{3}<\Delta_{4}<0$ implies that $x<y$.

Fig. 2 Kite-shape configuration


It's easy to verify that the Eqs. (5.3)-(5.6) are equivalent to the system

$$
\begin{aligned}
d & =x+y \\
d l & =4 x y \\
\frac{\Delta_{3}}{\Delta_{1}} & =-\frac{l}{2 x} \\
\frac{\Delta_{4}}{\Delta_{1}} & =-\frac{l}{2 y}
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $d(d-l)=(x-y)^{2}>0$, so $d>l$ as shown in Fig. 2.
Now, we consider the increasing function $\varphi: \mathbb{R}_{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ given by

$$
\varphi(s)=1-s^{a} \quad(a \leq-1)
$$

and remember that a Dziobek configuration $\left(s_{12}, \ldots, s_{34}, \Delta_{1}, \ldots, \Delta_{4}\right)$ is central, if and only if,

$$
m_{i} m_{j} \varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)=\Delta_{i} \Delta_{j} \quad \text { for any } i, j
$$

By imposing that the kite configuration be central and making $m_{1}=m_{2}$, we obtain the following relations

$$
\begin{aligned}
\varphi(l) & =\frac{\Delta_{1}^{2}}{m_{1}^{2}} \\
\varphi(x) & =\frac{\Delta_{1} \Delta_{3}}{m_{1} m_{3}} \\
\varphi(y) & =\frac{\Delta_{1} \Delta_{4}}{m_{1} m_{4}} \\
\varphi(d) & =\frac{\Delta_{3} \Delta_{4}}{m_{3} m_{4}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Remark 6 According to the signs of the $\Delta_{i}$ 's in (5.1), the Eqs. (5.12)-(5.15) together with the monotonicity of $\varphi$ provide the inequalities

$$
\varphi(x)<\varphi(y)<0<\varphi(l)<\varphi(d)
$$

and consequently,

$$
0<x<y<s_{0}<l<d
$$

where $s_{0}=1$ is the unique root of $\varphi$.
Once the variables $\Delta_{i}$ can not assume the value zero, we can make the ratios between the Eqs. (5.12)-(5.15) and we apply the relations (5.8)-(5.11) to simplify them. Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\varphi(x)}{\varphi(l)}=-\frac{m_{1}}{m_{3}} \frac{l}{2 x} \\
& \frac{\varphi(y)}{\varphi(l)}=-\frac{m_{1}}{m_{4}} \frac{l}{2 y} \\
& \frac{\varphi(x)}{\varphi(y)}=\frac{m_{4}}{m_{3}} \frac{y}{x} \\
& \frac{\varphi(d)}{\varphi(l)}=\frac{m_{1}^{2}}{m_{3} m_{4}} \frac{l}{d}
\end{aligned}
$$

The above system suggests the introduction of the function $f: \mathbb{R}_{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, f(s)=s \varphi(s)$ whose derivative is $f^{\prime}(s)=1-(1+a) s^{a} \geq 1$ for $a \leq-1$. After defining the relative masses $m_{3}^{\prime}=m_{3} / m_{1}$ and $m_{4}^{\prime}=m_{4} / m_{1}$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 m_{3}^{\prime} f(x)+f(l) & =0 \\
2 m_{4}^{\prime} f(y)+f(l) & =0 \\
m_{3}^{\prime} f(x)-m_{4}^{\prime} f(y) & =0 \\
m_{3}^{\prime} m_{4}^{\prime} f(d)-f(l) & =0
\end{aligned}
$$

where one sees that the Eqs. (5.17)-(5.19) are linearly dependent. By substituting $f(l)=$ $m_{3}^{\prime} m_{4}^{\prime} f(d)$ into (5.17) and combining it with (5.18) by eliminating $m_{4}^{\prime}$, we arrive to the following system

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 4 f(x) f(y)-f(l) f(d)=0 \\
& m_{3}^{\prime} f(x)-m_{4}^{\prime} f(y)=0 \\
& m_{3}^{\prime} m_{4}^{\prime} f(d)-f(l)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

which, together with (5.8) and (5.9), define the kite-shape central configurations on a circle.
Remark 7 By (5.16) and (5.23) and since $f$ is increasing, we have that the product $m_{3}^{\prime} m_{4}^{\prime}<1$. By the same argument, we should have that $\frac{m_{3}^{\prime}}{m_{4}^{\prime}}<1$ from (5.22). In what follows, let's insert two new parameters $p=m_{3}^{\prime} m_{4}^{\prime}$ and $q=\frac{m_{3}^{\prime}}{m_{4}^{\prime}}$, where both of them are in the open interval $(0,1)$.

# 5.1 Applications to the Vortex Problem, i.e., $a=-1$ 

In this case, the solution of (5.21)-(5.23) can be obtained explicitly. In fact, if $a=-1$, the function $f$ assumes the form $f(s)=s-1$ and the system (5.21)-(5.23) becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 3 x^{2}+2 x y+3 y^{2}-3 x-3 y=0 \\
& q x-q-y+1=0 \\
& p x^{2}+2(p-2) x y+p y^{2}+(1-p) x+(1-p) y=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, in order to find the common solutions of (5.24)-(5.26), we calculate the resultant of the two polynomials (5.24) and (5.26) with respect to the variable $y$. We obtain

$$
\operatorname{Res}=4 x^{2}\left[4(3-p)^{2} x^{2}-4(3-p)(4-p) x+3(4-p)\right]
$$

The positive zeroes of Res

$$
x^{\prime}=\frac{4-p-\sqrt{(1-p)(4-p)}}{2(3-p)} \text { and } x^{\prime \prime}=\frac{4-p+\sqrt{(1-p)(4-p)}}{2(3-p)}
$$

correspond to the values of $x$ for which the above system has a solution. By symmetry, the other solution of (5.24) and (5.26) is the pair $\left(x^{\prime \prime}, x^{\prime}\right)$. As $x<y$ we should take $x=x x^{\prime}$ and $y=x^{\prime \prime}$. By inserting these expressions into (5.25), we get

$$
q=\frac{2-p-\sqrt{(1-p)(4-p)}}{2-p+\sqrt{(1-p)(4-p)}}
$$

Thus, we have the complete solution of the system (5.21)-(5.23) parameterized by $p \in(0,1)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
x & =\frac{4-p-\sqrt{(1-p)(4-p)}}{2(3-p)} \\
y & =\frac{4-p+\sqrt{(1-p)(4-p)}}{2(3-p)} \\
d & =\frac{4-p}{3-p}, \quad l=\frac{3}{3-p} \\
m_{3}^{\prime}=\sqrt{p q} & =2-p-\sqrt{(1-p)(4-p)} \\
m_{4}^{\prime}=\sqrt{\frac{p}{q}} & =2-p+\sqrt{(1-p)(4-p)} \\
M=1 \Rightarrow & \frac{1}{m_{1}}=2+m_{3}^{\prime}+m_{4}^{\prime}=2(3-p) \\
\Rightarrow \quad m_{1} & =\frac{1}{2(3-p)} \\
m_{3} & =\frac{2-p-\sqrt{(1-p)(4-p)}}{2(3-p)} \\
m_{4} & =\frac{2-p+\sqrt{(1-p)(4-p)}}{2(3-p)}
\end{aligned}
$$

In Fig. 3 we present the evolution of the co-circular kites in the vortex problem according the parameter $p \in$.

This way, we have proved the following result



Fig. 3 Evolution of the co-circular kites in the vortex problem according the parameter $p \in$

Theorem 2 In the vortex four body-problem, there is a unique one-parameter family of kite shape co-circular central configurations described by the expressions (5.27)-(5.32).

Remark 8 The Newtonian case, i.e., $a=-3 / 2$, is not so friendly, for it produces polynomials of very higher degrees. Nevertheless, this case will be considered below.

# 5.2 Applications to Homogeneous Force Law 

Here, we consider $m_{3}^{\prime}$ and $m_{4}^{\prime}$ as variables to be obtained from (5.22)-(5.23) and we work with the system

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 4 f(x) f(y)-f(l) f(d)=0 \\
& d=x+y \\
& l=\frac{4 x y}{x+y}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(s)=s-s^{a+1}$ with $a<-1$. Note that the equation

$$
F(x, y)=4 f(x) f(y)-f\left(\frac{4 x y}{x+y}\right) f(x+y)=0
$$

is symmetric with respect to $x$ and $y$ which means that the trace of the zero level curve of $F$ is symmetric about the line $y=x$.

The domain of equation $F=0$ will be given by the restrictions in (5.16). There, we have that $0<x<y<1$, but by symmetry, we will leave $(x, y) \in \times$. Easily, one verifies three trivial solutions of $F(x, y)=0$ which are

$$
A=(1 / 3,1), \quad B=\left(\left(\frac{2}{1+2^{a}}\right)^{1 / a},\left(\frac{2}{1+2^{a}}\right)^{1 / a}\right) \quad C=(1,1 / 3)
$$

The point $B$ corresponds to the square configuration and the points $A$ and $C$ represent the kite with an equilateral triangle.

Fig. 4 Region $\Omega$ : the branch of hyperbola is the graph of $4 x y-x-y=0(l=1)$


The three points $A, B$ and $C$ lie in the square $[1 / 3,1] \times[1 / 3,1]$. For $0<x<1 / 3$ we have that $l=\frac{4 x y}{x+y}<1$ for any $y \in$. This would give us $f(l)<0$ and the configuration would not be central according to (5.12). Likewise, we will disregard the range $0<y<1 / 3$.

Once that $1 \leq \frac{4 x y}{x+y}$, we will take the region (see Fig. 4)

$$
\Omega=\left\{(x, y) \in\left[\frac{1}{3}, 1\right] \times\left[\frac{1}{3}, 1\right] / x+y \leq 4 x y\right\}
$$

as the domain of $F$ and we will show that $F(x, y)=0$ defines a decreasing curve in $\Omega$ passing through the points $A, B$ and $C$, regardless of the value of the exponent $a<-1$.

Proposition 1 For any $x \in[1 / 3,1]$ there exists a unique $y \in[1 / 3,1]$ such that $F(x, y)=0$.
Proof Remember that $f^{\prime}(s) \geq 1, \forall s>0$ and that $f(x) \leq 0$ and $f(d), f(l) \geq 0$ on $\Omega$. The partial derivative of $F$ with respect to $y$ is

$$
\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=4 f^{\prime}(y) f(x)-f^{\prime}(l) f(x+y) \frac{4 x^{2}}{d^{2}}-f(l) f^{\prime}(d)
$$

and then

$$
\frac{\partial F}{\partial y} \leq 4 f(x)-f(d) \frac{4 x^{2}}{d^{2}}-f(l) \leq 0
$$

so $\partial_{y} F=0$, if and only if,

$$
f(x)=f(d)=f(l)=0 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad x=d=l=1
$$

which is impossible. Thus, we have that $\partial_{y} F$ is a strictly negative continuous function on $\Omega$.
Given $x^{*} \in(1 / 3,1)$, let $y^{*} \in(1 / 3,1)$ be the unique ordinate such that $\left(x^{*}, y^{*}\right)$ is on the curve $l=1$. We have the following behavior of the function $h(y)=F\left(x^{*}, y\right)$ on the segment of the vertical line $x=x^{*}$ which goes from the curve $l=1$ up to the horizontal line $y=1$ :

- $h^{\prime}(y)=\partial_{y} F\left(x^{*}, y\right)<0$, i.e., $h$ is a strictly decreasing function

- $h\left(y^{*}\right)=F\left(x^{*}, y^{*}\right)=4 f\left(x^{*}\right) f\left(y^{*}\right)>0$
- $h(1)=F\left(x^{*}, 1\right)=-f\left(x^{*}+1\right) f\left(\frac{4 x^{*}}{x^{*}+1}\right)<0$.

By the continuity of $F$ on the region $\Omega$, we have that there is $y=\xi\left(x^{*}\right) \in\left(y^{*}, 1\right)$ such that $F\left(x^{*}, \xi\left(x^{*}\right)\right)=0$. The monotonicity of $h$ guarantees the uniqueness.

Naturally, the graph of the function $\xi:[1 / 3,1] \rightarrow[1 / 3,1]$ passes through the points $A, B$ and $C$ and since

$$
\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}(x, \xi(x)) \neq 0
$$

for all $x \in[1 / 3,1]$, the Implicit Function Theorem ensures that $\xi$ is differentiable. Furthermore, its derivative

$$
\xi^{\prime}(x)=-\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}\right)^{-1} \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}
$$

is negative and this lead us to conclude the following theorem.
Theorem 3 For any value of the exponent $a<-1$, there is a unique one-parameter family of kite shape co-circular central configurations of the four body-problem implicitly described by the Eq. (5.36) which goes from the kite with an equilateral triangle up to the square.

Remark 9 The Eqs. (5.22) and (5.23) give the following expressions for $q$ and $p$

$$
q(x)=\frac{f(\xi(x))}{f(x)}, \quad p(x)=\frac{f(l(x))}{f(x+\xi(x))}
$$

which are defined for $x \in[1 / 3,1]$.
In Fig. 5, we describe the behavior of $\xi$ for the Newtonian case.

Fig. 5 The concave curve is the graph of $\xi$ for $a=-3 / 2$. The points $A$ and $C$ are the extreme points on this curve. The point $B$ is its intersection with the bisectrix $y=x$


Remark 10 In the Ref. , the Newtonian case is considered and all the co-circular central configurations are determined. Using mutual distances as coordinates, it is shown that the set of co-circular central configurations with positive masses is a two-dimensional surface parameterized by two of the exterior side-lengths. Two symmetric families, the kite and isosceles trapezoid, are investigated extensively.

# 6 Co-Circular Central Configurations of Four Bodies with a Fifth Mass at the Center 

In this section, we consider a configuration of five bodies with the following shape: four masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}, m_{4}$ lying on a common circle and a fifth body with mass $m$ at the center of that circle (see Fig. 6). We will refer to this type of configuration as a co-circular (4,1)-configuration. By following A. Chenciner (see ), we raise the question: what are the co-circular (4,1)-central configurations? Again, let $M$ be the total mass of the system and whenever a tilde accent is used in the notation, we will be referring to the co-circular four-body configuration, e.g, $\tilde{M}=M-m$ and $\tilde{\beta}$ is the relative configuration of the four co-circular masses on the circle.

We will apply the tensorial approach presented in Sect. 2. In this context, the tensor $\beta$ has range 2 and by Remark 1, the differential $\alpha=d g(\beta)$ must have $\operatorname{rg} \alpha \leq 2$. This allows us to write

$$
\alpha=a Z_{1} \otimes Z_{1}+b Z_{2} \otimes Z_{2}, \quad Z_{1}, Z_{2} \in \mathcal{D}^{*}
$$

where either $a<0$ or $b<0$ by virtue of radial minimization (Remark 3). Without loss of generality, suppose that $a<0$ and consider the vector $Z_{1}$ factoring by $a=-(\sqrt{|a|})^{2}$, so that

$$
\alpha=-Z_{1} \otimes Z_{1}+b Z_{2} \otimes Z_{2}
$$

The two vectors $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are assumed to be linearly independent. By supposing that $\beta$ is a relative central configuration-what will be done from now on-by Definition 2, we must have that

$$
\beta \circ \alpha=-\left(\beta \circ Z_{1}\right) \otimes Z_{1}+b\left(\beta \circ Z_{2}\right) \otimes Z_{2}=0
$$

i.e., the contractions $Z_{1} \circ \beta$ and $Z_{2} \circ \beta$ should be zero in $\mathcal{D}$.

Fig. 6 Co-circular
$(4,1)$-configuration


Lemma $4 b \neq 0$.
Proof In fact, if $\alpha=-Z \otimes Z$ for some $Z=\left(z_{0}, z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}, z_{4}\right) \in \mathcal{D}^{*}$, then

$$
\alpha_{i j}=m_{i} m_{j} \varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)=z_{i} z_{j}
$$

By assuming that $z_{0} \neq 0$, we would have for any $j=1, \ldots, 4$,

$$
\frac{z_{j}}{m_{j}}=\varphi\left(R^{2}\right) \frac{m}{z_{0}}=k(\text { constant })
$$

so that, for $i \neq 0 \neq j$

$$
\varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)=\frac{z_{i} z_{j}}{m_{i} m_{j}}=k^{2} \Rightarrow s_{i j}=\text { constant }
$$

and this would imply that the four-body configuration $\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{4}\right)$ is spatial, which is a contradiction. So, we must have $z_{0}=0$ and $\varphi\left(R^{2}\right)=0$

$$
R^{2 a}=\frac{\lambda}{M} \Rightarrow \varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)=-s_{i j}^{a}+\rho^{a} . \quad\left(\rho=R^{2}\right)
$$

On the other hand, the nullity of the contraction $Z \circ \beta$ gives us that

$$
\sum_{j \neq 0, i} s_{i j} z_{j}=-2 z_{0} R^{2}=0, \quad \forall i=1, \ldots, 4
$$

This system together with the Eq. (6.1) for $i \neq 0 \neq j$ show that the four bodies $\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{4}\right)$ form a co-circular central configuration (see Sect. 4). By Lemma 1, one of the sides of the polygon must be greater than $\sqrt{2} R$ and so, one of the mutual distances $s_{13}, s_{14}, s_{23}, s_{24}$ must be greater than $2 \rho$. This implies that

$$
\varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)>0
$$

for some pair $(i, j)$ which corresponds to some side of the polygon. This is absurd, since according to estimates in the proof of Lemma 1, convex central configurations of the fourbody problem must have $\varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)<0$ for all external sides.

This way, we have shown that $b$ is not zero.
By Lemma 4, we can write

$$
\alpha=-Z_{1} \otimes Z_{1}+\sigma Z_{2} \otimes Z_{2}
$$

where $\sigma= \pm 1$ and the vectors $Z_{1}, Z_{2} \in \mathcal{D}^{*}$ are linearly independent.
In order to characterize the co-circular (4, 1)-central configurations, we will need a further constraint on the vectors $Z_{j}$. By writing

$$
Z_{1}=(\xi, \ldots) \quad \text { and } \quad Z_{2}=(\eta, \ldots)
$$

we have:
Lemma 5 If $\sigma=1$ then $|\xi| \neq|\eta|$.
Proof Firstly, $\xi$ and $\eta$ can not be simultaneously null, for in this case, we would have

$$
\tilde{\beta} \circ \tilde{Z}_{1}=\tilde{\beta} \circ \tilde{Z}_{2}=0
$$

That is, the two linearly independent vectors $\tilde{Z}_{1}$ and $\tilde{Z}_{2}$ would be in a 1D vector space, namely, $\operatorname{ker}\{\tilde{\beta}\}$.

Suppose that $\eta= \pm \xi$. By equating the coordinates of $\alpha$ in (2.4) and (6.2) and considering the hypothesis $\sigma=1$, we have

$$
m m_{i} \varphi\left(R^{2}\right)=\xi Z_{1 i}-\eta Z_{2 i}=\xi\left(Z_{1 i} \mp Z_{2 i}\right)
$$

for all $i=1, \ldots, 4$. This provides that the vector $Z_{1} \mp Z_{2}$ has all its coordinates either non-negative or non-positive. But this vector is in the hyperplane $\mathcal{D}^{*}$, so $Z_{1}= \pm Z_{2}$ and they are linearly dependent which is an absurd. Thus, if $\sigma=1$ then $\xi$ and $\eta$ must have different absolute values.

Lemma 6 There exists $\Delta \in \mathcal{D}^{*}$ whose first coordinate is zero and such that

$$
\alpha=-\Delta \otimes \Delta+\sigma Z \otimes Z
$$

Proof Let $\alpha$ be as written in (6.2). If $\sigma=-1$, take $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ given by

$$
a=\frac{-\eta}{\sqrt{\xi^{2}+\eta^{2}}} \quad \text { and } \quad b=\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{\xi^{2}+\eta^{2}}}
$$

so that $a^{2}+b^{2}=1$ and the vector

$$
\Delta=a Z_{1}+b Z_{2}=\left(0, \Delta_{1}, \Delta_{2}, \Delta_{3}, \Delta_{4}\right)
$$

has its first coordinate being zero. By defining

$$
Z=-b Z_{1}+a Z_{2}
$$

it is easy to see that

$$
\Delta \otimes \Delta+Z \otimes Z=Z_{1} \otimes Z_{1}+Z_{2} \otimes Z_{2}=-\alpha
$$

as stated. Now, if $\sigma=1$ take $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ as

$$
a=\frac{-\eta}{\sqrt{\left|\xi^{2}-\eta^{2}\right|}} \quad \text { and } \quad b=\frac{\xi}{\sqrt{\left|\xi^{2}-\eta^{2}\right|}}
$$

By Lemma 5, these expressions are well defined and the vector

$$
\Delta=a Z_{1}+b Z_{2}=\left(0, \Delta_{1}, \Delta_{2}, \Delta_{3}, \Delta_{4}\right)
$$

has its first coordinate null. By defining

$$
Z=b Z_{1}+a Z_{2}
$$

one has that

$$
\Delta \otimes \Delta-Z \otimes Z=\left(a^{2}-b^{2}\right)\left(Z_{1} \otimes Z_{1}-Z_{2} \otimes Z_{2}\right)=-\left(a^{2}-b^{2}\right) \alpha
$$

It only remains to demonstrate that $a^{2}-b^{2}=1$ to prove the lemma.
Supposing by absurd that $a^{2}-b^{2}=-1$, i.e., $\alpha=\Delta \otimes \Delta-Z \otimes Z$. In coordinates, this produces the relations

$$
m_{i} m_{j} \varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)=-\Delta_{i} \Delta_{j}+Z_{i} Z_{j}
$$

For $j=0$, we have that $s_{0 i}=R^{2}$ and $\Delta_{0}=0$, so

$$
m_{i} m \varphi\left(R^{2}\right)=Z_{0} Z_{i}, \quad \forall i \neq 0
$$

By remembering that $Z_{0}$ is not zero, we see that

$$
\frac{Z_{i}}{m_{i}}=\frac{m \varphi\left(R^{2}\right)}{Z_{0}}=k
$$

is constant for all $i=1, \ldots, 4$. Thus

$$
Z=k\left(m-M, m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}, m_{4}\right)
$$

and for $1 \leq i<j \leq 4$,

$$
m_{i} m_{j} \varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)=-\Delta_{i} \Delta_{j}+k^{2} m_{i} m_{j}
$$

Once the vector $\hat{\Delta}=\left(\Delta_{1}, \Delta_{2}, \Delta_{3}, \Delta_{4}\right) \in \mathcal{D}_{4}^{*}$ is in $\operatorname{ker}\{\hat{\beta}\}$, it is the unique vector, up to a scalar factor, such that

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{4} \Delta_{i}=0 \text { and } \sum_{i=1}^{4} \Delta_{i} \mathbf{q}_{i}=0
$$

Furthermore, a co-circular configuration of four bodies is convex and the previously adopted labeling gives us $\Delta_{3}, \Delta_{4}<0<\Delta_{1}, \Delta_{2}$. The equation

$$
\frac{\Delta_{i} \Delta_{j}}{m_{i} m_{j}}=k^{2}-\varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)
$$

and the distribution of the $\Delta_{i}$ 's signs imply that

$$
\varphi\left(s_{12}\right), \varphi\left(s_{34}\right)<k^{2}<\varphi\left(s_{13}\right), \varphi\left(s_{14}\right), \varphi\left(s_{23}\right), \varphi\left(s_{24}\right)
$$

Once $\varphi$ is increasing, both diagonals are smaller than any external side of the co-circular polygon and this is geometrically impossible.

The next theorem is the tensorial characterization of the co-circular $(4,1)$-central configurations.

Theorem 7 Let $\beta$ be a relative co-circular $(4,1)$-central configuration of the five bodyproblem. Then the tensor $\alpha=d g(\beta)$ admits the following parametrization

$$
\alpha=-\Delta \otimes \Delta-\gamma \Gamma \otimes \Gamma
$$

where

- $\Delta_{0}=0$ and $\hat{\Delta}=\left(\Delta_{1}, \ldots, \Delta_{4}\right) \in \mathcal{D}_{4}^{*}$ is a Dziobek cc of the co-circular 4 body-problem.
- $\Gamma=\left(M-m,-m_{1},-m_{2},-m_{3},-m_{4}\right)$
- $\gamma=-\frac{m}{M-m} \varphi\left(R^{2}\right)>0$.

Proof By the Lemma 6, there are vectors $\Delta, Z \in \mathcal{D}_{5}^{*}$ such that $\Delta_{0}=0$ and

$$
\alpha=-\Delta \otimes \Delta+\sigma Z \otimes Z
$$

Choose $\Delta_{1}>0$ and $Z_{0}>0$. Introducing coordinates, the tensor equation becomes

$$
m_{i} m_{j} \varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)=\Delta_{i} \Delta_{j}-\sigma Z_{i} Z_{j}
$$

By taking $j=0$ and $i \neq 0$, we get

$$
-\sigma Z_{0} Z_{i}=m m_{i} \varphi\left(R^{2}\right)
$$

whose summation gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sigma Z_{0}^{2} & =\sum_{i=1}^{4} Z_{0} Z_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{4} m m_{i} \varphi\left(R^{2}\right)=m(M-m) \varphi\left(R^{2}\right) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad Z_{0}^{2}=\sigma m(M-m) \varphi\left(R^{2}\right)>0
\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, all $Z_{i}$ coordinates must be non zero and their quotients by the respective masses $m_{i}$ are constants because of (6.4). Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{Z_{i}}{m_{i}} & =-\sigma \frac{m \varphi\left(R^{2}\right)}{Z_{0}}=-\frac{Z_{0}}{M-m} \\
Z & =\frac{Z_{0}}{M-m}\left(M-m,-m_{1},-m_{2},-m_{3},-m_{4}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

By defining

$$
\Gamma=\left(M-m,-m_{1},-m_{2},-m_{3},-m_{4}\right) \quad \text { and } \quad \gamma=\frac{Z_{0}^{2}}{(M-m)^{2}}
$$

we arrive to the expression

$$
\alpha=-\Delta \otimes \Delta+\sigma \cdot \gamma \cdot \Gamma \otimes \Gamma
$$

The Eq. (6.5) allows us to write the expression for $\gamma$ in another way

$$
\gamma=\sigma \frac{m}{M-m} \varphi\left(R^{2}\right)
$$

If $1 \leq i<j \leq 4$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& m_{i} m_{j} \varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)=\Delta_{i} \Delta_{j}-\sigma \gamma m_{i} m_{j} \\
& m_{i} m_{j}\left(\sigma \gamma+\varphi\left(s_{i j}\right)\right)=\Delta_{i} \Delta_{j} \\
& m_{i} m_{j} \tilde{\varphi}\left(s_{i j}\right)=\Delta_{i} \Delta_{j}
\end{aligned}
$$

where we have made $\tilde{\varphi}(s)=\sigma \gamma+\frac{\lambda}{M}-s^{a}$.
However

$$
\sigma \gamma+\frac{\lambda}{M}=\frac{m}{M-m} \varphi\left(R^{2}\right)+\frac{\lambda}{M}=\frac{m}{M-m}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-R^{2 a}\right)+\frac{\lambda}{M}=\frac{\lambda-m R^{2 a}}{M-m}
$$

We define

$$
\tilde{\lambda}=\lambda-m R^{2 a}
$$

to obtain the function

$$
\tilde{\varphi}(s)=\frac{\tilde{\lambda}}{M-m}-s^{a}
$$

and it follows that the four bodies lying on the circle must satisfy the equations

$$
m_{i} m_{j} \tilde{\varphi}\left(s_{i j}\right)=\Delta_{i} \Delta_{j}, \quad \sum_{i=1}^{4} \Delta_{i}=0, \quad \sum_{i=1}^{4} \Delta_{i} \mathbf{q}_{i}=0
$$

We claim that $\tilde{\lambda}>0$. In fact, if $\tilde{\lambda} \leq 0$ then we would have all the $\tilde{\varphi}\left(s_{i j}\right)$ to be negative, which does not hold, since at least two of $\Delta_{i}^{\prime} s$ have the same sign. Thus $\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{4}\right)$ is a co-circular Dziobek configuration associated to the multiplier $\tilde{\lambda}$.
By Remark (5), we have that

$$
0>\bar{\varphi}\left(R^{2}\right)=\frac{\lambda-m R^{2 a}}{M-m}-R^{2 a}=\frac{M}{M-m}\left(\frac{\lambda}{M}-R^{2 a}\right)=\frac{M}{M-m} \varphi\left(R^{2}\right)
$$
