They observed that there is exactly one class of convex central configurations and there is one or two classes of concave central configurations. Celli  established the exact number of central configurations for masses $x,-x, y,-y$. Albouy, Fu and Sun  recently proved the symmetric properties of convex central configurations for two equal masses and they conjecture that there is exactly one convex central configuration for any choice of four positive masses.

Here we consider a special case when $n=4, q_{i} \in \mathbf{R}^{2}, m_{1}=m_{3}=m_{4}=1$, and $m_{2} \in \mathbf{R}$. A central configuration in this case is either concave or convex, depending on whether the unequal mass $m_{2}$ is inside or outside of the triangle formed by the other three masses. Notice that a degenerate concave or convex configuration, i.e. three masses are collinear but not the fourth one, cannot be a central configuration, see for example, Xia . For concave or convex central configurations, recent results of Long and Sun , and Albouy, Fu and Sun  stated that such central configuration must possess a symmetry. More precisely, they proved

Lemma 1.1. (See Long and Sun .) Let $\alpha, \beta>0$ be any two given real numbers. Let $q=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3}, q_{4}\right) \in\left(\mathbf{R}^{2}\right)^{4}$ be a concave noncollinear central configuration with masses $(\beta, \alpha, \beta, \beta)$ respectively, with $q_{2}$ located inside the triangle formed by $q_{1}, q_{3}$, and $q_{4}$. Then the configuration $q$ must possess a symmetry, so either $q_{1}, q_{3}$, and $q_{4}$ form an equilateral triangle and $q_{2}$ is located at the center of the triangle, or $q_{1}, q_{3}$, and $q_{4}$ form an isosceles triangle, and $q_{2}$ is on the symmetrical axis of the triangle.

Lemma 1.2. (See Albouy, Fu and Sun .) Let four particles $\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3}, q_{4}\right)$ form a planar central configuration, which is a convex quadrilateral having $\left[q_{1}, q_{2}\right]$ and $\left[q_{3}, q_{4}\right]$ as diagonals. This configuration is symmetric with respect to the axis $\left[q_{1}, q_{2}\right]$ if and only if $m_{3}=m_{4}$.

Palmore  considered the one-parameter family consisting of three bodies of mass 1 at the vertices of an equilateral triangle and a fourth body of arbitrary mass $m_{2}$ at the centroid. We shall call this the equilateral central configuration. He showed that $m_{2}=m_{2}^{*}=(64 \sqrt{3}+81) / 249$ is the unique value of the mass parameter $m_{2}$ for which this central configuration is degenerate. Meyer and Schmidt  reproduced this result and further proved that another family of central configurations bifurcates from the equilateral central configuration when $m_{2}=m_{2}^{*}$. The other family, called the isosceles central

configuration, has three bodies of mass 1 at the vertices of an isosceles triangle and a fourth body of mass $m_{2}$ near the centroid and on the line of symmetry of the triangle.

Our goal here is to classify the concave (and convex) central configurations with masses ( $1, m_{2}, 1,1$ ) in $\mathbf{R}^{2}$ with $q_{2}$ located inside (or outside of) the triangle formed by $q_{1}, q_{3}$, and $q_{4}$ following the symmetry properties in Lemmas 1.1 and 1.2. For the concave case, an obvious solution is the equilateral triangle $q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$, and $q_{2}$ is located at the center of the triangle. In this case, $q$ is a central configuration for any mass $m_{2}>0$. This fact can be easily verified through Eq. (2). We use a different variational approach to reproduce Meyer and Schmidt's results and further prove that for $m_{2}=m_{2}^{*}$ there is exactly one concave central configuration (the isosceles family coincides with the equilateral family). We also proved the uniqueness of the convex central configuration with masses ( $1, m_{2}, 1,1$ ) in $\mathbf{R}^{2}$. Our bifurcation analysis involves a subtle rigorous analysis. The novelty is the use of symmetries ascertained in Lemmas 1.1, 1.2 and symbolic computation software Maple to handle the more tedious calculations.

For the stability of critical point $q$ of $E$, we recall that a critical point $q$ is non-degenerate if all eigenvalues of the Hessian $D^{2} E$ at $q$ are non-zero. Due to the invariance of $E$ with respect to the scaling and rotation, $E$ is degenerate at each critical point. Hence we call $E$ essentially degenerate if the degeneracy is not only due to the invariance. For planar central configurations, $q$ is essentially degenerate if the multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue of $D^{2} E(q)$ is greater than 2 ; and for central configurations in the space, $q$ is essentially degenerate if the multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue of $D^{2} E(q)$ is greater than 3 .

Our main results are summarized as follows.
Theorem 1.3. Let $E=I U^{2}$ and let $q$ be the equilateral triangle central configuration with central mass $m_{2}$. Then $E$ becomes essentially degenerate for only one value $m_{2}=m_{2}^{*}=(64 \sqrt{3}+81) / 249$. For given $0<m_{2}<m_{2}^{*}$, the equilateral central configuration is a local minimum of the energy functional $E$; for $m_{2}>m_{2}^{*}$, the equilateral central configuration is a saddle point of $E$.

Theorem 1.4. For any fixed isosceles triangle $q_{2} q_{3} q_{4}$ with $\angle q_{2} q_{3} q_{4}=\angle q_{2} q_{4} q_{3}<\pi / 3$, except when the height $b$ of the triangle is $b_{2} \approx 1.14090$ times $\left|q_{3}-q_{4}\right| / 2$ (see Theorem 3.1 for the definition of $b_{2}$ ), there is a unique $q_{1}$ (on the plane formed by $q_{2} q_{3} q_{4}$ ) and a unique (possibly negative) $m_{2}$, such that $\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3}, q_{4}\right)$ with masses $\left(1, m_{2}, 1,1\right)$ form a planar central configuration, with $q_{2}$ located inside the isosceles triangle $\triangle q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$. Moreover, any concave planar central configuration $\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3}, q_{4}\right)$ with masses $\left(1, m_{2}, 1,1\right)$ and $q_{2}$ located inside the isosceles triangle $\triangle q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$ is given by such an isosceles triangle one provided $m_{2}>0$.

Theorem 1.5. For any fixed isosceles triangle $q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$, except when the height $a$ of the triangle is $a_{1} \approx 0.43856$ times $\left|q_{3}-q_{4}\right| / 2$ (see Theorem 4.1 for the definition of $a_{1}$ ), there is a unique $q_{2}$ (on the plane formed by $q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$ ) and a unique (possibly negative) $m_{2}$, such that $\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3}, q_{4}\right)$ with masses $\left(1, m_{2}, 1,1\right)$ form a planar central configuration, with $q_{2}$ located outside the isosceles triangle $\triangle q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$. Moreover, any convex planar central configuration $\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3}, q_{4}\right)$ with masses $\left(1, m_{2}, 1,1\right)$ and $q_{2}$ located outside the isosceles triangle $\triangle q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$ is given by such a kite-shape central configuration provided $m_{2}>0$.

We remark that our uniqueness result is for a fixed isosceles triangle, then the position and the mass of the fourth particle is uniquely determined by the fixed isosceles triangle. Our method also provides efficient numerical algorithms for computing all these central configurations, so that the unique one-parameter concave and the unique one-parameter convex can be clearly calculated. The numerical results imply another type of uniqueness: for any $m_{2}$ in the admissible mass set, there is a unique isosceles triangle convex or concave with $m_{2}$ in the interior central configuration. However we cannot prove the latter result algebraically. See Sections 3 and 4 for more details.

We prove Theorem 1.3 in Section 2. Theorem 1.4 would be restated and proved in more details in Section 3. The dependence of $q_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ on $q_{2}$ is implicitly given by an equation. In Section 4 Theorem 1.5 will be proved and the relation between $m_{2}$ and position $q_{1}$ will be established.

# 2. Bifurcations of the equilateral triangle configuration 

We prove Theorem 1.3 in this section. We use a bifurcation approach with bifurcation parameter $m_{2}$, and we call the equilateral triangle solution $q^{0}$ to be the trivial solution. Then $\left(m_{2}, q^{0}\right)$ is the branch of trivial solutions. Notice that here $q^{0}$ is an equivalent class of configurations in $\mathbf{R}^{8}$, since the functional $E=I U^{2}$ possesses two invariances:

$$
E(k q)=E(q), \quad k \in \mathbf{R} \backslash\{0\}, \quad \text { and } \quad E(R(q))=E(q)
$$

here $k q$ is the scalar multiplication, and $R$ is a rotation about the origin (where $q_{2}$ is located). $E$ is a functional of eight variables which we order by introducing the 8 -vector $q=\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}, y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3}, y_{4}\right)$ and $q_{i}=\left(x_{i}, y_{i}\right), i=1,2,3,4$.

To find bifurcation points along the trivial solution branch, we notice that for $m_{2}>0, \nabla E\left(q^{0}\right)=0$, and we consider the Hessian matrix $H_{0}\left(m_{2}\right)$ of $E$ at $q^{0}$. The $8 \times 8$ matrix $H_{0}\left(m_{2}\right)$ has at least two zero eigenvalues from (5), but we look for values of $m_{2}$ such that $H_{0}\left(m_{2}\right)$ has additional zero eigenvalues. We fix the equilateral triangle configuration at

$$
q_{1}=\left(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right), \quad q_{2}=(0,0), \quad q_{3}=\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right), \quad q_{4}=(-1,0)
$$



Fig. 1. Triangle configuration.
and use symbolic computation software Maple (version 9.5) to calculate the characteristic polynomial $P\left(m_{2}, x\right)$ of $H_{0}\left(m_{2}\right)$. The result shows that $P\left(m_{2}, x\right)=x^{2}\left\{Q\left(m_{2}, x\right)\right\}^{2}$, where $Q\left(m_{2}, x\right)$ is a cubic polynomial in $x$ :

$$
Q\left(m_{2}, x\right)=Q_{0}\left(m_{2}\right)+Q_{1}\left(m_{2}\right) x+Q_{2}\left(m_{2}\right) x^{2}+x^{3}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& Q_{0}\left(m_{2}\right)=-\frac{6}{83}(5 \sqrt{3}-18)\left(249 m_{2}-81-64 \sqrt{3}\right) m_{2}\left(3 m_{2}+\sqrt{3}\right)^{4} \\
& Q_{1}\left(m_{2}\right)=6\left(18 m_{2}^{3}+(11 \sqrt{3}-18) m_{2}^{2}+5(1+3 \sqrt{3}) m_{2}+3\right)\left(3 m_{2}+\sqrt{3}\right)^{2} \\
& Q_{2}\left(m_{2}\right)=-\left(6 m_{2}^{2}+(27+2 \sqrt{3}) m_{2}+5 \sqrt{3}\right)\left(3 m_{2}+\sqrt{3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

This implies that all eigenvalues of $H_{0}\left(m_{2}\right)$ have even multiplicity. Since we look for $m_{2}$ such that $P\left(m_{2}, x\right)$ has more than two zero eigenvalues, we consider the roots $m_{2}$ of $Q\left(m_{2}, 0\right)=0$. Indeed Maple shows that

$$
Q\left(m_{2}, 0\right)=-\frac{6}{83}(-18+5 \sqrt{3}) m_{2}\left(249 m_{2}-81-64 \sqrt{3}\right)\left(3 m_{2}+\sqrt{3}\right)^{4}
$$

Hence the positive bifurcation point is $m_{2}=m_{2}^{*} \equiv(81+64 \sqrt{3}) / 249 \approx 0.77$. This value has been discovered by Palmore , Meyer and Schmidt  by using different formulations.

Note that $H_{0}\left(m_{2}\right)$ has eight real eigenvalues because the $8 \times 8$ Hessian matrix is symmetric. Note that $Q_{2}\left(m_{2}\right)<0$ and $Q_{1}\left(m_{2}\right)>0$ for all $m_{2}>0$, which implies that there are at least two positive roots by using Descartes' Rule of signs. $Q_{0}\left(m_{2}\right)$ will only change sign once at $m_{2}^{*}$ for $m_{2}>0$. For given $0<m_{2}<m_{2}^{*}, Q\left(m_{2}, x\right)=0$ has exactly three positive roots by using Descartes' Rule of signs, which implies the equilateral central configuration is a local minimum for the energy functional $E$. For $m_{2}>m_{2}^{*}, Q\left(m_{2}, x\right)=0$ has exactly two positive roots and one negative root, which implies the equilateral central configuration is a saddle point. This completes the proof of Theorem 1.3.

# 3. Concave central configurations 

From the symmetry property shown in Lemmas 1.1 and 1.2, to better understand the bifurcation occurring near $m_{2}^{*}$, we only need to consider the configuration

$$
q_{1}=(p, 0), \quad q_{2}=(k, 0), \quad q_{3}=(c, 1), \quad q_{4}=(c,-1)
$$

where $c<p$. Here $q_{1}, q_{3}$ and $q_{4}$ form an isosceles triangle in clockwise order, $q_{2}$ is in the symmetric axis of the triangle. (see Fig. 1). With this configuration, the degeneracy caused by (5) no longer exists.

Here we do not necessarily assume that $q_{2}$ is in the interior of the isosceles triangle $q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$. Let $a=p-c, b=k-c$, then $a-b=p-k$. Then with given isosceles triangle $q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$, the location of $q_{2}$ can be illustrated by the diagram in Fig. 1 (here we assume that $\Delta q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$ is isosceles but not equilateral):

1. (Concave case) If $q_{2}$ is in the interior of $\Delta q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$ (region $A$ in Fig. 1), then Lemma 1.1 asserts that $m_{2}$ is on the interior symmetric axis of the triangle. This corresponds to be configuration (9) with $a>b>0$, or equivalently $p>k>c$.

2. (Convex case) If $q_{2}$ is in region $B$, then Lemma 1.2 shows that all possible convex central configurations must have $m_{2}$ on the extended symmetric axis of $\Delta q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$. This corresponds to be configuration (9) with $a>0>b$, or equivalently $p>c>k$.
3. (Impossible cases) If $q_{2}$ is in region $D$ or $F$, then the configuration is convex but violates the result in Lemma 1.2, thus impossible. If $q_{2}$ is in region $C$ or $G$, then the configuration is concave but violates the perpendicular bisector theorem of Conley and Moeckel , thus impossible.
4. (Other cases) If $q_{2}$ is in region $E$, there exist central configurations since Albouy's isosceles configuration of four equal masses with one on the symmetric axis is such an example (see , or ), where $q_{1}$ is on the interior symmetric axis of the triangle $\Delta q_{2} q_{3} q_{4}$. By the perpendicular bisector theorem, $q_{2}$ must be on the symmetric axis of the isosceles triangle $\Delta q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$. But it is not known whether central configurations exist or not if $q_{2}$ is in region $E$ and $\Delta q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$ is not isosceles, and we do not consider these cases in this article.

Using the assumption of center of mass at origin, we have $p+m_{2} k+2 c=0$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p=\frac{-m_{2} b+2 a+m_{2} a}{m_{2}+3}, \quad k=\frac{-(a-3 b)}{m_{2}+3}, \quad c=\frac{-\left(m_{2} b+a\right)}{m_{2}+3} \\
& U=\frac{m_{2}}{a-b}+\frac{4}{\sqrt{a^{2}+1}}+\frac{2 m_{2}}{\sqrt{b^{2}+1}}+\frac{1}{8} \\
& I=\frac{\left(-m_{2} b+2 a+m_{2} a\right)^{2}+m_{2}(a-3 b)^{2}+2\left(m_{2} b+a\right)^{2}+2\left(m_{2}+3\right)^{2}}{\left(m_{2}+3\right)^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

By using these identities and $\lambda=U / 2 I$ in (4), the eight equations of central configuration in (2) are reduced to two equations with $m_{2}$ as a parameter:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f_{1}\left(a, b, m_{2}\right) \equiv \frac{3 b-a}{\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{m_{2}(b-a)-6 b}{\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{1}{4}(3 b-a)+\frac{m_{2}+3}{(a-b)^{2}}=0 \\
& f_{2}\left(a, b, m_{2}\right) \equiv \frac{m_{2}(a-b)+2 a}{\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{m_{2}(3 b-a)}{\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1}{4}\left(m_{2} b+a\right)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

With a linear elimination, we convert (10) and (11) to

$$
\begin{aligned}
& -\frac{m_{2}(b-a)^{2}+4 a b}{\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{a(3 b-a)}{4}+\frac{m_{2}(a-b)+2 a}{(a-b)^{2}}=0 \\
& \frac{m_{2}(b-a)^{2}+4 a b}{\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{b\left(m_{2}(a-b)+2 a\right)}{4}+\frac{m_{2}(3 b-a)}{(a-b)^{2}}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Then we rewrite (12) and (13) into

$$
s_{1} m_{2}-t_{1}=0, \quad s_{2} m_{2}-t_{2}=0
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& s_{1}:=-\frac{(a-b)^{2}}{\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{1}{a-b} \\
& t_{1}:=\frac{4 a b}{\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{a(a-3 b)}{4}-\frac{2 a}{(a-b)^{2}} \\
& s_{2}:=\frac{(a-b)^{2}}{\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{3 b-a}{(a-b)^{2}}-\frac{b(a-b)}{4} \\
& t_{2}:=-\frac{4 a b}{\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{a b}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

It is necessary that a solution of (12) and (13) satisfies $s_{1} t_{2}-s_{2} t_{1}=0$. With some elementary but tedious calculations, we obtain

$$
\Delta:=s_{1} t_{2}-s_{2} t_{1}=-\frac{a(a-3 b)(a-b-2)\left[(a-b)^{2}+2(a-b)+4\right]}{16\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}(a-b)^{4}\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}} P(a, b)
$$

where

$$
P(a, b):=4(a-b)^{3}\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}+8 b(a-b)^{2}\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}-\left[4+b(a-b)^{2}\right]\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}
$$

We shall consider the concave case in this section, and the convex case in the next section. For the concave case, we assume $0<b<a$ in this section. Theorem 1.4 can be stated more precisely as follows (note that here we include the case of negative mass $m_{2}$ )



Fig. 2. Bifurcation diagram of concave central configurations. Left: bifurcation diagram of $a$ with respect to $m_{2}$. Right: bifurcation diagram of $b$ with respect to $m_{2}, m_{2}^{*}=(64 \sqrt{3}+81) / 249$ is the unique bifurcation point.

Theorem 3.1. Let $m=\left(1, m_{2}, 1,1\right), q=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3}, q_{4}\right)$ (defined as in (9)) be a concave configuration with $q_{2}$ located inside the triangle $\triangle q_{1} q_{3} q_{4}$ (region $A$ in Fig. 1). Then all such central configurations are determined by the parameters $\left(a, b, m_{2}\right)$ as follows (see Fig. 3):
(A) The set of concave central configurations are contained in two curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Gamma_{0}=\left\{\left(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3} / 3, m_{2}\right): m_{2} \in \mathbf{R}\right\} \\
& \Gamma_{*}=\left\{\left(a_{0}(b), b, m_{2}\left(a_{0}(b), b\right)\right): 0<b<\sqrt{3}\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $a_{0}(b)$ is a function implicitly determined by $P\left(a_{0}(b), b\right)=0$, and $m_{2}\left(a_{0}(b), b\right)$ is computed as $m_{2}=t_{1} / s_{1}=t_{2} / s_{2}$ whenever $(a, b) \neq(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3} / 3),\left(\sqrt{3}, b_{1}\right)$ or $\left(a_{0}\left(b_{2}\right), b_{2}\right)$, where $b_{1} \approx 0.09943364929$ is the only positive root of $t_{1}(a, b)=t_{2}(a, b)=0$ other than $b=\sqrt{3} / 3$, and $b_{2} \approx 1.140903160$ is the only positive root of $s_{1}(a, b)=s_{2}(a, b)=0$ other than $b=\sqrt{3} / 3 ; \Gamma_{0}$ and $\Gamma_{*}$ has exactly one intersection point at $(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3} / 3, m_{2}^{*})$ which is the bifurcation point found in Theorem 1.3 (see Fig. 2).
(B) If $\left(a, b, m_{2}\right)$ is on the portion $\Gamma_{1}=\left\{\left(a_{0}(b), b, m_{2}\left(a_{0}(b), b\right)\right): b_{1}<b<b_{2}\right\}$, then $q$ is an isosceles triangular central configuration with positive mass $\infty>m_{2}>0$; for any $m \in(0, \infty)$, there exists at least one $b \in\left(b_{1}, b_{2}\right)$ such that $m=m_{2}\left(a_{0}(b), b\right)$.
(C) If $\left(a, b, m_{2}\right)$ is on the portion $\Gamma_{2}=\left\{\left(a_{0}(b), b, m_{2}\left(a_{0}(b), b\right)\right): 0<b<b_{1}\right\}$, then $q$ is an isosceles triangular central configuration with negative mass $0>m_{2}>-0.25$; for any $m \in(-0.25,0)$, there exists at least one $b \in\left(0, b_{1}\right)$ such that $m=m_{2}\left(a_{0}(b), b\right)$.
(D) If $\left(a, b, m_{2}\right)$ is on the portion $\Gamma_{3}=\left\{\left(a_{0}(b), b, m_{2}\left(a_{0}(b), b\right)\right): b_{2}<b<\sqrt{3}\right\}$, then $q$ is an isosceles triangular central configuration with negative mass $0>m_{2}>-2$; for any $m \in(-2,0)$, there exists at least one $b \in\left(b_{2}, \sqrt{3}\right)$ such that $m=m_{2}\left(a_{0}(b), b\right)$.

Note that $t_{1}(a, b)=t_{2}(a, b)=0$ is equivalent to $a=\sqrt{3}$ and $t_{1}(\sqrt{3}, b)=0$, which is equivalent to the algebraic expression:

$$
(3 b-\sqrt{3})\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}(\sqrt{3}-b)^{2}-16 b(\sqrt{3}-b)^{2}+8\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}=0
$$

Similarly $s_{1}(a, b)=s_{2}(a, b)=0$ is equivalent to

$$
\frac{\sqrt{b^{2}+1}}{\left(\left(b+\sqrt{b^{2}+1}\right)^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{2 b-\sqrt{b^{2}+1}}{\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{b}{4}=0
$$

The limit -0.25 of $m_{2}$ on $\Gamma_{2}$ when $b \rightarrow 0^{+}$can be obtained with (14), $b \rightarrow 0^{+}$and $a \rightarrow \infty$; similarly the limit -2 of $m_{2}$ on $\Gamma_{3}$ when $b \rightarrow(\sqrt{3})^{-}$can be obtained with (14), $b \rightarrow(\sqrt{3})^{-}$and $a \rightarrow \infty$.

For the proof of Theorem 3.1, we prove the following key lemma.
Lemma 3.2. Suppose that $P(a, b)$ is defined as in (20). Then for any $b \geqslant \sqrt{3}$ and $a \geqslant b, P(a, b)<0$; for any $0<b<\sqrt{3}$, there exists a unique $a=a_{0}(b)$ such that
(i) $P(a, b)<0$ for $b \leqslant a<a_{0}(b)$,
(ii) $P\left(a_{0}(b), b\right)=0$, and
(iii) $P(a, b)>0$ for $a>a_{0}(b)$.



Fig. 3. Possible concave central configurations on curve $\Gamma_{*}$.
Moreover $\Gamma_{*}=\left\{\left(a_{0}(b), b\right): 0<b<\sqrt{3}\right\}$ is a smooth curve in $\mathbf{R}_{+}^{2}$, and $\lim _{b \rightarrow 0^{+}} a_{0}(b)=\infty, \lim _{b \rightarrow(\sqrt{3})^{-}} a_{0}(b)=\infty$.
Proof. We rewrite $P(a, b)$ in the form:

$$
P(a, b)=b\left[8-\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right](a-b)^{2}\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}-4\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\left[\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}-(a-b)^{3}\right]
$$

When $b \geqslant \sqrt{3}$, we have $8-\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2} \leqslant 0$, then $P(a, b)<0$ for $a \geqslant b$ since $\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}-(a-b)^{3}>0$. For $b \in(0, \sqrt{3})$, $P(b, b)<0$ and $P(a, b) \rightarrow \infty$ as $a \rightarrow \infty$, then there exists $a \in(b, \infty)$ such that $P(a, b)=0$. We calculate $\partial P / \partial a$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial P}{\partial a}(a, b)= & b\left[8-\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right] \cdot\left[(a-b)\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{1 / 2}\left(5 a^{2}-3 a b+2\right)\right] \\
& -4\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2} \cdot 3\left[a\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{1 / 2}-(a-b)^{2}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

We notice that (23) and (24) can be written as

$$
\binom{P}{\partial P / \partial a}=M \cdot\binom{b\left[8-\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right]}{-4\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

where

$$
M:=\left(M_{i j}\right):=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
(a-b)^{2}\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2} & \left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}-(a-b)^{3} \\
(a-b)\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{1 / 2}\left(5 a^{2}-3 a b+2\right) & 3\left[a\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{1 / 2}-(a-b)^{2}\right]
\end{array}\right)
$$

and $M_{i j}$ is the entry of the matrix $M$. A simple calculation shows that

$$
\operatorname{Det}(M)=(a-b)\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\left\{2\left(a^{2}+1\right)\left[-\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}+(a-b)^{3}\right]-3 a b-3\right\}<0
$$

for any $0<b<\sqrt{3}$ and $a \geqslant b$. This implies that for any $0<b<\sqrt{3}$ and $a \geqslant b$,

$$
M_{21} P(a, b)-M_{11} \frac{\partial P}{\partial a}(a, b)=\operatorname{Det}(M) \cdot 4\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}<0
$$

Fix $b \in(0, \sqrt{3})$. Let $a=a_{0}(b)$ be the smallest $a>b$ such that $P(a, b)=0$, then $\partial P\left(a_{0}(b), b\right) / \partial a>0$ from (28). In fact whenever $P(a, b) \geqslant 0$ then $\partial P(a, b) / \partial a>0$ from (28). This implies $P(a, b)>0$ for all $a>a_{0}(b)$. Finally since $\partial P\left(a_{0}(b), b\right) / \partial a>0$ for any $b \in(0, \sqrt{3})$, then the set $\Gamma_{*}=\left\{\left(a_{0}(b), b\right): 0<b<\sqrt{3}\right\}$ is a smooth curve from the implicit function theorem, and the asymptotes of $a_{0}(b)$ follows easily from calculus.

Proof of Theorem 3.1. $\Gamma_{*}$ contains the trivial equilateral central configuration, which is well known. Hence we consider other possible central configurations by using (10) and (11), or equivalently (12) and (13). From discussion above, the set of



Fig. 4. Graph of $m_{2}(b), 0<b<\sqrt{3}$ along $\Gamma$.
concave central configurations must satisfy $\Delta=s_{1} t_{2}-s_{2} t_{1}=0$. From (19), for $b<a, \Delta=s_{1} t_{2}-s_{2} t_{1}=0$ has the following possibilities:

1. $a=0$. This does not give rise to a central configuration (see ).
2. $a-b=0$. With elementary computation, we can prove that it gives a central configuration only when $a=\sqrt{3}, b=$ $\sqrt{3} / 3$ which is the equilateral central configuration for any mass $m_{2} \in \mathbf{R}$, and it is included in $\Gamma_{0}$.
3. $a-b-2=0$. We can prove that it gives a central configuration only when $b=-1$ and $a=1$ which is a square configuration for mass $m_{2}=1$, and this is a convex central configuration which will be discussed in the next section.
4. $(a-b)^{2}+2(a-b)+4=(a-b+1)^{2}+3=0$ has no real valued solutions.
5. $P(a, b)=0$, which we shall discuss more below.

From Lemma 3.2, the level set $P(a, b)=0$ for $b>0$ is indeed a curve $\Gamma_{*}=\left\{\left(a_{0}(b), b\right): 0<b<\sqrt{3}\right\}$. For any $(a, b) \in \Gamma_{*}$, if $s_{1}=0$, then $t_{1}=0$ or $s_{2}=0$. In case $t_{1}=0$, one can deduce that $a=\sqrt{3}$ and $b=\sqrt{3} / 3$. In case $s_{2}=0$, one obtain positive values $(a, b)=(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3} / 3)$ and $(a, b)=(2.658025443,1.140903160=b_{2})$ from the equations. Similarly if $t_{2}=0$ and $a b \neq 0$, then $a=\sqrt{3}$, and $t_{1}=0$ or $s_{2}=0$. In case $s_{2}=0$, one obtain $(a, b)=(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3} / 3)$ and $(a, b)=(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3}-2)$. In case $t_{1}=0$, one obtain positive values $(a, b)=(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3} / 3)$ and $(a, b)=(\sqrt{3}, 0.09943364929=b_{1})$. Hence except at the $(a, b)=(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3} / 3),(a, b)=\left(\sqrt{3}, b_{1}\right)$ and $(a, b)=(2.658014, b_{2})$, for any other $(a, b) \in \Gamma_{*}$, the mass $m_{2}(a, b)=t_{1} / s_{1}=t_{2} / s_{2}$ is uniquely determined and we denote by $m_{2}(b):=m_{2}\left(a_{0}(b), b\right)$ with the domain $b \in(0, \sqrt{3})\backslash\left\{b_{1}, b_{2}, \sqrt{3} / 3\right\}$. The asymptotes of $m_{2}(b)$ for $b$ near $b=0, b_{1}, \sqrt{3} / 3, b_{2}, \sqrt{3}$ can be easily determined from calculus, which we omit the details. The function $m_{2}(b)$ is continuous in $\left(0, b_{1}\right) \cup\left(b_{1}, \sqrt{3} / 3\right) \cup\left(\sqrt{3} / 3, b_{2}\right) \cup\left(b_{2}, \sqrt{3}\right)$, which implies all results stated in theorem.

The numerical graph of $a_{0}(b)$ is shown in Fig. 3, and the numerical graph of $m_{2}(b)$ is shown in Fig. 4. We can observe the following facts from the numerical graphs of $a_{0}(b)$ and $m_{2}(b)$. When $b_{1} \leqslant b<b_{2}, m_{2}(b)$ increase from 0 to infinity. $b=b_{2}$ is a vertical asymptote of the curve $m_{2}=m_{2}(b)$. Each solution on the curve $\Gamma_{1}=\left\{\left(a_{0}(b), b, m_{2}(b)\right): b_{1}<b<b_{2}\right\}$ gives an isosceles triangle central configuration. If $b=\sqrt{3} / 3$, then $a_{0}(b)=\sqrt{3}$ and $m_{2}(b)=m_{2}^{*}$, which coincides to an equilateral triangle central configuration. $\left(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3} / 3, m_{2}^{*}\right)$ is the only intersection point between the curve $\Gamma_{0}$ and $\Gamma_{*}$. Let angles of isosceles triangle be $\phi, \theta, \theta$, the angle $\phi$ can be computed as $\phi=2 \arctan (1 / a)$. For $b_{1}<b<\sqrt{3} / 3,0<m_{2}<m_{2}^{*}$ and $a<\sqrt{3}$, so $\phi<\pi / 3$. For $\sqrt{3} / 3<b<b_{2}, m_{2}>m_{2}^{*}$ and $a>\sqrt{3}$, so $\phi>\pi / 3$.

When $0<b<b_{1}, a_{0}(b)$ decreases from infinity to $\sqrt{3}$ as shown in Fig. 3 and $m_{2}(b)$ increases from -0.25 to 0 as shown in Fig. 4. When $b_{2}<b<\sqrt{3}, a_{0}(b)$ increases from 2.658014 to infinity. But $m_{2}(b)$ is negative and is increasing from negative infinity to -2 .

Our result in this section classifies all concave central configurations with mass $(1, m_{2}, 1,1)$. It is shown that besides the equilateral triangular ones, all other isosceles ones lie on a smooth curve which can be parameterized by $b$, the distance



Fig. 5. Possible convex central configuration on curve $\Gamma^{\prime \prime}$.
from mass $m_{2}$ to the midpoint of the two symmetric vertices. The numerical graph (Fig. 4) suggest that $m_{2}(b)$ is always monotone.

# 4. Convex central configurations 

In this section, we consider the convex configurations, i.e. $b<0<a$ in the discussion in Section 3. In fact the analysis in Section 3 remain valid for convex case until Eq. (20). Theorem 1.5 can be stated more precisely as follows (note that we include the case of negative mass $m_{2}$ ).

Theorem 4.1. Let $m=\left(1, m_{2}, 1,1\right), q=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3}, q_{4}\right)$ (defined as in (9)) be a convex configuration with $q_{2}$ located in the region $B$ in Fig. 1. Then all such convex central configurations are determined by the parameters $\left(a, b, m_{2}\right)$ as follows (see Fig. 5):
(A) The set of convex central configurations are contained in the curve

$$
\Gamma^{\prime}=\left\{\left(a, b_{0}(a), m_{2}\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right)\right): 0<a<\infty\right\}
$$

where $b_{0}(a)$ is a function implicitly determined by $P\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right)=0$ such that $b_{0}(a)<0<a$, where $P$ is defined in (20), and $m_{2}\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right)$ is computed as $m_{2}=t_{1} / s_{1}=t_{2} / s_{2}$ whenever $(a, b) \neq\left(a_{1}, b_{0}\left(a_{1}\right)\right)$, or $\left(a_{2}, b_{0}\left(a_{2}\right)\right)$, where $a_{1} \approx 0.4385619887$ is the only positive root of $s_{1}(a, b)=s_{2}(a, b)=0$ such that $b_{0}\left(a_{1}\right) \approx-0.9208086952$ is negative, and $a_{2}=\sqrt{3}$ is the only positive root of $t_{1}(a, b)=t_{2}(a, b)=0$ such that $b_{0}\left(a_{2}\right) \approx-1.293021668$ is negative.
(B) If $\left(a, b, m_{2}\right)$ is on the portion $\Gamma_{4}=\left\{\left(a, b_{0}(a), m_{2}\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right)\right): a_{1}<a<a_{2}\right\}$, then $q$ is a convex central configuration with positive mass $\infty>m_{2}>0$; for any $m \in(0, \infty)$, there exists at least one $a \in\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right)$ such that $m=m_{2}\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right)$.
(C) If $\left(a, b, m_{2}\right)$ is on the portion $\Gamma_{5}=\left\{\left(a, b_{0}(a), m_{2}\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right)\right): 0<a<a_{1}\right\}$, then $q$ is a convex central configuration with negative mass $-\infty<m_{2}<0$; for any $m \in(-\infty, 0)$, there exists at least one $a \in\left(0, a_{1}\right)$ such that $m=m_{2}\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right)$.
(D) If $\left(a, b, m_{2}\right)$ is on the portion $\Gamma_{6}=\left\{\left(a, b_{0}(a), m_{2}\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right)\right): a_{2}<a<\infty\right\}$, then $q$ is a convex central configuration with negative mass $0>m_{2}>-2$; for any $m \in(-2,0)$, there exists at least one $a \in\left(a_{2}, \infty\right)$ such that $m=m_{2}\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right)$.

Note that $s_{1}(a, b)=s_{2}(a, b)=0$ is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{2 a \sqrt{a^{2}+1}}+\frac{4 a^{2}\left(a^{2}-3\right)}{\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3}}-\frac{a^{2}-1}{8 a}=0
$$

Similarly $t_{1}(a, b)=t_{1}(a, b)=0$ is equivalent to $a=\sqrt{3}$ and $t_{1}(\sqrt{3}, b)=0$ which is equivalent to the algebraic expression

$$
(3 b-\sqrt{3})\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}(\sqrt{3}-b)^{2}-16 b(\sqrt{3}-b)^{2}+8\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}=0
$$



Fig. 6. Graph of $Q(a, b)=0, P(a, b)=0$ and $b=-\sqrt{3}$.

Here we choose the positive zeros $a$ such that $b_{0}(a)$ is negative. The limit 0 of $m_{2}$ on $\Gamma_{5}$ when $a \rightarrow 0^{+}$can be obtained with (14), $a \rightarrow 0^{+}$and $b \rightarrow-1.139428225$; similarly the limit -2 of $m_{2}$ on $\Gamma_{6}$ when $a \rightarrow \infty$ can be obtained with (14), $b \rightarrow(-\sqrt{3})^{+}$and $a \rightarrow \infty$.

Before we give the proof, we first show the following key lemma.
Lemma 4.2. Recall that $P(a, b)$ is defined in (20) or equivalently (23). Then there exists a unique $b=b_{0}(a)$ such that
(i) $-\sqrt{3}<b=b_{0}(a)<0$
(ii) $P(a, b)<0$ for $b_{0}(a) \leqslant b<0$
(iii) $P\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right)=0$; and
(iv) $P(a, b)>0$ for $b<b_{0}(a)$.

Moreover $\Gamma^{\prime}=\left\{\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right): 0<a<\infty\right\}$ is a smooth curve in $\mathbf{R}_{+}^{2}$ as shown in Fig. 5, and $\lim _{a \rightarrow \infty} b_{0}(a)=-\sqrt{3}$.
Proof. For $b \leqslant-\sqrt{3}$ and $0 \leqslant a, P(a, b)>0$ because $8-\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}<0$ and $(a-b)^{3}-\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}>0$. For any $a>0$, $P(a, 0)=4 a^{3}-4\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}<0$. Then for any $a>0$, there exists at least one $b \in(-\sqrt{3}, 0)$ such that $P(a, b)=0$. Let

$$
Q(a, b)=(a-b)^{3}-\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}
$$

In the fourth quadrant, $Q(a, b)=0$ is equivalent to $b^{2}-2 a b-1=0$, which is implicitly defined a smooth function $b=b_{Q}(a)$ such that $Q\left(a, b_{Q}(a)\right)=0$ (see Fig. 6). By taking implicit derivative, we have $\frac{d}{d a} b_{Q}(a)>0$. So $b_{Q}(a)>b_{Q}(0)=-1$ for any $a>0$.

It is easy to check that $Q(a, b)<0$ when $0>b>b_{Q}(a)$, and $Q(a, b)>0$ when $-\sqrt{3}<b<b_{Q}(a)$. Therefore, $P(a, b)<0$ for $(a, b) \in\left\{a>0, b_{Q}(a)<b<0\right\}$. If $P(a, b)=0, b$ must be in the interval $\left(-\sqrt{3}, b_{Q}(a)\right)$. We calculate $\partial P / \partial b$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial P}{\partial b}(a, b)= & {\left[-12(a-b)^{2}\left(b^{2}+1\right)+12\left((a-b)^{3}-\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right) b\right] \cdot\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{1 / 2} } \\
& +\left[(a-b)(a-3 b)\left(8-\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right)-3 b^{2}(a-b)^{2}\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{1 / 2}\right] \cdot\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}
\end{aligned}
$$

We notice that (23) and (31) can be written as

$$
\binom{P}{\partial P / \partial b}=M \cdot\binom{\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{1 / 2}}{\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

where

$$
M:=\left(\begin{array}{ll}
M_{11} & M_{12} \\
M_{21} & M_{22}
\end{array}\right)
$$

and $M_{i j}$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M_{11}=4\left((a-b)^{3}-\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right)\left(b^{2}+1\right) \\
& M_{12}=\left(8-\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right) b(a-b)^{2} \\
& M_{21}=-12(a-b)^{2}\left(b^{2}+1\right)+12\left((a-b)^{3}-\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right) b \\
& M_{22}=(a-b)(a-3 b)\left(8-\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right)-3 b^{2}(a-b)^{2}\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{1 / 2}
\end{aligned}
$$

We claim that

$$
\operatorname{Det}(M)=M_{11} M_{22}-M_{12} M_{21}<0
$$

for any $a>0$ and $-\sqrt{3}<b<b_{\mathrm{Q}}(a)$, this implies that for any $a>0$ and $-\sqrt{3}<b<b_{\mathrm{Q}}(a)$,

$$
-M_{21} P(a, b)+M_{11} \frac{\partial P}{\partial b}(a, b)=\operatorname{Det}(M) \cdot\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}<0
$$

Assuming (34) and consequently (35), we prove the statements in Lemma 4.2. Fix $a>0$. Let $b=b_{0}(a)$ be the largest value such that $-\sqrt{3}<b<b_{\mathrm{Q}}(a)$ and $P(a, b)=0$. Then $\partial P\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right) / \partial b<0$ from (35) (note that $M_{11}>0$ and $M_{21}<0$ if $-\sqrt{3}<b<b_{\mathrm{Q}}(a)$ ). In fact whenever $P(a, b) \geqslant 0$ then $\partial P(a, b) / \partial b<0$ from (35). This implies $P(a, b)>0$ for all $b<b_{0}(a)$. Finally since $\partial P\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right) / \partial b<0$ for any $b \in\left(-\sqrt{3}, b_{\mathrm{Q}}(a)\right)$, then the set $\Gamma=\left\{\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right):-\sqrt{3}<b<b_{\mathrm{Q}}(a), a>0\right\}$ is a smooth curve from the implicit function theorem, and the asymptotes of $b_{0}(a)$ follows easily from calculus.

It remains to prove the claim that $\operatorname{Det}(M)=M_{11} M_{22}-M_{12} M_{21}<0$. Let

$$
A=\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{1 / 2}, \quad B=\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{1 / 2}, \quad C=a-b
$$

A simple calculation shows that

$$
\operatorname{Det}(M)=4 C \cdot S
$$

where

$$
S=B^{2}\left(8-B^{3}\right)\left[\left(C^{3}-A^{3}\right) a+3 b A^{3}\right]-24 b^{2} C\left(C^{3}-A^{3}\right)
$$

Then $\operatorname{Det}(M)<0$ is equivalent to $S<0$ because $C>0$. We compute $\partial S / \partial a$ :

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial a}=\left[3\left(C^{2}-A a\right) a+\left(C^{3}-A^{3}\right)+9 A b a\right] \cdot B^{2}\left(8-B^{3}\right)-24 b^{2} \cdot\left[\left(C^{3}-A^{3}\right)+3 C\left(C^{2}-A a\right)\right]
$$

$S$ and $\partial S / \partial a$ can be written as

$$
\binom{S}{\partial S / \partial a}=T \cdot\binom{B^{2}\left(8-B^{3}\right)}{-24 b^{2}}
$$

where

$$
T:=\left(T_{i j}\right):=\binom{\left(C^{3}-A^{3}\right) a+3 b A^{3}}{3\left(C^{2}-A a\right) a+\left(C^{3}-A^{3}\right)+9 A b a} \quad\left(C^{3}-A^{3}\right)+3 C\left(C^{2}-A a\right) .
$$

Note that $Q(a, b)=C^{3}-A^{3}>0$ and $C^{2}-A a>0$ for any $a>0,-\sqrt{3}<b<b_{\mathrm{Q}}(a)<0$. So $T_{22}>0, T_{12}>0$ and

$$
\operatorname{Det}(T)=3 b\left(A^{3}+3 a C A\right)\left(C^{3}-A^{3}\right)+9 b C A^{3}\left(C^{2}-A a\right)+b\left(C^{3}-A^{3}\right)^{2}<0
$$

for any $a>0,-\sqrt{3}<b<b_{\mathrm{Q}}(a)<0$. Thus

$$
T_{22} S-T_{12} \frac{\partial S}{\partial a}=\operatorname{Det}(T) \cdot B^{2}\left(8-B^{3}\right)<0
$$

If $S \geqslant 0$ at $\left(a_{0}, b_{0}\right)$ for some $a_{0}>0$ and $-\sqrt{3}<b_{0}<b_{\mathrm{Q}}(a)$, then $\partial S / \partial a>0$ from (38). In fact, whenever $S \geqslant 0$ then $\partial S / \partial a>0$ from (38). This implies that $S>0$ for all $a>a_{0}$. On the other hand, we note that for any fixed $-\sqrt{3}<b<0$, $S<0$ for sufficient large $a>0$. This is a contradiction. So $S<0$ for any $a>0$ and $-\sqrt{3}<b_{0}<b_{\mathrm{Q}}(a)$. We complete the proof.

Proof of Theorem 4.1. By a similar argument as in the proof of Theorem 3.1, the set of convex central configurations must satisfy $\Delta=s_{1} t_{2}-s_{2} t_{1}=0$ and $b<0<a$. From (19), for $b<0<a, \Delta=s_{1} t_{2}-s_{2} t_{1}=0$ has the following possibilities: (i) $a=0$; (ii) $a-3 b=0$; (iii) $a-b-2=0$; (iv) $(a-b)^{2}+2(a-b)+4=(a-b+1)^{2}+3=0$; (v) $P(a, b)=0$. From the



Fig. 7. Graph of $m_{2}(a),-\sqrt{3}<b<0$ along $p(a, b)=0$.


Fig. 8. Convex central configurations for $a_{1}<a<a_{2}$.
arguments for (i) to (iv) in the proof of Theorem 3.1, only case (iii) gives a convex central configuration when $b=-1$ and $a=1$ which is a square configuration for mass $m_{2}=1$, and it is included in $\Gamma^{\prime}$.

From Lemma 4.2, the level set $P(a, b)=0$ for $b<0<a$ is a parameterized curve $\Gamma^{\prime}=\left\{\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right): 0<a<\infty\right\}$. Then all the possible convex central configurations are along the curve $\Gamma^{\prime \prime}$. For any $(a, b) \in \Gamma^{\prime}$ and $b<0<a$, if $s_{1}=0$, then $t_{1}=0$ or $s_{2}=0$. In case $t_{1}=0$, one can deduce that $a=2-\sqrt{3}$ and $b=-\sqrt{3}$ which is not on $\Gamma^{\prime \prime}$. In case $s_{2}=0$, one obtain $(a, b)=(0.4385619887=a_{1},-0.9208086915)$ from the equations. Similarly if $t_{2}=0$ and $a b \neq 0$, then $a=\sqrt{3}$, and $t_{1}=0$ or $s_{2}=0$. In case $t_{1}=0$, one obtain $(a, b)=(\sqrt{3}=a_{2},-1.293021665)$ which is on $\Gamma^{\prime \prime}$. In case $s_{2}=0,(a, b)=(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3}-2)$ which is not on $\Gamma^{\prime \prime}$ but on $a-b-2=0$. Hence only except at the point $(a, b)=\left(a_{1}, b_{0}\left(a_{1}\right)\right)$, for any other $(a, b) \in \Gamma^{\prime \prime}$,

the mass $m_{2}(a, b)=t_{1} / s_{1}=t_{2} / s_{2}$ is uniquely determined and we denote by $m_{2}(a):=m_{2}\left(a, b_{0}(a)\right)$ with the domain $a \in$ $\left(0, a_{1}\right) \cup\left(a_{1}, \infty\right)$. The asymptotes of $m_{2}(a)$ for $a$ near $a=0, a_{1}, a_{2}, \infty$ can be easily determined from calculus, which we omit the details. The function $m_{2}(b)$ is continuous in $\left(0, b_{1}\right) \cup\left(b_{1}, \sqrt{3} / 3\right) \cup\left(\sqrt{3} / 3, b_{2}\right) \cup\left(b_{2}, \sqrt{3}\right)$, which implies all results stated in theorem.

The numerical graph of $b_{0}(a)$ is shown in Fig. 5, and the numerical graph of $m_{2}(a)$ is shown in Fig. 7.
We can observe the following facts from the numerical graphs of $b_{0}(a)$ and $m_{2}(a)$. When $a_{1} \leqslant a<a_{2}, m_{2}(a)$ decrease from infinity to $0 . a=a_{1}$ is a vertical asymptote of the curve $m_{2}=m_{2}(a)$. Each solution on the curve $\Gamma_{4}=\left[\left(a, b_{0}(a), m_{2}(a)\right)\right.$ : $\left.a_{1}<a<a_{2}\right\}$ gives a convex central configuration. When $a_{1}<a<1, m_{2}(a)>1$ and $\left|b_{0}(a)\right|>a$, which means that the heavier mass is further away the diagonal (see Fig. 8). When $a=1, b=-1$ and $m_{2}(a)=1$ which is a square central configuration. When $1<a<a_{2}, m_{2}(a)<1$ and $\left|b_{0}(a)\right|<a$, which means that the smaller mass is closer to the diagonal.

When $0<a<a_{1}, b_{0}(a)$ increase from -1.139428225 to -0.9208086915 as shown in Fig. 5 and $m_{2}(a)$ decrease from 0 to $-\infty$ as shown in Fig. 7. When $a_{2} \leqslant a<\infty, m_{2}(a)$ decrease from 0 to -2 and $b_{0}(a)$ decrease to $-\sqrt{3}$.

Our result in this section classifies all convex central configurations with mass $(1, m_{2}, 1,1)$. It is shown that all convex central configurations lie on a smooth curve which can be parameterized by $a$, the distance from mass $m_{2}$ to the midpoint of the two symmetric vertices. The numerical graph (Fig. 7) shows that $m_{2}(a)$ is always monotone.

# Central configurations of nested regular polyhedra for the spatial $2 n$-body problem 

## A B S T R A C T

We consider $2 n$ masses located at the vertices of two nested regular polyhedra with the same number of vertices. Assuming that the masses in each polyhedron are equal, we prove that for each ratio of the masses of the inner and the outer polyhedra there exists a unique ratio of the length of the edges of the inner and the outer polyhedra such that the configuration is central.
(c) 2008 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

## 1. Introduction

We consider the $N$-body problem in the $\ell$-dimensional space with $\ell=2,3$,

$$
m_{i} \overline{\mathbf{q}}_{i}=-\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{N} G m_{i} m_{j} \frac{\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}}{\left|\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right|^{3}}, \quad i=1, \ldots, N
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{\ell}$ is the position vector of the punctual mass $m_{i}$ in an inertial coordinate system and $G$ is the gravitational constant which can be taken equal to one by choosing conveniently the unit of time. We fix the center of mass $\sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i} \mathbf{q}_{i} / \sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i}$ of the system at the origin of $\mathbb{R}^{i N}$. The configuration space of the $N$-body problem in $\mathbb{R}^{\ell}$ is

$$
\mathscr{E}=\left\{\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{N}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{i N}: \sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i} \mathbf{q}_{i}=0, \mathbf{q}_{i} \neq \mathbf{q}_{j}, \text { for } i \neq j\right\}
$$

Given $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$, a configuration $\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{N}\right) \in \mathscr{E}$ is central if there exists a positive constant $\lambda$ such that

$$
\overline{\mathbf{q}}_{i}=-\lambda \mathbf{q}_{i}, \quad i=1, \ldots, N
$$
that is if the acceleration $\ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{i}$ of each point mass $m_{i}$ is proportional to its position $\mathbf{q}_{i}$ relative to the center of mass of the system and is directed towards the center of mass.

The central configurations of the $N$-body problem are important because they allow the computation of all the homographic solutions; every motion starting and ending in a total collision is asymptotic to a central configuration, and every parabolic motion of the $N$ bodies (i.e. the $N$ bodies tend to infinity as the time tends to infinity with zero radial velocity) is asymptotic to a central configuration (see ); there is a relation between central configurations and the bifurcations of the hypersurfaces of constant energy and angular momentum (see ); etc.

Two central configurations in $\mathbb{R}^{l}$ are in the same class if there exist a rotation and a homothecy of $\mathbb{R}^{l}$ which transform one into the other.

The first known central configurations are the three classes of collinear central configurations for the 3-body problem found in 1767 by Euler . In 1772 Lagrange  proved that when $N=3$, for each values of the masses $m_{1}, m_{2}$ and $m_{3}$, there are two classes of central configurations with the masses located at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. Those five classes are all the classes of central configurations of the 3-body problem. Only partial results on central configurations are known for $N>3$.

A central configuration of $\mathbb{R}^{l}$ is called planar if the configuration of the $N$ bodies is contained in a plane, and it is called spatial if there does not exist a plane containing the configuration of the $N$ bodies.

The simplest known planar central configuration of the $N$-body problem for $N \geqslant 2$ is obtained by taking $N$ equal masses at the vertices of a regular $N$-gon. We cannot find in the literature who was the first in discovering such planar central configurations. If we take $N$ equal masses at the vertices of a regular polyhedron with $N$ vertices, then we obtain a spatial central configuration of the $N$-body problem (see ).

A homographic solution is a solution of the $N$-body problem such that at every time the configuration of the $N$ bodies is central. If the central configuration is planar, then there exist three types of homographic solutions, the homothetic, the relative equilibrium and the composition of both. Let $\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots \mathbf{q}_{N}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{2 N}$ be a planar central configuration. A homothetic solution is of the form $\left(\varrho(t) \mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \varrho(t) \mathbf{q}_{N}\right)$, and a relative equilibrium solution is of the form $\left(A(t) \mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, A(t) \mathbf{q}_{N}\right)$ where $A(t)=\left(\begin{array}{cc}\cos \omega t & \sin \omega t \\ -\sin \omega t & \cos \omega t\end{array}\right)$. For the spatial central configurations the unique possible homographic solutions are the homothetic ones. For more details on homographic motions see Witner .

It is also known the existence of planar central configurations for the $2 n$-body problem where the masses are at the vertices of two nested regular $n$-gons with a common center. In such configurations all the masses on the same $n$-gon are equal but masses on different $n$-gons could be different. It seems that the first in studying these nested planar central configurations was Longley  in 1907, later on in 1927 and 1929 Bilimovitch (see ), and in 1967 Klemplerer  also studied them. More recently they have been also studied in .

We say that two regular polyhedra are nested if they have the same number of vertices $n$, the same center and the positions of the vertices of the inner polyhedron $\mathbf{r}_{i}$ and the ones of the outer polyhedron $\mathbf{R}_{i}$ satisfy the relation $\mathbf{R}_{i}=\rho \mathbf{r}_{i}$ for some scale factor $\rho>1$ and for all $i=1, \ldots, n$.

In this paper we shall prove that for convenient masses at the vertices of two nested regular polyhedra (see Fig. 1) we get spatial central configurations for the $2 n$-body problem in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. As in the planar case all the masses located at the vertices of the same polyhedron must be equal, but masses on different polyhedra could be different. There are five regular polyhedra: the tetrahedron, the octahedron, the cube, the icosahedron and the dodecahedron with $4,6,8,12$ and 20 vertices, respectively. Some preliminary results in this direction restricted to the tetrahedron and octahedron can be found in . Here we give an unified analytic proof for all five regular polyhedra.

The nested regular tetrahedra (octahedra, cube, icosahedra and dodecahedra) central configurations are characterized in Section 2 (3-6, respectively). The main results of these sections are summarized in the following theorem.

Theorem 1. We consider $2 n$ masses at the vertices of two nested regular polyhedra of $n$ vertices, where $n$ can be either $4,6,8,12$ or 20. Assume that the masses of the inner polyhedron are equal to $m_{1}$ and the masses of the outer polyhedron are equal to $m_{2}$. Then given two arbitrary positive values of $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ there exists a unique value of the scale factor $\rho$ of the nested polyhedra for which this configuration is central.

Assume that $\mathbf{q}_{i}=\left(x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$, then the equations of the spatial central configurations given by (1) can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
e x_{i} & =\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{N} \frac{m_{j}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)}{\left(\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{i}-y_{j}\right)^{2}+\left(z_{i}-z_{j}\right)^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\lambda x_{i}=0 \\
e y_{i} & =\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{N} \frac{m_{j}\left(y_{i}-y_{j}\right)}{\left(\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{i}-y_{j}\right)^{2}+\left(z_{i}-z_{j}\right)^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\lambda y_{i}=0 \\
e z_{i} & =\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{N} \frac{m_{j}\left(z_{i}-z_{j}\right)}{\left(\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{i}-y_{j}\right)^{2}+\left(z_{i}-z_{j}\right)^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\lambda z_{i}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

for $i=1, \ldots, N$.



Fig. 1. Nested regular polyhedra.

# 2. Nested tetrahedra 

In this section we study the spatial central configurations of the 8 -body problem when the masses are located at the vertices of two nested tetrahedra. Taking conveniently the unit of masses we can assume that all the masses of the inner tetrahedron are equal to one. We also choose the unit of length in such a way that the edges of the inner tetrahedron have length 2 . Recall that the set of central configurations is invariant under homothecies.

Proposition 2. Consider four equal masses $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=m_{4}=1$ located at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron with edge length 2 having positions $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1}\right)=(-1,-1 / \sqrt{3},-1 / \sqrt{6}),\left(x_{2}, y_{2}, z_{2}\right)=(1,-1 / \sqrt{3},-1 / \sqrt{6}),\left(x_{3}, y_{3}, z_{3}\right)=$ $\left(0,2 / \sqrt{3},-1 / \sqrt{6}\right)$, and $\left(x_{4}, y_{4}, z_{4}\right)=(0,0, \sqrt{3 / 2})$. Consider four additional equal masses $m_{5}=m_{6}=m_{7}=m_{8}=m$ at the vertices of a second nested regular tetrahedron having positions $\left(x_{i+4}, y_{i+4}, z_{i+4}\right)=\rho\left(x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i}\right)$ for $i=1, \ldots, 4$ and $\rho>1$ (see Fig. 1(a)). Then the following statements hold.
(a) Such configuration is central for the spatial 8-body problem when

$$
m=f_{8}(\rho)=\frac{\frac{(2 / 3)^{3 / 2}}{(\rho-1)^{2}}-\frac{\rho}{2}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(3 \rho+1)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}}{-\frac{1 / 2}{\rho^{2}}-\frac{(2 / 3)^{3 / 2} \rho}{(\rho-1)^{2}}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2} \rho(\rho+3)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}}
$$

and $\rho>\alpha=1.8899915758445007 \ldots$, where $\alpha$ is the unique real solution of $f_{8}(\rho)=0$ for $\rho>1$.
(b) For a fixed value of $m>0$ there exists a unique $\rho>\alpha$ for which the nested regular tetrahedra is a central configuration.

Proof. It is easy to check that in the statement of Proposition 2 the positions and the values of the masses have been taken so that the center of mass of the configuration is located at the origin.

We substitute the positions and the values of the masses into (2). After some computations we obtain that $e x_{3}=e x_{4}=$ $e x_{7}=e x_{8}=e y_{4}=e y_{8}=0, e x_{1}=-e x_{2}, e x_{5}=-e x_{6}, e y_{1}=e y_{2}=-e x_{2} / \sqrt{3}, e y_{3}=2 e x_{2} / \sqrt{3}, e y_{5}=e y_{6}=-e x_{6} / \sqrt{3}$, $e y_{7}=2 e x_{6} / \sqrt{3}, e z_{1}=e z_{2}=e z_{3}=-e x_{2} / \sqrt{6}, e z_{4}=\sqrt{3 / 2} e x_{2}, e z_{5}=e z_{6}=e z_{7}=-e x_{6} / \sqrt{6}$ and $e z_{8}=\sqrt{3 / 2} e x_{6}$. Therefore system (2) is equivalent to system

$$
\begin{aligned}
& e x_{2}=-\lambda+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{(2 / 3)^{3 / 2} m}{(\rho-1)^{2}}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2} m(\rho+3)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}=0 \\
& e x_{6}=-\lambda \rho+\frac{m}{2 \rho^{2}}+\frac{(2 / 3)^{3 / 2}}{(\rho-1)^{2}}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(3 \rho+1)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving system (3) with respect to the variables $\lambda$ and $m$ we get $\lambda=a(\rho) / f(\rho)$ and $m=b(\rho) / f(\rho)$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a(\rho)=-\frac{8 / 27}{(\rho-1)^{4}}-\frac{1 / 4}{\rho^{2}}+\frac{8\left(3 \rho^{2}+10 \rho+3\right)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3}}-\frac{16 /(3 \sqrt{3})}{(\rho-1)\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& b(\rho)=\frac{(2 / 3)^{3 / 2}}{(\rho-1)^{2}}-\frac{\rho}{2}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(3 \rho+1)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& f(\rho)=-\frac{1 / 2}{\rho^{2}}-\frac{(2 / 3)^{3 / 2} \rho}{(\rho-1)^{2}}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2} \rho(\rho+3)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\rho>1$ and equation $3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3=0$ has no real solutions, $a(\rho), b(\rho)$ and $f(\rho)$ are well defined for $\rho>1$. The function $f(\rho)$ has no real zeros when $\rho>1$. Indeed $f(\rho)$ can be written as

$$
\frac{36 \sqrt{2}(\rho-1)^{2} \rho^{3}(\rho+3)-\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}\left(4 \sqrt{6} \rho^{3}+9 \rho^{2}-18 \rho+9\right)}{18(\rho-1)^{2} \rho^{2}\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

So $f(\rho)=0$ if and only if

$$
36 \sqrt{2}(\rho-1)^{2} \rho^{3}(\rho+3)=\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}\left(4 \sqrt{6} \rho^{3}+9 \rho^{2}-18 \rho+9\right)
$$

We transform this equation into a polynomial one by squaring both sides of the equality. Solving numerically the resulting polynomial equation we see that there are no real solutions of $f(\rho)=0$ with $\rho>1$, in particular $f(\rho)<0$ for $\rho>1$. Therefore $\lambda$ and $m$ are well defined for $\rho>1$.

The solution of (3) gives a central configuration of the 8 -body problem if and only if $\lambda>0$ and $m>0$. Next we analyze the sign of $\lambda$ and $m$ for $\rho>1$. The function $a(\rho)$ can be written as

$$
a(\rho)=-\frac{a_{1}(\rho)+a_{2}(\rho)}{108(\rho-1)^{4} \rho^{2}\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{9 / 2}}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{1}(\rho)= & 192 \sqrt{3}(\rho-1)^{3} \rho^{2}\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3} \\
a_{2}(\rho)= & \left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}\left(729 \rho^{10}-1458 \rho^{9}-27 \rho^{8}-216 \rho^{7}+24642 \rho^{6}\right. \\
& \left.-30956 \rho^{5}+24642 \rho^{4}-216 \rho^{3}-27 \rho^{2}-1458 \rho+729\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

We solve numerically the polynomial equation $\left(a_{1}(\rho)\right)^{2}=\left(-a_{2}(\rho)\right)^{2}$ and we see that it has no real solutions. Therefore $\lambda$ is always different from zero. In particular it is positive for $\rho>1$.

Finally $b(\rho)$ can be written as

$$
\frac{36 \sqrt{2}(\rho-1)^{2}(3 \rho+1)-\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}\left(9 \rho^{3}-18 \rho^{2}+9 \rho-4 \sqrt{6}\right)}{18(\rho-1)^{2}\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

Solving numerically the equation

$$
\left(36 \sqrt{2}(\rho-1)^{2}(3 \rho+1)\right)^{2}=\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3}\left(9 \rho^{3}-18 \rho^{2}+9 \rho-4 \sqrt{6}\right)^{2}
$$

we see that it has only two real solutions with $\rho>1$, these solutions are $\rho=1.6903479049860676 \ldots$ and $\rho=\alpha=$ 1.8899915758445007 ..., but $\rho=\alpha$ is the unique one that satisfies equation $b(\rho)=0$. Furthermore, $b(\rho)>0$ for $1<\rho<\alpha$ and $b(\rho)<0$ for $\rho>\alpha$, so $m<0$ for $1<\rho<\alpha$, and $m>0$ for $\rho>\alpha$. This proves statement (a).

In order to prove statement (b) it is sufficient to prove that $m$ is an increasing function of $\rho$ for $\rho>\alpha$. The derivative of $m$ with respect to $\rho$ is

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d} m}{\mathrm{~d} \rho}=\frac{1}{f(\rho)^{2}}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~d} b}{\mathrm{~d} \rho}(\rho) f(\rho)-b(\rho) \frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{~d} \rho}(\rho)\right)
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{d} b}{\mathrm{~d} \rho}(\rho)=-\frac{12 \sqrt{2}\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho-1\right)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{2(2 / 3)^{3 / 2}}{(\rho-1)^{3}}-\frac{1}{2} \\
& \frac{\mathrm{~d} f}{\mathrm{~d} \rho}(\rho)=\frac{(2 / 3)^{3 / 2}(\rho+1)}{(\rho-1)^{3}}-\frac{2 \sqrt{2}\left(3 \rho^{3}+17 \rho^{2}-3 \rho-9\right)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{1}{\rho^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

We have seen that $f(\rho)<0$ and $b(\rho)<0$ for $\rho>\alpha$. Since $3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho-1>0$ for $\rho>1, \mathrm{~d} b / \mathrm{d} \rho$ is negative for $\rho>1$. Finally, we solve equation $\mathrm{d} f / \mathrm{d} \rho(\rho)=0$ by proceeding in a similar way as for the resolution of equation $f(\rho)=0$ and we see that this equation has no real zeros for $\rho>1$. In particular, $\mathrm{d} f / \mathrm{d} \rho(\rho)>0$ for $\rho>1$. Therefore $\mathrm{dm} / \mathrm{d} \rho>0$ for $\rho>\alpha$. This proves statement (b).

# 3. Nested octahedra 

In this section we study the spatial central configurations of the 12-body problem when the masses are located at the vertices of two nested octahedra. Taking conveniently the unit of masses we can assume that all the masses of the inner octahedron are equal to one. We also choose the unit of length in such a way that the edges of the inner octahedron have length 2 .

Proposition 3. Consider six equal masses $m_{i}=1$ for $i=1, \ldots, 6$ at the vertices of a regular octahedron with edge length 2 having positions $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1}\right)=(1,0,0),\left(x_{2}, y_{2}, z_{2}\right)=(-1,0,0),\left(x_{3}, y_{3}, z_{3}\right)=(0,1,0),\left(x_{4}, y_{4}, z_{4}\right)=(0,-1,0)$, $\left(x_{5}, y_{5}, z_{5}\right)=(0,0,1),\left(x_{6}, y_{6}, z_{6}\right)=(0,0,-1)$. Consider six additional equal masses $m_{i}=m$ for $i=7, \ldots, 12$ at the vertices of a second nested regular octahedron having positions $\left(x_{i+6}, y_{i+6}, z_{i+6}\right)=\rho\left(x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i}\right)$ for $i=1, \ldots, 6$ and $\rho>1$ (see Fig. 1(b)). Then the following statements hold.
(a) Such configuration is central for the spatial 12-body problem when

$$
m=f_{12}(\rho)=\frac{\frac{4 \rho}{\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{(1+4 \sqrt{2}) \rho}{4}+\frac{2\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)}{\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}}{-\frac{4 \rho^{2}}{\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}+\frac{4 \rho}{\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1+4 \sqrt{2}}{4 \rho^{2}}}
$$

and $\rho>\alpha=1.7298565115043054 \ldots$, where $\alpha$ is the unique real solution of $f_{12}(\rho)=0$ for $\rho>1$.
(b) For a fixed value of $m>0$ there exists a unique $\rho>\alpha$ for which the nested regular octahedra is a central configuration.

Proof. It is easy to check that the center of mass of the configuration defined in Proposition 3 is at the origin. We substitute the positions and the values of the masses into (2). After some computations we get that $e x_{3}=e x_{4}=e x_{5}=e x_{6}=e x_{9}=$ $e x_{10}=e x_{11}=e x_{12}=e y_{1}=e y_{2}=e y_{5}=e y_{6}=e y_{7}=e y_{8}=e y_{11}=e y_{12}=e z_{1}=e z_{2}=e z_{3}=e z_{4}=e z_{7}=e z_{8}=e z_{9}=$ $e z_{10}=0, e y_{3}=e z_{5}=e x_{1}, e x_{2}=e y_{4}=e z_{6}=-e x_{1}, e y_{9}=e z_{11}=e x_{7}$, and $e x_{8}=e y_{10}=e z_{12}=-e x_{7}$. Therefore system (2) is equivalent to system

$$
\begin{aligned}
& e x_{1}=\frac{4 m}{\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{4 \rho m}{\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}-\lambda+\sqrt{2}+\frac{1}{4}=0 \\
& e x_{7}=\frac{(1 / 4+\sqrt{2}) m}{\rho^{2}}-\lambda \rho+\frac{2\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)}{\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}+\frac{4 \rho}{\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving system (5) with respect to the variables $\lambda$ and $m$ we get $\lambda=a(\rho) / f(\rho)$ and $m=b(\rho) / f(\rho)$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a(\rho)=\frac{16 \rho}{\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3}}-\frac{8\left(\rho^{3}+\rho\right)}{\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{4}}-\frac{8}{\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{33+8 \sqrt{2}}{16 \rho^{2}} \\
& b(\rho)=\frac{4 \rho}{\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{(1+4 \sqrt{2}) \rho}{4}+\frac{2\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)}{\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}} \\
& f(\rho)=-\frac{4 \rho^{2}}{\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}+\frac{4 \rho}{\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1+4 \sqrt{2}}{4 \rho^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\rho>1, a(\rho), b(\rho)$ and $f(\rho)$ are well defined for $\rho>1$. The function $f(\rho)$ can be written as

$$
f(\rho)=\frac{f_{1}(\rho)-f_{2}(\rho)}{4(\rho-1)^{2} \rho^{2}(\rho+1)^{2}\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f_{1}(\rho)=16 \rho^{3}\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2} \\
& f_{2}(\rho)=\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}((17+4 \sqrt{2}) \rho^{4}-2(1+4 \sqrt{2}) \rho^{2}+1+4 \sqrt{2})
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving numerically the polynomial equation $\left(f_{1}(\rho)\right)^{2}=\left(f_{2}(\rho)\right)^{2}$ we see that $f(\rho)=0$ has no real solutions when $\rho>1$, in particular $f(\rho)<0$ for $\rho>1$. Therefore $\lambda$ and $m$ are well defined for $\rho>1$.

We can write

$$
a(\rho)=-\frac{a_{1}(\rho)+a_{2}(\rho)}{16(\rho-1)^{4} \rho^{2}(\rho+1)^{4}\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{9 / 2}}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{1}(\rho)= & 128 \rho^{2}\left(\rho^{4}-1\right)^{3} \\
a_{2}(\rho)= & \left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}((33+8 \sqrt{2}) \rho^{14}-(33+8 \sqrt{2}) \rho^{12}-128 \rho^{11} \\
& -3(33+8 \sqrt{2}) \rho^{10}+1536 \rho^{9}+3(33+8 \sqrt{2}) \rho^{8}-768 \rho^{7} \\
& +3(33+8 \sqrt{2}) \rho^{6}+1536 \rho^{5}-3(33+8 \sqrt{2}) \rho^{4}-128 \rho^{3}-(33+8 \sqrt{2}) \rho^{2}+33+8 \sqrt{2})
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving numerically the polynomial equation $\left(a_{1}(\rho)\right)^{2}=\left(-a_{2}(\rho)\right)^{2}$ we see that $a(\rho)$ has no real solutions for $\rho>1$. Therefore $\lambda$ is different from zero for $\rho>1$. In particular it is positive for $\rho>1$.

Finally we have

$$
b(\rho)=\frac{b_{1}(\rho)-b_{2}(\rho)}{4(\rho-1)^{2}(\rho+1)^{2}\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& b_{1}(\rho)=16 \rho\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2} \\
& b_{2}(\rho)=\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\left((1+4 \sqrt{2}) \rho^{5}-2(1+4 \sqrt{2}) \rho^{3}-8 \rho^{2}+4 \sqrt{2} \rho+\rho-8\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

We solve numerically equation $\left(b_{1}(\rho)\right)^{2}=\left(b_{2}(\rho)\right)^{2}$ and we see that it has only two real roots with $\rho>1$, they are $\rho=1.5419308914910530 \ldots$ and $\rho=\alpha=1.7298565115043054 \ldots$, but $\rho=\alpha$ is the unique one that satisfies equation $b(\rho)=0$. Furthermore, $b(\rho)>0$ for $1<\rho<\alpha$ and $b(\rho)<0$ for $\rho>\alpha$, so $m<0$ for $1<\rho<\alpha$, and $m>0$ for $\rho>\alpha$. This proves statement (a).

In order to prove statement (b) we proceed as in Section 2. The derivative $\mathrm{d} m / \mathrm{d} \rho$ is given by (4) where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{d} b}{\mathrm{~d} \rho}(\rho)=-\frac{4 \rho\left(\rho^{2}+3\right)}{\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{3}}-\frac{8 \rho^{2}-4}{\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{5 / 2}}-\sqrt{2}-\frac{1}{4} \\
& \frac{\mathrm{~d} f}{\mathrm{~d} \rho}(\rho)=\frac{4-8 \rho^{2}}{\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{8\left(\rho^{3}+\rho\right)}{\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{3}}+\frac{1+4 \sqrt{2}}{2 \rho^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

As above $f(\rho)<0$ and $b(\rho)<0$ for $\rho>\alpha$. Since $8 \rho^{2}-4>0$ for $\rho>1, \mathrm{~d} b / \mathrm{d} \rho$ is negative for $\rho>1$. We solve equation $\mathrm{d} f / \mathrm{d} \rho(\rho)=0$ by proceeding in a similar way as for the resolution of equation $f(\rho)=0$ and we get that it has no real solutions for $\rho>1$, in particular $\mathrm{d} f / \mathrm{d} \rho(\rho)>0$ for $\rho>1$. Therefore $m$ is increasing for $\rho>\alpha$. This proves statement (b).

# 4. Nested cube 

In this section we study the spatial central configurations of the 16-body problem when the masses are located at the vertices of two nested cubes. Taking conveniently the unit of masses we can assume that all the masses of the inner cube are equal to one. We also choose the unit of length in such a way that the edges of the inner cube have length 2 .

Proposition 4. Consider eight equal masses $m_{i}=1$ for $i=1, \ldots, 8$ at the vertices of a regular cube with edge length 2 having positions $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1}\right)=(1,1,1),\left(x_{2}, y_{2}, z_{2}\right)=(1,1,-1),\left(x_{3}, y_{3}, z_{3}\right)=(1,-1,1),\left(x_{4}, y_{4}, z_{4}\right)=(-1,1,1),\left(x_{5}, y_{5}, z_{5}\right)=$ $(1,-1,-1),\left(x_{6}, y_{6}, z_{6}\right)=(-1,1,-1),\left(x_{7}, y_{7}, z_{7}\right)=(-1,-1,1)$, and $\left(x_{8}, y_{8}, z_{8}\right)=(-1,-1,-1)$. Consider eight additional equal masses $m_{i}=m$ for $i=9, \ldots, 16$ at the vertices of a second nested regular cube having positions $\left(x_{i+8}, y_{i+8}, z_{i+8}\right)=\rho\left(x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i}\right)$ for $i=1, \ldots, 8$ and $\rho>1$ (see Fig. 1(c)). Then the following statements hold.
(a) Such configuration is central for the spatial 16-body problem when $m=b(\rho) / f(\rho)$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& b(\rho)=-\frac{1}{72}(18+9 \sqrt{2}+2 \sqrt{3}) \rho+\frac{2\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)}{3 \sqrt{3}\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}+\frac{3 \rho-1}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{3 \rho+1}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& f(\rho)=-\frac{18+9 \sqrt{2}+2 \sqrt{3}}{72 \rho^{2}}-\frac{4 \rho^{2}}{3 \sqrt{3}\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}-\frac{(\rho-3) \rho}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{(\rho+3) \rho}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

and $\rho>\alpha=1.643646762940176 \ldots$ where $\alpha$ is the unique real solution of $b(\rho)=0$ for $\rho>1$.

(b) For a fixed value of $m>0$ there exists a unique $\rho>\alpha$ for which the nested regular cube is a central configuration.

Proof. It is easy to check that the center of mass of the configuration defined in Proposition 4 is at the origin. We substitute the positions and the values of the masses into (2). After some computations we obtain that $e x_{2}=e x_{3}=e x_{5}=e y_{1}=$ $e y_{2}=e y_{4}=e y_{6}=e z_{1}=e z_{3}=e z_{4}=e z_{7}=e x_{1}, e x_{4}=e x_{6}=e x_{7}=e x_{8}=e y_{3}=e y_{5}=e y_{7}=e y_{8}=e z_{2}=$ $e z_{5}=e z_{6}=e z_{8}=-e x_{1}, e x_{10}=e x_{11}=e x_{13}=e y_{9}=e y_{10}=e y_{12}=e y_{14}=e z_{9}=e z_{11}=e z_{12}=e z_{15}=e x_{9}$, and $e x_{12}=e x_{14}=e x_{15}=e x_{16}=e y_{11}=e y_{13}=e y_{15}=e y_{16}=e z_{10}=e z_{13}=e z_{14}=e z_{16}=-e x_{9}$. Therefore system (2) is equivalent to system

$$
\begin{aligned}
& e x_{1}=\frac{1}{72}(18+9 \sqrt{2}+2 \sqrt{3})-\lambda-\frac{4 m \rho}{3 \sqrt{3}\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}-\frac{m(\rho-3)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{m(\rho+3)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}=0 \\
& e x_{9}=\frac{(18+9 \sqrt{2}+2 \sqrt{3}) m}{72 \rho^{2}}-\lambda \rho+\frac{2\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)}{3 \sqrt{3}\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}+\frac{3 \rho-1}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{3 \rho+1}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving system (6) with respect to the variables $\lambda$ and $m$ we get $\lambda=a(\rho) / f(\rho)$ and $m=b(\rho) / f(\rho)$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}
a(\rho)= & -\frac{83+54 \sqrt{2}+12 \sqrt{3}+6 \sqrt{6}}{864 \rho^{2}}-\frac{8\left(\rho^{3}+\rho\right)}{27\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{4}}+\frac{3 \rho^{2}+10 \rho+3}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3}}-\frac{3 \rho^{2}-10 \rho+3}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3}} \\
& -\frac{2(\rho+3)}{3 \sqrt{3}\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{2(\rho-3)}{3 \sqrt{3}\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& +\frac{16 \rho}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\rho>1$ and equations $3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3=0$ and $3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3=0$ have no real solutions, $a(\rho), b(\rho)$ and $f(\rho)$ are well defined for $\rho>1$. Next we find the real zeros of $f(\rho)$ when $\rho>1$. The function $f(\rho)$ can be written as

$$
f_{1}(\rho) /\left(72(\rho-1)^{2} \rho^{2}(\rho+1)^{2}\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}\right)
$$

where $f_{1}(\rho)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 72\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2} \rho^{3}\left[(\rho+3)\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}-(\rho-3)\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}\right] \\
& \quad-\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{3 / 2}\left((18+9 \sqrt{2}+34 \sqrt{3}\right) \rho^{4} \\
& \quad-2(18+9 \sqrt{2}+2 \sqrt{3}) \rho^{2}+18+9 \sqrt{2}+2 \sqrt{3})
\end{aligned}
$$

Then $f(\rho)=0$ if and only $f_{1}(\rho)=0$. Notice that equation $f_{1}(\rho)=0$ can be written as

$$
g_{1}(\rho) \sqrt{G_{1}(\rho)}+g_{2}(\rho) \sqrt{G_{2}(\rho)}=g_{3}(\rho) \sqrt{G_{1}(\rho) G_{2}(\rho)}
$$

Squaring both sides of this equation we get

$$
g_{1}(\rho)^{2} G_{1}(\rho)+g_{2}(\rho)^{2} G_{2}(\rho)-g_{3}(\rho)^{2} G_{1}(\rho) G_{2}(\rho)=-2 g_{1}(\rho) g_{2}(\rho) \sqrt{G_{1}(\rho) G_{2}(\rho)}
$$

Squaring again both sides of the last equation we get a polynomial equation. We solve it numerically and we see that it has a unique real solution $\rho=4.26968682884071 \ldots$ with $\rho>1$ which is not a solution of the initial equation $f_{1}(\rho)=0$. Therefore $f(\rho)=0$ has no real solutions with $\rho>1$ and consequently $\lambda$ and $m$ are well defined for $\rho>1$. Moreover $f(\rho)<0$ for $\rho>1$.

Repeating the same arguments for $b(\rho)$ we see that $b(\rho)$ has a unique real zero when $\rho>1$ which is given by $\rho=\alpha=1.643646762940176 \ldots$. Furthermore, $b(\rho)>0$ for $1<\rho<\alpha$ and $b(\rho)<0$ for $\rho>\alpha$, so $m<0$ for $1<\rho<\alpha$, and $m>0$ for $\rho>\alpha$.

Let $a_{1}(\rho)$ be the numerator of $a(\rho)$. It is easy to check that $a_{1}(\rho)=0$ can be written as

$$
g_{1}(\rho) \sqrt{G_{1}(\rho)}+g_{2}(\rho) \sqrt{G_{2}(\rho)}=g_{3}(\rho) \sqrt{G_{1}(\rho) G_{2}(\rho)}+g_{4}(\rho)
$$

Squaring both sides of this equation we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& g_{1}(\rho)^{2} G_{1}(\rho)+g_{2}(\rho)^{2} G_{2}(\rho)-g_{3}(\rho)^{2} G_{1}(\rho) G_{2}(\rho)-g_{4}(\rho)^{2} \\
& \quad=-\left(2 g_{1}(\rho) g_{2}(\rho)+2 g_{3}(\rho) g_{4}(\rho)\right) \sqrt{G_{1}(\rho) G_{2}(\rho)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring again both sides of the last equation we get a polynomial equation. We solve it numerically and we see that it has no real solutions with $\rho>1$. Therefore $a(\rho)$ is different from zero for $\rho>1$. This proves statement (a).

Now we prove statement (b). The derivative $\mathrm{d} m / \mathrm{d} \rho$ is given by (4) where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{d} b}{\mathrm{~d} \rho}(\rho)=-\frac{4 \rho\left(\rho^{2}+3\right)}{3 \sqrt{3}\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{3}}-\frac{18 \rho^{2}-12 \rho-6}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{5 / 2}}-\frac{6\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho-1\right)}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{5 / 2}}-\frac{1}{72}(18+9 \sqrt{2}+2 \sqrt{3}) \\
& \frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{~d} \rho}(\rho)=\frac{8 \rho\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)}{3 \sqrt{3}\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{3}}-\frac{3 \rho^{3}+17 \rho^{2}-3 \rho-9}{\left(3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho+3\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{3 \rho^{3}-17 \rho^{2}-3 \rho+9}{\left(3 \rho^{2}-2 \rho+3\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{18+9 \sqrt{2}+2 \sqrt{3}}{36 \rho^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

We have seen that $f(\rho)<0$ and $b(\rho)<0$ for $\rho>\alpha$. Since $18 \rho^{2}-12 \rho-6>0$ and $3 \rho^{2}+2 \rho-1>0$ for $\rho>1, \mathrm{~d} b / \mathrm{d} \rho$ is negative for $\rho>1$. Finally, we solve equation $\mathrm{d} f / \mathrm{d} \rho(\rho)=0$ by proceeding in a similar way as for the resolution of equation $f(\rho)=0$ and we get that it has no real zeros for $\rho>1$, in particular $\mathrm{d} f / \mathrm{d} \rho(\rho)>0$ for $\rho>1$. Therefore $\mathrm{d} m / \mathrm{d} \rho>0$ for $\rho>\alpha$. This proves statement (b).

# 5. Nested icosahedra 

In this section we study the spatial central configurations of the 24-body problem when the masses are located at the vertices of two nested icosahedra. Taking conveniently the unit of masses we can assume that all the masses of the inner icosahedron are equal to one. We also choose the unit of length in such a way that the edges of the inner icosahedron have length 2 .

Proposition 5. Consider twelve equal masses $m_{i}=1$ for $i=1, \ldots, 12$ located at the vertices of a regular icosahedron with edge length 2 having positions $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1}\right)=(0,1, \phi),\left(x_{2}, y_{2}, z_{2}\right)=(0,1,-\phi),\left(x_{3}, y_{3}, z_{3}\right)=(0,-1, \phi),\left(x_{4}, y_{4}, z_{4}\right)=$ $(0,-1,-\phi),\left(x_{5}, y_{5}, z_{5}\right)=(1, \phi, 0),\left(x_{6}, y_{6}, z_{6}\right)=(1,-\phi, 0),\left(x_{7}, y_{7}, z_{7}\right)=(-1, \phi, 0),\left(x_{8}, y_{8}, z_{8}\right)=(-1,-\phi, 0)$, $\left(x_{9}, y_{9}, z_{9}\right)=(\phi, 0,1),\left(x_{10}, y_{10}, z_{10}\right)=(\phi, 0,-1),\left(x_{11}, y_{11}, z_{11}\right)=(-\phi, 0,1)$, and $\left(x_{12}, y_{12}, z_{12}\right)=(-\phi, 0,-1)$, where $\phi=(1+\sqrt{5}) / 2$ is the golden ratio. Consider twelve additional equal masses $m_{i}=m$ for $i=12, \ldots, 24$ at the vertices of a second nested regular icosahedron having positions $\left(x_{i+12}, y_{i+12}, z_{i+12}\right)=\rho\left(x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i}\right)$ for $i=1, \ldots, 12$ and $\rho>1$ (see Fig. 1(d)). Then the following statements hold.
(a) Such configuration is central for the spatial 24-body problem when $m=b(\rho) / f(\rho)$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& b(\rho)=\frac{2 \sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5}}\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)}{5\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}-\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(\sqrt{5}-5 \rho)}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}-4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(5 \rho+\sqrt{5})}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}+4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1}{20}(5 \sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5}}) \rho \\
& f(\rho)=-\frac{4 \sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5}} \rho^{2}}{5\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}-\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(\sqrt{5} \rho-5) \rho}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}-4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(\sqrt{5} \rho+5) \rho}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}+4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{5 \sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5}}}{20 \rho^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

$\varphi=5+\sqrt{5}$ and $\rho>\alpha=1.549351115672993 \ldots$ where $\alpha$ is the unique real solution of $b(\rho)=0$.
(b) For a fixed value of $m>0$ there exists a unique $\rho>\alpha$ for which the nested regular icosahedra is a central configuration.

Proof. It is easy to check that the center of mass of the configuration defined in Proposition 5 is at the origin. We substitute the positions and the values of the masses into (2). After some computations we get that $e x_{1}=e x_{2}=e x_{3}=e x_{4}=e x_{13}=$ $e x_{14}=e x_{15}=e x_{16}=e y_{9}=e y_{10}=e y_{11}=e y_{12}=e y_{21}=e y_{22}=e y_{23}=e y_{24}=e z_{5}=e z_{6}=e z_{7}=e z_{8}=e z_{17}=$ $e z_{18}=e z_{19}=e z_{20}=0, e x_{6}=e y_{1}=e y_{2}=e z_{9}=e z_{11}=e x_{5}, e x_{7}=e x_{8}=e y_{3}=e y_{4}=e z_{10}=e z_{12}=-e x_{5}$, $e x_{9}=e x_{10}=e y_{5}=e y_{7}=e z_{1}=e z_{3}=\phi e x_{5}, e x_{11}=e x_{12}=e y_{6}=e y_{8}=e z_{2}=e z_{4}=-\phi e x_{5}, e x_{18}=e y_{13}=e y_{14}=$ $e z_{21}=e z_{23}=e x_{17}, e x_{19}=e x_{20}=e y_{15}=e y_{16}=e z_{22}=e z_{24}=-e x_{17}, e x_{21}=e x_{22}=e y_{17}=e y_{19}=e z_{13}=e z_{15}=\phi e x_{17}$, and $e x_{23}=e x_{24}=e y_{18}=e y_{20}=e z_{14}=e z_{16}=-\phi e x_{17}$. Therefore system (2) is equivalent to system

$$
\begin{aligned}
& e x_{5}=-\lambda-\frac{2 \sqrt{2} m(\sqrt{5} \rho-5)}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}-4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2} m(\sqrt{5} \rho+5)}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}+4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{4 \sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5}} m \rho}{5\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}+\frac{1}{20}(5 \sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5}}) \\
& e x_{17}=\frac{(5 \sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5}}) m}{20 \rho^{2}}-\lambda \rho+\frac{2 \sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5}}\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)}{5\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{2}}-\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(\sqrt{5}-5 \rho)}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}-4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(5 \rho+\sqrt{5})}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}+4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving system (7) with respect to the variables $\lambda$ and $m$ we get $\lambda=a(\rho) / f(\rho)$ and $m=b(\rho) / f(\rho)$ where $a(\rho)$ is given by

$$
\frac{8(2 \sqrt{5}-5)\left(\rho^{2}+1\right) \rho}{25\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{4}}-\frac{65-\sqrt{5}+5 \sqrt{5(5-2 \sqrt{5})}}{200 \rho^{2}}-\frac{4 \sqrt{10-4 \sqrt{5}}(\sqrt{5} \rho+5)}{5\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)\left(\varphi \rho^{2}-4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& +\frac{4 \sqrt{10-4 \sqrt{5}}(\sqrt{5} \rho-5)}{5\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)\left(\varphi \rho^{2}+4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{40\left(\sqrt{5} \rho^{2}-6 \rho+\sqrt{5}\right)}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}-4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3}}+\frac{40\left(\sqrt{5} \rho^{2}+6 \rho+\sqrt{5}\right)}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}+4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3}} \\
& +\frac{320 \rho}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}-4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3 / 2}\left(\varphi \rho^{2}+4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\rho>1$ and equations $\varphi \rho^{2}+4 \phi \rho+\varphi=0$, and $\varphi \rho^{2}-4 \phi \rho+\varphi=0=0$ have no real solutions, $a(\rho), b(\rho)$ and $f(\rho)$ are well defined for $\rho>1$. We proceed as in Section 4 and after doing a lot of tedious computations we prove that $f(\rho)<0$ for $\rho>1$, so $\lambda$ and $m$ are well defined for $\rho>1$. We also prove that $a(\rho)$ has no real zeros when $\rho>1$ and that $b(\rho)$ has a unique real zero when $\rho>1$ which is given by $\rho=\alpha=1.549351115672993 \ldots$. Furthermore, $b(\rho)>0$ for $1<\rho<\alpha$ and $b(\rho)<0$ for $\rho>\alpha$, so $m<0$ for $1<\rho<\alpha$, and $m>0$ for $\rho>\alpha$. This proves statement (a).

Now we prove statement (b). The derivative $\mathrm{d} m / \mathrm{d} \rho$ is given by (4) where

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} b}{\mathrm{~d} \rho}(\rho)= & -\frac{4 \sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5} \rho}\left(\rho^{2}+3\right)}{5\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{3}}-\frac{4 \sqrt{2}\left(5 \varphi \rho^{2}-20 \phi \rho-\varphi\right)}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}-4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{5 / 2}}-\frac{4 \sqrt{2}\left(5 \varphi \rho^{2}+20 \phi \rho-\varphi\right)}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}+4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{5 / 2}} \\
& -\frac{1}{20}(5 \sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5}}) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{~d} \rho}(\rho)= & \frac{8 \sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5} \rho}\left(\rho^{2}+1\right)}{5\left(\rho^{2}-1\right)^{3}}+\frac{2 \sqrt{2}\left(10 \phi \rho^{3}-9 \varphi \rho^{2}-10 \phi \rho+5 \varphi\right)}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}-4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{5 / 2}} \\
& -\frac{2 \sqrt{2}\left(10 \phi \rho^{3}+9 \varphi \rho^{2}-10 \phi \rho-5 \varphi\right)}{\left(\varphi \rho^{2}+4 \phi \rho+\varphi\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{5 \sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5}}}{10 \rho^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

We have seen that $f(\rho)<0$ and $b(\rho)<0$ for $\rho>\alpha$. We solve equations $\mathrm{d} b / \mathrm{d} \rho(\rho)=0$ and $\mathrm{d} f / \mathrm{d} \rho(\rho)=0$ by proceeding in a similar way as for the resolution of equation $f(\rho)=0$ and we get that they have no real solutions with $\rho>1$. In particular, $\mathrm{d} b / \mathrm{d} \rho(\rho)<0$ and $\mathrm{d} f / \mathrm{d} \rho(\rho)>0$ for $\rho>1$. Therefore $\mathrm{d} m / \mathrm{d} \rho>0$ for $\rho>\alpha$. This proves statement (b).

# 6. Nested dodecahedra 

In this section we study the spatial central configurations of the 40 -body problem when the masses are located at the vertices of two nested dodecahedra. Taking conveniently the unit of masses we can assume that all the masses of the inner dodecahedron are equal to one. We also choose the unit of length in such a way that the edges of the inner dodecahedron have length 2 .

Proposition 6.
