- Property 2. Every isolated solution of $H(x, 1)=P(x)=0$ can be reached by some path originating at $t=0$, that is, the path starts from a solution of the start system $H(x, 0)=Q(x)=0$.
A typical choice of a start system $Q(x)=0$ satisfying Property $0-2$ is

$$
Q(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{c}
q_{1}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)=a_{1} x_{1}^{d_{1}}-b_{1} \\
\vdots \\
q_{n}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)=a_{n} x_{n}^{d_{n}}-b_{n}
\end{array}\right.
$$



Figure 1: The solution set of classical homotopy.
where $d_{1}, \cdots, d_{n}$ are the degrees of polynomials $p_{1}(x), \ldots, p_{n}(x)$ respectively, and $a_{j}, b_{j}, j=1, \cdots, n$ are random complex numbers . The solutions of such start system $Q(x)=0$ can be explicitly obtained and the total number of solutions is $d=d_{1} \times d_{2} \times \cdots \times d_{n}$, which is known as the total degree or the Bézout number of the original polynomial system $P(x)=0$. We may then find all the isolated solutions of $P(x)=0$ by following the total degree number of paths originated from solutions of the start system $Q(x)=0$. But, a great majority of the polynomial systems arising in applications have fewer than, and in some cases only a small fraction of, $d=d_{1} \times$ $\cdots \times d_{n}$ isolated zeros. We call such a system deficient. In this case, many of the $d_{1} \times \cdots \times d_{n}$ paths will diverge to infinity as $t \rightarrow 1$ (see Figure 1), and those paths become extraneous, causing highly wasteful computations.

In the middle of 1990's, a major computational breakthrough emerged in solving deficient polynomial systems. The new method, called the polyhedral homotopy continuation method , takes a great advantage of the combinatorial root count, called mixed volume, in the Bernshteín's theorem , which generally provides a much tighter bound for the number of isolated zeros of a polynomial system in the algebraic torus $\left(\mathbb{C}^{*}\right)^{n}=(\mathbb{C} \backslash\{0\})^{n}$. When this method is employed, the number of homotopy paths that need to be traced agrees with the mixed volume of the polynomial system. Therefore, when the mixed volume of a polynomial system is far less than its total degree, the method will greatly reduce the extraneous paths and thereby considerably limit the wasteful computations.

However, this method involves a sometimes costly computation - the mixed cell computation. This mixed cell computation can become very costly for large polynomial systems. In 2005, a software package, MixedVol , emerged which led the existing codes for the mixed volume computation by a great margin in speed. However, soon after MixedVol was published, Mizutani, Takeda, and Kojima  developed a more

efficient algorithm which considerably outperformed MixedVol. Most recently Lee and Li  embedded the novel idea of dynamic enumeration of mixed cells of Mizutani, Takeda, and Kojima  into MixedVol and a new code, MixedVol-2.0, was produced which regained the lead by a substantial margin.

The software package HOM4PS , developed over the years by the group led by T. Y. Li at Michigan State University, implemented the polyhedral homotopy continuation method for solving polynomial systems. The code was widely considered as the most efficient polynomial systems solver. Recently many new curves tracing techniques and mixed cell computation algorithms, such as MixedVol-2.0 mentioned above, have been included in HOM4PS-2.0. By incorporating these new algorithms HOM4PS-2.0 is (as reported in ), in general, at least one order of magnitude faster than HOM4PS, as well as from one to three orders of magnitude faster than PHCpack , PHoM  and Bertini . Consequently, some large size polynomial systems can be solved in a reasonable number of hours. However, as the size of the polynomial system becomes larger, we need more computing resources to solve the system more efficiently. A natural way to attain more computing resources is to parallelize the homotopy continuation method which seems to be naturally parallel in the sense that each isolated zero is computed independently of the others. The parallel version of HOM4PS-2.0, HOM4PS-2.0para, has also been developed. Its excellent scalability in numerical results are reported in .

# 4 Computing central configurations 

The Albouy-Chenciner equations for the five-body problem with equal masses form a polynomial system consisting of 20 equations in 20 variables. For finding all the isolated solutions in complex field, the polyhedral homotopy method needs to trace $439,690,761$ curves. In order to trace so many curves efficiently, we use the subroutines in the MPI library (message passing interface ) to distribute data over multiple CPUs for parallel computation and we use the kernel of HOM4PS-2.0 to construct polyhedral homotopies and trace curves. Employing 32 Itanium 21.6 GHz CPUs, the computation is completed in 140 hours. As a result we obtain $101,062,826$ solutions in the complex field, 8775 of which are real solutions. Among those real solutions only 258 satisfy the physical condition (i.e. $r_{i j}>0$ for all $1 \leq i<j \leq 5$ ). We assume that any numerical solution with imaginary parts less than the threshold $\theta=10^{-7}$ corresponds to a real solution of the Albouy-Chenciner equations. This is reasonable since the set of real solutions remains the same when the threshold $\theta$ is chosen between $10^{-13}$ and $10^{-3}$. In addition, the residuals of the physical solutions are less than $2 \times 10^{-14}$ and their condition numbers are at most $3.8 \times 10^{2}$, which show that these solutions are numerically reliable.

To guarantee that in a small neighborhood of each numerical solution there is a unique exact physical solution, the interval Krawczyk method  is applied for verification. The method is based on the fact: For a smooth function $F: \mathbb{R}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and a point $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, let $\left\lceil\mathbf{x}\right\rceil_{r} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be the interval set centered at $\mathbf{x}$ with radius $r>0$. Namely,

$$
\lceil\mathbf{x}\rceil_{r}=\left\{\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}:\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|_{\infty} \leq r\right\}
$$

where $\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ is the infinity norm. Assume the derivative of $F$ at $\mathbf{x}$, denoted by $D F(\mathbf{x})$, is nonsingular, the Krawczyk set of $F$ associated with $[\mathbf{x}]_{r}$ is defined as

$$
K\left(F,[\mathbf{x}]_{r}\right)=\mathbf{x}-D F(\mathbf{x})^{-1} F(\mathbf{x})+\left[I-D F(\mathbf{x})^{-1} D F([\mathbf{x}]_{r})\right]\left([\mathbf{x}]_{r}-\mathbf{x}\right)
$$

If the Krawczyk set is contained in the interior of $[\mathbf{x}]_{r}$, then there exists a unique zero of $F$ in $[\mathbf{x}]_{r}$.

The task of verification is implemented by using the interval arithmetic in INTLAB (INTerval LABoratory) , developed by Siegfried M. Rump at Hamburg University of Technology, Germany. In this implementation each numerical solution $\mathbf{x}$ is taken as the midpoint of the interval set $[\mathbf{x}]_{r}$ with radius $r=10^{-8}$. The numerical solutions obtained by running HOM4PS-2.0 and the results of verification by using INTLAB are available for download at http://hom4ps.math.msu.edu/Nbody.htm.

# 5 Central Configurations of the 5 body problem 

In this section we present all the central configurations of the five-body problem with equal masses classified according to their dimensions. The dimension of the configuration was deduced by using Cayley-Menger determinants . For instance the CayleyMenger determinant for the volume $V$ of the four-dimensional simplex is

$$
-9216 V^{2}=\left|\begin{array}{cccccc}
0 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & r_{12}^{2} & r_{13}^{2} & r_{14}^{2} & r_{15}^{2} \\
1 & r_{12}^{2} & 0 & r_{23}^{2} & r_{24}^{2} & r_{25}^{2} \\
1 & r_{13}^{2} & r_{23}^{2} & 0 & r_{34}^{2} & r_{35}^{2} \\
1 & r_{14}^{2} & r_{24}^{2} & r_{34}^{2} & 0 & r_{45}^{2} \\
1 & r_{15}^{2} & r_{25}^{2} & r_{35}^{2} & r_{45}^{2} & 0
\end{array}\right|
$$

Configurations of dimension three or less were found by setting the determinant above to zero. Configurations of dimension two or less were found by setting to zero the determinant above plus the following determinants

$$
\left|\begin{array}{cccccc}
0 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & r_{12}^{2} & r_{13}^{2} & r_{14}^{2} \\
1 & r_{12}^{2} & 0 & r_{23}^{2} & r_{24}^{2} \\
1 & r_{13}^{2} & r_{23}^{2} & 0 & r_{34}^{2} \\
1 & r_{14}^{2} & r_{24}^{2} & r_{34}^{2} & 0
\end{array}\right|,\left|\begin{array}{cccccc}
0 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & r_{12}^{2} & r_{13}^{2} & r_{15}^{2} \\
1 & r_{12}^{2} & 0 & r_{23}^{2} & r_{25}^{2} \\
1 & r_{13}^{2} & r_{23}^{2} & 0 & r_{35}^{2} \\
1 & r_{14}^{2} & r_{24}^{2} & r_{35}^{2} & 0
\end{array}\right|,\left|\begin{array}{cccccc}
0 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & r_{23}^{2} & r_{24}^{2} & r_{25}^{2} \\
1 & r_{23}^{2} & 0 & r_{34}^{2} & r_{35}^{2} \\
1 & r_{24}^{2} & r_{34}^{2} & 0 & r_{45}^{2} \\
1 & r_{25}^{2} & r_{35}^{2} & r_{45}^{2} & 0
\end{array}\right|
$$

where, for example, the first of the three determinants above is the Cayley-Menger determinants for the tetrahedron formed by the masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}$ and $m_{4}$. One-dimensional configurations were obtained by setting to zero, in addition to the four Cayley-Menger determinants above, the ten Cayley-Menger determinants corresponding to all the possible triangles formed by a subset of three of the five masses. One of the ten determinants is

$$
-16 A^{2}=\left|\begin{array}{cccc}
0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & r_{12}^{2} & r_{13}^{2} \\
1 & r_{12}^{2} & 0 & r_{23}^{2} \\
1 & r_{13}^{2} & r_{23}^{2} & 0
\end{array}\right|
$$



Figure 2: Planar central configurations of the five body problem with equal masses.
where $A$ is the area for a plane triangle with side lengths $r_{12}, r_{13}$ and $r_{23}$.

# 5.1 Collinear and four-dimensional central configurations 

A complete count of the collinear central configurations has been known for almost one century. In 1910 Moulton  proved that there is a unique central configuration corresponding to each possible ordering of $n$ masses along a line, and thus there are $n!/ 2$ collinear central configurations. In 1970 Smale used tools of the theory of dynamical systems to give a modern proof of Moulton's result.

Our computations show, in agreement with Moulton's result, that there are $60=$ $5!/ 2$ solutions of the Albouy-Chenciner equations.

The four-dimensional central configurations of five bodies are also well understood. Saari  proved that the regular $n-1$ dimensional simplex is a central configuration of $n$ bodies for any value of the masses. In particular the case $n=4$ has been well known over a century . The fact that the tetrahedron is the unique spatial central configuration of four bodies was proved by Pizzetti . We find one 4-dimensional solution of the Albouy-Chenciner equations that, as we expected, is a regular 4-dimensional

# 5.2 Planar Central Configurations 

There are very few results concerning the planar five-body problem. Part of the work on the planar five body problem dates back to more than 50 years ago and is due to Williams ,. More recently, in 2005, Hampton  found new examples of (symmetric) central configurations in the planar five-body problem. Llibre and Mello  and Llibre, Mello, and Perez-Chavela  found some further central configurations using the same techniques employed by Hampton. Not much more is known in the planar five-body problem

It has been known for a long time that, in the equal mass case, the regular pentagon and the square with one mass at each of its vertices and with the fifth mass at its center are central configurations .

In the case of equal masses we find 147 planar solutions of the Albouy-Chenciner equations. Of these, 15 form a square with a particle in the middle (Figure 2 (a)), 12 form a regular pentagon (Figure 2 (b)), 60 form an isosceles triangle with the remaining particles in the convex hull of the first three (Figure 2 (c)), and 60 form an isosceles trapezoid with a mass in the convex hull of the first four (Figure 2 (d)). The configurations of Figure 2 (c) and Figure 2 (d) have been found numerically in 1989 by Moeckel  and rediscovered by Ferrario . Note that in  Williams erroneously states that a concave pentagon with three masses at the vertices of a pentagon and the remaining two in its interior cannot form central configurations. Our results (see figure Figure 2 (c)) show that such statement is incorrect.

It is interesting to remark that the number of solutions obtained can be explained using their symmetry. In the case of the configuration of Figure (2(a)) the four masses at the vertices of a square and one at the center are subject to an action of the group $S_{5}$ (symmetric group on 5 letters) permuting the masses and hence the set of mutual distances $r_{i j}$. But, the set of mutual distances $R$ for any particular numbering of the masses has an isotropy subgroup that is equal to the symmetries of the square (the dihedral group $D_{4}$ of order 8 ). Hence the set of $S_{5}$-orbits of configurations ( that is equal to the number of solutions of the Albouy-Chenciner equations) of this type should have $120 / 8=15$ elements. Similarly, the pentagon configurations in Figure (2(a)) have the dihedral group $D_{5}$ as isotropy subgroup and there are $120 / 10=12$ orbits. The configurations in Figure (2 (a)) and (2 (b)) have $C_{2}$ (i.e. the cyclic group of order 2) as isotropy subgroup and, in this case, there are $120 / 2=60$ orbits.

Another interesting fact is that, as in the four-body problem with equal masses , all the planar central configuration have an axis of symmetry that contains at least one mass.

### 5.3 Spatial Central Configurations

In 1908 Brehm  found some symmetric spatial central configurations of five bodies. Almost one century later Kotsireas and Lazard  used linear algebra and Gröbner bases to classify symmetric spatial central configurations of five bodies with equal masses. They found four distinct classes of central configurations. Kotsireas and



Figure 3: Convex spatial central configurations of five bodies with equal masses.

Lazard conjectured that their list of central configurations was complete. Xia proved, for general masses, that there is at least one convex central configuration that is a minimum of the configurational measure . Moeckel used Morse theory, under the assumption of nondegenerate critical points, to find 6 more central configurations of saddle type .

We find 50 spatial solutions of the Albouy-Chenciner equations. These correspond to four distinct classes of central configurations (two convex and two concave) that match the ones of Kotsireas and Lazard, thus proving their conjecture to be correct.

The first class has 10 solutions. These consist of an equilateral triangle and two symmetric points on the axis through the barycenter of the triangle that is orthogonal to it (Fig. 3(a)). The second one contains 15 solutions. These are pyramidal central configurations with a square base (Fig. 3(b)). The third class consists of 5 solutions. These consist of a regular tetrahedron with a point in its barycenter (Fig. 4(a)). The last class contains 20 solutions. These consist of an equilateral triangle and two points lying on the axis through the center of the triangle (Fig. 4(b)).

As in the planar case the number of central configurations can be explained using their symmetry. In the case of the configuration of Figure (3(a)) the masses are subject to an action of the group $S_{5}$. But, the set of mutual distances has the group $D_{3} \times C_{2}$ (of order 12) as isotropy subgroup. Hence the set of $S_{5}$-orbits of configurations of this type should have $120 / 12=10$ elements and thus there are 10 solutions of the Albouy Chenciner equations. The configuration in Figure (3(b)) has the dihedral group $D_{4}$ as isotropy subgroup and there are $120 / 8=15$ solutions. The configuration in Figure (4 (a)) has the tetrahedral group $T_{d}$ (that has order 24) as isotropy subgroup and hence there are $120 / 24=5$ solutions.



Figure 4: Concave spatial central configurations of five bodies with equal masses.

The configuration in Figure (4 (b)) has the dihedral group $D_{3}$ as isotropy subgroup and, in this case, there are $120 / 6=20$ solutions.

According to Moeckel  the convex central configurations would fit with the Morse theory as follows: 6 saddles plus 9 more $=15,1$ minimum plus 9 more $=10$.

# New classes of spatial central configurations for the 5-body problem 

## A B S T R A C T

In this paper, we show the existence of new families of spatial central configurations for the $n+3$-body problem, $n \geq 3$. We study spatial central configurations where $n$ bodies are at the vertices of a regular $n$-gon $\mathcal{T}$ and the other three bodies are symmetrically located on the straight line that is perpendicular to the plane that contains $\mathcal{T}$ and passes through the center of $\mathcal{T}$. The results have simple and analytic proofs.


## 1. Introduction

Consider $N$ punctual positive masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$ with position vectors $r_{1}, \ldots, r_{N}$, usually $r_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}, d=2,3$. In this paper, we denote the Euclidean distance between the bodies located at $r_{i}$ and $r_{j}$ by $r_{i j}=\left|r_{i}-r_{j}\right|$, and we use the inertial barycentric system, that is, the origin of the inertial system is the center of mass of the system, which is given by $\sum_{j=1}^{N} m_{j} r_{j} / M$, where $M=m_{1}+\ldots+m_{N}$ is the total mass. The space of configuration is defined by $\left\{\left(r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{N}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{d N}: r_{i} \neq r_{j}, i \neq j\right\}$.

The Newtonian $N$-body problem in celestial mechanics consists of studying the motion of these masses interacting amongst themselves through no other forces than their mutual gravitational attraction according to Newton's gravitational law .

At a given instant $t=t_{0}$, the $N$ bodies are in a central configuration if there exists $\lambda \neq 0$ such that $\bar{r}_{i}=-\lambda r_{i}$, for all $i=1, \ldots, N$. Two central configurations $\left(r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{N}\right)$ and $\left(\bar{r}_{1}, \bar{r}_{2}, \ldots, \bar{r}_{N}\right)$ of the $N$ bodies are related if we can pass from one to the other through a dilation and a rotation (centered at the center of mass). So we can study the classes of central configurations defined by the above equivalence relation.

The knowledge of central configurations allow us to compute homographic solutions (see ); there is a relation between central configurations and the bifurcations of the hypersurfaces of constant energy and angular momentum (see ); if the $N$ bodies are moving towards a simultaneous collision then the bodies tend to a central configuration (see ). See also .

Some examples of spatial central configurations are a regular tetrahedron with arbitrary positive masses at the vertices  and a regular octahedron with six equal masses at the vertices . Double nested spatial central configurations for $2 N$ bodies were studied for two nested regular polyhedra in . More recently, the same authors studied central configurations of three regular polyhedra for the spatial $3 N$-body problem in . See also , where nested regular tetrahedrons are studied.

Recently, Hampton and Santoprete  provided new examples of stacked spatial central configurations - central configurations for the $N$-body problem where a proper subset of the $N$ bodies are already on a central configuration - for the 7-body problem where the bodies are arranged as concentric three- and two-dimensional simplexes. New classes of stacked spatial central configurations for the 6-body problem which have four bodies at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron and

Fig. 1. Illustration of the configurations studied here for $n=3$. The position vectors $r_{1}, r_{2}$ and $r_{3}$ are located at the vertices of an equilateral triangle $\mathcal{T}, r_{4}$ and $r_{5}$ are located on $\mathcal{L}$, and $r_{6}$ is at the center of $\mathcal{T}$.
the other two bodies on a straight line connecting one vertex of the tetrahedron with the center of the opposite face were studied in .

In this paper, we study spatial central configurations for the $n+3$-body problem, for $n \geq 3$ (see Fig. 1 for $n=3$ ), that satisfy the following.

1. The position vectors $r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{n}$ are at the vertices of a regular $n$-gon $\mathcal{T}$ whose sides have length $a$.
2. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the straight line perpendicular to the plane that contains $\mathcal{T}$ and passes through the center of $\mathcal{T}$. The position vectors $r_{n+1}$ and $r_{n+2}$ are on $\mathcal{L}$ on opposite sides with respect to the plane that contains $\mathcal{T}$. The position vector $r_{n+3}$ is fixed at the center of $\mathcal{T}$.
The central configurations studied in this paper are much related to the double pyramidal central configurations studied in . This kind of configuration consists of $n$ masses on a plane $\Pi$ that are located at the vertices of a regular $n$-gon and two equal masses located on the line perpendicular to $\Pi$ passing through the center of the $n$-gon.

As far as we know, the spatial central configurations studied here are new, and they are, in a certain sense, generalizations of some nested planar central configurations studied in .

The main results of this paper are the following.
Theorem 1. Consider $n+3$ bodies with masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n}, m_{n+1}, m_{n+2}, m_{n+3}$ located according to the following (see Fig. 1 for the case $n=3$ ).
(i) $r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{n}$ are at the vertices of a regular $n$-gon $\mathcal{T}$ inscribed on a circle of radius $\rho$.
(ii) $r_{n+3}$ is at the center of $\mathcal{T}$.
(iii) $r_{n+1}$ and $r_{n+2}$ are on the straight line $\mathcal{L}$, on opposite sides with respect to the plane that contains $\mathcal{T}$, where $\mathcal{L}$ is the straight line that is perpendicular to $\mathcal{T}$ and passes through the center of $\mathcal{T}$. Let $b_{1}=\left|r_{n+1}-r_{n+3}\right|$ and $b_{2}=\left|r_{n+2}-r_{n+3}\right|$.

Suppose that $m_{n+1}=m_{n+2}$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{i} r_{i}=0$. In order that the $n+3$ bodies can be in a central configuration, the following statements hold.
(a) The masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n}$ are equal.
(b) The distances $b_{1}$ and $b_{2}$ are equal.

Define $b=b_{1}=b_{2}$. Then we have the following.

1. There is a non-empty interval $I_{1} \subset \mathbb{R}$ such that, for each $b \in I_{1}$, there are position vectors $r_{i}, i=1, \ldots, n+3$ and positive masses $m_{1}=\cdots=m_{n}, m_{n+1}=m_{n+2}$ and $m_{n+3}$ such that the bodies are in a central configuration according to items (i), (ii) and (iii).

2. Suppose that $m_{1}=\cdots=m_{n}=m_{n+1}=m_{n+2}=m$ and $n \neq 4$. Then there is a non-empty interval $I_{2} \subset \mathbb{R}$ such that, for each $b \in I_{2}$, there are position vectors $r_{i}, i=1, \ldots, n+3$ and positive masses $m$ and $m_{n+3}$ such that the bodies are in a central configuration according to items (i), (ii) and (iii).
3. Suppose that $m_{1}=\cdots=m_{n}=m_{n+1}=m_{n+2}=m$ and $n=4$. Then there is only one value $b=b_{*}>0$ such that the bodies are in a central configuration according to items (i), (ii) and (iii) for all values of positive masses $m$ and $m_{n+3}$.
4. Suppose that $m_{1}=\cdots=m_{n}=m_{n+1}=m_{n+2}=m_{n+3}=m$. Then there is only one value $b=b_{* *}>0$ such that the bodies with mass $m$ are in a central configuration according to items (i), (ii) and (iii).
The proof of Theorem 1 is given in the next section.

# 2. Proof of Theorem 1 

The equations of motion of the $N$-body problem are given by

$$
\ddot{r}_{i}=-\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\ j \neq i}}^{N} m_{j} \frac{r_{i}-r_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}
$$

for $i=1,2, \ldots, N$. In (1), the gravitational constant is taken equal to one. From the definition of central configuration, Eq. (1) can be written as

$$
\lambda r_{i}=\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\ j \neq i}}^{N} m_{j} \frac{r_{i}-r_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}
$$

Denote $r_{i}=\left(x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ and let $\hat{z}$ be the unit vector in the $z$-direction. Without loss of generality, consider $z_{1}=\cdots=z_{n}=0=z_{n+3}$.

Lemma 2. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, the following equations are verified.

$$
R_{n+1, i}=R_{n+1, j}=R_{n+2, i}=R_{n+2, j}
$$

for $1 \leq i \neq j \leq n$, and

$$
R_{n+1, n+3}=R_{n+2, n+3}
$$

where $R_{i, j}=\left|r_{i}-r_{j}\right|^{-3}$.
Proof. From the equation of central configurations (2), we have

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{n+3} m_{i} m_{j} R_{i, j}\left(r_{i}-r_{j}\right)=\lambda m_{i} r_{i}
$$

for $1 \leq i \leq n+3$. Taking the inner product of (5), for $i=1$ and $i=2$, by $\hat{z}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& m_{1} m_{n+1} R_{1, n+1}\left(z_{1}-z_{n+1}\right)+m_{1} m_{n+2} R_{1, n+2}\left(z_{1}-z_{n+2}\right)=\lambda m_{1} z_{1} \\
& m_{2} m_{n+1} R_{2, n+1}\left(z_{2}-z_{n+1}\right)+m_{2} m_{n+2} R_{2, n+2}\left(z_{2}-z_{n+2}\right)=\lambda m_{2} z_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

By our assumptions, the center of mass is at the origin; then we have

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j} z_{j}=0, \quad m_{n+1} z_{n+1}+m_{n+2} z_{n+2}=0
$$

From $m_{n+1}=m_{n+2} \neq 0$, we have

$$
z_{n+1}=-z_{n+2}
$$

Substituting (8) into (6) and (7), we obtain, respectively,

$$
R_{1, n+1}=R_{1, n+2}, \quad R_{2, n+1}=R_{2, n+2}
$$

As $r_{1}, \ldots, r_{n}$ are on a circle, we have

$$
R_{1, n+1}=\left(\left|r_{1}\right|^{2}+\left|z_{n+1}\right|^{2}\right)^{-3 / 2}=\left(\left|r_{2}\right|^{2}+\left|z_{n+1}\right|^{2}\right)^{-3 / 2}=R_{2, n+1}
$$

With similar arguments, we conclude that

$$
R_{i, n+1}=R_{j, n+1}=R_{i, n+2}=R_{j, n+2}
$$

for $1 \leq i, j \leq n$. This proves (3).

For the proof of (4), take the inner product of (5), for $i=n+3$, by $\hat{z}$. Thus

$$
m_{n+3} m_{n+1} R_{n+3, n+1}\left(z_{n+3}-z_{n+1}\right)+m_{n+3} m_{n+2} R_{n+3, n+2}\left(z_{n+3}-z_{n+2}\right)=\lambda m_{n+3} z_{n+3}
$$

Substituting (8) into (10), and using the information about the center of mass, we conclude that

$$
R_{n+3, n+1}=R_{n+3, n+2}
$$

The lemma is proved.
Eq. (4) of Lemma 2 proves item (b) of Theorem 1.
Lemma 3. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, the scalar $\lambda$ in Eq. (2) has the following value:

$$
\lambda=R_{n+3, n+1}\left(\frac{m_{n+2}}{4}+m_{n+3}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j} R_{n+1, j}
$$

Proof. From the equation of central configurations (2),

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{n+3} m_{i} m_{j} R_{i, j}\left(r_{i}-r_{j}\right)=\lambda m_{i} r_{i}
$$

for $1 \leq i \leq n+3$, or rewriting $m_{i} r_{i}$,

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{n+3} m_{i} m_{j} R_{i, j}\left(r_{i}-r_{j}\right)=\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{n+3} \frac{\lambda}{M} m_{i} m_{j}\left(r_{i}-r_{j}\right)
$$

where $M$ is the total mass of the system. Hence

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{n+3} m_{i} m_{j}\left(R_{i, j}-\frac{\lambda}{M}\right)\left(r_{i}-r_{j}\right)=0
$$

Substituting $i=n+1$ into (12) and taking the inner product by $\hat{z}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& m_{n+1} m_{n+3}\left(R_{n+1, n+3}-\frac{\lambda}{M}\right)\left(z_{n+1}-z_{n+3}\right)+m_{n+1} m_{n+2}\left(R_{n+1, n+2}-\frac{\lambda}{M}\right)\left(z_{n+1}-z_{n+2}\right) \\
& \quad+\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{n+1} m_{j}\left(R_{n+1, j}-\frac{\lambda}{M}\right)\left(z_{n+1}-z_{j}\right)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

From Lemma 2, it follows that $b=z_{n+1}-z_{n+3}$ and $z_{n+1}-z_{n+2}=2 b$. For $1 \leq i \leq n$ it holds that $z_{n+1}-z_{i}=b$ and $R_{n+1, n+3}=8 R_{n+1, n+2}$. With these considerations, Eq. (13) becomes

$$
m_{n+3}\left(R_{n+1, n+3}-\frac{\lambda}{M}\right) b+m_{n+2}\left(\frac{R_{n+1, n+3}}{8}-\frac{\lambda}{M}\right)(2 b)+\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j}\left(R_{n+1, j}-\frac{\lambda}{M}\right) b=0
$$

Solving for $\lambda$, we have

$$
\lambda=R_{n+3, n+1}\left(\frac{m_{n+2}}{4}+m_{n+3}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j} R_{n+1, j}
$$

The lemma is proved.
The proof of the following lemma is a direct consequence of the definition of central configuration taking into account that $r_{n+1}+r_{n+2}=0$.

Lemma 4. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, the following equality holds:

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{n} m_{i} m_{j} R_{i, j}\left(r_{i}-r_{j}\right)=\left[-2 m_{n+1}\left(R_{n+1, i}-\frac{\lambda}{M}\right)-m_{n+3}\left(R_{n+3, i}-\frac{\lambda}{M}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j} \frac{\lambda}{M}\right] m_{i} r_{i}
$$

Suppose that the radius $\rho$ of the circumscribed circle of $\mathcal{T}$ is equal to one. Without loss of generality, we can take a coordinate system such that the bodies have the following positions:

$$
r_{k}=\exp \left(\frac{2 k \pi}{n} \imath\right), \quad r_{n+1}=(0,0, x), \quad r_{n+2}=(0,0,-x), \quad r_{n+3}=(0,0,0)
$$

for $k=1, \ldots, n$, where $\imath=\sqrt{-1}, x>0$. It follows that $b=x$. In the rest of this paper we consider the above coordinates.
Lemma 5. Under the assumptions of Theorem 1, if the bodies are in a central configuration then the masses at the vertices of the regular $n$-gon $\mathcal{T}$ are equal; that is, $m_{1}=\cdots=m_{n}$.
Proof. In this proof, we use the concept of a circulant matrix as in . See also . Consider an $n \times n$ matrix $C=\left[c_{i, j}\right] . C$ is a circulant matrix if

$$
c_{i, j}=c_{i-1, j-1}
$$

where $c_{0, j}$ and $c_{i, 0}$ are identified with $c_{n, j}$ and $c_{i, n}$, respectively. From the right-hand side of expression (14), we define $A$ as

$$
A=-2 m_{n+1}\left(R_{n+1, i}-\frac{\lambda}{M}\right)-m_{n+3}\left(R_{n+3, i}-\frac{\lambda}{M}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j} \frac{\lambda}{M}
$$

Let $C$ be the $n \times n$ matrix defined as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& c_{i, i}=0, \quad \forall i=1, \ldots, n \\
& c_{i, j}=R_{i, j}\left(r_{i-j}-1\right)-\frac{A}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} m_{k}}, \quad \text { for } i \neq j
\end{aligned}
$$

Clearly $C$ is a circulant matrix, according to the above definition. In this way, Eq. (14) can be written as

$$
C \vec{m}=0
$$

where $\vec{m}=\left(m_{1}, \ldots, m_{n}\right)^{\top}$.
A positive vector is a vector, all of whose the components are real and positive. From (15), we are interested in positive vectors that belong to the kernel of $C$. There are well-known general formulas for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a circulant matrix :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \lambda_{k}=\sum_{j=1}^{n} c_{1, j} r_{k-1}^{j-1}, \quad \text { for } 1 \leq k \leq n, r_{0}=r_{n} \\
& v_{k}=\left(r_{k-1},\left(r_{k-1}\right)^{2}, \ldots,\left(r_{k-1}\right)^{n}\right), \quad \text { for } 1 \leq k \leq n
\end{aligned}
$$

For $n \geq 3$, we have just one positive eigenvector,

$$
v_{1}=(1,1, \ldots, 1)^{T}
$$

associated to the following eigenvalue:

$$
\lambda_{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{n} c_{1, j}
$$

Now, by the definition of $c_{1, j}$ and (14), we have

$$
\lambda_{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{n} c_{1, j}=\sum_{j=1, j \neq 1}^{n} R_{1, j}\left(r_{j-1}-1\right)-\frac{n A}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} m_{k}}=0
$$

Thus for $n \geq 3$ the possible positive vector solution of (15) is just $v_{1}$, or equivalently $m_{1}=m_{2}=\cdots=m_{n}=m$. The lemma is proved.

Lemma 5 proves item (a) of Theorem 1.
Lemma 6. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, the equation of central configurations (2) can be written as

$$
m\left(\frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc \frac{\pi j}{n}-\frac{n}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}\right)+2 \mu\left(\frac{1}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1}{8 x^{3}}\right)+m_{n+3}\left(1-\frac{1}{x^{3}}\right)=0
$$

Proof. From Eqs. (11) and (14), we have

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{n} m_{i} m_{j} R_{i, j}\left(r_{i}-r_{j}\right)=\left[\frac{1}{b^{3}}\left(\frac{m_{n+1}}{4}+m_{n+3}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j} R_{n+1, j}-2 m_{n+1} R_{n+1, i}-m_{n+3} R_{n+3, i}\right] m_{i} r_{i}
$$

From the above coordinates, Eq. (17) can be written as

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{n} m_{j} R_{i, j}\left(1-r_{i-j}\right)=\left[\frac{1}{x^{3}}\left(\frac{m_{n+1}}{4}+m_{n+3}\right)+\frac{1}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j}-\frac{2 m_{n+1}}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-m_{n+3}\right]
$$

Making the summation in (18) at the index $i$ and dividing both sides by $n$, we have

$$
\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{i}\right) \frac{1}{4 n} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc \frac{\pi j}{n}=\left[\frac{1}{x^{3}}\left(\frac{m_{n+1}}{4}+m_{n+3}\right)+\frac{1}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \sum_{j=1}^{n} m_{j}-\frac{2 m_{n+1}}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-m_{n+3}\right]
$$

Eq. (16) follows from Eq. (19) making $m_{1}=\cdots=m_{n}=m$ (see Lemma 5) and $m_{n+1}=m_{n+2}=\mu$. The lemma is proved.
Eq. (16) defines a plane through the origin in the space $\left(m, \mu, m_{n+3}\right)$. The normal vector of this plane is given by $\mathcal{N}=\left(n_{1}, n_{2}, n_{3}\right)$, where $n_{1}, n_{2}$ and $n_{3}$ are the coefficients of $m, 2 \mu$ and $m_{n+3}$, respectively, and are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& n_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc \frac{\pi j}{n}-\frac{n}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& n_{2}(x)=\frac{1}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1}{8 x^{3}}, \quad n_{3}(x)=1-\frac{1}{x^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $x>0$. Therefore, there will be positive masses $m, \mu$ and $m_{n+3}$ solutions of Eq. (16) if and only if two of the components of the normal vector $\mathcal{N}$ have opposite sign.
(a) Analysis of the function $n_{2}$ (see Fig. 2). The function $n_{2}$, for $x>0$, satisfies

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} n_{2}(x)=-\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} n_{2}(x)=0, \quad n_{2}^{\prime}(x)=\frac{-3 x}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{3}{8 x^{4}}
$$

The derivative of the function $n_{2}$ has only one zero at $1 /(\sqrt{2 \sqrt{2}-1})>0$ which is a maximum of $n_{2}$. So the function $n_{2}$ is increasing in the interval $(0,1 /(\sqrt{2 \sqrt{2}-1}))$ and it is decreasing and positive in the interval $(1 /(\sqrt{2 \sqrt{2}-1}), \infty)$. Thus the function $n_{2}$ has only one zero in the interval $(0, \infty)$. By a simple and elementary calculation it follows that $n_{2}(\sqrt{3} / 3)=0$.
(b) Analysis of the function $n_{3}$ (see Fig. 2). The function $n_{3}$, for $x>0$, satisfies

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} n_{3}(x)=-\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} n_{3}(x)=1, \quad n_{3}^{\prime}(x)=\frac{3}{x^{4}}>0
$$

Thus the function $n_{3}$ has only one zero in the interval $(0, \infty)$. By a simple and elementary calculation we have $n_{3}(1)=0$.
Let $x_{1}=\sqrt{3} / 3$ and $x_{2}=1$ be the zeros of the functions $n_{2}$ and $n_{3}$, respectively. Define the open interval $I_{1}$ as $I_{1}=\left(x_{1}, x_{2}\right)=(\sqrt{3} / 3,1)$ (see Fig. 2). In the open interval $I_{1}$ the function $n_{2}$ is positive and the function $n_{3}$ is negative. This is sufficient for the existence of positive masses $\left(m, \mu, m_{n+3}\right)$ for which we have central configurations as in our theorem. See Fig. 2.

From the above analysis, item 1 of Theorem 1 is proved.
Remark 7. The interval $I_{1}$ is not the largest interval for which there are central configurations as stated in Theorem 1. We can refine the result for each fixed value of $n$ taking into account the sign of the function $n_{1}$. In fact, $I_{1}$ is the best interval just for the case $n=8$.

Suppose that $m_{1}=\cdots=m_{n}=m_{n+1}=m_{n+2}=m$. From Eq. (16), we have

$$
m\left(\frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc \frac{\pi j}{n}-\frac{n}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{2}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{2}{8 x^{3}}\right)+m_{n+3}\left(1-\frac{1}{x^{3}}\right)=0
$$

Therefore there will be positive masses $m$ and $m_{n+3}$ solutions of Eq. (20) if and only if the coefficients of $m$ and $m_{n+3}$ have opposite signs, unless both coefficients vanish. The coefficient of $m_{n+3}$ is exactly $n_{3}$. Let $n_{4}$ be the coefficient of $m$. Therefore



Fig. 2. The graphs of the functions $n_{2}$ and $n_{3}$ and the interval $I_{1}=\left(x_{1}, x_{2}\right)$.
$n_{4}=n_{1}+2 n_{2}$. It is simple to see that

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} n_{4}(x)=-\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} n_{4}(x)=\frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc \frac{\pi j}{n}>0
$$

Furthermore, the derivative of $n_{4}$ is positive for $x>0$. Thus function $n_{4}$ is increasing in the interval $(0, \infty)$. It follows that $n_{4}$ has only one zero $x_{4}$ in this interval. By an elementary calculation, it follows that $n_{4}(1)<0$ for $n=3, n_{4}(1)=0$ for $n=4$ and $n_{4}(1)>0$ for $n \geq 5$. This implies that $x_{4}>1=x_{2}$ for $n=3, x_{4}=1=x_{2}$ for $n=4$ and $x_{4}<1=x_{2}$ for $n \geq 5$. Therefore, for $n=3$, the function $n_{4}$ is negative and the function $n_{3}$ is positive in the open interval $I_{2}=\left(x_{2}, x_{4}\right)$; for $n \geq 5$, the function $n_{4}$ is positive and the function $n_{3}$ is negative in the open interval $I_{2}=\left(x_{4}, x_{2}\right)$. For $n=4$, both functions $n_{3}$ and $n_{4}$ vanish at $x_{2}=x_{4}=1$. This implies the existence of a two-parameter family of central configurations for all values of positive masses $m$ and $m_{n+3}$. Define $b_{*}=1$. So items 2 and 3 of Theorem 1 are proved.

Suppose that $m_{1}=\cdots=m_{n}=m_{n+1}=m_{n+2}=m_{n+3}=m$. From Eq. (16), we have

$$
m\left(\frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc \frac{\pi j}{n}-\frac{n}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{2}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{2}{8 x^{3}}+1-\frac{1}{x^{3}}\right)=0
$$

The coefficient $n_{5}$ of $m$ in Eq. (21) is given by $n_{5}=n_{1}+2 n_{2}+n_{3}$. By an elementary calculation, we have

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} n_{5}(x)=-\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} n_{5}(x)=1+\frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc \frac{\pi j}{n}>0
$$

The derivative of $n_{5}$ is also positive for $x>0$. So function $n_{5}$ is increasing in the interval $(0, \infty)$. It follows that $n_{5}$ has only one zero $x_{5}$ in this interval. Defining $b_{* *}=x_{5}$, item 4 of Theorem 1 is proved.

In short, we have proved Theorem 1.
Finally, we consider the question of uniqueness of the masses $m, \mu$ and $m_{n+3}$ of Theorem 1 (item 1). Fix a mass vector $\left(m^{0}, \mu^{0}, m_{n+3}^{0}\right)$ and suppose that there are $y, z \in I_{1}=(\sqrt{3} / 3,1), y \neq z$, such that the bodies are in central configurations according to item 1 of Theorem 1. As the function $n_{2}$ is injective, we have $n_{2}(y) \neq n_{3}(z)$. It follows that $\mathcal{N}(y) \neq \mathcal{N}(z)$ and the two planes defined by (16) have a line through the origin and $\left(m^{0}, \mu^{0}, m_{n+3}^{0}\right)$ as intersection. Let $\mathfrak{s}(y, z)=\left(\mathfrak{s}_{1}(y, z), \mathfrak{s}_{2}(y, z), \mathfrak{s}_{3}(y, z)\right)=\mathcal{N}(y) \wedge \mathcal{N}(z)$ be the vector parallel to the straight line defined by the intersection of the two planes. The components of the vector $\mathfrak{s}(y, z)$ must have the same sign since the masses $m^{0}, \mu^{0}$ and $m_{n+3}^{0}$ are positive. From (16), we have

$$
\mathcal{N}(y)=\left(\frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc \frac{\pi j}{n}-\frac{n}{\left(1+y^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}, \frac{1}{\left(1+y^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1}{8 y^{3}}, 1-\frac{1}{y^{3}}\right)
$$

and

$$
\mathcal{N}(z)=\left(\frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc \frac{\pi j}{n}-\frac{n}{\left(1+z^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}, \frac{1}{\left(1+z^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1}{8 z^{3}}, 1-\frac{1}{z^{3}}\right)
$$

The components $\mathbb{\delta}_{1}$ and $\mathbb{\delta}_{3}$ of the vector $\mathbb{\delta}$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{\delta}_{1}(y, z)= & \left(\frac{1}{\left(1+y^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1}{8 y^{3}}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{z^{3}}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{\left(1+z^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1}{8 z^{3}}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{y^{3}}\right) \\
\mathbb{\delta}_{3}(y, z)= & \left(\frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc \frac{\pi j}{n}-\frac{n}{\left(1+y^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\left(1+z^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1}{8 z^{3}}\right) \\
& -\left(\frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc \frac{\pi j}{n}-\frac{n}{\left(1+z^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\left(1+y^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1}{8 y^{3}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

It is easy to see that $\mathbb{\delta}_{1}$ and $\mathbb{\delta}_{3}$ vanish when $y=z$. The function $\mathbb{\delta}_{1}$ is negative for $z>y$ and positive for $z<y$. The function $\mathbb{\delta}_{3}$ can be written as

$$
\mathbb{\delta}_{3}(y, z)=\left(\frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \csc \frac{\pi j}{n}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\left(1+z^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{1}{8 z^{3}}-\frac{1}{\left(1+y^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{1}{8 y^{3}}\right)+n\left(\frac{1}{z^{3}}-\frac{1}{y^{3}}\right)
$$

The first and second terms are positive for $z>y$ and negative for $z<y$. Therefore the same is true for $\mathbb{\delta}_{3}$. Thus $\mathbb{\delta}_{1}$ and $\mathbb{\delta}_{3}$ have opposite sign, where they are not null, in $(\sqrt{3} / 3,1) \times(\sqrt{3} / 3,1)$. We have a contradiction, and the uniqueness follows.
# The central configurations of four masses $x,-x, y,-y$ 

#### Abstract

The configuration of a homothetic motion in the $N$-body problem is called a central configuration. In this paper, we prove that there are exactly three planar non-collinear central configurations for masses $x,-x$, $y,-y$ with $x \neq y$ (a parallelogram and two trapezoids) and two planar non-collinear central configurations for masses $x,-x, x,-x$ (two diamonds). Except the case studied here, the only known case where the four-body central configurations with non-vanishing masses can be listed is the case with equal masses (A. Albouy, 1995-1996), which requires the use of a symbolic computation program. Thanks to a lemma used in the proof of our result, we also show that a co-circular four-body central configuration has nonvanishing total mass or vanishing multiplier.

## 1. Introduction

We are interested in configurations with $N$ punctual bodies which interact through gravitation, with masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$, and positions $\vec{r}_{1}, \ldots, \vec{r}_{N}$. The masses are positive or negative but do not vanish, the positions belong to a Euclidean vector space. The motion of the bodies is given by Newton's equations:

$$
\ddot{\vec{r}}_{i}=\vec{\gamma}_{i}\left(\vec{r}_{1}, \ldots, \vec{r}_{N}\right)=\sum_{j \in\{1, \ldots, N\} \backslash\{i\}} m_{j} \frac{\vec{r}_{j}-\vec{r}_{i}}{\left\|\vec{r}_{j}-\vec{r}_{i}\right\|^{3}}
$$

We have:

$$
\vec{\gamma}_{i}=\frac{1}{m_{i}} \frac{\partial U}{\partial \vec{r}_{i}}
$$

where $U$ is the Newtonian potential:

$$
U\left(\vec{r}_{1}, \ldots, \vec{r}_{N}\right)=\sum_{1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant N} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left\|\vec{r}_{j}-\vec{r}_{i}\right\|}
$$

We study a special class of configurations, which are called central configurations. A configuration is said to be central with multiplier $\xi$ if, and only if, for any $i, j$ :

$$
\vec{\gamma}_{j}\left(\vec{r}_{1}, \ldots, \vec{r}_{N}\right)-\vec{\gamma}_{i}\left(\vec{r}_{1}, \ldots, \vec{r}_{N}\right)=\xi\left(\vec{r}_{j}-\vec{r}_{i}\right)
$$

A motion is said to be homothetic if, and only if, there is a scalar $\alpha$ which depends on time, such that we have, for any $i, j$ :

$$
\vec{r}_{j}(t)-\vec{r}_{i}(t)=\alpha(t)\left(\vec{r}_{j}(0)-\vec{r}_{i}(0)\right)
$$

A motion is said to be homothetic with fixed center if, and only if, there is a scalar $\alpha$ which depends on time and a constant vector $\vec{\Omega}$, such that we have, for any $i$ :

$$
\vec{r}_{i}(t)-\vec{\Omega}=\alpha(t)\left(\vec{r}_{i}(0)-\vec{\Omega}\right)
$$

It can be shown that the motion associated with a configuration and vanishing initial velocities is homothetic if, and only if, the configuration is central. It can be shown that it is homothetic with fixed center if, and only if, the configuration is central with multiplier $\xi \neq 0$ . This motivates the study of central configurations.

The computation of central configurations is a difficult problem as soon as $N \geqslant 4$. Their finiteness up to similarities is the subject of Smale's sixth problem for the 21st century . It has only been proved recently in the case of four bodies with positive masses, and the proof requires a computer . On the other hand, there exists a continuum of five-body central configurations when we allow a negative mass . A continuum of four-body central configurations was also found for charged particles with electrostatic (not gravitational) interaction, which have positive masses and positive or negative charges . Four-body central configurations with positive masses were also studied numerically . Thanks to symbolic computation, they can be listed when one mass vanishes and the three others are equal $$ and when the four masses are equal $$.

In this article, we enumerate the four-body non-collinear planar central configurations with masses $x,-x, y,-y$, where $x$ and $y$ are two non-vanishing real numbers. The proof does not require the use of numerical or symbolic computation. We also prove that a co-circular four-body central configuration has non-vanishing total mass or vanishing multiplier.

# 2. The field generated by a gravitational or electric dipole is one-to-one 

The gravitational (respectively electric) field $\vec{\gamma}$ which is generated by two bodies with masses -1 and 1 (respectively with charges 1 and -1 ) and positions $\vec{r}_{1}=(-1,0)$ and $\vec{r}_{2}=(1,0)$ in the plane, is given by:

$$
\vec{\gamma}(\vec{r})=-\frac{\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}}{\left\|\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}}{\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}\right\|^{3}}
$$

Proposition 1. For every $\vec{r}, \vec{r}^{\prime}$ such as $\vec{\gamma}(\vec{r})=\vec{\gamma}\left(\vec{r}^{\prime}\right)$, we have: $\vec{r}=\vec{r}^{\prime}$ or $\vec{r}=-\vec{r}^{\prime}$.
Proof. Setting $\vec{r}=(u, v)$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma_{u}(u, v) & =\frac{1+u}{\left((1+u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{1-u}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
\gamma_{v}(u, v) & =\frac{v}{\left((1+u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{v}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
\frac{\partial \gamma_{u}}{\partial u}(u, v) & =\frac{v^{2}-2(u+1)^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}-\frac{v^{2}-2(1-u)^{2}}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}} \\
\frac{\partial \gamma_{u}}{\partial v}(u, v) & =\frac{\partial \gamma_{v}}{\partial u}(u, v)=-3 v\left(\frac{u+1}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{1-u}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right) \\
\frac{\partial \gamma_{v}}{\partial v}(u, v) & =\frac{(u+1)^{2}-2 v^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{2 v^{2}-(1-u)^{2}}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

We set:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& A(u, v)=\frac{(u+1)^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}-\frac{(1-u)^{2}}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}} \\
& B(u, v)=\frac{v^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}-\frac{v^{2}}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

We have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \gamma_{u}}{\partial u}(u, v) \frac{\partial \gamma_{v}}{\partial v}(u, v) & =(B(u, v)-2 A(u, v))(A(u, v)-2 B(u, v)) \\
& =-2(A(u, v)-B(u, v))^{2}+A(u, v) B(u, v)
\end{aligned}
$$

Let us denote by $J$ the determinant of the Jacobian matrix of $\vec{\gamma}$. We have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& J(u, v)=-\left(\frac{\partial \gamma_{u}}{\partial v}(u, v)\right)^{2}+\frac{\partial \gamma_{u}}{\partial u}(u, v) \frac{\partial \gamma_{v}}{\partial v}(u, v) \\
& J(u, v)=-9\left(\frac{(u+1) v}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{(1-u) v}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& -2\left(\frac{(u+1)^{2}-v^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{-(1-u)^{2}+v^{2}}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right)^{2} \\
& +\left(\frac{(u+1)^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}-\frac{(1-u)^{2}}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right) \\
& \times\left(\frac{v^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}-\frac{v^{2}}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right) \\
J(u, v)= & -8\left(\frac{(u+1) v}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{(1-u) v}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right)^{2} \\
& -2\left(\frac{(u+1)^{2}-v^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{-(1-u)^{2}+v^{2}}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right)^{2} \\
& -\left(\frac{(u+1) v}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{(1-u) v}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right)^{2} \\
& +\left(\frac{(u+1)^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}-\frac{(1-u)^{2}}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right) \\
& \times\left(\frac{v^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}-\frac{v^{2}}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right) \\
J(u, v)= & -8\left(\frac{(u+1) v}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{(1-u) v}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right)^{2} \\
& -2\left(\frac{(u+1)^{2}-v^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{-(1-u)^{2}+v^{2}}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right)^{2} \\
& -\frac{2(u+1)(1-u) v^{2}+(u+1)^{2} v^{2}+(1-u)^{2} v^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}, \\
J(u, v)= & -8\left(\frac{(u+1) v}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{(1-u) v}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right)^{2} \\
& -2\left(\frac{(u+1)^{2}-v^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}+\frac{-(1-u)^{2}+v^{2}}{\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right)^{2} \\
& -\frac{4 v^{2}}{\left((u+1)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}\left((1-u)^{2}+v^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}} \leqslant 0
\end{aligned}
$$

We have just proved that $\vec{\gamma}$ is a submersion for $\vec{r} \neq \overrightarrow{0}$.
We have, for every $\vec{r}: \vec{\gamma}(-\vec{r})=\vec{\gamma}(\vec{r})$. So Proposition 1 is equivalent to saying that for every $\vec{R}$, the following equation:

$$
\vec{\gamma}(\vec{r})=\vec{\gamma}(\vec{R})
$$

with unknown variable $\vec{r}$ has exactly one solution when $\vec{R}=\overrightarrow{0}$, and two solutions when $\vec{R} \neq \overrightarrow{0}$. This assertion is trivial for $\vec{R}=\overrightarrow{0}$. So it remains to prove that the restriction of $\vec{\gamma}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{2} \backslash\left\{\vec{r}_{1}, \overrightarrow{0}, \vec{r}_{2}\right\}$ is a 2 -fold covering map.

For $\vec{R}=(1 / 2,0)$, we easily check that Eq. (1) has two solutions: $(-1 / 2,0)$ and $(1 / 2,0)$. So it is enough to prove the following result: if Eq. (1) has exactly two solutions $\vec{R}$ and $-\vec{R}$ at a point $\vec{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{2} \backslash\left\{\vec{r}_{1}, \vec{0}, \vec{r}_{2}\right\}$, this is still true in a neighborhood of $\vec{R}$. Let us assume this to be false. Then there exists a sequence $\left(\vec{R}_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converging towards $\vec{R}$ such that the number of solutions of Eq. (1) associated with $\vec{R}_{n}$ is different from 2. As $d \vec{\gamma}(\vec{R})$ is invertible, there exists a neighborhood $\mathcal{U}$ of $\vec{R}$ such that for $\vec{R} \in \mathcal{U}$, Eq. (1) associated with $\vec{R}$ has exactly one solution $\vec{R}$ in $\mathcal{U}$. Then for $n$ large enough, the solutions in $\mathcal{U} \cup(-\mathcal{U})$ of Eq. (1) associated with $\vec{R}_{n}$ are $\vec{R}_{n}$ and $-\vec{R}_{n}$. This equation must have the third solution $\vec{R}_{n}^{\prime}$. If $\left(\vec{R}_{n}^{\prime}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ were bounded, we could extract a subsequence converging towards a solution $\vec{R}^{\prime}$ of Eq. (1) associated with $\vec{R}$. The solution $\vec{R}^{\prime}$ would not belong to the open sets $\mathcal{U}$ and $-\mathcal{U}$ and would be different from $\vec{R}$ and $-\vec{R}$, which is impossible. So the sequence $\left(\vec{R}_{n}^{\prime}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is not bounded. So we can assume (if necessary, we can consider a subsequence): $\left\|\vec{R}_{n}^{\prime}\right\| \rightarrow+\infty$. But this entails: $\left\|\vec{\gamma}\left(\vec{R}_{n}\right)\right\|=\left\|\vec{\gamma}\left(\vec{R}_{n}^{\prime}\right)\right\| \rightarrow 0$. Hence: $\vec{\gamma}(\vec{R})=\vec{0}$. Now we can check that this equality is false for every $\vec{R}$.

# 3. Planar non-collinear central configurations with masses $x,-x, y,-y$ and $\xi=0$ 

Theorem 2. Let $x$ be a real number. There is no planar non-collinear central configuration with vanishing multiplier for the masses $x,-x, x,-x$. Let $x$ and $y$ be two distinct non-vanishing real numbers. There exists exactly one planar non-collinear central configuration (up to similarities) with vanishing multiplier for the masses $x,-x, y,-y$. It is a parallelogram. The bodies with masses $x$ and $-x$ (respectively the bodies with masses $y$ and $-y$ ) are at the endpoints of the same diagonal. The bodies whose masses have the smaller absolute value are at the endpoints of the larger diagonal. The two parallel sides whose endpoints have masses with the same sign are the largest ones.

Proof. Let $x$ and $y$ be two non-vanishing real numbers. We can assume: $x, y>0$. If necessary, we can exchange body 1 and body 2 , or body 3 and body 4 . We can also assume: $x \leqslant y$. If necessary, we can exchange simultaneously body 1 and body 3 , body 2 and body 4 .

For any central configuration with vanishing multiplier, we have: $\vec{r}_{3}\left(\vec{r}_{1}, \ldots, \vec{r}_{4}\right)=$ $\vec{r}_{4}\left(\vec{r}_{1}, \ldots, \vec{r}_{4}\right)$. This is equivalent to: $\vec{\gamma}\left(\vec{r}_{3}\right)=\vec{\gamma}\left(\vec{r}_{4}\right)$, where $\vec{\gamma}$ is the function defined in the previous section. According to Proposition 1, the line segments $\left[\vec{r}_{1}, \vec{r}_{2}\right]$ and $\left[\vec{r}_{3}, \vec{r}_{4}\right]$ have the same midpoint, so the configuration is a parallelogram. The bodies with masses $x$ and $-x$ (respectively the bodies with masses $y$ and $-y$ ) are at the endpoints of a same diagonal.

Moreover, we have: $\vec{r}_{1}=\vec{r}_{3}$. This is equivalent to:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (x+y) \frac{\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{3}}{\left\|\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|^{3}}+(x-y) \frac{\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}} \\
& \quad=x \frac{\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{2}}{\left\|\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}+y \frac{\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|^{3}}=x \frac{\left(\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{3}\right)-\left(\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{3}\right)}{\left\|\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}+y \frac{\left(\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{3}\right)+\left(\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{3}\right)}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

As the bodies are assumed not to be collinear, the vectors $\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{3}$ and $\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{3}$ are not collinear. So this is equivalent to:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{2 x}{\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}=\frac{x+y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{x-y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}} \\
\frac{2 y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|^{3}}=\frac{x+y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{y-x}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}
\end{array}\right.
$$

Let us assume: $x=y$. These identities provide: $\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|=\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|=\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|$. This is impossible for a non-flat parallelogram. So there is no planar non-collinear central configuration with vanishing multiplier for the masses $x,-x, x,-x$.

From now on we assume: $x<y$. As we are looking for configurations up to similarities, we can also assume: $\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{2}+\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{2}=1$. Thus we have: $\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|,\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|<1$, and the previous system provides: $\frac{2 y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|^{3}}>2 y$, which is equivalent to: $\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|<1$. Let us write the parallelogram law:

$$
\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{2}+\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|^{2}=2\left(\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{2}+\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{2}\right)=2
$$

As $\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|<1$, we necessarily have: $\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|<1<\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|$. So the bodies whose masses have the smaller absolute value are at the endpoints of the larger diagonal. From this inequality we deduce:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2 x y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}} & <\frac{2 x y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|^{3}} \\
y\left(\frac{x+y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{x-y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}\right) & <x\left(\frac{x+y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{y-x}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence: $\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|<\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|$. So the two parallel sides whose endpoints have masses with the same sign are the largest ones.

Let us set:

$$
(u, v)=\left(\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}, \frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}\right), \quad\left(u^{\prime}, v^{\prime}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}, \frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|^{3}}\right)
$$

With these notations, the previously established system has the following expression:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
u^{\prime}=\frac{x+y}{2 x} u+\frac{x-y}{2 x} v \\
v^{\prime}=\frac{x+y}{2 y} u+\frac{y-x}{2 y} v
\end{array}\right.
$$

The condition: $\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{2}+\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{2}=1$ has the expression: $u^{-2 / 3}+v^{-2 / 3}=1$. The parallelogram law has the expression: $u^{\prime-2 / 3}+v^{\prime-2 / 3}=2$, which is equivalent to:

$$
\left(\frac{x+y}{2 x} u+\frac{x-y}{2 x} v\right)^{-2 / 3}+\left(\frac{x+y}{2 y} u+\frac{y-x}{2 y} v\right)^{-2 / 3}=2
$$

We are going to show that the system ( $\mathcal{S}$ ) which is defined by these two equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
f(u, v)=u^{-2 / 3}+v^{-2 / 3}=1 \\
g(u, v)=\left(\frac{x+y}{2 x} u+\frac{x-y}{2 x} v\right)^{-2 / 3}+\left(\frac{x+y}{2 y} u+\frac{y-x}{2 y} v\right)^{-2 / 3}=2
\end{array}\right.
$$

has exactly one solution $(u, v)$.

Let $\Gamma$ be the curve with equation: $g(u, v)=2$. Let us set:

$$
h(u, v)=\left(\frac{x+y}{2 x} u+\frac{x-y}{2 x} v, \frac{x+y}{2 y} u+\frac{y-x}{2 y} v\right)
$$

The set $\Gamma$ is the preimage of the curve with equation: $u^{-2 / 3}+v^{-2 / 3}=2$ by the invertible linear function $h$. This curve is diffeomorphic to a line, so $\Gamma$ is diffeomorphic to a line.

Let $\Delta_{1}$ be the ray defined by: $v=1, u \geqslant 1$. Let $\Delta_{2}$ be the ray defined by: $u=1, v \geqslant 1$. Let us set: $\Delta=\Delta_{1} \cup \Delta_{2}$. Let $\gamma$ be the set of the $(u, v)$ such that: $u, v>1$ and $g(u, v)=2$. Let us set: $G_{1}(u)=g(u, 1)$. The function $G_{1}$ is defined on $[1,+\infty[$ and strictly decreasing. Now $G_{1}(1)=2$, so $\Gamma \cap \Delta_{1}=\{(1,1)\}$. Let us set: $G_{2}(v)=g(1, v)$. The function $G_{2}$ is defined on $[1,(x+y) /(y-x)]$, and we have:

$$
\frac{d G_{2}}{d v}(v)=\frac{y-x}{3}\left(\frac{1}{x}\left(\frac{x+y}{2 x}+\frac{x-y}{2 x} v\right)^{-5 / 3}-\frac{1}{y}\left(\frac{x+y}{2 y}+\frac{y-x}{2 y} v\right)^{-5 / 3}\right)
$$

It can be checked that $d G_{2} / d v>0$ if, and only if:

$$
v>\frac{(x+y)\left(y^{2 / 5}-x^{2 / 5}\right)}{(y-x)\left(x^{2 / 5}+y^{2 / 5}\right)}
$$

Now it is easy to see that this inequality is always true if $y>x$ and $v \geqslant 1$. So $G_{2}$ is strictly increasing. As $G_{2}(1)=2$, we have: $\Gamma \cap \Delta_{2}=\{(1,1)\}$. Thus: $\Gamma \cap \Delta=\{(1,1)\}$. The set $\Gamma$ is diffeomorphic to a line, so $\Gamma \backslash\{(1,1)\}$ has two connected components, which are diffeomorphic to lines. As $\Gamma \cap \Delta=\{(1,1)\}$, each connected component is included in a side of $\Delta$. We can check that only one of the two components is in the quarter plane defined by the inequalities: $u>1$ and $v>1$. So this connected component is $\gamma$. Thus $\gamma$ is diffeomorphic to a line, an endpoint is $(1,1)$, the other is at infinity (Fig. 1).

When $u$ and $v$ tend to infinity, $f(u, v)$ tends to $0<1$. On the other hand, $f(1,1)=2>1$. The system ( $\mathcal{S}$ ) has at least one solution.

The arguments previously used in order to prove the inequality: $\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|<1<\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|$, enable to prove that:

$$
v^{\prime}=\frac{x+y}{2 y} u+\frac{y-x}{2 y} v>1>u^{\prime}=\frac{x+y}{2 x} u+\frac{x-y}{2 x} v
$$

on $\gamma$. Hence:

$$
\frac{1}{y}\left(\frac{x+y}{2 y} u+\frac{y-x}{2 y} v\right)^{-5 / 3}<\frac{1}{x}\left(\frac{x+y}{2 x} u+\frac{x-y}{2 x} v\right)^{-5 / 3}
$$

Thus on $\gamma$ we have:

$$
\frac{\partial g}{\partial v}(u, v)=\frac{y-x}{3}\left(\frac{1}{x}\left(\frac{x+y}{2 x} u+\frac{x-y}{2 x} v\right)^{-5 / 3}-\frac{1}{y}\left(\frac{x+y}{2 y} u+\frac{y-x}{2 y} v\right)^{-5 / 3}\right)>0
$$



Fig. 1.
We immediately check:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial u}(u, v)<0, \quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial v}(u, v)<0, \quad \frac{\partial g}{\partial u}(u, v)<0
$$

So $d f$ and $d g$ are collinear on $\gamma$. Thus the restriction of $f$ to $\gamma$ is strictly monotonic. There exists exactly one point $(u, v)$ of $\gamma$ such that $f(u, v)=1$. This point is the only solution of ( $\mathcal{S}$ ), which depends on $x$ and $y$ in a continuous way. So there exists at most one planar non-collinear central configuration (up to similarities) with vanishing multiplier for the masses $x,-x, y,-y$.

We are now going to show that the values of $u, v, u^{\prime}, v^{\prime}$ that we have just obtained actually define a non-collinear central configuration with vanishing multiplier. Let us hold $y$ constant. According to the following identity:

$$
0<u^{\prime}=\frac{x+y}{2 x} u-\frac{y-x}{2 x} v
$$

we have:

$$
\frac{y-x}{x+y} v<u
$$

Moreover: $u<v$ (as we established: $\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|<\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|$ ). So $u / v \rightarrow 1$ when $x \rightarrow 0$. According to the following identity:

$$
\frac{v^{\prime}}{v}=\frac{x+y}{2 y} \frac{u}{v}+\frac{y-x}{2 y}
$$

we also have: $v^{\prime} / v \rightarrow 1$ when $x \rightarrow 0$. So the homothety class of $\left(u^{-1 / 3}, v^{-1 / 3}, v^{\prime-1 / 3}\right)$ tends to the class of the lengths of the sides of an equilateral triangle when $x \rightarrow 0$. Thus, for $x$ close to 0 ,

the numbers $\left(u^{-1 / 3}, v^{-1 / 3}, v^{\prime-1 / 3}\right)$ are the lengths $\left(\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|,\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|,\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|\right)$ of a non-flat triangle, which is close to an equilateral triangle.

Let us now assume that for some $x<y$, the numbers $\left(u^{-1 / 3}, v^{-1 / 3}, v^{\prime-1 / 3}\right)$ are not the lengths of the sides of a non-flat triangle. Let us denote by $u(t), v(t), v^{\prime}(t)$ the values of $u, v, v^{\prime}$ associated with $x(t)=t x$ and $y(t)=y$. For $t$ close to 0 , we have just seen that $\left((u(t))^{-1 / 3},(v(t))^{-1 / 3},\left(v^{\prime}(t)\right)^{-1 / 3}\right)$ actually defines a non-flat triangle, whereas $\left((u(1))^{-1 / 3},(v(1))^{-1 / 3},\left(v^{\prime}(1)\right)^{-1 / 3}\right)$ does not define a non-flat triangle any more. The solutions $u, v, v^{\prime}$ depend on $x$ and $y$ in a continuous way. So at a certain time $t \leqslant 1$, the triangle is flat. Let us first assume that $\vec{r}_{3} \in] \vec{r}_{1}, \vec{r}_{4}[$ at this time. Let us set: $a=(u(t))^{-1 / 3}=\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|$, $b=\left(v^{\prime}(t)\right)^{-1 / 3}=\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|$. We have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\| & =(v(t))^{-1 / 3}=a+b \\
\left(u^{\prime}(t)\right)^{-2 / 3} & =g(u(t), v(t))-\left(v^{\prime}(t)\right)^{-2 / 3}=2-b^{2}=2 f(u(t), v(t))-b^{2} \\
& =2\left((u(t))^{-2 / 3}+(v(t))^{-2 / 3}\right)-b^{2}=2\left(a^{2}+(a+b)^{2}\right)-b^{2}=(2 a+b)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{2 x(t)}{(2 a+b)^{3}}=\frac{x(t)+y(t)}{a^{3}}+\frac{x(t)-y(t)}{(a+b)^{3}} \\
\frac{2 y(t)}{b^{3}}=\frac{x(t)+y(t)}{a^{3}}+\frac{y(t)-x(t)}{(a+b)^{3}}
\end{array}\right.
$$

Eliminating $x(t)$ and $y(t)$, we obtain:

$$
\left(\frac{1}{a^{3}}-\frac{1}{(a+b)^{3}}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{1}{a^{3}}+\frac{1}{(a+b)^{3}}-\frac{2}{(2 a+b)^{3}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{a^{3}}+\frac{1}{(a+b)^{3}}-\frac{2}{b^{3}}\right)
$$

For sake of convenience, we can study this equation under the assumption: $a=1$. Then we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(b^{3}+(b+2)^{3}\right)\left((b+1)^{3}+1\right) & =2\left(b^{3}(b+2)^{3}+(b+1)^{3}\right) \\
2 b^{6}+12 b^{5}+36 b^{4}+66 b^{3}+72 b^{2}+48 b+16 & =2 b^{6}+12 b^{5}+24 b^{4}+18 b^{3}+6 b^{2}+6 b+2
\end{aligned}
$$

No positive value of $b$ is a solution. So the triangle cannot be flat. We can obtain the same result for $\vec{r}_{4} \in] \vec{r}_{1}, \vec{r}_{3}[$. Lastly, as we have:

$$
v^{\prime}(t)=\frac{x(t)+y(t)}{2 y(t)} u(t)+\frac{y(t)-x(t)}{2 y(t)} v(t)
$$

we cannot simultaneously have: $u(t)>v^{\prime}(t)$ and $v(t)>v^{\prime}(t)$. Hence: $\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\| \geqslant\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|$ or $\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\| \geqslant\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|$. So we cannot have: $\vec{r}_{1} \in] \vec{r}_{3}, \vec{r}_{4}[$. Thus, the numbers $\left((u(t))^{-1 / 3},(v(t))^{-1 / 3}\right.$, $\left.\left(v^{\prime}(t)\right)^{-1 / 3}\right)$ cannot define a flat triangle. So the numbers

$$
\left(u^{-1 / 3}, v^{-1 / 3}, v^{\prime-1 / 3}\right)=\left((u(1))^{-1 / 3},(v(1))^{-1 / 3},\left(v^{\prime}(1)\right)^{-1 / 3}\right)
$$

are the mutual distances $\left(\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|,\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|,\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|\right)$ of a non-flat triangle.

Let $\vec{r}_{2}$ be the point such that $\left(\vec{r}_{1}, \vec{r}_{2}, \vec{r}_{3}, \vec{r}_{4}\right)$ is a parallelogram. We necessarily have: $\vec{\gamma}_{3}=\vec{\gamma}_{4}$. Moreover:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{2 x}{\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}=\frac{x+y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{x-y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}} \\
\frac{2 y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|^{3}}=\frac{x+y}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{y-x}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}
\end{array}\right.
$$

This enables to prove that $\vec{\gamma}_{1}=\vec{\gamma}_{3}$. Lastly:

$$
m_{2} \vec{\gamma}_{2}=-\left(m_{1} \vec{\gamma}_{1}+m_{3} \vec{\gamma}_{3}+m_{4} \vec{\gamma}_{4}\right)=-\left(m_{1}+m_{3}+m_{4}\right) \vec{\gamma}_{1}=m_{2} \vec{\gamma}_{1}
$$

As $\vec{r}_{1}, \vec{r}_{3}$ and $\vec{r}_{4}$ are not collinear, the parallelogram is not flat. So the configuration is noncollinear, central with vanishing multiplier for the masses $x,-x, y,-y$.

# 4. Planar non-collinear central configurations with masses $x,-x, y,-y$ and $\xi \neq 0$ 

Let us define the vector of inertia $\vec{\lambda}$ of an $N$-body system with vanishing total mass ( $M=$ $\left.m_{1}+\cdots+m_{N}=0\right)$ by:

$$
\vec{\lambda}=m_{1}\left(\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{a}\right)+\cdots+m_{N}\left(\vec{r}_{N}-\vec{a}\right)
$$

(the identity does not depend on the origin $\vec{a}$ ).
Proposition 3. For any central configuration with vanishing total mass: $\xi \vec{\lambda}=\overrightarrow{0}$.
Proof. We have to write:

$$
\overrightarrow{0}=\sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i} \vec{\gamma}_{i}\left(\vec{r}_{1}, \ldots, \vec{r}_{N}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{N} \xi m_{i}\left(\vec{r}_{i}-\vec{a}\right)=\xi \vec{\lambda}
$$

For every $N$-body configuration with dimension $N-2$, there exists exactly one $N$-tuple up to homotheties $\left(\Delta_{1}, \ldots, \Delta_{N}\right)$ such that $\Delta_{1}+\cdots+\Delta_{N}=0$ and $\Delta_{1}\left(\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{a}\right)+\cdots+\Delta_{N}\left(\vec{r}_{N}-\vec{a}\right)=\overrightarrow{0}$ (the identity does not depend on the origin $\vec{a}$ ). This follows from the fact that the linear map $\left(\xi_{1}, \ldots, \xi_{N}\right) \rightarrow \xi_{1}\left(\vec{r}_{1}-\vec{a}\right)+\cdots+\xi_{N}\left(\vec{r}_{N}-\vec{a}\right)$ with $\xi_{1}+\cdots+\xi_{N}=0$ has rank $N-2$ . So its kernel has dimension $(N-1)-(N-2)=1$. For every configuration with dimension $N-2$ and vanishing $\vec{\lambda}$, the $N$-tuples $\left(m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}\right)$ and $\left(\Delta_{1}, \ldots, \Delta_{N}\right)$ are collinear.

Proposition 4. A planar non-collinear four-body configuration is central with vanishing vector of inertia for a system of non-vanishing masses whose sum vanishes if, and only if:

- No three-body subconfiguration is collinear.
- The mutual distances satisfy the following identity, which does not involve the masses:

$$
\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|^{3}}=\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}=\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}
$$

Then $\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}, m_{4}\right)$ and $\left(\Delta_{1}, \Delta_{2}, \Delta_{3}, \Delta_{4}\right)$ are collinear.



Fig. 2.

Proof. For a non-collinear four-body configuration with vanishing $\vec{\lambda}$, the quadruples $\left(m_{1}, m_{2}\right.$, $m_{3}, m_{4}$ ) and $\left(\Delta_{1}, \Delta_{2}, \Delta_{3}, \Delta_{4}\right)$ are collinear. So $\Delta_{i} \neq 0$ for every $i$, and no three-body subconfiguration is collinear. The configuration is central if, and only if, it satisfies the Laura-Andoyer equations :

$$
m_{k} \Delta_{l}\left(\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{k}-\vec{r}_{l}\right\|^{3}}-\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{k}-\vec{r}_{j}\right\|^{3}}\right)=m_{l} \Delta_{k}\left(\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{l}-\vec{r}_{i}\right\|^{3}}-\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{l}-\vec{r}_{j}\right\|^{3}}\right)
$$

with $\{i, j, k, l\}=\{1,2,3,4\}$. Thanks to the collinearity of the vectors $\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}, m_{4}\right)$ and $\left(\Delta_{1}, \Delta_{2}, \Delta_{3}, \Delta_{4}\right)$, these equations are equivalent to:

$$
\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|^{3}}=\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}=\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}
$$

We can explain the degeneracy of the Laura-Andoyer equations by noticing that the condition: $\vec{\lambda}=\overrightarrow{0}$ enables to express the position of a body as a barycenter of the three others. Thus we have to deal with a three-body problem, with a different expression for the accelerations. Let us notice that this property is only the static variant of a more general fact: for $M=0$, the vector $\vec{\lambda}$ is the first integral which replaces the center of inertia. As it is invariant under translations, the $N$-body problem becomes 'more integrable' .

In the plane, we will call band of a line segment $[\vec{a}, \vec{b}]$ the set of the $\vec{r}+\vec{u}$, where $\vec{r} \in[\vec{a}, \vec{b}]$ and $\vec{u} \perp \vec{b}-\vec{a}$. We will call bands of a trapezoid the bands associated with its bases. Let us denote them by $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{B}^{\prime}$. If $\mathcal{B} \subset \mathcal{B}^{\prime}$ or $\mathcal{B}^{\prime} \subset \mathcal{B}$, we will say that the trapezoid is balanced. If $\mathcal{B} \cap \mathcal{B}^{\prime}=\emptyset$, we will say that the trapezoid is unbalanced. Otherwise, we will say that the trapezoid is semi-balanced (Fig. 2).

Theorem 5. For any two non-vanishing real numbers $x$ and $y$, there exist exactly two noncollinear central configurations (up to similarities) with non-vanishing multiplier for the masses $x,-x, y,-y$. These configurations are semi-balanced trapezoids. They are symmetrical with respect to a line which is orthogonal to the bases. If $x=y$ or $x=-y$, they are diamonds. The bodies with masses $x$ and $-x$ (respectively the bodies with masses $y$ and $-y$ ) are at the endpoints of one of the two parallel sides. Among the parallel sides, the side whose endpoints have the larger absolute value is the smaller. Two bodies which are on a same diagonal have masses with the same sign.

Proof. According to Proposition 3, we have, for such a central configuration: $\vec{\lambda}=\overrightarrow{0}$. So $x\left(\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right)=y\left(\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{4}\right)$ : the configuration is a trapezoid, and the bodies with masses $x$ and $-x$ (respectively the bodies with masses $y$ and $-y$ ) are at the endpoints of one of the two parallel sides. Among the parallel sides, the side whose endpoints have the larger absolute value is the smaller. Two bodies which are on a same diagonal have masses with the same sign.

We can assume: $x, y>0$. If necessary, we can exchange body 1 and body 2 , or body 3 and body 4 .

Let us assume the trapezoid to be balanced and, for instance: $y \leqslant x$. Then we have: $\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|<$ $\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|,\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|<\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|$. This is incompatible with the identity:

$$
\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}=\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}
$$

which follows from Proposition 4. So the trapezoid is not balanced. With a similar reasoning, we prove that the trapezoid is not unbalanced.

As we are looking for configurations up to similarities, we can assume $\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|=x$. The configuration is a trapezoid. Let us denote by $\vec{a}$ the intersection of $\left[\vec{r}_{1}, \vec{r}_{3}\right]$ and $\left[\vec{r}_{2}, \vec{r}_{4}\right]$, which are the diagonals of the trapezoid. The trapezoid up to isometries is defined by $\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{a}\right\|$ and $\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{a}\right\|$ such that $\left(\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{a}\right\|,\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{a}\right\|, x\right)$ satisfies the triangular inequalities. Let us set: $u=\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{2}$, $v=\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{2}$. We have: $\frac{\sqrt{v}}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{a}\right\|}=\frac{\sqrt{u}}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{a}\right\|}=\frac{x+y}{x}$. The trapezoid up to isometries is defined by $(u, v)$ such that $(\sqrt{u}, \sqrt{v}, x+y)$ are the lengths of the sides of a triangle.

Let us set:

$$
I(\vec{a})=\sum_{i=1}^{4} m_{i}\left\|\vec{r}_{i}-\vec{a}\right\|^{2}
$$

We have: $d I=-2 \vec{\lambda} . d \vec{a}=0$. Hence:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
I\left(\vec{r}_{2}\right)=I\left(\vec{r}_{1}\right) \\
I\left(\vec{r}_{2}\right)=I\left(\vec{r}_{3}\right)
\end{array}\right.
$$

This is equivalent to:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{2}+\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{2}=u+v-2 x y \\
(x+y)\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{2}=x u+y v-x y(x+y)
\end{array}\right.
$$

We set:

$$
\varphi\binom{u}{v}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\frac{x}{x+y} & \frac{y}{x+y} \\
\frac{y}{x+y} & \frac{x}{x+y}
\end{array}\right)\binom{u}{v}-x y\binom{1}{1}
$$

We have: $\varphi=\mathcal{T} \circ \mathcal{A}$, where $\mathcal{A}$ is the orthogonal scaling with respect to the first bisector with scale factor $\frac{x-y}{x+y}$ (it is an orthogonal projection for $x=y$ ), whose absolute value is smaller than 1 , and $\mathcal{T}$ is the translation with vector $-x y(1,1)$. The previous system is equivalent to: $\left(\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{2},\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{2}\right)=\varphi(u, v)$.



Fig. 3.

If the configuration is non-collinear central, we have, according to Proposition 4:

$$
\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{3}}+\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{3}}=\frac{1}{u^{3 / 2}}+\frac{1}{v^{3 / 2}}=\frac{1}{x^{3}}+\frac{1}{y^{3}}
$$

We set: $f(u, v)=\frac{1}{u^{3 / 2}}+\frac{1}{v^{3 / 2}}$. The previous identity is equivalent to:

$$
f(u, v)=f(\varphi(u, v))=f\left(x^{2}, y^{2}\right)
$$

Let $\Gamma$ be the contour line of $f$ associated with the value $f\left(x^{2}, y^{2}\right)$. Then $(u, v)$ satisfies Eq. (1) if, and only if: $(u, v) \in \Gamma \cap \varphi^{-1}(\Gamma)$. For every $x, y>0$, there exist exactly two solutions of (1) in $\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*} \times \mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}$, which can be written as $(u, v)$ and $(v, u)$. The solutions are the two intersections of $\Gamma$ and $\varphi^{-1}(\Gamma)$, and they depend on $x$ and $y$ in a continuous way (Fig. 3).

Conversely, let us consider one of the two solutions $(u, v)$ of (1). We have just seen that $(u, v)$ defines a trapezoid up to isometries if, and only if, the numbers $(\sqrt{u}, \sqrt{v}, x+y)$ are the lengths of the sides of a triangle. If $x=y=1$, the numbers $u$ and $v$ satisfy:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{1}{u^{3 / 2}}+\frac{1}{v^{3 / 2}}=2 \\
u+v=4
\end{array}\right.
$$

We obtain:

$$
(u, v) \approx(3.332979836 ; 0.6670201635) \quad \text { or } \quad(0.6670201635 ; 3.332979836)
$$

Thus for any $x=y$ :

$$
\begin{gathered}
(\sqrt{u}, \sqrt{v}, x+y) \approx(1.825645047 ; 0.8167130240 ; 2) x \\
\text { or } \quad(0.8167130240 ; 1.825645047 ; 2) x
\end{gathered}
$$

It can be checked that they are the sides of a non-flat triangle. If $x \neq y$, let us assume that $(\sqrt{u}, \sqrt{v}, x+y)$ are not the lengths of the sides of a non-flat triangle. Let us denote by $(u(t), v(t))$ a solution (depending on $t$ ) associated with $x(t)=x$ and $y(t)=x+t(y-x)$. We have $x(0)=y(0)$, and $(\sqrt{u(0)}, \sqrt{v(0)}, x(0)+y(0))$ actually defines a non-flat triangle, whereas $(\sqrt{u(1)}, \sqrt{v(1)}, x(1)+y(1))$ does not define a non-flat triangle any more. The solutions $u$ and $v$ depend on $x$ and $y$ in a continuous way. So at a certain time $t \leqslant 1$, the triangle is flat. So the configuration of the four bodies at time $t$ is a flat trapezoid. As the trapezoid is semi-balanced, the bodies are on a line in the order: $1,4,2,3$. Hence: $\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|<\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|$ and $\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|<\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|$. Thus:

$$
\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{2}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|}+\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{3}\right\|}<\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|}+\frac{1}{\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|}
$$

which is impossible. So $(\sqrt{u}, \sqrt{v}, x+y)=(\sqrt{u(1)}, \sqrt{v(1)}, x(1)+y(1))$ actually defines a nonflat triangle. So, according to Proposition 4, the solution $(u, v)$ defines a non-collinear central configuration with vanishing vector of inertia. If $x=y$, according to Theorem 2, we cannot have: $\xi=0$. According to the theorem, this is still true if $x \neq y$ as the bodies with masses $x$ and $-x$ cannot be at the endpoints of a same diagonal. Thus the solution $(u, v)$ actually defines a non-collinear central configuration with vanishing multiplier.

We obtain a central configuration from the other by exchanging $u$ and $v$. This is equivalent to exchanging body 1 and body 2 and to exchanging body 3 and body 4 . This is also equivalent to considering the image of the configuration by a symmetry whose axis is orthogonal to the bases of the trapezoid. For one solution, the endpoints of the larger diagonal of the trapezoid are the bodies with positive masses. For the other one, they are the bodies with negative masses.

For $x=y$, every central configuration is a parallelogram according to the vanishing of $\vec{\lambda}$. In fact, in this case, vector $\varphi(\vec{u}, \vec{v})$ is collinear with $(1,1)$ for every $(\vec{u}, \vec{v})$, so $\left(\left\|\vec{r}_{3}-\vec{r}_{2}\right\|^{2}\right.$, $\left\|\vec{r}_{4}-\vec{r}_{1}\right\|^{2})=\varphi(u, v)$ is collinear with $(1,1)$. Hence:
