$\left\{(a, b, c) \in \mathbb{R}^{3}: a \geq 1, b>c, D=0, r_{24} \geq r_{13}>r_{12} \geq r_{23} \geq r_{14} \geq r_{34}\right\}$, and the boundary of $\Omega$ is $\mathcal{C}_{1} \cup \mathcal{C}_{2} \cup \mathcal{C}_{3} \cup P_{1} \cup P_{2} \cup P_{3}$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathcal{C}_{1}=\{(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3}, c): c \in(-1 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3})\} \\
& \mathcal{C}_{2}=\left\{\left(\sqrt{1+c^{2}}, c+\sqrt{1+c^{2}}, c\right): c \in(-1 / \sqrt{3}, 0)\right\} \\
& \mathcal{C}_{3}=\{(a, b, c): a=b+c, f(b, c)=0, c \in(0,1 / \sqrt{3})\} \\
& P_{1}=(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3}) \\
& P_{2}=(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3},-1 / \sqrt{3}) \\
& P_{3}=(1,1,0)
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(b, c)= & \left((b+c)^{3}-\left(c^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right)\left(\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}-(b-c)^{3}\right)- \\
& \left(\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}-(b+c)^{3}\right)\left(\left(c^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}-(b-c)^{3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

See Figure 3 for the plot of the set $\Omega$.
The points of $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ provide configurations of the restricted problem with $m_{1}, m_{2}$ and $m_{3}$ in an equilateral triangle; the points of $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{3}$ provide rhombus and isosceles trapezoid central configurations, respectively; $P_{1}$ corresponds to an equilateral triangle configuration of the restricted problem with a collision of $m_{3}$ and $m_{4}$ at one of the vertices; $P_{2}$ corresponds to a configuration of the restricted problem with the masses at the vertices of a rhombus and such that the positions of $m_{1}, m_{2}$ and $m_{3}$ are the vertices of an equilateral triangle; and $P_{3}$ corresponds to the square central configuration.

Proof. Easily we can compute $r_{24}=\sqrt{1+(a-c)^{2}}, r_{13}=\sqrt{1+b^{2}}$, $r_{12}=a, r_{23}=\sqrt{1+(a-b)^{2}}, r_{14}=\sqrt{1+c^{2}}$, and $r_{34}=b-c$. Proposition 7 gives the characterization of the central configurations on the boundaries of $\Omega$. We prove the result by using this characterization and the parametrization $(a, b, c)$.

On the boundary with the masses $m_{1}, m_{2}$ and $m_{3}$ at the vertices of an equilateral triangle we have $r_{13}=r_{12}=r_{23}$. Solving the system of equations $r_{13}=r_{12}=r_{23}$, we get $a=2 / \sqrt{3}$ and $b=1 / \sqrt{3}$. Substituting

this solution into $r_{23}$ and $r_{14}$ and imposing the condition $r_{23} \geq r_{14}$, we get the condition $-1 / \sqrt{3} \leq c \leq 1 / \sqrt{3}$. It is easy to check that the solution $(a, b, c)=(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3}, c)$ with $c \in[-1 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3}]$ satisfies $r_{24} \geq r_{13} \geq r_{12} \geq r_{23} \geq r_{14} \geq r_{34}$. So the set $\mathcal{C}_{1} \cup P_{1} \cup P_{2}$ belongs to the boundary of $\Omega$. Moreover it is easy to check that the point $P_{1}$ correspond to an equilateral triangle configuration with the masses $m_{3}$ and $m_{4}$ colliding at the corresponding vertex of the triangle; and the point $P_{2}$ corresponds to a rhombus configuration such that $m_{1}, m_{2}$ and $m_{3}$ are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle.

On the rhombus configurations we have $r_{12}=r_{23}=r_{14}=r_{24}$. Solving the system of equations $r_{12}=r_{23}=r_{14}=r_{24}$ we get the solution $s(c)=(a, b)=\left(\sqrt{1+c^{2}}, c+\sqrt{1+c^{2}}\right)$. Imposing that this solution satisfies $r_{24} \geq r_{13}>r_{12}$ we get the condition $-1 / \sqrt{3}<c \leq 0$. So $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ belongs to the boundary of $\Omega$. Moreover $s(0)=(1,1)$ and $s(-1 / \sqrt{3})=(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3})$. So the endpoints of $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ are $P_{2}$ and $P_{3}$.

On the isosceles trapezoid, configurations $(a, b, c)$ are such that $r_{23}=$ $r_{14}, r_{24}=r_{13}$ and $D=0$. If $r_{23}=r_{14}$ and $r_{24}=r_{13}$, then the Dziobeck equation $D=0$ becomes

$$
\left(r_{14}^{3}-r_{13}^{3}\right)\left(\left(r_{12}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right)-\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)\left(r_{14}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right)\right)=0
$$

If $r_{14}=r_{13}$, then $r_{24}=r_{13}=r_{12}=r_{23}=r_{14}$. This corresponds to the point $P_{1}$ (see the proof of Proposition 6). Assume now that $r_{14} \neq r_{13}$. Solving system $r_{23}=r_{14}, r_{24}=r_{13}$ we get $a=b+c$. So $r_{24}=r_{13}=$ $\sqrt{b^{2}+1}, r_{12}=b+c, r_{23}=r_{14}=\sqrt{c^{2}+1}$, and $r_{34}=b-c$ and condition $D=0$ is equivalent to condition $f(b, c)=0$. Cors and Roberts in , using a different parametrization, proved the existence of a unique oneparameter family of isosceles trapezoid central configurations which is characterized by a differentiable function of one of the parameters in the parameter space. Moreover they prove that the endpoints of this family are the square configuration and the configuration consisting of an equilateral triangle with the masses $m_{3}=m_{4}=0$ at one of the vertices. In our parametrization the differentiable function of the parameter is the function $b(c)$ defined implicitly by $f(b, c)=0$ and the endpoints of the curve are the points $P_{1}$ and $P_{3}$. Thus $\mathcal{C}_{3}$ is the last curve in the boundary of $\Omega$ and it is a curve joining $P_{1}$ and $P_{3}$, see Figure 3.

Unfortunately we are not able to prove that $\Omega$ is a differentiable function over the two positions of the masses, as was stablish in the co-circular case, see . Nevertheless, in the next section we prove



Figure 3. The surface $\Omega$ of the trapezoid central configurations in the $a b c$-space.
that there exist a one-parameter family of trapezoid central configurations that divides $\Omega$ in two disjoint regions, namely the region that contains the trapezoid central configurations and the one that contains the obtuse trapezoid central configurations.

# 6. The RIGHT TrAPEZOID FAMILY 

We suppose again that we are in the hypotheses of Lemma 2; i.e. that $r_{12} \geqslant r_{23} \geqslant r_{14} \geqslant r_{34}$. We assume also that the position of the masses $m_{1}=1, m_{2}, m_{3}$ and $m_{4}$ are respectively $(0,0),(0, a),(1, b),(1,0)$ with $a \geqslant 1$ and $a \geqslant b>0$. Easily we can compute the mutual distances $r_{12}=a, r_{23}=\sqrt{1+(a-b)^{2}}, r_{14}=1, r_{34}=b$, and $r_{13}=\sqrt{1+b^{2}}$ and $r_{24}=\sqrt{1+a^{2}}$ (the diagonals).

First we give the set $\widetilde{\Omega}$ (see Lemma 2) on the right trapezoid family parameterized by the positions of the masses $(a, b)$. It is obvious that condition $r_{24}>r_{12}$ is always satisfied and that condition $r_{34} \leqslant r_{14}$ implies $b \leqslant 1$. On the other hand, it is easy to see that conditions $r_{13}>r_{12}$ and $r_{12} \geqslant r_{23}$ imply that $a<a_{1}(b)=\sqrt{1+b^{2}}$ and $a \geqslant a_{2}(b)=$ $\left(b^{2}+1\right) /(2 b)$ respectively. From here we get condition $a_{1}(b)>a_{2}(b)$ which is satisfied for $b>1 / \sqrt{3}$. In short, the set $\widetilde{\Omega}$ (see Lemma 2) on the right trapezoid family is
$\Omega_{r}=\left\{(a, b, c) \in \mathbb{R}^{3}: \frac{b^{2}+1}{2 b} \leqslant a<\sqrt{1+b^{2}}, \quad \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}<b \leqslant 1, \quad c=0\right\}$.



Figure 4. (a) The region $\Omega_{r}$ and the the curve $D=0$ for the right trapezoid family in the $a-b$ plane. (b) The the curve $D=0$ for the right trapezoid family on the region $\Omega$.

We can see that $a_{1}$ is a decreasing function in $b \in(1 / \sqrt{3}, 1]$ with $a_{1}(1 / \sqrt{3})=2 / \sqrt{3}$ and $a_{1}(1)=1$, whereas $a_{2}$ is an increasing function in $b \in(1 / \sqrt{3}, 1]$ with $a_{2}(1 / \sqrt{3})=2 / \sqrt{3}$ and $a_{2}(1)=\sqrt{2}$ (see Figure 4). Therefore $a \in(1, \sqrt{2})$.
Theorem 9. The curve $D=0$ is a graph with respect to the variable $a$ in the region $\Omega_{r}$ (see Figure 4). In fact, $\partial D / \partial a$ evaluated at the curve $D=0$ restricted to $\Omega_{r}$ is negative.

Proof. When $b=1$ equation $D=0$ becomes

$$
(1-2 \sqrt{2})\left(\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}-1\right)\left(a^{3}-\left(a^{2}-2 a+2\right)^{3 / 2}\right)=0
$$

which has a unique real solution with $a \geq 1$, the solution $a=1$. After straightforward computations we see that substituting $a=a_{2}(b)$ into $D$ we get a function of $b$ that is zero at $b=1$ and $b=1 / \sqrt{3}$ and positive for $b \in(1 / \sqrt{3}, 1)$. In a similar way substituting $a=a_{1}(b)$ into $D$ we get a function of $b$ that is zero at $b=0$ and $b=1 / \sqrt{3}$ and negative for $b \in(1 / \sqrt{3}, 1]$. Therefore each curve in $\Omega_{r}$ joining a point of the curve $a_{1}(b)$ with a point of the curve $a_{2}(b)$ has at least a point with $D=0$. Therefore there exist al least one set in $\Omega_{r}$ satisfying $D=0$. Next we see that this set is a graph in the variable $a$ that joins the points $(1,1)$ and $(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3})$, see Figure 4(a).

By simple computations we get

$$
\frac{\partial D}{\partial a}=\frac{\partial D}{\partial r_{12}} \frac{\partial r_{12}}{\partial a}+\frac{\partial D}{\partial r_{23}} \frac{\partial r_{23}}{\partial a}+\frac{\partial D}{\partial r_{24}} \frac{\partial r_{24}}{\partial a}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial r_{12}}{\partial a} & =1 \\
\frac{\partial r_{23}}{\partial a} & =\frac{a-b}{r_{23}}=\frac{r_{12}-r_{34}}{r_{23}} \\
\frac{\partial r_{24}}{\partial a} & =\frac{a}{r_{24}}=\frac{r_{12}}{r_{24}}
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial D}{\partial r_{12}} & =-3 r_{12}^{2}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{23}^{3}\right)\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right)-3 r_{12}^{2}\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)\left(r_{23}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right) \\
\frac{\partial D}{\partial r_{23}} & =3 r_{23}^{2}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)+3 r_{23}^{2}\left(r_{12}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right) \\
\frac{\partial D}{\partial r_{24}} & =3 r_{24}^{2}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)\left(r_{23}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right)-3 r_{24}^{2}\left(r_{12}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{23}^{3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms in a convenient way $\partial D / \partial a$ can be written in terms of the mutual distances as

$$
\frac{\partial D}{\partial a}=3\left(f_{1}+f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}+f_{5}+f_{6}\right)
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f_{1}=-r_{12}^{2}\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)\left(r_{23}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right) \\
& f_{2}=-r_{12}^{2}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{23}^{3}\right)\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right) \\
& f_{3}=r_{23}\left(r_{12}-r_{34}\right)\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right) \\
& f_{4}=r_{23}\left(r_{12}-r_{34}\right)\left(r_{12}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right) \\
& f_{5}=r_{12} r_{24}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)\left(r_{23}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right) \\
& f_{6}=-r_{12} r_{24}\left(r_{12}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{23}^{3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we will see that at the points of $\Omega_{r}$ satisfying $D=0$ the following conditions hold: $f_{1}+f_{4}<0, f_{2}+f_{5}<0$ and $f_{3}+f_{6} \leqslant 0$. Therefore $\partial D / \partial a$ evaluated at the curve $D=0$ restricted to $\Omega_{r}$ is negative.

From $D=0$ we get

$$
\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)\left(r_{23}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right)=\frac{\left(r_{12}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{233}^{}\right)\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right)}{r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}}
$$

Then $f_{1}+f_{4}$ can be written as

$$
f_{1}+f_{4}=\frac{g_{1}\left(r_{12}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right)}{r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}}
$$

where

$$
g_{1}=-r_{34} r_{23}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)-r_{12}\left(r_{12}-r_{23}\right)\left(r_{12} r_{23}\left(r_{12}+r_{23}\right)+r_{13}^{3}\right)
$$

Since $r_{13}>r_{12} \geqslant r_{23}$ on $\Omega_{r}$ and $g_{1}<0$ on $\Omega_{r}$, it follows that $f_{1}+f_{4}<0$ evaluated at the curve $D=0$ restricted to $\Omega_{r}$.

Proceeding as above, using that $D=0$ expression $f_{2}+f_{5}$ can be written as

$$
f_{2}+f_{5}=\frac{g_{2}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)\left(r_{23}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right)}{r_{12}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}}
$$

where

$$
g_{2}=-r_{12}\left(r_{24}-r_{12}\right)\left(r_{14}^{3}+r_{12}^{2} r_{24}+r_{12} r_{24}^{2}\right)
$$

Since $r_{24}>r_{12}$ on $\Omega_{r}, g_{2}<0$ on $\Omega_{r}$, we obtain that $f_{2}+f_{5}<0$ evaluated at the curve $D=0$ restricted to $\Omega_{r}$.

Finally, using that $D=0$ expression $f_{3}+f_{6}$ can be written as

$$
f_{3}+f_{6}=\frac{g_{3}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)}{r_{24}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}}
$$

where

$$
g_{3}=-r_{24} r_{12}\left(r_{23}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right)+r_{23}\left(r_{12}-r_{34}\right)\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right)
$$

There exists a curve in $\Omega_{r}$ such that $g_{3}=0$, so the previous arguments are not valid to prove that $f_{3}+f_{6}$ evaluated at the curve $D=0$ restricted to $\Omega_{r}$ is negative.

In order to avoid the last obstacle, by using resultants we will prove that there are no values $(a, b)$ in the interior of $\Omega_{r}$ for which $D$ and $g_{3}$ are zero simultaneously.

Let $\operatorname{Res}$ denote the resultant of the polynomials $P(x, y)$ and $Q(x, y)$ with respect to $x$. The resultant $\operatorname{Res}$ is a polynomial in the variable $y$ satisfying the following property: if $(x, y)=\left(x^{*}, y^{*}\right)$ is a solution of system $P(x, y)=0, Q(x, y)=0$ then $y=y^{*}$ is a zero of $\operatorname{Res}$. In other words, the set of zeroes of $\operatorname{Res}$ contains the components $y$ of all solutions of the system $P(x, y)=0$ and $Q(x, y)=0$. We observe that it may contain additional solutions that are not related with the solutions of the system $P(x, y)=0$ and $Q(x, y)=0$.

Let

$$
\begin{aligned}
& e_{1}=e_{1}\left(a, b, r_{13}, r_{23}, r_{24}\right)=0 \\
& e_{2}=e_{2}\left(a, b, r_{23}, r_{24}\right)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

be the system defined by the two equations $D=0$ and $g_{3}=0$ after performing the substitutions $r_{12}=a, r_{14}=1$ and $r_{34}=b$. Here we think that the mutual distances $r_{13}, r_{23}$ and $r_{24}$ are the positive solutions of system

$$
\begin{aligned}
& e_{3}=e_{3}\left(a, b, r_{13}\right)=r_{13}^{2}-\left(b^{2}+1\right)=0 \\
& e_{4}=e_{4}\left(a, b, r_{23}\right)=r_{23}^{2}-\left((a-b)^{2}+1\right)=0 \\
& e_{5}=e_{5}\left(a, b, r_{24}\right)=r_{24}^{2}-\left(a^{2}+1\right)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Using resultants we eliminate the variables $r_{13}, r_{23}$ and $r_{24}$ from the equations (18) in the following way. We eliminate the variable $r_{13}$ from $e_{1}$ by doing the resultant

$$
R_{1}=\operatorname{Res}\left[e_{1}, e_{3}, r_{13}\right]
$$

Then we eliminate the variable $r_{23}$ from $R_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ by doing the resultants

$$
S_{1}=\operatorname{Res}\left[R_{1}, e_{4}, r_{23}\right], \quad S_{2}=\operatorname{Res}\left[e_{2}, e_{4}, r_{23}\right]
$$

and the variable $r_{24}$ from $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ by doing the resultants

$$
T_{1}=\operatorname{Res}\left[S_{1}, e_{5}, r_{24}\right], \quad T_{2}=\operatorname{Res}\left[S_{2}, e_{5}, r_{24}\right]
$$

Here $T_{1}=16 a^{2} b^{2} \widetilde{T}_{1}$ and $T_{2}=b^{4} \widetilde{T}_{2}$, were $\widetilde{T}_{1}$ and $\widetilde{T}_{2}$ are polynomials of total degree 64 and 16 , respectively, in the variables $a$ and $b$. Note that by the properties of resultants the set of solutions of the new system of equations $\widetilde{T}_{1}=0, \widetilde{T}_{2}=0$ contains all solutions with $a, b \neq 0$ of system (18), or equivalently all the solutions with $a, b \neq 0$ of system $D=0$, $g_{3}=0$ (thinking $D$ and $g_{3}$ as a function of $a, b$ via the mutual distances $\left.r_{i j}\right)$.

Now we solve system $\widetilde{T}_{1}=0, \widetilde{T}_{2}=0$ by using resultants again. We compute $\operatorname{Res}\left[\widetilde{T}_{1}, \widetilde{T}_{2}, a\right]$ and we get the polynomial

$$
\begin{aligned}
W(b)= & (b-1)^{16} b^{96}\left(b^{2}+1\right)^{20}\left(b^{2}-b+1\right)^{4}\left(b^{2}+b+1\right)^{16} \\
& \left(3 b^{2}-4\right)^{2}\left(21 b^{4}+12 b^{2}+16\right)^{4}\left(21 b^{4}+24 b^{2}+16\right)^{2} \\
& W_{1}(b) W_{2}(b) W_{3}(b) W_{4}(b)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $W_{1}, W_{2}, W_{3}$ and $W_{4}$ are polynomials of degrees 162, 202, 210, and 214 respectively. From properties of resultants the set of zeroes of $W$ contains the component $b$ of all the solutions of system $\widetilde{T}_{1}=0$, $\widetilde{T}_{2}=0$. Recall that we are only interested in solutions belonging to $\Omega_{r}$, so we only consider zeroes with $1 / \sqrt{3}<b \leqslant 1$. We compute

analytically the zeroes of the first eight factors of $W$ and numerically the zeroes of the remaining four factors of $W$ and we get the following solutions with $1 / \sqrt{3}<b \leqslant 1$

$$
\begin{array}{rlr}
b & =0.61283303 \ldots, & b=0.69216326 \ldots \\
b & =0.71614387 \ldots, & b=0.76874157 \ldots \\
b & =0.79099409 \ldots, & b=0.82966657 \ldots \\
b & =0.91953907 \ldots, & b=1
\end{array}
$$

Next we compute $\operatorname{Res}\left[\widetilde{T}_{1}, \widetilde{T}_{2}, b\right]$ and we get the polynomial

$$
\begin{aligned}
w(a)= & (a-1)^{24} a^{64}\left(a^{2}+1\right)^{40}\left(a^{2}-a+1\right)^{4}\left(a^{2}+a+1\right)^{8} \\
& \left(3 a^{2}-1\right)^{2}\left(21 a^{4}+6 a^{2}+1\right)^{4}\left(21 a^{4}+54 a^{2}+49\right)^{2} \\
& w_{1}(a) w_{2}(a) w_{3}(a) w_{4}(a)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $w_{1}, w_{2}, w_{3}$ and $w_{4}$ are polynomials of degrees 162, 202, 210, and 214 respectively. The set of zeroes of $w$ contains the component $a$ of all the solutions of system $\widetilde{T}_{1}=0, \widetilde{T}_{2}=0$. Since we are only interested in solutions belonging to $\Omega_{r}$, we only consider zeroes with $1 \leqslant a \leqslant \sqrt{2}$. As above we compute analytically the zeroes of the first eight factors of $w$ and numerically the zeroes of the remaining four factors of $w$ and we get the following solutions with $1 \leqslant a \leqslant \sqrt{2}$

$$
\begin{array}{rlr}
a & =1, & a=1.04304633 \ldots \\
a & =1.07124596 \ldots, & a=1.08484650 \ldots \\
a & =1.09217286 \ldots, & a=1.10559255 \ldots \\
a & =1.16459040 \ldots &
\end{array}
$$

We consider $D$ and $g_{3}$ as a function of $(a, b)$ by substituting the expressions of the mutual distances $r_{i j}$. The possible solutions $(a, b)$ of system $D=0, g_{3}=0$ are the pairs $(a, b)=\left(a^{*}, b^{*}\right)$ formed by a zero $a^{*}$ of $w$ with $a^{*} \in[1, \sqrt{2}]$, and a zero $b^{*}$ of $W$ with $b^{*} \in(1 / \sqrt{3}, 1]$. Substituting all possible pairs $(a, b)=\left(a^{*}, b^{*}\right)$ into $D=0, g_{3}=0$ we see that $(a, b)=(1,1)$ is the unique pair that provides a solution of the system. This point belongs to the boundary of $\Omega_{r}$. Therefore the function $g_{3}$ does not change its sign on the solutions of $D=0$ that belong to $\Omega_{r}$.

It is easy to the check that the point $(a, b)=(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3})$, which belongs to the boundary of $\Omega_{r}$, satisfies $D=0$. Moreover the function $g_{3}$ evaluated at $(a, b)=(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3})$ is negative. Hence $g_{3} \leqslant 0$ in $\Omega_{r}$. This end the proof of the theorem.



Figure 5. The plot of the masses $m_{2}$ (upper line), $m_{3}$ (medium line) and $m_{4}$ (bottom line) along the right trapezoid family.

In short, the set of realizable right trapezoid central configurations is

$$
\Omega_{r}^{\prime}=\left\{(a, b, c) \in \Omega_{r}: D=0\right\}
$$

and it is plotted in Figure 4. In Figure 5 we plot the masses along the right trapezoid family parameterized by the parameter $a$. We note that the limit case $(a, b)=(1,1)$ correspond to the square with equal masses, and the limit case $(a, b)=(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3})$ corresponds to a right trapezoid central configurations with masses $m_{1}=1, m_{4}=0$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{2} & =\frac{7(8 \sqrt{3}-9)(49+8 \sqrt{7})}{2511}=0.94993335 \ldots \\
m_{3} & =\frac{2}{63}(8 \sqrt{3}-9)=0.15417163 \ldots
\end{aligned}
$$

such that the masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}$ form an equilateral triangle with edge length $2 / \sqrt{3}$.

# 7. Trapezoid CC with a couple of equal masses 

In this section we will study the trapezoid CC with a pair of equal masses. In  Cors and Roberts shown that for a given order of the mutual distances in any co-circular central configuration the set of masses is completely ordered. A similar result for the trapezoid central configurations has been obtained recently by Santoprete . Although in that case the masses are not totally ordered. With our particular choice of labeling, from  any trapezoid central configuration satisfies

$$
m_{4} \leq m_{3} \leq m_{1}=1 \quad m_{4} \leq m_{2}
$$



Figure 6. The image of $\Omega$ in $m_{2} m_{3} m_{4}$-space under equations $(14),(15)$ and $(16)$ with $m_{1}=1$.

Moreover, also from Santoprete , we know that if $m_{3}=m_{1}=1$ or $m_{2}=m_{4}$, then the central configuration is a rhombus and the remaining two masses have to be equal. And if $m_{3}=m_{4}$, then the central configuration is an isosceles trapezoid and again the two remaining masses are necessarily equal. Figure 6 shows the full set of masses for which a trapezoid central configuration exist.

From the previous results only two cases of trapezoid central configuration with only a pair of equal masses remains unknown, namely, $m_{2}=m_{3}$ and $m_{2}=m_{1}=1$. In the next two subsections we are going to show the existence of these two classes of trapezoid central configuration. Something remarkable is that we will proved analytically the existence of non-symmetric trapezoid central configurations with two equal masses. As far as we know this result was known numerically, but we think that is the first time that this result is proved analytically in the four-body problem.

Now we study the value of masses along the boundary of $\Omega$.
The equilateral triangle family. By substituting the points of $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ into (14), (15) and (16) we get $m_{4}=0$ and

$$
m_{2}=\mu_{2}(c)=\frac{\left(8 \sqrt{3}-9 k_{1}^{3}\right) k_{2}^{3}}{9 k_{1}^{3}\left(k_{2}^{3}-8\right)}, \quad m_{3}=\mu_{3}(c)=\frac{2(\sqrt{3}-3 c)^{2}\left(8 \sqrt{3}-9 k_{1}^{3}\right)}{27(\sqrt{3} c+1) k_{1}^{3} k_{2}^{2}}
$$

where $k_{1}=\sqrt{c^{2}+1}$ and $k_{2}=\sqrt{3 c^{2}-4 \sqrt{3} c+7}$. The function $\mu_{2}$ is defined for all $c \in[-1 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3}), \mu_{2}(-1 / \sqrt{3})=0$ and $\mu_{2}(c) \rightarrow 1$ when $c \rightarrow 1 / \sqrt{3}$; moreover it is increasing for $c \in\left[-1 / \sqrt{3}, c_{0}\right)$, it has a maximum at $c_{0}=0.27448350 \ldots$ with $\mu_{2}\left(c_{0}\right)=1.0912476 \ldots$ and

it is decreasing for $c \in\left(c_{0}, 1 / \sqrt{3}\right)$. The function $\mu_{3}$ is defined for all $c \in(-1 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3}], \mu_{3}(1 / \sqrt{3})=0, \mu_{3}(c) \rightarrow 1 / 2$ when $c \rightarrow-1 / \sqrt{3}$ and it is decreasing for $c \in(-1 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3}]$. The plot of the masses on $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ is given in Figure 7 (a).

The rhombus family. By substituting the points of $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ into (14), (16) and (17) we get $m_{1}=m_{3}=1$ and

$$
m_{2}=m_{4}=\mu_{r}(c)=-\frac{\left((c-k)^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\left(\left((c+k)^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}-k^{3}\right)}{\left(k^{3}-\left((c-k)^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right)\left((c+k)^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

where $k=\sqrt{1+c^{2}}$. Note that on the rhombus family expression (15) is not well defined and we should take expression (17) instead of it. We can see that $\mu_{r}$ is an increasing function defined for all $c \in[-1 / \sqrt{3}, 0]$, such that $\mu_{r}(-1 / \sqrt{3})=0$ and $\mu_{r}(0)=1$. The plot of the masses on $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ is given in Figure 7 (b).

The isosceles trapezoid family. On the isosceles trapezoid family we know that $m_{1}=m_{2}=1$ and $m_{3}=m_{4}=\mu$ (see for instance ), but since we do not have an explicit expression of the solutions of $f(b, c)=0$, we cannot give the explicit expression of $\mu$ as a function of the parameter $c$. Studying numerically the function $\mu$ we see that it is a decreasing function in $c \in(0,1 / \sqrt{3})$ such that $\mu \rightarrow 1$ when $c \rightarrow 0$ and $\mu \rightarrow 0$ when $c \rightarrow 1 / \sqrt{3}$. The plot of the masses on $\mathcal{C}_{3}$ is given in Figure 7 (c).

Note that if we approach to $P_{2}$ over the set $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ then $m_{3} \rightarrow 1$, whereas if we approach to $P_{2}$ over the set $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ then $m_{3} \rightarrow 1 / 2$. Thus the limit of $m_{3}$ as we approach to $P_{2}$ depends on the path you take and $m_{3}$ has a non removable discontinuity at $P_{2}$.
7.1. $m_{2}=m_{3}$. Take $f=m_{2}-m_{3}$. We are interested in the solutions of $f=0$. On $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ (corresponding to the rhombus family) we have $r_{12}=$ $r_{23}=r_{34}=r_{14}$ and $m_{1}=m_{3}=1$.

We know from equation (14) that on $\mathcal{C}_{2}$

$$
m_{2}=\frac{r_{23}^{3} r_{24}^{3}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{14}^{3}\right)}{r_{13}^{3} r_{14}^{3}\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{23}^{3}\right)}=\frac{r_{24}^{3}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)}{r_{13}^{3}\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)}
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{2}<1 & \Longleftrightarrow \quad r_{24}^{3}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)<r_{13}^{3}\left(r_{24}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right) \\
& \Longleftrightarrow \quad-r_{24}^{3} r_{12}^{3}<-r_{13}^{3} r_{12}^{3} \Longleftrightarrow r_{24}^{3}>r_{13}^{3}
\end{aligned}
$$



Figure 7. (a) The plot of the masses $m_{2}$ (continuous line) and $m_{3}$ (dashed line) on the boundary $\mathcal{C}_{1}$. (b) The plot of the masses $m_{2}=m_{4}$ (continuous line) and $m_{1}=$ $m_{3}=1$ (dashed line) along the rhombus family. (c) The plot of the masses $m_{1}=m_{2}=1$ (dashed line) and $m_{3}=m_{4}$ (continuous line) along the isosceles trapezoid family.

The last inequality follows from the fact that $r_{24}>r_{13}>1$. Therefore on $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ we have $f=m_{2}-m_{3}<0$.

Now on $\mathcal{C}_{3}$ (corresponding to the isosceles trapezoid family) we have $r_{23}=r_{14}, r_{24}=r_{13}$ and $m_{1}=m_{2}=1$. We also know that on this family $m_{3}=m_{4}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{3}=m_{4}<1 \Longleftrightarrow & \frac{r_{34}^{2}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)}{r_{12}^{2}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right)} \\
& \Longleftrightarrow r_{34}^{2}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{12}^{3}\right)<r_{12}^{2}\left(r_{13}^{3}-r_{34}^{3}\right) \\
& \Longleftrightarrow-r_{13}^{3}\left(r_{12}^{2}-r_{34}^{2}\right)<r_{12}^{2} r_{34}^{2}\left(r_{12}-r_{34}\right) \\
& \Longleftrightarrow-r_{13}^{3}\left(r_{12}-r_{34}\right)\left(r_{12}+r_{34}\right)<r_{12}^{2} r_{34}^{2}\left(r_{12}-r_{34}\right) \\
& \Longleftrightarrow-r_{13}^{3}\left(r_{12}+r_{34}\right)<r_{12}^{2} r_{34}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

That is, on $\mathcal{C}_{3}$ we have $f=m_{2}-m_{3}>0$. Therefore for any given path connecting $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{3}$ in $\Omega$, there exist $(a, b, c) \in \Omega$ such that $f=0$ or equivalently $m_{2}=m_{3}$.

Numerically we show that for any fixed path connecting $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{3}$ in $\Omega$ the solution of $f=0$ is unique. Curve representing the zeros of $f$ in $\Omega$ goes from $P_{3}$ to $(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3},-0.351839354 \ldots) \in \mathcal{C}_{1}$ (see Figure 8 ). To verify the last statement, we observe that the function $f$ on $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ becomes

$$
f=\frac{\left(\frac{8}{3 \sqrt{3}}-\left(c^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right)\left(-\frac{6\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}-c\right)^{2}}{8-\left(3 c^{2}-2 \sqrt{3} c+1\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{\left(3 c^{2}-4 \sqrt{3} c+7\right)^{3 / 2}}{8-\left(3 c^{2}-4 \sqrt{3} c+7\right)^{3 / 2}}\right)}{\left(c^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$



Figure 8. (a) In black, the curve $m_{2}=m_{3}$ on the region $\Omega$. (b) The curves $m_{1}=1, m_{2}=m_{3}$, and $m_{4}$ parametrized by $a$ on the curve in (a).

We apply Sturm Theorem to conclude that $f=0$, as a polynomial of degree 24 , has a unique real solution in $c \in(-1 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3})$, namely $c=-0.351839354 \ldots$
7.2. $m_{2}=m_{1}=1$. It is clear that $m_{2}=m_{1}=1$ along the isosceles trapezoid central configuration family, that is, on the boundary $\mathcal{C}_{3}$. Moreover $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=m_{4}=1$ on $P_{3}$, that is, on the square configuration, and $m_{2}-m_{1}<0$ on $\mathcal{C}_{2} \cup P_{2}$.

On the boundary $\mathcal{C}_{1} \cup\left\{P_{1}, P_{2}\right\}$ we have $m_{4}=0$ and $m_{1}, m_{2}$ and $m_{3}$ at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. Let $m_{2}=\mu_{2}(c)$ be the value of the mass $m_{2}$ on $\mathcal{C}_{1}$, see (23). We have seen that $\mu_{2}(c) \rightarrow 1$ when $c \rightarrow 1 / \sqrt{3}$, and that $\mu_{2}$ is decreasing for $c \in\left(c_{0}, 1 / \sqrt{3}\right)$ with $c_{0}=0.27448350 \ldots$, so $m_{2}-m_{1}>0$ near $P_{1}$. On the other hand at the point $Q=(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3}, 0)$ corresponding to the right trapezoid we have $m_{2}=0.15417163 \cdots<1$, see (21) which implies $m_{2}-m_{1}<0$. Therefore there exists a point $T$ on $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ such that $m_{2}=m_{1}$. Again applying Sturm Theorem to a polynomial of degree 22 in $c$, we can conclude that $T$ is unique, and its coordinates are $(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3}, c_{1})$ where $c_{1}=0.0517595932 \ldots$

Let $\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{1}=\left\{(a, b, c) \in \mathcal{C}_{1}: c<c_{1}\right\}$ and $\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{1}^{\prime}=\left\{(a, b, c) \in \mathcal{C}_{1}: c>c_{1}\right\}$. Therefore, for any given path connecting $\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{1}$ and $P_{3} \cup \mathcal{C}_{3} \cup P_{1} \cup \widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{1}^{\prime}$ in $\Omega$, there exist $(a, b, c) \in \Omega$ such that $m_{2}=m_{1}=1$.



Figure 9. (a) In black, the curve $m_{2}=1$ on the region $\Omega$. (b) The curves of $m_{3}$ and $m_{4}$, parameterized by $a$ on the curve in (a).

Numerically we show that for any fixed path connecting $\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{1}$ and $P_{3} \cup \mathcal{C}_{3} \cup P_{1} \cup \widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{1}^{\prime}$ in $\Omega$ the solution of $m_{2}-1=0$ is unique. Curve representing the zeros of $m_{2}-1$ joins the boundaries $\mathcal{C}_{3}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{1}$. This curve goes from $(1.13102016 \ldots, 0.896392974 \ldots, 0.234627188 \ldots) \in \mathcal{C}_{3}$ to $\left(2 / \sqrt{3}, 1 / \sqrt{3}, c_{1}\right) \in \mathcal{C}_{1}$ (see Figure 9 (a)). The values of the masses $m_{3}$ and $m_{4}$ along this curve are plotted in Figure 9 (b).

# 8. Conclusions 

Using the positions of the masses we have classified the set of trapezoid central configurations. This set is a two-dimensional surface whose boundaries are known families consisting in a rhombus, an isosceles trapezoid and an equilateral triangle with a zero mass off the triangle. Although a specific ordering of the masses has not hold for any trapezoid central configuration, we can split the two-dimensional surface in three disjoint regions where the set of masses is totally ordered. Somewhat we must remark that we have proved analytically the existence of non-symmetric trapezoid central configurations with a pair of equal masses.

There exist a one-parameter family of right trapezoid central configurations that also splits the two-dimensional surface in two disjoint regions, namely the acute and the obtuse regions. Along such a nonsymmetric family the masses are completely ordered, that is, the family belong to one of the previous three regions, concretely the middle one,

where the set of masses is totally ordered. Moreover, when the pair of equal masses belong to biggest parallel side, only acute trapezoid central configurations are allow. On the other hand, when the two equal masses belongs to the non-parallel side, only obtuse trapezoid central configurations are allow.

# Central configurations formed by two twisted regular polygons 

A B S T R A C T

In this paper, we study the necessary conditions and sufficient conditions for the central configurations formed by two twisted regular polygons (one $N$-regular polygon and one $L$-regular polygon). We wish to extend the results of the symmetrical central configurations formed by two twisted $N$-regular polygons, however, to our own surprise, it will be proved that the necessary condition on the central configurations is $L=N$.

## 1. Introduction

Central configurations play a very important role in Newtonian $N$-body problems. The numbers and shapes etc. about central configurations were studied by many mathematicians. Since finding concrete central configurations is very difficult, we can only find some special central configurations. In this paper, we study the necessary conditions and sufficient conditions for the central configurations formed by two twisted regular polygons (one $N$-regular polygon and one $L$-regular polygon), we try to extend some results in . The motivation of this paper comes mainly from .

Suppose two parallel regular polygons, one regular $N$-polygon and the other regular $L$-polygon with distance $h \geqslant 0$ (without loss of generality, we set $N \leqslant L$ ), are placed in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. Assume that the particles $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{N}$ with the same mass $m$ locate at the vertexes of the regular $N$-polygon; the particles $\tilde{P}_{1}, \tilde{P}_{2}, \ldots, \tilde{P}_{L}$ with the same mass $b m$ locate at the vertexes of the regular $L$-polygon. Similarly to , let $\rho_{k}$ be the $k$-th root of the $N$-roots of unity, $\xi_{l}$ be the $l$-th root of the $L$-roots of unity (i.e. $\rho_{k}=e^{i \theta_{k}}$, $\left.\xi_{l}=e^{i \varphi_{l}}\right)$, where $\theta_{k}=\frac{2 k \pi}{N}(k=1,2, \ldots, N), \varphi_{l}=\frac{2 l \pi}{L}(l=1,2, \ldots, L), a>0, i=\sqrt{-1}$; let $\tilde{\rho}_{l}=a \xi_{l} \cdot e^{i \theta}$, where $0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2 \pi$ and $\theta$ is called the twisted angle. The coordinates of the particles $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{N}$ and $\tilde{P}_{1}, \tilde{P}_{2}, \ldots, \tilde{P}_{L}$ are $q_{k}=\left(\rho_{k}, 0\right)(k=1,2, \ldots, N), \tilde{q}_{l}=\left(\tilde{\rho}_{l}, h\right)(l=1,2, \ldots, L)$ respectively. Then, similarly to , the necessary conditions and sufficient conditions for $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{N} ; \tilde{P}_{1}, \tilde{P}_{2}, \ldots, \tilde{P}_{L}$ forming a central configuration are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& A+b \sum_{j=1}^{L} \frac{1-a \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi j}{L}-\frac{2 \pi k}{N}+\theta\right)}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi j}{L}-\frac{2 \pi k}{N}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\mu \quad(1 \leqslant k \leqslant N) \\
& b B+\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1-a^{-1} \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi j}{N}-\frac{2 \pi k}{L}-\theta\right)}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi j}{N}-\frac{2 \pi k}{L}-\theta\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\mu \quad(1 \leqslant k \leqslant L) \\
& \sum_{j=1}^{L} \frac{\sin \left(\frac{2 \pi j}{L}-\frac{2 \pi k}{N}+\theta\right)}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi j}{L}-\frac{2 \pi k}{N}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=0 \quad(1 \leqslant k \leqslant N) \\
& \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{\sin \left(\frac{2 \pi j}{N}-\frac{2 \pi k}{L}-\theta\right)}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi j}{N}-\frac{2 \pi k}{L}-\theta\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=0 \quad(1 \leqslant k \leqslant L) \\
& h \sum_{j=1}^{L} \frac{1}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi j}{L}-\frac{2 \pi k}{N}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\frac{\mu L h}{N+b L} \quad(1 \leqslant k \leqslant N) \\
& h \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi j}{N}-\frac{2 \pi k}{L}-\theta\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\frac{\mu N h}{N+b L} \quad(1 \leqslant k \leqslant L)
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
A=\sum_{j=1}^{N-1} \frac{1-\rho_{j}}{\left|1-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}>0, \quad B=\sum_{j=1}^{L-1} \frac{1-\xi_{j}}{\left|1-\xi_{j}\right|^{3}}>0
$$

and $\mu$ is a positive constant.
For this type of central configurations, R. Moeckel and C. Simo  proved the following results with conditions $\theta=0, L=N$ :

Theorem 1.1 (R. Moeckel and C. Simo). There are exactly two planar central configurations $(h=0, \theta=0)$ consisting of two nested regular $N$-polygons for every mass ratio b. The ratio a of the sizes of the two polygons is less than 1 for one of them, and it is greater than 1 for the other. For most values of the parameters $N$ and $b$, these central configurations represent saddle points of the gradient flow of the configurational measure $I U^{2}$, where $U(q)=\sum \frac{m_{j} m_{k}}{\left|q_{j}-q_{k}\right|}, I(q)=\sum m_{j}\left|q_{j}\right|^{2}$. However, for $N \geq 473$, there is a constant $b_{0}(N)<1$ such that for $b<b_{0}$ and $b>\frac{1}{b_{0}}$, the central configuration with the smaller masses on the inner polygon is a repeller.

When $h^{2}>0, \theta=0$, they proved

Theorem 1.2 (R. Moeckel and C. Simo). If $N \geq 473$, there are no spatial central configurations of parallel regular $N$-polygon for $b<b_{0}(N)$. If $N<473$, there is a unique pair of such central configurations. A unique pair bifurcates from the planar central configuration with the smaller masses on the inner polygon at $b=b_{0}$. This remains the unique pair of spatial central configurations until $b=\frac{1}{b_{0}}$, where a similar bifurcation occurs in reverse, so that for $b>\frac{1}{b_{0}}$, only the planar central configurations remain.
X. Yu and S.Q. Zhang  proved the following results with condition $L=N$ :

Theorem 1.3. The twisted angle $\theta=0$ of the central configuration formed by two twisted regular $N$-polygons $(N \geq 2)$ with distance $h \geq 0$, cannot be anything but $\theta=0$ or $\theta=\pi / N$. Specifically, if two nested regular N -polygons are on the same unit circle (i.e., $a=1$ and $h=0$ ), then only $\theta=\pi / N$.

Corollary 1.4. For the central configuration formed by two nested regular $N$-polygons on the same unit circle, there is exactly one central configuration, which is the regular $2 N$-polygon.

Corollary 1.5. The equations of the central configurations formed by two twisted regular $N$-polygons $(N \geq 2)$ with distance $h \geq 0$ are as follows:
(i) When $h=0$ and $a \neq 1$, then

$$
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{1-a^{-1} \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)\right)^{3 / 2}}-A=b\left[\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{1-a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{A}{a^{3}}\right]
$$

or

$$
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{1-a^{-1} \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)\right)^{3 / 2}}-A=b\left[\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{1-a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{A}{a^{3}}\right]
$$

(ii) When $h>0$

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
A-\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=b a \sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=b a\left(\frac{A}{a^{3}}-\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}\right)
\end{array}\right.
$$

or

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
A-\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=b a \sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=b a\left(\frac{A}{a^{3}}-\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}\right)
\end{array}\right.
$$

In this paper, we wish to extend the results about the symmetrical central configurations formed by two twisted $N$-regular polygons. However, we will prove the following main result, which is unexpected:

Theorem 1.6. If $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{N} ; \tilde{P}_{1}, \tilde{P}_{2}, \ldots, \tilde{P}_{L}$ form a central configuration, then $N=L$, i.e., two stacked regular polygons forming a symmetrical central configuration have the same shape.

Then the necessary conditions and sufficient conditions for the central configurations formed by two twisted regular polygons are the conditions given in Corollaries 1.4 and 1.5. Furthermore, some particular cases are already completely known, specially, the case of $\theta=0$ in Theorems 1.1 and 1.2.

In the next section, we will get the important Lemma 2.4 which has been obtained in our paper , which can be regarded as a corollary of Lemma 2.3, we notice that there was a gap in our original proof about Lemma 2.3, so here we will fill the gap and give a complete proof of Lemma 2.3.

# 2. Some lemmas 

Lemma 2.1. Let $a_{j}>0,1 \leqslant j \leqslant k, A_{1} \geqslant A_{2} \geqslant \ldots \geqslant A_{k} \geqslant 0$, then

$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty}\left(\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant k} a_{j} A_{j}^{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{n}}=A_{1}
$$

Lemma 2.2. Given $a_{j}>0,1 \leq j \leq k, A_{1}>\cdots>A_{k}>0$. For the function $f(x)=\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq k} a_{j} A_{j}^{x}\right)^{\frac{1}{x}}$, $x \in(0, \infty)$, we have

$$
f^{\prime}(x)=\left(-A_{1} \ln a_{1}\right) \frac{1}{x^{2}}+o\left(\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)
$$

when $x \rightarrow \infty$.

# Proof. 

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{\prime}(x) & =\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq k} a_{j} A_{j}^{x}\right)^{\frac{1}{x}}\left[\frac{x \sum_{1 \leq j \leq k} a_{j} A_{j}^{x} \ln A_{j}}{\sum_{1 \leq j \leq k} a_{j} A_{j}^{x}}-\ln \sum_{1 \leq j \leq k} a_{j} A_{j}^{x}\right] / x^{2} \\
& =\frac{1}{x^{2}}\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq k} a_{j} A_{j}^{x}\right)^{\frac{1}{x}}\left[\frac{\ln A_{1}+\sum_{2 \leq j \leq k} b_{j} B_{j}^{x} \ln A_{j}}{1+\sum_{2 \leq j \leq k} b_{j} B_{j}^{x}} x-\ln \left(a_{1} A_{1}^{x}\right)-\ln 1+\sum_{2 \leq j \leq k} b_{j} B_{j}^{x}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

where $b_{j}=\frac{a_{j}}{a_{1}}, B_{j}=\frac{A_{j}}{A_{1}}(2 \leq j \leq k)$.
Then $B_{j}^{x} \rightarrow 0, x B_{j}^{x} \rightarrow 0$, when $x \rightarrow \infty$.
So $f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{1}{x^{2}}\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq k} a_{j} A_{j}^{x}\right)^{\frac{1}{x}}\left[-\ln a_{1}+o(1)\right]=\left(-A_{1} \ln a_{1}\right) \frac{1}{x^{2}}+o\left(\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)$.
Lemma 2.3. Let

$$
g(x, \alpha)=\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{\sin \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+x\right)^{\alpha}}
$$

where $\theta \in\left(0, \frac{x}{N}\right), a>0, \alpha>0, x \geq 0$. Then $g(x, \alpha)>0$ in $\{x: x \geq 0\}$ provided $\alpha$ is sufficiently large.
Proof. Set $t=\frac{2 a}{1+a^{2}+x}$, then $t \in\left(0, \frac{2 a}{1+a^{2}}\right]$ and we only need to prove that

$$
f(t, \alpha)=\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{\sin \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)}{\left(1-t \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)\right)^{\alpha}}
$$

is positive in $\left(0, \frac{2 a}{1+a^{2}}\right]$ for sufficiently large $\alpha$.
Firstly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(t, \alpha)= & \sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \sin \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right) \sum_{m \geq 0}\left[\frac{\alpha(\alpha+1) \cdots(\alpha+m-1)}{m!} t^{m} \cos ^{m}\left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)\right] \\
= & \sum_{m \geq 0}\left[\frac{\alpha(\alpha+1) \cdots(\alpha+m-1)}{m!}\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)^{m}\right] \sum_{1 \leq j \leq N}\left[\sin (m+1)\left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)\right. \\
& \left.+(m-1) \sin (m-1)\left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+\cdots\right] \\
= & \frac{\alpha(\alpha+1) \cdots(\alpha+N-2)}{(N-1)!}\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)^{N-1} N \sin (N \theta)+o\left(t^{N-1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

So there exists $\delta_{\alpha}$ for any given $\alpha$ such that $f(t, \alpha)$ is positive for $t \in\left(0, \delta_{\alpha}\right]$.
Let

$$
h(t, \alpha)=\left\{\sum_{0 \leq j \leq\lceil\frac{N-1}{2}\rceil} \frac{\sin \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)}{\left(1-t \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)\right)^{\alpha}}\right\}^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}-\left\{\sum_{1 \leq j \leq\lceil\frac{N}{2}\rceil} \frac{\sin \left(\theta_{j}-\theta\right)}{\left(1-t \cos \left(\theta_{j}-\theta\right)\right)^{\alpha}}\right\}^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}
$$

then $h(t, \alpha)$ and $f(t, \alpha)$ have the same sign.

We have $\frac{\partial h(t, \alpha)}{\partial \alpha}=\left[-\frac{\ln (\sin \theta)}{1-t \cos \theta}+\frac{\ln \left(\sin \left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}-\theta\right)\right)}{1-t \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}-\theta\right)}\right] \frac{1}{\alpha^{2}}+o\left(\frac{1}{\alpha^{2}}\right)$, since $\frac{\ln \left(\sin \left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}-\theta\right)\right)}{1-t \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}-\theta\right)}-\frac{\ln (\sin \theta)}{1-t \cos \theta}=$ $\frac{(1-t \cos \theta)\left[\ln \left(\sin \left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}-\theta\right)\right)-\ln (\sin \theta)\right]+t\left[\cos \left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}-\theta\right)-\cos \theta\right]}{[1-t \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}-\theta\right)](1-t \cos \theta)}>0$, hence $h(t, \alpha)$ is increasing about $\alpha$ provided $\alpha$ is sufficiently large.

So there exists some positive number $\delta$ (independent of $\alpha$ ) such that $h(t, \alpha)$ is positive in $(0, \delta]$ for sufficiently large $\alpha$.

Secondly, $h(t, \alpha) \rightarrow h(t)$ for any $t \in\left[\delta, \frac{2 a}{1+a^{2}}\right]$, where $h(t)=\frac{1}{1-t \cos \theta}-\frac{1}{1-t \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}-\theta\right)}$, and there exists some positive number $\epsilon$ such that $h(t) \geq \epsilon>0$ for any $t \in\left[\delta, \frac{2 a}{1+a^{2}}\right]$.

Since $h(t, \alpha)$ is increasing about $\alpha$ provided $\alpha$ is sufficiently large, by Dini's theorem, we know that $h(t, \alpha) \rightrightarrows h(t)$ on the compact interval $\left[\delta, \frac{2 a}{1+a^{2}}\right]$, thus $h(t, \alpha)$ is positive in $\left[\delta, \frac{2 a}{1+a^{2}}\right]$ for sufficiently large $\alpha$.

As a result, $g(x, \alpha)$ is positive in $\{x: x \geq 0\}$ provided $\alpha$ is sufficiently large.
Remark. We give some comments on Lemma 2.3. We found that there was a gap in our original proof of the important Lemma 2.10 in  since we didn't notice the problem about the uniform convergence of $h(t, \alpha)$ and the compactness of the whole interval we considered. So here we give the new proof of Lemma 2.3 to correct the error in Lemma 2.10 of .

Then we have the following important proposition which can be regarded as a corollary of Lemma 2.3.

# Lemma 2.4. If 

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{\sin \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=0
$$

then $\theta=\frac{j \pi}{N}(\bmod 2 \pi)$ for some $1 \leqslant j \leqslant 2 N$.
Proof. Here we give a brief proof, the other detailed proof can be found in .
Set

$$
g_{n}(x, \theta)=\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{\sin \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+x\right)^{(2 n+3) / 2}}
$$

where $\theta \in[0,2 \pi]$ and $a>0, n \in \mathbb{N}, x \geq 0$.
Firstly, it's easy to know that $g_{0}\left(x, \frac{\pi}{N}\right)=0, g_{0}(x,-\theta)=-g_{0}(x, \theta)$ and $g_{0}\left(x, \theta+\frac{2 \pi}{N}\right)=g_{0}(x, \theta)$. Thus, to prove Lemma 2.4, it is enough to prove that $g_{0}(x, \theta)>0$ for $x \in[0, \infty)$ and $\theta \in\left(0, \frac{\pi}{N}\right)$. Now we can claim that, by using the mathematical induction, if $g_{n}(x, \theta)>0(x \in[0, \infty), \theta \in\left(0, \frac{\pi}{N}\right)$ ) for some $n \geq 1$, then $g_{k}(x, \theta)>0(x \in[0, \infty), \theta \in\left(0, \frac{\pi}{N}\right)$ ) for $0 \leq k \leq n-1$. Hence we know that $g_{0}(x, \theta)>0$ for $x \in[0, \infty)$ and $\theta \in\left(0, \frac{\pi}{N}\right)$ from Lemma 2.3.

So Lemma 2.4 holds.

## 3. The proofs of the main results

By Eq. (3) and Lemma 2.4, for any $k \in\{1,2, \ldots, L\}$, there exists corresponding $l_{k}$ such that $1 \leqslant l_{k} \leqslant 2 L$ and

$$
\theta-\frac{2 \pi k}{N}=\frac{l_{k} \pi}{L} \quad(\bmod 2 \pi)
$$

Then there exists some $j \in\{1,2, \ldots, 2 L\}$ such that $\frac{2 \pi}{N}=\frac{j \pi}{L}(\bmod 2 \pi)$, moreover we have $N \mid(2 L)$. Similarly, by Eq. (4), for any $\nu \in\{1,2, \ldots, N\}$, there exists corresponding $n_{\nu}$ such that $1 \leqslant n_{\nu} \leqslant 2 N$ and

$$
-\theta-\frac{2 \pi \nu}{L}=\frac{n_{\nu} \pi}{N} \quad(\bmod 2 \pi)
$$

Then there exists some $j \in\{1,2, \ldots, 2 N\}$ such that $\frac{2 \pi}{L}=\frac{j \pi}{N}(\bmod 2 \pi)$, thus we also have $L \mid(2 N)$. Let $N=2^{n} \cdot N_{1}, L=2^{l} \cdot L_{1}$, where $N_{1}, L_{1}$ are odd, then we have $N_{1}=L_{1}$, and $n \leqslant l \leqslant n+1$, so $L=N$ or $L=2 N$.

In the following, we will prove $L \neq 2 N$. Otherwise, if $L=2 N$, we have $\theta=\frac{\left(4 k+l_{k}\right) \pi}{2 N}(\bmod 2 \pi)(1 \leq k \leq$ $2 N, 1 \leqslant l_{k} \leqslant 4 N)$ by (15) and $\theta=-\frac{\left(\nu+n_{\nu}\right) \pi}{N}(\bmod 2 \pi)\left(1 \leq \nu \leq N, 1 \leqslant n_{\nu} \leqslant 2 N\right)$ by (16), hence $l_{k}=2 l_{k}^{\prime}$ $\left(1 \leqslant l_{k}^{\prime} \leqslant 2 N\right)$ for any $k \in\{1,2, \ldots, 2 N\}$ and $2 k+l_{k}^{\prime}+\nu+n_{\nu}=0(\bmod 2 N)$ for any $k \in\{1,2, \ldots, 2 N\}$, $\nu \in\{1,2, \ldots, N\}$, furthermore, there are both even and odd number in the numbers $n_{\nu}(\nu \in\{1,2, \ldots, N\})$.

Then it's easy to know that $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{N} ; \check{P}_{1}, \check{P}_{2}, \ldots, \check{P}_{L}$ form a central configuration if and only if $a, b$, $h$ satisfy the following equations (in fact, by symmetry, one can get the same result):

$$
\begin{gathered}
A+b \sum_{j=1}^{2 N} \frac{1-a \cos \left(\frac{j \pi}{N}\right)}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{j \pi}{N}\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\mu \\
b B+\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1-a^{-1} \cos \left(\frac{2 j-1}{N} \pi\right)}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 j-1}{N} \pi\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\mu \\
b B+\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1-a^{-1} \cos \left(\frac{2 j}{N} \pi\right)}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 j}{N} \pi\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\mu \\
h \sum_{j=1}^{2 N} \frac{1}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{j \pi}{N}\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\frac{\mu L h}{N+b L} \\
h \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 j-1}{N} \pi\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\frac{\mu N h}{N+b L} \\
h \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 j}{N} \pi\right)+h^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\frac{\mu N h}{N+b L}
\end{gathered}
$$

Lemma 3.1. Let

$$
f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 j-1}{N} \pi\right)+x\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}-\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 j}{N} \pi\right)+x\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}} \quad x \in[0,+\infty)
$$

then for any $a \in(0, \infty)$, we have $f(x)<0$ for any $x \in[0,+\infty)$ except the unique singularity $a=1, x=0$.

Proof. Set $t=\frac{2 a}{1+a^{2}+x}$, then $t \in(0,1)$ and we only need to prove that

$$
g(t)=\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{1}{\left(1-t \cos \left(\theta_{j}-\frac{\pi}{N}\right)\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}-\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{1}{\left(1-t \cos \theta_{j}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}
$$

is negative in $(0,1)$.
In fact, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
g(t)= & \sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \sum_{m \geq 0}\left[\frac{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\left(\frac{3}{2}+1\right) \cdots\left(\frac{3}{2}+m-1\right)}{m!} t^{m}\left(\cos ^{m}\left(\theta_{j}-\frac{\pi}{N}\right)-\cos ^{m} \theta_{j}\right)\right] \\
= & \sum_{m \geq 0}\left[\frac{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\left(\frac{3}{2}+1\right) \cdots\left(\frac{3}{2}+m-1\right)}{m!}\left(\frac{t^{m}}{2^{m-1}}\right)\right] \sum_{1 \leq j \leq N}\left\{\left[\cos m\left(\theta_{j}-\frac{\pi}{N}\right)\right.\right. \\
& \left.\left.+m \cos (m-2)\left(\theta_{j}-\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+\cdots\right]-\left[\cos m\left(\theta_{j}\right)+m \cos (m-2)\left(\theta_{j}\right)+\cdots\right]\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $a_{m}=\left[\cos m\left(\theta_{j}-\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+m \cos (m-2)\left(\theta_{j}-\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+\cdots\right]-\left[\cos m\left(\theta_{j}\right)+m \cos (m-2)\left(\theta_{j}\right)+\cdots\right]$, then it's easy to know that $a_{m} \leq 0$ and $g(t)$ is negative in $(0,1)$.

By Eqs. (21), (22) and Lemma 3.1, we know $h=0$, and then there must be $a \neq 1$, otherwise, there will be collision. So $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{N} ; \bar{P}_{1}, \bar{P}_{2}, \ldots, \bar{P}_{L}$ form a central configuration if and only if $a, b, h$ satisfy the following equations

$$
\begin{gathered}
A+b \sum_{j=1}^{2 N} \frac{1-a \cos \left(\frac{j \pi}{N}\right)}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{j \pi}{N}\right)\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\mu \\
b B+\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1-a^{-1} \cos \left(\frac{2 j-1}{N} \pi\right)}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 j-1}{N} \pi\right)\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\mu \\
b B+\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1-a^{-1} \cos \left(\frac{2 j}{N} \pi\right)}{\left[1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\frac{2 j}{N} \pi\right)\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\mu
\end{gathered}
$$

Lemma 3.2. Let

$$
f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1-x^{-1} \cos \left(\frac{2 j-1}{N} \pi\right)}{\left[1+x^{2}-2 x \cos \left(\frac{2 j-1}{N} \pi\right)\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}-\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1-x^{-1} \cos \left(\frac{2 j}{N} \pi\right)}{\left[1+x^{2}-2 x \cos \left(\frac{2 j}{N} \pi\right)\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}, \quad x \in(0,1) \cup(1, \infty)
$$

then $f(x)<0$ for $x \in(1, \infty)$ and $f(x)>0$ for $x \in(0,1)$.
Proof. Let

$$
h(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1}{\left[1+x^{2}-2 x \cos \left(\frac{2 j-1}{N} \pi\right)\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}}-\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1}{\left[1+x^{2}-2 x \cos \left(\frac{2 j}{N} \pi\right)\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}}
$$

then

$$
\frac{d h(x)}{d x}=-x f(x)
$$

Firstly, we will prove that $f(x)$ is negative in $(1, \infty)$.
Set $t(x)=\frac{2 x}{1+x^{2}}$, then $t \in(0,1)$ and $\frac{d t(x)}{d x}=\frac{2\left(1-x^{2}\right)}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{2}}, \frac{d t(x)}{d x}>0$ for $x \in(0,1), \frac{d t(x)}{d x}<0$ for $x \in(1, \infty)$. Furthermore, we have $h(x)=\frac{1}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}} g(t)$, where

$$
g(t)=\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{1}{\left(1-t \cos \left(\theta_{j}-\frac{\pi}{N}\right)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}-\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{1}{\left(1-t \cos \theta_{j}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}
$$

Since

$$
\begin{aligned}
g(t)= & \sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \sum_{m \geq 0}\left[\frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+1\right) \cdots\left(\frac{1}{2}+m-1\right)}{m!} t^{m}\left(\cos ^{m}\left(\theta_{j}-\frac{\pi}{N}\right)-\cos ^{m} \theta_{j}\right)\right] \\
= & \sum_{m \geq 0}\left[\frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+1\right) \cdots\left(\frac{1}{2}+m-1\right)}{m!}\left(\frac{t^{m}}{2^{m-1}}\right)\right] \sum_{1 \leq j \leq N}\left\{\left[\cos m\left(\theta_{j}-\frac{\pi}{N}\right)\right.\right. \\
& \left.\left.+m \cos (m-2)\left(\theta_{j}-\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+\cdots\right]-\left[\cos m\left(\theta_{j}\right)+m \cos (m-2)\left(\theta_{j}\right)+\cdots\right]\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $a_{m}=\left[\cos m\left(\theta_{j}-\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+m \cos (m-2)\left(\theta_{j}-\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+\cdots\right]-\left[\cos m\left(\theta_{j}\right)+m \cos (m-2)\left(\theta_{j}\right)+\cdots\right]$, then it's easy to know that $a_{m} \leq 0$ and the first nonzero term is $a_{N}=-2$, furthermore, $g(t)$ and $\frac{d g(t)}{d t}$ is negative in $(0,1)$.

By (28), we have

$$
\frac{x\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{\frac{n}{2}} f(x)}{2}=\left(1+x^{2}\right) g(t)+\frac{\left(x^{2}-1\right)}{x} \frac{d g(t)}{d t}
$$

hence $f(x)<0$ for $x \in(1, \infty)$.
Secondly, let us prove that $f(x)$ is positive in $(0,1)$.
In the following, we will prove that $h(x)$ and $\frac{d h(x)}{d x}$ are both negative in $(0,1)$ by the method of R. Moeckel and C. Simo .

Let

$$
d(z)=\frac{1}{(1-z)^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\sum_{m \geq 0} d_{m} z^{m}
$$

then

$$
\begin{aligned}
h(x)= & \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1}{\left[1-x \exp \left(\frac{\sqrt{-1}(2 j-1)}{N} \pi\right)\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}} \frac{1}{\left[1-x \exp \left(\frac{-\sqrt{-1}(2 j-1)}{N} \pi\right)\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}} \\
& -\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1}{\left[1-x \exp \left(\frac{\sqrt{-1} 2 j}{N} \pi\right)\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}} \frac{1}{\left[1-x \exp \left(\frac{-\sqrt{-1} 2 j}{N} \pi\right)\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}} \\
= & \sum_{j=1}^{N} \sum_{m \geq 0} d_{m} x^{m} \exp \left(\frac{\sqrt{-1} m(2 j-1)}{N} \pi\right) \sum_{m \geq 0} d_{m} x^{m} \exp \left(\frac{-\sqrt{-1} m(2 j-1)}{N} \pi\right) \\
& -\sum_{j=1}^{N} \sum_{m \geq 0} d_{m} x^{m} \exp \left(\frac{\sqrt{-1} 2 m j}{N} \pi\right) \sum_{m \geq 0} d_{m} x^{m} \exp \left(\frac{-\sqrt{-1} 2 m j}{N} \pi\right) \\
= & \sum_{j=1}^{N} \sum_{m \geq 0} x^{m} \sum_{k+l=m} d_{k} d_{l} \exp \left(\frac{\sqrt{-1}(k-l)(2 j-1)}{N} \pi\right) \\
& -\sum_{j=1}^{N} \sum_{m \geq 0} x^{m} \sum_{k+l=m} d_{k} d_{l} \exp \left(\frac{\sqrt{-1} 2(k-l) j}{N} \pi\right) \\
= & N \sum_{m \geq 0} x^{m} \sum_{k+l=m, k \in l(\bmod N)} d_{k} d_{l} \cos \left(\frac{k-l}{N} \pi\right)-N \sum_{m \geq 0} x^{m} \sum_{k+l=m, k \in l(\bmod N)} d_{k} d_{l} \\
:= & \sum_{m \geq 0} b_{m} x^{m}
\end{aligned}
$$

It's easy to know that all of the coefficients $b_{m}$ are non-positive and infinitely many are negative, then $h(x)$ and $\frac{d h(x)}{d x}$ are both negative in $(0,1)$. Hence $f(x)>0$ for $x \in(0,1)$ by (28).

Proof of Theorem 1.6. By Eqs. (25), (26) and Lemma 3.2, we know that Eqs. (24), (25) and (26) have no solution, i.e., if $L=2 N, P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{N} ; \tilde{P}_{1}, \tilde{P}_{2}, \ldots, \tilde{P}_{L}$ cannot form a central configuration.


# Stacked central configurations: new examples in the planar five-body problem

#### Abstract

The main result of this paper is the existence of a new family of planar five-body central configurations. This family is unusual in that it is a stacked central configuration, i.e. a subset of the points also form a central configuration, in this case, the Lagrange equilateral solution to the three-body problem.

## 1. Introduction

The classical $n$-body problem consists of the study of the dynamics of $n$ point masses interacting according to Newtonian gravity (Newton 1687). We consider $n$ particles at $q_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ (usually with $d=2$ or $d=3$ ) with masses $m_{i} \in \mathbb{R}_{+}, i=1, \ldots, n$ and $\bar{q}_{i}=$ $\sum_{j \neq i} m_{j}\left(q_{j}-q_{i}\right) /\left|q_{j}-q_{i}\right|^{3}$. The $n$ particles form a central configuration (Wintner 1941) if there exists a mass vector $m \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$ and a parameter $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$such that

$$
\lambda q_{i}=\sum_{j \neq i} m_{j} \frac{q_{i}-q_{j}}{\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|^{3}}
$$

Each central configuration gives rise to a family of orbits in which each particle travels on a conic with a focus at the centre of mass. In particular, the circular orbits are relative equilibria, i.e. equilibria in a uniformly rotating coordinate system.

There has been steady progress in understanding central configurations and their dynamics, particularly in the three- and four-body problem. Much less is known in the five-body case. Strictly spatial five-body central configurations are analogous in some ways to the planar fourbody case, but the planar five-body central configurations present new challenges and there are very few results in this area.

In this paper we will exhibit a new family of central configurations which is quite simple and explicit, and which we hope will inspire further development. This family also has

an unusual property of being what we will call a stacked central configuration: a central configuration in which some subset of three or more points form a central configuration.

We will also discuss some open questions regarding stacked central configurations in section 3.

# 2. Three bodies to four 

It is a simple consequence of the perpendicular bisector theorem (Moeckel 1990), that a collinear three-body configuration cannot be extended to a non-collinear four-body central configuration. This argument is easily generalized to exclude the possibility of extending an $n-1$ collinear central configuration to a strictly planar $n$-body central configuration.

For our purposes, the most convenient equations for strictly planar central configurations seem to be the following 'Laura-Andoyer' equations (Laura 1905, Andoyer 1906, Albouy 2003):

$$
f_{i j}:=\sum_{k \neq i, j} m_{k}\left(R_{i k}-R_{j k}\right) \Delta_{i j k}=0
$$

where $\Delta_{i j k}$ is $\left(q_{i}-q_{j}\right) \wedge\left(q_{i}-q_{k}\right), q_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ and $R_{i j}=r_{i j}^{-3}=\left(\left|q_{i}-q_{j}\right|\right)^{-3}$. Usually the $\Delta_{i j k}$ will be replaced by the non-negative area $D_{i j k}$ in order to make the sign of the terms in our equations more apparent.

The equal mass Lagrange configuration can only be extended to a planar four-body central configuration by adding a mass to the centre of the triangle. This can be seen from equation (2), where if the equilateral points are $\{1,2,3\}$ then equation (2) forces $R_{14}=R_{24}=R_{34}$. In this case the mass of the added point is not uniquely determined. This also generalizes to the addition of a point to the centre of any equal mass regular polygon.

If we are willing to add dimensions, the Lagrange configuration can be extended to a regular tetrahedron for any four masses (Lehmann-Filhés 1891), a process which generalizes to the regular $n-1$ dimensional simplex with $n$ arbitrary masses (Saari 1980). However, there are no other spatial four-body central configurations (Pizzetti 1904).

## 3. Four bodies to five?

Here we have only questions and few answers.
(i) In addition to symmetric collinear configurations, the square or a regular tetrahedron with a mass at its centre and the square pyramidal configuration (Fayçal 1996) are there any five-body central configurations with a subset forming a four-body central configuration?
(ii) Are there any non-collinear five-body central configurations all of whose four-body subsets form a central configuration?

One might hope that a regular pentagon would furnish an example for the second question above. However, the trapezoids in a regular pentagon cannot be four-body central configurations for any choice of positive masses. This can be immediately seen from the fact that the diagonals of a convex four-body central configuration must be longer than any of the outer edges (MacMillan and Bartky 1932).

## 4. Outer Lagrange configurations for the five-body problem

In this section we will investigate configurations with the following symmetries and relations: $r_{12}=r_{23}=r_{13}=1, r_{14}=r_{25}, r_{15}=r_{24}$ and $r_{34}=r_{35}$. By assumption we will have $r_{14}>r_{15}$



Figure 1. A typical configuration.
and points 4 and 5 will be in the interior of the equilateral triangle formed by points 1,2 and 3 (figure 1).

From equation (2), with $i=1$ and $j=2$ we obtain

$$
f_{12}=m_{4}\left(R_{14}-R_{24}\right) D_{124}+m_{5}\left(R_{15}-R_{25}\right) D_{125}=0
$$

Since $D_{124}=D_{125}$ we find that $m_{4}=m_{5}$. Similarly with $i=4$ and $j=5$ we can see that $m_{1}=m_{2}$.

Also from equation (2), with $i=2$ and $j=3$ we obtain

$$
f_{23}=m_{5}\left[\left(R_{14}-R_{34}\right) D_{134}+\left(R_{15}-R_{34}\right) D_{135}\right]=0
$$

As long as $m_{5} \neq 0$ the rest of equation (4) gives us a relatively simple constraint on the geometry of our configuration:

$$
H:=-\left(R_{34}-R_{14}\right) D_{134}+\left(R_{15}-R_{34}\right) D_{135}=0
$$

Before analysing $H$ in more detail we note the following.
Lemma 1. Given a configuration with $r_{12}=r_{23}=r_{13}=1, r_{14}=r_{25}, r_{15}=r_{24}, r_{35}=r_{34}$ and $1>r_{14}>r_{34}>r_{15}$ which satisfies the relation $H=0$, there exist positive masses for which the configuration is a central configuration.

Proof. We have already seen that we must choose $m_{1}=m_{2}$ and $m_{4}=m_{5}$ to satisfy the relations $f_{12}=0$ and $f_{45}=0$. The remaining functions which must vanish are $f_{14}=f_{25}$, $f_{15}=f_{24}$ and $f_{34}=f_{35}$. These equations are linearly homogeneous in the masses $m_{1}, m_{3}$ and $m_{4}$. For a non-zero mass solution $\left(m_{1}, m_{3}, m_{4}\right)$ to exist, the determinant of this system must be zero. We find that
$\operatorname{Det}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\begin{array}{ccc}D_{124}\left(1-R_{15}\right) & D_{134}\left(R_{34}-1\right) & D_{145}\left(R_{45}-R_{15}\right) \\ D_{124}\left(1-R_{14}\right) & D_{135}\left(R_{34}-1\right) & D_{145}\left(R_{15}-R_{45}\right) \\ D_{134}\left(1-R_{14}\right)+D_{135}\left(R_{15}-1\right) & 0 & D_{345}\left(R_{34}-R_{45}\right)\end{array}\right]$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =-\left(D_{134}\left(1-R_{14}\right)+D_{135}\left(R_{15}-1\right)\right)\left(R_{34}-1\right)\left(-D_{134} D_{145} R_{14}\right. \\
& \left.-D_{135} D_{145} R_{15}+D_{124} D_{345} R_{34}+D_{134} D_{145} R_{45}+D_{135} D_{145} R_{45}\right. \\
& \left.-D_{124} D_{345} R_{45}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are assuming that $H=0$ we can substitute $D_{134} R_{34}+\left(R_{34}-R_{15}\right) D_{135}$ for $D_{134} R_{14}$ in the last factor of the above determinant, which then simplifies to

$$
\left(R_{34}-R_{45}\right)\left(D_{124} D_{345}-D_{135} D_{145}-D_{134} D_{145}\right)=0
$$

The fact that the second factor is 0 follows from an identity for any configuration of five points (Williams 1953).

Finally, the fact that the masses may be chosen to be all positive is a consequence of the sign pattern of the coefficient matrix. For configurations satisfying the given assumptions, there are only two sign patterns,

$$
\left[\begin{array}{rrr}
- & + & - \\
- & + & - \\
+ & 0 & -
\end{array}\right]
$$

and

$$
\left[\begin{array}{rrr}
- & + & + \\
- & + & - \\
+ & 0 & -
\end{array}\right]
$$

In both cases the last two rows of the matrix imply that all the components of a non-zero null vector will have the same sign.

It may be worth noting that the assumption that $r_{14}>r_{34}>r_{15}$ is necessary in this type of configuration for positive masses (Williams 1938).

Now note that $H$ is positive when $R_{14}=R_{34}$ and negative when $R_{15}=R_{34}$. Finally, note that $H$ is also negative when $r_{15}+r_{34}=1$ since $D_{135}=D_{234}=0$. If we consider a fixed $r_{15}$ in the interval $(0,1 / 2)$, this means equation (5) will be satisfied for some $r_{14}$ in $\left(\sqrt{r_{15}^{2}-\sqrt{3} r_{15}+1}, \sqrt{r_{15}^{2}-r_{15}+1}\right)$. Likewise for fixed $r_{15}$ in the interval $(1 / 2, \sqrt{3} / 3)$, equation (5) will be satisfied for some $r_{14}$ in $\left(\sqrt{r_{15}^{2}-\sqrt{3} r_{15}+1}, \sqrt{3} / 2-\sqrt{r_{15}^{2}-1 / 4}\right)$. Thus, there is always at least one such central configuration for each $r_{15} \in(0, \sqrt{3} / 3)$.

In fact we can show that there is only one such configuration for each $r_{15}$ by showing that $\mathrm{d} H / \mathrm{d} r_{14}<0$, where we consider $r_{34}$ to be determined by $r_{14}$ and $r_{15}$ by the planarity relation

$$
1-r_{14}^{2}+r_{14}^{4}-r_{15}^{2}-r_{14}^{2} r_{15}^{2}+r_{15}^{4}-r_{34}^{2}-r_{14}^{2} r_{34}^{2}-r_{15}^{2} r_{34}^{2}+r_{34}^{4}=0
$$

Then we have

$$
\frac{\partial r_{34}}{\partial r_{14}}=-\frac{r_{14}\left(1-2 r_{14}^{2}+r_{15}^{2}+r_{34}^{2}\right)}{r_{34}\left(1+r_{14}^{2}+r_{15}^{2}-2 r_{34}^{2}\right)}
$$

For the configurations under consideration it is easy to see that $\mathrm{d} r_{34} / \mathrm{d} r_{14} \leqslant 0$ for fixed $r_{15}$. Also note that

$$
\frac{\partial D_{135}}{\partial r_{14}}=\frac{\partial r_{34}}{\partial r_{14}}\left(\frac{2 r_{34}\left(r_{15}^{2}+1-r_{34}^{2}\right)}{D_{135}}\right)<0
$$

again for a fixed $r_{15}$.
The sign of $\mathrm{d} D_{134} / \mathrm{d} r_{14}$ is harder to verify but if equation (11) is substituted in for $\mathrm{d} r_{34} / \mathrm{d} r_{14}$ we can write

$$
\frac{\partial D_{134}}{\partial r_{14}}=\frac{2 r_{14}\left(r_{14}^{2}-r_{34}^{2}\right)\left(1+r_{14}^{2}+r_{34}^{2}-2 r_{15}^{2}\right)}{D_{134}\left(1+r_{14}^{2}+r_{15}^{2}-2 r_{34}^{2}\right)}
$$

which is positive for the values of $r_{15}, r_{14}$ and $r_{34}$ under consideration.



Figure 2. Outer Lagrange configurations


Figure 3. Normalized mass curve.

With these facts at hand it becomes clear that every summand of

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathrm{d} H}{\mathrm{~d} r_{14}}=-\frac{\mathrm{d} D_{134}}{\mathrm{~d} r_{14}}\left(R_{34}-R_{14}\right)+3 D_{134}\left(-r_{14}^{-4}+r_{34}^{-4} \frac{\mathrm{~d} r_{34}}{\mathrm{~d} r_{14}}\right)+\frac{\mathrm{d} D_{135}}{\mathrm{~d} r_{14}}\left(R_{15}-R_{34}\right) \\
+3 D_{135} r_{34}^{-4} \frac{\mathrm{~d} r_{34}}{\mathrm{~d} r_{14}}
\end{gathered}
$$

is negative, so there is unique zero of $H$ for each $r_{15}$ in $(0, \sqrt{3} / 3)$.
To summarize, we have proved the following.
Theorem 1. For every $r_{15} \in(0, \sqrt{3} / 3)$ there are positive masses $m_{1}=m_{2}, m_{4}=m_{5}$ and $m_{3}$ and distances $r_{12}=r_{13}=r_{23}=1,1>r_{14}=r_{25}>r_{35}=r_{34}>r_{24}=r_{15}$, such that the five points with these masses form a central configuration.

This family of configurations is illustrated in figure 2.
We show the corresponding masses in our family in figure 3, where the masses of the configuration have been normalized so that $m_{1}+m_{3}+m_{4}=1$.

This family can be continued further (so that the equilateral triangle is inside the convex hull), but then some of the masses become negative. The existence of the beginning of this family, where the interior masses ( 4 and 5 ) are near the centre of the triangle and infinitesimal, is a consequence of the theorems in Xia (1991).
