Let us apply this principle to $V$ which is a function on $\mathbb{R}^{3 N}$ and consider its average value with respect to the uniform distribution over $\left(B_{3}\left(R_{0}\right)\right)^{N}$ the product of $N$ balls of radius $R_{0}$, that is, we average over the sub-domain $0 \leq\left|\mathbf{r}_{a}\right| \leq R_{0}$. For a pair of particles, and if $n>-3$ the Williamson average (see Section 2.6) is

$$
\left\langle r_{i j}^{n}\right\rangle=\frac{72\left(2 R_{0}\right)^{n}}{(n+3)(n+4)(n+6)}
$$

and thus

$$
\left\langle V_{-1}\right\rangle=\frac{6 G}{5 R_{0}} \sum_{b<a} m_{a} m_{b}
$$

On the other hand

$$
\left\langle V_{2}\right\rangle=\frac{\Lambda R_{0}^{2}}{10} \sum m_{a}
$$

Therefore, the upper bound for the minimum value of $V^{\min }$ is, assuming that $\Lambda=3, G=$ $1, m_{a}=1$

$$
\frac{3}{10} N R_{0}^{2}+\frac{3}{5 R_{0}} N(N-1)
$$

The upper bound will be optimal, that is, smallest, if we choose $R_{0}^{3}=(N-1)$. Substituting back we get

$$
V^{\min } \leq \frac{9}{10} N(N-1)^{\frac{2}{3}}
$$

### 2.4.2 A lower bound for the energy

As explained in , Leib and Narnhoffer  proved a rigorous lower bound for $V_{O C P}$, at least in the case that $m_{1}=m_{2}=\ldots=m_{N}=m$. One defines an ion radius $a$ by

$$
N \frac{4 \pi}{3} a^{3}=A
$$

Thus in the case that $\Omega$ is a sphere of radius $R$

$$
a=\frac{R}{N^{\frac{1}{3}}}
$$

Note that in our solutions $a \approx 1$ with considerable accuracy. Now one has the extensive lower bound:

$$
V_{O C P} \geq-N \frac{9}{10} \frac{G m}{a}
$$

The interpretation is that the right hand side of (2.37) is the energy of $N$ non-overlapping spheres of radius $a$ with total charge zero, in other words of $N$ non-overlapping Thomson type Hydrogen atoms. The packing of these atoms plays an important role in determining the distribution of the points.

We may re-write the Leib-Narnhoffer bound (setting $G=m=a=1$ ) as

$$
V^{\min } \geq \frac{9}{10} N^{\frac{2}{3}}-N \frac{9}{10}
$$

# 2.5 Continuum limit 

This has already been alluded to above. It is most easily obtained by replacing the discrete distribution of masses by a continuous density distribution

$$
\sum m_{a} \delta\left(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{r}_{a}\right) \longrightarrow \rho(\mathbf{x})
$$

in the variational problem. Ignoring self-energies, we therefore need to extremize

$$
\frac{1}{2} G \iint \rho(\mathbf{x}) \rho(\mathbf{y}) \frac{1}{|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}|} d^{3} x d^{3} y+\frac{\Lambda}{6} \int \mathbf{x}^{2} \rho(\mathbf{x}) d^{3} x+\lambda \int \rho(\mathbf{x}) d^{3} x
$$

where $\lambda$ is a Lagrange multiplier enforcing the constraint that the total mass

$$
M=\int \rho(\mathbf{x}) d^{3} x
$$

is fixed. Variation of the density gives a linear integral equation for $\rho$

$$
G \int d^{3} y \rho(\mathbf{y}) \frac{1}{|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}|}+\frac{\Lambda}{6} \mathbf{x}^{2}+\lambda=0
$$

Acting on this equation with the Laplacian gives

$$
-4 \pi G \rho+\Lambda=0
$$

We have recovered our previous result that the density must be constant. But it is clear that the density cannot be everywhere constant and still satisfy the constraint that the total mass be fixed. Moreover we have not deduced that the boundary of the blob of uniform fluid must be spherically symmetric. This is presumably because we have not been sufficiently careful about boundary effects in the variation.

# 2.6 Separation probability distribution 

The cumulative probability for the separation of two points $\mathbf{r}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{r}_{2}$ uniformly distributed inside a sphere of radius $R$ seems to have been given originally by Williamson using an extremely ingenious geometrical argument . Below we rederive this result using differential forms.

The volume form on $\mathbb{R}^{3} \times \mathbb{R}^{3}$ is given in spherical polars about some fixed axis with origin $O$ by

$$
\omega=r_{1}^{2} \sin \theta_{1} d r_{1} \wedge d \theta_{1} \wedge d \phi_{1} \wedge r_{2}^{2} \sin \theta_{2} d r_{2} \wedge d \phi_{2}
$$

Consider the triangle $O 12$ with sides of length $r_{1}, r_{2}$ and $r_{12}$. Let $\psi$ be the angle $O 12$ and $\chi$ the angle of the plane of the triangle about an axis along the side $O 1$. Then by means of a rotation of the second set of spherical polars one has

$$
\omega=r_{1}^{2} \sin \theta_{1} d r_{1} \wedge d \theta_{1} \wedge d \phi_{1} \wedge r_{12}^{2} \sin \psi d r_{12} \wedge d \psi \wedge d \chi
$$

Now the cosine formula for the triangle tells us that

$$
r_{2}^{2}=r_{1}^{2}+r_{12}^{2}-2 r_{1} r_{12} \cos \psi
$$

and therefore

$$
r_{2} d r_{2}=\left(r_{1}-r_{12} \cos \psi\right) d r_{1}+\left(r_{12}-r_{1} \cos \psi\right) d r_{12}+r_{1} r_{12} \sin \psi d \psi
$$

Eliminating $d \psi$ gives

$$
\omega=r_{1} r_{2} r_{12} \sin \theta_{1} d r_{1} \wedge d r_{2} \wedge d r_{12} \wedge d \theta_{1} \wedge d \phi_{1} \wedge d \chi
$$

The integrals over $\theta_{1}, \phi_{1}, \chi$ may be done immediately so that

$$
\omega=8 \pi^{2} r_{1} r_{2} r_{12} d r_{1} \wedge d r_{2} \wedge d r_{12}
$$

In order to obtain $d P$ we set $r=r_{12}$ and integrate over $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ consistent with the points 1 and 2 being confined to lie inside a ball of radius $R$ and divide by $16 \pi^{2} R^{6} / 9$. To perform the integration it is convenient to introduce the coordinates $x=r_{1}+r_{2}$ and $y=r_{1}-r_{2}$. The ranges of integration are obtained by applying the triangle inequalities and are given by $r \leq x \leq 2 R-|y|$ and $|y| \geq r$.

The result is

$$
\operatorname{Prob}\left(\left|\mathbf{r}_{1}-\mathbf{r}_{2}\right| \leq r\right)=\frac{r^{3}}{R^{3}}-\frac{9 r^{4}}{16 R^{4}}+\frac{r^{6}}{32 R^{6}}
$$

One has of course $\operatorname{Prob}\left(\left|\mathbf{r}_{1}-\mathbf{r}_{2}\right| \leq 2 R\right)=1$. The probability density is thus

$$
d P=p(r) d r=\left(\frac{3 r^{2}}{R^{3}}-\frac{9 r^{3}}{4 R^{4}}+\frac{3 r^{5}}{16 R^{6}}\right) d r
$$

from which, the mean separation is

$$
\langle r\rangle=\int_{0}^{2 R} r p(r) d r=\frac{36}{35} R \approx 1.02857 R
$$

The numerical results described later agree with this rather well. In what follows we shall denote averages with respect to the Williamson distribution as above and averages taken over our numerically generated set of points (or pairs of points in this case) by an overbar. Thus numerically, as we shall show, we find that $\bar{r} \approx\langle r\rangle$ to a good accuracy. Of course to compare we must say what the value of $R$ is. This will usually be done using the formula $R=(N-1)^{\frac{1}{4}}$. Recall that this relation between $R$ and $N$ is the one derived in Section 2.4.1 in order to make the upper bound on $V^{\min }$ optimal.

The most likely separation is given by the root between $r=0$ and $r=2 R$ of the cubic equation

$$
6-\frac{27 r}{4 R}+\frac{15 r^{3}}{16 R^{3}}=0
$$

Because $r=2 R$, is a root, the cubic factorizes

$$
(r-2 R)\left(5 r^{2}+10 R r-16 R^{2}\right)=0
$$

and the solution we want is

$$
r=\frac{R}{5}(\sqrt{105}-5) \approx 1.04939 R
$$

# 2.7 Distribution of triangles 

Later we shall present the statistics of triples of points computed numerically. For points uniformly distributed inside a sphere an interesting quantity to consider is the distribution of angles over all triangles given by any three points. Unfortunately, it appears that no analytic expression for this distribution of angles is known. Deriving a formula for this distribution would therefore seem to be a very worthwhile exercise in geometric probability. One result that is known is that the probability that any angle is acute is given by $33 / 70$ . Numerically we shall find a good agreement with this value.

### 2.8 Point charges on a sphere

The problem here is to minimize the potential energy $V_{-1}$ subject to the constraint that the points lie on a sphere of some given radius. For reasons which are unclear to us, this problem has come to be associated with Thomson's name even though he appears not to have posed it explicitly. What he had in mind is perhaps that given the existence of a shell structure then one only needs to minimize the energy with respect to positions inside the shell. A large number of papers have investigated this problem; see  and references therein for details.

To see this more explicitly, note that in order to enforce the constraint one introduces $N$ Lagrange multipliers $\Lambda_{a}$. One obtains the equations

$$
\frac{\Lambda_{a}}{3} m_{a} \mathbf{r}_{a}+\sum_{b \neq a} \frac{G m_{a} m_{b}\left(\mathbf{r}_{b}-\mathbf{r}_{a}\right)}{\left|\mathbf{r}_{a}-\mathbf{r}_{b}\right|^{3}}=0
$$

The interpretation of the first term in (2.56), $\mathbf{F}_{a}=\frac{\lambda_{a}}{3} m_{a} \mathbf{r}_{a}$ is that it is the inward force exerted on the particle necessary to counteract the outward repulsion of the remaining particles. Thus on solving the equations and constraints, the Lagrange multipliers $\Lambda_{a}$ will turn out to be positive. If it happens that all the $\Lambda_{a}$ 's are equal then this is also a central configuration (it is a solution of (2.1)). This may be true only approximately if the distribution of points is sufficiently spherically symmetric.

# 2.9 Sphere packing problems 

As we have indicated above, there appears to be a close relation between central configurations and the classical sphere packing problem: to prove that there is no packing of congruent spheres in three dimensions with density or packing ratio $\eta$ exceeding that of a face-centred cubic (FCC) with $\eta=\pi / \sqrt{18} \approx 0.74048$. This long-standing conjecture, due originally to Harriot and Kepler has now been proved by Hales (see ref.  for an overview and references).

The highest packing density is achieved for FCC packing which is crystallographic, but it is well-known that there are uncountably many other packings, both crystallographic and non-crystallographic with the same packing density. Thus, viewed as an optimization problem, the sphere packing problem has infinitely many optima with essentially the same density. Moreover local optima with vacancies, that is with a finite number of isolated spheres missing, have in the infinite limit the same density. In the case of finite sphere packings there will clearly be many local optima very close to the closest packing. This feature is certainly shared by central configurations. The comparison of central configurations with sphere packings can be taken further. For example, a key fact about any sphere packing is, as stated first in print by Halley  in connection with his prior account of Olber's Paradox, that at most 12 congruent spheres may touch a thirteenth congruent sphere. In other words, the maximum coordination number (that is the number of nearest neighbours) for close-packing is 12 . This fact, asserted by Newton and denied by Gregory , would be a useful diagnostic tool in assessing whether our configurations are closepacked (they are certainly not FCC) but unfortunately for central configurations there is no unambiguous way to define a coordination number, and any numerical results computed are very sensitive to its definition.

One may refine the above discussion a little . The local cell for FCC packing is a rhombic dodecahedron. However, the local cell of smallest volume is a regular pentagonal dodecahedron. This cannot, because of it's five-fold symmetry, give a lattice packing of course but it can appear in small clusters and this happens in our case for 13 particles. In the same note it is remarked that most physicist's believe that the optimum for the One Component Plasma is a body-centred cubic (BCC) packing. As we discuss in Section 5.2 we have seen little evidence for that in our results. It is perhaps worth remarking here that the published energies of various lattices in the One Component Plasma problem  seem to be extremely close and this alone indicates it shares with the sphere packing problem the feature that there are many critical points very close to the minimum. It turns out to be worth exploring in more detail some further features of sphere packings since they

have some diagnostic value in understanding our numerical results. This is especially true in connection with the shell structure which will be discussed in Section 4.

# 3 Case I : small numbers of points 

Small numbers may be studied analytically and numerically; historical information may be found for example in ref.  or ref. , and we largely ignore planar solutions since (for $N>3$ ) these appear to be unstable. By symmetry, one expects any regular polyhedron to provide a solution but not necessarily a stable one. One can also place a mass point at the centre of a regular polyhedron. For the same reason it is also clear that pyramidal and bi-pyramidal solutions should exist for arbitrary numbers of particles as well as prism and anti-prism solutions. Again, placing a mass point at the centre of bi-pyramids, prisms and anti-prisms is possible. According to Hagihara , Blimovitch  claims two similar and similarly situated regular polyhedra are possible, as well as a regular polyhedron together with its dual.

### 3.1 N=3 Lagrange's triangle

Relative equilibria are planar solutions of (2.1) and include collinear solutions. They may also give rise to rigidly rotating solutions of Newton's equations of motion. Planar configurations will be the subject of another paper and so here we will restrict attention to the case when $N=3$. In that case, for arbitrary masses, the only non-collinear solution is Lagrange's equilateral triangle. In standard units the sides of the triangle are ${ }^{3} \sqrt{ } 3=1.4422496 \ldots$ which is larger than the distance ${ }^{3} \sqrt{ } 2=1.259921 \ldots$ of the dipole. In what follows it will be useful to envisage Lagrange's solution as three spheres touching one another. For some interesting recent work on the planar case including the relation to a hard disc model and with applications to the final shapes of systems of particles moving under repulsive inverse square law forces, see refs. . For other work on planar configurations see ref. . If one really were dealing with two dimensions, then the analogous problem would involve a logarithmic potential; for results on this case see ref. .

# 6 Discussion and conclusions 

By use of numerical algorithms we have investigated in detail central configurations where the interaction force is that of an inverse square law and the masses (charges) of all the particles are equal. We find that for low values of $N$ the configurations are generally convex deltrahedra which gives way to a multi-shell structure for $N>12$. As $N$ increases the number of shells increases and eventually the configuration tends towards having a constant density. The two-point probability distribution and also the probability of acute angle triangles agree to a high degree with those of a uniform distribution. The distribution of nearest neighbours is sharply peaked suggesting that each particle can be approximated by a sphere of diameter $d \approx 1.65$ and we have found, at this stage, no evidence for longrange orientational order in contrast to the situation in 2-dimensions, which we shall present elsewhere. It still remains an open question as to whether crystallization occurs, and the possibility remains that for large values of $N$ either we may not have found a minimum sufficiently close to the global one, or that we have not probed sufficiently large values of $N$. These aspects are currently under further investigation.

The specific types of central configurations that we have computed are examples for just one of a large set of models. As we have explained, the interaction potential we have studied has a number of special properties, and we should note that different force laws will lead to very different results. To illustrate this we have included fig. 17 which shows the density distribution as a function of radial distance for particles with $N=10000$ when the interaction force is an inverse cube law. Clearly in this case there is a decreasing trend



Figure 18: The distribution of 124 points, 100 of which have $m=1,20$ have $m=5$ and 4 have $m=25$. Each point with $m=1$ is represented by a sphere of diameter $d=1.65$ and the others by spheres with a diameter related to their mass by $d \propto m^{1 / 3}$.
See fig18.jpg for a colour version of this figure.
in the density with increasing radius, rather than the approach to uniform density that we have encountered so far in this paper. If the power in the interaction force is further increased then this downward trend becomes even more apparent.

Another interesting possibility is to consider situations in which the particles have different masses. Using the intuition that each of the particles can be represented by a sphere, our earlier analysis suggests that the diameter of this sphere should be taken to be proportional to $m^{1 / 3}$ and indeed we find this to be the case. This is illustrated in fig. 18, where the spheres can be seen to fit snugly together using the above prescription of taking the volume of the sphere proportional to the mass of the particle.

Clearly the current work is only the tip of the iceberg in terms of the full generality of the concepts involved in central configurations, but we believe it represents a good starting point for further work. Investigations into different power laws for the interactions, differ-

ent mass distributions and the all important question of whether crystallization occurs in these types of models are all underway.

# CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS OF THE PLANAR $1+N$ BODY PROBLEM 


#### Abstract

In this paper, we give a new derivation of the equations for the central configurations of the $1+n$ body problem. In the case of equal masses, we show that for $n$ large enough there exists only one solution. Our lower bound for $n$ improves by several orders of magnitude the one previously found by Hall.

## 1. Introduction

The problem of finding the central configurations of a system of $N$ particles in the plane has been the subject of many papers during the last two hundred years. One of the reasons why central configurations are interesting is that they allow us to construct exact solutions of the $N$-body problem. This was already pointed out by Laplace and, historically, the problem of central configurations was first formulated in this context.

But central configurations also have other interesting properties which show their relevance for the study of the $N$-body problem. Smale proved that there exists a relation between central configurations and the bifurcations of the surfaces of constant energy and angular momentum. He showed that, in the planar case, the set of classes of central configurations, modulus rotations and rescaling, completely determines the critical values of the energy and angular momentum map . Smale's paper marks the beginning of a renewed interest in this old problem, and many contributions have appeared in the last two decades, namely concerning Smale's conjecture on the finiteness of the number of classes of central configurations and the question of obtaining bounds for that number in some particular cases $[4,8,10-13,15,17]$, and concerning the relation between central configurations and limit escape and collision configurations $$. However, the problem is still far from being solved.



Fig. 1.

In this paper we consider a restricted version of the problem of planar central configurations, i.e., we study the limit case of one large mass and $n$ small equal masses as the small masses tend to zero. This problem was first considered by Maxwell in  trying to construct a model for Saturn's rings. In an interesting paper devoted to this subject, Hall  proved that, for $n$ large enough, there is only one central configuration, the regular $n$-gon with the large mass in the center. The bound he obtains for $n$, however, is rather large $\left(n \sim e^{27000}\right)$. We have used many of Hall's ideas and modified his proof to obtain the same result with a bound which improves the one above by many orders of magnitude $\left(n \sim e^{73}\right)$.

In Section 2 we derive the equations for the central configurations of the planar $1+n$ body problem (Proposition 2.3). Although these equations have already been obtained in , the proof given here is much simpler.

In Section 3 we restate the problem in terms of finding the critical points of a function defined on $(n-1)$-dimensional simplex, following Smale's approach to the general planar central configurations problem . Then, as in Smale's proof of Moulton's theorem, we obtain a lower bound for the number of central configurations of the planar $1+n$ body problem.

For $n$ small $(n \leq 8)$ and equal masses several solutions besides the regular $n$-gon have been found numerically in . In the case when $n=3$ the problem was completely solved in , and there exist exactly three classes of solutions, the equilateral triangle and two other configurations (see Figure 1). In Section 4 we prove the main result of this paper, namely that for equal masses and $n$ large enough there exists exactly one (modulus permutations) solution of the planar $1+n$ body problem. We also show that the bound given by our proof is of the order of $e^{73}$.

# 2. Equations and Definitions 

We shall start by defining the central configurations problem for $N$ particles in the plane and present some of its properties. These are classic results and can be found for instance in  or , but we have included here what is necessary for the text to be self-contained.

Consider $N$ particles of masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ subject to their mutual Newtonian gravitational interaction. In an inertial reference frame and choosing appropriate units, the equations of motion are

$$
m_{i} \ddot{q}_{i}=\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\ j \neq i}}^{N} m_{i} m_{j} \frac{q_{i}-q_{j}}{\left\|q_{j}-q_{i}\right\|^{3}}, \quad i=1, \ldots, N
$$

where $q_{i}$ is the position vector of the $i$ th particle. Denote by $M$ the mass matrix $M=\operatorname{diag}\left(m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right)$, by $q \in \mathbb{R}^{2 N}$ the vector $q=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}\right)$ and by $V$ the potential function

$$
V\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}\right)=-\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq N} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left\|q_{i}-q_{j}\right\|}
$$

With this notation, the equations of motion become

$$
M \ddot{q}=-V_{q}
$$

where $V_{q}=\left(\partial V / \partial q_{1}, \ldots, \partial V / \partial q_{N}\right)$.
Due to symmetries, the above equations have ten scalar first integrals, the energy

$$
h=\frac{1}{2} \dot{q}^{T} M \dot{q}+V
$$

the angular momentum

$$
C=\sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i}\left(q_{i} \wedge \dot{q}_{i}\right)
$$

the linear momentum

$$
P=\sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i} \dot{q}_{i}
$$

and the initial position of the center of mass

$$
A=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i} q_{i}-t \sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i} \dot{q}_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i}}
$$

According to (2.2), the center of mass moves with constant velocity. Hence, we may without loss of generality suppose that our reference frame has its origin at the center of mass, that is we shall fix $P=A=0$. Therefore, taking into account the singularities of (2.1), the configuration space of the planar $N$-body problem associated with the mass matrix $M=\operatorname{diag}\left(m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right)$ is

$$
\mathcal{M}\left(m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}\right)=\left\{q \in \mathbb{R}^{2 N}: \sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i} q_{i}=0, q_{i} \neq q_{j} \text { for } i \neq j\right\}
$$

Given a mass matrix $M$, we say that $q \in \mathcal{M}$ represents a central configuration of the associated planar $N$-body problem if there exists a positive constant $\lambda^{2}$ such that

$$
M^{-1} V_{q}=\lambda^{2} q
$$

i.e., if the acceleration vector of every particle is directed towards the center of mass and its modulus is proportional to the distance from the particle to the center of mass. We shall denote by $\mathcal{C}$ the set of planar central configurations associated to a given mass matrix $M$. Notice that $\mathcal{C}$ is invariant with respect to homotheties and rotations in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$. We shall denote by $\tilde{\mathcal{C}}$ the set of planar central configurations modulus the group $S O(2)$ of plane rotations.

Given $q_{i}=\left(x_{i}, y_{i}\right), i=1, \ldots, N$, let $r_{i j}=\left\|q_{i}-q_{j}\right\|$ be the distance between particles $i$ and $j$ and let

$$
(i, j, k)=\frac{1}{2}\left|\begin{array}{lll}
x_{i} & y_{i} & 1 \\
x_{j} & y_{j} & 1 \\
x_{k} & y_{k} & 1
\end{array}\right|
$$

by the oriented area of the triangle with vertices $q_{i}, q_{j}$ and $q_{k}$.
The following proposition (see, for instance, ) gives a characterization of $\tilde{\mathcal{C}}$ which we shall use to derive the equations of $\mathfrak{t} \boldsymbol{\iota}$ central configurations in the planar $1+n$ body problem.

PROPOSITION 2.1. Let $q=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}\right) \in \mathcal{M}\left(m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}\right)$ be a non-collinear planar central configuration. Then $q \in \mathcal{C}$ if and only if

$$
\sum_{\substack{k=1 \\ k \neq i, j}}^{N} m_{k}(i, j, k)\left(\frac{1}{r_{i k}^{3}}-\frac{1}{r_{j k}^{3}}\right)=0, \quad 1 \leq i \leq j \leq N
$$

From now one we shall study the limit problem of one large mass and $n$ small masses as the small masses tend to zero. This situation was first considered by Maxwell  trying to construct a model for Saturn's rings.

Let $q(\varepsilon)=\left(q_{0}(\varepsilon), q_{1}(\varepsilon), \ldots, q_{n}(\varepsilon)\right) \in \tilde{\mathcal{C}}$ be a central configuration of the planar $N$-body problem, $N=1+n$, associated to the masses $m_{0}=1, m_{i}=\mu_{i} \varepsilon$, $i=1, \ldots, n$, which depends continuously on $\varepsilon$ when $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$. We say that $q=$ $\left(q_{0}, q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$, is a central configuration of the planar $1+n$ body problem if there exists $\lim _{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} q(\varepsilon)$ and this limit is equal to $q$. In fact, the definition of a central configuration $q$ for the planar $1+n$ body problem can be weaker, saying that $q$ is the limit of a given sequence $q\left(\varepsilon_{k}\right)$ when $\varepsilon_{k} \rightarrow 0$. But since the more interesting cases correspond to central configurations of the planar $1+n$ body problem which can be prolongated to sufficiently small positive values of $\varepsilon$, we may as well work with the above definition. From (2.3), $q(\varepsilon)$ satisfies

$$
\lambda^{2} q_{0}(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon \sum_{j=1}^{n} \mu_{j} \frac{q_{0}(\varepsilon)-q_{j}(\varepsilon)}{\left\|q_{0}(\varepsilon)-q_{j}(\varepsilon)\right\|^{3}}
$$

$$
\lambda^{2} q_{i}(\varepsilon)=\frac{q_{i}(\varepsilon)-q_{0}(\varepsilon)}{\left\|q_{i}(\varepsilon)-q_{0}(\varepsilon)\right\|^{3}}+\varepsilon \sum_{\substack{j=1 \\ j \neq i}}^{n} \mu_{j} \frac{q_{i}(\varepsilon)-q_{j}(\varepsilon)}{\left\|q_{i}(\varepsilon)-q_{j}(\varepsilon)\right\|^{3}}, \quad i=1, \ldots, n
$$

When $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$ from the first equation we get $q_{0}=0$, and substituting in the other ones we have $\left\|q_{i}\right\|=\lambda^{-2 / 3}$ for $i=1, \ldots, n$. Therefore we have proved the following result.

PROPOSITION 2.2. All the central configurations of the planar $1+n$ body problem lie on a circle centered at $q_{0}=0$.

Let $q=\left(q_{0}, q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$ be a central configuration of the planar $1+n$ body problem. We say that $q$ is non-collision if $q_{i} \neq q_{j}$ for $i \neq j$. Notice that the definition of non-collision central configurations excludes the possibility that the distance between two or more particles tends to zero as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$.

PROPOSITION 2.3 Let $q=\left(q_{0}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$ be a non-collision central configuration of the planar $1+n$ body problem. Denoting by $\alpha_{i}$ the angle defined by the position of $q_{i}$ we have

$$
0=\sum_{\substack{j=1 \\ j \neq i}}^{n} \mu_{j} \sin \left(\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{i}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{8\left|\sin ^{3}\left(\left(\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{i}\right) / 2\right)\right|}\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n
$$

Proof. By hypothesis $q=\lim _{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} q(\varepsilon)$ and from Equations (2.4) we have that

$$
0=\varepsilon \sum_{\substack{k=1 \\ k \neq j}}^{n} \mu_{k}(0, j, k)\left(\frac{1}{r_{0 k}^{3}}-\frac{1}{r_{j k}^{3}}\right), \quad j=1, \ldots, n
$$

and

$$
0=(i, j, 0)\left(\frac{1}{r_{i 0}^{3}}-\frac{1}{r_{j 0}^{3}}\right)+\varepsilon \sum_{\substack{k=1 \\ k \neq i, j}}^{n} \mu_{k}(i, j, k)\left(\frac{1}{r_{i k}^{3}}-\frac{1}{r_{j k}^{3}}\right)
$$

for $1 \leq i<j \leq n$. We remark that the functions $(0, j, k), r_{0 k}, r_{j k},(i, j, 0), r_{i 0}$, $r_{j 0},(i, j, k), r_{i k}$ and $r_{j k}$ are evaluated at $q(\varepsilon)$ but we have omitted the dependence on $\varepsilon$ for the sake of simplicity.

We may factor out $\varepsilon$ in (2.6) so that in the limit $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0,(2.6)$ and (2.7) become, respectively

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 0=\sum_{\substack{k=1 \\
k \neq j}}^{n} \mu_{k}(0, j, k)\left(\frac{1}{r_{0 k}^{3}}-\frac{1}{r_{j k}^{3}}\right), \quad j=1, \ldots, n \\
& 0=(i, j, 0)\left(\frac{1}{r_{i 0}^{3}}-\frac{1}{r_{j 0}^{3}}\right), \quad 1 \leq i \leq j \leq n
\end{aligned}
$$

From Proposition 2.2, $r_{i 0}=r_{j 0}$ for $1 \leq i \leq j \leq n$ and consequently (2.9) is redundant. Moreover, Equations (2.5) correspond to Equations (2.8) written in angular coordinates.

In view of Proposition 2.3 we shall call any solution $\left(\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{n}\right)$ of Equations (2.5) a circular central configuration of the planar $1+n$ body problem. Since we are interested in central configurations modulus rotations and homotheties, to fix notation we shall assume that the circle has radius 1 and that $\alpha_{1}=0$. With this assumption there is a one-to-one correspondence between the solutions of (2.5) and the equivalence classes of circular central configurations.

# 3. The General Case 

From Equations (2.5), we see that the configuration space of the circular central configurations of the planar $1+n$ body problem is

$$
\mathcal{A}=\left\{\left(\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{n}\right) \in[0,2 \pi)^{n}: \alpha_{1}=0, \alpha_{i} \neq \alpha_{j} \text { for } i \neq j\right\}
$$

The set $\mathcal{A}$ has $(n-1)$ ! connected components, each of which corresponds to a given permutation of the $n$ particles on the circle. We shall restrict our study to one connected component of $\mathcal{A}$, i.e., to a given counterclockwise ordering of the $n$ particles. We may assume without loss of generality that $0=\alpha_{1}<\alpha_{2}<\ldots<$ $\alpha_{n}<2 \pi$. Let us take as coordinates on this connected component the angles between two consecutive particles, i.e.

$$
\theta_{i}=\alpha_{i+1}-\alpha_{i}, \quad i=1, \ldots, n-1
$$

It is convenient to work also with an $n$th redundant coordinate

$$
\theta_{n}=2 \pi-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \theta_{i}
$$

which measures the angular distance between particle $n$ and particle 1 . In this way the configuration space will be the simplex $S$ given by the intersection of the hyperplane $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \theta_{i}=2 \pi$ with the space $\left\{\left(\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{n}\right): \theta_{i}>0, i=1, \ldots, n\right\}$.

Let

$$
f(x)=\sin (x)\left(1-\frac{1}{8\left|\sin ^{3}(x / 2)\right|}\right)
$$

Note that Equations (2.5) for the circular central configurations may be expressed in terms of the function $f$.

PROPOSITION 3.1. The circular central configurations are given by the critical points on $S$ of the function

$$
U\left(\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{n}\right)=\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq n} \mu_{i} \mu_{j} F\left(\theta_{i}+\ldots+\theta_{j-1}\right)
$$

where

$$
F(x)=\frac{1}{2|\sin (x / 2)|}+2 \sin ^{2}(x / 2)
$$

Proof. The critical points of $U$ on $S$ are given by

$$
0=\frac{\partial U}{\partial \theta_{k}}+\rho, \quad k=1, \ldots, n
$$

where $\rho$ is the Lagrange multiplier. Since $\partial U / \partial \theta_{n}=0$ we obtain $\rho=0$. From the fact that $f(x)=F^{\prime}(x)$ we have

$$
\frac{\partial U}{\partial \theta_{1}}=0 \Leftrightarrow \mu_{1} \sum_{j=2}^{n} \mu_{j} f\left(\theta_{1}+\ldots+\theta_{j-1}\right)=0
$$

and this is Equation (2.5) for $i=1$.
For $k=1, \ldots, n-1$ we have

$$
0=\frac{\partial U}{\partial \theta_{k}}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} \mu_{i} \sum_{j=k+1}^{n} \mu_{j} f\left(\theta_{i}+\ldots+\theta_{j-1}\right)
$$

Then

$$
0=\frac{\partial U}{\partial \theta_{k+1}}-\frac{\partial U}{\partial \theta_{k}}
$$

becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
0= & \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{j=k+2}^{n} \mu_{i} \mu_{j} f\left(\theta_{i}+\ldots+\theta_{j-1}\right)-\sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{j=k+1}^{n} \mu_{i} \mu_{j} f\left(\theta_{i}+\ldots+\theta_{j-1}\right)+ \\
& +\mu_{k+1} \sum_{j=k+2}^{n} \mu_{j} f\left(\theta_{k+1}+\ldots+\theta_{j-1}\right) \\
= & \mu_{k+1}\left(\sum_{j=k+2}^{n} \mu_{j} f\left(\theta_{k+1}+\ldots+\theta_{j-1}\right)-\sum_{i=1}^{k} \mu_{i} f\left(\theta_{i}+\ldots+\theta_{k}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(x)$ is odd and $\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{i}=\theta_{i}+\ldots+\theta_{j-1}$ if $j>i$ and $\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{i}=$ $-\left(\theta_{j}+\ldots+\theta_{i-1}\right)$ if $j<i$, the above equation is Equation (2.5) with $i=k+1$. Hence the result follows.

THEOREM 3.2. For each choice of the mass parameters $\mu_{1}, \ldots, \mu_{n}$, there exist at least $(n-1)$ ! circular central configurations of the planar $1+n$ body problem.

Proof. Since there are $(n-1)$ ! different orderings of the $n$ particles on the circle, the result follows from Proposition 3.1 if we show that there exist at least

one critical point of $U$ on $S$. But the function $U$ tends to $+\infty$ on the boundary of $S$, and therefore $U$ has at least one minimum on $S$.

The function $f(x)$ defined in Equation (3.1) plays a key role in this problem. The following lemma states some properties of $f$ and its derivatives which will be used throughout this work.

LEMMA 3.3 . Let

$$
f(x)=\sin (x)\left(1-\frac{1}{8\left|\sin ^{3}(x / 2)\right|}\right), \quad x \in[0,2 \pi)
$$

Then the following hold.
(a) $f^{\prime}(x) \geq-7 / 8$, for all $x \in(0,2 \pi)$.
(b) $f^{\prime}(x)>19 /\left(10 x^{3}\right)$, for all $x \in(0, \pi / 2]$.
(c) $f^{\prime \prime \prime}(x) \geq 0$, for all $x \in(0,2 \pi)$.

The proof is straightforward and may be found in .

# 4. The Case of Equal Masses and $n$ Large 

Let $U: S \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be given by

$$
U\left(\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{n}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^{[(n+1) / 2]} \sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}} \mu_{i} \mu_{i+j} F\left(\theta_{i}+\ldots+\theta_{i+j-1}\right)
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& F(x)=\frac{1}{2|\sin (x / 2)|}+2 \sin ^{2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) \\
& \mu_{i+n}=\mu_{i} \\
& \theta_{i+n}=\theta_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

and the tilde means that when $j=[(n+1) / 2]$ the sum over $i$ skips those angles $\theta_{i}+\ldots+\theta_{i+j-1}$ whose complements $2 \pi-\theta_{i}-\ldots-\theta_{i+j-1}$ have appeared before in the sum. It is easy to check that the function $U$ thus defined coincides with the function $U$ given in Proposition 3.1.

The main result of this section is the following.
THEOREM 4.1. For equal mass parameters $\mu_{1}=\ldots=\mu_{n}$ and $n$ large enough, the function $U$ has exactly one critical point in $S$, a nondegenerate minimum.

In view of Proposition 3.1, we have

COROLLARY 4.2. For equal mass parameters $\mu_{1}=\ldots=\mu_{n}$ and $n$ large enough, there are exactly $(n-1)$ ! circular central configurations.

The idea of the proof is the following, well in the spirit of Smale's proof of Moulton's theorem. We consider the middle point $p=(2 \pi / n, \ldots, 2 \pi / n)$ of the simplex $S$, take an arbitrary $\bar{\theta}=\left(\bar{\theta}_{1}, \ldots, \bar{\theta}_{n}\right)$ on the boundary $\partial S$ (so that at least one of the $\bar{\theta}_{i}$ is zero) and consider the straight line which joins the two points, $\theta(t)=\left(\theta_{1}(t), \ldots, \theta_{n}(t)\right)$, with

$$
\theta_{i}(t)=(1-t) \frac{2 \pi}{n}+t \bar{\theta}_{i}, \quad i=1, \ldots, n, \quad t \in[0,1)
$$

We shall show that if $n$ is large enough, for any choice of $\bar{\theta}$, the function $u:[0,1) \rightarrow$ $\mathbb{R}$ given by $u(t)=U(\theta(t))$ is strictly convex in its whole domain. Since we also know that in the case of equal masses, $p$ is a critical point, it follows that $p$ must be a nondegenerate minimum and consequently the unique critical point of $U$ on $S$.

From (4.1),

$$
\frac{d u}{d t}=\sum_{j=1}^{[(n+1) / 2]} \sum_{i=1}^{\bar{n}} \mu_{i} \mu_{i+j} f\left(\theta_{i, j}(t)\right) \frac{d \theta_{i, j}}{d t}
$$

where

$$
\theta_{i, j}(t)=\theta_{i}(t)+\ldots+\theta_{i+j-1}(t)
$$

Notice that the numbers $d \theta_{i, j} / d t$ are constants. Hence

$$
\frac{d^{2} u}{d t^{2}}=\sum_{j=1}^{[(n+1) / 2]} \sum_{i=1}^{\bar{n}} \mu_{i} \mu_{i+j} f^{\prime}\left(\theta_{i, j}(t)\right)\left(\frac{d \theta_{i, j}}{d t}\right)^{2}
$$

and our purpose will be to show that, for $n$ large enough, (4.2) is always positive. For the proof of the theorem we shall need some preliminary results.

LEMMA 4.3. For each $j=1, \ldots, n-1$ and for every $t \in[0,1)$ we have $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \theta_{i, j}(t)=2 \pi j$.

Proof. It follows immediately from the equalities

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \theta_{i, j}(t) & =\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\theta_{i}(t)+\theta_{i+1}(t)+\ldots+\theta_{i+j-1}(t)\right) \\
& =\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(j(1-t) \frac{2 \pi}{n}+t\left(\bar{\theta}_{i}+\bar{\theta}_{i+1}+\ldots+\bar{\theta}_{i+j-1}\right)\right) \\
& =(1-t) 2 \pi j+t j \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bar{\theta}_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
=(1-t) 2 \pi j+t 2 \pi j=2 \pi j
$$

LEMMA 4.4. For any choice of $\bar{\theta}$ and any $t \in[0,1)$, the number $N$ of negative terms in the sum on the right-hand of (4.2) verifies

$$
N<\frac{3}{8} n^{2}+2 n
$$

Proof. By Lemmas 4.3 and 3.3(b), the number of pairs $(i, j), i=1, \ldots, n$ and $j$ fixed, which give rise to negative terms in the sum of (4.2) is strictly smaller than $4 j$. Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
N & <\sum_{j=1}^{[n / 4]} 4 j+\sum_{j=[n / 4]+1}^{[(n+1) / 2]} n \\
& =\frac{4}{2}\left(1+\left[\frac{n}{4}\right]\right)\left[\frac{n}{4}\right]+n\left(\left[\frac{n+1}{2}\right]-\left[\frac{n}{4}\right]\right) \\
& \leq 2\left(1+\frac{n}{4}\right) \frac{n}{4}+n\left(\frac{n+1}{2}-\frac{n}{4}+1\right) \\
& =\frac{3}{8} n^{2}+2 n
\end{aligned}
$$

LEMMA 4.5. If $\sum_{i=1}^{r}\left|a_{i}\right|=\eta$, then $\sum_{i=1}^{r} a_{i}^{2} \geq \eta^{2} / r$.
Proof. Since the minimum value of $\|a\|^{2}$ on the simplex $\left\{\left(a_{1}, \ldots, a_{r}\right): a_{i} \geq 0\right.$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{r} a_{i}=\eta\}$ takes place at the point $q=(\eta / r, \ldots, \eta / r)$, and $\|q\|^{2}=\eta^{2} / r$, the lemma follows.

PROPOSITION 4.6. For any choice of the mass parameters $\mu_{1}, \ldots, \mu_{n}, n$ large enough and for any $\bar{\theta} \in \partial S$ the function $d^{2} u / d t^{2}$ is strictly positive in $[0,1)$.

Proof. Denote by $\sum^{+}$the sum over the positive terms of (4.2) when $\mu_{1}=\ldots=$ $\mu_{n}=1$, by $M$ the ratio

$$
M=\frac{\max _{1 \leq i<j \leq n} \mu_{i} \mu_{j}}{\min _{1 \leq i<j \leq n} \mu_{i} \mu_{j}}
$$

and let

$$
\eta=\max _{\substack{i=1, \ldots, n \\ j=1, \ldots,(n+1) / 2}}\left|\frac{d \theta_{i, j}}{d t}\right|
$$

By Lemmas 3.3(a) and 4.4, the result follows if we prove that

$$
\sum^{+} \geq M\left(\frac{3}{8} n^{2}+2 n\right) \frac{7}{8} \eta^{2}
$$

We shall fix two parameters, $\alpha \in(0,1)$, and $c>2$, and consider two cases.
(a) There exist $i, j$ such that $j<n^{\alpha}$ and $d \theta_{i, j} / d t<-\eta / c$.
(b) For all $i, j$ such that $j<n^{\alpha}$ we have $d \theta_{i, j} / d t \geq-\eta / c$.

We shall prove that in case (a) (respectively (b)) there exists $A(\alpha, c, M)$ (respectively $B(\alpha, c, M))$ such that for $n>A(\alpha, c, M)$ (respectively $n>B(\alpha, c, M)$ ), (4.3) holds.

Case (a). If $d \theta_{i, j} / d t<-\eta / c$ with $j<n^{\alpha}$, then there exist $\theta_{k_{1}}, \ldots, \theta_{k_{r}}, r \leq j$ such that $d \theta_{k_{l}} / d t<0, l=1, \ldots, r$ and

$$
\sum_{l=1}^{r}\left|\frac{d \theta_{k_{l}}}{d t}\right| \geq \frac{\eta}{c}
$$

because $\theta_{i, j}(t)=\sum_{m=i}^{i+j-1} \theta_{m}(t)$.
Assume $n>4$ so that $2 \pi / n<\pi / 2$. Then, since $d \theta_{k_{l}} / d t<0$, by Lemma 3.3(b),

$$
f^{\prime}\left(\theta_{k_{l}}(t)\right)>\frac{19}{10\left(\theta_{k_{l}}(t)\right)^{3}} \geq \frac{19 n^{3}}{10(2 \pi)^{3}}
$$

for $l=1, \ldots, r$ and $t \in[0,1)$. Hence, using (4.4) and Lemma 4.5,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum^{+} & \geq \sum_{l=1}^{n} f^{\prime}\left(\theta_{k_{l}}(t)\right)\left(\frac{d \theta_{k_{l}}}{d t}\right)^{2} \\
& >\frac{19 n^{3}}{10(2 \pi)^{3}} \sum_{l=1}^{r}\left(\frac{d \theta_{k_{l}}}{d t}\right)^{2} \\
& \geq \frac{19 n^{3} \eta^{2}}{10(2 \pi)^{3} c^{2} r} \\
& >\frac{\eta^{2} 19 n^{3-\alpha}}{c^{2} 10(2 \pi)^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, (4.3) will hold provided that

$$
n^{1-\alpha} \geq \frac{70 \pi^{3} M c^{2}}{19}\left(\frac{3}{8}+\frac{2}{n}\right)>\frac{35 \pi^{3} M c^{2}}{19}
$$

assuming that

$$
n>16
$$

Case (b). From

$$
\eta=\max _{\substack{i=1, \ldots, n \\ j=1, \ldots,[(n+1) / 2]}}\left|\frac{d \theta_{i, j}}{d t}\right|
$$




Fig. 2.
there exist $l, k$ such that either $d \theta_{l, k} / d t=\eta$ or $d \theta_{l, k} / d t=-\eta$. Since the function $U$ given by (4.1) depends only on the distance between the different pairs of particles, we may choose between the smallest angle defined by the pair and its complementary. Clearly the function $F$ is invariant respect to this change, and so we may assume without loss of generality that $d \theta_{l, k} / d t=-\eta$. Therefore $k>n^{\alpha}$.

We shall consider partitions of $\theta_{l, k}$ in angles of the form $\theta_{i, m}$ for $m=$ $1, \ldots,\left[n^{\alpha}\right]$, and show that the angles of these partitions generate positive contributions to $\sum^{+}$, which are enough to cancel the negative terms.

Consider first the contribution of the angles of the form $\theta_{i}=\theta_{i, 1}$. Since $d \theta_{l, k} / d t=\sum_{i=l}^{l+k-1} d \theta_{i} / d t$, there exist $r$ angles, $\theta_{i_{p}}, p=1, \ldots, r, r \leq k$, such that $d \theta_{i_{p}} / d t<0$ and

$$
\sum_{p=1}^{r}\left|\frac{d \theta_{i_{p}}}{d t}\right| \geq \eta
$$

Hence, as in case (a), we have

$$
\sum_{p=1}^{r} f^{\prime}\left(\theta_{i_{p}}(t)\right)\left(\frac{d \theta_{i_{p}}}{d t}\right)^{2} \geq \frac{19 n^{3} \eta^{2}}{10(2 \pi)^{3} r} \geq \frac{19 n^{2} \eta^{2}}{10(2 \pi)^{3}}
$$

Consider now the contributions of the angles of the form $\theta_{i, m}, m>1$. For each $m \in$ $\left\{2, \ldots,\left[n^{\alpha}\right]\right\}$ we shall consider the following $m$ partitions of $\theta_{l, k}$ (see Figure 2).

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \theta_{l, k}=\theta_{l, m}+\theta_{l+m, m}+\ldots+\theta_{l+\left[\frac{k}{m}\right] m, k-m\left[\frac{k}{m}\right]} \\
& \theta_{l, k}=\theta_{l}+\theta_{l+1, m}+\ldots+\theta_{l+1+m\left[\frac{k-1}{m}\right], k-1-m\left[\frac{k-1}{m}\right]}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\theta_{l, k}=\theta_{l, m-1}+\theta_{l+m-1, m}+\ldots+\theta_{l+m-1+m\left[\frac{k-m+1}{m}\right], k-m+1-m\left[\frac{k-m+1}{m}\right]}
$$

Note that all the angles $\theta_{i, m}$ which appear in these partitions are different.
Consider the first partition, Since we are in case (b),

$$
\sum_{j=0}^{[k / m]-1} \frac{d}{d t}\left(\theta_{l+j m, m}\right)<-\eta+\frac{\eta}{c}
$$

As before, there must be $r$ angles $\theta_{l+j_{i} m, m}$ for $i=1, \ldots, r$ such that

$$
\frac{d}{d t}\left(\theta_{l+j_{i} m, m}\right)<0, \quad i=1, \ldots, r
$$

and

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{r}\left|\frac{d}{d t} \theta_{l+j_{i} m, m}\right| \geq\left(1-\frac{1}{c}\right) \eta
$$

Therefore, we have as in the previous cases,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{r} f^{\prime}\left(\theta_{l+j_{i} m, m}\right)\left(\frac{d \theta_{l+j_{i} m, m}}{d t}\right)^{2} & >\frac{19}{10}\left(\frac{n}{2 \pi m}\right)^{3}\left(1-\frac{1}{c}\right)^{2} \frac{\eta^{2}}{r} \\
& \geq \frac{19 n^{2}}{10(2 \pi)^{3} m^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{c}\right)^{2} \eta^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

where we have used $r \leq[k / m] \leq k / m, k \leq n$ and we have assumed that

$$
n^{1-\alpha}>4
$$

so that $2 \pi m / n<\pi / 2$.
For the remaining $m-1$ partitions the same reasoning holds, except that we must substitute the $(1-1 / c)$ factor by $(1-2 / c)$, because in these cases there may be two angles instead of just one, besides the $[k / m]$ of fixed 'width' $m$. Therefore, as in (4.8) and again using the fact that $k<n$, we have that

$$
\frac{19 n^{2}}{10(2 \pi)^{3} m^{2}}\left(1-\frac{2}{c}\right)^{2} \eta^{2}
$$

is a lower bound for the positive contribution of the angles of each partition. Summing over all the partitions, and after over $m$ up to $\left[n^{\alpha}\right]$ we have (see (4.7), (4.8) and (4.10))

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum^{+} & >\frac{19 \eta^{2}}{10(2 \pi)^{3}}\left(n^{2}+\sum_{m=2}^{\left[n^{\alpha}\right]}\left(1-\frac{2}{c}\right)^{2} \frac{n^{2}}{m}\right) \\
& =\frac{19 n^{2} \eta^{2}}{10(2 \pi)^{3}}\left(1-\left(1-\frac{2}{c}\right)^{2}+\left(1-\frac{2}{c}\right)^{2} \sum_{m=1}^{\left[n^{\alpha}\right]} \frac{1}{m}\right) \\
& >\frac{19 n^{2} \eta^{2}}{10(2 \pi)^{3}}\left(1-\frac{2}{c}\right)^{2} \log \left(n^{\alpha}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

because

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{m=1}^{\left[n^{\alpha}\right]} \frac{1}{m} & >1-\log 2+\int_{1}^{\left[n^{\alpha}\right]} \frac{1}{x} d x=1-\log 2+\log \left[n^{\alpha}\right] \\
& >1-\log 2+\log \left(n^{\alpha}-1\right)>\log \left(n^{\alpha}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where the last inequality follows if

$$
n>\left(\frac{e}{e-2}\right)^{1 / \alpha}
$$

From (4.3) and (4.6) the result holds if

$$
\log \left(n^{\alpha}\right)>\frac{35}{19} \pi^{3} M\left(1-\frac{2}{c}\right)^{-2}
$$

To sum up, we have shown that the sum in (4.2) is strictly positive for all $t \in[0,1)$ provided that (see (4.5), (4.6), (4.9), (4.11) and (4.12))

$$
n \geq \max \left\{16,4^{1 /(1-\alpha)},\left(\frac{e}{e-2}\right)^{1 / 2}, A(\alpha, c, M), B(\alpha, c, M)\right\}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& A(\alpha, c, M)=\left(N c^{2}\right)^{1 /(1-\alpha)} \\
& B(\alpha, c, M)=\exp \left(\frac{N c^{2}}{\alpha(c-2)^{2}}\right) \\
& N=\frac{35}{19} \pi^{3} M
\end{aligned}
$$

and the result follows.
Note that the result we have proved is much weaker than the convexity of the function $U$ on $S$. In fact, even for the case of equal masses, it may easily be seen that $U$ is not convex. Consider, for instance, the point $P$ in the simplex $S$ which corresponds to the configuration depicted in Figure 3, and the straight line $\tilde{\theta}(t)$ through $P$ which corresponds to changing the position of particle $k$ at $\alpha_{k}=\pi$ while keeping the other $n-1$ fixed. Denote by $\tilde{u}(t)$ the function $U(\tilde{\theta}(t))$. Then the second derivative of $\tilde{u}$ at $P$ will be given by an expression of the form of (4.2), where the only non-zero contributions come from the terms for which $i$ or $j$ is equal to $k$. Since $f^{\prime}(\pi)=-7 / 8$, it is clear that taking $\phi$ close to $\pi, \tilde{u}$ will have negative second derivative at $P$, and hence $U$ cannot be convex in $S$.

Proof of Theorem 4.1. Since $\mu_{1}=\ldots=\mu_{n}$ we know that the point $(2 \pi / n, \ldots$, $2 \pi / n) \in S$ is a critical point of $U$. Therefore, from Proposition 4.6 and (4.13) if

n \geq \max \left\{16,4^{1 /(1-\alpha)},\left(\frac{e}{e-2}\right)^{1 / \alpha}, A(\alpha, c, 1), B(\alpha, c, 1)\right\}
$$

then $p$ is a non-degenerate minimum and the unique critical point of $U$ on $S$.
The method used to prove Proposition 4.6 allows us to establish a lower bound for the number of particles $n$ for which Theorem 4.1 holds. This bound improves the one previously found by Hall  by many orders of magnitude. Consider again the number given by (4.14), and let us choose the values of the parameters $\alpha$ and $c$ that minimize this number. First we solve for $\alpha$ the equation $A(\alpha, c, 1)=B(\alpha, c, 1)$ :

\alpha=\frac{N c^{2}}{N c^{2}+(c-2)^{2} \log \left(N c^{2}\right)}
$$

where $N=35 \pi^{3} / 19$. The functions $A$ and $B$ attain their minimum on the curve (4.15) at the unique root $c_{0} \geq 2$ solution of the cubic

$$

# Stacked central configurations for Newtonian $N+2 p$-body problems 

## A B S T R A C T

We show the existence of spatial central configurations for the $N+2 p$-body problems. In such a configuration, $N$ bodies are at the vertices of a regular $N$-gon $T ; 2 p$ bodies are symmetric with respect to the center of $T$, and located on the straight line which is perpendicular to the regular $N$-gon $T$ and passes through the center of $T$. The masses located on the vertices of the regular $N$-gon are assumed to be equal; the masses located on the same line and symmetric with respect to the center of $T$ are equal.


## 1. Introduction and main results

The Newtonian $n$-body problems  are concerned with the motions of $n$ particles with masses $m_{j} \in R^{+}$and positions $q_{j} \in R^{3}(j=1, \ldots, n)$, the motion is governed by Newton's second law and the Universal law:

$$
m_{j} \ddot{q}_{j}=\frac{\partial U(q)}{\partial q_{j}}
$$

where $q=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$ with Newtonian potential:

$$
U(q)=\sum_{1 \leqslant j<k \leqslant n} \frac{m_{j} m_{k}}{\left|q_{j}-q_{k}\right|}
$$

Consider the space

$$
X=\left\{q=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{n}\right) \in R^{3 n}: \sum_{j=1}^{N} m_{j} q_{j}=0\right\}
$$

that is, suppose that the center of mass is fixed at the origin of the space. Because the potential is singular when two particles have the same position, it is natural to assume that the configuration avoids the collision set $\Delta=\left\{q=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}\right): q_{j}=q_{k}\right.$ for some $k \neq j$ ). The set $X \backslash \Delta$ is called the configuration space.

[^0]
[^0]:    * Correspondence to: Mianyang Normal University, Mianyang, Sichuan, 621000, PR China.

    E-mail address: zhaofurong2006@163.com (F. Zhao).



Fig. 1. $N+2 p$-body.
Definition 1.1 (). A configuration $q=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{n}\right) \in X \backslash \Delta$ is called a central configuration if there exists a constant $\lambda$ such that

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq k}^{n} \frac{m_{j} m_{k}}{\left|q_{j}-q_{k}\right|^{3}}\left(q_{j}-q_{k}\right)=-\lambda m_{k} q_{k}, \quad 1 \leqslant k \leqslant n
$$

The value of constant $\lambda$ in (1.4) is uniquely determined by

$$
\lambda=\frac{U}{I}
$$

where

$$
I=\sum_{k=1}^{n} m_{k}\left|q_{k}\right|^{2}
$$

Since the general solution of the $n$-body problem cannot be given, great importance has been attached to search for particular solutions from the very beginning. A homographic solution is a configuration which is preserved for all time. Central configurations and homographic solutions are linked by the Laplace theorem . Collapse orbits and parabolic orbits have relations with the central configurations [17-20], so finding central configurations becomes very important. The main general open problem for the central configurations is due to Wintner  and Smale : Is the number of central configurations finite for any choice of positive masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{n}$ ? Hampton and Moeckel  have proved this conjecture for any given four positive masses.

For 5-body problems, Hampton  provided a new family of planar central configurations, called stacked central configurations. A stacked central configuration is one that has some proper subset of three or more points forming a central configuration. Ouyang et al.  studied pyramidal central configurations for Newtonian $N+1$-body problems; Zhang and Zhou  considered double pyramidal central configurations for Newtonian $N+2$-body problems; Mello and Fernandes  analyzed new classes of spatial central configurations for the $N+3$-body problem. Llibre and Mello studied triple and quadruple nested central configurations for the planar $n$-body problem. There are many papers studying other central configuration problems such as $[2,4,3,5,8-14,16,21,22,25]$.

In this paper we shall prove the following result.
Theorem 1.1. For $N+2 p$-body problems in $R^{3}$ where $N \geq 2$ and $p \geq 1$, there is at least one central configuration such that $N$ bodies are at the vertices of a regular $N$-gon $T$, and $2 p$ bodies are symmetric with respect to the center of the regular $N$-gon $T$, and located on a line which is perpendicular to the regular $N$-gon $T$ and passes through the center of $T$. The masses at the vertices of the regular $N$-gon are equal and the masses symmetric with respect to the center of $T$ are equal. (See Fig. 1 for $N=4$ and $p=4$.)

# 2. The proof of Theorem 1.1 

To begin, we take a coordinate system which simplifies the analysis. The particles have positions given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& q_{j}=r_{0}\left(\cos \alpha_{j}, \sin \alpha_{j}, 0\right), \quad \text { where } \alpha_{j}=\frac{(j-1)}{N} 2 \pi, j=1, \ldots, N \\
& q_{N+j}=\left(0,0, r_{j}\right), \quad q_{N+j+p}=\left(0,0,-r_{j}\right), \quad \text { where } j=1, \ldots, p
\end{aligned}
$$

The masses are given by

$$
m_{1}=\cdots=m_{N}=M_{0}, \quad m_{N+j}=m_{N+j+p}=M_{j}
$$

Notice that $\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}, q_{N+1}, \ldots, q_{N+2 p}\right)$ is a central configuration if and only if

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq k}^{N+2 p} \frac{m_{j} m_{k}}{\left|q_{j}-q_{k}\right|^{3}}\left(q_{j}-q_{k}\right)=-\lambda m_{k} q_{k}, \quad 1 \leqslant k \leqslant N+2 p
$$

By the symmetries of the system, the Eq. (2.1) is equivalent to the following equations:

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq k}^{N+2 p} \frac{m_{j} m_{k}}{\left|q_{j}-q_{k}\right|^{3}}\left(q_{j}-q_{k}\right)=-\lambda m_{k} q_{k}, \quad k=1, N+1, \ldots, N+p
$$

That is,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& -\lambda r_{0}=-\frac{\beta M_{0}}{r_{0}^{2}}-\sum_{i=1}^{p} \frac{2 M_{i} r_{0}}{\left|r_{0}^{2}+r_{i}^{2}\right|^{3 / 2}}, \quad \text { where } \beta=\frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{N-1} \csc (\pi j / N) \\
& -\lambda r_{1}=-\frac{N M_{0} r_{1}}{\left|r_{0}^{2}+r_{1}^{2}\right|^{3 / 2}}-\frac{M_{1}}{4 r_{1}^{2}}+\sum_{i=2}^{p}\left(\frac{M_{i}}{\left|r_{i}-r_{1}\right|^{2}}-\frac{M_{i}}{\left|r_{i}+r_{1}\right|^{2}}\right) \\
& -\lambda r_{j}=-\frac{N M_{0} r_{j}}{\left|r_{0}^{2}+r_{j}^{2}\right|^{3 / 2}}-\sum_{1 \leq i<j}\left(\frac{M_{i}}{\left|r_{i}-r_{j}\right|^{2}}+\frac{M_{i}}{\left|r_{i}+r_{j}\right|^{2}}\right)-\frac{M_{j}}{4 r_{j}^{2}} \\
& -\sum_{j=1 \leq j j}\left(-\frac{M_{i}}{\left|r_{i}-r_{j}\right|^{2}}+\frac{M_{i}}{\left|r_{i}+r_{j}\right|^{2}}\right), \quad j=2, \ldots, p-1 \\
& -\lambda r_{p}=-\frac{N M_{0} r_{p}}{\left|r_{0}^{2}+r_{p}^{2}\right|^{3 / 2}}-\sum_{1 \leq i<p}\left(\frac{M_{i}}{\left|r_{i}-r_{p}\right|^{2}}+\frac{M_{i}}{\left|r_{i}+r_{p}\right|^{2}}\right)-\frac{M_{p}}{4 r_{p}^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

By (2.3)-(2.6), $\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}, q_{N+1}, \ldots, q_{N+2 p}\right)$ is a central configuration if and only if $\left(r_{0}, r_{1}, \ldots, r_{p}\right)$ is a critical point of $\tilde{U}\left(r_{0}, r_{1}, \ldots, r_{p}\right)$ on $\tilde{C}$, where:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \tilde{C}=\left\{\left(r_{0}, r_{1}, \ldots, r_{p}\right) \mid r_{0}>0,0<r_{1}<r_{2}<\cdots<r_{p}, \frac{1}{2} N M_{0} r_{0}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{p} M_{i} r_{i}^{2}=1\right\} \\
& \tilde{U}\left(r_{0}, r_{1}, \ldots, r_{p}\right)=\frac{\beta M_{0}^{2} N}{r_{0}}+\sum_{i=1}^{p} \frac{2 N M_{0} M_{i}}{\left|r_{0}^{2}+r_{i}^{2}\right|^{1 / 2}}+\sum_{i=1}^{p} \frac{M_{i}^{2}}{2 r_{i}}+\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq j j}\left(\frac{2 M_{i} M_{j}}{\left|r_{i}-r_{j}\right|}+\frac{2 M_{i} M_{j}}{\left|r_{i}+r_{j}\right|}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

$\tilde{C}$ is an open, simple connected and bounded set. $\tilde{U}\left(r_{0}, r_{1}, \ldots, r_{p}\right) \rightarrow+\infty$ at the boundary of the set $\tilde{C}$. Now there is at least one critical point of $\tilde{U}\left(r_{0}, r_{1}, \ldots, r_{p}\right)$ on $\tilde{C}$. The proof of Theorem 1.1 is completed.


# THREE-DIMENSIONAL CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS IN $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ AND $\mathrm{S}^{3}$ 


#### Abstract

We show that each central configuration in the three-dimensional hyperbolic sphere is equivalent to one central configuration on a particular twodimensional hyperbolic sphere. However, there exist both special and ordinary central configurations in the three-dimensional sphere that are not confined to any two-dimensional sphere.



## 1. INTRODUCTION

The curved $N$-body problem is a natural extension of the Newtonian $N$-body problem in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ to isotropic, complete, simply connected spaces of constant nonzero curvature, $\mathrm{S}^{3}$ and $\mathrm{H}^{3}$. For its history, we refer the readers to , where the equations of motion are written in extrinsic coordinates in $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ for $\mathbb{S}^{3}$, and the Minkowski space $\mathbb{R}^{3,1}$ for $\mathrm{H}^{3}$. This approach, different form more traditional ones like , led to fruitful results, especially in the study of relative equilibria, which are rigid motions that become fixed points in some rotating coordinates system, $$.

Based on the work of Diacu, especially , the authors of  proposed to study central configurations. Roughly speaking, central configurations are special arrangements of the point particles and the exact definition will be given later. The central configurations of the Newtonian $N$-body problem, first formulated by Laplace , are quite important in the study of the Newtonian $N$-body problem. In , the authors have also showed the importance of central configurations for the curved $N$-body problem. For instance, each central configuration gives rise to

a one-parameter family of relative equilibria, and central configurations are the bifurcation points in the topological classification of the curved $N$-body problem.

Some questions about these configurations were also raised in . For example, find all central configurations for $N$ point particles when $N$ is small (the threeparticles case has been recently solved and will appear in a forthcoming paper). Another interesting problem is to prove (or disprove) that for generic $N$ point particles, the number of equivalent classes of central configurations is finite. Though these questions are similar to those of the Newtonian $N$-body problem , the answers are quite different in general. For example, Moulton's theorem concerning the collinear central configurations has been generalized to $\mathrm{H}^{3}$, , but it can not be directly generalized to $\mathrm{S}^{3}$.

In this paper, we put into the evidence another difference: each central configuration on $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ is equivalent to one central configuration on $\mathrm{H}_{x y w}^{2}$, which will be defined later, whereas in $\mathrm{S}^{3}$ there are central configurations that are not confined to any two-dimensional sphere. In some sense, the number of central configurations in $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ is smaller than that of $\mathrm{S}^{3}$. When we consider the Wintner-Smale conjecture in $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ raised in  asking whether the number of classes of central configurations in $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ is finite or not for generic $N$ point particles, we only need to study the problem on $\mathrm{H}_{x y w}^{2}$.

The paper is organized as follows: in Section 2, we recall the basic setting of the curved $N$-body problem and the corresponding facts about central configurations; in Section 3, we prove the result about central configurations in $\mathrm{H}^{3}$; in Section 4, we construct a two-parameter family of three-dimensional central configurations in $\mathrm{S}^{3}$.

# 2. THE CURVED $N$-BODY PROBLEM AND CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS 

2.1. Equations of motion. As done in $$, the equations will be written in $\mathrm{R}^{4}$ for $\mathrm{S}^{3}$ and in the Minkowski space $\mathrm{R}^{3,1}$, for $\mathrm{H}^{3}$. For convenience, we understand the two linear spaces as $\mathrm{R}^{4}$ endowed with two inner products: for two vectors, $\mathbf{q}_{1}=\left(x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1}, w_{1}\right)^{T}$ and $\mathbf{q}_{2}=\left(x_{2}, y_{2}, z_{2}, w_{2}\right)^{T}$, the inner products are given by

$$
\mathbf{q}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{q}_{2}=x_{1} x_{2}+y_{1} y_{2}+z_{1} z_{2}+\sigma w_{1} w_{2}
$$

where $\sigma=1$ for the Euclidean space and $\sigma=-1$ for the Minkowski space. We define the unit sphere $\mathrm{S}^{3}$ and the unit hyperbolic sphere $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{S}^{3}:=\left\{(x, y, z, w)^{T} \in \mathrm{R}^{4} \mid x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+w^{2}=1\right\} \text { and } \\
& \mathrm{H}^{3}:=\left\{(x, y, z, w)^{T} \in \mathrm{R}^{4} \mid x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-w^{2}=-1, w>0\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

respectively. We can merge these two manifolds into

$$
\mathrm{M}^{3}:=\left\{(x, y, z, w)^{T} \in \mathrm{R}^{4} \mid x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+\sigma w^{2}=\sigma, \text { with } w>0 \text { for } \sigma=-1\right\}
$$

Given the positive masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$, whose positions are described by the configuration $\mathbf{q}=\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{N}\right) \in\left(\mathrm{M}^{3}\right)^{N}, \mathbf{q}_{i}=\left(x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i}, w_{i}\right)^{T}, i=\overline{1, N}$, we define the singularity set

$$
\Delta=\cup_{1 \leq i<j \leq N}\left\{\mathbf{q} \in\left(\mathrm{M}^{3}\right)^{N} ; \mathbf{q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf{q}_{j}= \pm 1\right\}
$$

Let $d_{i j}$ be the geodesic distance between the point masses $m_{i}$ and $m_{j}$, which is computed by

$$
d_{i j}(\mathbf{q})=\arccos \left(\mathbf{q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf{q}_{j}\right) \text { for } \mathrm{S}^{3}, \quad d_{i j}(\mathbf{q})=\arccosh \left(-\mathbf{q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf{q}_{j}\right) \text { for } \mathrm{H}^{3}
$$

The force function $U(-U$ being the potential function $)$ in $\left(\mathrm{M}^{3}\right)^{N} \backslash \Delta$ is

$$
U(\mathbf{q}):=\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq N} m_{i} m_{j} \operatorname{ctnd}_{i j}(\mathbf{q})
$$

where $\operatorname{ctn}(x)$ stands for $\cot (x)$ in $\mathrm{S}^{3}$ and $\operatorname{coth}(x)$ in $\mathrm{H}^{3}$. We also introduce two more notations, which unify the trigonometric and hyperbolic functions,

$$
\operatorname{sn}(x)=\sin (x) \text { or } \sinh (x), \quad \operatorname{csn}(x)=\cos (x) \text { or } \cosh (x)
$$

Define the kinetic energy as $T(\dot{\mathbf{q}})=\sum_{1 \leq i \leq N} m_{i} \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{i} \cdot \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{i}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}=\left(\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{1}, \ldots, \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{N}\right)$. Then the curved $N$-body problem is given by the Lagrange system on $T\left(\left(\mathrm{M}^{3}\right)^{N} \backslash \Delta\right)$, with

$$
L(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}):=T(\dot{\mathbf{q}})+U(\mathbf{q})
$$

Using variational methods, we obtain the equations of motion in $\mathrm{S}^{3}$ and in $\mathrm{H}^{3}$, . Merged into one, they are

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{i}=\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{N} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}\left[\mathbf{q}_{j}-\operatorname{csnd}_{i j} \mathbf{q}_{i}\right]}{\operatorname{sn}^{3} d_{i j}}-\sigma m_{i}\left(\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{i} \cdot \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{i}\right) \mathbf{q}_{i} \\
\mathbf{q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf{q}_{i}=\sigma, \quad i=\overline{1, N}
\end{array}\right.
$$

The first part of the acceleration access from the gradient of the force function, $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} U(\mathbf{q})$, and we will denote it by $\mathbf{F}_{i}$. It is the sum of $\mathbf{F}_{i j}=\frac{m_{i} m_{j}\left[\mathbf{q}_{j}-\operatorname{csnd}_{i j} \mathbf{q}_{i}\right]}{\operatorname{sn}^{3} d_{i j}}$ for $j \neq i$.

# 2.2. Central configurations. 

Definition 1. A configuration $\mathbf{q} \in\left(\mathrm{M}^{3}\right)^{N} \backslash \Delta$ is called a central configuration if there is some constant $\lambda$ such that

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} U(\mathbf{q})=\lambda \nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} I(\mathbf{q}), i=\overline{1, N}
$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient operator in $\mathrm{M}^{3}, I(\mathbf{q})=\sum_{i=1}^{N} m_{i}\left(x_{i}^{2}+y_{i}^{2}\right)$, and the explicit form of $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} I$ is

$$
2 m_{i}\left[\begin{array}{c}
x_{i}\left(w_{i}^{2}+z_{i}^{2}\right) \\
y_{i}\left(w_{i}^{2}+z_{i}^{2}\right) \\
-z_{i}\left(x_{i}^{2}+y_{i}^{2}\right) \\
-w_{i}\left(x_{i}^{2}+y_{i}^{2}\right)
\end{array}\right] \text { in } T\left(\mathrm{~S}^{3}\right)^{N} \text { and } 2 m_{i}\left[\begin{array}{l}
x_{i}\left(w_{i}^{2}-z_{i}^{2}\right) \\
y_{i}\left(w_{i}^{2}-z_{i}^{2}\right) \\
z_{i}\left(x_{i}^{2}+y_{i}^{2}\right) \\
w_{i}\left(x_{i}^{2}+y_{i}^{2}\right)
\end{array}\right] \text { in } T\left(\mathrm{H}^{3}\right)^{N}
$$

Since the two functions $U$ and $I$ are both invariant under the group action of $S O(2) \times S O(2)$ (in the case of $\mathrm{S}^{3}$ ) and $S O(2) \times S O(1,1)$ (in the case of $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ ), it is easy to check that a central configuration remains a central configuration after an $S O(2) \times S O(2)$ action (or an $S O(2) \times S O(1,1)$ action), . Two central configurations are said to be equivalent if one can be transformed to the other by these group actions. When we say a central configuration, we mean a class of central configurations as defined by the equivalence relation.

A central configuration with $\lambda=0$ is called a special central configuration, which only occurs in $\mathrm{S}^{3}$, . Otherwise, it is called an ordinary central configuration. A central configuration lying on a geodesic is called a geodesic central configuration. A central configuration lying on a two-dimensional sphere is called an $\mathrm{S}^{2}$ central configuration, a central configuration lying on a two-dimensional hyperbolic sphere is called an $\mathrm{H}^{2}$ central configuration. All the other central configurations are called three-dimensional central configurations.

Here, a two-dimensional sphere (hyperbolic sphere) means a sphere (hyperbolic sphere) isometric to the unit sphere (hyperbolic sphere) in $\mathrm{R}^{3}\left(\mathrm{R}^{2,1}\right)$. It is the nonempty intersection of $\mathrm{M}^{3}$ with a three-dimensional linear subspace: $\left\{(x, y, z, w)^{T} \in\right.$ $\left.\mathrm{R}^{4} \mid a x+b y+c z+d w=0\right\},$. We begin with the following result.
Proposition 1. Let $V=\left\{(x, y, z, w)^{T} \in \mathrm{R}^{4} \mid c z+\sigma d w=0\right\}$. If a configuration $\mathbf{q}=\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \cdots, \mathbf{q}_{N}\right)$ lies on the two-dimensional sphere (hyperbolic sphere): $V \cap \mathrm{M}^{3}$, then $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} I$ is in $V$ for $i=\overline{1, N}$.

Proof. By the explicit form of $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} I$, equation (2), we get

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} I \cdot(0,0, c, d)^{T}=-\sigma 2 m_{i}\left(x_{i}^{2}+y_{i}^{2}\right)\left(c z_{i}+\sigma d w_{i}\right)=0
$$

This equation completes the proof.

# 3. Central CONFigurations on $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ 

Let us define $\mathrm{H}_{x y w}^{2}:=\left\{(x, y, z, w)^{T} \in \mathrm{R}^{4} \mid z=0\right\} \cap \mathrm{H}^{3}$. We can prove the following result.

Theorem 1. Each central configuration in $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ is equivalent to some central configuration on $\mathrm{H}_{x y w}^{2}$.

Proof. We first show that all central configurations in $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ must lie on a twodimensional hyperbolic sphere. Then we show that there is some action $\chi \in$

$S O(2) \times S O(1,1)$ which transforms that hyperbolic sphere to $\mathrm{H}_{x y w}^{2}$. Thus by the definition of equivalent central configurations, each central configuration in $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ is equivalent to some central configuration on $\mathrm{H}_{x y w}^{2}$.

Consider the two-dimensional hyperbolic sphere: $\mathrm{H}_{\phi}^{2}:=\left\{(x, y, z, w)^{T} \in \mathrm{R}^{4} \mid \cosh \phi z-\right.$ $\sinh \phi w=0\} \cap \mathrm{H}^{3}$. The intersection is not empty, since the linear subspace and $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ share the point $(0,0, \sinh \phi, \cosh \phi)^{T}$. We show that each central configuration will be confined to only one such two-dimensional hyperbolic sphere.

Assume that this is not the case. Suppose that there is a central configuration $\mathbf{q}=\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \cdots, \mathbf{q}_{N}\right)$ with $\mathbf{q}_{i} \in \mathrm{H}_{\phi_{i}}^{2}, \phi_{1} \geq \phi_{i}$ for $i \neq 1$ and there is at least one $i$ such that $\phi_{1}>\phi_{i}$. Then $\mathbf{q}_{i}$ can be written as $\left(x_{i}, y_{i}, \rho_{i} \sinh \phi_{i}, \rho_{i} \cosh \phi_{i}\right)^{T}$ with $\rho_{i}>0$ since $w_{i}=\rho_{i} \cosh \phi_{i}>0$. By Proposition $1, \nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{1}} I$ is in the linear subspace $\left\{(x, y, z, w)^{T} \in \mathrm{R}^{4} \mid \cosh \phi_{1} z-\sinh \phi_{1} w=0\right\}$. In order to have a central configuration, $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{1}} U$ must be in the linear subspace, i.e.,

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{1}} U \cdot\left(0,0, \cosh \phi_{1}, \sinh \phi_{1}\right)^{T}=\mathbf{F}_{1 z} \cosh \phi_{1}-\mathbf{F}_{1 w} \sinh \phi_{1}=0
$$

where $\mathbf{F}_{1 z}$ and $\mathbf{F}_{1 w}$ stand for the $z$-coordinate and $w$-coordinate of $\mathbf{F}_{1}$, respectively. However, using the explicit form of $\mathbf{F}_{1}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathbf{F}_{1 z} \cosh \phi_{1}-\mathbf{F}_{1 w} \sinh \phi_{1} \\
= & \sum_{i=2}^{N} m_{i} m_{1}\left(\frac{z_{i}-\cosh d_{i 1} z_{1}}{\sinh ^{3} d_{i 1}} \cosh \phi_{1}-\frac{w_{i}-\cosh d_{i 1} w_{1}}{\sinh ^{3} d_{i 1}} \sinh \phi_{1}\right) \\
= & \sum_{i=2}^{N} m_{i} m_{1} \frac{\rho_{i} \sinh \phi_{i} \cosh \phi_{1}-\rho_{i} \cosh \phi_{i} \sinh \phi_{1}-\cosh d_{i 1}\left(z_{1} \cosh \phi_{1}-w_{1} \sinh \phi_{1}\right)}{\sinh ^{3} d_{i 1}} \\
= & \sum_{i=2}^{N} m_{i} m_{1} \frac{\rho_{i} \sinh \left(\phi_{i}-\phi_{1}\right)}{\sinh ^{3} d_{i 1}}<0
\end{aligned}
$$

since $\phi_{i} \leq \phi_{1}$ for $i \neq 1$ and there is at least one $i$ such that $\phi_{i}<\phi_{1}$.
Thus any central configuration must lie on only one such hyperbolic sphere, say $\mathrm{H}_{\phi}^{2}$. Let

$$
\chi=\left(\begin{array}{ll}
1 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\cosh \phi & -\sinh \phi \\
-\sinh \phi & \cosh \phi
\end{array}\right] \in S O(2) \times S O(1,1)
$$

Since $\left[\begin{array}{cc}\cosh \phi & -\sinh \phi \\ -\sinh \phi & \cosh \phi\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}\rho_{i} \sinh \phi \\ \rho_{i} \cosh \phi\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ \rho_{i}\end{array}\right], \chi\left(\mathrm{H}_{\phi}^{2}\right)=\mathrm{H}_{x y w}^{2}$. This calculation completes the proof.

To offer more insight into this result, we provide a heuristic argument. Recall that the Poincaré ball model of $\mathrm{H}^{3}$ is

$$
\left(\bar{x}^{2}+\bar{y}^{2}+\bar{z}^{2}<1, d s^{2}=\frac{4\left(d \bar{x}^{2}+d \bar{y}^{2}+d \bar{z}^{2}\right)}{\left(1-\bar{x}^{2}-\bar{y}^{2}-\bar{z}^{2}\right)^{2}}\right)
$$

In this model, a two-dimensional hyperbolic sphere is the intersection of the threedimensional ball with a two-dimensional Euclidean sphere that orthogonally intersects the boundary of the ball. The hyperbolic spheres $\mathrm{H}_{\phi}^{2}$ defined above are those that intersect the $\bar{z}$-axis orthogonally, . For example, $\mathrm{H}_{x y w}^{2}$ in this model is the disk in the plane $\bar{z}=0$. Now suppose that $\mathbf{q}_{i} \in \mathrm{H}_{\phi_{i}}^{2}$ and $\phi_{1}>\phi_{2}$. Proposition 1 implies that $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{1}} I \in T_{\mathbf{q}_{1}} \mathrm{H}_{\phi_{1}}^{2}$, as showed in Figure 1. However, $\mathbf{F}_{12}$ points towards the lower hyperbolic sphere $\mathrm{H}_{\phi_{2}}^{2}$. Thus $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{1}} I$ and $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{1}} U$ cannot be collinear.


Figure 1. A configurations in the Poincaré ball model.

Remark 1. Recall that there are central configurations not in a plane (called spatial central configurations) in the Newtonian $N$-body problem, such as the regular tetrahedron for any given four masses. However, those spatial configurations do not lead to rigid motions. Thus if we defined central configurations in $\mathrm{R}^{3}$ as those that lead to rigid motions, there would be no spatial ones.

# 4. Central Configurations in $\mathrm{S}^{3}$ 

Apparently, the compactness of $\mathrm{S}^{3}$ makes the set of central configuration in it richer than in $\mathrm{H}^{3}$. With computations similar to the ones we performed in $\mathrm{H}^{3}$, we can get the following necessary conditions for central configurations in $\mathrm{S}^{3}$,

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{N} m_{i} m_{j} \frac{\rho_{j} \sin \left(\phi_{j}-\phi_{i}\right)}{\sin ^{3} d_{i j}}=0, i=\overline{1, N}
$$

These equations, however, do not rule out the existence of three-dimensional central configurations. For example, we have the pentatope special central configuration of five equal masses, ,

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
x_{1}=1, & y_{1}=0, & z_{1}=0, & w_{1}=0 \\
x_{2}=-1 / 4, & y_{2}=\sqrt{15} / 4, & z_{2}=0, & w_{2}=0 \\
x_{3}=-1 / 4, & y_{3}=-\sqrt{5} /(4 \sqrt{3}), & z_{3}=\sqrt{5} / \sqrt{6}, & w_{3}=0 \\
x_{4}=-1 / 4, & y_{4}=-\sqrt{5} /(4 \sqrt{3}), & z_{4}=-\sqrt{5} /(2 \sqrt{6}), & w_{4}=\sqrt{5} /(2 \sqrt{2}) \\
x_{5}=-1 / 4, & y_{5}=-\sqrt{5} /(4 \sqrt{3}), & z_{5}=-\sqrt{5} /(2 \sqrt{6}), & w_{5}=-\sqrt{5} /(2 \sqrt{2})
\end{array}
$$

However, all known three-dimensional central configurations are special central configurations (i.e., $\lambda=0$ ). We will further construct a two-parameter family of ordinary three-dimensional central configurations of five masses. Suppose that the masses are $m_{1}=m_{2}=m, m_{3}=m_{4}=m_{5}=1$, and their positions are given by

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
x_{1}=0, & y_{1}=0, & z_{1}=\cos \theta, & w_{1}=\sin \theta \\
x_{2}=0, & y_{2}=0, & z_{2}=\cos \theta, & w_{2}=-\sin \theta \\
x_{3}=r, & y_{3}=0, & z_{3}=c, & w_{3}=0 \\
x_{4}=r \cos \frac{2 \pi}{3}, & y_{4}=r \sin \frac{2 \pi}{3}, & z_{4}=c, & w_{4}=0 \\
x_{5}=r \cos \frac{4 \pi}{3}, & y_{5}=r \sin \frac{4 \pi}{3}, & z_{5}=c, & w_{5}=0
\end{array}
$$

where $c \in(-1,1) \backslash\{0\}, r>0, r^{2}+c^{2}=1$ and $\theta \in(0, \pi) \backslash\left\{\frac{\pi}{2}\right\}$. Such configurations depend on two parameters, $c$ and $\theta$, and we denote them by $\mathbf{q}(c, \theta)$. It is easy to see that these configurations are not confined to any two-dimensional sphere. In Figure 2, we illustrate such a configuration in a $\mathrm{R}^{3}$ hyperplane by the stereographic projection of $S^{3}$ from $(0,0,1,0)$ onto the corresponding equatorial $\mathrm{R}^{3}$ hyperplane, i.e.,

$$
\bar{x}=\frac{x}{1-z}, \quad \bar{y}=\frac{y}{1-z}, \bar{w}=\frac{w}{1-z}
$$

Proposition 2. For any $(c, \theta) \in(-1,0) \times\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, and $(c, \theta) \in(0,1) \times\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)$, the configurations $\mathbf{q}(c, \theta)$ constructed above are central configurations if

$$
m=-\frac{3 c\left|\sin ^{3} 2 \theta\right|}{2 \cos \theta\left(1-c^{2} \cos ^{2} \theta\right)^{3 / 2}}
$$

Generally, they are ordinary central configurations.



Figure 2. A configuration $\mathbf{q}(c, \theta)$ with $(c, \theta) \in(-1,0) \times\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

Proof. We check that the central configuration equations $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} U=\lambda \nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} I, i=$ $1, \cdots, 5$, are satisfied. The function $U$ can be written as $U=U_{1}+U_{2}$, where

$$
U_{1}=\cot d_{34}+\cot d_{45}+\cot d_{35}, U_{2}=m^{2} \cot d_{12}+m \sum_{i=3}^{5}\left(\cot d_{1 i}+\cot d_{2 i}\right)
$$

Note that the three equal masses $m_{3}, m_{4}$, and $m_{5}$ form an ordinary central configuration themselves, i.e., $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} U_{1}=\lambda_{1} \nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} I$, for $i=3,4,5, \lambda_{1}=\frac{3}{2 \sin ^{3} d_{34}}$. . Note that $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{1}} I=\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{2}} I=0$ by equation (2). Thus $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} U=\lambda \nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} I$ is satisfied if and only if there is some constant $\lambda_{2}$ such that

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} U_{2}=\lambda_{2} \nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} I, i=3,4,5, \text { and } \mathbf{F}_{1}=\mathbf{F}_{2}=0
$$

By symmetry, we only need to check $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{3}} U_{2}=\lambda_{2} \nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{3}} I$, and $\mathbf{F}_{1}=0$.
Note that $d_{13}=d_{23}=d_{14}=d_{24}=d_{15}=d_{25}, d_{34}=d_{45}=d_{35}$, and

$$
\cos d_{12}=\cos 2 \theta, \cos d_{13}=c \cos \theta, \quad \cos d_{34}=\frac{3}{2} c^{2}-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Some straightforward computation shows

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{3}} U_{2} & =\mathbf{F}_{31}+\mathbf{F}_{32}=\frac{m\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}-\cos d_{13} \mathbf{q}_{3}\right)}{\sin ^{3} d_{13}}+\frac{m\left(\mathbf{q}_{2}-\cos d_{23} \mathbf{q}_{3}\right)}{\sin ^{3} d_{23}} \\
& =\frac{m}{\sin ^{3} d_{13}}\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}+\mathbf{q}_{2}-2 \cos d_{13} \mathbf{q}_{3}\right)=\frac{m}{\sin ^{3} d_{13}}\left((0,0,2 \cos \theta, 0)^{T}-2 c \cos \theta(r, 0, c, 0)^{T}\right) \\
& =\frac{-2 m r \cos \theta}{\sin ^{3} d_{13}}(c, 0,-r, 0)^{T}
\end{aligned}
$$

Using equation (2), we obtain $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{3}} I=2 r c(c, 0,-r, 0)^{T}$. Thus we can write that

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{3}} U_{2}=\lambda_{2} \nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{3}} I, \quad \lambda_{2}=\frac{-m \cos \theta}{c \sin ^{3} d_{13}}
$$

By direct computation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{F}_{1} & =\mathbf{F}_{12}+\sum_{j=3}^{5} \mathbf{F}_{1 j}=\frac{m^{2}}{\left|\sin ^{3} 2 \theta\right|}\left(\mathbf{q}_{2}-\cos 2 \theta \mathbf{q}_{1}\right)+\sum_{i=3}^{5} \frac{m}{\sin ^{3} d_{13}}\left(\mathbf{q}_{i}-\cos d_{13} \mathbf{q}_{1}\right) \\
& =\frac{m^{2}}{\left|\sin ^{3} 2 \theta\right|}\left(\mathbf{q}_{2}-\cos 2 \theta \mathbf{q}_{1}\right)+\frac{m}{\sin ^{3} d_{13}}\left(\sum_{i=3}^{5} \mathbf{q}_{i}-3 c \cos \theta \mathbf{q}_{1}\right) \\
& =m \sin \theta\left(\frac{2 m \cos \theta}{\left|\sin ^{3} 2 \theta\right|}+\frac{3 c}{\sin ^{3} d_{13}}\right)(0,0, \sin \theta,-\cos \theta)^{T}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\mathbf{F}_{1}=0$ if and only if $m=-\frac{3 c\left|\sin ^{3} 2 \theta\right|}{2 \cos \theta\left(1-c^{2} \cos ^{2} \theta\right)^{3 / 2}}$. Since we need positive masses, $c \cos \theta$ needs to be negative.

We have thus obtained a two-parameter family of central configurations $\mathbf{q}(c, \theta)$ for any $(c, \theta) \in(-1,0) \times\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, and $(c, \theta) \in(0,1) \times\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)$. The central configuration equations $\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} U=\lambda(c, \theta) \nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}} I, i=1, \cdots, 5$, are satisfied, and the constant is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda(c, \theta) & =\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}=\frac{-3}{2 \sin ^{3} d_{34}}-\frac{m \cos \theta}{c \sin ^{3} d_{13}}=\frac{-3}{2 \sin ^{3} d_{34}}+\frac{3\left|\sin ^{3} 2 \theta\right|}{2 \sin ^{6} d_{13}} \\
& =\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{-8}{3 \sqrt{3}\left(1+3 c^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}\left(1-c^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}+\frac{\left|\sin ^{3} 2 \theta\right|}{\left(1-c^{2} \cos ^{2} \theta\right)^{3}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

which is zero on a one-dimensional manifold. Factually, it is homeomorphic to two open unit intervals. Thus generally, $\mathbf{q}(c, \theta)$ are ordinary central configurations. This remark completes the proof.

Moreover, if $(c, \theta) \in(-1,0) \times\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, then the masses $m_{3}, m_{4}, m_{5}$ are contained in the unit ball, $\bar{x}^{2}+\bar{y}^{2}+\bar{w}^{2} \leq 1$, and the masses $m_{1}, m_{2}$ are outside, see Figure 2. This happens because

$$
\bar{w}_{1}=\frac{w_{1}}{1-z_{1}}=\frac{\sin \theta}{1-\cos \theta}>1, \bar{x}_{3}^{2}+\bar{y}_{3}^{2}=\left(\frac{x_{3}}{1-z_{3}}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{y_{3}}{1-z_{3}}\right)^{2}=\frac{1+c}{(1-c)}<1
$$

Similarly, if $(c, \theta) \in(0,1) \times\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)$, then masses $m_{3}, m_{4}, m_{5}$ are outside, but the masses $m_{1}, m_{2}$ are inside the ball.

Obviously, we can still obtain central configurations if we substitute the equilateral triangle by a regular $n$-gon with equal masses, and generally they are ordinary ones.
