# Double pyramidal central configurations of Newtonian $(N+2)$-body problem 

## A B STR A C T

For double pyramidal central configurations of the Newtonian $(N+2)$-body problem where $N$ point particles are positioned at the vertices of a regular $N$-polygon, and the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point-particles are positioned the opposite sides of the plane containing the polygon, and the two point particles are located on a line, which is perpendicular to the regular $N$-polygon, we obtain some properties of the positions, masses and values of $N$ of these $N+2$ point-particles

## Introduction and main result

The classical Newtonian $n$-body problem concerns the motion of $n$ point particles with masses $m_{j} \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$and positions $q_{j} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ with $j=1,2, \ldots, n$ where the equations of motion for the $n$ positive masses can be described by Newton's second law of classical mechanics and Newton's universal gravitation law:

$$
m_{j} \ddot{q}_{j}=\frac{\partial U(q)}{\partial q_{j}}, \quad q=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{n}\right) \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{3}\right)^{n}, \quad j=1, \ldots, n
$$

with force function $U(q)=\sum_{1 \leq j<k \leq n} m_{j} m_{k} /\left|q_{j}-q_{k}\right|$.
When $n=2$, system (1) has well-known closed form solutions given in terms of elementary functions. For the case of $n=3$, Hilbert  regarded it as a good mathematical proble - the simplicity of its statement belies the complexity of its solutions - and remains notoriously resistent to solution. For the case $n>3$, the force of gravitation between the $n$ point particles becomes increasingly complicated and difficult to handle . There is then considerable focus on particular solutions and the instructive value they may possess.

In order to avoid collisions, we consider the configuration space
$\Delta=\bigcup_{1 \leq k \neq s \leq n} \Delta_{k, s}=\left\{x=\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{3}\right)^{n} \mid x_{k} \neq x_{s}, 1 \leq k \neq s \leq n\right\}$.
A configuration of the Newtonian $n$-body problem is a central configuration if the acceleration of each point particle is proportional to its position relative to the inertial barycentric system. To be precise, the definition of a central configuration can be stated in the following manner :

Definition 1. A configuration $q=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{n}\right) \in \Delta$ is a central configuration at some instant if there exists a constant $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ such that

$$
\sum_{\substack{s \leq n \\ 1 \leq s \leq n}} \frac{m_{s} m_{j}\left(q_{s}-q_{j}\right)}{\left|q_{s}-q_{j}\right|^{3}}=-\lambda m_{j}\left(q_{j}-x_{0}\right), \quad j=1,2, \ldots, n
$$

where the barycenter of masses is given by $x_{0}=\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq n} m_{j}\right.$ $\left.q_{j}\right) /\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq n} m_{j}\right)$.

Among the particular types of solutions for Newtonian $n$-body problem, an interesting class is formed by the homographic solution. It is well-known that central configurations and homographic solutions are linked by the Laplace theorem . The links between collapse and parabolic orbits with central configurations is a fruitful relationship . These are just a few reasons which promote the study of central configurations in the broader research of Newtonian $n$-body problem. The study of central configurations for Newtonian $n$-body problem date back to the early classical work of Euler, and it is the discovery of the well-known collinear central configuration which often bears his name . For the planar non-collinear central configuration with $n=3$, there is only one kind of central configuration - the Lagrange equilateral-triangle central configuration . It is important to note that in this configuration, the masses of the three point particles which lie at the vertices of the regular 3-polygon may not be equal to each other (see Fig. 1); in contrast, for the planar non-collinear central configuration with $n \geq 4$, if the $n$ point particles lie at the vertices of a regular $n$-polygon (see Fig. 2), then the $n$ masses must all be equal .


Fig. 1. Planar 3-body problem.


Fig. 2. Planar $N$-body problem $(N \geq 4)$.


Fig. 3. Spatial 4-body problem.

For more results on planar non-collinear central configurations with different geometrical shapes for $n \geq 4$, we refer the interested reader to $[10-14]$.

The focus of the present paper is on a restricted class of spatial central configurations. Before recalling previous works which are relevant for the present development, we introduce the definitions of pyramidal central configurations and double pyramidal central configurations (see $$ ).

Definition 2. A central configuration of $N+1$ point particles, $N$ of which are coplanar and the $(N+1)$-th is not contained in the plane, is called a pyramidal central configuration; equivalently, we will say that the central configuration has the shape of a pyramid.


Fig. 4. Spatial 5-body problem.


Fig. 5. Spatial $(N+1)$-body problem.


Fig. 6. Spatial $(N+2)$-body problem.

Definition 3. A central configuration of $N+2$ point-particles, $N$ of which are coplanar and the remaining two point particles are above and below the plane, is called a double pyramidal central configuration.

For the spatial Newtonian four-body $(n=4)$ problem, the regular tetrahedron (see Fig. 3) is the unique spatial central configuration . We note that it is indeed a pyramidal central configuration, and the three masses of the vertices of the equilateral-triangle base may not be equal to each other. For a pyramidal central configuration of the spatial Newtonian five-body $(n=5)$ problem with a square base, Fayçal  proved that the masses on the vertices of the square base must all be equal (see Fig. 4). For pyramidal central configurations of the Newtonian $n$-body $(n=N+1 \geq 5)$ problem with $N$ point particles at the vertices of a regular $N$-polygon base (see Fig. 5), Ouyang, Xie and Zhang  proved that the $N$ point particles located at the vertices of the regular $N$-polygon must all have equal masses. For the Newtonian $(N+2)$-body problem with $n=N+2 \geq 5$, Zhang and Zhou  obtained the existence of double pyramidal central configurations where $N$ point particles are located at the vertices of a regular $N$-polygon, and with the remaining two point particles positioned outside the plane containing the polygon (see Fig. 6). For more details in this direction, we refer the interested reader to [20-24].

Note that in , Corbera and Llibre investigated double pyramidal central configurations where the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles were positioned on the same side of the plane containing a regular $N$-polygon, and they showed that the masses of the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles may differ, but any of the results in  is based on the assumption that the two point particles located on a line $\bar{L}$ perpendicular to the regular $N$-polygon, but the vertical line $\bar{L}$ passes through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon.

We also note that for the double pyramidal central configurations where the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles being positioned on opposite sides of the plane containing a regular $N$-polygon, and the two point particles located on a line $\bar{L}$, which is perpendicular to the regular $N$-polygon: Zhang and Zhou  obtained that the $N$ point particles located at the vertices of the regular $N$-polygon have equal masses, but made additional assumptions that the barycenter of masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{N+2}$ aligns with the geometrical center of the regular $N$ polygon, the vertical line $\bar{L}$ passes through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, and the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles have equal masses, and the two point particle are positioned respect to the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon.

Now, in this paper we investigate some properties of double pyramidal central configurations in which the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles are positioned on opposite sides of the plane containing the regular $N$-polygon, with the two point particles located on a line perpendicular to the regular $N$-polygon (see Fig. 6). The corresponding result is described as the following.

Theorem 1. For the double pyramidal central configurations of the spatial Newtonian ( $N+2$ )-body $(N \geq 3)$ problem with $N$ point particles at the vertices of a regular $N$-polygon, and the remaining two point particles being positioned on opposite sides of the plane containing the regular $N$-polygon (see Fig. 6), if the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles are located on a line $\bar{L}$, which is perpendicular to the regular $N$-polygon, then we have:
(1) when the line $\bar{L}$ does not pass through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, then the $(N+1)$-th point particle and $(N+2)$-th point particle have equal masses;
(2) when the line $\bar{L}$ passes through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, then the $N$ point particles located at the vertices of the regular $N$-polygon have equal masses;
(3) when the line $\bar{L}$ passes through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, and the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles are positioned respect to the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, then either $3 \leq N \leq 472$, or the barycenter of masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{N+2}$ aligns with the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon.

Remark 1. Different from , in Theorem 1(1), we study double pyramidal central configurations where the vertical line $\bar{L}$ does not pass through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, and we find that the masses of the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point-particles must be equal, which is different from .

Remark 2. Contrast to , in Theorem 1(2), we also obtain that the masses of the $N$ point particles positioned at the vertices of the regular $N$-polygon are all equal, but we only need the assumption that the vertical line $\bar{L}$ passes through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon. Moreover, in the case where the vertical line $\bar{L}$ passes through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, Theorem 1(3) shows that if with the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles are positioned respect to the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, and the barycenter of masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{N+2}$ does not align with the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, then $3 \leq N \leq 472$.

# Some useful lemmas 

In order to prove Theorem 1, we introduce the definition of circulant matrix as follows.

Definition 4 ([25, Pages 65-66]). A matrix $B=\left(b_{k, i}\right)_{N \times N}(1 \leq k, j \leq$ $N, N \geq 4)$ is circulant if $b_{k, j}=b_{k-1, j-1}$, where $b_{k, 0}=b_{k, N}$ and $b_{0, j}=b_{N, j}$.

Let us consider the circulant matrix $B$ with
$b_{n, j}= \begin{cases}\frac{1-\rho_{j-1}}{\left(1-\rho_{j-1}\right)^{2}}, & k \neq j, \\ 0, & k=j,\end{cases}$ and $\rho_{k-j}=e^{i \frac{2(\rho-\mu)}{N}}=\cos \frac{2(k-j) \pi}{N}+i \sin \frac{2(k-j) \pi}{N}$

Then we list some properties of the circulant matrix $B$.
Lemma 1 (). The circulant matrix $B$ has the same form of the eigenvalues $\lambda_{j}$ and the corresponding eigenvectors $\xi_{j}$, i.e.
$\lambda_{j}=\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N} b_{1, k} \rho_{j-1}^{k-1}, \quad \xi_{j}=\left(\rho_{j-1}, \rho_{j-1}^{2}, \ldots, \rho_{j-1}^{N}\right)^{T}, j=1,2, \ldots, N$,
where $\rho_{j-1}=e^{i[2(j-1) \pi / N]}=\cos [2(j-1) \pi / N]+i \sin [2(j-1) \pi / N]$.
Lemma 2 (). The eigenvalues of the circulant matrix $B$ have the property that for any $N \geq 4$, we have $\lambda_{j}>0$ except that $\lambda_{\frac{N+1}{2}}=0$ for odd $N$.

Lemma 3 ([20, Proposition 2.2]). The eigenvectors $\xi_{j}(j=1,2, \ldots, N)$ of the circulant matrix $B$ constitute a basis for $\mathbb{C}^{N}$.

Lemma 4 (). For any integer $j, k \in\{1,2, \ldots, N\}$, let $\left(\xi_{j}\right)^{T}$ be the conjugate transpose of $\xi_{j}$, then
$\left(\xi_{j}\right)^{T} \xi_{k}= \begin{cases}0, & j \neq k, \\ N, & j=k,\end{cases} \quad\left(\rho_{-1}, \rho_{-2}, \ldots, \rho_{-N}\right)\left(\xi_{N}\right)=N$.
To prove Theorem 1
Since the distance is translation invariant, without loss of generality, in the proof of Theorem 1, we choose the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon as the origin of our coordinate system.

## To prove Theorem 1(1)

By (2), the $N+2$ point particles form a central configuration if and only if

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{\substack{\lambda \leq k \leq N \\
\left\lvert\, \lambda_{k-2, N}\right.}} \frac{\sum^{-q_{k-1}}}{\left(q_{k}-q_{k}\right)^{2}} m_{j} m_{k}+\frac{\sum_{k+1}-\alpha_{k}}{\left(q_{N+1}-q_{k}\right)^{2}} m_{N+1} m_{k}+\frac{\sum_{k+2}-\alpha_{k}}{\left(q_{N+2}-q_{k}\right)^{2}} m_{N+2} m_{k} \\
& =-\lambda m_{k}\left(q_{k}-x_{0}\right), \\
& k=1,2, \ldots, N, \\
& \sum_{\left\{k \geq 2, N\right.} \frac{\sum^{-q_{N+1}}}{\left(q_{k}-q_{N+1}\right)^{2}} m_{j} m_{N+1}+\frac{\sum_{N+2}-\alpha_{N+1}}{\left(q_{N+2}-q_{N+1}\right)^{2}} m_{N+2} m_{N+1} \\
& =-\lambda m_{N+1}\left(q_{N+1}-x_{0}\right), \\
& \sum_{k \geq 2, N} \frac{\sum^{-q_{N+1}}}{\left(q_{k}-q_{N+1}\right)^{2}} m_{j} m_{N+2}+\frac{\sum_{N+2}-\alpha_{N+1}}{\left(q_{N+1}-q_{N+2}\right)^{2}} m_{N+3} m_{N+2}
\end{aligned}
$$

where the barycenter of $N+2$ point particles is

$$
x_{0}=\frac{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} q_{k}}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}
$$

Employing the assumption that $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles are located on a line $\bar{L}$, which is perpendicular to the regular $N$-polygon, we can assume that

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
q_{k}=\left(\rho_{k}, 0\right)=\left(e^{\frac{2 k \pi}{N}}, 0\right)=\left(\cos \frac{2 k \pi}{N}+i \sin \frac{2 k \pi}{N}, 0\right), \quad k=1, \ldots, N \\
q_{N+1}=\left(a_{1} e^{i \pi}, h_{N+1}\right)=\left(a_{1} \cos \alpha+\left(a_{1} \sin \alpha, h_{N+1}\right)\right. \\
a_{1}>0, \quad 0 \leq \alpha<2 \pi, \quad h_{N+1}>0 \\
q_{N+2}=\left(a_{1} e^{i \pi}, h_{N+2}\right)=\left(a_{1} \cos \alpha+\left(a_{1} \sin \alpha, h_{N+2}\right)\right. \\
h_{N+2}<0
\end{array}\right.
$$

For simplicity, we use $D_{s, j}$ to denote the mutual distance between $q_{s}$ and $q_{j}$ with $s, j \in\{1,2, \ldots, N, N+1, N+2\}$. Then for the third component of the position coordinate, it follows from (5)-(7) that

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{m_{N+1} h_{N+1}}{D_{N+1, j}^{2}}+\frac{m_{N+2} h_{N+2}}{D_{N+2, j}^{2}}=\lambda \frac{m_{N+1} h_{N+2}+m_{N+2} h_{N+2}}{m_{k}}, \quad j=1,2, \ldots, N \\
-\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{h_{N+1}}{D_{N+1, j}^{2}} m_{j} m_{N+1}+\frac{h_{N+2}-h_{N+1}}{D_{N+2, N+1}^{2}} m_{N+2} m_{N+1} \\
\quad=-\lambda m_{N+1}\left(h_{N+1}-\frac{m_{N+1} h_{N+1}+m_{N+2} h_{N+2}}{m_{k}}\right) \\
-\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{h_{N+2}}{D_{N+2, j}^{2}} m_{j} m_{N+2}+\frac{h_{N+1}-h_{N+2}}{D_{N+2, N+1}^{2}} m_{N+1} m_{N+2} \\
\quad=-\lambda m_{N+2}\left(h_{N+2}-\frac{m_{N+1} h_{N+1}+m_{N+2} h_{N+2}}{m_{k}}\right)
\end{array}\right.
$$

Notice that the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles are located on a line, which is perpendicular to the regular $N$-polygon, we can assume that $m_{N+2} h_{N+2}=-s m_{N+1} h_{N+1}$ for some $s>0$. Employing (8), we have

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{1}{D_{N+1, j}^{2}}=\frac{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}{m_{k}}+\frac{1}{D_{N+2, j}^{2}}, \quad j=1,2, \ldots, N \\
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{m_{j}}{D_{N+1, j}^{2}}+\frac{s m_{N+1}}{D_{N+2, N+1}^{2}}+\frac{m_{N+2}}{D_{N+2, N+1}^{2}}=\lambda-\frac{j(1-s) m_{N+1}}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}} \\
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{s m_{j}}{D_{N+2, j}^{2}}+\frac{m_{N+2}}{D_{N+2, N+1}^{2}}+\frac{s m_{N+1}}{D_{N+2, N+1}^{2}}=\lambda s+\frac{j(1-s) m_{N+1}}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}
\end{array}\right.
$$

Assuming that

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{1}{D_{N+1, k}^{2}}=\max \left\{\frac{1}{D_{N+1,1}^{2}} \cdot \frac{1}{D_{N+1,2}^{2}}, \ldots \cdot \frac{1}{D_{N+1, N}^{2}}\right\}\right. \\
\left\{\frac{1}{D_{N+1, k}^{2}}=\min \left\{\frac{1}{D_{N+1,1}^{2}} \cdot \frac{1}{D_{N+1,2}^{2}}, \ldots \cdot \frac{1}{D_{N+1, N}^{2}}\right\}\right.
\end{array}\right.
$$

and in the following, we divide the proof of Theorem 1(1) into 3 cases.
Case (i): $s>1$. Notice that the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles are located on a line $\bar{L}$, which is perpendicular to the regular $N$-polygon, and the line $\bar{L}$ does not pass through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, then for Case (i), it suffices to prove that when $1 / D_{N+1,1}^{2}, 1 / D_{N+1,2}^{2} \ldots$ and $1 / D_{N+1, N}^{2}$ are not all equal, Theorem 1(1) holds, and we will prove that when there exists an integer $l \in\{1,2, \ldots, N\}$ such that $1 / D_{N+1, l}^{2}<1 / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$, Theorem 1(1) holds.

In fact, since $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, it is easy to see that one of the three inequalities must hold: $\lambda=\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}, \lambda<\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$ and $\lambda>\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$.

Firstly, if $\lambda=\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$, then for any $j \in\{1,2, \ldots, N\}$, by the first part of (10), we have $\lambda \geq \sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, j}^{2}$. Combining the first equation of (9) and $s>1$, there is $1 / D_{N+2, j}^{2} \leq 1 / D_{N+1, j}^{2}$ with $j=1,2, \ldots, N$.

Notice that there exists an integer $l \in\{1,2, \ldots, N\}$ such that $1 / D_{N+1, l}^{2}<1 / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$, we conclude $\lambda \geq \sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, l}^{2}$, then
with the help of the first equation (9) with $j=l$, there is $1 / D_{N+2, l}^{2}<$ $1 / D_{N+1, l}^{2}$.

Employing $1 / D_{N+2, j}^{2} \leq 1 / D_{N+1, j}^{2}$ with $j=1,2, \ldots, N$ and $1 / D_{N+2, l}^{2}<$ $1 / D_{N+1, l}^{2}$, we use the third equation of (9) to minus the second equation of (9), then

$$
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{(s-1) m_{j}}{D_{N+2, j}^{2}}>\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{s m_{j}}{D_{N+2, j}^{2}}-\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{m_{j}}{D_{N+1, j}^{2}}=\frac{\lambda(s-1) \sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} m_{j}}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}
$$

Moreover, by the first equation of (9) and the first part of (10), we have

$$
\frac{1}{D_{N+2, k}^{2}}=\max \left\{\frac{1}{D_{N+2,1}^{2}} \cdot \frac{1}{D_{N+2,2}^{2}}, \ldots \cdot \frac{1}{D_{N+2, N}^{2}}\right\}
$$

Thanks to $s>1$, (11) and (12), we have

$$
\frac{\lambda(s-1) \sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} m_{j}}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}<\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{(s-1) m_{j}}{D_{N+2, j}^{2}} \leq \frac{(s-1) \sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} m_{j}}{D_{N+2, k}^{2}}
$$

which implies that $\lambda<\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+2, k}^{2}<\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$, and it contradicts with $\lambda=\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$. Therefore, for Case (i), $\lambda=\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$ is impossible.

Secondly, if $\lambda<\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$, then by $1-s<0$ and the first equation of (9), we have $D_{N+2, k}>D_{N+1, k}$. Combining (7) and

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
D_{N+1, k}=\sqrt{\left(a_{1} \cos \alpha-\cos \frac{2 k \pi}{N}\right)^{2}+\left(a_{1} \sin \alpha-\sin \frac{2 k \pi}{N}\right)^{2}+h_{N+1}^{2}} \\
D_{N+2, k}=\sqrt{\left(a_{1} \cos \alpha-\cos \frac{2 k \pi}{N}\right)^{2}+\left(a_{1} \sin \alpha-\sin \frac{2 k \pi}{N}\right)^{2}+h_{N+2}^{2}}
\end{array}\right.
$$

one computes that $h_{N+2}^{2}>h_{N+1}^{2}$, and then $D_{N+2, j}>D_{N+1, j}$ with $j=1,2, \ldots, N$.

By the second part of (10) and the first equation of (9) with $j=\bar{k}$, we have

$$
\frac{1}{D_{N+2, k}^{2}}=\min \left\{\frac{1}{D_{N+2,1}^{2}} \cdot \frac{1}{D_{N+2,2}^{2}}, \ldots \cdot \frac{1}{D_{N+2, N}^{2}}\right\}
$$

On the one hand, when $\lambda<\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$, if $\lambda \geq$ $\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$, then combining the first equation of (9) and $1-s<0$, we have $D_{N+2, k} \leq D_{N+1, k}^{2}$. Then thanks to (13), we have $h_{N+2}^{2} \leq h_{N+1}^{2}$, which contradicts with $h_{N+2}^{2}>h_{N+1}^{2}$. So $\lambda<$ $\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$. From the first equation of (9) with $j=\bar{k}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(\frac{1}{D_{N+1, k}^{2}}-\frac{\lambda}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}\right) m_{N+1} h_{N+1} \\
& \quad=\left(\frac{\lambda}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}-\frac{1}{D_{N+2, k}^{2}}\right) m_{N+2} h_{N+2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Inserting $h_{N+1}>0, h_{N+2}<0$ and $\lambda<\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}$ into (15), we see that when $\lambda<\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{2}: \lambda<\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+2, k}^{2}$.

On the other hand, by the second and third equations of (8), we have

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{-h_{N+1}}{D_{N+1, j}^{2}} m_{j} m_{N+1}+\frac{h_{N+2}-h_{N+1}}{D_{N+2, N+1}^{2}} m_{N+2} m_{N+1} \\
\quad=-\lambda m_{N+1}\left(h_{N+1}-\frac{m_{N+1} h_{N+1}+m_{N+2} h_{N+2}}{N^{2}} m_{k}\right) \\
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{-h_{N+2}}{D_{N+2, j}^{2}} m_{j} m_{N+2}-\frac{h_{N+1}-h_{N+2}}{D_{N+2, N+1}^{2}} m_{N+1} m_{N+2} \\
\quad=-\lambda m_{N+2}\left(h_{N+2}-\frac{m_{N+1} h_{N+2}+m_{N+2} h_{N+2}}{N^{2}} m_{k}\right)
\end{array}\right.
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& -\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N}\left\{\frac{h_{N+1}}{D_{N+1, j}^{3}} m_{j} m_{N+1}-\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N} \frac{h_{N+2}}{D_{N+2, j}^{3}} m_{j} m_{N+2}\right. \\
& \left.\quad=-\lambda\left(m_{N+1} h_{N+1}+m_{N+2} h_{N+2}\right) \frac{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N} m_{k}}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

Combining $D_{N+2, j}>D_{N+1, j}$ with $j=1,2, \ldots, N$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& -\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N}\left\{\frac{h_{N+1}}{D_{N+2, j}^{3}} m_{j} m_{N+1}+\frac{h_{N+2}}{D_{N+2, j}^{3}} m_{j} m_{N+2}\right\} \\
& \quad>-\lambda\left(m_{N+1} h_{N+1}+m_{N+2} h_{N+2}\right) \frac{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N} m_{k}}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}
\end{aligned}
$$

then using (14), one computes that $\lambda>\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+2, k}^{3}$, and it contradicts with $\lambda<\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+2, k}^{3}$. Hence, for Case (i), $\lambda<$ $\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{3}$ is impossible, too.

Thirdly, if $\lambda>\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, k}^{3}$, employing $1-s<0$ and the first equation of (9), we have $D_{N+2, k}<D_{N+1, k}$. Combining (7) and (13), we have $h_{N+2}^{3}<h_{N+1}^{2}$, and then $D_{N+2, j}<D_{N+1, j}$ with $j=1,2, \ldots, N$.

On the one hand, using the first equation of (8) with $j=\bar{k}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(\frac{1}{D_{N+1, \bar{k}}^{3}}-\frac{\lambda}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}\right) m_{N+1} h_{N+1} \\
& \quad=\left(\frac{\lambda}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}-\frac{1}{D_{N+2, \bar{k}}^{3}}\right) m_{N+2} h_{N+2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Inserting $h_{N+1}>0, h_{N+2}<0$ and $\lambda>\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, \bar{k}}^{3}$ into (17), we see that $\lambda>\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+2, \bar{k}}^{3}$.

On the other hand, employing the second and third equations of (8) and $D_{N+2, j}<D_{N+1, j}$ with $j=1,2, \ldots, N$, similar to obtain (16), we deduce that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& -\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N}\left\{\frac{h_{N+1}}{D_{N+2, j}^{3}} m_{j} m_{N+1}+\frac{h_{N+2}}{D_{N+2, j}^{3}} m_{j} m_{N+2}\right\} \\
& \quad<-\lambda\left(m_{N+1} h_{N+1}+m_{N+2} h_{N+2}\right) \frac{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N} m_{k}}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}
\end{aligned}
$$

then using (12), we have $\lambda<\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+2, \bar{k}}^{3}$, and it contradicts with $\lambda>\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+2, \bar{k}}^{3}$. Therefore, for Case (i), $\lambda>$ $\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, \bar{k}}^{3}$ is impossible.

By now, we prove that for the double pyramidal central configurations of the Newtonian $(N+2)$-body problem, Case (i) cannot occur.

Case (ii): $0<s<1$. For the case of $0<s<1$, by the second part of (10), it suffices to prove that when there exists an integer $d \in\{1,2, \ldots, N\}$ such that $1 / D_{N+1, d}^{3}>1 / D_{N+1, \bar{k}}^{3}$, Theorem 1(1) holds.

Since $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, it is easy to see that one of the three inequalities must hold: $\lambda=\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, \bar{k}}^{3}, \lambda<\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, \bar{k}}^{3}$ and $\lambda>\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, \bar{k}}^{3}$. The following proof of Case (ii) is similar to the procedure of Case (i), and the only difference is that if $\lambda<$ $\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, \bar{k}}^{3}$, we use

$$
\begin{aligned}
& -\sum_{1 \leq j \leq N}\left\{\frac{h_{N+1}}{D_{N+1, j}^{3}} m_{j} m_{N+1}+\frac{h_{N+2}}{D_{N+1, j}^{3}} m_{j} m_{N+2}\right\} \\
& \quad>-\lambda\left(m_{N+1} h_{N+1}+m_{N+2} h_{N+2}\right) \frac{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N} m_{k}}{\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<s<1$ and $D_{N+2, j}<D_{N+1, j}$ with $j=1,2, \ldots, N$ to substitute (16), thus $\lambda>\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, \bar{k}}^{3}$, which contradicts with $\lambda<\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k} / D_{N+1, \bar{k}}^{3}$, and then we can conclude that Case (ii) cannot happen, too.

Case (iii): $s=1$.
From $s=1$ and the first equation of (9), we see that $D_{N+1, j}=D_{N+2, j}$ with $j=1,2, \ldots, N$. Combining the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles are located on a line $\bar{L}$, which is perpendicular to the regular $N$-polygon, then $h_{N+1}^{2}=h_{N+2}^{2}$. Combining with $h_{N+1}>0$ and $h_{N+2}<0$, we have $h_{N+2}=-h_{N+1}$. Moreover, by $s=1, h_{N+2}=-h_{N+1}$ and $m_{N+2} h_{N+2}=-s m_{N+1} h_{N+1}=-m_{N+1} h_{N+1}$, then when $s=1, m_{N+1}=$ $m_{N+2}$.

## To prove Theorem 1(2)

Notice that the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles are located on a line $\bar{L}$, which is perpendicular to the regular $N$-polygon, and the line $\bar{L}$ passes through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, there is $D_{N+1,1}=D_{N+1,2}=-\cdots=D_{N+1, N}$ and $D_{N+2,1}=D_{N+2,2}=-\cdots=$ $D_{N+2, N}$. The rest of the proof of Theorem 1(2) is divided into 2 cases.

Case 1: $N \geq 4$. By $D_{N+1,1}=D_{N+1,2}=\cdots=D_{N+1, N}$ and $D_{N+2,1}=$ $D_{N+2,2}=\cdots=D_{N+2, N}$, then using (6) and (7), we can assume that

Then by (18), for any $j, k \in\{1,2, \ldots, N\}$, we have $\rho_{j}-\rho_{k}=\left(e^{i \frac{2 k \pi}{N}}, 0\right)$ $\left(e^{i \frac{2 k \pi}{N}}, 0\right)=e^{i \frac{2 k \pi}{N}}\left(e^{i \frac{2 k \pi}{N}, \alpha}, 0\right)=\rho_{k}\left(1-\rho_{j-k}\right)$. Then inserting (18) into the first part of (5), for any $k \in\{1,2, \ldots, N\}$, we have

$$
\sum_{j \neq k} \frac{1-\rho_{j-k}}{\left(1-\rho_{j-k}\right)^{3}} m_{j}=\left[\lambda-\left(\frac{m_{N+1}}{D_{N+1,1}^{3}}+\frac{m_{N+2}}{D_{N+2,1}^{3}}\right)\right]-\left(\lambda \bar{q}_{0}\right) \rho_{-k}
$$

Then, it follows from (3), (4) and (19) that (see [26, Page 6, (3.13)])

$$
\begin{aligned}
& B\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{N}\right)^{T} \\
= & {\left[\lambda-\left(m_{N+1}+m_{N+2}\right)\right](1,1, \ldots, 1)^{T}-\left(\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N} m_{k} \rho_{k}\right)\left(\rho_{-1}, \rho_{-1}^{2}, \ldots, \rho_{-1}^{N}\right)^{T} } \\
= & {\left[\lambda-\left(m_{N+1}+m_{N+2}\right)\right] \xi_{j}-\left(\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N} m_{k} \rho_{k}\right) \xi_{N} }
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $N \geq 4$, we can use Lemmas 1-4 and argue in a manner similar to the procedure of [26, Pages 6-7] to prove that $m_{1}=m_{2}=\cdots=m_{N}$.

Case 2: $N=3$. Thanks to (7), we can assume that

By the first part of (5), we have

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{\left(q_{1}-q_{1}\right) m_{2}}{D_{1,1}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{2}-q_{2}\right) m_{1}}{D_{1,1}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{3}-q_{3}\right) m_{4}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{3}-q_{3}\right) m_{3}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}=-\lambda\left(q_{1}-x_{0}\right) \\
\frac{\left(q_{1}-q_{1}\right) m_{1}}{D_{1,2}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{2}-q_{2}\right) m_{1}}{D_{1,2}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{3}-q_{3}\right) m_{4}}{D_{2,2}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{3}-q_{3}\right) m_{3}}{D_{2,2}^{3}}=-\lambda\left(q_{2}-x_{0}\right) \\
\frac{\left(q_{1}-q_{1}\right) m_{1}}{D_{1,3}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{2}-q_{2}\right) m_{2}}{D_{2,3}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{3}-q_{3}\right) m_{4}}{D_{2,3}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{3}-q_{3}\right) m_{3}}{D_{3,3}^{3}}=-\lambda\left(q_{3}-x_{0}\right)
\end{array}\right.
$$



Fig. 7. Spatial 5-body problem $(N=3)$.

Since $N=3, D_{4,1}=D_{4,2}=D_{4,3}$ and $D_{5,1}=D_{5,2}=D_{5,3}$. Then by (21) and $D_{2,1}=D_{1,2}=D_{5,1}=D_{1,3}=D_{5,2}=D_{2,3}$, one computes that

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{\left(q_{2}-q_{1}\right) m_{2}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{2}-q_{1}\right) m_{1}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{4}-q_{3}\right) m_{4}}{D_{4,1}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{2}-q_{1}\right) m_{3}}{D_{4,1}^{3}}=-\lambda q_{1}+\lambda x_{0} \\
\frac{\left(q_{1}-q_{2}\right) m_{1}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{2}-q_{1}\right) m_{2}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{2}-q_{2}\right) m_{4}}{D_{4,1}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{2}-q_{3}\right) m_{5}}{D_{4,1}^{3}}=-\lambda q_{2}+\lambda x_{0} \\
\frac{\left(q_{1}-q_{2}\right) m_{1}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{2}-q_{3}\right) m_{2}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{4}-q_{3}\right) m_{4}}{D_{4,1}^{3}}+\frac{\left(q_{2}-q_{3}\right) m_{3}}{D_{4,1}^{3}}=-\lambda q_{3}+\lambda x_{0}
\end{array}\right.
$$

Summing over the three equations of (22), and combining $q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}=$ $(0,0,0)$, we have

$$
\frac{3 m_{1} q_{1}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}+\frac{3 m_{2} q_{2}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}+\frac{3 m_{3} q_{3}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}+\frac{3 m_{4} q_{4}}{D_{4,1}^{3}}+\frac{3 m_{5} q_{5}}{D_{5,1}^{3}}=3 \lambda x_{0}
$$

If we note that $N=3$, then

$$
q_{1}=\left(-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 0\right), \quad q_{2}=\left(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 0\right), \quad q_{3}=(1,0,0)
$$

Thus for the second component of the position coordinate, it follows from (20), (23) and the barycenter $x_{0}=\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j} q_{j}\right) /\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j}\right)$ that

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} m_{1}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} m_{2}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}=\lambda \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} m_{1}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} m_{2}}{\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j}}
$$

Hence $\lambda=\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j}\right) / D_{2,1}^{3}$ or $m_{1}=m_{2}$. Next, we will show that $\lambda=$ $\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j}\right) / D_{2,1}^{3}$ is impossible, and we assume that $\lambda=$ $\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j}\right) / D_{2,1}^{3}$.

Let the coordinate of barycenter $x_{0}$ be $\left(x_{0}^{(1)}, x_{0}^{(2)}, x_{0}^{(3)}\right)$. Inserting (24), $q_{4}=\left(0,0, h_{4}\right), q_{5}=\left(0,0, h_{5}\right)$ and $m_{4}=m_{5}$ (here $m_{N+1}=m_{N+2}$ with $N=3$ ) into the first two equations of (22), then for the second component of the position coordinate, one computes that

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{3 m_{3}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}-\frac{m_{3}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}-\frac{m_{4}}{D_{4,1}^{3}}-\frac{m_{5}}{D_{5,1}^{3}}=-\lambda+\lambda x_{0}^{(2)} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\
\frac{2 m_{1}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}-\frac{m_{5}}{D_{5,1}^{3}}+\frac{m_{4}}{D_{5,1}^{3}}+\frac{m_{5}}{D_{5,1}^{3}}=\lambda+\lambda x_{0}^{(2)} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
\end{array}\right.
$$

which implies that

$$
\frac{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}{D_{2,1}^{3}} \times \frac{m_{4}}{D_{4,1}^{3}}+\frac{m_{5}}{D_{5,1}^{3}}=\lambda
$$

In view of (25) and $\lambda=\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j}\right) / D_{2,1}^{3}$, then

$$
\frac{m_{4}}{D_{4,1}^{3}}+\frac{m_{5}}{D_{5,1}^{3}}=\frac{m_{4}+m_{5}}{D_{5,1}^{3}}
$$

Moreover, inserting $\lambda=\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j}\right) / D_{2,1}^{3}$ into the first equation of (9) with $N=3$ and $j=1$, there is

$$
\frac{1}{D_{4,1}^{3}}-\frac{s}{D_{5,1}^{3}}=\frac{1-s}{D_{5,1}^{3}}
$$

It follows from $s>0$, (26) and (27) that

$$
\frac{1}{D_{4,1}^{3}}\left[1-(1-s) \frac{m_{4}}{m_{4}+m_{5}}\right]=\frac{1}{D_{5,1}^{3}}\left[1-(1-s) \frac{m_{4}}{m_{4}+m_{5}}\right]
$$

Then by $s>0$, we have $D_{4,1}=D_{5,1}$. Combining (20) with $N=3$, we have $h_{5}=-h_{4}$. Moreover, employing $D_{4,1}=D_{5,1}$, (25) and $D_{2,1}=D_{1,1}$, we see $D_{2,1}=D_{3,1}=D_{4,1}=D_{5,1}$. Then for the second component of the position coordinate, by $m_{4}=m_{5}$, and the second and third parts of (5) with $N=3$, we have

$$
\frac{-2 h_{4} m_{4}\left(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}\right)}{D_{4,1}^{3}}+\frac{-4 h_{4} m_{4}^{2}}{D_{5,4}^{3}}=-2 \lambda m_{4} h_{4}
$$

Thus combining $h_{4}>0, \lambda=\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j}\right) / D_{2,1}^{3}$ and $D_{2,1}=D_{4,1}$, we have $\lambda=\left(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}\right) / D_{4,1}^{3}+(2 m_{4}) / D_{5,4}^{3}$, which implies that $D_{5,4}=D_{4,1}(=:$ $y)$. Thus $\left|q_{1}-O\right|=(y / 2) / \sin (\pi / 3)=\sqrt{3} \gamma / 3$ (see Fig. 7). Moreover, by the second and third parts of (20) with $N=3$,
$D_{5,4}=\left|q_{5}-q_{4}\right|=2\left|q_{4}-O\right|=2 \sqrt{y^{2}-\left(\frac{\sqrt{3} \gamma}{3}\right)^{2}}=\frac{2 \sqrt{6} \gamma}{3}>y=D_{5,4}$.
which is a contradiction. Hence $\lambda=\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j}\right) / D_{2,1}^{3}$ is impossible, and it must be that $m_{1}=m_{2}$.

Inserting $m_{1}=m_{2}, q_{4}=\left(0,0, h_{4}\right), q_{5}=\left(0,0, h_{5}\right), h_{5}=-h_{4}$, (6) and (24) into (23), then for the first component of the position coordinate, we have

$$
\frac{m_{3}-m_{1}}{D_{2,1}^{3}}=\lambda \frac{m_{3}-m_{1}}{\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j}}
$$

Hence $\lambda=\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j}\right) / D_{2,1}^{3}$ or $m_{1}=m_{3}$. Combining $\lambda \neq$ $\left(\sum_{1 \leq j \leq 5} m_{j}\right) / D_{2,1}^{3}$, and thus we conclude that $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}$.

By analyzing for $N \geq 4$ and $N=3$, we have $m_{1}=m_{2}=\cdots=m_{N}$

In this part, notice that the vertical line $\bar{L}$ passes through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, then all the assumptions of Theorem 1(2) are satisfied, so by Theorem 1(2), we have $m_{1}=m_{2}=$ $\cdots=m_{N}$. Therefore,

Then by (29), we have $f(N):=\sum_{j \leq j \leq N}\left(1-\rho_{j-k}\right) /\left(\left|1-\rho_{j-k}\right|^{3}\right)<N$ with $N \geq 3$. On the other hand, it follows from , $f(N) / N$ is increasing in $N$, and $f(472) \approx 0.99990875$ and $f(473) \approx 1.00024558$. So if $\lambda=\left(\sum_{1 \leq k \leq N+2} m_{k}\right) / D_{N+1,1}^{3}$, then $3 \leq N \leq 472$.

By now, we arrive at the conclusion that if the vertical line $L$ passes through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, and the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles are positioned respect to the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, then either $3 \leq N \leq 472$, or the barycenter $x_{0}=0$.

## Conclusions

For double pyramidal central configurations of the spatial Newtonian ( $N+2$ )-body problem where $N$ point particles are at the vertices of a regular $N$-polygon, and the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point-particles are positioned on opposite sides of the plane containing the polygon, and the two point particles are located on a line, which is perpendicular to the polygon, and the vertical line passes through the geometrical center of the regular $N$-polygon, Zhang-Zhou  investigated the existence of the double pyramidal central configurations. In this paper, we investigate the properties of double pyramidal central configurations that the $(N+1)$-th and $(N+2)$-th point particles are positioned on opposite sides of the plane containing the polygon and they are located on a line $L$, where $L$ passes or does not pass through the geometrical center of the polygon.

# ON THE EQUILATERAL PENTAGONAL CENTRAL CONFIGURATIONS 


#### Abstract

An equilateral pentagon is a polygon in the plane with five sides of equal length. In this paper we classify the central configurations of the 5 -body problem having the five bodies at the vertices of an equilateral pentagon with an axis of symmetry. We prove that there are two unique classes of such equilateral pentagons providing central configurations, one concave equilateral pentagon and one convex equilateral pentagon, the regular one. A key point of our proof is the use of rational parameterizations to transform the corresponding equations, which involve square roots, into polynomial equations.


## 1. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF THE RESULT

The Newtonian planar 5-body problem describes the dynamics of five point particles of positive masses $m_{i}$ at positions $\mathbf{q}_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ moving according to the Newton's laws under their mutual gravitational forces. The equations of motion of this 5 -body problem are

$$
m_{i} \ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{i}=-\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{5} G m_{i} m_{j} \frac{\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}, \quad 1 \leq i \leq 5
$$

where $r_{i j}=\left|\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}\right|$ is the mutual distances between the masses $m_{i}$ and $m_{j}$, and $G$ is the gravitational constant. We take conveniently the time unit so that $G=1$.

The configuration space is defined by

$$
\mathcal{E}=\left\{\mathbf{q}=\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{5}\right) \in\left(\mathbb{R}^{2}\right)^{5}: \mathbf{q}_{i} \neq \mathbf{q}_{j}, \quad i \neq j\right\}
$$

The configuration $\mathbf{q}=\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{5}\right)$ is called central if the position vector of each body with respect to the center of mass is proportional to the corresponding acceleration vector. In other words, if there exists a positive constant $\lambda$ such that

$$
\ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{i}=\lambda\left(\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{c}_{m}\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, 5
$$

where $\mathbf{c}_{m}=\left(m_{1} \mathbf{q}_{1}+\cdots+m_{5} \mathbf{q}_{5}\right) / M$ and $M=m_{1}+\cdots+m_{5}$, being $\mathbf{c}_{m}$ and $M$ the center of mass of the five bodies and the total mass, respectively. Hence a given configuration $\left(\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{5}\right) \in \mathcal{E}$ of the 5 -body problem with positive masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{5}$, is central if there exists a $\lambda$ such that $\left(\lambda, \mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{5}\right)$ is a solution of the system

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{5} m_{j} \frac{\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{q}_{j}}{r_{i j}^{3}}=\lambda\left(\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{c}_{m}\right), \quad 1 \leq i \leq 5
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    2010 Mathematics Subject Classification. 70F10 (70F15).
    Key words and phrases. Central configuration, 5-body problem, equilateral pentagon.

A central configuration is convex if no body belongs to the convex hull of the other four bodies; otherwise it is called concave. A planar central configuration is called a relative equilibrium when they become equilibrium solutions in a rotating coordinate system $$.

Since equations (1) are invariant under rotations, translations and dilations, when we consider the number of central configurations, this will be restricted to count the classes of central configurations modulo these mentioned transformations.

The central configurations are of special importance in Celestial Mechanics for several reasons. For instance, central configurations are the initial conditions for the homographic orbits of the $n$-body problem. Central configurations play an important role in the description of the topology of the integral manifolds in the $n$-body problem. Moreover, in the planar case the central configurations are initial positions for periodic solutions. For more information on this subject, recent advances and open questions, the reader is addressed to  and references therein.

In this paper we will investigate some central configurations of the 5 -body problem, for which there are few known results. The first results concerning this issue take us back decades ago to the work due to Williams , who settled necessary and sufficient conditions for any plane central configuration of five bodies. In what follows we offer a non-exhaustive list of some interesting works concerning this topic, which have been published more recently.

Albouy and Kaloshin  proved that for a choice of five positive masses in the complement of a codimension-two algebraic variety in the mass space, there are only a finite number of equivalence classes of central configurations of the Newtonian 5-body problem. In  Chen and Hsiao provided necessary conditions for strictly convex central configurations of the planar 5 -body problem.

In the last times the interest in stacked central configurations has grown a lot, that is, central configurations in which some subset of three or more masses also forms a central configuration. This concept was introduced by Hampton , who was arguably the first to find stacked central configurations in the 5 -body problem, where two bodies can be removed and the remaining three bodies are already in a central configuration. After, several papers have been published showing the existence of other stacked central configurations in the planar 5 -body problem; see, among others, , .

Other studies have focused on restricting the problem to a particular shape, in  it was proved that the unique co-circular central configuration in the planar 5 -body problem is the regular 5 -gon with equal masses, while in  was proved the existence of three families of planar central configurations where three bodies are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle and the other two bodies are on a perpendicular bisector. Later on in  was studied the central configuration in a symmetric 5 -body problem with three masses on an axis of symmetry and two other masses outside this axis, placed in symmetric positions. A complete classification of the isolated central configurations of the planar 5 -body problem with equal masses was given in . Recently in  were studied the central configurations of the planar 5 -body problem having four bodies at the vertices of a rhombus.



Figure 1. Pentagonal configurations: a convex one in the left hand picture and two different type of concave ones

For the reader's convenience, we summarize here some basic facts about the pentagon, which is a polygon with five sides and five angles. It is said that it is convex if all its vertices are pointing outwards, otherwise it is concave; see Figure 1. A pentagon with five sides of equal length is named equilateral. Moreover, a pentagon is called regular when all the sides are equal in length, and five angles are of equal measures. If the pentagon does not have equal side length and angle measure, then it is called irregular. The regular pentagon is unique, up to similarity transformations, because it is equilateral and its five angles are equal.

The goal in this paper is to characterize the equilateral pentagonal central configurations with an axis of symmetry for the planar 5 -body problem whose five positive masses are at the vertices of an equilateral pentagon.


Figure 2. The two equilateral pentagonal central configurations with an axis of symmetry of the 5 -body problem.

Then our main result is the following one, which will be proved in the next section.
Theorem 1. There are two classes of equilateral pentagonal central configuration having an axis of symmetry for the 5 -body problem.
(a) The convex regular pentagon with equal five masses, see Figure 2(a).
(b) The equilateral concave pentagon with the masses normalized, i.e. $\sum_{i=1}^{5} m_{i}=$ 1 , equal to $m_{1}=m_{2} \approx 0.0922539749, m_{3}=m_{4} \approx 0.3860948766$ and $m_{5} \approx$ 0.04330242730 . In Figure 2(b) we show a representative of its class where the bodies of masses $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are fixed at $(0,1 / 2)$ and $(0,-1 / 2)$, respectively. The other bodies of masses $m_{3}, m_{4}$ and $m_{5}$ are located at $\left(x_{3}, y_{3}\right),\left(-x_{3}, y_{3}\right)$ and

$\left(0, y_{5}\right)$, respectively, where $x_{3} \approx 0.5402091568, y_{3} \approx 0.9991912848$ and $y_{5} \approx$ 0.1576604970 . See Remark 2 for some comments of how these values are obtained.

Remark 2. From the proof of Theorem 1 and the results of Appendix B we obtain a value $t=t^{*} \approx 0.7332148086$ which is the smallest root of the quadratic polynomial $t^{2}-u^{*} t+1=0$, where $u=u^{*} \approx 2.0970716051$ is the unique root in the interval $[205 / 100,210 / 100]$ of the polynomial of degree 60 with integer coefficients, $R_{60}(u)$, given in Appendix B. This polynomial is constructed from a reciprocal polynomial of degree 120 and also with integer coefficients that appears in (10). Then $y_{5}=\left(1-\left(t^{*}\right)^{2}\right) /\left(4 t^{*}\right)$ and all the other values in the theorem, $x_{3}, y_{3}, m_{j}, j=1,2, \ldots, 5$, can be obtained from this $t^{*}$ by elementary computations: sums, subtractions, multiplications, divisions and square roots. Recall that, although we do not know the exact value of $u^{*}$, the classical use of Sturm sequences allows to obtain explicit intervals, with rational endpoints, containing $u^{*}$ and with arbitrarily small length.

At this stage the reader should be warned that there is a previous work by Perko and Walter , who showed that $n$ equal masses at the vertices of a regular polygon, for $n \geq 4$, forms a central configuration if and only if the masses are equal. Therefore it was known that the regular pentagon with equal masses is a central configuration for the 5 -body problem, but it was unknown that it is the unique equilateral convex pentagonal central configuration with an axis of symmetry.

One of the key points of our approach is the use of rational parameterizations to eliminate some of the square roots that appear in the equations governing the central configurations, converting in this way these equations into polynomial ones. Then these equations can be treated analytically by using some classical tools, like for instance the Sturm sequences or the computation of resultants.

# 2. Preliminaries 

Central configurations are invariant under composition of translations, rotations, and scaling through its center of mass, hence without loss of generality we can assume that the position of the masses $m_{i}>0$ for $i=1 \ldots, 5$ at the vertices of an equilateral pentagon with an axis of symmetry are $p_{k}=\left(x_{k}, y_{k}\right)$ for $k=1,2,3,4,5$, where $y_{1}=0$, $x_{2}=-x_{1}, y_{2}=0, x_{4}=-x_{3}, y_{4}=y_{3}$ and $x_{5}=0$. Note that we can assume that $x_{1}>0$, $x_{3}>0, y_{3}>0, y_{5}>0$ and $y_{3} \neq y_{5}$, because we want that the points $\left(x_{i}, y_{i}\right)$ be the vertices of a pentagon.

Next we will obtain the coordinates for the equilateral pentagon vertices. By a suitable scaling we may assume that $r_{12}=1$, so $x_{1}=1 / 2$. Now we substitute this value into the equation $r_{13}=1$, obtaining that $y_{3}^{2}=\left(3+4 x_{3}-4 x_{3}^{2}\right) / 4$. These values replaced in the equation $r_{35}=1$ provides $x_{3}$ in terms of $y_{5}$,

$$
x_{3}=\Psi^{ \pm}\left(y_{5}\right)=\frac{1}{4} \pm \frac{y_{5}}{2} \Phi\left(y_{5}\right), \quad \text { where } \quad \Phi(y)=\sqrt{\frac{15-4 y^{2}}{1+4 y^{2}}}
$$

Since we are interested in central configurations, with an axis of symmetry, modulus rotations and homothetic transformations, without loss of generality, we have the next result.

Proposition 3. Suppose that $\mathbf{q}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{5}$ form an equilateral pentagon, with $\mathbf{q}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{q}_{2}$ fixed on the $x$-axis and with the $y$-axis as an axis of symmetry. Then

$$
\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)=(0,1 / 2), \quad\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)=(-1 / 2,0), \quad\left(x_{3}, y_{3}\right), \quad\left(-x_{3}, y_{3}\right) \quad \text { and } \quad\left(0, y_{5}\right)
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { (a) either } x_{3}=\Psi^{+}\left(y_{5}\right)=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{y_{5}}{2} \Phi\left(y_{5}\right), \quad y_{3}=\frac{y_{5}}{2}+\frac{1}{4} \Phi\left(y_{5}\right), \quad \text { and } \quad y_{5} \in(0, \sqrt{15} / 2) \\
& \text { (b) or } x_{3}=\Psi^{-}\left(y_{5}\right)=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{y_{5}}{2} \Phi\left(y_{5}\right), \quad y_{3}=\frac{y_{5}}{2}-\frac{1}{4} \Phi\left(y_{5}\right), \quad \text { and } \quad y_{5} \in(1+ \\
& \quad \sqrt{3} / 2, \sqrt{15} / 2)
\end{aligned}
$$

The geometrically distinct equilateral pentagon are shown in Figure 3. It follows from the case (a) of Proposition 3 that the equilateral pentagon is concave when $y_{5} \in$ $(0, \sqrt{3} / 2)$, and convex if $y_{5} \in(\sqrt{3} / 2, \sqrt{15} / 2)$. While in case (b) of Proposition 3 the equilateral pentagon is always concave.


Figure 3. Gallery of possible pentagon equilateral configurations, according whether $x_{3}=\Psi^{+}\left(y_{5}\right)$ or $x_{3}=\Psi^{-}\left(y_{5}\right)$ and the value of $y_{5}$, together with the boundary cases, that are no more pentagons.

In the next section we will see that the only values of $y_{5}$ that give rise to central configurations will be $x_{3}=\Psi^{+}\left(y_{5}\right)$, where $y_{5}=(\sqrt{5+2 \sqrt{5}}) / 2 \approx 1.539$ is associated to the regular pentagon, while $y_{5} \approx 0.1576605$ gives a concave central configuration.

# 3. Proof of Theorem 1 

By a suitable scaling we may assume that $m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}+m_{4}+m_{5}=1$. Then the center of mass of the five bodies is

$$
\mathbf{c}_{m}=\left(x_{m}, y_{m}\right)=\left(\frac{m_{1}-m_{2}+2\left(m_{3}-m_{4}\right) x_{3}}{2}, \frac{\left(m_{3}+m_{4}\right) \sqrt{3+4 x_{3}-4 x_{3}^{2}}+2 m_{5} y_{5}}{2}\right)
$$

Since we are studying equilateral pentagons we can assume that $r_{12}=r_{13}=r_{35}=$ $r_{45}=r_{24}=1$. Then the others mutual distances are

$$
r_{14}=r_{2,3}=\sqrt{1+2 x_{3}}, \quad r_{1,5}=r_{2,5}=\sqrt{y_{5}^{2}+1 / 4}, \quad r_{3,4}=2 x_{3}
$$

From (1) we obtain the ten equations for the central configurations of the 5 -body problem in the plane:

$$

& e_{j+5}=\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{5} \frac{m_{j}\left(y_{i}-y_{j}\right)}{r_{i, j}^{3}}-\lambda\left(y_{j}-y_{m}\right)=0, \quad 1 \leq j \leq 5
\end{aligned}

A straightforward computation shows that $\sqrt{3+4 x_{3}-4 x_{3}^{2}}\left(-1+\sqrt{1+2 x_{3}}+2 x_{3} \sqrt{1+2 x_{3}}\right)=$ 0 for $x_{3}=-1 / 2,0,3 / 2$. Since $e_{3}+e_{4}=\left(m_{3}-m_{4}\right)\left(1+8 \lambda x_{3}^{3}\right) /\left(4 x_{3}^{2}\right)=0$. It follows that either $m_{4}=m_{3}$, or $\lambda=-1 /\left(8 x_{3}^{3}\right)$. In this last case we obtain
