L_{1}= & -2\left(1+2 x_{3}\right)\left(2 E_{1} E_{3} x_{3}^{3}-E_{1} E_{3} x_{3}^{2}+x_{3}^{2} E_{3}-4 E_{1}\right) y_{5}-E_{2} E_{3} x_{3}^{2}\left(2 x_{3} E_{1}+E_{1}-1\right) \\
L_{2}= & \left(1+2 x_{3}\right)\left(12 E_{1} E_{3} x_{3}^{3}-2 E_{1} E_{3} x_{3}^{2}-64 x_{3}^{3} E_{1}+2 x_{3}^{2} E_{3}-E_{1} E_{3}\right) y_{5} \\
& +E_{2} E_{3} x_{3}^{2}\left(2 x_{3} E_{1}+E_{1}-1\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\lambda$ from equation $g_{3}=0$ we obtain the two solutions

$$
\lambda_{1}=-\frac{8}{E_{3}}, \quad \lambda_{2}=\frac{L_{1}}{L_{2}}
$$

The solution $\lambda=\lambda_{1}$ is not suitable because then $m_{3}=0$. Substituting the solution $\lambda=\lambda_{2}$ in the equations $g_{1}=0$ and $g_{4}=0$, we get that $g_{4} \equiv 0$, and the equation $g_{1}=0$ reduces to

$$
\bar{h}_{1}=\left(2 x_{3}^{3} y_{5} E_{1} E_{3}\left(E_{3}-8\right)^{2}\left(2 x_{3}-1\right)\left(1+2 x_{3}+4 x_{3}^{2}\right) h_{1}=0\right.
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_{1}= & -4\left(1+2 x_{3}\right)^{2}\left(4 E_{1}^{2}\left(E_{3}-16\right) x_{3}^{4}-8 E_{1}\left(E_{1} E_{3}-4 E_{1}-4\right) x_{3}^{3}-E_{3}\left(E_{1}-1\right)^{2} x_{3}^{2}\right. \\
& \left.+E_{1}^{2}\left(E_{3}-8\right)\right) y_{5}^{2}-2 E_{2}\left(1+2 x_{3}\right)\left(16 E_{1}^{2}\left(E_{3}-4\right) x_{3}^{4}+4 E_{1}\left(3 E_{1} E_{3}-8 E_{1}-E_{3}-8\right) x_{3}^{3}\right. \\
& \left.+2 E_{3}\left(E_{1}-1\right)^{2} x_{3}^{2}-2 E_{1}^{2}\left(E_{3}-8\right) x_{3}-E_{1}^{2}\left(E_{3}-8\right)\right) y_{5}+E_{2}^{2} E_{3} x_{3}^{2}\left(2 x_{3} E_{1}+E_{1}-1\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $2 x_{3}^{3} y_{5} E_{1} E_{3}\left(1+2 x_{3}+4 x_{3}^{2}\right)$ does not vanish because $x_{3} \in(0,1), y_{5}>0$ and $E_{1}=r_{1,4}>0$.

At this step we shall prove that condition $\left(E_{3}-8\right)\left(2 x_{3}-1\right)=0$ implies that $m_{5}=0$. This is so, because

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{5}= & 1-\left(m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}+m_{4}\right)=1-2\left(m_{1}+m_{3}\right) \\
= & \frac{2 E_{1} y_{5} x_{3}^{3} E_{2} E_{3}\left(2 x_{3}-1\right)\left(4 x_{3}^{2}+2 x_{3}+1\right)\left(E_{3}-8\right)}{L_{2}^{2}} \\
& \times\left(-\left(1+2 x_{3}\right)\left[8 E_{1}^{2}\left(E_{3}-16\right) x_{3}^{4}+8 E_{1}\left(E_{3}-8\right)\left(E_{1}+1\right) x_{3}^{3}+2 E_{3}\left(E_{1}-1\right)^{2} x_{3}^{2}\right.\right. \\
& \left.\left.-2 E_{1}^{2}\left(E_{3}-16\right) x_{3}-E_{1}\left(E_{1} E_{3}-16 E_{1}+E_{3}\right)\right] y_{5}+E_{2} E_{3} x_{3}^{2}\left(2 E_{1} x_{3}+E_{1}-1\right)^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where we have used the expressions (6) for $m_{1}, m_{3}$ and substituted $\lambda=\lambda_{2}$ where $\lambda_{2}$ is given in equation (7). In short we have proved that the equations $\bar{h}_{1}=0$ and $h_{1}=0$ are equivalent.

From Proposition 3 we have that

$$
x_{3}=\frac{1}{4} \pm \frac{y_{5}}{2} \sqrt{\frac{15-4 y_{5}^{2}}{1+4 y_{5}^{2}}}
$$

or equivalently,

$$
h_{2}=\left(1-4 x_{3}\right)^{2}\left(1+4 y_{5}^{2}\right)+4 y_{5}^{2}\left(4 y_{5}^{2}-15\right)=0
$$

Hence the central configurations are the solutions of the simultaneous solution of both equations $h_{1}=0$ and $h_{2}=0$, with the two unknowns $x_{3}$ and $y_{5}$. Indeed it provides positive masses $m_{j}$. In order to avoid the square roots which appear in $E_{1}, E_{2}$ and $E_{3}$ in $h_{1}$, we do a change of variables such that the expressions appearing inside each square root are equal to some new squared expressions. These changes of variables are given by the so called rational parameterizations and correspond to parameterizations of planar algebraic curves given by rational functions. Due to the famous Cayley-Riemann's Theorem $$ they exist if and only if the corresponding surfaces have genus zero. There are effective methods to find one of these parameterizations see for instance [20, Chap. $4 \& 5]$. In fact, many programs of symbolic calculus have implemented some

methods and algorithms for obtaining them. For more information on this subject the reader is addressed to  and references therein, where there are several examples of applications of this approach.

In our case, for instance, we have that $E_{1}=\sqrt{1+2 x_{3}}, E_{2}=\sqrt{3+4 x_{3}-4 x_{3}^{2}}$. Hence if we write $x_{3}=\left(u^{2}-1\right) / 2$ we get that $E_{1}=\sqrt{u^{2}}$. Then

$$
3+4 x_{3}-\left.4 x_{3}^{2}\right|_{x_{3}=\left(u^{2}-1\right) / 2}=u^{2}\left(4-u^{2}\right)
$$

Consider now the algebraic curve $F(u, v)=u^{2}\left(4-u^{2}\right)-v^{2}=0$. It has genus 0 , and by the Cayley-Riemann's theorem it admits a rational parameterization. For example, for all $s$,

$$
F\left(\frac{4(2 s-1) s}{5 s^{2}-4 s+1}, \frac{8 s(s-1)(3 s-1)(2 s-1)}{\left(5 s^{2}-4 s+1\right)^{2}}\right)=0
$$

As a consequence, by taking

$$
x_{3}=\left.u^{2}\left(4-u^{2}\right)\right|_{u=\frac{4(2 s-1) s}{5 s^{2}-4 s+1}}=\frac{\left(3 s^{2}-1\right)\left(13 s^{2}-8 s+1\right)}{2\left(5 s^{2}-4 s+1\right)^{2}}
$$

we obtain that

$$
E_{2}=\sqrt{v^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{(8 s(s-1)(3 s-1)(2 s-1))^{2}}{\left(5 s^{2}-4 s+1\right)^{4}}}
$$

The rational parameterization of $E_{3}=\left(1+4 y_{5}^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}$ is much simpler and can be obtained similarly. It suffices to consider the algebraic curve of genus $0, G\left(y_{5}, w\right)=1+4 y_{5}^{2}-w^{2}=$ 0 . A good parameterization for $y_{5}$ is $y_{5}=\left(1-t^{2}\right) /(4 t)$.

We are interested on values $y_{5} \in(0, \sqrt{15} / 2)$ and $x_{3} \in(0,1)$. In short, we do the change of variables $\left(x_{3}, y_{5}\right) \rightarrow(s, t)$ where

$$
x_{3}=\frac{\left(3 s^{2}-1\right)\left(13 s^{2}-8 s+1\right)}{2\left(5 s^{2}-4 s+1\right)^{2}}, \quad y_{5}=\frac{1-t^{2}}{4 t}
$$

Then we have that $t$ varies in the interval $T:=(4-\sqrt{15}, 1)$ and similarly, the values of $x_{3} \in(0,1)$ are covered for instance for $s \in S:=(\sqrt{3} / 3,(6+\sqrt{3}) / 11)$. Hence,

$$
E_{1}=\frac{4 s(2 s-1)}{5 s^{2}-4 s+1}, \quad E_{2}=\frac{-8 s(s-1)(3 s-1)(2 s-1)}{\left(5 s^{2}-4 s+1\right)^{2}}, \quad E_{3}=\frac{\left(t^{2}+1\right)^{3}}{8 t^{3}}
$$

In the variables $(s, t)$ the two equations $h_{1}=0$ and $h_{2}=0$ become

$$
\begin{aligned}
& h_{1}=\frac{8 s^{2}(2 s-1)^{2}}{\left(5 s^{2}-4 s+1\right)^{2} t^{3}} H_{1}=0 \\
& h_{2}=\frac{1}{16\left(5 s^{2}-4 s+1\right)^{4} t^{4}} H_{2}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

respectively, where

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_{2}= & \left(5 s^{2}-4 s+1\right)^{4}\left(t^{8}+1\right)-4\left(47 s^{4}-152 s^{3}+150 s^{2}-56 s+7\right) \\
& \times\left(153 s^{4}-168 s^{3}+58 s^{2}-8 s+1\right)\left(t^{6}+t^{2}\right)+\left(101222 s^{8}-258784 s^{7}+326904 s^{6}\right. \\
& \left.-286240 s^{5}+183428 s^{4}-79776 s^{3}+21432 s^{2}-3168 s+198\right) t^{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

and $H_{1}$ ia a huge polynomial of total degree 34 and with $\operatorname{deg}_{s}\left(H_{1}\right)=24$ and $\operatorname{deg}_{t}\left(H_{1}\right)=$ 10 , which is given in Appendix A.

Taking into account that $t \in T$ and $s \in S$ to solve system (9), we see that this can be reduced to solve the system $H_{1}=0, H_{2}=0$, because $s(2 s-1)\left(s^{2}+2 s-1\right) \neq 0$. Hence, to find the real solutions of the systems $h_{1}=0, h_{2}=0$, is equivalent to find the real solutions, $(s, t) \in S \times T$, of the polynomial system $H_{1}=0, H_{2}=0$.

To study the above planar systems of equations we will use a mixture of the classical approach applying resultants together with simple inequalities in the original variables $x_{3}$ and $y_{5}$. For our problem this approach is very suitable because of the simplicity of the equation $h_{2}=0$, given in (8).

We start with the polynomials system $H_{1}(s, t)=0, H_{2}(s, t)=0$. Recall that if $(\hat{s}, \hat{t})$ is one of its solutions (real or complex), then $t=\hat{t}$ must be a zero of the one variable polynomial

$$
P(t)=\operatorname{Res}_{s}\left(H_{1}, H_{2}\right)
$$

where $\operatorname{Res}_{s}(\cdot, \cdot)$ denotes the resultant of two polynomials with respect the variable $s$, see for instance . After some computations (implemented for instance in Maple or Mathematica) we get that

$$
P(t)=\left(1+t^{2}\right)^{6} p_{4}(t) q_{4}(t) p_{120}(t) p_{132}(t)
$$

where $p_{4}(t)=1+4 t-14 t^{2}+4 t^{3}+t^{4}, q_{4}(t)=1-4 t-14 t^{2}-4 t^{3}+t^{4}$ and $p_{k}$ denotes a polynomial with integer coefficients of degree $k$ that we do not detail. We only remark that precisely $p_{120}$ is the polynomial that gives rise to the polynomial $R_{60}$, detailed in Appendix B and that gives rise to the values $t^{*}$ and $u^{*}$ that appear in Remark 2. Hence, by computing the Sturm sequences of each of the four polynomials, $p_{4}, q_{4}, p_{120}$ and $p_{132}$, we get that they have respectively, $4,4,28$ and 32 real roots and, moreover, that all them are simple. Furthermore, since we are only interested on the roots $t \in T \sim(0.127,1)$, we consider a slightly bigger interval $T \subset T^{\prime}=(3 / 25,100)$, with rational endpoints. Again, the corresponding Sturm sequences allow to prove that their number of roots in $T^{\prime}$ are $1,1,7$ and 9 , respectively. We will denote them by $t_{1} ; t_{2} ; t_{3}, \ldots, t_{9}$ and $t_{10}, \ldots t_{18}$, where for each $p_{k}$ the roots are ordered. Their approximated ordered value are

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
t_{10} \approx 0.1278827, & t_{3} \approx 0.1296657, & t_{11} \approx 0.1318307, & t_{12} \approx 0.1535285, & t_{2} \approx 0.1583844 \\
t_{13} \approx 0.1690804, & t_{4} \approx 0.1818971, & t_{5} \approx 0.1871837, & t_{14} \approx 0.4693713, & t_{1} \approx 0.5095254 \\
t_{15} \approx 0.5490528, & t_{16} \approx 0.5930556, & t_{6} \approx 0.7095411, & t_{7} \approx 0.7332148, & t_{8} \approx 0.9432977 \\
t_{17} \approx 0.9681690, & t_{9} \approx 0.9958185, & t_{18} \approx 0.9962499
\end{array}
$$

In fact, the roots $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ are $t_{1}=-1+\sqrt{5}-\sqrt{5-2 \sqrt{5}} \approx 0.5095254$ and $t_{2}=$ $1+\sqrt{5}-\sqrt{5+2 \sqrt{5}} \approx 0.1583844$, while each of the other sixteen roots can be obtained, again using the Sturm sequences, with any desired error.

Therefore, each $t_{j}, j=3, \ldots, 18$, can be bounded by $\underline{t}_{j}<t_{j}<\bar{t}_{j}$, with $\underline{t}_{j}, \bar{t}_{j} \in \mathbb{Q}$ and $0<\bar{t}_{j}-\underline{t}_{j}$ as small, as desired. For each of these values of $t_{j}$ we can use that the function $t \rightarrow\left(1-t^{2}\right) /(4 t)$ is decreasing in $(0,1)$ and that $y_{5}=\left(1-t^{2}\right) /(4 t)$ to get that if $\left(1-t_{j}^{2}\right) /\left(4 t_{j}\right)=y_{5}(j)$, then

$$
\underline{y}_{5}(j)=\frac{1-\bar{t}_{j}^{2}}{4 \bar{t}_{j}}<y_{5}(j)<\frac{1-\underline{t}_{j}^{2}}{4 \underline{t}_{j}}=\bar{y}_{5}(j), \quad \text { with } \quad \underline{y}_{5}(j), \bar{y}_{5}(j) \in \mathbb{Q}
$$

Recall that in (2) we have introduced the functions

$$
\Psi^{ \pm}(y)=\frac{1}{4} \pm \frac{y}{2} \sqrt{\frac{15-4 y^{2}}{1+4 y^{2}}}
$$

By simple derivation we get that $\Psi^{+}$(resp. $\Psi^{-}$) is increasing (resp. decreasing) for $y \in(0, \sqrt{3} / 2)$ and decreasing (resp. increasing) for $y \in(\sqrt{3} / 2,1)$. Hence, if we define $x_{3}^{ \pm}=\Psi^{ \pm}\left(y_{5}\right)$ it holds that

- If $j$ is such that $y_{5}(j)<\sqrt{3} / 2$ then

$$
\Psi^{+}\left(\underline{y}_{5}(j)\right)<x_{3}^{+}(j)<\Psi^{+}\left(\bar{y}_{5}(j)\right), \quad \Psi^{-}\left(\bar{y}_{5}(j)\right)<x_{3}^{-}(j)<\Psi^{-}\left(\underline{y}_{5}(j)\right)
$$

- If $j$ is such that $y_{5}(j)>\sqrt{3} / 2$ then

$$
\Psi^{+}\left(\bar{y}_{5}(j)\right)<x_{3}^{+}(j)<\Psi^{+}\left(\underline{y}_{5}(j)\right), \quad \Psi^{-}\left(\underline{y}_{5}(j)\right)<x_{3}^{-}(j)<\Psi^{-}\left(\bar{y}_{5}(j)\right)
$$

From these inequalities it is easy to find rational values $\underline{x}_{3}^{ \pm}(j)$ and $\bar{x}_{3}^{ \pm}(j)$ such that

$$
\underline{x}_{3}^{ \pm}(j)<x_{3}^{ \pm}(j)<\bar{x}_{3}^{ \pm}(j)
$$

and with $0<\bar{x}_{3}^{ \pm}(j)-\underline{x}_{3}^{ \pm}(j)$ as small as desired. Finally, the functions that define $E_{1}, E_{2}$ and $E_{3}$, given by $\psi_{1}(x)=\sqrt{1+2 x}, \psi_{2}(x)=\sqrt{3+4 x-4 x^{2}}$ and $\Psi_{3}(y)=\left(1+4 y^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}$ are increasing, increasing for $x \in(0, \sqrt{3} / 3)$ and decreasing for $x \in(\sqrt{3} / 3,1)$, and increasing, respectively. Similarly that for $x^{ \pm}(j)$ we can find rational bounds, $\underline{E}_{j}$ and $\bar{E}_{j}, j=1,2,3$, as sharp as desired and satisfying

$$
\underline{E}_{1}<E_{1}<\bar{E}_{1}, \quad \underline{E}_{2}<E_{2}<\bar{E}_{2}, \quad \underline{E}_{3}<E_{3}<\bar{E}_{3}
$$

In short, we have found sharp rational upper and lower bound of any possible solution $y_{5}=y_{5}(j), x_{3}^{ \pm}(j)$, corresponding to each $t=t_{j}, j=1,2, \ldots, 18$. These rational bounds give also rational bounds for $E_{1}, E_{2}$ and $E_{3}$. Gluing these bounds we prove that some candidates to be solutions of our system can be discarded. That other candidates are actual solution of our problem can be easily proved from Bolzano's theorem. We detail two examples, one of each type and skip the computations for all the rest.

A suitable way is to write $h_{1}$ in function of the variables $x_{3}, y_{5}, E_{1}, E_{2}$ and $E_{3}$, namely

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_{1}= & -128 x_{3}^{3} y_{5}^{2}\left(4 x_{3}^{2}+4 x_{3}+1\right) E_{1}+4 x_{3}^{2} y_{5}^{2}\left(4 x_{3}^{2}+4 x_{3}+1\right) E_{3} \\
& +32 y_{5}^{2}\left(32 x_{3}^{6}+16 x_{3}^{5}-8 x_{3}^{4}-4 x_{3}^{3}+4 x_{3}^{2}+4 x_{3}+1\right) E_{1}^{2}+64 x_{3}^{3} y_{5}\left(1+2 x_{3}\right) E_{1} E_{2} \\
& -8 x_{3}^{2} y_{5}^{2}\left(4 x_{3}^{2}+4 x_{3}+1\right) E_{1} E_{3}-4 x_{3}^{2} y_{5}\left(1+2 x_{3}\right) E_{3} E_{2} \\
& +16 y_{5}\left(16 x_{3}^{5}+16 x_{3}^{4}+4 x_{3}^{3}-4 x_{3}^{2}-4 x_{3}-1\right) E_{1}^{2} E_{2} \\
& -4 y_{5}^{2}\left(16 x_{3}^{6}-16 x_{3}^{5}-32 x_{3}^{4}-12 x_{3}^{3}+3 x_{3}^{2}+4 x_{3}+1\right) E_{1}^{2} E_{3} \\
& +8 x_{3}^{2} y_{5}\left(2 x_{3}^{2}+3 x_{3}+1\right) E_{1} E_{2} E_{3}+E_{2}^{2} E_{3} x_{3}^{2} \\
& -2 y_{5}\left(32 x_{3}^{5}+40 x_{3}^{4}+16 x_{3}^{3}-2 x_{3}^{2}-4 x_{3}-1\right) E_{1}^{2} E_{2} E_{3} \\
& -2 x_{3}^{2}\left(1+2 x_{3}\right) E_{1} E_{2}^{2} E_{3}+x_{3}^{2}\left(4 x_{3}^{2}+4 x_{3}+1\right) E_{1}^{2} E_{2}^{2} E_{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

We remark that the addends of $h_{1}$ can be bounded using the inequalities given above. For instance

$$
\underline{E}_{2}^{2} \underline{E}_{3} \underline{x}_{3}^{2}<E_{2}^{2} E_{3} x_{3}^{2}<\bar{E}_{2}^{2} \bar{E}_{3} \bar{x}_{3}^{2}
$$

and

$$
-4 \bar{x}_{3}^{2} \bar{y}_{5}\left(1+2 \bar{x}_{3}\right) \bar{E}_{3} \bar{E}_{2}<-4 x_{3}^{2} y_{5}\left(1+2 x_{3}\right) E_{3} E_{2}<-4 \underline{x}_{3}^{2} \underline{y}_{5}\left(1+2 \underline{x}_{3}\right) \underline{E}_{3} \underline{E}_{2}
$$

Let us prove for instance that the value $y_{5}=y_{5}(5)$ corresponding to $t=t_{5} \approx$ 0.1871837 , together with $x_{3}=x_{3}^{+}(5)=\Psi^{+}\left(y_{5}(5)\right)$ does not provide a solution of our system. From the Sturm sequence we get that

$$
\frac{1871}{10000}<t_{5}<\frac{1872}{10000}
$$

From these inequalities and all the above considerations we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}
1.2886701 \approx \frac{94234}{73125} & <y_{5}<\frac{96499359}{74840000} \approx 1.2894088, \quad \frac{9235}{10000}<x_{3}^{+}<\frac{9238}{10000} \\
\frac{16873}{10000} & <E_{1}<\frac{16873}{10000}, \quad \frac{18118}{10000} \leq E_{2}<\frac{18115}{10000}, \quad \frac{21128}{1000}<E_{3}<\frac{21161}{1000}
\end{aligned}
$$

By using all these inequalities we obtain that the corresponding value of $h_{1}>242$ and the system has no solution for the value of $y_{5}$, and its corresponding $x_{3}^{+}(5)$ associated to $t=t_{5}$.

On the other hand, let us prove that the value $y_{5}=y_{5}(7)$ corresponding to $t=t_{7}=$ $t^{*} \approx 0.7332148$ together with $x_{3}=x_{3}^{+}(7)=\Psi^{+}\left(y_{5}(7)\right)$ does provide an actual solution. This is a simple consequence of Bolzano's theorem, because if we denote as $h_{1}(\tau)$ the value of the expression of $h_{1}$ when all the values $y_{5}, x_{5}^{+}, E_{1}, E_{2}$ and $E_{3}$ are obtained when $t=\tau$ we get for instance that

$$
h_{1}\left(\frac{7332}{10000}\right) h_{1}\left(\frac{7333}{10000}\right)<0
$$

We carry out similar computations for $y_{5}=y_{5}(j)$, corresponding to $t=t_{j}$, and $x_{3}=x_{3}^{ \pm}(j)=\Psi^{ \pm}\left(y_{5}(j)\right)$. We conclude that among the 36 candidates that could be a solution of the system $h_{1}\left(x_{3}, y_{5}\right)=0, h_{2}\left(x_{3}, y_{5}\right)=0$ the only couples $\left(x_{3}, y_{5}\right)$ that do solve it are:
(I) $\left(x_{3}^{+}(2), y_{5}(2)\right)=\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{4}, \frac{\sqrt{5+2 \sqrt{5}}}{2}\right) \approx(0.8090170,1.5388418)$ corresponding
to $t=t_{2}$,
(II) $\left(x_{3}^{+}(7), y_{5}(7)\right) \approx(0.5402091,0.1576605)$ corresponding to $t=t_{7}=t^{*}$,
(III) $\left(x_{3}^{+}(9), y_{5}(9)\right) \approx(0.2540572,0.0020951)$ corresponding to $t=t_{9}$,
(IV) $\left(x_{3}^{-}(4), y_{5}(4)\right) \approx(-0.4091526,1.3289291)$ corresponding to $t=t_{4}$,
(V) $\left(x_{3}^{-}(14), y_{5}(14)\right) \approx(-0.3542470,0.4152845)$ corresponding to $t=t_{14}$,
(VI) $\left(x_{3}^{-}(18), y_{5}(18)\right) \approx(0.2463622,0.0018786)$ corresponding to $t=t_{18}$.

Clearly, solutions in items (IV) and (V) can be discarded because the corresponding values of $x_{3}$ are negative. The solutions given in items (III) and (VI) are not good either, since both options result in negative $m_{5}$ values. In short the central configurations are:
(I) $\left(x_{3}, y_{3}\right)=\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{4}, \frac{\sqrt{10+2 \sqrt{5}}}{4}\right)$ and $y_{5}=\frac{\sqrt{5+2 \sqrt{5}}}{2}$, with masses $m_{j}=\frac{1}{5}$, for all $j$.

(II) $\left(x_{3}, y_{3}\right)=\left(x_{3}^{+}(7), y_{3}^{+}(7)\right) \approx(0.5402091,0.9991913)$ and $y_{5}=y_{5}(7) \approx 0.1576605$ with masses $m_{1}=m_{2} \approx 0.0922539, m_{3}=m_{4} \approx 0.3860949$ and $m_{5} \approx 0.04330243$.

The values of $y_{3}$ and $m_{j}$ are obtained from Proposition 3 and the expressions (6) and (7).

The first solution provides the regular pentagon of Figure 2(a) as a convex central configuration of the 5 -body problem with masses equal to $1 / 5$. While the second one provides the equilateral concave pentagon of Figure 2(b) as a concave central configuration of the 5 -body problem with the masses given in the statement (b) of the theorem. This completes the proof of Theorem 1.
3.1. Alternative approaches to solve system $h_{1}=0, h_{2}=0$. In this section we comment about to alternative approaches two solve this system and its equivalent one $H_{1}=0, H_{2}=0$.

A first one consists on computing the Gröbner basis of the two polynomials $H_{1}$ and $H_{2}$ with respect to the two variables $s$ and $t$. Doing this we obtain three polynomial equations whose common solutions are also the solutions of system $H_{1}=0, H_{2}=0$. We do not provide explicitly these three polynomials, but only comment that they are huge and their expressions need many pages. The first one essentially coincides with $P(t)$ given in (10). The second one $P_{2}(s, t)=\left(1+t^{2}\right)^{2} p_{259}(s, t)$. depends on both variables $s$ and $t$, and $P_{2}$ is linear in the variable $s$. Consequently each root $t=t_{j}$ of the polynomial $P$ provides a single value of $s$ from $P_{2}\left(s, t_{j}\right)=0$, say $s=s_{j}$. Then we only need to keep the $j^{\prime}$ s such that $s_{j} \in S$. Finally, the third polynomial $P_{3}(s, t)$ of the Gröbner basis has degree 262 but it is only cubic in the variable $s$. By keeping only the values $s_{j} \in S$ that also satisfy $P_{3}\left(s_{j}, t_{j}\right)=0$ we arrive to the actual solutions. We have used our approach instead of this one because it is not easy to check analytically all the above facts because only two of the eighteen roots of $P$ are known analytically. Moreover, we prefer our point of view because the computation of a resultant is simple and self contained while the computation of a Gröbner basis is implemented in the computer algebra systems but the user has no control on what the algorithm is doing.

A second alternative approach would consist on computing also $Q(s)=\operatorname{Res}_{t}\left(H_{1}, H_{2}\right)$. In this case we arrive to

$$
Q(s)=q_{2}^{6}(s) q_{4}^{2}(s) q_{120}(s) q_{132}(s)
$$

for some polynomials $q_{k}$ of degree $k$, where here $q_{4}$ is different to the one given in (10). Their respective number of real roots are $0,4,28$ and 32 . Moreover, only $1,0,4$ and 6 of them are in $S$. Call them $s_{m}, m=1,2, \ldots, 11$. Hence all the possible solutions of system $H_{1}=0, H_{2}=0$ in $S \times T$ are given by $11 \times 18$ values $\left(s_{m}, t_{j}\right)$. Then, a discarding process, similar to the one done in our proof of Theorem 1 can be done. On the other hand, a proof that the non discarded candidates to be solutions are actual solutions can be done for instance by using the nice Poincaré-Miranda theorem. See for instance  to have more details of how to utilize this approach. We have not used it in our work because the expression of $h_{2}$ is much simpler that the one of $Q$.


# Central Configurations with Many Small Masses 


#### Abstract

By using the method of analytical continuation, we find the exact numbers of central configurations for some open sets of $n$ positive masses for any choice of $n$. It turns out that the numbers increase dramatically as $n$ increases; e.g., for some open set of 18 positive masses, some $2.08766 \times 10^{20}$ classes of distinctive central configurations are found. In the mean time, we obtained some results about the Hausdorff measure for the set of $n$ positive masses where degenerate central configuration arises. (C) 1991 Academic Press, Inc.


## 1. InTRODUCTION

Consider $N$ point masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{N}>0$ with positions $q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{N}$, $q_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ in the Euclidean plane. These points form a central configuration, if, for some positive constant $\lambda$, the following system of algebraic equations is satisfied

$$
\lambda m_{i} q_{i}=\sum_{j \neq i} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left\|q_{i}-q_{j}\right\|^{3}}\left(q_{j}-q_{i}\right)=\frac{\partial U_{n}}{\partial q_{i}}
$$

for $i=1,2, \ldots, N$, and where

$$
U_{N}=\sum_{i<j} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left\|q_{i}-q_{j}\right\|}
$$

The central configurations are important in $n$-body problems because they are bifurcation points for the topological classification of the co-planar $n$-body problem (see Easton  and Smale ); they are the limiting configurations for colliding particles and for completely parabolic orbits (see D. Saari $$ ); they are the only configurations which can be maintained all the time in the $n$-body system; and often they are the starting
points for finding some new classes of periodic solutions. Questions about these configurations were raised by Wintner , Smale , Palmore , and many others. Recently there has been an active interest in finding and classifying the central configurations, e.g., the recent work of Meyer and Schmidt , Hall , Moeckel , and others.

For $n=3$, this problem is completely solved and it is a classical result: There are exactly 3 collinear solutions and 2 equilateral triangular solutions for any 3 positive masses. In case of $n=4$, even for 4 equal masses, the exact number of central configurations is unknown. On the other hand, Arenstorf  obtained the number of central configurations with one of four masses being very small. He started with one zero mass and then analytically continue it into positive masses. A very interesting phenomenon arises in this case, i.e., there are two sets of masses such that the numbers of central configurations corresponding to these two sets are different. In this paper, we are going to find the exact number of central configuration for some open sets of $N$ masses for any $N$. It turns out that for any $N \geqslant 4$, the same phenomenon arises; there are always two open sets of masses such that the numbers of central configurations corresponding to these masses are different. From this we conclude that for any $N \geqslant 4$, the set of masses for which the degenerate central configuration exists has a positive ( $N-1$ )-dimensional measure (Haussdorff). This was proved first by Palmore , but it seems difficult to complete all the steps in his proof.

The method we are going to use is analytical continuation. We start with two zero masses and find the corresponding central configurations, especially the ones in which two zero masses are at the same point. Under certain conditions, these central configurations can be analytically continued into a full $n$-body problem with all masses positive. We will see that the central configuration with two zero masses at the same point will bifurcate into several distinctive central configurations of a full $n$-body problem. By repeating this processes, for any choice of $n$, we can find the exact number of central configurations for at least some open subset of $N$ positive masses.

The central configurations are also called relative equilibria. However, throughout this paper we only use the name central configuration and save the relative equilibria for those special central configurations with one or more zero masses.

# 2. Restricted Problem of $(n+2)$-Body 

Let $q^{*}=\left(q_{1}^{*}, q_{2}^{*}, \ldots, q_{N}^{*}\right)$ be a solution of Eq. (1), i.e., $q_{1}^{*}, q_{2}^{*}, \ldots, q_{N}^{*}$ form a central configuration; then it is easy to see that $k q^{*}=\left(k q_{1}^{*}, k q_{2}^{*}, \ldots, k q_{N}^{*}\right)$ and $A q^{*}=\left(A q_{1}^{*}, A q_{2}^{*}, \ldots, A q_{N}^{*}\right)$ is also a solution of (1), where $k$ is a constant and $A \in S O(2, R)$ is a rotation matrix. We can define an equivalence

relation by $q \sim k q$ and $q \sim A q$. By a central configuration, we will actually mean an equivalence class of central configurations. An equivalent definition of central configuration is the critical points of the potential function $U$ restricted to the sphere $I=1$, where $I=(1 / 2) \sum m_{i}\left\|q_{i}\right\|^{2}$ is the moment of inertia. Then (1) is exactly the equation given by the Lagrange multiplier method for finding the critical point and $\lambda$ is the Lagrange multiplier. Note that there is a degenerate direction for $U$ restricted on the sphere $I=1$ due to $S O(2, R)$ action. To remove this degeneracy, let $S / \sim$ be the quotient space of the sphere $I=1$ with relation $q \sim A q, A \in S O(2, R)$; then the equivalence classes of central configurations are the critical points of $U()$ on $S / \sim$, where $$ is the equivalent class of $q$.

A central configuration is called nondegenerate if its equivalence class is a nondegenerate critical point of $U($; i.e., the Hessian is nonsingular at the critical point. By the implicit function theorem, any nondegenerate central configuration can be analytically continued to nearby masses.

We remark that, in (1), the equation for central configuration, one may fix $\lambda=1$. This only fixes the scale of the central configuration. For any equivalence class of central configurations, the one with $\lambda=1$ can be found. From now on, we fix $\lambda=1$.

Let $q^{*}=\left(q_{1}^{*}, q_{2}^{*}, \ldots, q_{N}^{*}\right)$ be a nondegenerate central configuration for the $N$-body problem; now we consider an $n$-body system with $n=N+2$ in which we add two small masses to the $N$-body system. We want to find the central configurations to this system in which $q=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{N}\right)$ is close to $q^{*}=\left(q_{1}^{*}, q_{2}^{*}, \ldots, q_{N}^{*}\right)$. The corresponding equations for the central configurations are

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{i} q_{i}= & \frac{\partial U_{N}}{\partial q_{i}}+\frac{m_{i} m_{N+1}}{\left\|q_{N+1}-q_{i}\right\|^{3}}\left(q_{N+1}-q_{i}\right) \\
& +\frac{m_{i} m_{N+2}}{\left\|q_{N+2}-q_{i}\right\|^{3}}\left(q_{N+2}-q_{i}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

for $i=1,2, \ldots, N$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{N+1} q_{N+1}= & \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i} m_{N+1}}{\left\|q_{N+1}-q_{i}\right\|^{3}}\left(q_{i}-q_{N+1}\right) \\
& +\frac{m_{N+1} m_{N+2}}{\left\|q_{N+1}-q_{N+2}\right\|^{3}}\left(q_{N+2}-q_{N+1}\right) \\
m_{N+2} q_{N+2}= & \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i} m_{N+2}}{\left\|q_{N+2}-q_{i}\right\|^{3}}\left(q_{i}-q_{N+2}\right) \\
& +\frac{m_{N+1} m_{N+2}}{\left\|q_{N+1}-q_{N+2}\right\|^{3}}\left(q_{N+1}-q_{N+2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that in Eqs. (3) and (4) there are factors $m_{N+1}$ and $m_{N+2}$, respectively. When dealing with small masses it is convenient to factor out $m_{N+1}, m_{N+2}$. Assume this is done. Our next step is to consider the extreme case where $m_{N+1}=m_{N+2}=0$. For $m_{N+1}=m_{N+2}=0$, (2) reduces to (1), and (3) and (4) become

$$
\begin{aligned}
& q_{N+1}=\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|q_{n+1}-q_{i}^{*}\right\|^{3}}\left(q_{N+1}-q_{i}^{*}\right) \\
& q_{N+2}=\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|q_{N+2}-q_{i}^{*}\right\|^{3}}\left(q_{N+2}-q_{i}^{*}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the equations for $q_{N+1}, q_{N+2}$ are identical; we may write them in a different way as

$$
D V_{N}\left(q_{N+1}\right)=0, \quad D V_{N}\left(q_{N+2}\right)=0
$$

where

$$
V_{N}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|q_{i}^{*}-x\right\|}+\frac{1}{2}\|x\|^{2}
$$

Let $x^{*}$ be a solution of $D V_{N}(x)=0$; then it is called a relative equilibrium of the restricted ( $n+1$ )-body problem, and it is nondegenerate if the Jacobian of $D V_{N}(x)$ has a rank 2 ; i.e., if $\left|D^{2} V_{N}(x)\right| \neq 0$ at $x=x^{*}$. Since $D^{2} V_{N}(x)$ is symmetric, it has two real valued eigenvalues, say $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$, and by selecting appropriate coordinates, we may write

$$
D^{2} V_{N}\left(q_{N+1}\right)=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
a_{1} & 0 \\
0 & a_{2}
\end{array}\right]
$$

The objective of this section is to find some central configurations of the $(n+2)$-body problem with two small masses from a known relative equilibrium of the restricted $(n+1)$-body problem. The following proposition shows how to find the central configurations where two small masses are far apart from each other.

Proposition 1. Let $q_{1}^{*}, q_{2}^{*}, \ldots, q_{N}^{*}$ be a nondegenerate central configuration for $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{N}>0$. Let $q_{N+1}^{*}, q_{N+2}^{*}$ be nondegenerate relative equilibria of the restricted $(n+1)$-body problem, and $q_{N+1}^{*} \neq q_{N+2}^{*}$; then the central configuration $q_{1}^{*}, q_{2}^{*}, \ldots, q_{N}^{*}, q_{N+1}^{*}, q_{N+2}^{*}$ for the masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{N}, 0,0$, can be analytically continued to a central configuration for any masses in an open neighborhood of $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{N}, 0,0$ in $\mathbb{R}_{+}^{N+2}$.

In this proposition, $q_{N+1}^{*} \neq q_{N+2}^{*}$ is required so that the influences of the two small masses on each other are of high order, therefore the implicit function theorem applies. In fact, the Jacobian at $q_{1}^{*}, q_{2}^{*}, \ldots, q_{N}^{*}$, $q_{N+1}^{*}, q_{N+2}^{*}$ for (2), (3), and (4) breaks into three parts, one for (2) at $q_{1}^{*}, q_{2}^{*}, \ldots, q_{N}^{*}$, and the other two for (3) and (4) at $q_{N+1}^{*}$ and $q_{N+2}^{*}$, respectively. All of them are nondegenerate, so the implicit function theorem gives the proposition.

Observe that, if we have $k$ nondegenerate relative equilibria for the restricted $(n+1)$-body problem, this proposition gives $k \cdot(k-1)$ distinctive central configurations for the full $(n+2)$-body problem with two small masses and it is easy to see that, for $m_{N+1}, m_{N+2}$ sufficiently small, this gives all the central configurations with $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{N}$ near $q_{1}^{*}, q_{2}^{*}, \ldots, q_{N}^{*}$ and $m_{N+1}, m_{N+2}$ away from one another. It is still possible that there are some central configurations for which the two small masses $m_{N+1}, m_{N+2}$ are close together; i.e., as the limits of $m_{N+1}, m_{N+2}$ tend to zero, $m_{N+1}$, $m_{N+2}$ occupy the same point. We consider this case next.

In case of $q_{N+1}^{*}=q_{N+2}^{*}$, the influences between two small masses become very large as their masses become positive, since the distance between them is very small. Therefore we can not apply the implicit function theorem directly. In fact, $m_{N+1}=0=m_{N+2}, q_{N+1}^{*}=q_{N+2}^{*}$ is a singular point for Eqs. (2), (3), and (4), we will see that the bifurcation of the central configuration occurs here.

When $m_{N+1}>0, m_{N+2}>0$ are very small, and $q_{N+1}-q_{N+2}$ is very small, it is convenient to introduce some new coordinates for $m_{N+1}$ and $m_{N+2}$; let

$$
r_{1}=\left(m_{N+1} q_{N+1}+m_{N+2} q_{N+2}\right) /\left(m_{N+1}+m_{N+2}\right)
$$

and

$$
r_{2}=q_{N+2}-q_{N+1}
$$

Then, for $q_{N+1}-q_{N+1}^{*}, q_{N+2}-q_{N+2}^{*}$ very small, Eqs. (2), (3), and (4) become

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{i} q_{i} & =\frac{\partial U_{N}}{\partial q_{i}}+O\left(m_{N+1}, m_{N+2}\right) \quad i=1,2, \ldots, N \\
r_{1} & =\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{m_{i}}{\left\|q_{i}-r_{1}\right\|}\left(q_{1}-r_{1}\right)+O\left(m_{N+1}, m_{N+2}, r_{2}\right) \\
D^{2} V_{N}\left(r_{1}\right) r_{2} & =\frac{m_{N+1}+m_{N+2}}{\left\|r_{2}\right\|^{3}} r_{2}+O\left(m_{N+1}, m_{N+2}, r_{2}^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

We still have a singularity for (10) at $m_{N+1}=0, m_{N+2}=0$, and $r_{2}=0$; a scaling of variables will remove this singularity. Let $r_{2}=\left(m_{N+1}+m_{N+2}\right)^{1 / 3} r_{2}^{\prime}$; (10) becomes

$$
\left(D^{2} V_{N}\left(r_{1}\right)-1 /\left\|r_{2}^{\prime}\right\|^{3}\right) r_{2}^{\prime}=O\left(m_{N+1}, m_{N+2}\right)
$$

Now, $m_{N+1}=m_{N+2}=0, r_{2}=0$ is no longer a singular point for (8), (9), and (11) and therefore we may use this set of equations for finding the central configurations with two small masses close together.

Let $m_{N+1}=0, m_{N+2}=0$ and let $r_{1}^{*}=q_{N+1}^{*}=q_{N+2}^{*}$ be a nondegenerate relative equilibrium of the restricted ( $N+1$ )-body problem; (11) gives

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc}
a_{1}-1 /\left\|r_{2}^{\prime}\right\|^{3} & 0 \\
0 & a_{2}-1 /\left\|r_{2}^{\prime}\right\|^{3}
\end{array}\right] r_{2}^{\prime}=0
$$

where $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ are the eigenvalues of $D V_{N}\left(r_{1}^{*}\right)$ and $a_{1} \neq 0, a_{2} \neq 0$. There are three cases for the solutions of this equation depending on different values of $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ :
(i) $a_{1}<0, a_{2}<0$, i.e., $r_{1}^{*}$ is a local maximum of $V(x)$; then there is no solution at all.
(ii) $a_{1}<0, a_{2}>0$ (or similarly, $a_{1}>0, a_{2}<0$ ), $r_{1}^{*}$ is a saddle point of $V(x)$; there are two solutions, $r_{2}^{\prime}= \pm\left(0, a_{2}^{-1 / 3}\right)$, and the Jacobian at these solutions is

$$
\left|\begin{array}{cc}
a_{1}-a_{2} & 0 \\
0 & 3 a_{2}
\end{array}\right|=3\left(a_{1}-a_{2}\right) a_{2} \neq 0
$$

so these two solutions can be continued into two classes of central configurations for a full $(n+2)$-body problem.
(iii) $a_{1}>0, a_{2}>0$; there are four solutions in this case,

$$
r_{2}^{\prime}= \pm\left(0, a_{2}^{-1 / 3}\right), \quad r_{2}= \pm\left(a_{1}^{-1 / 3}, 0\right)
$$

and the Jacobians at these solutions are

$$
\left|\begin{array}{cc}
a_{1}-a_{2} & 0 \\
0 & 3 a_{2}
\end{array}\right|, \quad\left|\begin{array}{cc}
3 a_{1} & 0 \\
0 & a_{2}-a_{1}
\end{array}\right|
$$

Both of them do not vanish provided that $a_{1} \neq a_{2}$, and hence if $a_{1} \neq a_{2}$ these four solutions can be continued into four different classes of central configurations for the full $(N+2)$-body problem with two small masses.

The following graph illustrates the relative positions of two small masses in a $(4+2)$-body problem.


Now we have a way for finding the central configurations of the $(N+2)$ body problem with two small masses even when these two small masses have the same limit position as their masses tend to zero. We point out that the central configurations thus found exhaust all the possible ones with two sufficient small masses and with the large masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{N}$ close to $q_{1}^{*}, q_{2}^{*}, \ldots, q_{N}^{*}$.

In case (iii), when $a_{1}=a_{2}<0$, more complicated bifurcation occurs, and it depends on high order terms of $V_{N}(x)$ at $x^{*}$, it is possible that we have more than four solutions that can be continued into a full $(N+2)$-body problem instead of four solutions in the case of $a_{1} \neq a_{2}, a_{1}<0$, and $a_{2}<0$. For example, let us put $N$ equal masses at the vertices of a regular $N$-polygon; then the origin is a relative equilibrium and is a local minimum of $V_{N}(x)$, by symmetry, $a_{1}=a_{2}<0$. One can show that at least $2 N$ classes of central configurations of the $(N+2)$-problem, with two small masses at the origin, can be obtained, again by symmetry.

As an application of above results, let us consider a 4-body problem with two small masses. There are five relative equilibria for a restricted 3-body problem; two of them are equilateral triangle solutions which are minima of $V_{2}(x)$, and two eigenvalues of $D^{2} V(x)$ are different at these two points, and the other three of them are collinear solutions which are saddle points of $V_{2}(x)$. All of the five relative equilibria are nondegenerate. Thus, Proposition 1 gives $5 \times 4=20$ classes of central configurations for the 4 -body problem with two small masses which are away from each other and there are $2 \times 4+3 \times 2=14$ classes of central configurations with two small masses close to each other; therefore, there are totally 34 classes of central configurations for the 4 -body problem with two small masses. This same result was obtained by Arenstorf  by a different method.

# 3. The Numbers of Central Configurations 

In last section, we developed a method to find the number of relative equilibria of the $(N+2)$-body problem from that of the restricted $(N+1)$ body problem, and we continued these into the central configurations of the full $(N+1)$-body problem. If we keep $m_{N+2}=0$ and only continue $m_{N+1}$ into positive values, then what we obtain are some relative equilibria of the restricted $((N+1)+1)$-body problem, so we can use the same technique again to obtain some central configurations of the $(N+3)$-body problem, and so on. Before we do that, we must first find the eigenvalues of $D^{2} N_{N+1}(x)$ at these new relative equilibria of the restricted $((N+1)+1)$-body problem.

For the relative equilibria given by Proposition 1, i.e., when two small masses are away from each other, for $m_{N+1}$ small enough, $D^{2} V_{N+1}(x)$ has the same property as that of $D^{2} V_{N}(x)$, and therefore the method of the last section applies again.

In the case of two small masses close to each other, if $m_{N+1}$ is small enough, then $V_{N+1}(x)$ can be approximated by

$$
V_{N+1}(x)=V_{N}+m_{N+1} /\left\|r_{2}\right\|+O\left(m_{N+1}\right)
$$

with

$$
D^{2} V_{N}(x)=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
a_{1} & 0 \\
0 & a_{2}
\end{array}\right]
$$

Corresponding to that three cases of the last section, local properties of $V_{N+1}(x)$ can be shown to be the following.
(i) $a_{1}<0, a_{2}<0$; no relative equilibrium for the $(N+1)+1$ )-body problem;
(ii) $a_{1}<0, a_{2}>0$ (and similarly for $a_{1}>0, a_{2}<0$ ), $r_{2}^{\prime}= \pm\left(0, a_{2}^{-1 / 3}\right)$,

$$
D^{2} V_{N+1}(x)=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
a_{1}-a_{2} & 0 \\
0 & 3 a_{2}
\end{array}\right]+O\left(m_{N+1}\right)
$$

again, the relative equilibria are saddle points;
(iii) $a_{1}>0, a_{2}>0, a_{1} \neq a_{2}$; for the solution $r_{2}^{\prime}= \pm\left(0, a_{2}^{-1 / 3}\right)$,

$$
D^{2} V_{N+1}(x)=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
a_{1}-a_{2} & 0 \\
0 & 3 a_{2}
\end{array}\right]+O\left(m_{N+1}\right)
$$

and for the solution $r_{2}^{\prime}= \pm\left(a_{1}^{-1 / 3}, 0\right)$,

$$
D^{2} V_{N+1}(x)=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
3 a_{1} & 0 \\
0 & a_{2}-a_{1}
\end{array}\right]+O\left(m_{N+1}\right)
$$

So two of the relative equilibria are saddle points, while the other two are minimal of $V_{N+1}(x)$.

We conclude that, for any saddle point of $V_{N}(x)$, then for each central configuration continued from this relative equilibrium, with $m_{N+1}$ sufficiently small, there are always two saddle points of $V_{N+1}(x)$ nearby $m_{N+1}$, and correspondingly, for any minimum of $V_{N}(x)$, there will always be two minima and two saddle points nearby $m_{N+1}$ for $V_{N+1}(x)$.

Now, we come back to the 4 -body problem we discussed at the end of the last section. First consider the case with $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ large and $m_{3}$ sufficiently small. From the above result, there are together $2 \times 4+3 \times 2+5 \times 4=34$ relative equilibria. Among these 34 relative equilibria of the restricted $(3+1)$-body problem, 16 belong to the equilateral triangle formed by $m_{1}, m_{2}$, and $m_{3}$ with $2 \times 3=6$ local minima and $2 \times 5=10$ local saddle points. The other 18 belong the collinear central configurations of $m_{1}, m_{2}$, and $m_{3}$ with $3 \times 2$ local minima and $3 \times 4$ local saddle points. By a very careful counting, we conclude that there are altogether $2 \times 3 \times 4+2 \times 3 \times 7+2 \times 5 \times 3+2 \times 5 \times 6+3 \times 2 \times 3+3 \times 2 \times 6+$ $3 \times 4 \times 2+3 \times 4 \times 5=294$ relative equilibria for the restricted $(4+1)$-body problem.

We now turn our attention to the central configurations with three large masses. First for any three positive masses, there are five classes of central configurations; three of them are collinear and two of them are equilateral. Arenstorf  and Palmore  showed that for any collinear central configuration there are six relative equilibria for the restricted 4 -body problem; two of them are local minima and the other four of them are saddles. For the equilateral central configuration, an interesting phenomenon happens. Arenstorf  showed that there are 8 or 10 relative equilibria of the restricted 4 -body problem depending on the three positive masses, and for most of the masses they are all nondegenerate. A simple topological argument shows that in the nondegenerate case, among these 8 (or 10 ) relative equilibria, 3 (or 4) of them must be local minima and the other 5 (or 6) must be saddle points. Since thee eigenvalues continuously depend on the masses, it can be shown easily that for most of the masses, at the minima relative equilibria, $D^{2} V_{3}(x)$ has distinct eigenvalues.

Therefore for the restricted 4 -body problem, for some open set of three large masses, there are totally 34 relative equilibria. Among them, 22 are saddle points and the other 12 are local minima, and for some other open set of three large masses, the total number of relative equilibria is 36 . Among them 24 are saddle points and 14 are local minima. From these results about the restricted $(3+1=4)$-body problem and the technique we developed above, it is easy to see (again, by carefully counting the numbers), for a 5 -body problem, for some open set of masses (with two large masses, one small mass, and two even smaller masses), there are 294

classes of central configurations, while for some other open set of masses (with three large masses and two small masses), there are 374 classes of central configurations, and all of them are nondegenerate.

Repeating the above procedure, for any $N$ there are two open sets of masses for which we can find the exact number of central configurations corresponding to these two sets of masses. For $n$ from 4 through 10, the numbers thus found are listed in Table I.

It would be nice if we could develop a general formula depending on the number of bodies for the number of central configurations thus found. It turns out that it is even hard to write a recursive formula for these numbers. In fact, the numbers in Table I are produced by a small Fortran program.

It is interesting to see how fast the number of the central configurations increases as $n$ increases. Let $t_{n}$ be the total number of central configurations we find for some $n$ positive masses. Since local minima produce more central configurations when continued into positive masses, $t_{n}$ must be greater than the number obtained by considering all local minima as saddle points. In this way, we have a simple estimate:

$$
t_{n}>(n+2)!/ 24 \quad \text { for } \quad n \geqslant 4
$$

By a topological argument, Palmore  showed that there is a lower bound, $(3 n-4)(n-1)!/ 2$, on the numbers of central configurations for any choice of $n$ positive masses. It is interesting to note that the numbers that are actually found here far exceeds the lower bound as $n$ becomes large.

Observe that, for any $n \geqslant 4$, there are two open sets of $n$ positive masses such that all the corresponding central configurations are nondegenerate and the numbers of central configurations corresponding to these two sets are different. This shows the complexity of the problem of central configurations and also give us some information about degeneracy of central configurations.

Numbers of Central Configurations

| $n$ | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 |
| :-- | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| 2 Large masses | 34 | 294 | 3096 | 38,250 | $5,536,800$ | $9,036,729$ | $165,191,000$ |
| 3 Large masses | 38 | 374 | 4512 | 64,248 | $1,051,440$ | $19,399,000$ | $397,737,000$ |
