# 4. Measure of Degenerate Central Configuration 

A long-standing problem in central configurations of the $n$-body problem is whether there is only a finite number of central configurations for any choice of $n$ positive masses. This problem concerns the nature of degenerate central configurations. The first example of degenerate central configurations was given by Palmore  in a 4-body problem. By using some results of the last section, we can prove the following theorem concerning of the masses for which the degenerate central configuration exists.

Theorem. Let $\Sigma_{N}$ be the set of masses $\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{N}\right) \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{N}$ for which the degenerate central configuration exists; then $\Sigma_{N}$ has a positive $(N-1)$ dimensional Hausdorff measure.

This is a theorem of Palmore , but there is a step in his proof that seems difficult to complete. Here we give a different proof.

Proof. We have shown that for any $n \geqslant 4$, there exist $m \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{N}$ and $m^{*} \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{N}$, such that $m \notin \Sigma_{N}$ and $m^{*} \notin \Sigma_{N}$ and the numbers of central configurations corresponding to $m$ and $m^{*}$ are different. Let $\Gamma$ be any arc in $\mathbb{R}_{+}^{N}$ joining $m$ and $m^{*}$, then $\Gamma \cap \Sigma_{N} \neq \phi$; otherwise, by analytical continuation of the central configuration along the arc, we will get the same number for both $m$ and $m^{*}$ but that is impossible. This proves the theorem.

## 5. Some Remarks

While it seems impossible to find all central configurations and classify them for any choice of $n$ positive masses, the method we introduced here can solve this problem for at least some open sets of $n$ positive masses for any choice of $n$. It is amazing to see how fast the number of central confiigurations grows as $n$ increases.

Note that our open sets of masses consist of two or three large masses and a small mass, an even smaller mass, ..., and so on. An immediate way to extend our results is to consider three, four, or even more zero masses as a starting point, i.e., consider first the restricted $(N+n)$-body problem and find corresponding central configurations and then continue them into the full $(N+n)$-body problem. It turns out that, after some changing and rescaling of variables, the resulting equations are not much easier to solve than solving the original equations with $N+n$ positive masses. However, it might be interesting to solve the problem for $n=3$.

Finally, we remark that the above method can also be used to find the central configurations in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and in this way, the author suspects that the

nonplanar central configurations contribute most to the total number of central configurations as the number of bodies becomes large.

# On the central configurations of the planar $1+3$ body problem 

#### Abstract

We consider the Newtonian 4 body problem in the plane with a dominat mass $M$. We study the planar central configurations of this problem when the remaining masses are infinitesimal. We obtain two different classes of central configurations depending on the mutual distances between the infinitesimal masses. Both classes exhibit symmetric and non-symmetric configurations. And when two infinitesimal masses are equal, with the help of extended precision arithmetics, we provide evidence that the number of central configurations varies from five to seven.

## 1. Introduction

We study configurations with one massive central mass and several infinitesimal coorbital satellites describing the same circular orbit around the central massive mass. Such configurations are called relative equilibra, because in a rotation frame the satellites remain fixed. Recently these configurations have attracted the attention of astronomers. Renner and Sicardy (2004), suggest that the presence of coorbital satellites might explain, at least partly, the confinement of Neptune's ring arcs.

When the configuration of the coorbital satellites changes its size, but keep the shape, the motion is called homographic. In that case each satellite describe a Keplerian orbit around the central mass.

A configuration that allows relative equilibria and homographic motions is called a central configuration and equals to configurations such that the total Newtonian acceleration of every mass is equal to a constant multiplied by the position vector of this mass with respect to the center mass of the configuration, see (Lee and Santoprete, 2009) and the references quoted there.
(c) 2010 Kluwer Academic Publishers. Printed in the Netherlands.

The central configurations in the case of one large mass and $n$ infinitesimal arbitrary masses are called central configurations of the $1+n$ body problem.

Maxwell (Maxwell, 1859) studied the case of $n$ equal masses orbiting Saturn at a common radius and uniformly distributed about a cercle of this radius. He concluded that, for large $n$, the ring is stable if a convenient inequality between the mass of the ring and the mass of Saturn is satisfied. More recently, Moeckel (Moeckel, 1994) studied the linear stability of the $N$-body problem when the motion is a rotation about the center of mass and under the condition that all the masses except one become vanishingly small. Notice that the $1+n$ body problem is a particular case. Moeckel shows that the $1+n$-gon (when the small equal masses are uniformly distributed) is stable if and only if $n \geq 7$. For $n \leq 6$, he gives some exemples of the stable configurations where the small equal bodies are not uniformly distributed. Additionally Roberts (Roberts, 2000) carries the analysis a step further showing that the large mass has to grow proportionally to $n^{3}$ to ensure the linear stability. Such a criteria agrees with those given by Scheeres and Vinh (1991).

For large values of $n$, Hall (1988) shows that if $n \geq e^{27,000}$, then there is a unique class of central configurations, the regular $1+n$-gon. In (Casasayas, Llibre and Nunes, 1994) the same result is proved under the assumption that $n \geq e^{73}$.

When $n$ is small and the small masses are equal, in (Cors, Llibre and Ollé, 2004) the authors obtain numerically that the $1+n$-gon is the only configuration when $n \geq 9$. In the case $n=4$ they proved that there are only three symmetric central configurations. Recently Albouy and $\mathrm{Fu}(2009)$ proved that any central configuration of the $1+4$ body problem must be symmetric.

In (Renner and Sicardy, 2004) the authors removed the condition that the infinitesimal masses are identical and obtained results about the inverse problem, that is, given a configuration of the coorbital satellites, find the infinitesimal masses making it a central configuration. They also studied the linear stability.

In this paper we study the planar central configurations of the $1+$ 3 body problem without collision between two infinitesimal satellites when two infinitesimal masses are equal. The characterization of these central configurations is summarized in Section 5.

# 2. Definitions and equations 

In this section we present the equations of the central configurations of the $1+n$ body problem. More details can be found in (Casasayas, Llibre and Nunes, 1994) and (Cors, Llibre and Ollé, 2004).

Consider $N$ particles of masses $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ subject to their mutual Newtonian gravitational attraction. In an inertial reference frame with the origin at the center of mass of the $N$ bodies and choosing suitable units, the equations of motion of the $N$ body problem in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ are

$$
M q^{\prime \prime}=-V_{q}
$$

where $M$ is the mass matrix $M=\operatorname{diag}\left(m_{1}, m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}, m_{N}\right), q=$ $\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}\right)$ is the position vector with $q_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}, V$ the potential vector

$$
V\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}\right)=\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq N} \frac{m_{i} m_{j}}{\left\|q_{i}-q_{j}\right\|}
$$

and $V_{q}=\left(\partial V / \partial q_{1}, \ldots, \partial V / \partial q_{N}\right)$. Note that the Newtonian gravitational constant has been taken equal to one choosing conveniently the unit of time. Taking into account the singularities of equation (1), the configuration space of the planar $N$ body problem associated with the mass matrix $M$ is

$$
\mathcal{M}\left(m_{1}, \ldots, m_{N}\right)=\left\{q \in \mathbb{R}^{2 N}: \sum_{i=1}^{N} q_{i}=0, q_{i} \neq q_{j}, \quad \text { for } \quad i \neq j\right\}
$$

Given a matrix $M$, we say that $q \in \mathcal{M}$ represents a central configuration of the associated planar $N$ body problem if there exists a positive constant $\lambda^{2}$ such that

$$
M^{-1} V_{q}=\lambda^{2} q
$$

i.e., if the acceleration vector of every particle is directed towards the center of mass and its modulus is proportional to the distance from the particle to the center of mass. We shall denote by $\mathcal{C}$ the set of planar central configurations associated with a given mass matrix $M$. Notice that $\mathcal{C}$ is invariant with respect to homothetic transformations and rotations of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$. We shall denote by $\tilde{\mathcal{C}}$ the set of planar central configurations modulus the group $S O(2)$ of plane rotations.

Now we concentrate our interest on the central configurations of the planar $1+n$ body problem with infinitesimal unequal masses. That is, we consider $N=1+n$ and let $q(\varepsilon)=\left(q_{0}(\varepsilon), q_{1}(\varepsilon), \ldots, q_{n}(\varepsilon)\right) \in \tilde{\mathcal{C}}$ be a central configuration of the planar $1+n$ body problem with masses $m_{0}=1, m_{i}=\mu_{i} \varepsilon, i=1, \ldots, n$, which depends continuously on $\varepsilon$. We

say that $q=\left(q_{0}, q_{1}, \ldots, q_{N}\right)$ is a central configuration of the planar $1+n$ body problem if there exists $\lim _{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} q(\varepsilon)$ and this limit is equal to $q$.

The following two results can be found in the unpublished paper of Hall (1988) and in (Casasayas, Llibre and Nunes, 1994).

PROPOSITION 2.1. All the central configurations of the planar $1+n$ body problem lie on a circle centered at $q_{0}=0$.

Let $q=\left(q_{0}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$ be a central configuration of the planar $1+n$ body problem. We say that $q$ is non-collision if $q_{i} \neq q_{j}$ for $i \neq j$. That is, we exclude the possibility that the distance between two or more masses tends to zero as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$.

PROPOSITION 2.2. Let $q=\left(q_{0}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)$ be a non-collision central configuration of the planar $1+n$ body problem. Denoting by $\vartheta_{i}$ the angle defined by the position of $q_{i}$ for $i=1, \ldots, n$., we have

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq i}^{n} \mu_{j} \sin \left(\vartheta_{j}-\vartheta_{i}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{2} \sqrt{\left(1-\cos \left(\vartheta_{j}-\vartheta_{i}\right)\right)^{3}}}\right)=0
$$

for $i=1, \ldots, n$.
We call any solution $\left(\vartheta_{1}, \cdots, \vartheta_{n}\right)$ of system (2) a coorbital central configuration of the planar $1+n$ body problem. Since we are interested in central configurations modulus rotations and homothetic transformations, without loss of generality we can assume that the circle has radius 1 and that $\vartheta_{1}=0$. Then the configuration space of the coorbital central configurations of the planar $1+n$ body problem is

$$
\mathcal{A}=\left\{\left(\vartheta_{1}, \cdots, \vartheta_{n}\right) \in[0,2 \pi)^{n}: \vartheta_{1}=0, \vartheta_{i} \neq \vartheta_{j} \quad \text { for } \quad i \neq j\right\}
$$

The set $\mathcal{A}$ has $(n-1)$ ! connected components, each of which corresponds to a given permutation of the $n$ satellites on the circle. We shall consider one connected component of $\mathcal{A}$, i.e. a given counterclockwise ordering of the $n$ satellites. Without loss of generality we can assume that $0=\vartheta_{1}<$ $\vartheta_{2}<\cdots<\vartheta_{n}<2 \pi$. In this case it is natural to take as coordinates the angles between two consecutive satellites

$$
\theta_{i}=\vartheta_{i+1}-\vartheta_{i}, \quad i=1, \ldots, n-1
$$

Also it is convenient to work with an $n$th redundant coordinate angle

$$
\theta_{n}=2 \pi-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \theta_{i}
$$

which measures the angular distance between particle n and particle 1 . In this way the configuration space will be the simplex $S$ given by the intersection of the hyperplane $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \theta_{i}=2 \pi$ and the space $\left\{\left(\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{n}\right)\right.$ : $\left.\theta_{i}>0\right\}$.

In the coordinates $\left(\theta_{1}, \cdots, \theta_{n}\right)$ system (2) becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{2} f\left(\theta_{1}\right)+\mu_{3} f\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)+\cdots+\mu_{n} f\left(\theta_{1}+\ldots+\theta_{n-1}\right) & =0 \\
\mu_{3} f\left(\theta_{2}\right)+\mu_{4} f\left(\theta_{2}+\theta_{3}\right)+\cdots+\mu_{1} f\left(\theta_{2}+\ldots+\theta_{n}\right) & =0 \\
\mu_{4} f\left(\theta_{3}\right)+\mu_{5} f\left(\theta_{3}+\theta_{4}\right)+\cdots+\mu_{2} f\left(\theta_{3}+\ldots+\theta_{n}+\theta_{1}\right) & =0 \\
\cdots & \\
\mu_{1} f\left(\theta_{n}\right)+\mu_{2} f\left(\theta_{n}+\theta_{1}\right)+\cdots+\mu_{n-1} f\left(\theta_{n}+\theta_{1}+\cdots+\theta_{n-2}\right) & =0 \\
\theta_{1}+\cdots+\theta_{n} & =2 \pi
\end{aligned}
$$

where the function $f(\theta)=\sin \theta\left(1-\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{2} \sqrt{(1-\cos \theta)^{3}}}\right)$.
In the case of three satellites system (3) is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{2} f\left(\theta_{1}\right)+\mu_{3} f\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right) & =0 \\
\mu_{3} f\left(\theta_{2}\right)+\mu_{1} f\left(\theta_{2}+\theta_{3}\right) & =0 \\
\mu_{1} f\left(\theta_{3}\right)+\mu_{2} f\left(\theta_{3}+\theta_{1}\right) & =0 \\
\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}+\theta_{3} & =2 \pi
\end{aligned}
$$

or equivalently

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{2} f\left(\theta_{1}\right)-\mu_{3} f\left(\theta_{3}\right) & =0 \\
\mu_{3} f\left(\theta_{2}\right)-\mu_{1} f\left(\theta_{1}\right) & =0 \\
\mu_{1} f\left(\theta_{3}\right)-\mu_{2} f\left(\theta_{2}\right) & =0 \\
\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}+\theta_{3} & =2 \pi
\end{aligned}
$$

because $f(2 \pi-\theta)=-f(\theta)$.
Notice that the first three equations in (4) are linearly dependent. So one equation is irrelevant. We also chose the unit of mass so that $\mu_{3}=1$. Under these assumptions equations (4) are equivalent to the system

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{1} f\left(\theta_{1}\right)-f\left(\theta_{2}\right) & =0 \\
\mu_{2} f\left(\theta_{1}\right)-f\left(\theta_{3}\right) & =0 \\
\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}+\theta_{3} & =2 \pi
\end{aligned}
$$

Next results allows us to classify the coorbital central configurations of the $1+3$ body problem in two main classes, as we shall see latter on.

PROPOSITION 2.3. Let $\left(\theta_{1}, \theta_{2}, \theta_{3}\right)$ be a coorbital central configuration solution of system (5).

(i) If $f\left(\theta_{i}\right)=0$ for some $i=1,2,3$, then $\mu_{j}=0$ for some $j=1,2$.
(ii) The sign of $f\left(\theta_{i}\right)$ must be positive or negative for all $i=1,2,3$.

Proof. Suppose that $f\left(\theta_{1}\right)=0$, then from system (5) $f\left(\theta_{2}\right)=f\left(\theta_{3}\right)=0$. The zeros of the function $f$ are $\pi / 3, \pi$ and $5 \pi / 3$. Clearly the sum of any choice of these three values never equals to $2 \pi$.

Consider now $f\left(\theta_{2}\right)=0$. Then either $\mu_{1}=0$ or $f\left(\theta_{1}\right)=0$ (previous case). Finally if $f\left(\theta_{3}\right)=0$ implies, using the same argument, that $\mu_{2}=0$. So statement (i) follows

On the other hand, suppose that $f\left(\theta_{1}\right)<0$, then from system (5) clearly $f\left(\theta_{2}\right)<0$ and $f\left(\theta_{3}\right)<0$, as well. The other cases run in a similar way.

Proposition 2.3 says that any coorbital central configuration of the $1+3$ body problem cannot posses an angle $\theta_{i}$ equal to $\pi / 3, \pi$ or $5 \pi / 3$ for $i=1,2,3$.

COROLLARY 2.4. Let $\left(\theta_{1}, \theta_{2}, \theta_{3}\right)$ be a coorbital central configuration solution of system (5). Then either $\theta_{i} \in(\pi / 3, \pi)$ for all $i=1,2,3$, or two angles are less than $\pi / 3$ and the third belongs to the interval $(4 \pi / 3,5 \pi / 3)$.

Proof. This follows from the Proposition 2.3 and the plot of the function $f$.

In short, the $1+3$ body problem have two unconnected classes of coorbital central configurations. We call coorbital central configuration of class $A$ the one having two angles less than $\pi / 3$, and coorbital central configuration of class $B$ the one having the three angles greater than $\pi / 3$.

# 3. Symmetric central configurations 

A coorbital central configuration $\left(\theta_{1}, \theta_{2}, \ldots, \theta_{n}\right)$ of the planar $1+n$ body problem is symmetric with respect to a straight line $L$ containing the central body, if modulus a cyclic permutation of the angles we have, when $n$ is even either

$$
\theta_{1}=\theta_{n}, \quad \theta_{2}=\theta_{n-1}, \quad \ldots, \quad \theta_{\frac{n}{2}}=\theta_{\frac{n+2}{2}}
$$

(in this case the symmetry axis $L$ contains two satellites), or

$$
\theta_{1}=\theta_{n-1}, \quad \theta_{2}=\theta_{n-2}, \quad \ldots, \quad \theta_{\frac{n-2}{2}}=\theta_{\frac{n+2}{2}}, \quad \theta_{\frac{n}{2}}, \quad \theta_{n}
$$

(in this case the symmetry axis $L$ contains no satellites) and when $n$ is odd

$$
\theta_{1}=\theta_{n}, \quad \theta_{2}=\theta_{n-1}, \quad \ldots, \quad \theta_{\frac{n-1}{2}}=\theta_{\frac{n+3}{2}}
$$

(in this case the symmetry axis $L$ contains one satellite).
From the definition of symmetric coorbital central configuration in the case of three satellites the configuration is symmetric if and only if two of the angles $\left(\theta_{1}, \theta_{2}, \theta_{3}\right)$ are equal.

PROPOSITION 3.1. If the coorbital central configuration of the $1+3$ body problem is symmetric, with respect to a straight line $L$ containing the central body, then $\mu_{i}=\mu_{j}$ for some $i, j=1,2,3$ with $i \neq j$

Proof. Suppose that $\theta_{2}=\theta_{3}$ then from system (5) we have that $\mu_{1} f\left(\theta_{1}\right)=\mu_{2} f\left(\theta_{1}\right)$ and so $\mu_{1}=\mu_{2}$. Similar arguments can be used to prove cases $\theta_{1}=\theta_{2}$ or $\theta_{1}=\theta_{3}$.

Without loss of generality, we assume that $\mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=\mu$. So system (5) is equivalent to system

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu f\left(\theta_{1}\right)-f\left(\theta_{2}\right) & =0 \\
\mu f\left(\theta_{1}\right)-f\left(\theta_{3}\right) & =0 \\
\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}+\theta_{3} & =2 \pi
\end{aligned}
$$

By setting $\alpha=\theta / 2$ we see that $f(\theta)$ can be written as

$$
g(\alpha)=\frac{\cos \alpha}{4 \sin ^{2} \alpha}\left(8 \sin ^{3} \alpha-1\right)
$$

Let $\alpha_{1}=\theta_{1} / 2$ and $\alpha_{2}=\theta_{2} / 2$ and $\alpha_{3}=\theta_{3} / 2=\pi-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}$. By writing $g\left(\alpha_{3}\right)$ in terms of $\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$ we get

$$
g\left(\alpha_{3}\right)=\frac{\cos \left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\right)\left(1-8\left(\sin \left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\right)\right)^{3}\right)}{4\left(\sin \left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\right)\right)^{2}}
$$

where $\alpha_{1} \in(0, \pi)$ and $\alpha_{2} \in(0, \pi)$. Since $\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2} \neq 0$ and $\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2} \neq$ $\pi$ (notice that if $\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}=\pi$ then $\alpha_{3}=0$ which is not possible), the denominator of $g\left(\alpha_{3}\right)$ is different from zero. Let $e_{1}\left(\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2} ; \mu\right)=$ $\mu g\left(\alpha_{1}\right)-g\left(\alpha_{2}\right)$ and $e_{2}\left(\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{3} ; \mu\right)=\mu g\left(\alpha_{1}\right)-g\left(\alpha_{3}\right)$. The system (6) becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
& e_{1}\left(\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2} ; \mu\right)=0 \\
& e_{2}\left(\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{3} ; \mu\right)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2} \in(0, \pi)$ and $\alpha_{3}=\pi-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2} \in(0, \pi)$.
Under the assumption $\mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=\mu$, the symmetric coorbital central configurations satisfy $\theta_{2}=\theta_{3}$, or equivalently $\alpha_{2}=\alpha_{3}$. Analyzing the solutions of (7) with $\alpha_{2}=\alpha_{3}$ depending on the values of $\mu$ we obtain the following result.

PROPOSITION 3.2. Let $u_{1}=0.89616 \ldots$ The $1+3$ body problem has the following symmetric coorbital central configurations:
(a) One symmetric coorbital central configuration $A^{s}$ belonging to class $A$ for $\mu \in\left(0, u_{1}\right)$.
(b) Two symmetric coorbital central configurations for $\mu=u_{1}$, one belonging to class $A\left(A^{s}\right)$ and one belonging to class $B\left(B_{1,2}^{s}\right)$.
(c) Three symmetric coorbital central configurations for $\mu>u_{1}$, one belonging to class $A\left(A^{s}\right)$ and two belonging to class $B\left(B_{1}^{s}\right.$, $\left.B_{2}^{s}\right)$. The two symmetric coorbital central configurations of class $B$ coincide at $\mu=u_{1}$.

Proof. The proof is structured as follows. First, by using appropriate variables, we transform system (7) with $\alpha_{2}=\alpha_{3}$ into a system of polynomial equations. Then by using resultant theory we obtain all the values of $\mu$ at which the number of solutions of that system changes, and we count the number of solutions of the system for the different values of $\mu$. Finally we analyze the solution of the system in function of $\mu$.

The assumption $\alpha_{2}=\alpha_{3}$ implies that $\alpha_{1}=\pi-2 \alpha_{2}$, so $\alpha_{2} \in(0, \pi / 2)$. Since $\cos \alpha_{1}=\sin ^{2} \alpha_{2}-\cos ^{2} \alpha_{2}$ and $\sin \alpha_{1}=2 \sin \alpha_{2} \cos \alpha_{2}$, system (7) can be written in terms of $c=\cos \alpha_{2}$ and $s=\sin \alpha_{2}$. Then eliminating the denominators we get the following system equivalent to system (7)

$$
-s^{2} \mathcal{E}_{1}=0, \quad-s^{2}\left(c^{2}+s^{2}\right) \mathcal{E}_{2}=0, \quad F=0
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{E}_{1}= & 32 s^{3} c^{3}-4 c^{3}+\left(64 s^{3} c^{5}-64 s^{5} c^{3}-c^{2}+s^{2}\right) \mu \\
\mathcal{E}_{2}= & 32 s^{3} c^{9}+96 s^{5} c^{7}+96 s^{7} c^{5}+32 s^{9} c^{3}-4 c^{3} \\
& +\left(64 s^{3} c^{7}-c^{4}-64 s^{7} c^{3}+s^{4}\right) \mu \\
F= & c^{2}+s^{2}-1
\end{aligned}
$$

and $0<s \leqslant 1$ and $0 \leqslant c<1$ because $\alpha_{2} \in(0, \pi / 2)$. Clearly $c^{2}+s^{2} \neq 0$ and $s \neq 0$. Therefore system (8) can be written as

$$
\mathcal{E}_{1}=0, \quad \mathcal{E}_{2}=0, \quad F=0
$$

We perform the following substitutions: $c^{2}=1-s^{2}, c^{3}=c\left(1-s^{2}\right)$, $c^{4}=\left(1-s^{2}\right)^{2}, c^{5}=c\left(1-s^{2}\right)^{2}, c^{7}=c\left(1-s^{2}\right)^{3}$, and $c^{9}=c\left(1-s^{2}\right)^{4}$. After these substitutions $\mathcal{E}_{1}=\mathcal{E}_{2}$ and system (9) becomes $E=0, F=0$ where
$E=-32 c s^{5}+32 c s^{3}+4 c s^{2}-4 c+\left(128 c s^{7}-192 c s^{5}+64 c s^{3}+2 s^{2}-1\right) \mu$.

From now on instead of writing the system $E=0, F=0$, we also shall write $E=F=0$.

Using the resultant theory we can eliminate the variable $c$ in the equations $E=F=0$. The resultant of the polynomials $E$ and $F$ with respect to the variable $c$ is the polynomial

$$
\begin{aligned}
R= & \left(16384 s^{16}-65536 s^{14}+102400 s^{12}-77824 s^{10}+28672 s^{8}\right. \\
& \left.-4096 s^{6}+4 s^{4}-4 s^{2}+1\right) \mu^{2}+\left(-8192 s^{14}+28672 s^{12}\right. \\
& +1024 s^{11}-36864 s^{10}-3584 s^{9}+20480 s^{8}+4608 s^{7}-4096 s^{6} \\
& \left.-2560 s^{5}+512 s^{3}\right) \mu+1024 s^{12}-3072 s^{10}-256 s^{9}+3072 s^{8} \\
& +768 s^{7}-1008 s^{6}-768 s^{5}-48 s^{4}+256 s^{3}+48 s^{2}-16
\end{aligned}
$$

in the variables $s$ and $\mu$, and $R$ satisfies the following property: if $(c, s)=\left(c^{*}(\mu), s^{*}(\mu)\right)$ is a common root of the polynomials $E$ and $F$, then $s^{*}(\mu)$ is a root of the polynomial $R$ (see for instance (Lang, 1993) and (Olver, 1999) for more details on the resultant theory). Therefore the solutions of equation $R=0$ give at least all the values $s(\mu)$ of the common solutions $(c(\mu), s(\mu))$ of $E=F=0$. Notice that equation $R=0$ could also give solutions $s(\mu)$ that do not provide common solutions of $E=F=0$.

We are interested in the set of values of $\mu$ at which the number of real solutions $(c(\mu), s(\mu))$ of system $E=F=0$ changes. Since equation $R=0$ provides all the values $s(\mu)$ of the common solutions $(c(\mu), s(\mu))$ of $E=F=0$, the set of the values of $\mu$ at which the number of real solutions of $R=0$ changes contains at least all the values of $\mu$ at which the number of real solutions of $E=F=0$ changes.

The number of real solutions of $R=0$ can change only at the values of $\mu$ that provide solutions with multiplicity greater than 1 , that is, at the values of $\mu$ where $R=d R / d s=0$.

Again using resultant theory we can eliminate the variable $s$ in the system $R=d R / d s=0$. The resultant of the polynomials $R$ and $d R / d s$ with respect to $s$ is the polynomial

$$
H=k_{0} \mu^{34}(\mu-4)(\mu+4) H_{0}
$$

where $k_{0} \neq 0$ is a large constant and $H_{0}$ is the following polynomial of degree 22

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_{0}= & 544400220773632720896 \mu^{22}-11491835434562035187712 \mu^{20} \\
& +2898856085837444554752 \mu^{19}+45101390498475214934016 \mu^{18} \\
& -50207178662075239133184 \mu^{17}-3597828247551090484224 \mu^{16} \\
& +54441252684647804362752 \mu^{15}-90330266881601149980672 \mu^{14}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& +105029467560226902200832 \mu^{13}-87060482984162666161152 \mu^{12} \\
& +53192685061230729315840 \mu^{11}-25608023464518181047260 \mu^{10} \\
& +9249906747903520991616 \mu^{9}-1771852062223329593868 \mu^{8} \\
& -159500845521348320736 \mu^{7}+119990316536124348321 \mu^{6} \\
& +12123699015371647968 \mu^{5}-11384652544065195120 \mu^{4} \\
& +400296455761238280 \mu^{3}+345472406710968960 \mu^{2} \\
& +2678966190976320 \mu-8438743501575408
\end{aligned}
$$

By the properties of the resultant, the solutions of equation $H=0$ provide at least all the values of $\mu$ of the common solutions $(s, \mu)$ of system $R=d R / d s=0$, although they also can provide values of $\mu$ that do not correspond to common solutions of the system. Therefore the real solutions of $H=0$ with $\mu>0$ provide all the possible values of $\mu$ at which the number of real solutions of system $R=0$ changes.

We compute all the solutions of the polynomial equation $H_{0}=0$ with the help of Mathematica and we find 22 different solutions of which only 3 are real solutions with $\mu>0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu & =u_{1}=0.8961616399532140 \ldots \\
\mu & =u_{2}=1.2506375233635711 \ldots \\
\mu & =u_{4}=4.0000142922001194 \ldots
\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, equation $H=0$ has the additional real solution with $\mu>0$

$$
\mu=u_{3}=4
$$

In short there are four possible values of $\mu$ at which the number of real solutions of $E=F=0$ could change, $\mu=u_{1}, u_{2}, u_{3}, u_{4}$.

Since we only are interested in studying the solutions of $E=F=0$ satisfying $0<s \leqslant 1$ and $0 \leqslant c<1$ we need to control not only the changes in the number of real solutions of the system $E=F=$ 0 without constraints. We also need to control when a real solution $(s(\mu), c(\mu))$ starts to satisfy the conditions $0<s \leqslant 1$ and $0 \leqslant c<1$ for some values of $\mu$.

Next we find values of $\mu$ where the number of real solutions of system $E=F=0$ does not change but the number of real solutions satisfying $0<s \leqslant 1$ and $0 \leqslant c<1$ can change. For doing that, since all the solutions $s(\mu)$ of $E=F=0$ are solutions of $R=0$, we find the values of $\mu$ at which either $s=0$ or $s=1$ is a solution of $R=0$. Evaluating $R=0$ at $s=0$ and $s=1$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left.R\right|_{s=0}=\mu^{2}-16=0 \\
& \left.R\right|_{s=1}=\mu^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the unique values of $\mu$ at which the number of real solutions of system $E=F=0$ satisfying $0<s \leqslant 1$ and $0 \leqslant c<1$ can change are $\mu=u_{1}, u_{2}, u_{3}, u_{4}$.

Finally we compute the number of real solutions of system $E=F=$ 0 satisfying $0<s \leqslant 1$ and $0 \leqslant c<1$ at values $\mu=\left\{v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}, v_{4}, v_{5}\right\}$ with $0<v_{1}<u_{1}<v_{2}<u_{2}<v_{3}<u_{3}<v_{4}<u_{4}<v_{5}$ in the following way. Let Res $$ denote the resultant of the polynomials $P$ and $Q$ with respect to $X$. Fixed $\mu=v_{i}$ we compute the resultants Res $$ and Res $$, which are polynomials of the single variable $c$ and $s$ respectively. Using the properties of resultants, if $\left(c_{0}, s_{0}\right)$ is a solution of system $E=F=0$, then $\operatorname{Res}\left(c_{0}\right)=0$ and $\operatorname{Res}\left(s_{0}\right)=0$. We compute with the help of Mathematica all the solutions of the polynomial equations $\operatorname{Res}=0$ and $\operatorname{Res}=0$. Finally we check which pairs $(c, s)$ formed by a real solution $c$ of $\operatorname{Res}=0$ with $0 \leqslant c<1$ and a real solution $s$ of $\operatorname{Res}=0$ with $0<s \leqslant 1$ provide a solution of system $E=F=0$. Using this procedure for each $v_{i}, i=1, \ldots, 5$ we get one solution for $\mu=v_{1}$ and three solutions for $\mu=\left\{v_{2}, v_{3}, v_{4}, v_{5}\right\}$, so the number of real solutions of system $E=F=0$ with $0<s \leqslant 1$ and $0 \leqslant c<1$ changes at $\mu=u_{1}$.

Analyzing the solutions of system $E=F=0$ as a function of $\mu$ we observe that the solution $(s(\mu), c(\mu))$ that we have obtained for $0<\mu<u_{1}$ persists for all $\mu$ and it gives a family of symmetric coorbital central configurations of class $A$, denoted by $A^{s}$. At $\mu=u_{1}$ appears a new symmetric coorbital central configuration of class $B$, denoted by $B^{s}$ which bifurcates in two families of symmetric coorbital central configurations, denoted by $B_{1}^{s}$ and $B_{2}^{s}$ for $\mu>u_{1}$. See Figures 1 and 2 where the angles $\theta_{1}(\mu)$ and $\theta_{2}(\mu)$ have been computed. Also see Figures 3 and 4 where qualitative pictures of coorbital central configurations have been plotted for different values of $\mu$.

# 4. Non-symmetric central configurations 

In Section 3 we have analyzed the symmetric coorbital central configurations of the $1+3$ body problem and we have found the value of $\mu$ at which the number of symmetric coorbital central configurations changes. Here we analyze the values $\mu$ where the number of coorbital central configurations change independently if such configurations are symmetric or not. In particular we prove the following result.

PROPOSITION 4.1. The following statements hold.
(a) At $\mu=1.4238513 \ldots$, the symmetric coorbital central configuration $B_{1}^{s}$ given in Proposition 3.2, bifurcates to two non-symmetric

coorbital central configurations $\left(B_{1}, B_{2}\right)$, which persist for all $\mu \in$ $(0,1.4238513 \ldots)$.
(b) From the non-symmetric coorbital central configurations of the $1+3$ body problem do not bifurcate any non-symmetric coorbital central configurations.

Proof. System (7) can be written in terms of $c_{1}=\cos \alpha_{1}$ and $s_{1}=$ $\sin \alpha_{1}, c_{2}=\cos \alpha_{2}$ and $s_{2}=\sin \alpha_{2}$, then by eliminating the denominators and by doing the substitutions

$$
\begin{aligned}
& c_{1}^{2}=1-s_{1}^{2}, c_{1}^{3}=c_{1}\left(1-s_{1}^{2}\right), c_{1}^{4}=\left(1-s_{1}^{2}\right)^{2} \\
& c_{2}^{2}=1-s_{2}^{2}, c_{2}^{3}=c_{1}\left(1-s_{2}^{2}\right), c_{2}^{4}=\left(1-s_{2}^{2}\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

system (7) is equivalent to system $E_{1}=E_{2}=F_{1}=F_{2}=0$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{1}= & -8 c_{2} s_{1}^{2} s_{2}^{3}+c_{2} s_{1}^{2}+\left(8 c_{1} s_{1}^{3} s_{2}^{2}-c_{1} s_{2}^{2}\right) \mu \\
E_{2}= & 64 c_{2} s_{2}^{2} s_{1}^{6}-32 c_{2} s_{2} s_{1}^{6}+64 c_{1} s_{2}^{4} s_{1}^{5}-64 c_{1} s_{2}^{2} s_{1}^{5}+8 c_{1} s_{1}^{5}-64 c_{2} s_{2}^{3} s_{1}^{4} \\
& +24 c_{2} s_{2} s_{1}^{4}-32 c_{1} s_{2}^{4} s_{1}^{3}+24 c_{1} s_{2}^{2} s_{1}^{3}+s_{2} s_{1}^{3}+8 c_{2} s_{2}^{3} s_{1}^{2}-c_{1} c_{2} s_{1}^{2} \\
& +\left(-16 c_{2} s_{2} s_{1}^{6}-16 c_{1} s_{2}^{2} s_{1}^{5}+8 c_{1} s_{1}^{5}+16 c_{2} s_{2} s_{1}^{4}+8 c_{1} s_{2}^{2} s_{1}^{3}\right. \\
& \left.+2 c_{2} s_{2} s_{1}^{3}+2 c_{1} s_{2}^{2} s_{1}^{2}-c_{1} s_{1}^{2}-2 c_{2} s_{2} s_{1}-c_{1} s_{2}^{2}\right) \mu \\
F_{1}= & c_{1}^{2}+s_{1}^{2}-1 \\
F_{2}= & c_{2}^{2}+s_{2}^{2}-1
\end{aligned}
$$

We are interested in solutions of this system with $0<s_{1} \leqslant 1,0<s_{2} \leqslant$ $1,-1<c_{1}<1,-1<c_{2}<1$, and such that $\alpha_{3}=\pi-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2} \in(0, \pi)$, here $\alpha_{i}=\arctan \left(s_{i} / c_{i}\right)$ when $s_{i} / c_{i}>0$ and $\alpha_{i}=\arctan \left(s_{i} / c_{i}\right)+\pi$ when $s_{i} / c_{i}<0, i=1,2$. Next we will find the values of $\mu$ at which the number of real solutions of system $E_{1}=E_{2}=F_{1}=F_{2}=0$ satisfying those conditions changes. First we find the values of $\mu$ at which the number of real solutions of $E_{1}=E_{2}=F_{1}=F_{2}=0$ changes.

We eliminate the variable $c_{1}$ by doing the resultants

$$
R_{1}=\operatorname{Res}\left[E_{1}, E_{2}, c_{1}\right], R_{2}=\operatorname{Res}\left[E_{1}, F_{1}, c_{1}\right], R_{3}=\operatorname{Res}\left[E_{1}, F_{2}, c_{1}\right]
$$

Next we eliminate the variable $c_{2}$ by doing the resultants

$$
S_{1}=\operatorname{Res}\left[R_{3}, R_{1}, c_{2}\right], S_{2}=\operatorname{Res}\left[R_{3}, R_{2}, c_{2}\right]
$$

The factorization of the polynomials $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ contains factors with multiplicity greater than 1 . We define two new polynomials $\bar{S}_{1}$ and $\bar{S}_{2}$ as the polynomials that contain exactly the same factors than $S_{1}$ and

$S_{2}$ but all of them with multiplicity one. Then we eliminate the variable $s_{2}$ by doing the resultant

$$
T=\operatorname{Res}\left[\bar{S}_{1}, \bar{S}_{2}, s_{2}\right]
$$

The factorization of $T$ is formed by a large constant, a power of $\mu$ and five factors in the variables $s_{1}$ and $\mu$. We eliminate the constant, the power of $\mu$ (we are only interested in solutions with $\mu>0$ ) and the multiplicities of the factors and we obtain a new polynomial

$$
\bar{T}=\bar{T}_{1} \cdot \bar{T}_{2} \cdot \bar{T}_{3} \cdot \bar{T}_{4} \cdot \bar{T}_{5}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{T}_{1}= & s_{1} \\
\bar{T}_{2}= & 2 s_{1}-1 \\
\bar{T}_{3}= & 4 s_{1}^{2}+2 s_{1}+1 \\
\bar{T}_{4}= & \left(4096 s_{1}^{16}-8192 s_{1}^{14}-2048 s_{1}^{13}+4096 s_{1}^{12}+4096 s_{1}^{11}+384 s_{1}^{10}\right. \\
& -2048 s_{1}^{9}-768 s_{1}^{8}-32 s_{1}^{7}+384 s_{1}^{6}+64 s_{1}^{5}+s_{1}^{4}-32 s_{1}^{3}-2 s_{1}^{2} \\
& +1) \mu^{4}+\left(2048 s_{1}^{14}-2048 s_{1}^{12}-512 s_{1}^{11}-768 s_{1}^{10}+512 s_{1}^{9}\right. \\
& +1824 s_{1}^{8}+192 s_{1}^{7}-1056 s_{1}^{6}-448 s_{1}^{5}-12 s_{1}^{4}+256 s_{1}^{3}+28 s_{1}^{2} \\
& -16) \mu^{2}+\left(256 s_{1}^{10}-1280 s_{1}^{8}-32 s_{1}^{7}+1024 s_{1}^{6}+160 s_{1}^{5}\right. \\
& \left.-128 s_{1}^{3}\right) \mu+256 s_{1}^{12}+192 s_{1}^{8}-252 s_{1}^{6}
\end{aligned}
$$

and $\bar{T}_{5}$ is a polynomial depending on $s_{1}$ and $\mu$ of degree 44 in the variable $s_{1}$.

By the properties of resultants, the new equation $\bar{T}=0$ contains all the values $s_{1}(\mu)$ of the solutions $\left(c_{1}(\mu), s_{1}(\mu), c_{2}(\mu), s_{2}(\mu)\right)$ of the system $E_{1}=E_{2}=F_{1}=F_{2}=0$ and probably values $s_{1}(\mu)$ that do not provide solutions of the initial system. Therefore the values of $\mu$ at which the number of real solutions of $E_{1}=E_{2}=F_{1}=F_{2}=0$ changes are also values of $\mu$ at which the number of real solutions of $T=0$ changes.

The number of real solutions of $\bar{T}=0$ can change either at the values of $\mu$ at which a real root of a factor $\bar{T}_{i}$ has multiplicity greater than one, or at the values of $\mu$ at which a real root of a factor $\bar{T}_{i}$ is also a root of a factor $\bar{T}_{j}$ with $i \neq j$.

Clearly the root of the factor $\bar{T}_{1}, s_{1}=0$ is not a root of the factors $\bar{T}_{2}$ and $\bar{T}_{3}$. Moreover

$$
\left.\bar{T}_{4}\right|_{s_{1}=0}=\mu^{4}-16 \mu^{2},\left.\quad \bar{T}_{5}\right|_{s_{1}=0}=-\mu^{10}-4 \mu^{8}
$$

So $\mu=4$ is the unique value of $\mu>0$ at which the root of the factor $\bar{T}_{1}$ is a root of some of the other factors. Proceeding in a similar way for the root of the factor $\bar{T}_{2}, s_{1}=1 / 2$, we get

$$
\left.\bar{T}_{3}\right|_{s_{1}=1 / 2}=3,\left.\quad \bar{T}_{4}\right|_{s_{1}=1 / 2}=-25 / 8,\left.\quad \bar{T}_{5}\right|_{s_{1}=1 / 2}=2197 / 4096
$$

so $s_{1}=1 / 2$ is only root of the factor $\bar{T}_{2}$. The roots of factor $\bar{T}_{3}$ are non-real, therefore we do not consider them.

Next we compute at which values of $\mu>0$ there are real roots of $\bar{T}_{4}$ that are roots of $\bar{T}_{5}$ by solving the polynomial equation $\operatorname{Res}\left[\bar{T}_{4}, \bar{T}_{5}, s_{1}\right]=$ 0 and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{1}=0.1325450004033988 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{3}=0.1541643785502070 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{6}=0.5250057176263389 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{8}=0.6784610926616778 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{13}=1.0011322554499964 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{15}=1.0076481112559950 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{16}=1.0606474258429618 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{19}=1.4238513421761745 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{20}=2.5123408303563733 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{21}=3.2950663210056425 \ldots
\end{aligned}
$$

Now we find the values of $\mu>0$ at which the factor $\bar{T}_{4}$ has real roots with multiplicity greater than ones by solving the polynomial equation $\operatorname{Res}\left[\bar{T}_{4}, \partial \bar{T}_{4} / \partial s_{1}, s_{1}\right]=0$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{5}=0.4816163432110476 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{7}=0.6154472608017034 \ldots \\
& \mu=u_{1}=\widetilde{u}_{10}=0.8961616399532140 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{11}=0.8977353306077976 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{17}=1.2506375233635711 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{18}=1.2615567635193134 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{22}=4 \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{23}=4.0000142922001194 \ldots

$$

Finally we find the values of $\mu>0$ at which the factor $\bar{T}_{5}$ has real roots with multiplicity greater than ones by solving the polynomial equation $\operatorname{Res}\left[\bar{T}_{5}, \partial \bar{T}_{5} / \partial s_{1}, s_{1}\right]=0$ and we get

$$
\mu=\widetilde{u}_{2}=0.1424427964946848 \ldots
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{4}=0.2055692659990572 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{9}=0.6791080539220485 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{12}=0.9939202640321302 \ldots \\
& \mu=\widetilde{u}_{14}=1.0072825044062513 \ldots
\end{aligned}
$$

In short, the possible values of $\mu>0$ at which the number of real solutions of $\bar{T}=0$ can change are $\mu=\widetilde{u}_{i}$ for $i=1, \ldots, 23$.

We are interested in the values of $\mu$ at which the number of real solutions of $E_{1}=E_{2}=F_{1}=F_{2}=0$ with $0<s_{1} \leqslant 1,0<s_{2} \leqslant 1$, $-1<c_{1}<1,-1<c_{2}<1$, and $\alpha_{3}=\pi-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2} \in(0, \pi)$. Using the same argument as in Section 3 we need to control not only the changes in the number of real solutions of the system $E_{1}=E_{2}=F_{1}=F_{2}=0$ without constraints. We also need to control when a real solution starts to satisfy the conditions $0<s_{j} \leqslant 1$ and $-1<c_{j}<1, j=1,2$ for some values of $\mu$. Since the set of real solutions $s_{1}(\mu)$ of system $E_{1}=E_{2}=F_{1}=F_{2}=0$ is contained in the set of real solutions of $\bar{T}=0$, in order to find these last possible values of $\mu$ it is sufficient to find the values $\mu$ at which a solution $s_{1}(\mu)$ of $\bar{T}=0$ satisfies that $s_{1}(\mu)=0$ or $s_{1}(\mu)=1$. Notice that $s_{1}=0$ is a solution of $\bar{T}=0$ but this solution does not depend on $\mu$ so we do not consider it. Evaluating $\bar{T} / s_{1}$ at $s=0$ and $s=1$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left.\left(\bar{T} / s_{1}\right)\right|_{s_{1}=0} & =-\left(\mu^{4}-16 \mu^{2}\right)\left(-\mu^{10}-4 \mu^{8}\right) \\
\left.\left(\bar{T} / s_{1}\right)\right|_{s_{1}=1} & =92747200
\end{aligned}
$$

So we do not obtain new possible values of $\mu$ at which the number of solutions real solutions of the system $E_{1}=E_{2}=F_{1}=F_{2}=0$ with satisfying the desired conditions changes.

Finally we compute the number of real solutions of the system $E_{1}=$ $E_{2}=F_{1}=F_{2}=0$ with $0<s_{1} \leqslant 1,0<s_{2} \leqslant 1,-1<c_{1}<$ $1,-1<c_{2}<1$, and $\alpha_{3}=\pi-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2} \in(0, \pi)$ at values $\mu=v_{i}$ with $v_{1} \in\left(0, \widetilde{u}_{1}\right), v_{i+1} \in\left(\widetilde{u}_{i}, \widetilde{u}_{i+1}\right)$ for $i=1, \ldots, 23$ and $v_{24}>\widetilde{u}_{23}$ by proceeding of the following way. System (7) can be written in terms of $c_{1}=\cos \alpha_{1}$ and $s_{1}=\sin \alpha_{1}, c_{2}=\cos \alpha_{2}$ and $s_{2}=\sin \alpha_{2}$. In order to simplify our computations we introduce two new variables $z_{1}=e^{i \alpha_{1}}$ and $z_{2}=e^{i \alpha_{2}}$ where $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Using these variables, $\cos \alpha_{j}=\left(z_{j}^{2}+\right.$ 1) $/\left(2 z_{j}\right)$ and $\sin \alpha_{j}=\left(z_{j}^{2}-1\right) /\left(2 i z_{j}\right)$ for $j=1,2$. Then by doing the previous substitutions and by eliminating the denominators system (7) is equivalent to system $\bar{e}_{1}=\bar{e}_{2}=0$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{e}_{1}= & i z_{1}^{6} z_{2}^{8}-2 i z_{1}^{4} z_{2}^{8}+i z_{1}^{2} z_{2}^{8}-2 i z_{1}^{6} z_{2}^{6}+4 i z_{1}^{4} z_{2}^{6}-2 i z_{1}^{2} z_{2}^{6}-z_{1}^{6} z_{2}^{5}+2 z_{1}^{4} z_{2}^{5} \\
& -z_{1}^{2} z_{2}^{5}-z_{1}^{6} z_{2}^{3}+2 z_{1}^{4} z_{2}^{3}-z_{1}^{2} z_{2}^{3}+2 i z_{1}^{6} z_{2}^{2}-4 i z_{1}^{4} z_{2}^{2}+2 i z_{1}^{2} z_{2}^{2}-i z_{1}^{6}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& +2 i z_{1}^{4}-i z_{1}^{2}+\left(-i z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{8}+2 i z_{2}^{4} z_{1}^{8}-i z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{8}+2 i z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{6}-4 i z_{2}^{4} z_{1}^{6}\right. \\
& +2 i z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{6}+z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{5}-2 z_{2}^{4} z_{1}^{5}+z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{5}+z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{3}-2 z_{2}^{4} z_{1}^{3}+z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{3}-2 i z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{2} \\
& \left.+4 i z_{2}^{4} z_{1}^{2}-2 i z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{2}+i z_{2}^{6}-2 i z_{2}^{4}+i z_{2}^{2}\right) \mu \\
\overline{\boldsymbol{e}}_{2}= & i-i z_{2}^{8} z_{1}^{12}+2 i z_{2}^{8} z_{1}^{10}+2 i z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{10}+z_{2}^{5} z_{1}^{9}-i z_{2}^{8} z_{1}^{8}-4 i z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{8}-2 z_{2}^{5} z_{1}^{7} \\
& +z_{2}^{3} z_{1}^{7}+2 i z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{6}-2 i z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{6}+z_{2}^{5} z_{1}^{5}-2 z_{2}^{3} z_{1}^{5}+4 i z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{4}+i z_{1}^{4}+z_{2}^{3} z_{1}^{3} \\
& -2 i z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{2}-2 i z_{1}^{2}+\left(-i z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{12}+2 i z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{10}+2 i z_{2}^{4} z_{1}^{10}+z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{9}\right. \\
& -4 i z_{2}^{4} z_{1}^{8}-i z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{8}+z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{7}-2 z_{2}^{4} z_{1}^{7}-2 i z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{6}+2 i z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{6}-2 z_{2}^{4} z_{1}^{5} \\
& \left.+z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{5}+i z_{2}^{6} z_{1}^{4}+4 i z_{2}^{4} z_{1}^{4}+z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{3}-2 i z_{2}^{4} z_{1}^{2}-2 i z_{2}^{2} z_{1}^{2}+i z_{2}^{2}\right) \mu
\end{aligned}
$$

and $\left|z_{1}\right|=\left|z_{2}\right|=1$. Since we are interested in solutions of (7) with $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2} \in(0, \pi)$ and $\alpha_{3}=\pi-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2} \in(0, \pi)$, we only consider solutions of $\bar{e}_{1}=\bar{e}_{2}=0$ with $\left|z_{1}\right|=\left|z_{2}\right|=1$ such that $\operatorname{Im}\left(z_{1}\right), \operatorname{Im}\left(z_{2}\right)>0$ and $\alpha_{3}=\pi-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2} \in(0, \pi)$ where $\alpha_{i}=\arctan \left(\operatorname{Im}\left(z_{i}\right) / \operatorname{Re}\left(z_{i}\right)\right)$ when $\operatorname{Im}\left(z_{i}\right) / \operatorname{Re}\left(z_{i}\right)>0$ and $\alpha_{i}=\arctan \left(\operatorname{Im}\left(z_{i}\right) / \operatorname{Re}\left(z_{i}\right)\right)+\pi$ when $\operatorname{Im}\left(z_{i}\right) / \operatorname{Re}\left(z_{i}\right)<0, i=1,2$.

Fixed $\mu=v_{i}$ for $i=1, \ldots, 24$ we solve the polynomial system $\bar{e}_{1}=\bar{e}_{2}=0$ by means of resultants. With the help of Mathematica, we compute the resultants $\operatorname{Res}\left[\bar{e}_{1}, \bar{e}_{2}, z_{1}\right]$ and $\operatorname{Res}\left[\bar{e}_{1}, \bar{e}_{2}, z_{2}\right]$, which are polynomials of the single variable $z_{2}$ and $z_{1}$ respectively. Then we compute all the solutions of the polynomial equations $\operatorname{Res}\left[\bar{e}_{1}, \bar{e}_{2}, z_{1}\right]=0$ and $\operatorname{Res}\left[\bar{e}_{1}, \bar{e}_{2}, z_{2}\right]=0$. We check which pairs $\left(z_{1}, z_{2}\right)$ formed by a solution $z_{2}$ of $\operatorname{Res}\left[\bar{e}_{1}, \bar{e}_{2}, z_{1}\right]=0$ and a solution $z_{1}$ of $\operatorname{Res}\left[\bar{e}_{1}, \bar{e}_{2}, z_{2}\right]=0$ provide a solution of system $\bar{e}_{1}=\bar{e}_{2}=0$. Finally we chose the solutions $\left(z_{1}, z_{2}\right)$ of system $\bar{e}_{1}=\bar{e}_{2}=0$ satisfying the conditions $\left|z_{1}\right|=\left|z_{2}\right|=1$, $\operatorname{Im}\left(z_{1}\right), \operatorname{Im}\left(z_{2}\right)>0$ and $\alpha_{3}=\pi-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2} \in(0, \pi)$.

After all these computations we get the following: system $\bar{e}_{1}=$ $\bar{e}_{2}=0$ has 5 solutions for $\mu=v_{1}, \ldots, v_{10}$, four corresponding to nonsymmetric coorbital central configuration and one corresponding to a symmetric one; it has 7 solutions for $\mu=v_{11}, \ldots, v_{19}$, four corresponding to non-symmetric coorbital central configurations and three corresponding to symmetric ones; it has 5 solutions for $\mu=v_{20}, \ldots, v_{24}$, two corresponding to non-symmetric coorbital central configurations and three corresponding to symmetric ones. So the number of solutions of system $\bar{e}_{1}=\bar{e}_{2}=0$ satisfying the desired conditions changes at $\mu=\widetilde{u}_{10}=u_{1}$ and at $\mu=\widetilde{u}_{19}$.

We remark that we have studied all the bifurcations values using the changes of solutions in the variable $s_{1}$, we have a similar study using the changes of solutions in the variable $s_{2}$, obtaining exactly the same results.

Notice that $\mu=u_{1}$ is the bifurcation value that we have obtained in Section 3. Analyzing the solutions of system $\bar{e}_{1}=\bar{e}_{2}=0$ as a function of $\mu$ in a neighbourhood of $\mu=u_{1}$ and $\mu=\widetilde{u}_{19}$ we observe the following. In a neighbourhood of $\mu=u_{1}$ the four solutions corresponding to non-symmetric coorbital central configurations that we have found for $\mu<u_{1}$ persist when $\mu \geqslant u_{1}$, and at $\mu=u_{1}$ appears a new solution that bifurcates into two ones for $\mu>u_{1}$ providing symmetric coorbital central configurations. Two of the four solutions corresponding to non-symmetric coorbital central configurations that we have found for $\mu<\widetilde{u}_{19}$ match to one of the solutions providing a symmetric coorbital central configuration at $\mu=\widetilde{u}_{19}$ and these last solution persist for $\mu>\widetilde{u}_{19}$. In short, at $\mu=\widetilde{u}_{19}$ a symmetric coorbital central configuration bifurcates to two non-symmetric ones for $\mu<\widetilde{u}_{19}$. This proves statements (a), and since there is no other bifurcation value (except $\mu=u_{1}$ ) it follows statement (b).

Analyzing the solutions of system $E_{1}=E_{2}=F_{1}=F_{2}=0$ (or equivalently of system $\bar{e}_{1}=\bar{e}_{2}=0$ ) as a function of $\mu$ we observe that we have five families of coorbital central configurations for $\mu<u_{1}$, the symmetric family $A^{\mathrm{s}}$ found in Section 3, two non-symmetric families of class $A$ denoted by $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ and two non-symmetric families of class $B$ denoted by $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$; seven families of coorbital central configurations for $u_{1}<\mu<\widetilde{u}_{19}$, the symmetric family $A^{s}$, the two symmetric families $B_{1}^{s}$ and $B_{2}^{s}$ found in Section 3, which match at $\mu=u_{1}$, plus the four non-symmetric families $A_{1}, A_{2}, B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$; and finally five families of coorbital central configurations for $\mu>\widetilde{u}_{19}$, the three symmetric families $A^{s}, B_{1}^{s}$ and $B_{2}^{s}$ plus the two non-symmetric families $A_{1}, A_{2}$. We note that the two non-symmetric families $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ match at $\mu=\widetilde{u}_{19}$ to one of the symmetric families of class $B$, exactly $B_{1}^{s}$. Again see Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4.

# 5. Conclusions 

We have derived results concerning to the number of coorbital central configurations of the planar $1+3$ body problem when two infinitesimal masses are equal, that is, $m_{1}=m_{2}=\mu$ and $m_{3}=1$. The problem exhibits two unconnected classes of central configurations denoted $A$, when two angles are less than $\pi / 3$ and $B$, when the three angles are greater than $\pi / 3$. Each class have symmetric (denoted by $A^{s}, B_{1}^{s}$ and $B_{2}^{s}$ ) and non-symmetric configurations.

The results obtained in Sections 3 and 4 can be summarized as follows.

The coorbital central configurations of the $1+3$ body problem with two equal infinitesimal masses are the following ones.
(a) For $\mu \in(0,0.89616 \ldots)$ there are 5 coorbital central configurations, 3 of class $A\left(A^{s}, A_{1}\right.$ and $\left.A_{2}\right)$ and 2 of class $B\left(B_{1}\right.$ and $\left.B_{2}\right)$.
(b) For $\mu=0.89616 \ldots$ there are 6 coorbital central configurations, 3 of class $A\left(A^{s}, A_{1}\right.$ and $\left.A_{2}\right)$ and 3 of class $B\left(B_{1}, B_{2}\right.$ and $\left.B_{1,2}^{s}\right)$.
(c) For $\mu \in(0.89616 \ldots, 1.42385 \ldots)$ there are 7 coorbital central configurations, 3 of class $A\left(A^{s}, A_{1}\right.$ and $\left.A_{2}\right)$ and 4 of class $B\left(B_{1}, B_{2}\right.$, $B_{1}^{s}$ and $\left.B_{2}^{s}\right)$.
(d) For $\mu=1.42385 \ldots$ there are 5 coorbital central configurations, 3 of class $A\left(A^{s}, A_{1}\right.$ and $\left.A_{2}\right)$ and 2 of class $B\left(B_{1}^{s}\right.$ and $\left.B_{2}^{s}\right)$.
(e) For $\mu>1.42385 \ldots$ there are 5 coorbital central configurations, 3 of class $A\left(A^{s}, A_{1}\right.$ and $\left.A_{2}\right)$ and two of class $B\left(B_{1}^{s}\right.$ and $\left.B_{2}^{s}\right)$.

Notice that the proof of the results stated are analytical with the exception that we have computed numerically the real roots of some polynomials of one variable. For all polynomials of one variable that we have found we have computed (with mathematica) as many roots as of its degree (of course some are complex), we have checked that every root obtained once it is substituted in its polynomial, this vanishes. We have done these computations with 100 decimals for each root. We thus provide numerical evidence that we have obtained all the real roots of the polynomials that we have studied and that we do not forget any real root.

In order to see how the classes $A$ and $B$ of the coorbital central configurations change in function of the parameter $\mu$, we have computed numerically the values of the angles $\theta_{1}(\mu)$ and $\theta_{2}(\mu)$, for each family of coorbital central configurations, see Figures 1 and 2.

In Figures 3 and 4 qualitative pictures of the classes $A$ and $B$ of the coorbital central configurations are showed for different values of $\mu$.

Figure 2. The angles $\theta_{1}(\mu)$ and $\theta_{2}(\mu)$ along the class $B$.

# Twisted angles for central configurations formed by two twisted regular polygons* 

## A B S T R A C T

In this paper, we study the necessary conditions and sufficient conditions for the twisted angles of the central configurations formed by two twisted regular polygons, in particular, we prove that for the 2 N -body problem, the twisted angles must be $\theta=0$ or $\theta=\pi / N$.

## 1. Introduction and main results

The problem on the numbers for central configurations is so important that S. Smale  took it as one of the most important 18 mathematical problems for the 21st century. Central configurations are important in the Newtonian N-body problems, for example, it's well known that finding the relative equilibrium solutions of the classical N-body problem and planar central configurations is equivalent. Central configurations also play other important roles, there were a lot of works on the existence and multiplicity and the shapes of central configurations ([1-11] etc.). But finding concrete central configurations is very difficult, here we consider some particular situations: the central configurations formed by two twisted regular polygons, we will explain it more clearly in the following.

Definition. (See .) A configuration $q=\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right) \in X \backslash \Delta$ is called a central configuration if there exists a constant $\lambda \in \mathbf{R}$ such that

$$
\sum_{j=1, j \neq k}^{n} \frac{m_{j} m_{k}}{\left|q_{j}-q_{k}\right|^{3}}\left(q_{j}-q_{k}\right)=-\lambda m_{k} q_{k}, \quad 1 \leqslant k \leqslant n
$$

The value of $\lambda$ in (1.1) is uniquely determined by

$$
\lambda=\frac{U(q)}{I(q)}
$$

where

$$
\begin{gathered}
X=\left\{q=\left(q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{n}\right) \in \mathbf{R}^{3 n}: \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{i} q_{i}=0\right\} \\
\Delta=\left\{q: q_{j}=q_{k} \text { for some } j \neq k\right\} \\
U(q)=\sum_{1 \leqslant j<k \leqslant n} \frac{m_{j} m_{k}}{\left|q_{j}-q_{k}\right|} \\
I(q)=\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant n} m_{j}\left|q_{j}\right|^{2}
\end{gathered}
$$

Consider the central configurations in $\mathbf{R}^{3}$ formed by two twisted regular N -gons $(N \geqslant 2)$ with distance $h \geqslant 0$. It is assumed that the lower layer regular N -gons lies in horizontal plane, and the upper regular N -gons parallels to the lower one and $z$-axis passes through both centers of two regular N gons. Suppose that the lower layer particles have masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{N}$ and the upper layer particles have masses $m_{1}^{\prime}, m_{2}^{\prime}, \ldots, m_{N}^{\prime}$ respectively. For convenience, we treat $\mathbf{R}^{3}$ as the direct product of the complex plane and real axis when choosing the coordinates. More precisely, let $\rho_{k}$ be the $k$ th complex root of unity, i.e.,

$$
\rho_{k}=\mathrm{e}^{i \theta_{k}}
$$

And we let

$$
\rho_{k}^{\prime}=a \rho_{k} \cdot e^{i \theta}
$$

where $a>0, i=\sqrt{-1}, \theta_{k}=\frac{2 k \pi}{N}(k=1, \ldots, N), 0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2 \pi, \theta$ is called twisted angle (see Fig. 1, we only draw the situation of $N=4$ ).

It is assumed that $m_{k}(k=1, \ldots, N)$ locates at the vertex $q_{k}$ of the lower layer regular N -gons; $m_{k}^{\prime}$ $(k=1, \ldots, N)$ locate at the vertex of the upper layer regular N -gons:

$$
\begin{gathered}
q_{k}=\left(\rho_{k}, 0\right) \\
q_{k}^{\prime}=\left(\rho_{k}^{\prime}, h\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

where $h \geqslant 0$ is the distance between the two layers. Then the center of mass is

$$
z_{0}=\frac{\sum_{j}\left(m_{j} q_{j}+m_{j}^{\prime} q_{j}^{\prime}\right)}{M}
$$



Fig. 1. The symmetrical configurations considered here.
where

$$
M=\sum_{j}\left(m_{j}+m_{j}^{\prime}\right)
$$

Let

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
P_{k}=q_{k}-z_{0}, & P=\left(P_{1}, \ldots, P_{N}\right) \\
P_{k}^{\prime}=q_{k}^{\prime}-z_{0}, & P^{\prime}=\left(P_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, P_{N}^{\prime}\right)
\end{array}
$$

If $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{N} ; P_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, P_{N}^{\prime}$ form a central configuration, then $\exists \lambda \in \mathbf{R}^{+}$, such that

$$
\begin{gathered}
\sum_{j=1, j \neq k}^{N} \frac{m_{j}}{\left|P_{k}-P_{j}\right|^{3}}\left(P_{k}-P_{j}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{m_{j}^{\prime}}{\left|P_{k}-P_{j}^{\prime}\right|^{3}}\left(P_{k}-P_{j}^{\prime}\right)=\lambda P_{k}, \quad 1 \leqslant k \leqslant N \\
\sum_{j=1, j \neq k}^{N} \frac{m_{j}^{\prime}}{\left|P_{k}^{\prime}-P_{j}^{\prime}\right|^{3}}\left(P_{k}^{\prime}-P_{j}^{\prime}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{m_{j}}{\left|P_{k}^{\prime}-P_{j}\right|^{3}}\left(P_{k}^{\prime}-P_{j}\right)=\lambda P_{k}^{\prime}, \quad 1 \leqslant k \leqslant N \\
\lambda=\frac{U\left(P, P^{\prime}\right)}{I\left(P, P^{\prime}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

In the following, we only consider the case of $m_{1}=\cdots=m_{N}=m$ and $m_{1}^{\prime}=\cdots=m_{N}^{\prime}=b m$. Then

$$
z_{0}=\sum_{j}\left(m_{j} q_{j}+m_{j}^{\prime} q_{j}^{\prime}\right) / M=\left(0,0, \frac{b h}{1+b}\right)
$$

And (1.15), (1.16) and (1.17) are equivalent to

$$
\begin{gathered}
\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \frac{\left(1-\rho_{j}, 0\right)}{\left|1-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}+b \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\left(1-\rho_{j}^{\prime},-h\right)}{\left(\left|1-\rho_{j}^{\prime}\right|^{2}+h^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\frac{\lambda}{m}\left(1,0,-\frac{b h}{1+b}\right) \\
\frac{b}{a^{3}} \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \frac{\left(a e^{i \theta}-\rho_{j}^{\prime}, 0\right)}{\left|1-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}+\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\left(a e^{i \theta}-\rho_{j}, h\right)}{\left(\left|a e^{i \theta}-\rho_{j}\right|^{2}+h^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\frac{\lambda}{m}\left(a e^{i \theta}, \frac{h}{1+b}\right) \\
\frac{\lambda}{m}=\frac{\left(1+\frac{b^{2}}{a}\right) \sum_{1 \leqslant j<k \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left|\rho_{j}-\rho_{k}\right|}+b N \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left(\left|1-\rho_{j}^{\prime}\right|^{2}+h^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}}}{N\left(1+b a^{2}+\frac{b h^{2}}{1+b}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

In the following, let $\mu=\frac{\lambda}{m}$, and we only consider the case of $0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \frac{2 \pi}{N}$ or $-\frac{\pi}{N} \leqslant \theta \leqslant \frac{\pi}{N}$ because of the symmetry.

When $\theta=0$, R. Moeckel and C. Simo  proved the following results:
Theorem 1.1 (R. Moeckel and C. Simo). When $h=0, \theta=0$, for every mass ratio $b$, there are exactly two planar central configurations consisting of two nested regular N-gons. For one of these, the ratio a of the sizes of the two polygons is less than 1, and for the other it is greater than 1. However, for $N \geqslant 473$ there is a constant $b_{0}(N)<1$ such that for $b<b_{0}$ and $b>\frac{1}{b_{0}}$, the central configuration with the smaller masses on the inner polygon is a repeller.

Theorem 1.2 (R. Moeckel and C. Simo). When $h>0, \theta=0$, if $N<473$, there is a unique pair of spatial central configurations of parallel regular N-gons. If $N \geqslant 473$, here are no such central configurations for $b<b_{0}(N)$. At $b=b_{0}$ a unique pair bifurcates from the planar central configuration with the smaller masses on the inner polygon. This remains the unique pair of spatial central configurations until $b=\frac{1}{b_{0}}$, where a similar bifurcation occurs in reverse, so that for $b>\frac{1}{b_{0}}$, only the planar central configurations remain.

Zhang and Zhou  studied the necessary and sufficient conditions for the masses of the central configurations consisting of two planar twisted regular N-gons. They proved the following theorem:

Theorem 1.3. If the central configuration is formed by two twisted regular N-gons $(N \geqslant 2)$ with distance $h=0$, then

$$
\begin{gathered}
\lambda \frac{N}{M}=\frac{1}{1+b}\left(\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \frac{1-\rho_{j}}{\left|1-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}+\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{b\left(1-a \rho_{j} e^{i \theta}\right)}{\left|1-a \rho_{j} e^{i \theta}\right|^{3}}\right) \\
\lambda \frac{N}{M}=\frac{e^{-i \theta}}{a(1+b)}\left(\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \frac{b\left(1-\rho_{j}\right) e^{i \theta}}{a^{2}\left|1-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}+\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{a e^{i \theta}-\rho_{j}}{\left|a e^{i \theta}-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

From their theorem, a series of conclusions are derived, especially they have the following corollaries:

Corollary 1.4. (See MacMillan and Bartky .) For $N=2$ and $\theta=\pi / 2$, then $b=1$ if and only if $a=1$.
Corollary 1.5. (See Perko and Walter .) For $N \geqslant 2, a=1$ and $\theta=\pi / N$, if (1.15), (1.16) and (1.17) hold, then $b=1$.

When $h>0$ Xie, Zhang and Zhou  proved:



Fig. 2. Theorem 1.8.

Theorem 1.6 (Xie-Zhang-Zhou). The configuration formed by two twisted regular N-gons $(N \geqslant 2)$ with distance $h>0$ is a central configuration if and only if the parameters $a, b, h, \theta$ satisfy the following relationships:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\lambda \frac{N}{M}=\frac{1}{1+b}\left(\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \frac{1-\rho_{j}}{\left|1-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}+\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{b\left(1-a e^{i \theta} \rho_{j}\right)}{\left(\left|1-a e^{i \theta} \rho_{j}\right|^{2}+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}\right) \\
\lambda \frac{N}{M}=\frac{e^{-i \theta}}{a(1+b)}\left(\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \frac{b\left(1-\rho_{j}\right) e^{i \theta}}{a^{2}\left|1-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}+\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{a e^{i \theta}-\rho_{j}}{\left(\left|a e^{i \theta}-\rho_{j}\right|^{2}+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}\right) \\
\lambda \frac{N}{M}=\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left(\left|1-a e^{i \theta} \rho_{j}\right|^{2}+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{gathered}
$$

Zhang and Zhu  proved the following result for a special case:
Theorem 1.7 (Zhang-Zhu). When $h>0$, if $a=1, b=1$, and $\theta=\pi / N$, then for every $N$, there exists a unique central configuration. Particularly, they proved that

$$
\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{j}+\pi / N\right)+1}{\left(2-2 \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\pi / N\right)\right)^{3 / 2}}-\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \frac{1-\rho_{j}}{\left|1-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}>0
$$

In the following, we let

$$
A=\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \frac{1-\rho_{j}}{\left|1-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}
$$

In this paper we will prove the following main results:
Theorem 1.8. If the central configuration is formed by two twisted regular N-gons $(N \geqslant 2)$ with distance $h \geqslant 0$, then only $\theta=0$ or $\theta=\pi / N$ (see Fig. 2). Specifically, if $a=1$ and $h=0$, i.e., two nested regular $N$-gons are on the same unit circle, then only $\theta=\pi / N$.



Fig. 3. Corollary 1.9.

Corollary 1.9. For $N \geqslant 2, h=0$, if $a=1$, then $b=1$ and $\theta=\pi / N$, i.e., there is exactly one central configuration formed by two nested regular N-gons on the same unit circle, which is the regular 2 N -gons (see Fig. 3).

Corollary 1.10. The configuration formed by two twisted regular N-gons $(N \geqslant 2)$ with distance $h \geqslant 0$ is a central configuration if and only if the parameters $a, b, h$ satisfy the following relationships:
(i) When $h=0$ and $a \neq 1$

$$
b\left[\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1-a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{A}{a^{3}}\right]=\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1-a^{-1} \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)\right)^{3 / 2}}-A
$$

or

$$
b\left[\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1-a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)\right)^{3 / 2}}-\frac{A}{a^{3}}\right]=\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1-a^{-1} \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)\right)^{3 / 2}}-A
$$

(ii) When $h>0$

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
b a \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=A-\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
b a\left(\frac{A}{a^{3}}-\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}\right)=\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{array}\right.
$$



Fig. 4. Corollary 1.11.

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
b a \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
=A-\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
b a\left(\frac{A}{a^{3}}-\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}\right) \\
=\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{j}\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\frac{\pi}{N}\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{array}\right.
$$

Corollary 1.11. For $N \geqslant 2, h>0, a=1$, if the configuration formed by two twisted regular $N$-gons $(N \geqslant 2)$ with distance $h \geqslant 0$ is a central configuration, then $b=1, \theta=0$ or $\pi / N$, and there exists a unique $h$ for each $\theta$. In other words, there are exactly two spatial central configurations formed by parallel regular $N$-gons which have the same sizes (see Fig. 4).

# 2. Some lemmas 

First of all, let's establish some identical equations to simplify the problem.

## Lemma 2.1.

$$
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{1 \leqslant j<k \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left|\rho_{j}-\rho_{k}\right|}=\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \frac{1-\rho_{j}}{\left|1-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}=\frac{1}{4} \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \csc \left(\frac{\pi j}{N}\right)
$$

Proof. It's easy to know

$$
\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \frac{1-\rho_{j}}{\left|1-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}=\frac{1}{4} \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \csc \left(\frac{\pi j}{N}\right)>0
$$

We only need to prove

$$
\sum_{1 \leqslant j<k \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left|\rho_{j}-\rho_{k}\right|}=\frac{N}{4} \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \csc \left(\frac{\pi j}{N}\right)
$$

In fact, we have

$$
2 \sum_{1 \leqslant j<k \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left|\rho_{j}-\rho_{k}\right|}=\sum_{j \neq k} \frac{1}{\left|\rho_{j}-\rho_{k}\right|}=N \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \frac{1}{\rho_{j}-1}=\frac{N}{2} \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \csc \left(\frac{\pi j}{N}\right)
$$

Then we have

$$
A=\frac{1}{N} \sum_{1 \leqslant j<k \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left|\rho_{j}-\rho_{k}\right|}=\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \frac{1-\rho_{j}}{\left|1-\rho_{j}\right|^{3}}=\frac{1}{4} \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N-1} \csc \left(\frac{\pi j}{N}\right)
$$

Lemma 2.2. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{j}-\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}-\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}-\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}}=\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}-\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}} \\
& \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\sin \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=-\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\sin \left(\theta_{j}-\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}-\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Proof. For (2.3), we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} & =\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\cos \left(2 \pi-\theta_{j}-\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(2 \pi-\theta_{j}-\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& =\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{N-j}-\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{N-j}-\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& =\sum_{1 \leqslant k \leqslant N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{k}-\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{k}-\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}} \\
& =\sum_{1 \leqslant k \leqslant N} \frac{\cos \left(\theta_{k}-\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{k}-\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we can get (2.4), (2.5) and (2.6).
From (1.19), (1.20) and (1.21), and using (2.1)-(2.6) we can get five equivalent equations.

Lemma 2.3. (1.19), (1.20) and (1.21) can be simplified into the following equations:

$$
\begin{gathered}
A+b \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1-a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=\mu \\
\frac{b}{a^{3}} A+\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1-a^{-1} \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=\mu \\
\sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{\sin \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=0 \\
h \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=\frac{\mu h}{1+b} \\
\mu=\frac{\left(1+\frac{b^{2}}{a}\right) A+b \sum_{1 \leqslant j \leqslant N} \frac{1+a^{2}+h^{2}-2 a \cos (\theta+\theta)}{\left(1+a^{2}-2 a \cos \left(\theta_{j}+\theta\right)+h^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}}{\left(1+b a^{2}+\frac{b h^{2}}{1+b}\right)}
\end{gathered}
$$

Proof. We write every vector in the equations of (1.19) and (1.20) into the forms of components, and apply (2.1)-(2.6), then (2.7)-(2.10) are obvious. (2.11) is also clear from (2.1)-(2.6) and (1.21).
